history: Dominant rule: Chavez (2018) anchors both slices: the Virginia Court of Appeals affirms a conviction supported by evidence even if it might have reached a different result, overturning only judgments that are plainly wrong or without evidence. Credibility and weight belong to the factfinder (Pijor 2017; Kelley 2019; 2018), intent is usually proved circumstantially (2009), and the factfinder may reasonably reject a defendant's theories (2017); Hudson (2003) limits the reasonable-hypothesis-of-innocence rule to theories advanced at trial. Preservation is strict: a due-process objection does not preserve a confrontation claim (Juniper, 2006), and the court reviews only assigned errors (Banks, 2017). How it changed: Vasquez (2016) held Graham inapplicable to aggregate term-of-years sentences for juveniles, a leading case in 2020-24. In the partial 2025-29 slice Pijor leads and a Tennessee criminal unit merges in (Sneed 2010, Rye 2015, TWB Architects 2019), which is drift rather than a change in Virginia law. The earlier Virginia slices (criminal, capital and termination appeals before 2020) are no longer part of this lineage.
rule: Virginia appellate courts affirm a conviction unless it is plainly wrong or without evidence to support it, deferring to the factfinder's credibility findings and rejection of hypotheses of innocence, and review only properly preserved arguments and assignments of error.

changes.what: The exclusion of reasonable hypotheses of innocence is limited to theories the accused advanced at trial, and whether a hypothesis is reasonable is a question of fact.
A general due-process objection does not preserve a Confrontation Clause claim.
Graham v. Florida does not reach aggregate term-of-years sentences exceeding life expectancy.
Review is limited to the assignments of error the litigant presents.
Convictions supported by evidence are not overturned even if the appellate court would have reached a different result; anchors both slices.

round1.name: Virginia Court of Appeals: plainly-wrong review and Rule 5A:18 preservation
round1.description: Virginia appellate review: judgments stand unless plainly wrong or without supporting evidence, and Rule 5A:18 bars new arguments unless the record affirmatively shows a miscarriage of justice (Redman, 1997; Ohree, 1998). Anchors shift: criminal sufficiency and capital cases in 1995-2004 (Martin, Coleman, Higginbotham), termination-of-parental-rights cases in 2005-19 (Farley, Logan, Kaywood, Toms), and deferential criminal review from 2020 (Chavez, 2018; Pijor, 2017).
round1.history: Dominant rule: deferential review by the Virginia Court of Appeals and the Supreme Court of Virginia, with strict preservation. Rule 5A:18 bars arguments not made below, even constitutional ones (Ohree, 1998), and the ends-of-justice exception applies only if the record affirmatively shows the offense did not occur (Redman, 1997). How it changed: the anchor and subject shift. In 1995-99 Martin (1987) anchors criminal trial issues, with Higginbotham (1975) on circumstantial evidence and Drew (1986) on constructive possession. In 2000-04 Coleman (1983) anchors, alongside capital cases (Cherrix, 1999; Lovitt, 2000; Burns, 2001) on future dangerousness and parole-eligibility instructions. From 2005-09 to 2015-19 termination-of-parental-rights and custody appeals dominate: Farley (1990) anchors 2005-09 and Logan (1991) 2010-19, with Kaywood (1990) and Toms (2005) on services and best interests. From 2020-24 the criminal line returns, anchored by Chavez (2018), with Pijor (2017), Hudson (2003) on hypotheses of innocence, Vasquez (2016) on aggregate juvenile sentences and Banks (2017) on assignments of error. In 2025-29 Tennessee cases merge in, which is drift.
round1.rule: A Virginia trial court's judgment, whether a criminal conviction or a custody or termination ruling, is affirmed unless plainly wrong or without evidence to support it, and arguments not made below are barred by Rule 5A:18 unless the ends-of-justice exception applies because the record affirmatively shows a miscarriage of justice.

changes.case: Farley v. Farley; Kaywood v. Halifax County DSS; Logan v. Fairfax County DHD
changes.what: In custody and termination cases the child's best interests are paramount and the court's judgment, heard ore tenus, is reversed only if plainly wrong; a child need not wait indefinitely for a parent to resume responsibility.
The ends-of-justice exception requires the record to show affirmatively that an element did not occur; mere failure of proof is not enough.
Rule 5A:18 bars even constitutional claims raised for the first time on appeal.
Hypotheses of innocence that must be excluded are those advanced at trial, and rejecting them is a fact question.
Affirming termination subsumes a challenge to the foster-care goal of adoption; § 16.1-283(C)(2) requires proof that reasonable and appropriate services were offered.
Graham does not reach aggregate term-of-years sentences for multiple crimes.

Review is confined to preserved objections and assigned errors (Juniper 2006, Banks 2017). Vasquez (2016) refused to extend Graham to aggregate sentences. Tennessee cases merge in during 2025-29.

name: Hypnotically refreshed testimony and Frye general acceptance (Mack, Shirley, Hurd)
description: Admissibility of hypnotically refreshed testimony under Frye (1923), 1980-89: after early cases treated hypnosis as going to weight (Harding 1968), Mack (1980, anchor 1980-84), Shirley (1982) and Bundy (1985) barred such testimony per se, while Hurd (1981) and Collins (1982) admitted it under safeguards or limited to prehypnotic memory. Frye anchors 1985-89 as rape-trauma and child-abuse syndrome evidence (Bledsoe 1984) joins.
history: Dominant rule: scientific evidence must be generally accepted in its field (Frye 1923), and courts applying that test in 1980-89 concluded that hypnosis does not reliably restore memory. How it changed: older cases admitted hypnotically induced testimony, leaving reliability to the jury (Harding, Md. 1968; McQueen 1978; Smrekar 1979). Mack (Minn. 1980), anchor of 1980-84, rejected it because hypnosis need not produce accurate memory; Nazarovitch (Pa. 1981) excluded testimony without prior recollection; Shirley (Cal. 1982) barred hypnotised witnesses even from prehypnotic recollections, later partly abrogated by Cal. Evid. Code § 795. Hurd (N.J. 1981) instead adopted Dr. Orne's procedural safeguards, and Collins (Ariz. 1982) and Quintanar (1982) limited testimony to recollections recorded before hypnosis. Frye anchors 1985-89, with Hughes (1983), Peoples (1984) and Bundy (Fla. 1985, per se inadmissible) continuing the hypnosis line, and the test spreading to expert testimony on rape-trauma syndrome (Bledsoe, Cal. 1984, rejected to prove rape; Middleton 1983 allowed but not on truthfulness) and child-victim behaviour (Myers 1984). The lineage splits three ways in 1990-94.
rule: Novel scientific evidence is admissible only if generally accepted in the relevant field (Frye), and because hypnosis is not accepted as reliable for restoring memory, many states barred hypnotically refreshed testimony, either per se or unless strict safeguards were met, while allowing prehypnotic recollections.

changes.what: General-acceptance test for scientific evidence.

changes.case: Harding v. State (Md.); State v. McQueen; Smrekar
changes.what: Early cases admitted hypnotically induced testimony, treating hypnosis as going to weight, if the hypnotist was competent and the jury was told.

changes.case: State v. Mack (Minn.); People v. Shirley (Cal.); Commonwealth v. Nazarovitch (Pa. 1981)
changes.what: Hypnotically refreshed testimony held inadmissible under Frye; Shirley barred even prehypnotic recollection (later partly abrogated by Cal. Evid. Code § 795).

changes.case: State v. Hurd (N.J.); State ex rel. Collins v. Superior Court (Ariz.)
changes.what: Admission only under procedural safeguards, or only of facts demonstrably recalled before hypnosis.

changes.case: People v. Bledsoe (Cal.); Bundy v. State (Fla.)
changes.what: Frye applied to rape-trauma-syndrome evidence offered to prove rape; Florida adopted a per se bar on hypnotically refreshed testimony.

name: Civil or punitive? Sex-offender commitment and registration (Hendricks, Smith v. Doe)
description: A 2005-09 cluster anchored by Kansas v. Hendricks (1997): sex-offender civil commitment and registration are civil schemes, not punishment, so ex post facto and double-jeopardy challenges fail unless the Mendoza-Martinez (1963) factors show punitive effect (Hudson, 1997; Smith v. Doe, 2003). Commitment needs clear and convincing proof (Addington, 1979; Foucha, 1992) and serious difficulty controlling behavior (Crane, 2002).
history: Dominant rule: whether a nominally civil statute imposes punishment. Hendricks (1997) anchors the only slice, 2005-09, after merging with a federal civil-rights unit: Kansas's Sexually Violent Predators Act is civil, so commitment does not violate the Ex Post Facto or Double Jeopardy Clauses. The test asks first what the legislature intended and then whether the scheme is so punitive in purpose or effect as to negate that intent, using the Mendoza-Martinez (1963) factors (Ward, 1980; Hudson, 1997, judging the statute on its face). Smith v. Doe (2003) extended this to sex-offender registration. Alongside: due-process limits on commitment, with clear and convincing proof (Addington, 1979), release once mental illness ends (Foucha, 1992) and proof of serious difficulty in controlling behavior (Crane, 2002); state SVP statutes upheld (Young, Wash. 1993; Hubbart, Cal. 1999; Thorell, Wash. 2003). Ex post facto doctrine itself: Calder (1798) categories, Weaver (1981) on good-time credits, Collins (1990) excluding procedural changes, and Morales (1995) and Garner (2000) on parole-hearing frequency. The unit splits on into 2010-14.
rule: A statute the legislature labels civil, such as sex-offender civil commitment or registration, is not punishment for ex post facto or double-jeopardy purposes unless the clearest proof shows it is punitive in purpose or effect under the Mendoza-Martinez factors (Hendricks, Smith v. Doe).

changes.case: Kennedy v. Mendoza-Martinez; United States v. Ward
changes.what: Factors for deciding whether a nominally civil sanction is in fact punitive; the legislature's intent is the first step.

changes.case: Addington v. Texas; Foucha v. Louisiana
changes.what: Civil commitment requires clear and convincing proof of mental illness and dangerousness, and a person no longer mentally ill must be released.

changes.case: Weaver v. Graham; Collins v. Youngblood; California Dept. of Corrections v. Morales
changes.what: The Ex Post Facto Clause bars retroactive increases in the quantum of punishment, as Calder defined it, but not procedural changes or reduced parole-hearing frequency that create only a speculative risk.

changes.what: Kansas's Sexually Violent Predators Act is civil, so commitment does not violate ex post facto or double jeopardy; the civil-penalty inquiry looks at the statute on its face.
Commitment requires proof of serious difficulty controlling behavior, though not total lack of control.

name: Speedy trial's formative era, 1970-94: Barker balancing and when the right attaches
description: The formative federal speedy-trial era, 1970-94: Hooey (1969) anchors 1970-74 on prisoners held elsewhere, then Barker v. Wingo (1972) balancing of delay, reason, assertion and prejudice. The right attaches only on accusation (Marion 1971), pre-indictment delay is a due-process matter (Lovasco 1977), dismissal is the sole remedy (Strunk 1973) and time without pending charges is excluded (MacDonald 1982). State rules (Pa. Rule 1100, Hicks, Vickery) run alongside.
history: Dominant rule: speedy-trial claims are decided by Barker v. Wingo's (1972) balancing of length of delay, reason, assertion of the right and prejudice, and Barker anchors from 1975-79 on. How it changed: in 1970-74 the anchor is Smith v. Hooey (1969), with Dickey (1970) and Klopfer (1967), on the states' duty to try prisoners held elsewhere and the incorporation of the right. Marion (1971) held that the right attaches only on accusation, so earlier delay is a due-process question; Lovasco (1977) held investigative delay does not violate due process. Strunk (1973) made dismissal the sole remedy and Moore (1973) rejected a need to prove prejudice. MacDonald (1982) and Loud Hawk (1986) excluded periods when no charge was pending. Doggett (1992) enters in 1990-94 on presumptive prejudice. Alongside: state speedy-trial rules (Pennsylvania Rule 1100 cases, Maryland's Hicks, Georgia's Vickery).
rule: Whether a defendant was denied the Sixth Amendment right to a speedy trial is decided by balancing the length of delay, the reason for it, the defendant's assertion of the right and prejudice (Barker), the right attaching only on arrest or formal accusation, with earlier delay governed by due process (Marion, Lovasco).

changes.what: The speedy-trial right is incorporated through the Fourteenth Amendment and binds the states.

changes.case: Smith v. Hooey; Dickey v. Florida
changes.what: A state must make a diligent good-faith effort to bring to trial a defendant held in another jurisdiction's prison.
The Sixth Amendment right does not attach until a person is accused, so pre-indictment delay is not a Sixth Amendment violation.
Four-factor balancing test (length, reason, assertion, prejudice); no affirmative showing of prejudice is required.
Dismissal is the only remedy for a speedy-trial violation.
Investigative pre-indictment delay does not violate due process even if the defense is somewhat prejudiced.
The guarantee does not apply to the period between dismissal of charges and a later indictment.
Excessive delay can presumptively prejudice the defense without proof of specific harm.

name: Second Amendment after Bruen: felon-in-possession challenges (Rahimi, Range)
description: Second Amendment litigation in the partial 2025-29 slice, anchored by Bruen (2022): regulations must fit the Nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation, building on Heller (2008) and McDonald (2010). Rahimi (2024) upheld disarming dangerous persons. Most cases test the felon ban, § 922(g)(1), where circuits split: Jackson (8th Cir.) upholds it categorically, Range (3d Cir.) allows as-applied relief, Diaz and Williams look to dangerousness.
history: Dominant rule: Bruen (2022) anchors this single partial 2025-29 slice: a firearm regulation is valid only if consistent with the Nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation, after asking whether the Second Amendment's text covers the person and conduct. Heller (2008) recognised an individual right to keep arms for self-defence, not a right to carry any weapon for any purpose, and McDonald (2010) incorporated it against the states. How it changed: Rahimi (2024) held that temporary disarmament of people who pose a credible threat fits that tradition, and that analogues need only share its principles. Most cases apply this to § 922(g)(1). Courts agree felons are among 'the people' (Williams, Travis, Brooks) but divide at the historical step: Jackson (8th Cir. 2024) needs no felony-by-felony litigation; Range (3d Cir. 2024) relied on founding-era disarmament of distrusted groups to grant as-applied relief; Diaz (5th Cir. 2024) and Williams (6th Cir. 2024) uphold the statute by analogy to punishments for crime and dangerousness. Pre-Bruen authority such as Rozier (2010) and Kanter v. Barr (2019, dissent cited on dangerousness) survives in the reasoning; Texas's § 46.04 was upheld facially (Burns, 2024).
rule: A firearm regulation is constitutional only if it is consistent with the Nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation (Bruen), judged by whether it fits the principles underlying that tradition (Rahimi); courts split on whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(1) may be challenged as applied to individual felons.

changes.case: District of Columbia v. Heller; McDonald v. City of Chicago
changes.what: The Second Amendment protects an individual right to keep and bear arms for self-defence, incorporated against the states.

changes.case: New York State Rifle & Pistol Ass'n v. Bruen
changes.what: Means-end scrutiny gave way to a text-and-history test; anchors the slice.
Disarming individuals who pose a credible threat to others is consistent with the historical tradition; laws need only fit its principles.

changes.case: Range v. Attorney General (3d Cir.); United States v. Jackson (8th Cir.); United States v. Diaz (5th Cir.); United States v. Williams (6th Cir.)
changes.what: Circuits divide on § 922(g)(1): Jackson rejects felony-by-felony litigation, Range sustains an as-applied challenge, Diaz and Williams uphold it on historical analogues and dangerousness.

name: Iowa dissolution property and physical care (Sullins, Hansen), then termination
description: Iowa family appeals led by dissolution of marriage, 2005-19: Sullins (2006) anchors 2005-14 on valuing and dividing property, with premarital property weighed case by case, and Hansen (2007), anchor 2015-19, opened joint physical care under § 598.41(3); McDermott (2013) treats equal division as often equitable. Only from 2020-24, after a merger, does the anchor move to termination of parental rights under P.L. (2010).
history: Dominant rule: de novo review of Iowa family-court decrees. In 2005-09 and 2010-14 Sullins (2006) anchors dissolution cases: property is divided equitably, courts may give premarital property different weight, and valuations must follow accepted methods (Witten, 2003; Benson, 1996); workers' compensation benefits are separate property (Schriner, 2005); joint physical care anticipates roughly equal time (Hynick, 2007); and modest alimony can correct inequity after a long marriage (Geil, 1993). How it changed: Hansen (2007) rejected the near-irrebuttable presumption against joint physical care, requiring case-specific analysis with the § 598.41(3) factors, and anchors 2015-19; McDermott (2013), Fennelly (2007) and Kimbro (2013) favour equal division after long marriages, and Gust (2015) addresses spousal support. Okland (2005) governs rule 1.904(2) motions and appeal time. In 2020-24, after a merger, the anchor shifts to termination of parental rights: P.L. (2010) and D.W. (2010) set the three-step § 232.116 analysis, A.B. (2012) treats chronic addiction as unfitness and A.M. (2014) refuses to delay permanency. P.L. anchors 2025-29 with Hansen still leading.
rule: Iowa appellate courts review dissolution decrees de novo, dividing marital property equitably, which is often but not necessarily equally, and deciding physical care, including joint physical care, on the child's best interests under the § 598.41(3) factors (Sullins, Hansen).

changes.what: Modest alimony can remedy the financial inequity of dissolving a long marriage.

changes.case: In re Marriage of Schriner; In re Marriage of Okland
changes.what: Workers' compensation benefits are the injured spouse's separate property; an untimely rule 1.904(2) motion does not extend the time to appeal.
Courts may weigh the premarital status of property differently and must value and divide property by accepted methods.
Joint physical care is examined on each case's facts using § 598.41(3) factors, ending the near-irrebuttable presumption against it.

changes.case: In re P.L.; In re D.W.
changes.what: Termination of parental rights follows a three-step analysis under § 232.116(1), (2) and (3).
Equitable distribution does not require equal division, though equality is often most equitable.

phases.rule: dissolution: equitable property division and physical care (Sullins, Hansen)
termination of parental rights under § 232.116 (P.L.)

name: California criminal appeals 1970-84: Daniels kidnapping, Sedeno, Watson
description: Pre-1985 California criminal appeals, before the death-penalty docket dominates: Daniels (1969) limits kidnapping to movement more than incidental to the crime (anchor 1970-74); Sedeno (1974) sets the sua sponte duty to instruct on lesser included offenses (anchor 1975-79); Watson (1956) harmless error anchors 1980-84. Also Beagle (1972) on prior-conviction impeachment, Pope and Flannel (1979).
history: Dominant rule: California's harmless-error test for state-law trial error, under which reversal requires a reasonable probability of a more favourable result (Watson, 1956), across a mixed body of California criminal-appeal doctrine. How it changed: in 1970-74 Daniels (1969) anchors, narrowing the kidnapping statute to movement that is more than incidental to the underlying crime. In 1975-79 Sedeno (1974) anchors, on the duty to instruct sua sponte on lesser included offenses and when its breach is harmless, with Beagle (1972) on excluding prior convictions offered for impeachment. In 1980-84 Watson itself anchors, joined by Flannel (1979, imperfect self-defense), Pope (1979, ineffective assistance) and Green (1980, special circumstances). Alongside: Ibarra (1963) on counsel's failure to move to suppress, and Neal (1960) on multiple punishment. The lineage splits in 1985-89, partly into federal habeas.
rule: In California criminal appeals, a state-law trial error requires reversal only if it is reasonably probable that the defendant would have obtained a more favourable result without it (Watson), applied chiefly to instructional error on lesser offenses and defenses, evidentiary rulings and counsel's performance.

changes.what: Kidnapping statute applies only when the victim's movement is more than incidental to the underlying assault or robbery.
Trial courts have discretion to exclude a prior felony conviction offered to impeach the defendant when its prejudice outweighs its probative value.
Duty to instruct sua sponte on lesser included offenses supported by the evidence; the omission can be harmless where the jury necessarily resolved the question under other instructions.
California standard for ineffective assistance of counsel: performance below that of a reasonably competent attorney that withdrew a potentially meritorious defense.
An honest but unreasonable belief in the need for self-defense negates malice (imperfect self-defense).

Noncapital 1970-84 doctrine, decades before the 2000-24 capital forfeiture-and-misconduct unit (Crittenden, Doolin).
1970-84 general criminal appeals, not the 2005-09 Moon unit on capital jury selection and counsel.
1970-84 general criminal appeals, not the 1995-99 Arias unit on penalty-phase argument and voir dire.

name: FOIA exemptions, adequate search and Vaughn indexes (Reporters Committee, SafeCard)
description: FOIA litigation in the D.C. courts: disclosure is the Act's dominant objective (Rose 1976), so the agency must show an adequate search (Oglesby, Morley) and justify each exemption with specific affidavits or a Vaughn index and a segregability finding (Vaughn, Mead Data). Reporters Committee (1989) anchors 2010-14 on privacy balancing; SafeCard (1991) anchors 2015-19.
history: Dominant rule: FOIA favours disclosure (Rose, 1976), and an agency that withholds records bears the burden of justifying it. It must describe an adequate search with the terms used and how it was done (Oglesby 1990, Morley 2007), itemize withholdings in a Vaughn index (Vaughn v. Rosen, 1973), and explain why no reasonably segregable parts exist (Mead Data, 1977). Exemption 5 tracks the deliberative-process privilege (Sears 1975, Coastal States 1980, Klamath 2001); privacy exemptions balance personal interests against the public interest in agency conduct (Reporters Committee, 1989). How it changed: Reporters Committee anchors 2010-14; in 2015-19 SafeCard (1991) anchors, with official-acknowledgment doctrine (Wolf 2007, ACLU 2011), request scope (Larson 2009) and fee entitlement (Brayton 2011) entering. The lineage covers only 2010-19.
rule: Under FOIA disclosure is the dominant objective; an agency withholding records bears the burden to show an adequate search and to justify each exemption claimed with specific, segregability-aware affidavits or a Vaughn index.

changes.what: An agency withholding documents must itemize what it withholds and the exemptions claimed, as in an index.
Privacy exemptions weigh the individual's interest against the public interest in shedding light on an agency's performance of its duties.
Names and addresses of private individuals in law-enforcement files are categorically exempt under Exemption 7(C); SafeCard anchors 2015-19.

name: Massachusetts summary-judgment burden: Kourouvacilis, Cassesso, Pederson
description: Massachusetts summary judgment: Cassesso (1983, anchor 1995-99) and Dawes (1976) set the movant's burden; Kourouvacilis (1991, anchor 2000-14) adopted Celotex, letting a movant show the opponent cannot prove an element, after which the opponent must offer specific facts (Pederson 1989). Flesner (1991) cautions on state-of-mind issues. Also New York summary judgment (Zuckerman, Alvarez) until it splits off in 2005-09, Chapter 93A and the implied covenant.
history: Dominant rule: the Massachusetts summary-judgment standard under Mass. R. Civ. P. 56. Cassesso (1983) anchors 1995-99 and Kourouvacilis (1991) anchors 2000-04 through 2010-14. How it changed: Dawes (1976) and Cassesso put the burden on the movant to show no triable issue; Pederson (1989) shifted the burden to the opponent once that showing is made; Kourouvacilis adopted the Celotex approach, so a movant without the trial burden may rely on the opponent's lack of evidence, and it required expert proof of a product defect. Flesner (1991) warns against summary judgment on state-of-mind questions. In 2000-04 a New York unit merges in, bringing Zuckerman (1980), Alvarez (1986) and Winegrad (1985), and splits off as New York civil summary judgment in 2005-09. Alongside: the implied covenant of good faith in employment (Fortune 1977) and Chapter 93A unfairness (Anthony's Pier Four 1991; Clinton Hospital 1990); quasi-judicial immunity for court-appointed evaluators (LaLonde 1989); new-trial discretion (Nicastro 1985); and the anti-SLAPP statute (Duracraft 1998). The unit dissolves into a much larger one in 2015-19.
rule: In Massachusetts a party moving for summary judgment that will not bear the burden at trial need not disprove the opponent's case but may show the opponent has no reasonable expectation of proving an essential element, after which the opponent must respond with specific facts (Kourouvacilis; Pederson).

changes.what: Summary judgment is proper where the movant carries its burden and the opponent responds without specific facts showing a triable issue.
The moving party bears the burden of showing there is no genuine issue of material fact and that it is entitled to judgment as a matter of law.
Once the movant establishes the absence of a triable issue, the burden shifts to the opponent to offer affirmative evidence.
Adopted the Celotex approach: a movant without the trial burden may prevail by showing the opponent has no reasonable expectation of proving an essential element.
Summary judgment is often inappropriate where motive, intent or other state of mind is at issue.

name: Tennessee criminal appeals: sufficiency review and sentencing review (Ashby to Bise)
description: Tennessee criminal appeals: on sufficiency review the State gets the strongest legitimate view of the evidence (Cabbage, 1978; Tuggle, 1982; Bland, 1997). Dorantes (2011, anchor 2015-19) put circumstantial evidence on the same footing as direct evidence. Sentencing review moved from Ashby's (1991, anchor 2000-04) presumption of correctness to Bise's (2012) abuse of discretion. Also Baxter on counsel and Smith (2000) on plain error.

history: Dominant rule: the appellate court gives the State the strongest legitimate view of the evidence and leaves credibility to the jury (Cabbage, 1978; Tuggle, 1982, anchor 2005-09; Bland, 1997, anchor 2010-14, which also sets comparative proportionality review of death sentences). How it changed: Ashby (1991) anchors 2000-04, with de novo sentencing review and a presumption of correctness when the record shows the court weighed sentencing principles. Burns (1999) reset the lesser-included-offense test, and Smith (2000) tightened plain-error review under Adkisson. In 2005-09 guilty-plea and counsel cases join (Boykin, Alford, Hill, Baxter), and Gomez (2005) upheld the 1989 Act against Blakely before the 2005 amendments made enhancement factors advisory (Carter, 2008). Dorantes (2011) enters in 2010-14 and anchors 2015-19: circumstantial evidence is reviewed like direct evidence. Bise (2012) replaced Ashby with abuse-of-discretion review and a presumption of reasonableness. Also: Odom (1996) on the serious-physical-abuse aggravator and Hanson (2009) on the knowing mens rea.
rule: On appeal in Tennessee the State gets the strongest legitimate view of the evidence and all reasonable inferences, with credibility and weight left to the jury, and sentencing review moved from de novo review with a presumption of correctness (Ashby) to abuse of discretion with a presumption of reasonableness (Bise).

changes.case: State v. Cabbage; State v. Tuggle
changes.what: The State is entitled to the strongest legitimate view of the evidence; credibility, weight and factual disputes are for the trier of fact.
Sentences are reviewed de novo with a presumption of correctness, conditioned on the record showing the trial court considered the sentencing principles and facts.
Adopted a Model Penal Code-based test for lesser-included offenses and required instructions where the evidence supports them.
Plain-error relief requires all Adkisson factors, including breach of a clear and unequivocal rule of law; a court may stop once one factor fails.

changes.case: State v. Gomez; 2005 Sentencing Act amendments
changes.what: Gomez held the 1989 Sentencing Reform Act consistent with Blakely; the 2005 amendments then made enhancement factors advisory.
Circumstantial evidence alone can sustain a conviction and is reviewed under the same standard as direct evidence, abandoning the requirement that it exclude every reasonable hypothesis but guilt.
Sentences within the statutory range are reviewed for abuse of discretion with a presumption of reasonableness, and disagreement with the weighing of factors is no longer a ground for appeal.

name: Punitive-damages limits in Alabama and under due process (Haslip, Gore)
description: A 1995-99 cluster anchored by West (Ala. 1989) on Alabama's substantial-evidence standard. Its main rule is punitive-damages review: Alabama's Hammond (1986) and Hornsby (1989) factors and the due-process line from Haslip (1991) and TXO (1993) to Gore (1996), which first struck an award as grossly excessive. Alongside: federal common law and the FDIC (Erie, D'Oench, Kimbell Foods, O'Melveny 1994) and Feres.
history: Dominant rule: excessive punitive damages are checked by state post-verdict review and by the Due Process Clause. The cluster exists only in 1995-99, anchored by West v. Founders Life Assurance (Ala. 1989), which set the substantial-evidence standard that Alabama courts cite for reviewing verdicts. How it developed: Alabama required trial courts to review punitive awards on stated factors (Hammond 1986; Green Oil v. Hornsby 1989). Haslip (1991), an Alabama case, upheld an award because jury instructions and that review limited discretion, and TXO (1993) allowed potential harm to count. BMW v. Gore (1996), also from Alabama, held a $2 million award on $4,000 of harm grossly excessive, setting the reprehensibility, ratio and comparable-penalty guideposts. Alongside: when federal law displaces state law, from Erie (1938) and D'Oench (1942, with Langley 1987 on § 1823(e)) to Kimbell Foods (1979) and O'Melveny (1994), which declined to make federal common law for the FDIC; Feres (1950) on military injuries; Alabama workers' compensation causation (Trinity Industries 1996); and CERCLA (Alcan 1992). The unit splits in 2000-04.
rule: A punitive award is reviewed for excessiveness under due process (Haslip; TXO; Gore's reprehensibility, ratio and comparable-penalty guideposts) and, in Alabama, under the Hammond and Green Oil v. Hornsby factors, with facts tested by the substantial-evidence standard (West).

changes.case: Hammond v. City of Gadsden (Ala.); Green Oil Co. v. Hornsby (Ala.)
changes.what: Alabama trial courts must state reasons on post-verdict review of punitive awards, weighing factors such as culpability, deterrence and impact on the parties.
Defined the substantial-evidence standard that replaced Alabama's scintilla rule.

changes.case: Pacific Mutual v. Haslip; TXO v. Alliance Resources
changes.what: Upheld large punitive awards where jury instructions and post-verdict review limited discretion, and allowed potential harm to count.

changes.case: BMW of North America v. Gore
changes.what: A $2 million punitive award on $4,000 of economic harm was grossly excessive under the Due Process Clause.
Courts may not create federal common law to supplement comprehensive statutes; the FDIC as receiver takes subject to state-law defenses.

name: Michigan appeals family: civil precedent (Boodt) to Carines plain error
description: The Michigan appellate family, 2010-29, which begins civil and turns criminal. In 2010-14 Boodt (2008) anchors a mixed unit with civil cases on dicta, fees (Khouri, 2008) and notice provisions (Rowland, 2007). From 2015-19 Carines (1999) anchors a large criminal cluster: plain error for unpreserved errors, ineffectiveness proved at a Ginther (1973) hearing with outcome-determinative prejudice (Trakhtenberg, 2012), and Lockridge (2015) advisory guidelines.

previous.name: Michigan criminal appeals: plain error and counsel
previous.description: Michigan criminal precedent: plain-error review of unpreserved issues (Carines), ineffective assistance and Ginther hearings, futile objections, other-acts evidence and the sentencing guidelines after Lockridge.

history: Dominant rule: Carines (1999) plain-error review and Ginther (1973) ineffectiveness claims, anchoring from 2015-19 to 2025-29. Unpreserved errors, constitutional or not, are reviewed for clear or obvious error affecting substantial rights, and reversal is discretionary even then; Vaughn (2012) treats structural errors as meeting the prejudice prong. Ineffective assistance requires deficient performance and outcome-determinative prejudice (Trakhtenberg, 2012), with the factual predicate on the defendant (Solloway, 2016). How it changed: in 2010-14 Boodt (2008) anchors a unit that still carries Michigan civil cases: obiter dicta make no rule (Boodt), fees follow the totality of circumstances (Khouri, 2008), and statutory notice is strictly enforced (Rowland, 2007, overruling Hobbs and Brown). From 2015-19 criminal cases dominate: Unger (2008), Ericksen (2010) and Dobek (2007) on evidence and intent, Bahoda (1995) on prosecutorial argument, and sentencing, where Milbourn's (1990) proportionality principle, Francisco (2006) and Hardy (2013) on guideline scoring, and Lockridge (2015) making the guidelines advisory all enter. The rule is stable through 2025-29.
rule: Michigan appellate courts review unpreserved error, constitutional or not, for plain error that affected substantial rights (Carines), and ineffective-assistance claims require deficient performance and outcome-determinative prejudice, with factual support developed at a Ginther hearing (Trakhtenberg).

changes.what: Created the evidentiary hearing for ineffective-assistance claims resting on matters outside the record.
Replaced the shock-the-conscience test with a principle of proportionality for sentences.
Plain-error review extends to unpreserved constitutional error.

changes.case: Rowland v. Washtenaw County Road Comm'n; Khouri v. Citizens Insurance
changes.what: Statutory notice provisions are strictly enforced (overruling Hobbs and Brown); reasonable attorney fees are set on the totality of the circumstances.

changes.case: People v. Vaughn; People v. Trakhtenberg
changes.what: Unobjected-to courtroom closure is forfeited, not waived, and structural error satisfies Carines' third prong; ineffectiveness requires outcome-determinative deficiency.
Facts scoring the sentencing guidelines are reviewed for clear error and need a preponderance of evidence.
Mandatory guidelines violated the Sixth Amendment; they became advisory and departures are reviewed for reasonableness.

round1.name: Michigan criminal appeals: Carines plain error and Ginther ineffectiveness
round1.description: Michigan criminal appeals: unpreserved error, including constitutional error, gets Carines (1999) plain-error review; ineffectiveness needs deficient performance and outcome-determinative prejudice, developed at a Ginther (1973) hearing (Trakhtenberg, 2012); futile objections are not ineffective (Ericksen, 2010). Lockridge (2015) made the guidelines advisory. Carines anchors from 2015-19; 2000-14 the cluster is mostly Michigan civil and statutory-interpretation cases.
round1.history: Dominant rule: from 2015-19 to 2025-29 Carines (1999) anchors a large criminal-appeals cluster. Unpreserved errors, constitutional or not, are reviewed for plain error, and the defendant must show prejudice; reversal is discretionary even then. Ginther (1973) hearings develop ineffectiveness claims, Trakhtenberg (2012) states the two-part test, and Ericksen (2010), Unger (2008), Dobek (2007) and Payne (2009) supply futile-objection, misconduct, other-acts and abandonment rules. How it changed: the cluster's subject shifts. In 1995-99 Farrington (1993) anchors with Milbourn (1990), which replaced shock-the-conscience with proportionality, and Stanaway (1994) on in camera review of privileged records. In 2000-04 to 2010-14 Michigan civil and statutory-construction cases dominate (In re MCI, 1999; Maiden, 1999; Boodt, 2008), with Washington Public Records Act cases merged in, which is drift. When criminal cases return in 2015-19, Lockridge (2015) enters: Michigan's mandatory guidelines violated the Sixth Amendment after Alleyne, so they became advisory and departures are reviewed for reasonableness, with Milbourn proportionality reviving. Hardy (2013) sets review of scoring findings, and Vaughn (2012) treats unpreserved public-trial claims as forfeited, not waived.
round1.rule: Unpreserved claims in Michigan, constitutional or not, are reviewed for plain error: an error that was clear or obvious and affected substantial rights, with reversal only if it resulted in conviction of an innocent defendant or seriously affected the fairness, integrity or public reputation of the proceedings (Carines); ineffectiveness requires deficient performance and outcome-determinative prejudice, developed at a Ginther hearing.

changes.what: Claims of inadequate counsel resting on facts outside the record are developed at an evidentiary hearing in the trial court.

history: Dominant rule: McDonnell Douglas (1973) anchors every slice from 1980-84, after Griggs (1971) anchors 1975-79 with Albemarle (1975), Franks (1976) and remedial cases merged from labor and public-law clusters. history: Dominant rule: in the single slice 1985-89, formed when federal Brady and confrontation clusters merged, Ohio v. Roberts (1980), the anchor, admits hearsay of an unavailable declarant only with adequate indicia of reliability, which a firmly rooted exception supplies. It builds on Mattox (1895), Pointer (1965), Douglas (1965) and Barber (1968, unavailability). Green (1970) admitted prior statements of a testifying witness; Dutton (1970) admitted reliable coconspirator hearsay. How it changed: Bruton (1968) barred a non-testifying codefendant's confession at a joint trial, Lee v. Illinois (1986) treated such confessions as presumptively unreliable, and Cruz (1987) extended Bruton to interlocking confessions. Inadi (1986) dropped unavailability for coconspirator statements and Bourjaily (1987) let courts decide their foundation by a preponderance. Davis (1974) protected cross-examination on bias, and Chambers (1973) barred mechanistic rules that defeat a defense. Alongside: entrapment (Russell 1973, Hampton 1976). The round-1 Connecticut Evans and Golding material lies outside this slice.
rule: Hearsay of an unavailable declarant may be admitted against an accused only if it bears adequate indicia of reliability, inferred when it falls within a firmly rooted exception; a non-testifying codefendant's confession implicating the defendant is barred at a joint trial, and effective cross-examination must be allowed.

changes.case: Pointer v. Texas; Douglas v. Alabama; Barber v. Page; Bruton v. United States
changes.what: Confrontation applies to the states; the state must show unavailability; a codefendant's incriminating confession is inadmissible at a joint trial despite a limiting instruction.

changes.case: California v. Green; Dutton v. Evans
changes.what: Prior statements of a testifying witness and preliminary-hearing testimony may be admitted; coconspirator hearsay with indicia of reliability does not violate confrontation.
Barring cross-examination of a witness's bias (probation status) is constitutional error.
Unavailability plus adequate indicia of reliability, presumed for firmly rooted hearsay exceptions.

changes.case: Lee v. Illinois; United States v. Inadi; Bourjaily v. United States; Cruz v. New York
changes.what: Codefendant confessions are presumptively unreliable; coconspirator statements need no unavailability showing and need no separate reliability inquiry; Bruton applies to interlocking confessions.

round1.name: Connecticut review of unpreserved constitutional claims: Evans and Golding
round1.description: Connecticut appellate review of unpreserved constitutional claims: Evans (1973), anchor 1985-89, allowed review for clear deprivation of a fundamental right, and Golding (1989), anchor 1990-99, restated it as a four-part test ending in harmless error. The claims reviewed are mostly Confrontation Clause claims under Ohio v. Roberts (1980), Wright (1990), Craig (1990) and White (1992), and Brady disclosure claims (Agurs 1976, Bagley 1985).
round1.history: Dominant rule: Connecticut courts review unpreserved constitutional claims only under Evans (1973) and its restatement in Golding (1989): an adequate record, a claim of constitutional magnitude, a clear violation that deprived the defendant of a fair trial, and failure of the state to show harmlessness beyond a reasonable doubt. How it changed: Evans anchors 1985-89, when the claims are mostly Brady disclosure (Brady 1963, Agurs 1976 without request, Bagley 1985 extending to impeachment) and confrontation (Pointer 1965, Green 1970, Dutton 1970, Davis 1974 on bias cross-examination, Roberts 1980), with Manson (1977) on identifications and Kurvin (1982) warning against trial by ambuscade. Golding anchors 1990-99. In 1990-94 confrontation cases lead: Van Arsdall (1986), Bruton (1968), Lee v. Illinois (1986), Wright (1990), Craig (1990) and White (1992), with Coy (1988) and Allen (1970) on presence. In 1995-99 Connecticut decisions lead: Sivri (1994) on DNA statistics, Greenfield (1993) on reviewing constitutional facts, Ross (1994) on the state death penalty, and Prioleau (1995) on intent instructions. The lineage splits into an unlabelled group in 2000-04, before Crawford.
round1.rule: A Connecticut defendant may prevail on an unpreserved constitutional claim only if the record is adequate, the claim is of constitutional magnitude alleging violation of a fundamental right, the violation clearly exists and clearly deprived him of a fair trial, and the state cannot show harmlessness beyond a reasonable doubt; the claims so reviewed are chiefly confrontation and disclosure claims under the pre-Crawford Roberts framework and Brady.

changes.what: An exceptional circumstance permits review of an unpreserved claim when the record shows a clear deprivation of a fundamental constitutional right and a fair trial.
An unavailable declarant's hearsay is admissible under the Confrontation Clause only with adequate indicia of reliability, such as a firmly rooted exception.
Brady covers impeachment evidence, material if it may make the difference between conviction and acquittal.

changes.case: Coy v. Iowa; Maryland v. Craig
changes.what: Face-to-face confrontation may yield to closed-circuit child testimony on a case-specific finding of trauma, though a screen without findings violates the Clause.
Restated Evans as a four-part test, the last being that the claim survives harmless-error analysis.

changes.case: Idaho v. Wright; White v. Illinois
changes.what: Reliability requires a firmly rooted exception or particularized guarantees not drawn from corroboration; firmly rooted exceptions need no showing of unavailability.

name: Texas sufficiency under Jackson, 1980-2029: Geesa, Clewis, Brooks (family)
description: The family's shared rule, from the 1980s on, is Jackson v. history: Dominant rule: Jackson v. Virginia (1979) anchors every slice: evidence is sufficient if any rational trier of fact, viewing it for the verdict, could find each element beyond a reasonable doubt, with credibility for the jury (Cain 1997). How it changed: 1980-89 mix Texas with Louisiana and Georgia review (Sepulvado, Bonanno, Hawes); Almanza (1985) set egregious-harm review for unobjected charge error. Butler (1989) and Geesa (1991) lead 1990-94, rejecting the any-evidence and reasonable-hypothesis tests. Clewis (1996) leads 1995-2009 with factual-sufficiency review; Malik (1997) tied sufficiency to the hypothetically correct charge; Johnson (2000) adopted the full civil factual-insufficiency formulation; Watson (2006) reclarified Clewis and overruled Zuniga in part. Brooks (2010) leads from 2010-14, abolishing factual sufficiency in favor of Jackson alone, with Hooper and Clayton (2007) on inferences and circumstantial evidence. Also: Montgomery (1991) on Rule 403 and abuse of discretion, Mosley (1998) on improper argument under Rule 44.2(b). The partial 2025-29 slice merges in Tennessee review.
rule: A conviction stands if, viewing all the evidence in the light most favorable to the verdict, any rational trier of fact could find each element beyond a reasonable doubt, measured against a hypothetically correct jury charge; since Brooks (2010) this Jackson standard is the only sufficiency standard in Texas.

changes.what: Unobjected-to jury-charge error requires reversal only for egregious harm; preserved error requires reversal unless harmless.
Rejected the reasonable-hypothesis-of-innocence construct for appellate sufficiency review.
Recognized factual-sufficiency review alongside Jackson legal sufficiency.
Sufficiency is measured by the elements of the offense as defined by the hypothetically correct jury charge.
Clewis read as adopting the complete civil factual-insufficiency formulation.
Reclarified Clewis and overruled Zuniga v. State (2004) in part.
Jackson legal sufficiency is the only standard for reviewing the evidence; separate factual-sufficiency review ends.

name: Negligence duty of care, 1990-99: Rowland, Dillon-Thing bystanders, premises
description: The scope of the tort duty of care, 1990-99 only, in California, New York and Washington cases, anchored by Zuckerman (1980) on proof opposing summary judgment: Rowland (1968) and Basso (1976) replaced landowner status categories with reasonable care; Dillon (1968) allowed bystander distress claims and Thing (1989) confined them to close relatives present. In 1995-99 social-host liability (Hansen 1992), premises notice (Gordon 1986) and crime on premises lead.
history: Dominant rule: the scope of the duty of care in negligence and when a court may decide it on summary judgment. Zuckerman (1980) anchors both slices: the opponent of summary judgment must lay bare admissible proof of a triable issue (with Alvarez 1986 on expert proof). How it changed: in 1990-94 the leading cases are Dillon (1968), which abandoned the zone-of-danger rule for bystanders, Thing (1989), which limited that recovery to close relatives present at the scene, Rowland (1968), which replaced landowner status categories with reasonable care (later superseded in part by statute), and Molien (1980) on direct-victim distress. In 1995-99 Washington and New York premises cases lead: Hansen (1992) imposed a social-host duty not to serve minors, Gordon (1986) required notice of the specific hazard, Nallan (1980) and Hutchins (1991) addressed duties against third-party crime, and Christen (1989) limited dram-shop liability by foreseeability. Also: primary assumption of risk (Turcotte 1986, Knight 1992), loss of consortium (Lee 1986, Gray 1987, Villareal 1989), and new-trial discretion (Nicastro 1985).
rule: Negligence duty is limited by foreseeability and policy: landowners owe reasonable care to entrants rather than status-based duties (Rowland, Basso), bystander emotional-distress recovery is confined to close relatives present at the scene (Thing, narrowing Dillon), and a defendant moving for summary judgment shifts the burden to the plaintiff to produce admissible evidence of a triable issue (Zuckerman).

changes.case: Rowland v. Christian (Cal.); Dillon v. Legg (Cal.)
changes.what: Replaced the trespasser-licensee-invitee categories with a general duty of reasonable care, and abandoned the zone-of-danger rule for bystanders in favour of foreseeability.
New York likewise adopted a single standard of reasonable care for landowners.

changes.case: Zuckerman v. City of New York; Nallan v. Helmsley-Spear
changes.what: The opponent of summary judgment must produce evidentiary proof in admissible form; a landlord must take reasonable precautions against foreseeable crime. Zuckerman anchors both slices.

changes.case: Turcotte v. Fell (N.Y.); Knight v. Jewett (Cal.)
changes.what: Primary assumption of risk: sports participants owe co-participants only a duty to avoid intentional or reckless injury.
Bystander recovery limited to close relatives present at the scene, aware of the injury and suffering serious distress.

name: Mandamus as an extraordinary remedy (Kerr, Cheney) with recusal and contempt
description: A 2005-09 cluster anchored by Kerr (1976): mandamus is drastic and issues only on a clear and indisputable right with no other adequate remedy (Allied Chemical, 1980; Cheney, 2004). Related limits on judicial power ride along: recusal for extrajudicial bias (Liteky, 1994), contempt (Bagwell, 1994) and inherent sanctions (Chambers, 1991), with attorney-client privilege (Upjohn, 1981), FOIA privacy (Reporters Committee, 1989) and excusable neglect (Pioneer, 1993).
history: Dominant rule: mandamus as an extraordinary writ. Kerr (1976) anchors the only slice, 2005-09, formed with an attorney's fees and sanctions lineage: the remedy is drastic and reserved for extraordinary situations. Roche (1943) limits it to confining a lower court to its jurisdiction or compelling a required act; Allied Chemical (1980) denies it where the matter is discretionary; Cheney (2004) restates the three conditions, no other adequate means, a clear and indisputable right and the court's satisfaction that the writ is appropriate. Alongside: recusal requires personal, extrajudicial bias rather than adverse rulings (Liteky, 1994; Beard, 1987); civil contempt coerces or compensates, while serious criminal contempt carries a jury right (Bagwell, 1994; Gompers, 1911); courts may sanction bad-faith litigation under inherent power (Chambers, 1991). Also cited here are Upjohn (1981) on corporate attorney-client privilege, Reporters Committee (1989) and Favish (2004) on FOIA privacy, Pioneer (1993) on excusable neglect and Mallard (1989) barring coercive appointment of counsel under § 1915. The unit splits in 2010-14.
rule: Mandamus is a drastic remedy for extraordinary situations, available only when the petitioner has no other adequate means of relief, the right to the writ is clear and indisputable, and the court is satisfied the writ is appropriate (Kerr, Allied Chemical, Cheney).

changes.what: Mandamus confines an inferior court to its lawful jurisdiction or compels it to exercise authority it must exercise.

changes.case: Kerr v. U.S. District Court; Allied Chemical v. Daiflon
changes.what: Mandamus is reserved for extraordinary situations; where a matter is committed to discretion the right to a result cannot be clear and indisputable.
Three conditions: no other adequate means, a clear and indisputable right, and the court's discretionary satisfaction that the writ is appropriate.

changes.case: Chambers v. NASCO; International Union, UMWA v. Bagwell
changes.what: Courts have inherent power to sanction bad faith; serious criminal contempt needs a jury, while civil contempt coerces or compensates.
Bias requiring recusal ordinarily comes from an extrajudicial source, not from rulings or courtroom conduct.

history: Dominant rule: appellate review of trial errors in criminal cases, with the anchor moving from sufficiency to plain error. Jackson v. Virginia (1979) anchors 1980-94: the question is whether any rational trier of fact could find guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. How it changed: in 1980-89 the cluster is mostly state appeals: Louisiana capital and sentencing review (Sepulvado, 1979; Bonanno, 1980; Lanclos, 1982), Georgia penalty arguments (Hawes, Fleming), and Texas charge-error and sufficiency rules (Almanza, 1985; Carlsen, 1983). Geesa (1991) abandoned the Texas reasonable-hypothesis rule. In 1990-94 a federal unit merges in: Glasser (1942) substantial evidence, Pinkerton (1946) co-conspirator liability, Brady and Bagley (1985) disclosure, Young (1985) prosecutorial comment, Kotteakos harmless error and Bourjaily (1987) co-conspirator statements. The cluster then flows into federal sentencing.

Virginia), and in federal appeals forfeited errors are corrected only if plain, affecting substantial rights, and seriously affecting the fairness or integrity of the proceedings (Olano).

name: Confrontation Clause in 2005-09: Crawford, Bruton and limits on cross-examination
description: The family's shared rule in 2005-09, the whole Confrontation Clause: Crawford (2004, anchor) bars testimonial statements unless the declarant is unavailable and was cross-examined, displacing Roberts (1980); Davis (2006) set the primary-purpose test. The cluster also carries cross-examination limits (Davis v. Alaska, 1974; Van Arsdall, 1986), codefendant confessions (Bruton, 1968) and Connecticut's Golding (1989) review.
history: Dominant rule: Crawford v. Washington (2004), which anchors the only slice, 2005-09: testimonial hearsay is admissible only if the declarant is unavailable and the defendant had a prior opportunity to cross-examine. How it changed: Crawford displaced Ohio v. Roberts (1980), which had admitted hearsay with adequate indicia of reliability; lower courts first held that Roberts still governed nontestimonial statements (Saget, 2004) and divided over 911 calls and statements to police (Cromer, 2004; Corella, 2004; Mungo, 2004). Davis v. Washington (2006) then defined testimonial statements by the primary purpose of the interrogation, separating emergency statements from accounts of past events. Alongside: the clause binds the states (Pointer, 1965), bars a nontestifying codefendant's confession at a joint trial (Bruton, 1968; Lilly, 1999), admits prior statements of a testifying witness (Green, 1970), and protects cross-examination on bias subject to reasonable limits (Davis v. Alaska, 1974; Van Arsdall, 1986); child testimony by closed circuit is allowed (Craig, 1990). Connecticut's Golding (1989) test for unpreserved constitutional claims rides along. The unit splits into three in 2010-14.
rule: The Confrontation Clause bars testimonial out-of-court statements unless the declarant is unavailable and the defendant had a prior opportunity to cross-examine; statements are testimonial when their primary purpose is to establish past events for prosecution (Crawford, Davis).

changes.case: Pointer v. Texas; Bruton v. United States; California v. Green
changes.what: The clause binds the states, bars a nontestifying codefendant's incriminating confession at a joint trial, and admits prior statements of a witness who testifies.

name: Federal preemption of state law: express, field and conflict (Cipollone, ERISA)
description: A 2005-09 cluster on federal preemption: express clauses read narrowly against a presumption for state police powers (Cipollone, 1992; Lohr, 1996; English, 1990), conflict preemption (Crosby, 2000) and ERISA preemption (Ingersoll-Rand, 1990; Dillingham, 1997; Egelhoff, 2001), with Bruch (1989) on review of benefit denials. Tennessee summary-judgment (Byrd, 1993) and statutory-construction cases ride along.
history: Dominant rule: preemption of state law by federal statute. Cipollone (1992) anchors the only slice, 2005-09, formed by a merger with an ERISA and labor-law preemption lineage. Express clauses are read for their scope, so the Cigarette Labeling Act preempts some but not all common-law claims (Cipollone), Lohr (1996) left state device tort claims standing, and English (1990) requires clear and manifest intent before displacing traditional state fields. Conflict preemption reaches state law that frustrates federal objectives (Crosby, 2000). Alongside: ERISA's broad preemption clause covers claims tied to pension plans (Ingersoll-Rand, 1990) and beneficiary-revocation statutes (Egelhoff, 2001), but not laws with indirect effects (Dillingham, 1997); Bruch (1989) sets de novo review of benefit denials absent discretionary authority. Reilly (2001) struck state tobacco-advertising limits, and Barnett Bank (1996) protected national-bank powers. Tennessee cases on summary judgment (Byrd, 1993), statutory construction (Mooney, 2000) and appellate fact review (Realty Shop, 1999) also cluster here; the unit splits on into 2010-14.
rule: Federal law preempts state law expressly, by occupying a field, or by conflict that frustrates federal objectives, but preemption of areas traditionally occupied by the states requires clear and manifest congressional intent.

changes.what: ERISA benefit denials are reviewed de novo unless the plan gives the administrator discretionary authority.

name: Due-process burden of proof: Winship, Mullaney and Patterson
description: Due process and the burden of proof in 1975-79: the prosecution must prove every element beyond a reasonable doubt (Winship, 1970), and must disprove provocation once raised in a homicide case (Mullaney, 1975, anchor). Patterson (1977) let states place true affirmative defenses on the defendant. Also: statutory presumptions (Tot, Leary, Turner, Barnes) and due process in juvenile and civil-commitment proceedings (Gault, Kent, Jackson v. Indiana).
history: Dominant rule: due process requires proof beyond a reasonable doubt of every fact necessary to constitute the crime (Winship, 1970), and Mullaney (1975), the anchor of the single 1975-79 slice, barred states from making a homicide defendant prove provocation to reduce murder to manslaughter. How it changed: Patterson (1977) confined Mullaney, letting states put on the defendant an affirmative defense that does not negate an element, and Hankerson (1977) applied Mullaney retroactively. Statutory presumptions were tested for rationality (Tot, 1943; Leary, 1969; Turner, 1970; Barnes, 1973). Alongside: due process in juvenile proceedings (Kent, 1966; Gault, 1967; McKeiver, 1971, no jury right) and in civil commitment and incompetency (Lessard, 1972; Jackson v. Indiana, 1972, limits on indefinite commitment of incompetent defendants; O'Connor, 1975). The lineage merges into a federal habeas cluster in 1980-84.
rule: Due process requires the prosecution to prove beyond a reasonable doubt every fact necessary to constitute the crime charged (Winship), so a state may not presume an element or shift to the defendant the burden of disproving it (Mullaney), though it may assign affirmative defenses that do not negate an element (Patterson).

changes.what: A statutory presumption is invalid unless the presumed fact more likely than not follows from the proved fact.

changes.what: Juvenile proceedings must meet the essentials of due process, including notice and counsel.

changes.case: Patterson v. New York; Hankerson v. North Carolina
changes.what: A state may require the defendant to prove an affirmative defense such as extreme emotional disturbance that does not negate an element; Mullaney applies retroactively.

name: Tennessee and Maryland summary judgment (Byrd, Beatty) and fear-of-AIDS claims
description: A 1995-99 state civil cluster anchored by Byrd v. Hall (Tenn. 1993): the nonmovant must answer a supported summary-judgment motion with specific facts. Maryland adds that summary judgment decides only law (Beatty 1993; Heat & Power 1990). Fear-of-AIDS emotional distress divides courts: Faya (Md. 1993) allowed recovery without proven exposure; K.A.C. (1995) and Bain (Tenn. 1997) required exposure. Also discovery-rule accrual (Carvell 1995).
history: Dominant rule: the summary-judgment burden in state courts, chiefly Tennessee and Maryland. The cluster exists only in 1995-99, anchored by Byrd v. Hall (Tenn. 1993), after two earlier units merge; it splits in 2000-04, the Tennessee part continuing as the Tennessee summary-judgment lineage. How it developed: Byrd required a nonmovant facing a properly supported motion to set out specific facts rather than rely on pleadings. Maryland's Heat & Power (1990), Beatty (1993) and Eaton (1994) held that summary judgment and directed verdicts decide questions of law only, and Zenobia (1992) treated pleading admissions as substantive evidence. A second strand concerns emotional distress from fear of HIV: Maryland's Faya (1993) adopted a foreseeable-risk standard allowing recovery without proof of exposure, while K.A.C. v. Benson (1995) and Tennessee's Bain (1997) required actual exposure, following Burk (1990). Also: Tennessee's discovery-rule accrual (Carvell 1995) and duty as a matter of reasonable care (McCall 1995), limits on agents giving away a principal's property (King 1985), and Maryland's Little Miller Act (Seaboard Surety 1992).
rule: A nonmovant facing a properly supported summary-judgment motion may not rest on its pleadings but must set out specific facts showing a genuine issue (Byrd), and the court decides only issues of law (Beatty); fear-of-HIV emotional-distress claims generally require actual exposure.

changes.what: Once the movant makes a properly supported motion, the burden shifts to the nonmovant to set forth specific facts showing a genuine dispute; the court views evidence for the nonmovant.

name: Patent infringement: all-limitations rule and doctrine of equivalents (Pennwalt)
description: Early Federal Circuit patent law in a single 1990-94 slice anchored by Loctite (1985): every claim limitation must be met literally or equivalently (Pennwalt 1987, ZMI 1988, Johnston 1989) under Graver Tank's (1950) function-way-result test, with Hughes (1983) on flexible prosecution-history estoppel. Also obviousness (Graham 1966), inequitable conduct (Kingsdown 1988), jury trial of patent issues (Connell, Railroad Dynamics) and antitrust attempt claims.
history: Dominant rule: patent infringement in the early Federal Circuit, where every claim limitation must be found in the accused product literally or by a substantial equivalent. Loctite (1985) anchors the lineage's only slice, 1990-94, which passed through an employment-discrimination lineage before and after. How it changed: no change within the span; the leading cases set the 1980s rules. Graver Tank (1950) supplies the function-way-result test; Hughes Aircraft (1983) treated prosecution-history estoppel as flexible; Pennwalt (en banc 1987) required equivalence limitation by limitation and made it a question of fact; ZMI (1988) and Johnston (1989) restated the all-limitations rule and that attorney argument is not evidence; Palumbo (1985) addressed means-plus-function claims and Moleculon (1986) circumstantial proof of direct infringement. Alongside: Graham (1966) on obviousness, Kingsdown (1988) on inequitable conduct, Connell (1983) and Railroad Dynamics (1984) on jury trial of patent issues, Perkin-Elmer (1984) and Shatterproof (1985) on new trials, and Loctite on attempted monopolization claims.
rule: Infringement requires that every claim limitation be found in the accused device literally or by a substantial equivalent (Pennwalt's all-elements rule), an equivalent being one that performs substantially the same function in substantially the same way to obtain the same result (Graver Tank), with equivalence a question of fact.

name: New York family law: support agreements (Brescia), then custody (Eschbach)
description: New York family law where the child's interests override parental agreements, 1980-2029. To 2004 the axis is child support fixed by separation agreements: Boden (1977) and Brescia (1982) on upward modification, with equitable distribution (Hartog 1995) entering. From 2005 Eschbach (1982) anchors: custody turns on the totality of circumstances and best interests; Bennett (1976) governs non-parents; Tropea (1996) set relocation review.
history: Dominant rule: New York courts refuse to let parents' agreements fix outcomes that belong to the child. Phase one (1980-2004): Brescia (1982) anchors 1980-99 and Boden (1977) 2000-04. Boden allowed upward modification of agreed child support only on an unanticipated and unreasonable change, while Brescia held that when the child's own right to support is asserted the test is the child's needs. Christian (1977) set the unconscionability standard for separation agreements, and Kleila (1980) and Goldman (1940) addressed the court's power to modify. Later entrants address maintenance and equitable distribution (Merl 1986, McSparron 1995, Hartog 1995, O'Brien 1985, Majauskas 1984). How it changed: from 2005-09 Eschbach (1982) anchors through 2025-29: custody is decided on the totality of circumstances, no agreement binds the court, and Friederwitzer (1982) allows modification of agreed custody when best interests require. Bennett (1976) gives a parent priority over non-parents absent extraordinary circumstances, and Tropea (1996) replaced the exceptional-circumstances relocation test with best-interests weighing. Nicholson (2004) and Gooler (2013) enter in 2015-19; the partial 2025-29 slice drifts toward child-protective proceedings (Sheila G., Jamie M. 1984).
rule: In New York, a parental agreement cannot bind the court on matters affecting a child: child support fixed by a separation agreement may be modified when the child's needs are not met, and custody is decided on the totality of circumstances in the child's best interests.

changes.what: A parent has custody priority over a non-parent unless extraordinary circumstances are shown; then best interests govern.

changes.what: Child support in an incorporated agreement may be raised on a showing of unanticipated and unreasonable change or unmet needs; agreements are set aside only if unconscionable or fraudulent.
Where the child's own right to adequate support is asserted, the Boden standard does not limit modification; the test is the child's needs.

changes.case: Eschbach v. Eschbach; Friederwitzer v. Friederwitzer

Replaced the 'exceptional circumstances' presumption against relocation with a best-interests weighing of all factors.

name: FTCA discretionary-function exception (Gaubert) with international-law claims
description: A single 2000-04 cluster anchored by Gaubert (1991): the FTCA discretionary-function exception covers policy-grounded judgment unless a rule prescribes the conduct (Varig, 1984; Berkovitz, 1988). Beside it: Alien Tort Statute suits for torture (Filartiga, 1980; Marcos, 1994), foreign sovereign immunity (Amerada Hess, 1989; Nelson, 1993) and Vienna Convention claims without suppression (Breard, 1998; Lombera-Camorlinga, 2000).
history: Dominant rule: the FTCA's discretionary-function exception. Gaubert (1991) anchors the only slice, 2000-04: the exception covers conduct involving judgment that is susceptible to policy analysis, including day-to-day operations, and Berkovitz (1988) withholds it where a statute, regulation or policy prescribes a specific course of action; Varig Airlines (1984) applied it to the FAA's choice of a spot-checking program. Alongside: the cluster merged with a personal-jurisdiction unit from 1995-99 and carries suits that test the reach of U.S. courts over foreign conduct and states: the Alien Tort Statute for torture and jus cogens violations (Filartiga, 1980; Tel-Oren, 1984; Marcos, 1994; Kadic, 1996), the FSIA as the sole basis of jurisdiction over foreign states and its commercial-activity exception (Amerada Hess, 1989; Nelson, 1993), abduction not barring trial (Alvarez-Machain, 1992) and Vienna Convention Article 36, where Breard (1998) applied procedural default and Lombera-Camorlinga (9th Cir. en banc 2000) refused suppression. description: The later Texas termination cluster, 2010-29: C.H. (2002) anchors every slice, with J.F.C. (2002) firm-belief review of a predicate ground and best interest (Holley 1976). Distinctive here: J.O.A. (2009) and Boyd (1987) inferring endangerment from conduct not aimed at the child, A.V. (2003) holding one ground suffices, and a 2010-19 influx of Tennessee (Valentine, Kaliyah S., Carrington H.) and federal family-rights cases.

previous.name: Texas parental termination: sufficiency review and Santosky/Troxel
previous.description: Texas termination-of-parental-rights appeals built on In re C.H. and In re J.F.C. (factual and legal sufficiency under the clear-and-convincing standard) and the Holley best-interest factors, grounded in Santosky, Stanley and Troxel on the constitutional weight of the parent-child relationship. Boyd (endangerment and imprisonment) is a frequent companion.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session subagents, from cocite evidence; second pass differentiated near-duplicates)

history: Dominant rule: Texas termination requires clear and convincing evidence of a § 161.001(b)(1) ground and of best interest, and appellate courts apply heightened sufficiency review. In re C.H. (2002) anchors every slice from 2010-14 to 2025-29, with J.F.C. (2002) leading beside it: legal sufficiency disregards evidence a factfinder could reasonably disbelieve, and factual sufficiency asks whether disputed evidence prevents a firm belief or conviction. The core rule is stable. Holley (1976) supplies the best-interest factors, Holick (1985) reads 'provide' to include arranging support, Boyd (1987) and J.O.A. (2009) allow endangerment to be inferred from misconduct not directed at the child, A.V. (2003) holds one predicate suffices, and H.R.M. (2006) and J.P.B. (2005) require deference to the factfinder on credibility. How it changed: the 2010-14 slice forms from two 2005-09 units and brings in constitutional cases (Stanley, 1972; Troxel, 2000) and Tennessee termination cases (Valentine, 2002; Angela E., 2010). In 2015-19 Tennessee's Kaliyah S. (2015) dropped reasonable efforts as a precondition and Carrington H. (2016) required review of every ground found. The unit is Texas-led again in 2020-29.
rule: Texas termination requires clear and convincing evidence of a ground under Family Code § 161.001(b)(1) and that termination is in the child's best interest, reviewed under heightened legal and factual sufficiency standards asking whether a factfinder could reasonably form a firm belief or conviction (C.H., J.F.C.).

changes.case: Stanley v. Illinois; Santosky v. Kramer
changes.what: Parental rights are a fundamental liberty interest, and termination needs at least clear and convincing evidence.
A predicate ground and best interest must both be proved; nonexclusive factors guide best interest.

changes.case: Texas Department of Human Services v. Boyd
changes.what: Endangerment may be inferred from parental misconduct, including imprisonment.

changes.case: In re C.H.; In re J.F.C.
changes.what: Heightened legal and factual sufficiency review under the firm-belief-or-conviction standard.
One predicate finding suffices when there is also a best-interest finding.
Endangering conduct need not be directed at the child.

changes.case: In re Kaliyah S.; In re Carrington H. (Tenn.)
changes.what: Tennessee: reasonable efforts are not a precondition to termination, and appellate courts must review every ground found, challenged or not.

changes.what: Both a predicate ground and the child's best interest must be shown, and best interest is weighed by non-exclusive factors such as the parent's abilities and excuses for acts or omissions.
Due process requires clear and convincing proof to terminate parental rights.

changes.what: Endangerment may be inferred from parental misconduct, and imprisonment is a factor; the court disapproved a contrary holding.

changes.what: One predicate finding plus a best-interest finding suffices, and parents have a right to effective counsel in termination cases.

name: Statutes of repose and open-courts challenges (Rosenberg, Pullum)
description: Statutes of repose in 1985-89: Rosenberg (N.J. 1972, anchor) held a builders' repose statute prevents a claim from arising and is valid, and Freezer Storage (1978) agreed. Florida's Sirmons (1979) and Battilla (1980) struck repose statutes under the access-to-courts clause until Pullum (1985) receded from Battilla. Also limits on duties to third parties (Lucas 1961, Ultramares 1931, De Long 1983 special duty).
history: Dominant rule: Rosenberg v. North Bergen (N.J. 1972), anchor of the single slice (1985-89), treats a statute of repose as extinguishing a cause of action at an ascertainable time, so that no claim arises after the period, and upholds it. Freezer Storage (Pa. 1978) held that a constitutional remedies clause does not stop the legislature from abolishing common-law actions, and Burmaster (1978) found rational the line between architects and owners; Reeves (1976) and Anderson (1981) applied the statutes to suppliers and old buildings. How it changed: Florida's Supreme Court struck builders' and products repose statutes under its access-to-courts clause (Sirmons 1979, Battilla 1980), and Phillips (1980) did the same on open-courts and equal-protection grounds; Pullum (1985) then upheld Florida's products-liability repose statute and receded from Battilla. Klein (1982) addressed standing and warranty periods. Alongside: limits on duties to non-clients and the public, including Ultramares (1931) for accountants, Lucas v. Hamm (1961) for will drafters, De Long (1983) on a municipality's special duty to 911 callers, and Miller (1984) on a college's duty as landlord. The cluster continues into 1990-94.
rule: A statute of repose, which bars a claim a fixed time after construction or sale whether or not injury has occurred, prevents a cause of action from arising and is generally a valid legislative choice, though some state courts struck such statutes under open-courts guarantees when they abolished common-law remedies without an overpowering public necessity.

changes.case: Rosenberg v. Town of North Bergen (N.J.)
changes.what: A builders' statute of repose does not bar an accrued claim but prevents a cause of action from ever arising, and is constitutional.

changes.case: Freezer Storage v. Armstrong Cork (Pa.); Burmaster (Ill.)
changes.what: Legislatures may limit causes of action; distinctions between architects and owners are rational.

changes.case: Overland Construction v. Sirmons (Fla.); Battilla v. Allis Chalmers (Fla.); Phillips (Ala.)
changes.what: Statutes of repose violated access-to-courts provisions by abolishing common-law rights without overpowering public necessity.
Receded from Battilla and upheld the products-liability statute of repose as a valid legislative means.
