name: Federalism revival: Seminole Tribe sovereign immunity and Lopez commerce limits
description: Federalism in the late 1990s: Seminole Tribe (1996) barred abrogation of state immunity under Article I, Alden (1999) extended immunity to state courts, and Boerne's (1997) congruence-and-proportionality test defeated ADEA and ADA abrogation (Kimel, 2000; Garrett, 2001). Ex parte Young (1908) and Edelman (1974) set the prospective-relief line. Lopez (1995) and Morrison (2000) limited the commerce power. 2000-04 adds standing (Lujan) and Rooker-Feldman.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Eleventh Amendment immunity and federalism (late 1990s)
previous.description: State sovereign immunity and limits on federal power: Seminole Tribe, Hans, Edelman and Ex parte Young on suits against states and officials, Pennhurst and Atascadero, and City of Boerne and Lopez on congressional power to abrogate or regulate.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session subagents, from cocite evidence; second pass differentiated near-duplicates)

history: Dominant rule: renewed limits on federal power over states. Lopez (1995) anchors 1995-99 and Seminole Tribe (1996) 2000-04. Sovereign immunity rests on Hans (1890): states cannot be sued by private parties without consent, Ex parte Young (1908) allows prospective injunctions against officers, and Edelman (1974), Pennhurst (1984) and Atascadero v. Scanlon (1985) bar retroactive money relief and state-law claims and require unmistakably clear waiver or abrogation. How it changed: Seminole Tribe (1996) held Article I powers cannot abrogate immunity, overruling Union Gas. City of Boerne (1997) required § 5 legislation to be congruent and proportional, and Alden (1999) extended immunity to suits in state courts. In 2000-04 Kimel (2000) and Garrett (2001) enter, holding the ADEA and ADA Title I do not validly abrogate immunity, and Morrison (2000) struck VAWA's civil remedy. Lopez and New York v. United States (1992) set commerce and anti-commandeering limits. Also: Lujan (1992) standing, Rooker-Feldman, Younger abstention and Cleburne equal protection in a broad public-law mix; the cluster splits in 2005-09.
rule: States are immune from private suits for damages that Congress cannot abrogate under its Article I powers (Seminole Tribe), subject to Ex parte Young suits for prospective relief against officials and valid § 5 abrogation that is congruent and proportional (City of Boerne); Congress's commerce power stops at noneconomic intrastate activity (Lopez).

changes.case: Hans v. Louisiana; Ex parte Young
changes.what: States are immune from suit by their own citizens without consent, but federal courts may enjoin state officers' unconstitutional acts.

changes.case: Edelman v. Jordan; Pennhurst v. Halderman; Atascadero v. Scanlon
changes.what: No retroactive monetary relief from the state treasury, no federal suit on state-law claims against a state, and waiver or abrogation must be unmistakably clear.
Congress exceeded the commerce power with the Gun-Free School Zones Act.

changes.case: Seminole Tribe of Florida v. Florida
changes.what: Congress cannot abrogate state sovereign immunity under Article I, overruling Pennsylvania v. Union Gas.
Section 5 legislation must be congruent and proportional to identified constitutional violations; RFRA exceeded it as applied to states.
Sovereign immunity bars private suits against states in their own courts on federal claims such as the FLSA.

changes.case: Kimel v. Florida Board of Regents; Board of Trustees v. Garrett; United States v. Morrison
changes.what: The ADEA and ADA Title I do not validly abrogate state immunity, and VAWA's civil remedy exceeded both the commerce and § 5 powers.

name: Substantial evidence for agency findings (Perales): disability and NLRB, 1985-94
description: The family rule shared by disability and labor review, 1985-94: agency findings stand if supported by substantial evidence on the whole record (Consolidated Edison 1938, Universal Camera 1951; Perales 1971, anchor of both slices). Circuits shaped review of the grids (Kirk 1981), pain testimony (Polaski 1984, Bunnell 1991) and vocational hypotheticals (Magallanes 1989). Also NLRB discharge cases (Transportation Management 1983) and black-lung benefits.
history: Dominant rule: courts review agency fact findings for substantial evidence, defined in Consolidated Edison (1938) and applied to the whole record in Universal Camera (1951). Richardson v. Perales (1971), anchor in 1985-89 and 1990-94, held that written medical reports can be substantial evidence in disability hearings and that the ALJ resolves conflicts. Courts may not try the case de novo or decide credibility (Garner 1984). How it changed: the slices are dominated by circuit law on disability adjudication. Heckler v. Campbell (1983) upheld the grids, and Kirk (6th Cir. 1981) limited them where nonexertional impairments narrow the range of work. Polaski (8th Cir. 1984) set factors for subjective pain, Duncan (1986) stressed the ALJ's view of demeanor, and in 1990-94 Williams (1988) and Bunnell (9th Cir. en banc 1991) required articulated reasons for disbelieving symptoms, while Magallanes (1989) required complete vocational hypotheticals. Thomas v. Arn (1985) let courts condition appeal on objections to a magistrate's report. Alongside: NLRB mixed-motive discharges (Transportation Management 1983), black-lung presumptions (Mullins Coal 1988) and prisoner medical-care claims (Wright v. Collins 1985). The lineage splits in 1995-99.
rule: Agency fact findings, including Social Security disability denials, are upheld if supported by substantial evidence, meaning such relevant evidence as a reasonable mind might accept as adequate, on the record as a whole; the court does not reweigh evidence or decide credibility, but the ALJ must give reasons for rejecting testimony and evidence.

changes.case: Consolidated Edison v. NLRB; Universal Camera v. NLRB
changes.what: Substantial evidence is what a reasonable mind might accept as adequate, judged on the whole record including contrary examiner findings.
Written medical reports can be substantial evidence in disability hearings even if contradicted, where the claimant did not subpoena the doctors.

changes.case: Kirk v. Secretary of HHS (6th Cir.); Heckler v. Campbell
changes.what: The medical-vocational grids are valid but apply only where nonexertional limits do not restrict the full range of work.
Subjective pain complaints must be weighed under factors such as daily activities and may be discounted only if inconsistent with the whole record.
Courts may condition appellate review on timely objections to a magistrate's recommendation.

changes.case: Mullins Coal v. Director, OWCP; Magallanes v. Bowen; Bunnell v. Sullivan (9th Cir. en banc)
changes.what: Deference to agency regulations; vocational hypotheticals must include all limitations; symptom testimony cannot be rejected solely for lack of objective support.

name: Selective Service and conscientious objectors: Estep basis-in-fact, Seeger, Welsh
description: Judicial review of Selective Service decisions in the Vietnam era. Estep (1946, anchor 1965-69) allows challenge to classifications lacking a basis in fact; Dickinson (1953) and Witmer (1955) govern denial of objector claims; Seeger (1965, anchor 1970-74) and Welsh (1970) broadened religious belief; Oestereich (1969), Breen and Mulloy (1970) curbed lawless board action.
history: Dominant rule: courts review draft classifications narrowly, for a basis in fact, but boards must follow the statute and regulations and may not deny conscientious-objector claims on speculation. Estep (1946) anchors 1965-69 with Dickinson (1953), Witmer (1955) and Burns (1953): a registrant prosecuted for refusing induction may challenge a classification lacking a basis in fact. How it changed: Seeger (1965) anchors 1970-74 and, with Welsh (1970), extended the exemption to sincere beliefs parallel to traditional religion, including those based largely on moral grounds. Oestereich (1969) allowed pre-induction review of lawless board action and Breen (1970) of punitive delinquency reclassification, while Gabriel (1968) barred it for factual judgments. McKart (1969) relaxed exhaustion in criminal cases, Mulloy (1970) required reopening on a prima facie claim, Ehlert (1971) addressed late-crystallizing beliefs, and Haughton (1969) and Hammond (1968) applied fair-procedure requirements. The cluster then dissolves into agency-review lineages as the draft ended.
rule: Draft-board classifications are reviewed only for a basis in fact, but a board may not deny a conscientious-objector claim on suspicion alone, and a sincere objection to all war rooted in deeply held moral or religious belief qualifies.

changes.what: In a prosecution for refusing induction, a classification may be challenged if it has no basis in fact or the board exceeded its jurisdiction.

changes.case: Dickinson v. United States; Witmer v. United States
changes.what: A prima facie exemption claim cannot be denied on suspicion and speculation, though sincerity is a subjective question for the board.
Religious training and belief includes a sincere belief that occupies a place parallel to that filled by God in traditional believers.

changes.case: Oestereich v. Selective Service Board; Clark v. Gabriel; McKart v. United States
changes.what: Pre-induction review is available for blatantly lawless board action but not for fact-based judgments; failure to appeal a classification does not always bar a defense in a criminal case.

changes.case: Welsh v. United States; Breen v. Selective Service Board; Mulloy v. United States; Ehlert v. United States
changes.what: Objection based in part on moral beliefs qualifies; punitive delinquency reclassification is reviewable; boards must reopen on a prima facie claim; late-crystallizing claims need a fair hearing.

name: Ohio summary judgment, 1995-99 cluster: Dresher arrives; employer torts, Savoie
description: The one-slice 1995-99 Ohio cluster in which Dresher v. Burt (1996) first anchors: the movant must point to record evidence, then the nonmovant must show specific facts (building on Harless 1978, Mitseff 1988, Murphy 1992). Its distinctive settings are employer intentional torts (Fyffe 1991, Van Fossen 1988), per-person limits for wrongful-death claims (Savoie 1993), public records (Steckman 1994) and at-will promissory estoppel (Wing 1991).
history: Dominant rule: Ohio's summary-judgment standard under Civ.R. 56. The cluster exists only in 1995-99, anchored by Dresher v. Burt (1996), after an earlier unit merges in; it splits in 2000-04. How it developed: Harless (1978) stated the three-part test, Mitseff (1988) required the movant to specify the grounds it relies on, and Murphy v. City of Reynoldsburg (1992) required the trial court itself to examine the evidence. Dresher then held that the movant must identify record evidence showing the nonmovant lacks proof of an essential element, not merely assert it, after which the nonmovant must set out specific facts for trial. Alongside, the substantive Ohio law that the cases test: product defects and the duty to warn (Temple 1977), promissory estoppel and at-will employment (Wing 1991), employer intentional torts (Fyffe 1991), trespass by emissions (Brown 1993), legal-malpractice harm (Vahila 1997, extending Krahn), separate per-person limits for wrongful-death claims (Savoie 1993), and public-records proceedings (Steckman 1994).
rule: Under Ohio Civ.R. 56 the movant must identify the specific grounds and the record evidence showing the nonmovant has no evidence on an essential element, after which the nonmovant must set out specific facts showing a genuine issue for trial (Dresher v. Burt).

changes.what: Summary judgment is proper only if no genuine fact issue remains, the movant is entitled to judgment as a matter of law, and reasonable minds viewing the evidence for the nonmovant could reach only one conclusion.
The movant must specify the grounds for summary judgment; a motion does not put the nonmovant on notice that the whole claim is challenged.
The trial court must itself examine the evidence before granting summary judgment; appellate review cannot substitute for that.
A movant cannot rest on conclusory assertions but must point to record evidence; the nonmovant then bears a reciprocal burden to set forth specific facts.
A legal-malpractice plaintiff need not always prove the underlying case would have been won; other harm, such as a lost settlement opportunity, can suffice.

name: Maryland statutory interpretation: plain meaning and purpose (Kaczorowski, Oaks)
description: Maryland Court of Appeals rules of statutory interpretation in 1995-2004: plain meaning first (MVA 1997; Buckman 1994; Mauzy 1979), read with purpose and common sense to avoid absurd results (Kaczorowski 1987, anchor 1995-99; Oaks 1995, anchor 2000-04). Also narrow review of agency action (UPS 1994), mootness exceptions (Coburn 1996), and summary judgment and contract cases (Beatty 1993; Gross 1993; Colomiris 1999).
history: Dominant rule: the cardinal rule of Maryland statutory construction is to find and carry out legislative intent, starting with the plain, ordinary meaning of the words. Kaczorowski (1987) anchors 1995-99 and Oaks v. Connors (1995) anchors 2000-04, after three earlier units merge; the cluster splits in 2005-09. How it developed: Mauzy (1979) refused to narrow plain statutory terms, Buckman (1994) and MVA (1997) confined courts to unambiguous language, and Kaczorowski allowed reading a statute in light of its purpose to avoid absurd results. Weiss (1958) addresses whether code revisions change substance. Statutes applied include real estate disclosure (Romm 1995), police certification after termination (Stanford 1997), and local ordinances (Tidewater/Havre de Grace 1995). Alongside: narrow judicial review of agency decisions on the agency's stated reasons (UPS 1994), deciding moot cases of public importance (Coburn 1996), local-government tort liability for constitutional torts (Ashton 1995), summary judgment as a ruling of law (Beatty 1993; Heat & Power 1990), material misrepresentation (Gross 1993), plain-meaning contract interpretation (Colomiris, Ashton 1999), powers of attorney (King 1985) and lex fori for procedure (Goodwich 1996).
rule: Maryland courts seek legislative intent first in the plain, ordinary meaning of the statute's words, looking beyond unambiguous language only to read the statute in light of its purpose and avoid absurd or illogical results (Kaczorowski; Oaks).

changes.case: Bureau of Mines v. George's Creek Coal (Weiss)
changes.what: A change in wording in a code revision is presumed substantive only where the record shows that was intended; studied revisions can carry substantive change.

changes.case: Kaczorowski v. Mayor and City Council of Baltimore
changes.what: Statutes are read in light of their purpose and context, adopting a construction that comports with common sense and avoids illogical or absurd results.
Where statutory language is clear, the court applies its plain meaning without resort to other aids; a statute in derogation of common law is construed accordingly.
Courts do not look beyond statutory language that is free from ambiguity.

changes.case: United Parcel Service v. People's Counsel
changes.what: Judicial review of agency action is narrow, and a decision may be affirmed only on the agency's own findings and reasons.

name: CGL coverage for pollution: duty to defend, 'sudden and accidental' (Outboard Marine)
description: Insurance coverage for pollution claims, 1990-2004: ambiguities favour the insured, the duty to defend arises whenever a claim may be covered (Gray 1966, Montrose 1993), and courts split on the 'sudden and accidental' exclusion (Claussen 1989 v. Belleville 1990). Broadwell (1987) anchors 1990-94 and Outboard Marine (1992) 1995-2004; by 2000-04 the cluster drifts to Illinois civil review standards (Pedrick, Maple).
history: Dominant rule: how comprehensive general liability policies apply to environmental contamination. Broadwell Realty (1987) anchors 1990-94, holding certain cleanup costs covered, with Foley (1988), Technicon (1989, whether an EPA demand is a 'suit'), Waste Management of Carolinas (1986, gradual leaching as an accident) and Claussen (1989, pollution exclusion ambiguous). Belleville (1990) read the exclusion as clear, and USF&G (1988) defined occurrence by unexpected damage. How it changed: Outboard Marine (1992) anchors 1995-99 and 2000-04, construing ambiguities for the insured and reviewing summary judgment de novo; Montrose (1993) set the potential-for-coverage duty to defend, Morton International (1993) and Queen City Farms (1995) entered, and Waller (1995) barred bad-faith claims absent coverage. The dominant rule drifts in 2000-04 as Illinois cases merge in: Pedrick (1967) on directed verdicts, Maple (1992) on new trials, Hodge (1993), and public-law cases (Michigan Avenue National Bank 2000, City of Belvidere 1998). Also: Bank of the West (1992) on the UCL and Illinois premises liability (Ward 1990).
rule: Insurance policies are construed for the insured where ambiguous, an insurer must defend whenever the underlying claim may fall within coverage (Gray, Montrose), and comprehensive general liability policies cover environmental cleanup unless a clear pollution exclusion bars it, with courts split on whether 'sudden and accidental' is ambiguous.

changes.what: An insurer must defend where the facts alleged could support a covered claim, even if the complaint pleads only an intentional tort.

changes.case: Waste Management of Carolinas (N.C.); Broadwell Realty; Claussen (Ga.); Lumbermens Mutual v. Belleville Industries (Mass.)
changes.what: Courts divided on whether gradual contamination is an accident and whether the 'sudden and accidental' pollution exclusion is ambiguous (Claussen) or clear (Belleville).
Response and cleanup costs are covered 'damages', with ambiguities resolved in favour of coverage.

changes.case: Outboard Marine Corp. v. Liberty Mutual (Ill.)
changes.what: Ambiguous provisions, including 'sudden and accidental', are construed for the insured; summary judgment rulings are reviewed de novo. Outboard Marine anchors 1995-2004.

changes.case: Montrose Chemical Corp. v. Superior Court (Cal.)
changes.what: The insured need only show the underlying claim may fall within coverage; the insurer must prove it cannot.

phases.rule: CGL coverage of environmental contamination: duty to defend, 'damages', 'suit', 'occurrence' and the pollution exclusion

name: Jury-exclusion claims 1965-74: Smith v. Texas, Glasser, Whitus, Swain
description: Racial exclusion from juries as litigated in 1965-74 only: Smith v. Texas (1941) anchors 1965-69 and Glasser (1942), on the jury's representative character, anchors 1970-74; Fay (1947) and Brown v. Allen (1953) also lead. Systematic exclusion shown by long-term disparities makes a prima facie case (Cassell 1950; Hernandez 1954); Whitus (1966) and Alexander (1972) refined statistical proof, while Swain (1965) limited peremptory-challenge claims.
history: Dominant rule: the state may not purposefully exclude members of a race or ethnic group from grand or petit juries, and long-standing or large statistical disparities shift to the state the burden of rebutting discrimination. Smith v. Texas (1941) anchors 1965-69 and Glasser (1942), cited for the jury's representative character and the substantial-evidence standard, anchors 1970-74. How it changed: the core is the line from Strauder (1880) and Neal (1881) through Norris (1935), Hill (1942), Akins (1945), Patton (1947), Cassell (1950), Avery (1953), Eubanks (1958) and Arnold (1964), which inferred exclusion from decades without Black jurors, and Hernandez (1954), extending protection to Mexican-Americans. Swain (1965) required proof of systematic peremptory strikes across cases. Whitus (1966) found a prima facie case in a 27.1% versus 9.1% disparity; in 1970-74 Turner and Carter (1970) let excluded citizens challenge selection systems and Alexander (1972) required case-by-case inquiry, while Comeaux (1968) upheld a literacy requirement. The cluster then splits.
rule: Purposeful exclusion of a racial or ethnic group from grand or petit juries denies equal protection; a long-standing, substantial disparity between the group's share of the population and of jury lists makes a prima facie case that the state must rebut.

changes.case: Strauder v. West Virginia; Neal v. Delaware
changes.what: Excluding Black citizens from jury service, by statute or in practice under a neutral statute, violates equal protection.

changes.case: Norris v. Alabama; Smith v. Texas; Hill v. Texas; Akins v. Texas; Patton v. Mississippi; Cassell v. Texas; Avery v. Georgia
changes.what: Long-term absence of Black jurors makes a prima facie case of systematic exclusion; purposeful discrimination is required, and limiting jurors to token numbers is unlawful.
Mexican-Americans are a distinct class protected against systematic exclusion from juries.
Discriminatory use of peremptory challenges must be shown by systematic exclusion over many cases, not in a single trial.

changes.case: Whitus v. Georgia; Turner v. Fouche; Carter v. Jury Commission; Alexander v. Louisiana
changes.what: Statistical disparities on jury lists and venires, with opportunity to discriminate, establish a prima facie case, and excluded Black citizens may sue to challenge selection systems.

name: Texas criminal trials: indictment notice and extraneous offenses (Albrecht, Drumm)
description: Texas Court of Criminal Appeals trial-error law, 1980-84: extraneous offenses are admissible only for a relevant purpose such as rebutting a defense (Albrecht 1972, anchor; Young 1953), and an indictment must give notice of the manner and means the State will prove (Drumm 1977, Ferguson 1981, Gorman 1982). Also lesser offenses in homicide (Cumbie, Simpkins 1979) and improper jury argument (Jones 1978, Alejandro 1973).
history: Dominant rule: a Texas accused is entitled to be tried on the accusation in the State's pleading and not for being a criminal generally (Young 1953), so extraneous offenses come in only for a relevant purpose, notably to rebut a defensive theory (Albrecht 1972, anchor of the single slice, 1980-84). How it changed: the leading cases from the late 1970s and early 1980s tightened charging-instrument notice. Drumm (1977) judged a timely notice objection from the accused's perspective; Ferguson (1981) and Gorman (1982) required the State, on a motion to quash, to specify which statutory type of conduct or appropriation it would prove, while Thomas (1981) held statutorily defined terms need not be further alleged and American Plant Food (1974) addressed disjunctive elements. Cumbie (1979) and Simpkins (1979) addressed homicide charging and lesser-offense issues. Alongside: improper prosecutorial argument referring to facts outside the record (Alejandro 1973, Jones 1978) and abatement on appeal (Barfield 1979). The cluster continues in 1985-89 in Texas sufficiency-of-the-evidence appeals.
rule: A Texas accused must be tried only on the offense charged, with an indictment giving notice of the manner and means the State will prove, and extraneous offenses are admissible only for a relevant purpose such as rebutting a defensive theory.

changes.case: Young v. State; Albrecht v. State
changes.what: The accused is tried on the charge, not as a criminal generally; extraneous offenses may be used to rebut defensive theories.
A timely notice objection to the charging instrument is judged from the perspective of the accused.

changes.case: Ferguson v. State; Thomas v. State; Gorman v. State
changes.what: On a motion to quash, the State must specify which statutorily defined manner of conduct it will prove, though defined terms need not be further alleged.

changes.case: Cumbie v. State; Simpkins v. State
changes.what: Lesser-offense and accident issues in homicide: death necessarily involves bodily injury, and accidental discharge does not necessarily raise criminally negligent homicide.

name: California dependency family: Autumn H. permanency, then I.J. jurisdiction
description: The California dependency family, 2010-29, whose anchor moves from permanency to jurisdiction. Autumn H. (1994) anchors 2010-19: adoption is preferred after reunification fails unless a parent proves a beneficial relationship outweighing adoption's benefits (Casey D., 1999; Jasmine D., 2000). From 2020-24 In re I.J. (2013) anchors jurisdictional findings of risk under § 300, joined by R.T. (2017) and Drake M. (2012) on substance abuse.
history: Dominant rule: California dependency law's preference for permanency once reunification has failed. Autumn H. (1994) anchors 2010-14 and 2015-19: at a section 366.26 hearing adoption is preferred, and the beneficial-relationship exception requires a parental bond that promotes the child's well-being to a degree outweighing the security of an adoptive home (Casey D., 1999; Jasmine D., 2000). Marilyn H. (1993) shifts the focus to the child's need for stability after services end, Stephanie M. (1994) sets abuse-of-discretion review, and Celine R. (2003) treats the sibling exception from the child's perspective. In 2015-19 special immigrant juvenile findings (Maria P.E.A., 2013) and other custody rulings enter. How it changed: from 2020-24 the anchor moves to jurisdiction. In re I.J. (2013) held that a father's abuse of a daughter can support jurisdiction over sons without empirical evidence of risk, R.T. (2017) dropped any parental-fault requirement under § 300(b)(1), and Drake M. (2012) defined substance abuse by diagnosis or the DSM. I.J. anchors the partial 2025-29 slice, with Kimberly F. (1997) on section 388 petitions.
rule: Once reunification ends in a California dependency case, the focus shifts to the child's need for permanency and stability, and adoption is preferred unless a parent proves an exception such as a beneficial relationship so significant that terminating it would harm the child more than adoption would benefit (Autumn H., Marilyn H., Stephanie M.).

changes.what: After reunification services end, the parent's interest yields to the child's interest in permanency and stability.
The beneficial-relationship exception applies only where the relationship promotes the child's well-being enough to outweigh the benefits of adoption.
Placement and custody rulings are reviewed for abuse of discretion, with the child's best interests paramount.
The sibling-relationship exception is applied from the adoptive child's perspective and rarely defeats adoption.

changes.case: L.A. County DCFS v. Drake M.
changes.what: Substance abuse for jurisdiction requires a medical diagnosis or conduct meeting the DSM definition.
A father's sexual abuse of a daughter can support jurisdiction over her brothers without expert proof of risk.
Jurisdiction under § 300(b)(1) for failure to protect does not require parental fault.

name: Regulatory takings, 1985-2009: Lucas wipeouts, Williamson ripeness, Lingle
description: Regulatory takings in 1985-2009, the era of Lucas and ripeness: Agins (1980) anchors 1985-89 with Penn Central (1978) and Williamson County's (1985) ripeness rule; Nollan and First English (1987) and Dolan (1994) add exaction and temporary-taking rules; Lucas (1992) anchors 1995-2004 with its total-wipeout rule, limited by Palazzolo (2001) and Tahoe-Sierra (2002). Lingle (2005) discarded Agins's test and Penn Central anchors 2005-09.
history: Dominant rule: when a land-use or other regulation is a taking that requires just compensation. Agins (1980) anchors 1985-89 with Penn Central's ad hoc balancing, Mahon's 'too far' test, Euclid and Williamson County's ripeness rule (final decision and state compensation procedures first). How it changed: Nollan and First English (1987) added the exaction nexus and compensation for temporary takings; Lucas (1992) set a categorical rule for regulations that remove all economically beneficial use and anchors 1995-2004, with Dolan (1994) adding rough proportionality. Palazzolo (2001) and Tahoe-Sierra (2002) enter in 2000-04, limiting the categorical rule and keeping Penn Central for moratoria. Lingle (2005) rejected Agins's 'substantially advances' formula, and Penn Central anchors again in 2005-09, alongside Kelo (2005) on public use and San Remo (2005) on preclusion. Also: Contract Clause cases (U.S. Trust, Romein) join in 1995-99.
rule: A regulation is a compensable taking if it permanently physically occupies property (Loretto), deprives land of all economically beneficial use (Lucas), or fails the Penn Central ad hoc balancing; exactions need a nexus and rough proportionality (Nollan, Dolan), and a federal takings claim is not ripe without a final decision and resort to state compensation procedures (Williamson County).

changes.case: Penn Central Transportation Co. v. New York City
changes.what: Ad hoc balancing of economic impact, interference with investment-backed expectations and the character of the government action.

changes.case: Williamson County Regional Planning Commission v. Hamilton Bank
changes.what: A takings claim is not ripe until the government reaches a final decision (here, no variance sought) and state compensation remedies are pursued.
Permit conditions demanding an easement need an essential nexus to the government's interest; a temporary regulatory taking requires compensation for the period before invalidation.

changes.case: Lucas v. South Carolina Coastal Council
changes.what: A regulation depriving land of all economically beneficial use is a categorical taking unless background principles of property law already barred the use; Lucas anchors 1995-2004.
Exactions must be roughly proportional to the impact of the proposed development.
Acquiring property after a regulation does not bar a claim; a temporary moratorium is analysed under Penn Central, not as a categorical taking.
Rejected Agins's 'substantially advances a legitimate state interest' formula as a takings test; Penn Central again anchors 2005-09.

name: Georgia capital appeals family, 1985-94: Spivey voir dire, Moore proportionality
description: The Georgia death-penalty family, 1985-94, led by capital jury selection: Spivey (1984, anchor 1985-89) on voir dire about parole and juror qualification, with Isaacs (1989) and Mincey, inside the Supreme Court's review of each death sentence for excessiveness against similar cases (Moore 1975). Goodwin (1976) anchors 1990-94. Also sentencing-phase evidence (Berryhill 1982), no weighing requirement (Ford 1987), mitigation charges (Taylor 1991).
history: Dominant rule: the Georgia Supreme Court's direct review of death sentences, combining ordinary error review with a statutory check that the sentence is not excessive or disproportionate compared with similar cases. Spivey (1984) anchors 1985-89, with Ingram, Moore (1975), Roberts and Berryhill (1982). How it changed: Goodwin (1976) anchors 1990-94, when Isaacs (1989), Hall, Taylor (1991) and Lee (1988) enter. Isaacs adopted the McDonough test for juror nondisclosure and upheld reverse-Witherspoon rulings; Taylor holds the court need not identify the defendant's mitigating circumstances in its charge; Ford (1987) holds Georgia juries need not weigh aggravation against mitigation; Patillo (1992) overruled Foster (1988) in part. Alongside: voir dire on parole (Spivey) and juror bias (Mincey), funds for defense investigators (Roberts), voluntariness of statements (Amadeo, Ingram), lesser-offense charges (Dick), and mental retardation (Stripling 1991).
rule: On direct appeal of a Georgia death sentence the Supreme Court reviews the trial for error and compares the sentence with similar cases to ensure it is not excessive or disproportionate, deferring to the trial court on juror qualification and the conduct of voir dire.

changes.what: A death sentence was held excessive because the case was less aggravated than the death cases to which it was compared.
No pretrial notice is needed to reuse guilt-phase evidence at sentencing; the jury reconsiders all of it.
Adopted the McDonough Power Equipment v. Greenwood test for juror nondisclosure on voir dire.
Overruled Foster v. State (1988) in part on other grounds.

Bruch (1989) anchors ERISA: de novo review absent discretion, broad 'relate to' preemption (Shaw 1983, Holliday 1990), exclusive § 502(a) remedies (Pilot Life 1987, Ingersoll-Rand 1990), then narrowing in Travelers (1995) and Dillingham (1997), plus Pegram (2000) and Great-West (2002). history: Dominant rule: the cluster's anchor doctrine changes by period. Strickland (1984) anchors 1990-99, when the cluster also holds habeas and capital material (Brecht 1993, Coleman 1991, Teague 1989, Lindh 1997) and guilty-plea review (Boykin 1969). How it changed: Apprendi (2000) anchors 2000-04, alongside Williams v. Taylor (2000) on AEDPA and Olano (1993) on plain error. Booker (2005) anchors 2005-09, after Blakely (2004), with Gall, Rita and Kimbrough (2007) entering; habeas and Texas strands split off. Gall anchors from 2010-14 through the partial 2025-29 slice: sentences are reviewed for procedural error, then substantive reasonableness. Anders (1967) and Penson (1988) lead in 2010-14 before an Anders unit splits off. In 2015-19 Johnson (2015), Descamps (2013) and Mathis (2016) bring the categorical approach, with Molina-Martinez (2016) on Guidelines errors. changes.what: Ineffective assistance requires deficient performance and a reasonable probability of a different result.
Four-part plain-error test for forfeited errors; waived errors are not reviewable.

name: California arbitration, 2020-29: Armendariz unconscionability and FAA preemption
description: California-centred enforcement of arbitration agreements, 2020-24: Armendariz (2000, anchor) requires minimum protections and bilaterality in employment arbitration and both procedural and substantive unconscionability (Kho, 2019); Kaplan (1995) and Henry Schein (2019) govern who decides; Concepcion preemption (Iskanian 2014), Epic (2018) and Lamps Plus (2019) shape the FAA. The partial 2025-29 slice drifts to mandamus (Cheney 2004).
history: Dominant rule: courts enforce arbitration agreements by their terms, deciding contract formation and, absent clear delegation, arbitrability (First Options v. Kaplan, 1995, which reverses the presumption for who decides; AT&T Technologies, 1986). Armendariz (2000) anchors 2020-24: mandatory employment arbitration of statutory claims must provide minimum protections and a modicum of bilaterality, and unconscionability requires both procedural and substantive elements (Kho, 2019, on surprise and time to consider; Baltazar, 2016; Pinnacle, 2012). Review of awards is narrow (Moncharsh, 1992); waiver by unreasonable delay (Engalla, 1997); Moses H. Cone (1983) and Volt (1989) frame FAA scope. How it changed: Iskanian (2014) held Gentry preempted after Concepcion; Sanchez (2015) applied Concepcion to the CLRA; Epic Systems (2018) enforced individual-arbitration terms; Henry Schein (2019) rejected the wholly-groundless exception; Lamps Plus (2019) required consent to class arbitration. In the partial 2025-29 slice the anchor moves to Cheney (2004) on mandamus, with Rooker-Feldman and Younger, and Moriana (2022) on PAGA arbitration, which is drift.
rule: Courts decide whether a valid arbitration agreement exists and who decides arbitrability unless the parties clearly delegated it (First Options, Henry Schein), enforce agreements by their terms under the FAA, and refuse employment agreements that are both procedurally and substantively unconscionable or lack a modicum of bilaterality (Armendariz).

changes.case: First Options of Chicago v. Kaplan
changes.what: Who decides arbitrability is presumptively for the court unless there is clear and unmistakable evidence the parties agreed otherwise.
Mandatory employment arbitration of unwaivable statutory claims must meet minimum requirements and have a modicum of bilaterality; anchors 2020-24.
Under Concepcion the FAA preempts California's Gentry rule against class waivers.

changes.case: Epic Systems v. Lewis; Henry Schein v. Archer & White; Lamps Plus v. Varela; OTO v. Kho
changes.what: Individual-arbitration terms are enforced; a delegation clause binds even if the arbitrability claim is wholly groundless; class arbitration needs affirmative consent; surprise and time pressure inform unconscionability.

name: Illinois tort appeals: Pedrick directed verdicts and duty as policy
description: Illinois tort appeals in a single 1990-94 slice anchored by Pedrick (1967): directed verdicts only when the evidence overwhelmingly favours the movant. Companion rules: duty as a policy question (Kirk 1987, Rowe 1988, Ward 1990, child trespassers in Corcoran and Cope), medical standard of care (Purtill 1986), retaliatory discharge (Kelsay 1978), and a split on the discovery rule for childhood sexual abuse (Tyson, Hammer, E.W.).
history: Dominant rule: Illinois appellate control of jury verdicts in tort cases under Pedrick (1967), which allows a directed verdict or judgment n.o.v. only when all the evidence, viewed most favourably to the opponent, so overwhelmingly favours the movant that no contrary verdict could stand. Pedrick anchors the lineage's only slice, 1990-94. How it changed: no change to the Pedrick standard within the span. Alongside: duty as a question of law shaped by policy (Kirk 1987, also adopting the learned-intermediary doctrine), no broad landlord duty against third-party crime (Rowe 1988), foreseeable distraction from obvious hazards (Ward 1990), and the child-trespasser rules of Corcoran (1978) and Cope (1984); the medical standard of care and expert qualifications (Purtill 1986); and Kelsay (1978) on retaliatory discharge. A second group concerns the discovery rule for childhood sexual abuse: Tyson (Wash. 1986) refused it, Hammer (Wis. 1987) applied it, Meiers-Post (Mich. 1988) required corroboration, and E.W. (Mont. 1988) was superseded by statute in 1989.
rule: An Illinois directed verdict or judgment n.o.v. is proper only when all the evidence, viewed most favourably to the opponent, so overwhelmingly favours the movant that no contrary verdict could stand (Pedrick); duty is a question of law shaped by foreseeability and policy.

changes.what: Set the overwhelming-evidence standard for directed verdicts and judgments n.o.v.; Pedrick anchors the slice.

changes.case: Tyson v. Tyson (Wash.); Hammer v. Hammer (Wis.); Meiers-Post v. Schafer (Mich.); E.W. v. D.C.H. (Mont.)

name: Scientific evidence: Daubert reliability versus the Frye general-acceptance test
description: Admissibility of scientific evidence in 1995-99: Daubert (1993, anchor) replaced Frye's (1923) general-acceptance test in federal court with judicial screening for reliability, reviewed for abuse of discretion (Joiner 1997), while Arizona (Bible 1993), Washington (Cauthron 1993) and California (Leahy 1994) kept Frye, often for DNA evidence. Arizona and Washington capital-case rulings (Gretzler, Atwood, Gentry, Pirtle, Benn) fill out the cluster.
history: Dominant rule: whether and how a court screens expert scientific evidence. The cluster exists only in 1995-99, anchored by Daubert (1993), after three earlier units merge, and it splits in 2000-04. How it developed: Frye (1923) admitted scientific evidence only if generally accepted in its field. Daubert held that Federal Rule of Evidence 702 superseded Frye and made the trial judge a gatekeeper of reliability and relevance; Joiner (1997) set abuse-of-discretion review. State supreme courts divided: Arizona (Bible 1993), Washington (Cauthron 1993) and California (Leahy 1994) kept Frye, largely in DNA cases, holding that Frye asks only about general acceptance of the method, while questions of human error go to weight. name: Washington dissolution property division, 2015-19: just and equitable (Rockwell)
description: Washington dissolution appeals in 2015-19, anchored by Littlefield (1997): broad trial-court discretion over just and equitable property division, with Rockwell (2007) aiming long marriages at roughly equal positions for life, characterization of pensions and disability pay (Muhammad 2005, Brewer 1999), maintenance tied to division (Crosetto 1996), and relocation presumptions (Horner 2004). Findings stand on substantial evidence (Burrill 2002, Rideout 2003).
history: Dominant rule: Littlefield (1997) anchors this single 2015-19 slice of Washington family-law appeals. Trial courts have broad discretion in dissolutions: property is divided justly and equitably, and in long-term marriages the goal is to leave the parties in roughly equal financial positions for the rest of their lives, with any value between the parties' figures available (Rockwell, 2007). Characterization matters: private disability payments are separate property even if premiums were community funds (Brewer, 1999), and pensions accrued before marriage are addressed in Muhammad (2005); maintenance and property division may be considered together (Crosetto, 1996), and maintenance may be paid from business income (Valente, 2014). Review is deferential: findings stand on substantial evidence even if other evidence contradicts them (Burrill, 2002), including documentary evidence (Rideout, 2003), and credibility is not reviewed. Alongside: parenting restrictions need not await actual harm (Chandola, 2014; Katare, 2012 on expert weight), relocation is presumptively allowed (Horner, 2004; Fahey, 2011), and choice of law follows the most significant relationship (Wright, 2013). Littlefield was superseded by statute on other grounds.
rule: In a Washington dissolution the trial court has broad discretion to divide all property justly and equitably under RCW 26.09.080, aiming in long marriages to leave the parties in roughly equal positions for life, and its findings stand if supported by substantial evidence, with credibility left to the trier of fact.

history: Dominant rule: Barker v. Wingo (1972) anchors all four slices: courts balance the length of delay, the reason for it, the defendant's assertion of the right and prejudice, and the burden of bringing a case to trial rests on courts and prosecutors. Marion (1971) limits the right to accused persons, so pre-indictment delay falls outside it. How it changed: Doggett (1992) let an excessive delay establish presumed prejudice even without bad faith. In 2005-09 Texas Court of Criminal Appeals cases lead: Barker governs the state constitution (Zamorano, 2002), delay for good-faith plea negotiations does not count against the state (Munoz, 1999), unchallenged testimony of anxiety counts as prejudice, prejudice arguments must be raised below (Dragoo, 2003), and delay near a year triggers the inquiry (Shaw, 2003); Cantu (2008) required an actual violation before dismissal with prejudice. From 2010-14 the cluster merges with New Mexico criminal appeals, so Rojo (1998), Cunningham (2000) on sufficiency, Tollardo (2012) and Montoya (2015) lead beside Barker, and New Mexico speedy-trial cases apply the same test. Also: Georgia (Ruffin, 2008) and Ohio statutory tolling (Brown, 2002). The cluster splits in 2025-29.
rule: Whether a defendant's speedy-trial right was violated is decided by balancing the length of delay, the reason for it, the defendant's assertion of the right and prejudice to the defendant, with a presumptively prejudicial delay needed to trigger the inquiry (Barker v. Wingo).

changes.what: The Sixth Amendment right attaches only on arrest or formal charge, so pre-indictment delay does not violate it.

name: Illinois criminal appeals of the 1970s: confessions, identification, sentences
description: Illinois criminal appeals in 1975-79 (anchor People v. Williams, 1975, on refusing to answer a jury's factual questions): voluntariness of confessions under the totality test (Prim, 1972; Johnson, 1970, on delay before presentment), sufficiency of a single eyewitness identification (Stringer, 1972) and limits on consecutive sentences for one course of conduct (Whittington, 1970). history: Dominant rule: the ordinary review standards of the Illinois appellate courts in the 1970s, in a single 1975-79 slice anchored by People v. Williams (1975), which upheld a trial court's refusal to answer jurors' factual questions. How it changed: no rule changes appear in the evidence. Confessions are voluntary if made freely without compulsion or inducement (Prim, 1972), and delay before presentment to a magistrate bears on voluntariness without being decisive (Johnson, 1970). A single credible eyewitness with an adequate opportunity to observe is enough to convict (Stringer, 1972), and an identification is not tainted merely because the defendant was the only black man at the defense table (Clark, 1972). Consecutive sentences require independently motivated offenses (Whittington, 1970). Also: comparing offence seriousness by penalty range (Duszkewycz, 1963) and the Pickett and Lilly decisions of 1973-74. The lineage merges into an Illinois criminal-appeals cluster in 1980-84.
rule: Illinois reviewing courts asked whether a confession was made freely and without compulsion, the defendant's will not being overborne (Prim), whether a single credible eyewitness with an adequate opportunity to observe sufficed to convict (Stringer), and whether multiple sentences rested on independently motivated acts (Whittington).

changes.what: Unreasonable delay before presentment to a magistrate is a factor in, not decisive of, the voluntariness of a confession.
A confession is voluntary if made freely and without compulsion or inducement, the defendant's will not being overcome.
The testimony of a single credible identifying witness who had an adequate opportunity to view the offender is sufficient to convict.
Consecutive sentences are barred where the second offense was not independently motivated.

name: Daubert reliability gatekeeping for expert testimony, with Delaware demand futility
description: A 2005-09 cluster anchored by Daubert (1993): trial judges screen expert testimony for reliability under Rule 702, displacing Frye's general-acceptance test (1923), with Joiner (1997) setting abuse-of-discretion review and Kumho Tire (1999) reaching all expert testimony. history: Dominant rule: judicial gatekeeping of expert testimony. Daubert (1993) anchors the only slice, 2005-09, a merger of several 2000-04 units: the Federal Rules of Evidence superseded Frye (1923), so the judge must ensure that expert testimony rests on reliable methods and fits the case. Joiner (1997) makes those rulings reviewable for abuse of discretion and lets courts reject opinions connected to data only by the expert's say-so, and Kumho Tire (1999) extends gatekeeping to all specialized knowledge. State courts weighed adopting Daubert (Avara, 2005, Mississippi). Alongside: Delaware derivative-suit demand futility, where Aronson (1984) asks whether particularized facts raise reasonable doubt about director independence or business judgment, Rales (1993) covers boards that did not make the challenged decision, and Brehm (2000) sets de novo review; the FTCA discretionary-function exception (Varig, 1984; Berkovitz, 1988; Gaubert, 1991) and Boyle's (1988) government-contractor defence; and Mississippi notice-of-claim statutes requiring strict compliance (Easterling, Arceo, 2006). The unit splits three ways in 2010-14.

name: Indiana criminal appeals family, 2010-29: sentence review under Anglemyer and Rule 7(B)
description: Indiana sentence review, 2010-29: a sentence within the statutory range is reviewed for abuse of discretion in finding aggravators and mitigators (Anglemyer, 2007, anchor in most slices), and separately revised under Appellate Rule 7(B) only if the defendant shows it inappropriate given the offense and character (Childress, 2006; Cardwell, 2008, judging the aggregate sentence). Stephenson (2015) requires compelling positive evidence.
history: Dominant rule: Indiana's two-track sentence review. Anglemyer (2007) anchors 2010-14, 2015-19 and 2025-29, and Cardwell (2008) 2020-24. Under Anglemyer a sentence within the range is reviewed for abuse of discretion in the sentencing statement, and a claim that the court overlooked a mitigator needs proof that it was significant and clearly supported. Separately, Appellate Rule 7(B) lets the court revise a sentence that is inappropriate in light of the nature of the offense and the character of the offender, with the burden on the defendant (Childress, 2006), and King (2008) keeps the two claims distinct. How it changed: Cardwell (2008) directed 7(B) review to the aggregate sentence, Davidson (2010) to all penal consequences, and Prewitt (2007) excluded probation-violation sanctions. Stephenson (2015) enters in 2015-19 and declines relief absent compelling positive evidence about the offense and the defendant. Alongside: sufficiency review on probative evidence only (Drane, 2007), criminal history weighing on character (Rutherford, 2007), Richardson (1999) double jeopardy, waiver for lack of cogent argument (Cooper, 2006), the incredible dubiosity rule (Moore, 2015) and juvenile life sentences after Miller (Conley, 2012).

name: New Jersey agency review, partial 2025-29 slice: arbitrary or capricious (Stallworth)
description: New Jersey judicial review of agency action in the partial 2025-29 slice, anchored by Stallworth (2011): a final agency decision stands unless arbitrary, capricious or unreasonable or unsupported by sufficient credible evidence (Taylor 1999, Brady 1997), with de novo review of statutory questions (Lavezzi 2014, Saccone 2014). history: Dominant rule: In re Stallworth (2011) anchors this single partial 2025-29 slice, which split from a 2020-24 New Jersey appellate unit: appellate courts reverse a final agency decision only if it is arbitrary, capricious or unreasonable, violates legislative policy, or lacks sufficient credible evidence in the record. Courts accept supported findings even if they would decide otherwise (Taylor, 1999; Brady, 1997) and defer to expertise (Greenwood, 1992), but agencies have no superior ability on purely legal questions, so statutory interpretation is reviewed de novo (Lavezzi 2014; Saccone 2014). Civil-service discipline is a main application: the Commission reviews discipline de novo (Henry, 1980), consistency is a legislative goal (Herrmann, 2007), and serious infractions can justify removal despite a good record (Carter, 2007); the Department bears the burden on prohibited-act charges against inmates (Figueroa, 2010). Pension claims are the other: Richardson (2007) set the accidental-disability test, and Russo (2011) applied it after Patterson's horror-inducing event standard for mental injuries. Allstars Auto (2018) restates the standard. No rule change appears in the slice.

name: Double jeopardy 1965-84: incorporation (Benton), mistrial, retrial, resentencing
description: The whole Double Jeopardy Clause in its formative period, 1965-84: Green (1957) on implied acquittal anchors 1965-69; Benton (1969, anchor 1970-74) incorporated the Clause, Ashe (1970) added collateral estoppel and Pearce (1969) limited harsher resentencing; Jorn (1971, anchor 1975-79) and Dinitz (1976) set mistrial rules; Burks (1978) barred retrial after evidentiary reversal; Pearce anchors 1980-84 as Blockburger cases rise.

history: Dominant rule: the anchor shifts through the Clause's protections. Green (1957) anchors 1965-69: a conviction for a lesser offense implicitly acquits of the greater, with Tateo (1964) allowing retrial after reversal for trial error and Downum (1963) on mistrials. How it changed: Benton (1969) anchors 1970-74, incorporating the Clause, with Ashe (1970) on collateral estoppel, Pearce (1969) on resentencing, and Waller (1970) on dual sovereignty. Jorn (1971) anchors 1975-79 as mistrial and appeal cases enter: Somerville (1973) and Dinitz (1976) on manifest necessity and defendant-requested mistrials, Perez (1824) on hung juries, and Wilson, Jenkins and Serfass (1975) on government appeals and attachment. Pearce anchors 1980-84 as Blockburger (1931), Burks (1978), Brown v. Ohio (1977), Whalen (1980), Albernaz (1981) and DiFrancesco (1980) lead on same-offense analysis, evidentiary reversals and sentence appeals. The cluster then becomes part of the 1985-89 federal criminal cluster.
rule: The Double Jeopardy Clause, binding the states since Benton (1969), bars retrial after an acquittal or an evidentiary reversal and after a mistrial declared without manifest necessity or the defendant's consent, and bars successive prosecution or cumulative punishment for the same offense under Blockburger, though retrial after reversal for trial error is allowed.

changes.case: United States v. Perez; Blockburger v. United States
changes.what: Retrial after a mistrial is allowed on manifest necessity; offenses are distinct when each requires proof of an element the other does not.

changes.case: Green v. United States; Downum v. United States; United States v. Tateo
changes.what: A conviction on a lesser offense implicitly acquits of the greater; retrial after reversal for trial error is permitted.

changes.case: Benton v. Maryland; North Carolina v. Pearce; Ashe v. Swenson; Waller v. Florida
changes.what: The Clause binds the states, includes collateral estoppel, and treats a municipality and its state as one sovereign; a harsher sentence after retrial needs non-vindictive reasons.

changes.case: United States v. Jorn; Illinois v. Somerville; United States v. Dinitz
changes.what: Abrupt sua sponte mistrials bar retrial, a mistrial for an incurable defect satisfies manifest necessity, and a defendant-requested mistrial generally permits retrial.

changes.case: United States v. Wilson; Serfass v. United States; Burks v. United States
changes.what: The government may appeal a post-verdict ruling for the defendant, jeopardy must attach before the bar applies, and reversal for insufficient evidence bars retrial.

changes.case: Brown v. Ohio; Whalen v. United States; United States v. DiFrancesco; Albernaz v. United States
changes.what: Greater and lesser included offenses are the same offense; multiple punishment turns on legislative intent; government sentence appeals are permitted.

round1.description: Federal double jeopardy law 1970-99: incorporation and collateral estoppel (Benton 1969, Ashe 1970, anchor 1970-74), mistrials and manifest necessity (Jorn 1971, Dinitz 1976), no retrial after acquittal or evidentiary reversal (Burks 1978), resentencing (Pearce 1969), and the Blockburger same-offense test (anchor 1985-89). changes.what: Incorporated double jeopardy, allowed resentencing after a successful appeal subject to due process limits on vindictiveness, and embodied collateral estoppel.

name: Patent claim construction (Phillips, Markman) and § 101 eligibility (Bilski, Mayo)
description: Federal patent law, 2005-14, anchored by Phillips (en banc 2005): claims are construed by the court from the specification and prosecution history (Markman, 1995-96), reviewed de novo (Cybor, 1998). In 2010-14 KSR (2007) on obviousness and Bilski (2010) and Mayo (2012) on abstract ideas and natural laws join, with i4i (2011) on proving invalidity. Judicial estoppel (New Hampshire v. Maine, 2001) rides along.
history: Dominant rule: patent claim construction. Phillips v. AWH (en banc 2005) anchors both slices: claim terms take the meaning a skilled artisan would give them in the context of the specification and prosecution history, extrinsic evidence such as dictionaries is secondary, and importing limitations from the written description is error. Markman (1995, 1996) made construction a question for the court, Vitronics (1996) disfavoured constructions excluding the preferred embodiment, and Cybor (en banc 1998) set de novo review. In 2005-09 judicial estoppel cases ride along, from New Hampshire v. Maine (2001) to bankruptcy nondisclosure (Hamilton, 2001; Cunningham, 2005). How it changed: in 2010-14 validity doctrines enter the core. KSR (2007) rejected the rigid teaching-suggestion-motivation test under the Graham (1966) framework. Bilski (2010) held hedging an abstract idea, drawing on Benson (1972), Flook (1978) and Diehr (1981), and Mayo (2012) held that claims adding nothing significant to a natural law are ineligible. i4i (2011) required clear and convincing proof of invalidity, and Lucent (2009) addressed method-claim damages. The unit splits in 2015-19.
rule: Patent claims are construed as a matter of law by the court, giving terms their ordinary meaning to a skilled artisan read in light of the specification and prosecution history, with extrinsic evidence secondary (Markman, Phillips).

changes.what: Obviousness turns on the scope of the prior art, the differences, the level of skill and objective indicia.

changes.what: Algorithms and abstract ideas are not patentable as such, but a process applying a formula in a practical industrial process can be.

changes.what: Hedging was an unpatentable abstract idea, and claims adding nothing significant to a natural law fall outside § 101.

history: Dominant rule: Watson (1956) anchors every slice: state-law error requires reversal only on a reasonable probability of a better result, while federal constitutional error must be harmless beyond a reasonable doubt (Chapman, 1967). Chiu (2014) barred first-degree premeditated murder liability under the natural and probable consequences doctrine. In 2020-24 the weight shifts to ameliorative change: In re Estrada (1965) applies reduced penalties to nonfinal judgments, Senate Bill 1437 (effective 2019) narrowed murder liability with a resentencing petition (Gentile, 2020; Lewis, 2021; Strong, 2022), and Dueñas (2019) required an ability-to-pay hearing. In the partial 2025-29 slice Crawford leaves and Erlinger (2024), Alleyne (2013), Romero and Carmony lead, shifting toward sentencing.

name: Dividing pensions and military retired pay on divorce: Brown, McCarty
description: Pensions and retirement benefits as divisible marital or community property. Brown (Cal. 1976) overruled French and made nonvested pensions divisible; McCarty (1981) held that federal law preempted division of military retired pay, following Hisquierdo (1979); Congress reversed McCarty in 1982 (USFSPA). Also degrees as property (Graham) and reimbursement support (Hubbard).
history: Dominant rule: retirement benefits earned during marriage are marital or community property divisible on divorce. How it changed: in 1970-74 the early military-pension cases lead (Mora, Busby, LeClert), treating military retired pay as divisible rather than a gratuity. In 1975-79 In re Marriage of Brown (1976) anchors: it overruled French v. French (1941) and held nonvested pension rights to be a divisible contingent interest (followed in Cearley, 1976). In 1980-84 McCarty (1981) anchors: building on Hisquierdo (1979), it held that federal military retirement statutes preempted state division; Congress reversed McCarty with the Uniformed Services Former Spouses' Protection Act (1982). In 1985-89 McCarty still leads with Majauskas (N.Y. 1984) on deferred compensation as marital property. Alongside: whether a professional degree is property (Graham, 1978), reimbursement for a supporting spouse (Hubbard, 1979) and spousal-support modification.
rule: Pension and retirement rights earned during marriage, vested or not, are marital or community property divisible on divorce, except where federal law preempts state division (McCarty for military retired pay, later reversed by statute).

name: Washington termination of parental rights: RCW 13.34.180 and implied unfitness
description: Washington termination of parental rights in 2020-24, anchored by K.M.M. (2016): proof of the RCW 13.34.180(1) elements implies parental unfitness. Services must be offered and tailored (I.M.-M. 2016, H.O. 2016) unless futile (M.R.H. 2008); whether improvement is likely in the near future is judged from the child's view (T.R. 2001). Review is for substantial evidence (Schermer 2007); due-process notice claims may be raised first on appeal (Mares 2014).
history: Dominant rule: K.M.M. (2016) anchors this single 2020-24 slice: when the State proves every element of RCW 13.34.180(1), a finding of parental unfitness is implied, and the court then decides the child's best interests. How it applies: the Department must offer all necessary services, tailored to known impairments (I.M.-M., 2016), and failure to provide bonding services required reversal (H.O., 2016), but services are futile when the parent refuses them (M.R.H., 2008, which also upheld the statute without a less-restrictive-alternative requirement). The near-future question is measured from the child's perspective (T.R., 2001: another year was too long for a six-year-old), special medical needs may be considered while hostility alone is not unfitness (T.L.G., 2005), and long uncertainty supports termination (K.N.J., 2011). Dependency uses a preponderance standard consistent with Mathews (Schermer 2007; T.P. 2015), review is for substantial evidence, a void dependency order invalidates termination (Jenkins, 2011), and a due-process notice claim may be raised first on appeal (Mares, 2014). The slice merged in from a Texas termination unit and splits in 2025-29.
rule: Washington terminates parental rights when the State proves the six RCW 13.34.180(1) elements by clear, cogent and convincing evidence, which implies a finding of parental unfitness, and termination is in the child's best interests; the Department must offer necessary, tailored services unless they would be futile.

changes.what: A further year of services was not a future near enough for a six-year-old.
A child's special medical needs may be weighed; mere hostility to services does not establish unfitness.
Services are futile where the parent refuses to participate; the statute need not require considering guardianship or open adoption.

changes.case: In re Parental Rights to K.M.M.
changes.what: Proof of all RCW 13.34.180(1) elements carries an implied finding of parental unfitness; anchors the slice.

changes.what: Knowledge of a parent's cognitive impairment triggers a duty to tailor services; failure to offer bonding services required reversal.

name: Habeas appeals: certificates of appealability and jurisdictional deadlines
description: A 2005-09 cluster on getting a habeas case to the court of appeals: a certificate of appealability needs a showing that reasonable jurists could debate the ruling (Slack, 2000; Miller-El, 2003), Rule 60(b) motions are screened as successive petitions (Winestock, 2003; Reid, 2004), and statutory appeal deadlines are jurisdictional (Bowles, 2007) while rule-based limits are claim-processing rules (Kontrick, 2004; Eberhart, 2005).
history: Dominant rule: the threshold requirements for federal habeas appeals. Rose (2001) anchors the only slice, 2005-09, a split from the habeas ineffective-assistance lineage, with Slack (2000) and Miller-El (2003) leading: a certificate of appealability requires a substantial showing that reasonable jurists could debate the constitutional claim or the procedural ruling. Winestock (4th Cir. 2003) requires district courts to treat reconsideration motions that are really successive applications as such, and Reid v. Angelone (2004) requires a COA to appeal a Rule 60(b) denial. How it changed: the Supreme Court sorted time limits into jurisdictional and claim-processing rules. Kontrick (2004) and Eberhart (2005) held rule-based limits forfeitable, and Bowles (2007) held the statutory deadline for a civil notice of appeal jurisdictional, following Browder (1978) and Robinson (1960). Pace (2005) denied AEDPA tolling to untimely state petitions, and Irwin (1991) frames equitable tolling. Also: Thomas v. Arn (1985) lets circuits require objections to a magistrate's report. Rose (4th Cir. 2001) on a state court's wrong prejudice standard under Strickland anchors.
rule: A habeas petitioner needs a certificate of appealability, granted on a substantial showing that reasonable jurists could debate the constitutional claim or the procedural ruling (Slack, Miller-El), and statutory deadlines for appeal are jurisdictional while court-made time limits are claim-processing rules (Bowles, Eberhart).

name: Equal protection: school desegregation (Brown) to one person, one vote
description: Equal protection in the Warren Court. Sweatt (1950) anchors the graduate-school cases; Brown (1954, 1955) anchors 1955-64, with Shelley (1948), Cooper v. Aaron (1958) and Goss (1963) enforcing desegregation; then Baker v. Carr (1962) and Reynolds v. Sims (1964, anchor 1965-69) required both legislative houses to be apportioned by population.
history: Dominant rule: the Equal Protection Clause bars state-imposed racial classifications and, from 1964, unequal weighting of votes. Carr (1962) made it justiciable, and Reynolds v. Sims (1964) with Lucas, Tawes, Lomenzo, Davis and Roman (1964) required population-based districts for both houses. history: Dominant rule: speech, assembly and association are protected against vague, overbroad or standardless restrictions, with narrowly defined unprotected categories and reasonable time, place and manner limits. name: Washington summary-judgment burden, 2015-19 (Young v. Key Pharmaceuticals)
description: Washington civil appeals in 2015-19 centred on the summary-judgment burden: under Young v. Key Pharmaceuticals (1989, anchor) a defendant movant can shift the burden by showing the plaintiff lacks evidence on an element, and the nonmovant must then set out specific facts (Ranger Insurance 2008). Applied to negligence duty and causation (Hertog 1999, Folsom 1998, Hartley 1985), CPA claims (Hangman Ridge 1986) and Deeds of Trust Act claims (Bain 2012, Frias 2014).
history: Dominant rule: Young v. Key Pharmaceuticals (1989) anchors this single 2015-19 slice: a summary-judgment movant may meet its initial burden by pointing out that the plaintiff cannot establish an element, and the inquiry then shifts to the plaintiff, who must set forth specific facts rebutting the motion (Ranger Insurance, 2008); review is de novo (Jones, 2002), and negligence and proximate cause are generally not susceptible to summary judgment (Owen, 2005). The cases test elements of particular claims: duty, breach, injury and proximate cause in negligence, with cause in fact and legal causation (Hartley, 1985); special-relationship duties under Restatement § 319 (Hertog, 1999) but no franchisor duty without control (Folsom, 1998); CPA causation and per se violations (Hangman Ridge, 1986); and Deeds of Trust Act claims, where Bain (2012) bars contracting around the beneficiary definition and Frias (2014) denies damages absent a completed sale. Also: judicial estoppel (New Hampshire v. Maine, 2001), Burnet factors for excluding witnesses (Keck, 2015), PRA exemption logs (Sanders, 2010) and WLAD following Title VII (Scrivener, 2014).

name: Fourth Amendment from Boyd and Weeks to Terry: probable cause and exclusion
description: Fourth Amendment reasonableness: probable cause for warrantless searches, reasonable suspicion for Terry stops (1968, the anchor from 1975-79), and suppression of fruits (Weeks 1914, Mapp 1961, Wong Sun). Gates (1983) replaced Aguilar-Spinelli with totality of the circumstances; Leon (1984) added good faith; Ornelas (1996) and Guzman (1997) set de novo review. Miranda is a constant companion.

The lineage runs back to Boyd and Weeks and passes through Mapp; Miranda appears as a frequent companion in suppression litigation.

history: Dominant rule: searches and seizures must be reasonable; a warrantless search needs probable cause and an exception, a brief stop needs reasonable suspicion, and unlawfully obtained evidence and its fruits are suppressed. How it changed: before 1915 the lineage is Boyd and Counselman on compelled papers and self-incrimination. Weeks (1914) anchors 1920-29 and created the federal exclusionary rule; Carroll (1925) allowed vehicle searches on probable cause and anchors 1930-34. Rabinowitz (1950) leads the 1950s until Chimel (1969) narrowed searches incident to arrest. Mapp (1961) anchors 1960-64 and extended exclusion to the states. Aguilar (1964) anchors 1970-74; from 1975-79 Terry (1968) anchors every slice. Gates (1983) replaced the Aguilar-Spinelli test with totality of the circumstances, Leon (1984) added the good-faith exception, and Ornelas (1996) with Texas's Guzman (1997) set de novo review of probable cause and reasonable suspicion. Rodriguez (2015) limited prolonged traffic stops. Also: Wong Sun fruits, Schneckloth consent, Royer and Mendenhall seizures, and Miranda in suppression practice.
rule: A search or seizure must be reasonable: warrantless searches need probable cause and an exception, a brief stop needs reasonable suspicion (Terry), and evidence obtained in violation is excluded subject to limits such as good faith.

changes.what: Compelled production of papers and testimony tied the Fourth and Fifth Amendments; immunity must be as broad as the privilege.

Totality-of-the-circumstances test for probable cause from informants' tips replaced the Aguilar-Spinelli two-prong test.

changes.what: Reasonable suspicion and probable cause are reviewed de novo, with deference to historical facts and credibility findings.

name: New York custody and relocation (Eschbach, Daghir); Tennessee drift 2000-04
description: Custody cluster, 1975-2004, sharing New York's best-interests test: the child's interests on the totality of circumstances control over any agreement (Eschbach 1982, anchor 1990-99; Friederwitzer 1982); a parent beats a nonparent absent extraordinary circumstances (Bennett 1976); Strahl, Weiss and Daghir (1979-82) limited relocation. Tennessee divorce cases join in 1995-99, and Tennessee summary judgment (Byrd 1993) anchors 2000-04.
history: Dominant rule: the best-interests standard in New York custody and relocation disputes. How it changed: in 1975-79 Obey (1975) anchors with Bennett v. Jeffreys (1976), which limited nonparent custody to extraordinary circumstances. In 1980-84 Strahl (1979) anchors, and Weiss (1981) and Daghir (1981-82) restrict a custodial parent's relocation that would cut off visitation. Daghir anchors 1985-89, and Eschbach (1982) anchors 1990-94 and 1995-99: custody turns on the totality of the circumstances and no agreement binds the court, while Friederwitzer (1982) allows modification without proof of unfitness. In 1995-99 Tennessee divorce cases merge in, on separate versus marital property (Brown, 1994; Batson, 1988) and retirement benefits (Cohen, 1996). In 2000-04 the anchor shifts to Tennessee civil law: Byrd v. Hall (1993) on the summary-judgment burden, Carvell (1995) and Hunter (1997) on discovery-rule accrual, McCall (1995) and Staples (2000) on duty, and Robinson (1997) on negligent misrepresentation.

Jeffreys).

name: Batson challenges: three-step test for race-based peremptory strikes
description: Batson (1986) anchors this 2020-24 cluster: race-based peremptory strikes violate equal protection, tested in three steps. Johnson v. California (2005) lowered the prima facie bar; Purkett (1995) and Hernandez (1991) shaped the race-neutral step; Miller-El (2005), Snyder (2008), Foster (2016) and Flowers (2019) used comparative analysis and strike history to find pretext. A smaller strand covers Rule 11 sanctions and Seventh Circuit procedure.
history: Dominant rule: Batson v. Kentucky (1986) anchors this single 2020-24 slice: the Equal Protection Clause forbids peremptory strikes based on race. The test runs in three steps. Johnson v. California (2005) requires at step one only evidence sufficient to permit an inference of discrimination; Hernandez (1991) treats the prima facie question as moot once the prosecutor explains, and considers disparate impact as evidence of intent; Purkett (1995) deems a reason race neutral unless discrimination inheres in it. At step three courts look for pretext: Miller-El (2005) found the state court's finding rebutted by clear and convincing evidence using side-by-side juror comparisons, Snyder (2008) rejected a pretextual reason, Foster (2016) relied on the prosecution's notes, and Flowers (2019) weighed the prosecutor's history of strikes and allowed any type of evidence. How it changed: the doctrine is stable; the later cases apply it more searchingly. Also: a Seventh Circuit procedural strand on Rule 11 and sanctions (Yagman 1986, Orlett 1992, Gravel 1990), conflict waivers (Wheat 1988), summary-judgment credibility (Lisle 2019) and sentencing explanation (Patel 2019, Solomon 2018).
rule: A peremptory strike based on race violates equal protection; the objector makes a prima facie case by evidence permitting an inference of discrimination, the prosecutor offers a race-neutral reason, and the court decides whether purposeful discrimination is proved, considering pretext, comparative juror analysis and the whole history of strikes.

changes.what: Race-based peremptory strikes violate the Equal Protection Clause; anchors the slice.

changes.case: Hernandez v. New York; Purkett v. Elem
changes.what: Once a race-neutral reason is offered the prima facie step is moot; a reason is race neutral unless discriminatory intent is inherent in it.

changes.what: Step one needs only evidence permitting an inference of discrimination; side-by-side comparison of jurors can show pretext.

changes.case: Snyder v. Louisiana; Foster v. Chatman; Flowers v. Mississippi

name: Illinois appeals: Foutch record rule, parental unfitness, pretrial detention
description: Illinois appellate cases in 2020-24, anchored by Foutch (1984): an appellant must supply a complete record, or the trial court is presumed correct. The slice mixes juvenile termination appeals (unfitness on one section 1(D) ground, reasonable efforts and progress: C.N. 2001, D.T. 2004, Daphnie E. 2006, J.L. 2010) with 2023 pretrial-detention appeals after Rowe v. Raoul (Stock, Inman, Trottier).
history: Dominant rule: Foutch v. O'Bryant (1984) anchors this single 2020-24 slice: the appellant bears the burden of a complete record, and without one the reviewing court presumes the trial court acted lawfully. The largest strand is juvenile termination: a finding of unfitness stands on any one statutory ground of section 1(D) (Daphnie E., 2006), reasonable efforts and reasonable progress are independent grounds (C.N., 2001), progress is not mere service-plan compliance, incarceration does not excuse it (J.L., 2010), and once unfitness is found the focus shifts to the child's best interests (D.T., 2004, which also requires a new hearing when the wrong standard of proof was used). Neglect concerns the child, not the parents (Arthur H., 2004), and neglect of one child may bear on fitness as to another (D.F., 2002). How it changed: in 2023 the pretrial-release reform upheld in Rowe v. Raoul produced detention appeals: the State must prove by clear and convincing evidence that a defendant poses a real and present threat (Stock), and Rule 604(h) does not make the court the appellant's advocate (Inman). Also: de novo review of summary judgment and construing insurance ambiguities for the insured (Outboard Marine, 1992).
rule: An Illinois appellant must supply a complete record, and doubts from an incomplete record are resolved against him (Foutch); in termination cases one proven statutory ground of unfitness under section 1(D) of the Adoption Act suffices before the focus shifts to the child's best interests.

changes.what: The appellant must present a complete record; absent one, the reviewing court presumes the trial court's order was lawful and factually supported. Anchors the slice.

name: Relaxed causation: loss of chance (Hamil, Herskovits) and DES market share (Sindell)
description: Relaxed causation in tort, a single 1990-94 slice anchored by Hamil (1978): loss of chance lets a jury find causation where malpractice destroyed a substantial chance of recovery (Herskovits 1983, Aasheim 1985, McKellips 1987), against Cooper's (1971) more-likely-than-not rule. DES market-share liability (Sindell 1980, Martin 1984, Hymowitz 1989) and strict products liability (Berkebile 1975, Azzarello 1978) appear alongside.
history: Dominant rule: when a plaintiff may reach the jury on causation without traditional but-for proof. Hamil v. Bashline (1978) anchors the lineage's only slice, 1990-94, which splits three ways in 1995-99. How it changed: loss of chance spread through the 1980s: Herskovits (1983) allowed recovery for a reduced chance of survival below 50%, Aasheim (1985) and DeBurkarte (1986) left the substantial-factor question to the jury, and McKellips (1987) adopted a substantial-chance approach, while Cooper (1971) had required survival odds above 50% and Kallenberg (1974) let a 20-40% chance reach the jury. A parallel line relaxed product identification for DES: Sindell (1980) created market-share liability, Martin (1984) chose an alternative-liability variant, Hymowitz (1989) adopted a national market share without exculpation, and Brown (1988) refused it for fraud and warranty. Alongside: strict products liability and warnings (Berkebile 1975; Azzarello 1978, no 'unreasonably dangerous' in instructions), hospital transfer duties (Thompson 1984), and assumption of risk (Suter 1979).
rule: Where a defendant's negligence destroys a substantial chance of recovery, causation may go to the jury without proof that the chance exceeded 50% (loss of chance), and DES plaintiffs who cannot identify the manufacturer may recover in proportion to market share (Sindell, Hymowitz).

history: Dominant rule: a manufacturer is strictly liable in tort for personal injury caused by a defective product it put on the market (Greenman, 1963, the 1970-74 anchor; Suvada, 1965), but tort does not reach purely economic loss, which belongs to warranty (Seely, 1965, the 1980-84 anchor; Moorman, 1982). round1.name: Federal sentencing: mandatory Guidelines to Apprendi, Booker and Gall review
round1.description: Federal criminal sentencing whose anchor moves with doctrine: Diaz-Villafane (1989) in 1990-94, Olano (1993) in 1995-99, Apprendi (2000) in 2000-04, Booker (2005) in 2005-09, and Gall (2007) from 2010-14 on. Booker made the Guidelines advisory; Gall, Rita and Kimbrough set review. Also recidivist enhancements and the categorical approach (Almendarez-Torres, Taylor, Shepard, Mathis, Johnson 2015) and plain error (Puckett 2009).
round1.history: Dominant rule: the cluster tracks federal sentencing review, and its anchor doctrine shifts. In 1990-94 Diaz-Villafane (1st Cir. 1989) anchors Guidelines review, with McMillan (1986) on sentencing factors and Zannino (1990) on waived arguments, after merging with a Brady and confrontation unit. How it changed: Olano (1993) anchors 1995-99, with Koon (1996) on departures, Gaudin (1995) on jury findings and Bailey (1995) on § 924(c). round1.rule: The anchor rule shifts: under the mandatory Guidelines (1990s), departures were reviewed deferentially and forfeited errors under Olano's plain-error test; from 2000 facts raising the statutory maximum must go to a jury (Apprendi); from 2005 the Guidelines are advisory and sentences are reviewed for procedural and substantive reasonableness under an abuse-of-discretion standard (Booker, Gall).
