name: Florida criminal appeals: DiGuilio harmless error and habitual-offender sentencing
description: Florida criminal appeals, 1990-99: DiGuilio (1986) harmless-error review anchors 1990-94, alongside guidelines departures (Lambert 1989, Ree 1990) and the habitual-offender statute upheld in King, Barber and Arnold (1990). Callaway (1995) anchors 1995-99, applying Hale (1993, no consecutive habitual terms for one episode) retroactively; Gray (1995) abolished attempted felony murder. Also capital aggravators (Rogers 1987 on CCP, Campbell 1990 on mitigation).
history: Dominant rule: Florida's harmless-error test (DiGuilio, 1986), under which the State must show beyond a reasonable doubt that an error did not contribute to the verdict, applied together with the sentencing rules most often litigated on appeal. DiGuilio anchors 1990-94 with Rogers (1987, cold-calculated-premeditated requires a careful plan), Lambert (1989, no departure for probation-violation factors) and Ree (1990, contemporaneous written departure reasons); King, Barber and Arnold (1990) upheld the 1988 habitual-felony-offender act. How it changed: Hale (1993) barred consecutive habitual-offender sentences for a single episode, and Callaway (1995) enters and anchors 1995-99, making Hale retroactive under Witt. Davis (1995) and Mancino (1998) define when sentences can be corrected under rule 3.800(a); Gray (1995) abolished attempted felony murder, a ruling later superseded by statute. Also: Campbell (1990) on weighing mitigation, Holton (1991) on the CCP aggravator, Law (1989) on circumstantial evidence, and Shaughnessy (1954) on agencies following their own rules.
rule: A Florida conviction stands despite error only if the State shows beyond a reasonable doubt that the error did not contribute to the verdict (DiGuilio); sentencing errors such as consecutive habitual-offender terms for a single episode (Hale) are corrected under the rules on illegal sentences and retroactivity.

changes.what: Harmless error requires the State to show beyond a reasonable doubt that the error did not contribute to the verdict; DiGuilio leads both slices.

changes.case: Lambert v. State; Ree v. State; King; Barber; Arnold
changes.what: Probation-violation factors cannot justify a guidelines departure, written departure reasons are required, and the rewritten habitual-offender act survives equal-protection, due-process and burden-shifting challenges.
Consecutive habitual-offender sentences for crimes from a single criminal episode are not authorised by statute.
Hale applies retroactively under the Witt standard; Callaway anchors 1995-99.

name: Federal appellate jurisdiction: final-judgment rule and Cohen collateral orders
description: Lineage whose anchor shifts: Erie (1938) and the law applied in diversity (1960-64), then interest-analysis choice of law under Babcock (1963) in 1965-69. From 1970-89 Cohen (1949) anchors: appeals lie only from final decisions (Catlin, Cobbledick), except collateral orders, with Abney (1977) allowing double-jeopardy appeals and Livesay (1978) and Firestone (1981) refusing class-certification and disqualification appeals. Will (1967) limits mandamus.

previous.description: Appealability: the final-judgment rule (Catlin, Cobbledick), the collateral-order doctrine (Cohen), class-certification orders (Livesay, Eisen), mandamus (Will) and interlocutory criminal appeals (Abney).

history: Dominant rule: the anchor doctrine changes. 1960-64: Erie (1938) and its successors on the law applied in diversity (Guaranty Trust 1945, Byrd 1958), with intergovernmental tax immunity cases (Detroit, Murray, Muskegon 1958). 1965-69: Babcock (1963) anchors as state courts replace lex loci delicti with interest analysis (Griffith 1964, Wilcox 1965, Reich 1967) and refuse foreign damage caps (Kilberg 1961). How it changed: from 1970-74 Cohen (1949) anchors every slice. Finality under § 1291 means an order that ends the litigation on the merits (Catlin 1945), and grand-jury subpoena orders are reviewed only through contempt (Cobbledick 1940, Ryan 1971), while IRS summons enforcement follows Powell (1964) and Donaldson (1971). Will (1967) restricts mandamus. Eisen (1974) and FOIA cases (Mink, Sears, Vaughn) lead in 1975-79. In 1980-84 Abney (1977) lets defendants appeal double-jeopardy denials, while Livesay (1978) rejects the death-knell doctrine for class certification and Firestone (1981) bars appeal of orders refusing to disqualify counsel. In 1985-89 press-access cases join (Richmond Newspapers 1980, Globe 1982, Press-Enterprise 1984, 1986), before the cluster splits into arbitration and fees units.
rule: From 1970 the anchor rule is that federal courts of appeals review only final decisions under § 1291, ones that end the litigation on the merits (Catlin), save for the small class of collateral orders that conclusively decide an important question separate from the merits and are effectively unreviewable after judgment (Cohen); in 1960-69 the lineage instead centred on the law a federal court applies (Erie) and interest-analysis choice of law (Babcock).

changes.case: Erie R. Co. v. Tompkins; Guaranty Trust v. York; Byrd v. Blue Ridge; Hanna v. Plumer
changes.what: Federal courts in diversity apply state substantive law, subject to countervailing federal interests (Byrd) and the Federal Rules (Hanna).

changes.case: Babcock v. Jackson (N.Y.); Griffith v. United Air Lines (Pa.); Reich v. Purcell (Cal.)
changes.what: State courts abandoned lex loci delicti for interest analysis or the most-significant-relationship approach.

changes.case: Cobbledick v. United States; United States v. Ryan
changes.what: Orders denying motions to quash subpoenas are not final; review comes through contempt.

changes.case: Cohen v. Beneficial Industrial Loan Corp.
changes.what: The collateral-order doctrine for decisions finally resolving claims separable from the merits.

changes.case: Abney v. United States; Coopers & Lybrand v. Livesay; Firestone Tire v. Risjord
changes.what: Denials of double-jeopardy claims are immediately appealable, but class-certification orders and orders refusing to disqualify counsel are not collateral orders.

name: Ohio criminal appeals 2010-29: Thompkins evidence review, plain error, merger
description: The family of Ohio criminal-appeal standards, 2010-29, anchored by Thompkins (1997): sufficiency (Jenks 1991) and manifest weight (Martin 1983) are distinct tests, alongside plain error (Long 1978; Barnes 2002), ineffectiveness (Bradley 1989) and abuse of discretion (Blakemore 1983). Changes: allied-offense merger reworked by Johnson (2010) and Ruff (2015); Eastley (2012) carried weight review to civil cases; Marcum (2016) on felony sentences.
history: Dominant rule: the two Ohio standards for reviewing the evidence. Thompkins (1997) anchors every slice from 2010-14 to 2025-29: sufficiency is a question of law, judged by whether any rational juror viewing the evidence for the state could find the elements (Jenks, 1991, which abandoned the reasonable-theory-of-innocence rule for circumstantial evidence), while manifest weight lets the court act as a thirteenth juror and reverse only where the jury clearly lost its way and created a manifest miscarriage of justice (Martin, 1983); a sufficiency reversal bars retrial but a weight reversal does not (Tibbs, 1982). DeHass (1967) leaves credibility to the factfinder. Alongside: plain error under Crim.R. 52(B) (Long, 1978; Barnes, 2002; Rogers, 2015), ineffective assistance (Bradley, 1989), abuse of discretion as an unreasonable, arbitrary or unconscionable decision (Blakemore, 1983) and Seasons Coal (1984) on deference to findings. How it changed: Johnson (2010) and then Ruff (2015) reworked allied-offense merger under R.C. 2941.25, Eastley (2012) carried the weight standard to civil appeals, and Marcum (2016) set felony-sentence review. The cluster merged in from a habeas lineage in 2010-14.
rule: Ohio appellate courts test sufficiency by asking whether, viewing the evidence for the prosecution, any rational trier of fact could find the elements proved beyond a reasonable doubt (Jenks), and separately review manifest weight as a thirteenth juror, reversing only where the jury clearly lost its way (Thompkins, Martin).

changes.what: Weight and credibility are primarily for the trier of fact.

changes.case: State v. Long; State v. Barnes
changes.what: Unobjected-to error is reviewed only for plain error: an obvious deviation from a legal rule that affected the outcome, noticed only to prevent a manifest miscarriage of justice.
On manifest weight the court weighs the evidence and credibility and reverses only where the jury clearly lost its way.
Ineffective assistance requires deficient performance and a reasonable probability of a different outcome.
Adopted the Jackson v. Virginia sufficiency test and abandoned the rule that circumstantial evidence must exclude every reasonable theory of innocence.
Sufficiency and manifest weight are distinct; a weight reversal does not bar retrial, but a sufficiency reversal does.

changes.case: State v. Johnson; State v. Ruff
changes.what: Allied offenses under R.C. 2941.25 are judged by the defendant's conduct, and offenses with separate victims or separate harm do not merge.
The criminal manifest-weight standard applies in civil cases.

name: Maritime tort remedies against the vessel: Sieracki unseaworthiness, Ryan indemnity
description: Tort remedies of injured longshoremen against the vessel, not compensation coverage: Sieracki (1946) gave them the seaman's unseaworthiness claim, and Ryan (1956), Nacirema (1958), Crumady (1959) and Italia (1964) let vessels recover over from stevedores; Moragne (1970) added maritime wrongful death. After the 1972 LHWCA amendments ended Sieracki and Ryan, the anchor moves to Caputo (1977), Scindia (1981) and admiralty jurisdiction (Executive Jet, Foremost).
history: Dominant rule: through 1979 the vessel owes longshoremen doing a seaman's work the absolute warranty of seaworthiness (Sieracki, 1946, anchoring 1950-54 and 1970-74), and the vessel may recover from the stevedore for breach of its warranty of workmanlike performance (Ryan, 1956, anchoring 1965-69 and 1975-79). How it changed: Hawn (1953, anchor 1955-59) applied admiralty law in any forum, and Petterson (1954) held defective stevedore equipment makes a ship unseaworthy. Crumady (1959) anchors 1960-64, and Nacirema (1958), Waterman (1960) and Italia (1964) widened indemnity; Gutierrez (1963) reached injuries ashore caused by ship's gear. Moragne (1970) created a maritime wrongful-death action. The anchor then shifts: Caputo (1977) anchors 1980-84 on LHWCA coverage after the 1972 amendments ended Sieracki and Ryan for covered workers, and Executive Jet (1972) anchors 1985-89 with Foremost (1982) on admiralty tort jurisdiction and Scindia (1981) on vessel negligence duties. Also: Pfeifer (1983) and Liepelt (1980) on damages.
rule: Until the 1972 LHWCA amendments, a longshoreman doing a seaman's work could recover from the vessel for unseaworthiness (Sieracki), and the vessel could recover over from the stevedore for breach of its implied warranty of workmanlike performance (Ryan).

changes.what: State workers' compensation could not reach a longshoreman's injury on navigable waters.

changes.case: Seas Shipping Co. v. Sieracki; Pope & Talbot v. Hawn
changes.what: The warranty of seaworthiness extends to longshoremen doing a seaman's work, and admiralty law governs such claims in any forum.

changes.case: Ryan Stevedoring v. Pan-Atlantic; Weyerhaeuser v. Nacirema; Crumady v. The Joachim Hendrik Fisser; Italia Societa v. Oregon Stevedoring
changes.what: The vessel may obtain indemnity from the stevedore for breach of its implied warranty of workmanlike performance, even without stevedore negligence.
General maritime law supplies a wrongful-death action for breach of maritime duties.

changes.case: Executive Jet Aviation v. City of Cleveland
changes.what: Admiralty tort jurisdiction requires a significant relationship to traditional maritime activity, not location alone.

changes.case: 1972 LHWCA amendments (33 U.S.C. § 905(b)); Northeast Marine Terminal v. Caputo; Scindia Steam Navigation v. De Los Santos
changes.what: Longshoremen lost the unseaworthiness and indemnity scheme, gained broader LHWCA coverage, and may sue vessels only for negligence under Scindia's duties.

phases.rule: longshoremen's unseaworthiness claims and stevedore indemnity (Sieracki, Ryan)
admiralty tort jurisdiction and the amended LHWCA (Executive Jet, Foremost, Scindia, Caputo)

name: Alabama civil appeals: substantial evidence (West) and State-agent immunity (Cranman)
description: Alabama civil appeals, 2010-19. West (1989) anchors 2010-14: summary judgment turns on substantial evidence after a prima facie showing (Dow, 2004), with deference to ore tenus findings in divorce and property cases (Philpot, 2002; Fadalla, 2005; Parrish, 1993). In 2015-19 Davis (1992) anchors as State immunity and State-agent immunity under Cranman and Butts (2000) join the core.
history: Dominant rule: Alabama civil appellate review, built on West (1989): the nonmovant must answer a properly supported summary-judgment motion with substantial evidence, evidence from which fair-minded persons could reasonably infer the fact. How it changed: in 2010-14 West anchors a unit merged from a personal-jurisdiction lineage and another 2005-09 unit, with Philpot (2002), Fadalla (2005, equitable reformation of deeds), Ex parte Perkins (1994) and Parks (2007) leading: ore tenus findings are presumed correct and not reweighed (Hall, 1986; Stone, 2009), undisputed facts get de novo review (Skelton, 1996), property division and alimony are reviewed together (Parrish, 1993), and the court will not research arguments for a party (Dykes, 1994; Jimmy Day Plumbing, 2007). In 2015-19 Davis (1992) anchors and immunity enters: state agencies are immune (Davis; Atkinson, 2007, holding sovereign immunity jurisdictional and unwaivable), and Butts (2000) adopted Cranman's State-agent immunity test, applied to coaches in Nall (2003). Ex parte BOC Group (2001) and Integon (1995) concern mandamus review. The unit splits three ways in 2020-24.
rule: An Alabama summary-judgment movant must make a prima facie showing of no genuine issue, after which the nonmovant must present substantial evidence, meaning evidence of such weight and quality that fair-minded persons could reasonably infer the fact (West); State agents are immune for discretionary functions unless they act willfully, maliciously, fraudulently, in bad faith or beyond their authority (Cranman, Butts).

changes.what: Defined substantial evidence as evidence of such weight and quality that fair-minded persons could reasonably infer the fact to be proved.

changes.case: Davis v. Alabama Dep't of Human Resources (Ala. Civ. App.)
changes.what: The Department of Human Resources is immune from civil liability as a state agency.
The appellate court will not do a party's legal research or make arguments for it.

changes.what: Butts adopted the Cranman plurality's test: State agents are immune for listed discretionary functions unless acting willfully, maliciously, fraudulently, in bad faith or beyond authority.
Public-school coaches exercising judgment were immune as State agents.

changes.case: Dow v. Alabama Democratic Party; Jimmy Day Plumbing & Heating v. Smith
changes.what: The movant must first make a prima facie showing; briefs lacking the citations Rule 28(a)(10) requires waive the argument.

phases.rule: summary judgment on substantial evidence and ore tenus deference (West, Philpot, Fadalla)
State and State-agent immunity (Davis, Cranman, Butts)

history: Dominant rule: forfeiture and plain error in Illinois criminal appeals. Enoch (1988) anchors 1995-99 and 2005-09: an issue is preserved only by a trial objection plus a written post-trial motion. Albanese (1984) adopted Strickland and Collins (1985) Jackson v. Virginia. In 2000-04 the anchor is Coleman (1998) on postconviction review, with West, Evans, Buss and Hobley (1998, freestanding actual innocence). How it changed: Herron (2005) enters in 2005-09 and anchors 2010-14. It rejected Olano's four-part test and set two prongs: clear error where the evidence is closely balanced, or clear error so serious it threatened the trial's integrity. Piatkowski (2007) puts the burden of prejudice on the defendant under the first prong and presumes it under the second; Thompson (2010) held a Rule 431(b) error is not automatically second-prong error. The dominant topic shifts in 2015-19, when Miller (2012) anchors and Roper (2005), Graham (2010) and Montgomery (2016) enter on Eighth Amendment limits on juvenile sentences. In 2020-24 those leave and the anchor is In re D.T. (2004) with Foutch (1984) on the appellant's duty to supply a record, which is drift.
rule: To preserve an issue an Illinois defendant must both object at trial and raise it in a written post-trial motion (Enoch); forfeited errors are reviewed only as plain error, when the evidence is closely balanced or the error is so serious it undermined the fairness of the trial (Herron, Piatkowski).

changes.what: Illinois adopted Strickland's two-part ineffectiveness test (Albanese) and Jackson v. Virginia's sufficiency standard (Collins).
Preservation requires a trial objection and a written post-trial motion; without a motion, review is limited to constitutional issues raised at trial, sufficiency and plain error.

Overton Park (1971) anchors 1975-84 with Abbott Laboratories (1967), Data Processing (1970) and State Farm (1983); Chevron (1984) anchors from 1985, as standing tightens (Warth 1975, Allen 1984, Lujan 1992) and asylum review grows (Cardoza-Fonseca 1987, Elias-Zacarias 1992).

history: Dominant rule: the anchor shifts with the agencies before the courts. 1960-69: Federal Power Commission gas regulation, with Atlantic Refining (1959) as anchor, Hope (1944) on end-result rate review, Mobile-Sierra (1956) on contracts, and NBC (1943) and Sanders Bros. (1940) on licensing and competitor standing. How it changed: Permian Basin (1968) anchors 1970-74, as Abbott Laboratories (1967), Data Processing v. Camp (1970), Barlow (1970) and Sierra Club v. Morton (1972) open review and define standing. Overton Park (1971) anchors 1975-84: review is on the record and asks whether the decision was arbitrary, with Udall (1965) deference, Chenery (1947), Vermont Yankee (1978) and State Farm (1983) on reasoned explanation. Warth (1975) and Simon (1976) tighten standing. Chevron (1984) anchors 1985-99 with its two-step deference, while Valley Forge (1982) and Allen (1984) require traceable, redressable injury and Lujan (1992) concrete injury. From 1990 immigration cases join: Cardoza-Fonseca (1987) sets a lower asylum standard, and Elias-Zacarias (1992) requires evidence compelling reversal and proof of the persecutor's motive. Landgraf (1994) on retroactivity enters in 1995-99 before the cluster splits into immigration and public-law units.
rule: Agency action is reviewable unless Congress precludes it (Abbott Laboratories), on the administrative record for arbitrariness and reasoned explanation (Overton Park, State Farm, Chenery), with deference to reasonable agency readings of ambiguous statutes (Chevron); only a litigant with an injury fairly traceable to the challenged action and redressable by the court may sue (Warth, Allen, Lujan).

changes.case: Warth v. Seldin; Simon v. EKWRO; Valley Forge; Allen v. Wright

name: Federal criminal appeals 1975-84: Glasser sufficiency review and Brady disclosure
description: Federal criminal appeals of 1975-84, centred on sufficiency and disclosure: Glasser's (1942) substantial-evidence review anchors both slices, with Kotteakos (1946) for harmless error; Brady (1963), Giglio (1972) and Agurs (1976) govern disclosure. Confrontation (Bruton 1968, Davis 1974, Roberts 1980) rides along. In 1980-84 Bell (5th Cir. en banc 1982) on circumstantial evidence and Turkette (1981) on RICO enter.

history: Dominant rule: the trial-error standards of federal criminal appeals. Glasser (1942) anchors 1975-79 and 1980-84: a verdict must be sustained if substantial evidence, taken most favourably to the Government, supports it. Kotteakos (1946) supplies the substantial-and-injurious-effect harmless-error test. How it changed: on disclosure, Brady (1963) and Giglio (1972, impeachment evidence) were extended by Agurs (1976) to evidence not requested, which enters the leading cases in 1980-84; Napue (1959) governs false testimony. On confrontation, Bruton (1968) leads in 1975-79; Davis (1974) on cross-examination for bias leads in 1980-84, when Roberts (1980) enters with its reliability test for hearsay. Also in 1980-84: the Fifth Circuit en banc in Bell (1982) on circumstantial evidence, RICO under Turkette (1981), and coconspirator statements under James (1979). The cluster splits in 1985-89 into federal Brady and RICO units and a Connecticut criminal unit.
rule: A federal jury verdict stands if substantial evidence, viewed most favourably to the Government, supports it (Glasser), subject to the due-process duty to disclose material favourable evidence (Brady) and the confrontation right, with nonconstitutional error harmless unless it had a substantial and injurious effect (Kotteakos).

changes.case: Brady v. Maryland; Giglio v. United States; United States v. Agurs
changes.what: Suppressing material favourable evidence violates due process; this covers impeachment evidence (Giglio) and, where material, evidence not requested (Agurs).

changes.case: Bruton; California v. Green; Dutton v. Evans; Ohio v. Roberts
changes.what: A nontestifying codefendant's confession is barred at a joint trial (Bruton); hearsay from an unavailable declarant needs adequate indicia of reliability (Roberts).
Denying cross-examination of a witness about bias violates the Confrontation Clause.

changes.case: United States v. Bell (5th Cir. en banc)
changes.what: Circumstantial evidence no longer had to exclude every reasonable hypothesis of innocence; the test is whether a reasonable jury could find guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.
RICO's enterprise covers wholly illegitimate associations; enterprise and pattern are distinct elements whose proof may coalesce.

round1.history: Dominant rule: the trial-error standards of federal criminal appeals. Glasser (1942) anchors 1975-84: a verdict must be sustained if substantial evidence, taken most favorably to the Government, supports it, and the Fifth Circuit en banc in Bell (1982) dropped the requirement that circumstantial evidence exclude every reasonable hypothesis of innocence. Kotteakos (1946) supplies the substantial-and-injurious-effect harmless-error test. How it changed: on disclosure, Brady (1963) and Giglio (1972) were extended by Agurs (1976) to evidence not requested and refined by Bagley (1985), which adopted a reasonable-probability materiality standard and enters in 1985-89; Napue (1959) governs false testimony. On confrontation, Bruton (1968) leaves after 1975-79 and returns in 1985-89, when Roberts (1980) becomes the anchor with Green (1970), Dutton (1970) and Davis (1974) on cross-examination for bias. round1.rule: A federal jury verdict stands if substantial evidence, viewed most favorably to the Government, supports it (Glasser); the prosecution must disclose material evidence favorable to the accused, including impeachment evidence (Brady, Giglio, Bagley); and hearsay against the accused must satisfy the Confrontation Clause (Bruton, Roberts).

changes.case: Brady v. Maryland; Giglio; United States v. Agurs
changes.what: Suppression of material favorable evidence violates due process, impeachment evidence counts, and the duty exists without a specific request.

changes.case: Bruton; California v. Green; Dutton v. Evans; Ohio v. Roberts
changes.what: A nontestifying codefendant's incriminating confession cannot be admitted at a joint trial; other hearsay is admissible if the declarant is unavailable and it bears adequate indicia of reliability; Roberts anchors 1985-89.

changes.case: United States v. Bell (5th Cir. en banc)
changes.what: The evidence need not exclude every reasonable hypothesis of innocence; the test is whether a reasonable trier of fact could find guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.
Brady materiality is a reasonable probability of a different result, for exculpatory and impeachment evidence alike.

name: Michigan civil appeals: summary disposition (Maiden), open and obvious (Hoffner)
description: Michigan civil appeals: summary disposition under MCR 2.116(C)(10) (Maiden 1999, the anchor in every slice; Quinto 1996), no speculative causation (Skinner, 1994), retaliation causation (West, 2003), open-and-obvious premises liability (Lugo 2001, Hoffner 2012, until Kandil-Elsayed 2023), abandonment of unbriefed issues (Berger), and Daubert gatekeeping. Preclusion cases (Taylor v. Sturgell) join in 2020-24.

history: Dominant rule: Maiden v. Rozwood (1999) anchors every slice: summary disposition is reviewed de novo on the evidence actually before the trial court, and the nonmovant must offer admissible, specific evidence, not conclusory affidavits or promises of proof (Quinto, 1996; Gorman, 2013). Skinner (1994) bars causation theories resting on conjecture, and West (2003) holds temporal proximity alone does not show retaliation. How it changed: premises liability leads in 2015-19 and 2020-24: Lugo (2001) and Hoffner (2012) deny a duty for open and obvious dangers, including snow and ice, without special aspects (Allison, 2008; Buhalis, 2012). Both leave the partial 2025-29 slice, consistent with Kandil-Elsayed (2023) moving the doctrine to breach. Daubert and Kumho lead in 2015-19, drop out in 2020-24, and return in 2025-29. In 2020-24 federal preclusion cases enter: Taylor v. Sturgell (2008) on nonparty preclusion, Semtek (2001), Parklane Hosiery (Shore, 1979), New Hampshire v. Maine (2001) on judicial estoppel. Also: contracts enforced as written (Rory, Klapp), and abandonment of inadequately briefed claims (Berger, 2008).
rule: Michigan courts grant summary disposition under MCR 2.116(C)(10) when the admissible evidence before the court, viewed for the nonmovant, shows no genuine issue of material fact, and causation cannot rest on speculation (Maiden, Quinto, Skinner).

changes.what: A causation theory that is merely as possible as another, or rests on supposition, cannot survive summary disposition.

changes.case: Quinto v. Cross & Peters; Maiden v. Rozwood
changes.what: The nonmovant must answer a supported motion with admissible, specific evidence of a genuine dispute, judged on the record before the court at the motion.

changes.case: Lugo v. Ameritech; Hoffner v. Lanctoe
changes.what: A premises possessor owes no duty for open and obvious hazards, including wintry conditions, absent special aspects making them unreasonably dangerous or effectively unavoidable.
Nonparty preclusion is confined to six recognised exceptions; virtual representation was rejected.

changes.case: Kandil-Elsayed v. F & E Oil (overruling Lugo in part)
changes.what: The Michigan Supreme Court moved open-and-obvious analysis from duty to breach and comparative fault.

name: Maritime torts: admiralty jurisdiction and wrongful-death remedies (Miles, Moragne)
description: Maritime and federal-employee tort remedies in a single 1990-94 slice anchored by Miles (1990): general maritime wrongful death (Moragne 1970) exists but, to match the Jones Act, allows no loss-of-society recovery. Admiralty jurisdiction follows Executive Jet (1972), Foremost (1982) and Sisson (1990); East River (1986) bars admiralty products claims for pure economic loss. Also FELA (Urie, Buell) and the Tucker Act (Testan).
history: Dominant rule: federal maritime tort law, its reach and its remedies. Miles (1990) anchors the lineage's only slice, 1990-94, which later feeds an attorney's-fees lineage. How it changed: within the span the main development is Miles, which kept Moragne's (1970) general maritime wrongful-death action but held that Congress's limit of Jones Act recovery to pecuniary loss bars loss-of-society damages for unseaworthiness, narrowing Gaudet (1974). Jurisdiction rests on locality plus a maritime nexus: Executive Jet (1972), extended to small-boat collisions by Foremost (1982) and to a marina fire by Sisson (1990), which left open whether the Limitation Act is an independent basis. East River (1986) barred products claims for injury to the product itself, and Tallentire (1986) read the Death on the High Seas Act. Alongside: FELA cases (Urie 1949 on occupational disease; Buell 1987, FELA claims not precluded by the RLA), Jensen (1916) on state compensation laws, and federal jurisdiction statutes (Testan 1976 on the Tucker Act; § 2410 quiet-title suits).
rule: Admiralty jurisdiction over a tort requires a maritime locality and a substantial relationship to traditional maritime activity (Executive Jet, Foremost, Sisson), and general maritime wrongful-death remedies exist (Moragne) but are confined to the pecuniary losses Congress allowed under the Jones Act, barring loss-of-society damages (Miles).

changes.case: Moragne v. States Marine Lines; Sea-Land Services v. Gaudet
changes.what: Recognised a general maritime cause of action for wrongful death, with damages that could include loss of society.

changes.case: Executive Jet Aviation; Foremost Insurance v. Richardson; Sisson v. Ruby
changes.what: Admiralty tort jurisdiction requires maritime locality plus a nexus to traditional maritime activity, extended beyond aviation to pleasure-boat collisions and a yacht fire at a marina.

changes.case: East River Steamship Corp. v. Transamerica Delaval
changes.what: No admiralty products-liability claim lies when the only injury is to the product itself (economic loss).
The Jones Act did not displace the maritime wrongful-death action, but no loss-of-society damages are recoverable for unseaworthiness death; Miles anchors the slice.

name: North Carolina parental-rights termination 2005-09: neglect (Ballard), late orders
description: North Carolina termination of parental rights in the single 2005-09 slice, with no criminal component: one statutory ground suffices (Shermer 2003), neglect needs prior neglect and a likelihood of repetition (Ballard 1984), and Huff (2000) anchors on medical neglect and parental religion. Court of Appeals rulings in 2004-05 held that orders entered past the 30-day deadline require reversal only when prejudicial (J.L.K.; C.J.B.; T.L.T.).
history: Dominant rule: North Carolina termination under the Juvenile Code (Chapter 7B) requires only one statutory ground (Shermer, 2003), proved by clear, cogent and convincing evidence, with findings reviewed for competent supporting evidence (McMillon, 2001; Montgomery, 1984). In re Huff (2000) anchors the only slice, 2005-09, formed from three 2000-04 units: medical neglect is a proper consideration, and questioning a parent on how religious beliefs affect care was permitted (Huff, 2001). Ballard (1984) requires more than a prior neglect adjudication, namely a probability of repetition, and Montgomery (1984) looks to the child's conditions rather than parental culpability. How it changed: after the 2001 amendments the reasonable-progress inquiry is no longer limited to the twelve months before the petition (C.L.C., 2005). In 2004-05 the Court of Appeals addressed late written orders: delay alone was not prejudice per se (J.L.K., 2004; C.J.B., 2005), but long delays of five to seven months were held prejudicial and required reversal (C.J.B.; T.L.T.; L.E.B., 2005). Oghenekevebe (1996) applies the criminal ineffective-assistance test. The unit splits in 2010-14.
rule: North Carolina may terminate parental rights on proof of one statutory ground, such as neglect shown by prior neglect plus a probability of its repetition (Ballard), and a late written order requires a new hearing only when the delay prejudiced the parties.

changes.case: In re Ballard; In re Montgomery
changes.what: A prior adjudication of neglect is relevant but not enough; the court must find a probability of repeated neglect, judged by the child's circumstances rather than parental fault.
Ineffective-assistance claims in termination cases follow essentially the criminal test.
Medical neglect and the effect of a parent's religious practices on care may be considered despite First Amendment objections.
Willful failure to make reasonable progress is no longer measured solely by the twelve months before the petition.

changes.case: In re J.L.K.; In re C.J.B.; In re T.L.T.; In re L.E.B.
changes.what: Orders entered after the 30-day statutory deadline are reversed only on a showing of prejudice, found for delays of five months or more.

name: Kansas criminal appeals: preservation and briefing (Ward, King, Godfrey), sentencing
description: Kansas criminal appeals, 2010-24, centred on getting issues before the court: Ward (2011) anchors throughout; issues need a specific objection (King 2009) and adequate briefing, and Godfrey (2015) and Williams (2014) enforce Rule 6.02(a)(5) for issues raised first on appeal. Also sentencing rules (Keel and Dickey 2015) and Dunn (2016), which overruled the jurisdictional view of defective charges.
history: Dominant rule: preservation and the structure of Kansas appellate review. Ward (2011) anchors all three slices, with harmless-error analysis and abandonment of issues not carried forward. In 2010-14 King (2009) requires a specific contemporaneous objection under K.S.A. 60-404, McCaslin (2011) finds a brief argument sufficient to preserve, and Reid (2008) leaves probativeness to the district court. How it changed: Plummer (2012) and Williams (2012) set a four-step review of jury instructions. In 2015-19 the Kansas Supreme Court tightened briefing: Williams (2014) and Bowen (2014) treat poorly briefed issues as abandoned, Kelly (2014) bars new issues, and Godfrey (2015) requires a Rule 6.02(a)(5) explanation for any issue first raised on appeal. Sentencing changes entered too: Keel (2015) classifies prior convictions as of the current crime, Dickey (2015) lets illegal-sentence claims be raised first on appeal, and Ivory (2002) excludes criminal history from Apprendi. Dunn (2016) overruled precedent treating defective charging documents as jurisdictional, and Gunby (2006) abolished res gestae. In 2020-24 Butler and Chandler (2018) lead on counsel's strategy and limiting instructions; the cluster then splits.
rule: Kansas appellate courts decide only issues preserved by timely, specific objection and adequately briefed, and a party raising an issue for the first time on appeal must explain under Rule 6.02(a)(5) why it may be considered, or the issue is abandoned (Kelly, Godfrey, Williams).

changes.what: Using prior convictions in the criminal history score needs no jury finding under Apprendi.
Res gestae is no longer an independent basis for admitting other-crimes evidence outside K.S.A. 60-455.
K.S.A. 60-404 requires a timely, specific objection to preserve evidentiary issues; prosecutors may comment on witnesses' motives.
Constitutional harmless-error test for Kansas cases; issues not raised in the petition for review are abandoned.

changes.case: State v. Plummer; State v. Williams
changes.what: Jury-instruction issues follow a four-step progression of reviewability, legal appropriateness, factual appropriateness and harmlessness.

changes.case: State v. Williams; State v. Godfrey
changes.what: Failing to explain under Rule 6.02(a)(5) why an issue may be raised first on appeal waives it; inadequately briefed issues are abandoned.

changes.case: State v. Keel; State v. Dickey

history: Dominant rule: the Texas Supreme Court's standards of review for civil judgments: legal sufficiency, factual sufficiency, summary judgment, abuse of discretion, and jurisdiction. How it changed: Garza (1965) anchors 1980-89 with King's Estate (1951) and Glover (1981) on no-evidence and insufficiency points; tort and damages cases (Borel 1973, Cavnar 1985) ride along. Nixon (1985) anchors 1990-2004: summary-judgment evidence favorable to the nonmovant is taken as true, with Clear Creek (1979) on burden shifting and Cain (1986) on factual insufficiency. Walker (1992) set the mandamus standard; Texas Ass'n of Business (1993) made standing non-waivable; Havner (1997) required reliable evidence for more than a scintilla. Blue (2000) let courts weigh evidence on pleas to the jurisdiction, and Miranda (2004) required express Tort Claims Act waiver and a summary-judgment-like process. City of Keller v. Wilson (2005) anchors 2005-24, settling how reviewing courts credit and disregard evidence; Knott (2003) and Dorsett (2005) govern summary-judgment grounds and contract construction. Miranda anchors the partial 2025-29 slice. Also: TCPA cases (Lipsky 2015) enter in 2015-24.
rule: Texas civil review credits evidence favorable to a finding if reasonable jurors could and disregards contrary evidence unless they could not (legal sufficiency), sets aside a finding as factually insufficient only if clearly wrong and manifestly unjust, takes nonmovant evidence as true on summary judgment, and requires a governmental unit's immunity to be expressly waived, tested by plea to the jurisdiction.

changes.case: In re King's Estate; Garza v. Alviar
changes.what: Distinct no-evidence and factual-insufficiency standards; factual review weighs all the evidence.

changes.case: Nixon v. Mr. Property Management; Downer v. Aquamarine Operators
changes.what: On summary judgment the nonmovant's evidence is taken as true; abuse of discretion means acting without reference to guiding rules or principles.
A verdict is reversed for factual insufficiency only if the supporting evidence is so weak as to be clearly wrong and manifestly unjust.

changes.case: Texas Ass'n of Business v. Texas Air Control Board
changes.what: Standing is a component of subject-matter jurisdiction that cannot be waived and may be raised for the first time on appeal.
More than a scintilla requires evidence on which fair-minded people could differ; opinions resting on unreliable data are no evidence.

changes.case: Bland ISD v. Blue; Texas Dept. of Parks & Wildlife v. Miranda
changes.what: Courts consider evidence on a plea to the jurisdiction, applying a summary-judgment-like standard; immunity stands unless the Tort Claims Act expressly waives it.
Legal-sufficiency review credits favorable evidence if reasonable jurors could and disregards contrary evidence unless reasonable jurors could not.

name: Erie and federal common law: Guaranty Trust, Hanna, Clearfield Trust
description: Choosing federal or state law, 1975-79: diversity courts apply state substantive law, including limitations (Guaranty Trust, 1945, anchor) and choice of law (Klaxon, 1941), under Erie (1938), but valid Federal Rules control (Hanna, 1965). Federal common law governs the United States' rights (Clearfield Trust, 1943) and federal lien priority (New Britain, 1954). Also Federal Tort Claims Act limits (Dalehite, Feres, Indian Towing).
history: Dominant rule: when federal courts must apply state law and when federal law governs. In the single 1975-79 slice Guaranty Trust v. York (1945) anchors: a state limitations period is substantive under Erie (1938) because it determines the outcome. Klaxon (1941) requires the forum's choice-of-law rules, and Hanna (1965) holds that a valid Federal Rule displaces a conflicting state rule. How it changed: no change within the slice. On the federal side, Clearfield Trust (1943) applies a uniform federal rule to the United States' commercial paper, New Britain (1954), Pioneer American (1963) and lower-court cases set first-in-time and choateness rules for federal lien priority, and Milwaukee (1972) recognized § 1331 jurisdiction over federal common-law claims. Also: Federal Tort Claims Act limits, the discretionary-function exception (Dalehite, 1953), the Feres (1950) bar for service members and Indian Towing (1955); and prejudgment interest as substance or procedure (Busik, 1973). The cluster splits in 1980-84.
rule: In diversity cases federal courts apply state substantive law, including statutes of limitations and choice-of-law rules (Erie; Guaranty Trust; Klaxon), but valid Federal Rules govern procedure (Hanna), while the United States' own rights, such as on commercial paper and lien priority, are governed by uniform federal common law (Clearfield Trust).

changes.what: There is no general federal common law; diversity courts apply state law.
Diversity courts apply the forum state's choice-of-law rules.

changes.case: Clearfield Trust Co. v. United States
changes.what: The rights of the United States on commercial paper it issues are governed by a uniform federal rule.
Outcome-determinative test: state statutes of limitations are substantive for Erie purposes.

name: Washington appeals, 2025-29: waiver of unargued issues and family-law discretion
description: Washington Court of Appeals practice in the partial 2025-29 slice, led by waiver: issues not argued in the opening brief, or given passing treatment, are waived (Cowiche Canyon 1992, Holland 1998); contracts mean what they say (Hearst 2005); summary judgment follows Young (1989) and Ranger (2008). history: Dominant rule: Littlefield (1997) anchors this single partial 2025-29 slice, which merged a Washington appellate-practice unit with a family-law unit. Two threads dominate. Family law: trial courts have broad discretion, a private agreement is a factor but not binding (Littlefield), pensions are characterized by when they accrued (Muhammad, 2005), parenting restrictions need only be reasonably calculated to prevent the harm (Chandola, 2014), and Wilcox (2024) read RCW 26.09.090 as requiring the court only to consider maintenance factors. Termination findings require clear, cogent and convincing evidence (Sego, 1973), and proof of the RCW 13.34.180(1) elements implies unfitness (K.M.M., 2016). Civil matters: Young (1989) and Ranger (2008) govern summary judgment, and Hearst (2005) holds courts interpret what was written, limiting extrinsic evidence under Berg. Littlefield was superseded by statute on other grounds.

name: Delaware pleading-stage review: Aronson demand futility, then Central Mortgage
description: Delaware corporate litigation. name: Failed-bank litigation: D'Oench doctrine and FTCA discretionary function
description: Litigation over failed banks and federal regulators in a single 1990-94 slice anchored by D'Oench (1942): unrecorded side agreements cannot be asserted against the FDIC or FSLIC (Langley 1987, Beighley 1989, Bowen 1990). FTCA claims against bank regulators meet the discretionary-function exception (Dalehite, Varig, Berkovitz 1988, Gaubert 1991). Also federal common law under Kimbell Foods (1979).
history: Dominant rule: the D'Oench, Duhme doctrine (1942), codified in 12 U.S.C. § 1823(e), which bars borrowers from using secret or unrecorded agreements as defenses or claims against the FDIC and FSLIC. D'Oench anchors the lineage's only slice, 1990-94, formed when securities and banking units merged during the savings-and-loan crisis. How it changed: Langley (1987) extended § 1823(e) to conditions of payment such as warranties; Beighley (1989) applied the doctrine without intent to deceive; FSLIC v. Two Rivers (1989) protected the agencies in receiver and corporate capacities; and Bowen (1990) barred claims on unrecorded promises to lend, though Howell (1981) excluded bilateral obligations on the instrument's face. McClanahan (1986) put the loss on the borrower. Alongside: suits against bank regulators under the FTCA, where the discretionary-function exception follows Dalehite (1953), Varig Airlines (1984), Berkovitz (1988, no immunity where a mandatory policy prescribes conduct) and Gaubert (1991, day-to-day supervision covered). Kimbell Foods (1979) governs when federal law borrows state rules.
rule: Under D'Oench, Duhme and 12 U.S.C. § 1823(e) a borrower cannot assert against the FDIC or FSLIC any secret or unrecorded agreement that would diminish the agency's interest in an asset, even without intent to deceive; and the FTCA's discretionary-function exception bars claims against regulators for policy-based judgments unless a statute or regulation prescribes the course of action.

name: Louisiana excessive-sentence review and habitual-offender sentences (Dorthey)
description: Louisiana criminal appeals in a single 2005-09 cluster anchored by Dorthey (1993): sentences within statutory limits are reviewed for constitutional excessiveness, with wide discretion for the sentencing judge (Bonanno, 1980; Lanclos, 1982), and Dorthey allows a reduction below a habitual-offender minimum when it is excessive. Sufficiency review leaving credibility to the jury (King, 1983) and drug intent to distribute (Duncan, 1982) ride along.
history: Dominant rule: review of Louisiana sentences for excessiveness. Dorthey (1993) anchors the only slice, 2005-09, after the unit merged in from a Texas sufficiency-of-the-evidence lineage: under La. Const. art. I, § 20 even a sentence within the statutory range may be excessive, and a court may depart below a mandatory habitual-offender minimum when that sentence makes no measurable contribution to acceptable goals of punishment; the multiple-offender hearing is not a trial, so double jeopardy does not apply. Bonanno (1980), Lanclos (1982) and Smith (1983) give the sentencing judge wide discretion within statutory limits and hold that imperfect compliance with art. 894.1 does not automatically invalidate a sentence. Also: credibility and weight are for the jury alone (King, 1983), quantity and packaging can prove intent to distribute (Duncan, 1982), and a physician can violate the controlled-substances law (Moody, 1981). The evidence is thin and the cluster reverts to a sufficiency lineage in 2010-14.
rule: A Louisiana sentence within statutory limits may still be unconstitutionally excessive under La. Const. art. I, § 20, but the sentencing judge has wide discretion, and a court may depart below a mandatory habitual-offender minimum only when that sentence is shown to be excessive as applied (Dorthey).

changes.case: State v. Bonanno; State v. Lanclos; State v. Smith
changes.what: Sentences within statutory limits are reviewed for excessiveness, the judge has wide discretion, and failure to follow art. 894.1 does not by itself invalidate a sentence.

name: Indiana tort duty and summary judgment: Webb, Goodwin, Hughley
description: Indiana tort appeals. Hughley (2014) anchors 2015-29: Indiana denies summary judgment whenever designated evidence, even a self-serving affidavit, shows a genuine issue. Duty follows Webb (1991), with Goodwin (2016) and Rogers (2016) assessing foreseeability generally, as in barroom shootings. In 2010-14 Kalal (2004) anchors a mixed unit of school and premises duty (Mangold, 2001; Rhodes, 2004) and CGL coverage (J.S.U.B., 2007).
history: Dominant rule: duty and summary judgment in Indiana negligence cases. How it changed: in 2010-14 Kalal (2004, Wisconsin, on statutory construction from text and context) anchors a unit merged in from New Jersey and other units, with Mangold (2001) extending a school's duty off campus, Rhodes (2004) on premises duty, Plonski (2010) on foreseeability of an assault on a store patron, Dreaded (2009) on notice to insurers, and CGL coverage cases reading 'accident' and 'arising out of' (J.S.U.B., 2007; Kvaerner, 2006; Taurus, 2005). In 2015-19 Hughley (2014) enters and anchors through 2025-29: Indiana's summary-judgment standard is stricter than the federal one, and a self-serving affidavit can create a triable issue. Webb (1991) supplies the duty factors, and Goodwin (2016) and Rogers (2016) make foreseeability for duty a general inquiry, distinct from the fact-specific proximate-cause analysis. Alongside: respondeat superior for employees' criminal acts (Barnett, 2008; Stropes, 1989; Konkle, 1996), organizational knowledge of molestation (Vaughan, 2000), defamation and truth (Tharp, 2009), fraud elements (Rice, 1996) and unjust enrichment (Reed, 2012).
rule: Indiana courts decide duty as a question of law under Webb's relationship, foreseeability and public-policy factors, assessing foreseeability at a general level, and deny summary judgment whenever designated evidence, even a self-serving affidavit, raises a genuine issue (Webb, Goodwin, Hughley).

name: South Carolina appellate review: de novo family-court review (Lewis) and preservation
description: South Carolina appellate review: Lewis (2011) anchors from 2010-14, reviewing family-court rulings de novo but leaving the appellant to show error, refined by Stoney (2017); fee awards follow Glasscock (1991) and E.D.M. (1992), and issues not raised and ruled on below are not preserved (Wilke, 1998; Adams, 2003). In 2005-09 the unit centres on preservation and scope of review in criminal and municipal appeals (Wilson, 2001; Landis, 2004).
history: Dominant rule: the scope of South Carolina appellate review and preservation. How it changed: in 2005-09 Landis (2004) anchors, with Wilson (2001), Adams (2003), Lark (1981) and Wood (2004): criminal appeals review errors of law only, an issue must be raised and ruled on below, a motion in limine does not preserve an objection, and agency findings need substantial evidence. In 2010-14 Lewis v. Lewis (2011) enters and anchors through 2025-29: family-court appeals are reviewed de novo, but the appellant must convince the court the findings are wrong, and alimony may be modified on a substantial change of circumstances; Simmons (2011) confirms de novo review. Stoney (2017) enters in 2015-19 and holds that de novo review leaves the family court's advantage on credibility intact. Alongside: attorney's fees under the Glasscock (1991) factors and E.D.M. (1992); Futch (1999) on not reaching nondispositive issues; Hancock (2009) on the scintilla standard for summary judgment; harmless error (Baccus, 2006; Pagan, 2006); and plain-meaning statutory construction (Hodges, 2000; Morgan, 2002).

name: Forum and law in tort suits with products liability, 1985-89 (Gilbert, Piper, Duncan)
description: Diversity and transnational tort litigation in 1985-89, paired with products liability: Erie (1938), Klaxon (1941), Guaranty Trust (1945) and Hanna (1965) fix the law applied, and Gulf Oil v. Gilbert (1947, anchor) and Piper v. Reyno (1982) govern forum non conveniens. Duncan (Tex. 1984) adopted the most-significant-relationship test. Products doctrines merge in: economic loss (Moorman 1982), market share (Sindell 1980), creeping-disease accrual (Cathcart 1984).
history: Dominant rule: Gulf Oil v. Gilbert (1947), anchor of the single slice (1985-89), with Erie (1938), the heaviest case, frames where and under what law multistate tort suits are tried. Erie abolished federal general common law; Klaxon (1941) requires the forum state's choice-of-law rules and Guaranty Trust (1945) treats limitations as substantive, while Hanna (1965) lets valid Federal Rules govern. Gilbert set the private and public interest factors for forum non conveniens, and Piper Aircraft v. Reyno (1982) kept the doctrine flexible, allowing dismissal to Scotland despite less favourable law. Lauritzen (1953) and Bailey (1983) give maritime and extraterritorial contact tests. How it changed: the slice merged products-liability and Texas civil units, adding Duncan v. Cessna (Tex. 1984), which adopted the Restatement (Second) most-significant-relationship test; Moorman (Ill. 1982), barring tort recovery of purely economic loss for defective products except for intentional or negligent misrepresentation; Sindell (Cal. 1980) on market-share liability for DES; Cathcart (1984) on accrual in creeping-disease cases; and Pedrick (Ill. 1967) on directed verdicts. The unit splits in 1990-94.
rule: A federal court in diversity applies state substantive law, including the forum state's choice-of-law rules and limitations periods, and may dismiss for forum non conveniens on a flexible balance of private and public interests.

changes.case: Erie R.R. v. Tompkins; Klaxon v. Stentor; Guaranty Trust v. York
changes.what: No federal general common law; diversity courts follow state substantive law, state choice-of-law rules and state limitations.

name: Alabama capital appeals cluster: Batson strikes (Branch) and plain-error review
description: Alabama capital and serious-felony appeals, 1990-2014, whose shared rule is Batson (1986), anchor of 1990-99 and 2010-14, applied through Ex parte Branch (1987) and refined by Powers, Hernandez (1991) and Purkett (1995). Kuenzel (1990-91) anchors 2000-04 and Hall (1999) 2005-09 as plain-error review, prosecutorial argument (Young, Darden) and aggravators (Bankhead, Haney) lead; Harris (1995) upheld judicial override.
history: Dominant rule: Batson (1986) bars racially motivated peremptory strikes; Alabama courts apply it through Ex parte Branch (1987), and it anchors 1990-94, 1995-99 and 2010-14. How it changed: in 1990-94 Powers (1991), Edmonson (1991) and Hernandez (1991) broadened standing and civil coverage and held a race-neutral explanation moots the prima facie step. Purkett (1995) and Witt (1985, death-qualification) enter in 1995-99 with Kuenzel (1990-91), Taylor (1994-95) and Harris v. Alabama (1995), upholding Alabama's capital statute. Kuenzel anchors 2000-04 as Lockett (1978) and Eddings (1982) bring in individualized mitigation, and Ingram (1999) holds calling the jury's verdict a recommendation does not violate Caldwell. Hall (1999) anchors 2005-09 with Ex parte Waldrop (2002) on aggravating circumstances, Price (1998) and Williams (1996, plain-error review of issues first raised in a new-trial motion). Batson anchors again in 2010-14. Also: prosecutorial argument judged in context (Young 1985, Darden 1986) and the heinous-atrocious-cruel and Tison factors (Bankhead, Haney).
rule: Peremptory strikes based on race violate equal protection (Batson), tested in Alabama by the Ex parte Branch prima facie factors and a race-neutral explanation that need not be persuasive (Purkett), with Alabama's appellate courts reviewing death cases for plain error and prosecutorial argument for fundamental unfairness (Young, Darden).

changes.what: Equal protection forbids peremptory strikes based solely on race; Batson anchors 1990-99 and 2010-14.
Set out Alabama's factors for a prima facie Batson case, including disparate treatment of similarly situated veniremembers.

changes.case: Powers v. Ohio; Edmonson v. Leesville Concrete; Hernandez v. New York
changes.what: A defendant may object whatever his race, Batson applies in civil cases, and offering a race-neutral reason moots the prima facie question.
A reason is race-neutral unless discriminatory intent is inherent in it; it need not be persuasive at step two.
Alabama's capital statute, which lets the judge override a jury recommendation, does not violate the Eighth Amendment.

name: Colorado criminal appeals: preservation and plain error (Hagos), prosecutor argument
description: Colorado criminal appeals: Hagos (2012), anchor from 2015-19, ties the standard of review to preservation, so unpreserved errors are reversed only for obvious error undermining fundamental fairness. Applied mostly to prosecutorial misconduct in argument (Domingo-Gomez 2005, Wend 2010, People v. Miller 2005 as 2010-14 anchor). Novotny (2014) and Reyna-Abarca (2017) changed reversal and lesser-offense rules.
history: Dominant rule: Colorado appellate courts choose the standard of reversal by preservation. People v. Miller (2005) anchors 2010-14: error is not normally plain where guilt is overwhelming. Hagos (2012) anchors from 2015-19 through 2025-29, restating that preserved errors are reviewed for harmlessness and unpreserved ones for plain error, which must be obvious and cast serious doubt on the conviction's reliability (Conyac, 2014). How it changed: prosecutorial argument is a constant theme: calling defence witnesses liars (Domingo-Gomez, 2005), asking jurors to 'do justice' (McBride, 2009), and Wend (2010) on improper remarks regardless of intent; failure to object weighs in the analysis (Strock, 2010). Novotny (2014) held a peremptory-challenge shortfall is not structural error, Reyna-Abarca (2017) adopted a new lesser-included test, and Rediger (2018) treated defence-tendered instructions as invited error. From 2020-24 Howard-Walker (2019) limits cumulative error and McCoy (2019) restates statutory construction; Rojas (2022) on CRE 404(b) enters. Also: lay versus expert testimony (Stewart, 2002) and child-credibility vouching (Eppens, 1999).
rule: In Colorado, preservation fixes the standard of review: preserved errors are reviewed for harmlessness, unpreserved ones only for plain error that is obvious and so undermines the trial's fundamental fairness as to cast serious doubt on the conviction (Hagos), a test applied especially to improper prosecutorial argument.

changes.case: People v. Miller; Domingo-Gomez v. People
changes.what: Error is not normally plain where evidence of guilt is overwhelming; prosecutor's 'lying' remarks without objection were not plain error. Miller anchors 2010-14.
Improper prosecutorial statements, regardless of intent, can corrupt the fundamental fairness of the trial.
Restated Colorado's standards of reversal, keyed to preservation; anchors from 2015-19.

Cumulative-error analysis is required only when multiple errors have been identified.

name: New Jersey capital appeals: Ramseur and heightened state protections
description: New Jersey death-penalty appeals, 1990-2004, anchored throughout by Ramseur (1987): the state constitution and fundamental fairness add safeguards, including weighing beyond a reasonable doubt (Biegenwald 1987), intent to kill for eligibility (Gerald 1988), no waiver of mitigation (Koedatich 1988) and no non-statutory aggravation (Rose 1988). Marshall (1991), Martini (1993), DiFrisco (1994), Loftin (1996) and Timmendequas (1999) follow.
history: Dominant rule: New Jersey's Capital Punishment Act, upheld in Ramseur (1987), is applied with safeguards beyond the federal minimum. Ramseur anchors all three slices. How it changed: the core rules come from the 1987-88 cases leading 1990-94: Biegenwald required weighing beyond a reasonable doubt, Gerald limited death eligibility to intentional killers under Article I, paragraph 12, Bey (1988) addressed confessions, Williams (1988) and Rose (1988) policed prosecutorial argument, Koedatich (1988) barred waiving mitigation and Zola (1988) allowed an unsworn plea for mercy. In 1995-99 Marshall (1991), Martini (1993, res gestae uncharged acts), DiFrisco (1994, guilty-plea prejudice) and Brown (1994) enter. In 2000-04 Roth (1984) on appellate sentence review, Loftin (1996, informing the jury of sentencing options), Timmendequas (1999) and Koskovich (2001) lead, as proportionality review continues. Also: Hunt (1989, the depravity aggravator), Pennington (1990, impeachment with prior murders) and Coyle (1990, sequential charges).
rule: New Jersey's Capital Punishment Act is constitutional but, under the state constitution and fundamental fairness, requires heightened safeguards: an intent to kill for death eligibility (Gerald), aggravating factors that outweigh mitigation beyond a reasonable doubt (Biegenwald), searching voir dire (Ramseur), and confinement of argument to statutory aggravators.

changes.what: Upheld the Act while requiring structured sentencing that prevents discrimination and thorough voir dire on bias; Ramseur anchors every slice.
The jury must find that aggravating factors outweigh mitigating factors beyond a reasonable doubt; failure to so charge requires reversal.
Article I, paragraph 12 gives greater protection: a defendant who intended only serious bodily injury is not death-eligible.

changes.case: State v. Koedatich; State v. Zola; State v. Rose
changes.what: A capital defendant may not waive mitigation, may make an unsworn plea for mercy, and the prosecutor may not argue non-statutory future dangerousness.
The capital sentencing jury must be fully informed of the range of sentencing options.

name: Rule 10b-5 limits and implied rights (Hochfelder, Blue Chip, Cort)
description: From 1970 the dominant rule limits the implied Rule 10b-5 action: scienter (Hochfelder 1976), purchaser-seller standing (Blue Chip 1975), deception, not mismanagement (Santa Fe 1977), with presumed reliance for omissions (Affiliated Ute 1972). Cort (1975) and Redington (1979) tied implied rights to congressional intent. Earlier slices cover intergovernmental tax immunity (1930-44) and Erie and Guaranty Trust (1945-69).

name: Iowa parental-rights termination 2005-19: three-step § 232.116 test (P.L.)
description: Iowa termination of parental rights, 2005-19, with no divorce cases: P.L. and D.W. (2010) set the three-step analysis under Iowa Code § 232.116, a statutory ground, best interests, then permissive exceptions. P.L. anchors 2010-19; A.M. (2014) refuses to deny children permanency on hope of improvement, and A.B. (2012) treats chronic addiction as unfitness. Arizona severance cases (Michael J. 2000; Kent K. 2005) join in 2015-19.
history: Dominant rule: Iowa's three-step termination analysis under § 232.116. How it changed: in 2005-09 L.L. (1990) anchors a small unit with C.K. (1997), J.E. (2006), Dameron (1981) and S.R. (1999): past conduct predicts future care, statutory timelines give parents a limited window, and once those lapse proceedings carry urgency (C.B., 2000). In 2010-14 P.L. (2010) enters and anchors: a statutory ground under § 232.116(1), then best interests under § 232.116(2) giving primary weight to safety and permanency, then the permissive exceptions in § 232.116(3), with steps the parent does not challenge left unaddressed. D.W. (2010) frames the bond exception as whether termination disadvantages the child, A.B. (2012) holds severe chronic addiction can make a parent unfit and bars new arguments on appeal, and A.M. (2014) refuses to delay permanency on hope. In 2015-19 the unit merges with Arizona severance cases: affirmance on one ground suffices (Michael J., 2000; Jesus M., 2002), best interests require a benefit from severance or detriment from continuing the relationship, an adoption plan suffices (Mary Lou C., 2004), and Kent K. (2005) sets the standards of proof. It splits in 2020-24.
rule: Iowa terminates parental rights in three steps: the State must prove a ground under Iowa Code § 232.116(1), the court must find termination in the child's best interests under § 232.116(2), and then decide whether any permissive exception in § 232.116(3) should preclude it (P.L., D.W.).

changes.case: In re L.L.; In re C.B.
changes.what: Termination proceedings must be viewed with urgency once statutory time limits lapse, and showing the child cannot be returned implicates reasonable efforts.
A parent's past conduct predicts future care, within the limited statutory time frame for parents to show ability.

changes.what: Termination is a three-step analysis under § 232.116(1), (2) and (3); unchallenged steps need not be addressed, and the exceptions are permissive.

changes.case: In re A.B.; In re A.M.

name: Self-incriminating registration laws and statutory presumptions: Marchetti, Leary
description: Fifth Amendment limits on registration and tax schemes: Marchetti, Grosso and Haynes (1968, anchor 1965-69) barred prosecutions for failing to register wagering or firearms; Leary (1969, anchor 1970-74) and Turner (1970) invalidated irrational statutory presumptions. In 1975-79 the anchor moves to IRS summons enforcement (Donaldson 1971, Powell 1964) and records cases (Couch 1973, Fisher 1976).
history: Dominant rule: through 1974 the cluster concerns statutes that force self-incrimination or presume guilt from proved facts. Marchetti (1968) anchors 1965-69 with Grosso and Haynes (1968), holding that the privilege bars prosecution for failing to register or pay occupational taxes where compliance exposes the registrant to real hazards, following Albertson (1966); Gainey and Romano (1965) tested statutory inferences. How it changed: Leary (1969) anchors 1970-74, striking the presumption that a marijuana possessor knew of illegal importation, and Turner (1970) applied the same test to heroin and cocaine. Murphy (1964), Garrity (1967) and Gardner (1968) enter on immunity and employment compulsion, and Coin & Currency (1971) applied the privilege to forfeiture. In 1975-79 the anchor shifts to Donaldson (1971) and IRS summons enforcement under Powell (1964), Reisman (1964) and Walling (1946), with Couch (1973), Bellis (1974) and Fisher (1976) limiting the privilege for records held by others. The cluster then merges into a federal-procedure cluster.
rule: The privilege against self-incrimination bars prosecution for failing to register or pay taxes where compliance would expose a person to real hazards of incrimination, and a statutory presumption is valid only if the presumed fact more likely than not flows from the proved fact.

changes.case: United States v. Gainey; United States v. Romano
changes.what: A statutory inference must be rational; presence at a still supports an inference of carrying on the business but not of possession or control.

name: Florida capital appeals: Spencer hearings, aggravators and DiGuilio harmless error
description: Florida Supreme Court capital review in a single 2010-14 cluster anchored by Spencer (1993) sentencing hearings: aggravators need competent, substantial evidence (Swafford, 1988; Willacy, 1997), weighing is qualitative (Porter, 1990), and proportionality looks at the totality (Urbin, 1998). DiGuilio (1986) sets harmless error, Ring claims failed (Bottoson, 2002), and Montgomery (2010) found fundamental error in the manslaughter instruction.
history: Dominant rule: Florida's capital sentencing and appellate review. Spencer (1993) anchors the only slice, 2010-14: before imposing sentence the trial court holds a hearing where both sides may argue and present further evidence. On appeal an aggravator stands if competent, substantial evidence supports it (Swafford, 1988; Willacy, 1997), and the court may strike one where the evidence fails, as for heinous, atrocious or cruel in Williams (2010); the cold, calculated and premeditated aggravator rests on reflective, execution-style killing (Lynch, 2003). Weighing is qualitative (Porter, 1990), expert mitigation can be rejected only if inconsistent with other evidence (Coday, 2006), and proportionality compares the totality of circumstances with other death cases (Urbin, 1998), which led to a life sentence in Offord (2007). How it changed: Bottoson (2002) and Coday (2006) denied relief under Ring, so aggravators need not be charged or found by a jury under the law then in force. Montgomery (2010) held the standard manslaughter-by-act instruction fundamental error. Alongside: DiGuilio (1986) harmless error, inextricably intertwined evidence subject to § 90.403 (Bradley, 2001; Wright, 2009), victim-impact limits (Franklin, 2007) and preservation (Terry, 1996).
rule: In Florida capital cases the Supreme Court reviews aggravators only for competent, substantial evidence, weighs aggravators and mitigators qualitatively rather than by count, conducts proportionality review on the totality of circumstances, and finds error harmless only if it did not contribute to the verdict beyond a reasonable doubt (DiGuilio).

changes.what: Error is harmless only if the state shows beyond a reasonable doubt that it did not contribute to the verdict.

changes.what: An established aggravator stands if competent, substantial evidence supports it; the appellate court does not reweigh the evidence.
Weighing is qualitative, not a comparison of the number of aggravators and mitigators.

name: Idaho sentencing review (State v. Toohill) and post-conviction relief
description: Idaho sentencing review: a sentence within statutory limits is reviewed for abuse of discretion, with protection of society the primary objective (Toohill, 1982, anchor 2000-04 and 2010-24), codefendant disparity allowed (Lopez, 1984) and mitigation weighed (Knighton, 2006). Post-conviction relief runs alongside and leads the partial 2025-29 slice: the petition is civil and needs prima facie evidence (Rhoades, 2009; Kelly, 2010).
history: Dominant rule: Toohill (1982) anchors 2000-04 and every slice from 2010-14 to 2020-24: a sentence within statutory limits is reasonable if it is necessary to protect society and serves deterrence, rehabilitation or retribution, and protection of society comes first. Codefendants may receive different sentences (Lopez, 1984), restitution of buy money may be ordered (Hernandez, 1991), and mitigating factors such as remorse, a first offence and family support are weighed (Knighton, 2006). How it changed: in 2005-09 Gonzales (1991) anchors a post-conviction unit, with Clark (1969) holding that a guilty plea waives nonjurisdictional defects and Murray (1992) on summary dismissal. From 2010-14 the post-conviction strand grows inside the sentencing unit: the petition is civil (Rhoades, 2009), must make a prima facie case on each element (Kelly, 2010; Berg, 1998; Roman, 1994), and summary dismissal is reviewed by the trial court's standard (Ridgley, 2010); Oliver (2007) and Sheahan (2008) lead with Toohill. In the partial 2025-29 slice Rhoades anchors.
rule: An Idaho sentence within statutory limits is reviewed for abuse of discretion, asking whether it is reasonable given the protection of society, the primary objective, and the related goals of deterrence, rehabilitation and retribution (Toohill).

changes.what: Protection of society is the primary consideration in sentencing; other objectives are subservient to it.

changes.what: Codefendants may receive different sentences on their individual circumstances; restitution of investigative buy money may be ordered.

changes.case: Clark v. State; Murray v. State
changes.what: A valid guilty plea waives nonjurisdictional defects, and summary dismissal of a post-conviction petition is proper when the relief sought is unavailable.

changes.case: Rhoades v. State; Kelly v. State; Ridgley v. State
changes.what: A post-conviction petition is a civil proceeding; the petitioner must present prima facie evidence on each element, and summary dismissal is reviewed by the trial court's standard.

post-conviction petitions are civil and need prima facie evidence (Rhoades)

name: Mississippi divorce framework, 1990-2029: Ferguson division, Armstrong alimony
description: The family rule of Mississippi divorce, 1990-2029: chancellors classify marital property (Hemsley 1994), divide it under the Ferguson (1994) factors, award alimony under Armstrong (1993) only where a deficit remains (Johnson 1994), and decide custody under Albright (1983). Cheatham (1988, lump-sum alimony) anchors 1990-94; Ferguson anchors nearly every slice after, to 2025-29. Also McKee fees and, in 1995-2004, Tort Claims Act notice (Lumpkin 1997, Carr 1999).
history: Dominant rule: the Mississippi framework for dividing property, awarding alimony and setting custody on divorce. How it changed: in 1990-94, before the framework, Cheatham (1988) anchors on lump-sum alimony after a long marriage, with Jones (1988) on Watts-based equitable distribution, Brown (1983), Holleman (1988) on chancellors' broad discretion and Tilley (1992). The 1993-94 cases then set the modern rules: Armstrong (1993) listed the alimony factors, Ferguson (1994) the equitable-distribution factors, Hemsley (1994) a presumption of marital property, and Johnson (1994) made alimony depend on a deficit after division. Ferguson anchors 1995-2004 and 2010-29; Albright (1983, custody factors) anchors 2005-09. Later entrants apply the same rules: Magee (1995) on pensions, Lowrey (2009), Mabus (2003) and recent chancery decisions (Smith 2012, Vassar 2017). Also: McKee (1982) on reasonable attorney's fees, Nichols (1989) on child support, and Mississippi Tort Claims Act notice (Lumpkin 1997, Carr 1999) in 1995-2004.
rule: A Mississippi chancellor classifies assets as marital or separate (Hemsley), divides marital property equitably under the Ferguson factors, considers alimony under the Armstrong factors only if the division leaves a deficit (Johnson v. Johnson), and decides custody by the child's best interest under Albright, with appellate deference absent manifest error or abuse of discretion.

history: Dominant rule: two burden-allocation frameworks. Under Aguilar (2001), the anchor in 2000-04 and again from 2015-19 to 2020-24, a defendant moving for summary judgment may show the plaintiff cannot reasonably obtain evidence on an element. Under § 425.16, the defendant first shows the claim arises from protected activity and the plaintiff must then show minimal merit. How it changed: in 2000-04 Briggs (1999) and Wollersheim (1996) lead the anti-SLAPP cases, and Waller (1995), Guz (2000) and Cel-Tech (1999) add insurance bad faith, employment and UCL law. Equilon (2002) anchors 2005-09 and 2010-14 with Navellier and Cashman, and Noerr-Pennington petitioning immunity and dormant Commerce Clause cases join in 2005-09. Flatley (2006) and Soukup (2006) refine the test, and fee law joins in 2010-14 (Hensley, Ketchum). Arbitration cases join in 2015-19 (Armendariz, 2000; Iskanian, 2014). Baral (2016) and Park (2017) lead 2020-24, and Jameson v. Desta (2018) anchors the partial 2025-29 slice with Denham's presumption of correctness.
rule: California civil practice centred on two burden-allocating rules: on summary judgment a defendant may shift the burden by showing the plaintiff has not and cannot reasonably obtain evidence of an element (Aguilar), and on an anti-SLAPP motion the defendant shows the claim arises from protected activity before the plaintiff must show minimal merit (Equilon, Navellier).

name: Pennsylvania criminal appeals: Maroney ineffectiveness, waiver and sentencing
description: Pennsylvania criminal appeals: counsel is effective if the chosen course had a reasonable basis (Maroney, 1967, anchor 1980-89), ineffectiveness must be raised at the earliest opportunity (Hubbard, 1977), and Pierce (1987) equated the test with Strickland. Earlier, Futch (1972) suppression for pre-arraignment delay; in 1990-94 Frye's general-acceptance test for DNA evidence (Castro, Schwartz) anchors.
history: Dominant rule: Pennsylvania's standard for ineffective assistance and the waiver rules around it. How it changed: in 1975-79 Futch (1972) anchors, suppressing evidence obtained during unnecessary delay before arraignment, with Clair (1974) adopting waiver of claims not raised at trial. From 1980-84 Maroney (1967) anchors: counsel is effective if the course chosen had some reasonable basis. Hubbard (1977) required ineffectiveness claims at the earliest opportunity, and Martin (1976) and Riggins (1977) required sentencing judges to state reasons; Tuladziecki (1987) enforced Rule 2119(f) for discretionary sentencing appeals. Pierce (1987) held the state test is the same rule as Strickland. In 1990-94 the anchor shifts to Frye (1923) and DNA evidence (Castro, Schwartz, 1989). In 1995-99 Pennsylvania capital and ineffectiveness cases return, led by the 1982 decision upholding the death penalty statute and Pierce.
rule: In Pennsylvania, counsel is not ineffective if the course chosen had some reasonable basis designed to serve the client's interests (Maroney), claims must be raised at the earliest opportunity or are waived, and from Pierce (1987) the state test is treated as the same rule as Strickland.

name: Michigan appellate practice: plain-meaning statutory construction, Carines, Maiden
description: Michigan Supreme Court appellate practice of 2000-09: statutes are construed by plain text, read as a whole and without surplusage (MCI, Ward, 1999), and erroneous statutory precedent may be overruled (Robinson, 2000; Pohutski, 2002). Carines (1999) governs unpreserved error and Maiden (1999) summary disposition. Gilbert v. DaimlerChrysler (2003) anchors 2005-09, with Fieger (2006) on attorney conduct.

name: Patent obviousness under Graham and nonmutual collateral estoppel
description: Patent nonobviousness under Graham (1966, anchor 1975-84), with combination patents scrutinized (A&P, 1951; Anderson's-Black Rock, 1969; Sakraida, 1976) until the Federal Circuit stressed secondary considerations (Stratoflex, 1983). In 1980-84 preclusion leads: Blonder-Tongue (1971) dropped mutuality, Parklane (1979) allowed offensive estoppel, and Allen (1980) and Kremer (1982) gave state judgments preclusive effect.
history: Dominant rule: Graham v. John Deere (1966) anchors both slices: obviousness turns on the prior art, the differences from the claims and the level of ordinary skill, with secondary considerations as indicia. How it changed: in 1975-79 the Supreme Court's combination-patent cases lead, A&P (1951), Anderson's-Black Rock (1969), Dann (1976) and Sakraida (1976), treating combinations of old elements as obvious despite commercial success; Graver Tank (Linde, 1950) supplies the doctrine of equivalents. In 1980-84 preclusion joins the leaders. Blonder-Tongue (1971) let defendants invoke a prior judgment of invalidity without mutuality; Parklane v. Shore (1979) allowed offensive nonmutual estoppel; Montana (1979) required a full and fair opportunity to litigate; Allen v. McCurry (1980) and Kremer (1982) gave state judgments preclusive effect in federal court; Sunnen (1948) and Cromwell (1877) supply the older rules. Stratoflex (Fed. Cir. 1983) made secondary considerations mandatory evidence. The cluster splits in 1985-89.
rule: A patent is invalid as obvious under § 103 when the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art, assessed with secondary considerations, would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill (Graham), and a patentee or other party who had a full and fair opportunity to litigate an issue and lost may be estopped from relitigating it against a new party (Blonder-Tongue).

history: Dominant rule: Strickland's two-part test for ineffective assistance, applied in federal habeas through AEDPA's § 2254(d). How it changed: in 2005-09 Williams v. Taylor (2000) anchors a broad cluster of collateral-review law that also covers certificates of appealability (Slack, 2000; Miller-El, 2003), Crawford (2004), Ring (2002) and Brady. From 2010-14 Strickland anchors every slice. name: Virginia Court of Appeals: criminal sufficiency, then parental-rights termination
description: The Virginia Court of Appeals. In 1995-2004 criminal appeals lead (Martin 1987, Coleman 1983 anchors): sufficiency and constructive possession (Josephs, Burchette), excited utterances, and preservation (Ohree 1998; Redman 1997). From 2005-09 family cases dominate, anchored by Farley (1990) and Logan (1991): the child's best interests govern custody and termination under Code § 16.1-283 (Kaywood 1990; Toms 2005; Fields 2005).

Martin (1986) separates permanent foster care from termination; Toms and Fields (2005) treat other subsections and adoption goals as subsumed in an affirmed termination.
