name: Forum and law in tort suits with dram-shop liability, 1980-84 (Gilbert, Rappaport)
description: A 1980-84 cluster with two strands: diversity procedure, under Erie (1938), Klaxon (1941), Guaranty Trust (1945) and Hanna (1965), and forum non conveniens under Gulf Oil v. Gilbert (1947, anchor) and Piper v. Reyno (1982); and common-law dram-shop negligence, where Rappaport (1959), Adamian (1968), Vesely (1971) and Ono (1980) made liquor sellers liable to third parties injured by intoxicated patrons.
history: Dominant rule: the cluster joins two bodies of law that met in tort suits brought across state lines. First, Erie (1938) abolished federal general common law, Klaxon (1941) required the forum state's choice-of-law rules, Guaranty Trust (1945) treated limitations as substantive, and Hanna (1965) let valid Federal Rules govern. Gulf Oil v. Gilbert (1947), anchor of the single slice (1980-84), set the private and public interest factors for forum non conveniens, and Piper Aircraft v. Reyno (1982) kept the doctrine flexible and allowed dismissal despite less favourable foreign law; Lauritzen (1953) gave the maritime choice-of-law factors. How it changed: the second strand shows state courts abandoning the common-law rule that the drinker, not the seller, causes the harm. Rappaport (N.J. 1959) and Adamian (Mass. 1968) imposed liability on taverns serving minors or intoxicated patrons; Vesely (Cal. 1971) and Peterson (1979) treated statutory violations as negligence per se; Elder (1966), Campbell (Or. 1977), Lewis (Iowa 1977) and Ono (Haw. 1980) extended a common-law duty to injured third parties, while Holmes (1976) left the question to the legislature. The cluster splits in 1985-89.

name: Public access to criminal proceedings (Richmond Newspapers, Press-Enterprise)
description: Public access to criminal proceedings, 1985-89: Richmond Newspapers (1980, anchor) found a First Amendment right to attend trials, Globe (1982) required case-specific closure findings, and Press-Enterprise I (1984) and II (1986) extended access to voir dire and preliminary hearings under an experience-and-logic test; Waller (1984) applied the defendant's public-trial right. Also Fifth Amendment act-of-production cases (Fisher 1976, Doe 1984) and grand jury secrecy.
history: Dominant rule: Richmond Newspapers (1980), anchor of the single slice (1985-89), held that the First Amendment protects a right of the public and press to attend criminal trials, a right DePasquale (1979) had denied under the Sixth Amendment, which is personal to the defendant. How it changed: Globe Newspaper (1982) struck a mandatory closure statute for minor sex-offense victims' testimony, requiring case-by-case findings under strict scrutiny. Press-Enterprise I (1984) extended access to voir dire, holding that closure must be rare and justified by findings that it is essential to higher values and narrowly tailored, and Press-Enterprise II (1986) applied an experience-and-logic test to open preliminary hearings. Waller (1984) applied the same standard to a defendant's public-trial right at suppression hearings. Nixon (1978) recognised a common-law right of access to judicial records, while Douglas Oil (1979) and Branzburg (1972) protect grand jury secrecy and subpoenas. Alongside: the Fifth Amendment act-of-production doctrine for subpoenaed papers (Bellis 1974, Fisher 1976, Doe 1984), IRS summons enforcement (Powell 1964) and contempt power (United Mine Workers 1947). The cluster splits in 1990-94.

name: Connecticut Golding review of unpreserved constitutional claims, 1990-2004
description: Connecticut criminal appeals, 1990-2004, anchored by State v. Golding (1989): an unpreserved constitutional claim is reviewable if the record is adequate and the claim is constitutional, and succeeds if a clear violation deprived the defendant of a fair trial and was not harmless. In 1990-94 confrontation cases lead (Roberts, Van Arsdall, Bruton, Davis); by 2000-04 Connecticut civil and zoning cases (Bloom 1995) merge in.

name: Tennessee habeas corpus: void judgments and illegal sentences (Archer, Summers)
description: Tennessee habeas corpus, 2005-29: relief only for void judgments, shown on the face of the judgment or the original record, or expired sentences; voidable judgments go to post-conviction (Archer, 1993, anchor 2005-09; Potts, 1992). A sentence in direct contravention of a statute is void (Taylor, 1999; Stephenson, 2000). Summers (2007), anchor from 2010-14, set procedural requirements and overruled McLaney in part; Cantrell (2011) restated illegal-sentence analysis.

Potts (1992) and Newsom (1968) confine the writ to void judgments, Passarella (1994) allows summary dismissal of petitions stating no cognizable claim, and Dykes (1998) and Wyatt (2000) treat a fatally defective indictment as jurisdictional. Taylor (1999) and Stephenson (2000) define an illegal sentence as one in direct contravention of a statute, and Ritchie (2000) and Hickman (2004) limit review to the original record and to judgments that themselves restrain the petitioner. How it changed: Summers (2007) enters and anchors from 2010-14 through 2025-29, requiring strict compliance with the statutory petition requirements and overruling McLaney (2001) in part. In 2010-14 Edwards (2008), Davis (2010), Tucker (2009, pretrial jail credits) and Cantrell (2011) refine which sentencing errors make a judgment void. Faulkner (2007) bars attacks on federal judgments in state court. The rule is stable thereafter.

name: Georgia death penalty after Furman: Gregg and proportionality review
description: Capital sentencing after Furman (1972), centred on Georgia: guided-discretion statutes with aggravating circumstances and appellate proportionality review were upheld in Gregg v. Georgia (1976), with Proffitt and Jurek, while mandatory death statutes fell (Woodson, Roberts). Georgia Supreme Court review (Floyd, 1974, anchor; Jarrell, Moore, 1975) compared each sentence with similar cases.
history: Dominant rule: a death sentence must rest on a guided-discretion statute and survive appellate review for arbitrariness and proportionality. How it changed: Furman (1972) struck down unguided death sentences. Georgia's new statute required the state supreme court to compare each death sentence with similar cases; Gregg v. State (1974) disallowed death for armed robbery, Jarrell (1975) asked whether juries generally impose death in comparable cases, and Moore (1975) set aside a sentence as excessive. Gregg v. Georgia (1976), Proffitt (1976) and Jurek (1976) upheld guided-discretion schemes; Woodson and Roberts (1976) struck mandatory ones and required individualized sentencing. name: Mississippi death-penalty appeals family, 1985-2019: bars, argument, aggravators
description: The Mississippi capital-appeals family over 1985-2019 as a whole: on direct review of death sentences the court enforces the contemporaneous-objection bar (Billiot 1984, Conner 1994), polices prosecutorial argument outside the record (Cabello 1985) and limits aggravators (Shell 1990; Willie and Hansen 1991). name: Takings in 2020-24: Cedar Point physical-taking rule, Knick, COVID closures
description: Takings Clause cases in 2020-24, marked by Cedar Point v. history: Dominant rule: Penn Central (1978) anchors this single 2020-24 slice: most regulatory takings claims are judged by ad hoc factors, building on Mahon (1922), where regulation that goes too far is a taking. Per se categories sit alongside: permanent physical invasions (Loretto, 1982) and regulations denying all economically beneficial use (Lucas, 1992). Exactions must have an essential nexus (Nollan, 1987) and rough proportionality (Dolan, 1994), extended to monetary conditions (Koontz, 2013). How it changed: Tahoe-Sierra (2002) refused per se treatment for a 32-month moratorium, and Lingle (2005) discarded the 'substantially advances' test. Knick (2019) overruled the state-litigation requirement, so plaintiffs need not exhaust state remedies before suing in federal court. Cedar Point Nursery v. Hassid (2021) held that a regulation granting union organizers access to farms is a per se physical taking because it appropriates the right to exclude; pandemic-era challenges to shutdown orders drew on these cases. (2002) leading: on legal sufficiency the court views the evidence for the finding and disregards evidence a factfinder could reasonably disbelieve, and on factual sufficiency it asks whether disputed evidence is so significant that a factfinder could not reasonably form a firm belief or conviction. C.H. holds that a lack of definitive placement plans is relevant to best interest but not dispositive. Holley (1976) supplies the best-interest factors, and G.M. (1980) and Santosky (1982) the heightened standard of proof. Boyd (1987) lets endangerment be inferred from parental misconduct, including imprisonment, Holick (1985) reads 'provide' to include arranging support, and D.T. (2000) and J.P.B. (2005) apply constructive abandonment and drug-use endangerment. M.S. (2003) recognised the right to effective counsel, applied deferentially in H.R.M. (2006). Only one ground need be proved (J.L., 2005). The cluster splits in 2010-14, part continuing as a Texas termination lineage.
rule: Termination of the parent-child relationship under Tex. Fam. Code § 161.001 requires clear and convincing proof of a statutory ground and that termination is in the child's best interest, and appellate courts review legal and factual sufficiency under that heightened standard (J.F.C., C.H.).

changes.what: Listed nonexclusive factors for the child's best interest; a predicate ground and best interest must both be proved.

changes.case: In re G.M.; Santosky v. Kramer
changes.what: Due process requires clear and convincing evidence to terminate parental rights.

changes.case: Texas Dept. of Human Services v. Boyd
changes.what: Endangerment can be inferred from parental misconduct, and imprisonment is a factor in endangerment.

changes.case: In re J.F.C.; In re C.H.
changes.what: Legal and factual sufficiency in termination cases is reviewed for whether a factfinder could reasonably form a firm belief or conviction, disregarding evidence a factfinder could reasonably disbelieve.

name: Ohio summary judgment, 2015-29 cluster: Dresher plus Industrial Commission mandamus
description: The 2015-29 Ohio cluster: Dresher (1996) anchors 2015-24 with Harless, Mitseff, Murphy and de novo review (Grafton 1996), but unlike its sub-cluster it also gathers claim preclusion (Grava 1995) and mandamus against the Industrial Commission (Pressley 1967) from 2020-24; in the partial 2025-29 slice Hanson (1992) on Civ.R. 12(B)(6) anchors as the summary-judgment cases split away.
history: Dominant rule: Dresher v. Burt (1996) anchors 2015-19 and 2020-24: a party moving for summary judgment bears the initial burden of identifying record evidence showing no genuine issue on an essential element, and the nonmovant then has a reciprocal burden to set forth specific facts showing a genuine issue. Harless (1978) states the three-part Civ.R. 56 test; Grafton (1996) makes review de novo, yet Murphy (1992) insists the trial court make the initial determination, and Mitseff (1988) bars adding grounds not raised. The cases apply it to products liability (Temple, 1977, adopting § 402A), employer intentional torts (Mitchell, 1988), legal malpractice harm short of losing the case (Vahila, 1997), parental pre-injury releases (Zivich, 1998), negligence per se (Smiddy, 1987) and foreclosure standing (Schwartzwald and McLean, 2012). How it changed: from 2020-24 claim preclusion on a common nucleus of operative facts (Grava, 1995) and mandamus against the Industrial Commission (Pressley, 1967) join; in the partial 2025-29 slice Hanson (1992) on Civ.R. 12(B)(6) anchors as the summary-judgment cases split away.
rule: In Ohio a summary-judgment movant must identify the parts of the record showing no genuine issue on the elements of the nonmovant's claim, after which the nonmovant has a reciprocal burden under Civ.R. 56(E) to set out specific facts showing a genuine issue for trial; appellate review is de novo.

changes.what: Three-part Civ.R. 56 standard: no genuine issue, judgment as a matter of law, and reasonable minds reaching only one conclusion adverse to the nonmovant.
A motion must specify its grounds; a summary-judgment motion does not put the nonmovant on notice that the whole claim is challenged.
The movant must point to record evidence; the nonmovant then has a reciprocal burden to set forth specific facts. Anchors 2015-19 and 2020-24.
Appellate courts review summary judgment de novo.

name: First Circuit early Guidelines sentencing: departure review (Diaz-Villafane)
description: First Circuit sentencing in the first Guidelines years, a single 1990-94 slice anchored by Diaz-Villafane (1989) on review of departures. Mistretta (1989) upheld the Guidelines, McMillan (1986) and Wright (1989) let judges find sentencing facts and relevant conduct, and Williams (1992) made policy statements binding guides. Also drug-conspiracy sufficiency (Rivera-Santiago, Ortiz) and juror contact (Boylan).
history: Dominant rule: how a federal appellate court reviews sentences under the new Guidelines, especially departures. Diaz-Villafane (1st Cir. 1989) anchors the lineage's only slice, 1990-94, which later splits into the national Guidelines and Apprendi/Booker lineage. How it changed: Mistretta (1989) upheld the Guidelines against delegation and separation-of-powers challenges. McMillan (1986) held there is no jury right for sentencing factors, and Wright and Mocciola (1989) allowed relevant conduct and even acquitted conduct to raise a sentence; Batista-Polanco (1991) upheld the obstruction enhancement for false testimony. Williams (1992) held that a departure on a factor the policy statements reject misapplies the Guidelines, and Taylor (1990) required a categorical approach to prior convictions. Alongside: drug-conspiracy membership and presence (Rivera-Santiago 1989, Ortiz 1992), juror contact limited to egregious tampering (Boylan 1990), plea promises (Santobello) and proportionality (Solem).
rule: Under the new Sentencing Guidelines the First Circuit reviews a departure by asking whether the circumstances are unusual enough to warrant it, whether the facts are supported, and whether its direction and degree are reasonable, without reducing departures to arithmetic; judges may find sentencing facts, including relevant conduct, without a jury.

changes.what: A sentencing factor such as a weapons enhancement may be found by the judge; there is no Sixth Amendment right to jury sentencing.
Upheld the Guidelines as a valid delegation of legislative authority.
Framework for appellate review of departures, which should not become mechanistic bean-counting.
A policy statement prohibiting an action is an authoritative guide to the Guideline, and a departure on an expressly rejected factor is a misapplication.

name: At-will employment 1985-89: handbook and assurance contracts (Toussaint)
description: Contract limits on at-will employment, 1985-89: employer handbooks and assurances create enforceable just-cause promises (Toussaint 1980, anchor; Weiner 1982; Mettille 1983; Woolley 1985). Alongside, discharge contrary to public policy is a tort (Tameny 1980, Palmateer 1981), and California implied a good-faith covenant (Cleary 1980, Pugh 1981), whose tort remedy Foley (1988) later disapproved. Seaman's (1984) extended bad-faith tort to commercial contracts.
history: Dominant rule: Toussaint (Mich. 1980), anchor of the single slice (1985-89), held that an employer's announced policy of discharge only for cause can bind it as a contract term even without mutual negotiation. How it changed: other states followed with handbook and assurance theories: Weiner (N.Y. 1982) found consideration in an employee's reliance on assurances, Mettille (Minn. 1983) treated a handbook as a unilateral-contract offer the employer may reserve the right to amend, Thompson (Wash. 1984) recognised manual-based claims, and Woolley (N.J. 1985) enforced implied promises in manuals. The public-policy tort continued to grow from Petermann (1959) and Nees (1975) through Tameny (Cal. 1980), Sheets (Conn. 1980) and Palmateer (Ill. 1981), which protected employees who report crime. California also implied a covenant of good faith (Cleary 1980) and promises from the whole relationship (Pugh 1981); Fortune (Mass. 1977) had done so for commissions. Seaman's (1984) allowed a bad-faith tort for denying a commercial contract's existence, and Foley (1988) later disapproved tort remedies for the employment covenant. The unit continues into 1990-94 under another lineage.
rule: An at-will employee may enforce an employer's handbook or policy promise not to discharge without cause as an implied contract, and may sue in tort for a discharge contravening a clear public policy; some states also implied a covenant of good faith.

changes.case: Toussaint v. Blue Cross & Blue Shield of Michigan
changes.what: Employer policy statements, such as discharge only for cause, can create enforceable contractual rights without mutual negotiation.

changes.case: Tameny v. Atlantic Richfield (Cal.); Palmateer v. International Harvester (Ill.); Sheets v. Teddy's Frosted Foods (Conn.)
changes.what: Tort for discharge in violation of public policy, including for reporting crime or food-labelling violations.

changes.case: Cleary v. American Airlines; Pugh v. See's Candies (Cal. App.)
changes.what: Implied covenant of good faith and implied-in-fact promises from the totality of the relationship limit at-will discharge.

changes.case: Weiner v. McGraw-Hill (N.Y.); Pine River State Bank v. Mettille (Minn.); Thompson v. St. Regis Paper (Wash.); Woolley v. Hoffmann-La Roche (N.J.)
changes.what: Handbook and assurance-based promises bind employers under unilateral-contract principles unless clearly disclaimed.
Disapproved tort remedies for breach of the implied covenant in employment (Cleary), leaving contract damages.

name: Agency review, then asylum review: Overton Park, Chevron, Elias-Zacarias
description: A cluster whose anchor moves: standing and reviewability (Data Processing 1970, anchor 1970-74); record review (Overton Park 1971, anchor 1975-84); Chevron deference (1984, anchor 1985-99; overruled 2024) with standing (Warth, Allen, Lujan); then asylum review under Elias-Zacarias (1992, anchor 2000-14), Second Circuit credibility cases (Xiu Xia Lin 2008, anchor 2015-19) and Ninth Circuit nexus cases (Zetino 2010, Duran-Rodriguez 2019).

previous.name: Immigration and agency review
previous.description: Judicial review of agency fact-finding, dominated since the 1990s by asylum petitions: Elias-Zacarias and Cardoza-Fonseca on persecution, with Second Circuit adverse-credibility cases (Secaida-Rosales, Zhang, Xiao Ji Chen, Xiu Xia Lin) deferring to the IJ and BIA. Earlier slices run through Overton Park (Volpe) and Chevron on deference to agencies.

history: Dominant rule: courts defer to agencies on facts and reasonable judgments while reviewing on the record. The anchor changes doctrine plainly. How it changed: in 1970-74 Data Processing v. Camp and Barlow (1970), with Flast (1968) and Abbott Laboratories (1967), loosen standing and ripeness. Overton Park (1971) anchors 1975-84: review is on the record before the agency, with Bowman (1975) on arbitrary-and-capricious review and Vermont Yankee (1978) barring added procedures; Warth (1975) and Simon (1976) tighten standing. Chevron (1984) anchors 1985-99 with Valley Forge (1982), Allen (1984) and Lujan (1992) on standing, Cardoza-Fonseca (1987) on the well-founded-fear standard, and Perales (1971) and Universal Camera (1951) on substantial evidence. From 2000-04 the cluster becomes asylum review: Elias-Zacarias (1992) requires evidence compelling a contrary finding and proof of motive; St. Cyr (2001) and Ventura (2002, remand to the agency) enter; Second Circuit cases settle credibility and review of IJ decisions (Secaida-Rosales 2003, Zhang 2004, Xiao Ji Chen 2006, Xiu Xia Lin 2008, applying the REAL ID Act's totality standard). Matter of M-E-V-G- (2014) on social groups, Zetino (2010) on nexus and Duran-Rodriguez (2019) lead 2020-29; Loper Bright (2024) overruled Chevron.
rule: Courts review agency action on the administrative record, deferring to agency fact-finding and (until 2024) to reasonable interpretations of ambiguous statutes, and in asylum cases reverse only where the evidence compels a contrary conclusion.

changes.case: Data Processing v. Camp; Barlow v. Collins
changes.what: Injury in fact plus the zone-of-interests test for standing to challenge agency action.

changes.case: Citizens to Preserve Overton Park v. Volpe; Vermont Yankee v. NRDC
changes.what: Review on the administrative record, and courts may not impose procedures beyond the APA.

changes.case: Chevron v. NRDC; INS v. Cardoza-Fonseca
changes.what: Deference to reasonable agency interpretations; well-founded fear is a lower standard than more likely than not.
The BIA is reversed only if the evidence compels a contrary finding, and persecution must be motivated by a protected ground.
Courts must remand matters placed primarily in agency hands rather than decide them first.

changes.case: Xiu Xia Lin v. Mukasey (2d Cir.)
changes.what: Under the REAL ID Act an IJ may rely on any inconsistency in the totality of the circumstances.
Overruled Chevron; courts decide statutory meaning independently.

round1.name: Review of agency action: Overton Park, Chevron, and asylum (Elias-Zacarias)
round1.description: A cluster whose anchor moves: Sherman Act price fixing and patent misuse (Socony-Vacuum 1940, anchor 1940-54); standing and reviewability (Ickes 1938, Data Processing 1970); record review (Overton Park 1971, anchor 1975-84); Chevron deference (1984, anchor 1985-99; overruled 2024); and asylum review (Elias-Zacarias 1992, anchor 2000-14), with Second Circuit credibility cases and BIA social-group rulings later.
round1.history: Dominant rule: across its main span, courts defer to agencies on facts and reasonable interpretations while keeping review on the record and of pure legal questions. The anchor changes doctrine plainly. How it changed: in 1940-59 the cluster is antitrust: Socony-Vacuum (1940) made price fixing per se illegal, Morton Salt (1942) and Masonite tied patents to antitrust limits, and Paramount (1948) and Standard Oil (1910) lead; A&P Tea (1951) anchors 1960-64. Agency law begins in 1965-69 with Ickes (1938) on standing, then Data Processing v. Camp (1970) and Abbott Laboratories (1967). Overton Park (1971) anchors 1975-84 with Vermont Yankee (1978) and standing cases (Warth, Simon). Chevron (1984) anchors 1985-99 alongside Cardoza-Fonseca (1987) and Lujan (1992). Elias-Zacarias (1992) anchors 2000-14 as Mead (2001), St. Cyr (2001) and Ventura (2002) enter and Second Circuit credibility cases dominate. Xiu Xia Lin (2008) anchors 2015-19, Zetino (2010, 9th Cir.) on nexus 2020-24, and Duran-Rodriguez (2019) 2025-29, with Wilkinson (2024) entering.
round1.rule: Courts review agency action on the administrative record, defer to reasonable agency readings of ambiguous statutes (Chevron, until 2024), and uphold agency fact-findings, including asylum determinations, unless the evidence compels a contrary conclusion (Elias-Zacarias); the earliest slices instead carry Sherman Act antitrust doctrine.

changes.case: United States v. Socony-Vacuum Oil; Morton Salt v. Suppiger; United States v. Paramount Pictures
changes.what: Price fixing is illegal per se, whatever its form; a patentee using a patent to restrain trade in unpatented goods is denied relief; Socony-Vacuum anchors 1940-54.

changes.what: The legal-right test for standing gave way to injury in fact and zone of interests, with a presumption of reviewability and ripeness for pre-enforcement review; Ickes anchors 1965-69 and Camp 1970-74.

changes.case: Citizens to Preserve Overton Park v. Volpe; Vermont Yankee v. NRDC
changes.what: Arbitrary-and-capricious review on the record before the agency; courts may not impose procedures beyond the APA's; Volpe anchors 1975-84.

changes.case: Chevron v. NRDC; INS v. Cardoza-Fonseca
changes.what: Two-step deference to reasonable agency interpretations of ambiguous statutes; pure questions of statutory construction remain for courts; well-founded fear needs less than a probability; Chevron anchors 1985-99.
Asylum findings are reversed only if the evidence compels it; the applicant must show the persecutor's motive tied to a protected ground; Elias-Zacarias anchors 2000-14.

changes.case: Christensen v. Harris County; INS v. St. Cyr; United States v. Mead; INS v. Ventura
changes.what: Chevron applies only to interpretations carrying the force of law; habeas preserved for legal questions; courts must remand issues the agency has not decided.

changes.what: Deferential credibility review under the REAL ID Act; particular social groups need immutability, particularity and social distinction; a notice to appear lacking time and place does not stop the clock; Xiu Xia Lin anchors 2015-19.

changes.what: Loper Bright overruled Chevron; Wilkinson held that applying a legal standard to established facts is a reviewable question of law.

name: Federal civil litigation: Rule 23 class certification (Wal-Mart) and patent validity
description: A single 2015-19 federal cluster mixing two doctrines. Class certification leads: Wal-Mart (2011), the anchor, with Amchem (1997) and Comcast v. Behrend (2013), requires rigorous proof of each Rule 23 element and bars altering substantive rights; Hensley (1983) governs fees. Patent law runs alongside: claim construction (Phillips 2006, Teva 2015), eligibility (Mayo 2012, Enfish 2016) and obviousness (Graham 1966, KSR 2007).
history: Dominant rule: Wal-Mart v. Dukes (2011) anchors this single 2015-19 slice: the class proponent bears the burden on every Rule 23 requirement (Amchem, 1997), proven through rigorous analysis that may overlap with the merits, and Rule 23 cannot abridge, enlarge or modify substantive rights. Comcast v. Behrend (2013) requires a classwide damages model for predominance; Amchem stresses small claims as the core of the class device; Hensley (1983) reduces fees for limited success. Alongside: a large patent strand. Phillips (2006) bars importing limitations from the specification; Teva (2015) reviews claim construction de novo but subsidiary fact-finding for clear error; Gartside (2000) applies substantial-evidence review to the Board; Graham (1966) and KSR (2007) set flexible obviousness; Mayo (2012), Ultramercial (2014) and Enfish (2016) mark the § 101 line, with Diamond v. Diehr (1981). Also: substantial evidence defined (Consolidated Edison, 1938) and waiver of arguments first raised on appeal (1981). The slice splits in 2020-24 toward Social Security review and other units.
rule: A party seeking class certification must affirmatively prove each Rule 23 requirement through rigorous analysis that may overlap the merits, without enlarging substantive rights (Wal-Mart, Comcast); alongside, patent claims are construed under Phillips and Teva and tested for eligibility (Mayo) and obviousness (KSR, Graham).

changes.what: The party seeking certification bears the burden of establishing Rule 23's requirements.
Commonality requires a common question whose answer drives resolution, and the Rules Enabling Act bars using Rule 23 to alter substantive rights; anchors the slice.
Predominance fails where the damages model cannot measure damages classwide; certification analysis may overlap the merits.

changes.case: Mayo v. Prometheus; Teva v. Sandoz; Enfish v. Microsoft
changes.what: Claims to a law of nature adding nothing significant are ineligible; subsidiary facts in claim construction are reviewed for clear error; software claims improving computer function are not abstract.

name: Public-policy discharge tort, 1980-84: Frampton, Petermann, Tameny
description: The tort exception to at-will employment, 1980-84: discharge contrary to a clear mandate of public policy is a tort (Petermann 1959; Frampton 1973, anchor, workers' compensation retaliation; Nees 1975; Kelsay 1978; Harless 1978; Tameny 1980), while Geary (1974) denied claims without such a mandate. Monge (1974) and Fortune (1977) implied a covenant of good faith. Insurance bad-faith torts (Gruenberg 1973, Neal 1978) share the cluster.
history: Dominant rule: the at-will rule yields where a discharge contravenes a clear mandate of public policy, and the employee may recover in tort. Petermann (Cal. 1959) recognised the exception for refusing to commit perjury. Frampton (Ind. 1973), the anchor of the single slice (1980-84), allowed full damages for discharge in retaliation for a workers' compensation claim, and Sventko (Mich. 1976) and Kelsay (Ill. 1978) followed. How it changed: state courts extended the tort to jury service (Nees, Or. 1975), reporting violations of consumer-credit law (Harless, W. Va. 1978) and refusing to join illegal schemes (Tameny, Cal. 1980), while Geary (Pa. 1974) refused relief absent a clear public-policy mandate. A parallel contract theory implied good faith into at-will employment: Monge (N.H. 1974) for a refusal to date a foreman and Fortune (Mass. 1977) for a firing to avoid paying commissions. Alongside: first-party insurance bad faith (Fletcher 1970, Gruenberg 1973, Neal 1978) and punitive damages in products cases (Day 1979). The cluster continues in 1985-89 under another lineage.
rule: An employer may discharge an at-will employee for any reason except one that contravenes a clear mandate of public policy, such as retaliation for a workers' compensation claim, jury service or refusing to commit perjury, which gives rise to a tort action.

changes.what: Discharge for refusing to commit perjury violates public policy.
Retaliatory discharge for filing a workers' compensation claim is actionable in damages.

changes.case: Monge v. Beebe Rubber (N.H.); Fortune v. National Cash Register (Mass.)
changes.what: Bad-faith or retaliatory termination of an at-will employee breaches the employment contract's implied covenant.
No action lies where no clear mandate of public policy is violated.

changes.case: Nees v. Hocks (Or.); Kelsay v. Motorola (Ill.); Harless v. First National Bank (W. Va.); Tameny v. Atlantic Richfield (Cal.)
changes.what: Tort recovery for discharges for jury service, workers' compensation claims, reporting consumer-law violations and refusing illegal acts.

name: Foreseeability-based negligence duties, 1975-89 family: Dillon bystander distress
description: The 1975-89 family on widening negligence duty through foreseeability, anchored by Dillon (1968) in every slice: a bystander who sees a close relative injured may recover outside the zone of danger (adopted by Sinn, Pa. 1979, and Portee, N.J. 1980), and Rowland (1968) dropped land-entrant categories. Its sub-clusters hold the birth-related claims (wrongful pregnancy; wrongful birth and life); Tarasoff (1976) rises by 1985-89.
history: Dominant rule: courts defined negligence duty by foreseeability rather than fixed categories, chiefly in emotional-distress and birth-related claims. Dillon (1968) anchors every slice: a bystander who sees a close relative injured may recover without being in the zone of danger. How it changed: in 1975-79 Dillon leads with Rowland (1968, a general duty of care to land entrants), Vesely (1971, dram-shop liability) and the first-party bad-faith torts of Fletcher (1970) and Gruenberg (1973). In 1980-84 wrongful-conception and wrongful-birth claims lead: Troppi (1971) and Sherlock (1977) on negligent sterilization and benefit offsets, Becker (1978) and Berman (1979) allowing parents' claims for lost prenatal choice, while Sinn (1979) and Portee (1980) adopted Dillon and Molien (1980) extended direct-victim recovery. In 1985-89 Tarasoff (1976) joins the leaders on the therapist's duty to protect identified victims, with Harbeson (1983) on wrongful life. The lineage splits in 1990-94.
rule: Negligence duty is defined by foreseeability of harm rather than fixed categories, so a bystander who witnesses injury to a close relative may recover for emotional distress (Dillon), and physicians owe duties for negligent sterilization, prenatal counselling and threats by patients (Troppi, Becker, Tarasoff).

changes.case: Dillon v. Legg; Rowland v. Christian
changes.what: Dillon replaced the zone-of-danger rule with a foreseeability test for bystander distress; Rowland replaced land-entrant categories with a general duty of reasonable care.

changes.case: Custodio v. Bauer; Troppi v. Scarf; Sherlock v. Stillwater Clinic
changes.what: Parents may sue for a negligent sterilization or contraceptive failure, with the child's benefits offset against the damages.
An insurer that unreasonably refuses to pay a covered first-party claim breaches the implied covenant of good faith in tort.

changes.case: Tarasoff v. Regents of University of California
changes.what: A therapist whose patient presents a serious danger of violence to an identifiable victim must use reasonable care to protect that victim.

changes.case: Becker v. Schwartz; Berman v. Allan; Harbeson v. Parke-Davis
changes.what: Parents may recover for wrongful birth where a physician's failure to advise of prenatal testing deprived them of the choice to terminate; most courts rejected the child's own wrongful-life claim for general damages.

changes.case: Sinn v. Burd; Molien v. Kaiser; Portee v. Jaffee
changes.what: Other states adopted Dillon's foreseeability test for bystanders, and Molien let a direct victim recover for distress without physical injury.

name: Missouri review 1990-2024: Murphy v. Carron, ITT summary judgment, briefing
description: All Missouri civil standards of appellate review, 1990-2024: Murphy v. Carron (1976) anchors every slice for judge-tried cases, ITT Commercial Finance (1993) sets de novo summary-judgment review, and Thummel (1978) and Rule 84.04 govern points relied on; White (2010) and Ivie (2014) refined the evidentiary challenges. history: Dominant rule: standards of review in Kentucky's appellate courts. Commonwealth v. English (1999) anchors 2015-19 and 2020-24, requiring that prior sexual misconduct be part of a common scheme with the charged offences before it is admitted under KRE 404(b), which courts apply cautiously against propensity proof (1994). Benham (1991) governs directed verdicts: acquittal only if a guilty verdict would be clearly unreasonable on the whole evidence. Steelvest (1991) restricts civil summary judgment to cases the nonmovant cannot possibly win, and Martin (2006) defines palpable error as manifest injustice, applied to unanimity errors in Johnson and Kingrey (2013; Martin 2015). Thompson (2000) adopted Kumho Tire for experts. How it changed: from 2020-24 Yanero (2001) and Sloas (2006) on qualified official immunity enter, with obvious dangers in premises cases (Scifres, 1996) and forfeiture (Brewer, 2006). In the partial 2025-29 slice a Michigan unit merges in and Daubert (1993), Maiden (1999) and Kumho (1999) join the leading cases, so the lineage drifts.

name: Pennsylvania civil appeals: mortgage-foreclosure summary judgment (Murray)
description: Pennsylvania civil appeals in 2015-19, anchored by Murray (2013): a foreclosing mortgagee needs proof of default and of holding the note, and summary judgment fails if possession of the original note is disputed; a general denial of the amount owed admits it (Strausser 1995), and business-record loan histories suffice (Bank of America 2014). Also zoning variances (Hertzberg 1998), family-court support and fees, and waiver of undeveloped issues.
history: Dominant rule: Murray (2013) anchors this single 2015-19 slice of Pennsylvania Superior and Commonwealth Court cases. In foreclosure the mortgagee must show default and that it holds the note; summary judgment is improper if possession of the original note is a disputed material fact (Murray), though an averment of owning the mortgage implies holding the note (Mallory, 2009), loan histories are admissible business records (Bank of America, 2014), and a general denial of the amount owed is an admission (Strausser, 1995). Alongside: summary judgment on limitations in malpractice where discovery is disputed (Fine, 2005) and expert conclusions not rejected at that stage (Summers, 2010); the factfinder may believe all, part or none of the evidence (Smith v. Smith, 2006); support and counsel-fee awards reviewed for abuse of discretion (Childress 2011, Teodorski 2004); preliminary injunctions need concrete irreparable harm (Summit Towne, 2003); and zoning, where Hertzberg (1998) relaxed hardship for dimensional variances and Robinson Township (2013) struck limits on municipal zoning of oil and gas operations. Appellate courts will not scour the record for an appellant (Schenk, 2005).
rule: In a Pennsylvania mortgage foreclosure the mortgagee is entitled to summary judgment when the record shows default and that it holds the note and mortgage, and the mortgagor's general denial of the amount owed is an admission; possession of the note left genuinely in dispute defeats summary judgment.

name: Prosecutorial false testimony and suppression: Mooney, Napue, Brady
description: Prosecutorial duties of candor: Mooney (1935), Pyle (1942), Alcorta (1957) and Napue (1959, anchor 1960-64) bar knowing use of false testimony; Brady (1963, anchor 1965-74) bars suppressing material favorable evidence, extended to police files (Barbee 1964) and misleading evidence (Pate 1967). history: Dominant rule: due process forbids a conviction obtained through evidence the prosecution knows is false or through suppression of material evidence favorable to the accused. Napue (1959) anchors the small 1960-64 slice with Mooney (1935), Pyle (1942) and Alcorta (1957): the prosecutor must not use and must correct false testimony, including on a witness's credibility. How it changed: Brady (1963) enters and anchors 1965-74, requiring disclosure of material favorable evidence on request. Barbee (4th Cir. 1964) imputed police knowledge to the prosecution, Giles (1967) and Miller v. Pate (1967) addressed suppressed and misrepresented evidence, Dennis (1966) required disclosure of grand-jury testimony, and Jencks (1957) and Palermo (1959) governed witness statements. In 1970-74 the cluster grows and capital-sentencing cases join the leaders: Witherspoon (1968) on excluding jurors opposed to the death penalty (with Boulden 1969 and Maxwell 1970) and Furman (1972). The cluster then splits into Brady/Giglio and capital lineages.
rule: Due process is violated when the prosecution knowingly uses or fails to correct false testimony or misleading evidence, or suppresses evidence favorable to the accused that is material to guilt or punishment.

name: Federal appeal deadlines: timely notice of appeal is jurisdictional (Browder, Griggs)
description: Federal appellate jurisdiction over late appeals, a single 1990-94 slice anchored by Browder (1978): the notice-of-appeal deadline is mandatory and jurisdictional. Griggs (1982) and Osterneck (1989) void notices filed during pending Rule 59 motions; Houston v. Lack (1988) set the prison mailbox rule; Mallis (1978) the separate-document rule. Also excusable neglect (Baker 1989) and Rule 60(b) finality (Peake 1983).
history: Dominant rule: a timely notice of appeal is a mandatory and jurisdictional prerequisite to federal appellate review. Browder (1978) anchors the lineage's only slice, 1990-94, which split from the attorney's-fees and sanctions lineage. How it changed: within the span the rule is settled by Supreme Court cases of 1978-89. Browder held that an untimely reconsideration motion does not toll the time to appeal the judgment; Mallis (1978) tied the start of the period to a separate document; Griggs (1982) made a notice filed during a pending motion to alter or amend a nullity; Osterneck (1989) treated a prejudgment-interest motion as a Rule 59(e) motion; Houston v. Lack (1988) dated a pro se prisoner's notice by delivery to prison officials. Circuit cases fill gaps: Peake (1983) on Rule 60(b) not affecting finality, Baker v. Raulie (1989) on busy counsel not being excusable neglect, McMillan (1987) on a pro se filing serving as a notice, and Denley (1984) on Thompson's (1964) unique-circumstances exception. Also: Robinson (1960) on rulemaking, Ackermann (1950) on deliberate choices not to appeal, and Liljeberg (1988) on recusal and Rule 60(b)(6).
rule: The time limit for a federal notice of appeal is mandatory and jurisdictional (Browder); a notice filed while a timely Rule 59 motion is pending is a nullity (Griggs, Osterneck), a Rule 60(b) motion does not affect finality, and only narrow devices such as the prison mailbox rule (Houston v. Lack) or excusable neglect extend the deadline.

Crawford and Apprendi join in the 2010s; Estrada retroactivity, Dueñas (2019) and SB 1437 resentencing (Gentile, Lewis, Strong) lead the 2020s.

history: Dominant rule: from 2010-14 Watson (1956) anchors and Chapman (1967) stays second: errors of state law reverse only on a reasonable probability of a more favourable outcome, federal constitutional errors only if not harmless beyond a reasonable doubt. Breverman (1998) puts noncapital lesser-included instruction errors under Watson. How it changed: the dominant doctrine shifts across slices. In 1995-99 and 2000-04 the cluster is California capital appeals anchored by People v. Crittenden (1994) with Hill (1998), Frye and Hines. In 2005-09 Batson (1986) anchors as a jury-selection unit merges in. In 2010-14 Crawford (2004), Melendez-Diaz (2009) and Davis (2006) on confrontation, and Apprendi (2000), Blakely (2004) and Ring (2002) on jury findings, enter as federal habeas and Washington units merge, and Watson takes the anchor. In 2020-24 Apprendi, Batson and Blakely drop out and new state rules lead: In re Estrada (1965) on ameliorative amendments, Dueñas (2019) on ability to pay fines, and the Senate Bill 1437 resentencing cases Gentile (2020), Lewis (2021) and Strong (2022), which also lead the partial 2025-29 slice.
rule: State-law error in a California criminal case is reversible only if it is reasonably probable the defendant would have obtained a more favourable result without it (Watson), while federal constitutional error must be shown harmless beyond a reasonable doubt (Chapman).

description: The family's shared rule is Washington appellate review of criminal convictions: McFarland (1995, anchor from 2010-14) confines direct review to the trial record, unpreserved claims are heard only as manifest constitutional error under RAP 2.5(a)(3) (Kirkman 2007), and its members cover ineffective assistance (Grier 2011), prosecutorial misconduct (Emery 2012) and legal financial obligations (Blazina 2015). history: Dominant rule: McFarland (1995) anchors 2010-14 through 2020-24. Direct review is confined to the trial record, unpreserved claims are heard only as manifest constitutional error under RAP 2.5(a)(3), and counsel's conduct is presumed reasonable. How it changed: in 2005-09 the cluster is Confrontation Clause law anchored by Crawford (2004), which replaced Roberts for testimonial statements, with Davis (2006) and circuit cases on what is testimonial. In 2010-14 it becomes Washington criminal practice. Statutory interpretation (Campbell & Gwinn, 2002) and public-trial closure (Bone-Club, 1995; Momah, 2009; Presley, 2010) join alongside sufficiency review (Salinas, 1992; Thomas, 2004) and substitution of counsel (Stenson, 1997). Kirkman (2007) narrowed the manifest-error exception, Kyllo (2009) and Grier (2011) refined ineffective assistance, and Thorgerson (2011) and Emery (2012) required a showing that a curative instruction could not cure prosecutorial misconduct. Blazina (2015) and Ramirez (2018) govern legal financial obligations. Emery anchors the partial 2025-29 slice.
rule: Washington appellate courts generally refuse to review errors not raised below unless they are manifest constitutional errors shown on the trial record (RAP 2.5(a)(3), McFarland), and ineffective-assistance claims fail unless the record shows no conceivable legitimate tactic and resulting prejudice (McFarland, Grier).

name: Fair-trial rights: juvenile due process and jury trial (Gault, Winship, Duncan)
description: Fair-trial rights, 1970-74 (one slice): Gault (1967, anchor) and Kent (1966) brought due process to juvenile cases; Winship (1970) required proof beyond a reasonable doubt. Duncan (1968) incorporated the jury right for serious crimes, Baldwin (1970) set the line at six months, and Bloom (1968) applied it to contempt. Publicity cases (Irvin, Rideau, Estes, Sheppard) and Mayberry (1971) protect an impartial tribunal.
history: Dominant rule: the Due Process Clause and incorporated Sixth Amendment guarantee the essentials of a fair trial in state proceedings. In re Gault (1967), the anchor, required notice, counsel, confrontation and the privilege against self-incrimination in juvenile delinquency hearings, after Kent (1966) required a full hearing before transfer to adult court; In re Winship (1970) required proof beyond a reasonable doubt of every element, in juvenile and adult cases alike. Duncan v. Louisiana (1968) held the jury right fundamental and binding on the States for serious offenses, and Baldwin v. New York (1970) set the line at offenses punishable by more than six months. Bloom v. Illinois (1968) treated serious criminal contempt as a criminal prosecution requiring a jury, with Cheff (1966) classifying contempt by the sentence imposed; In re Oliver (1948) and Cooke (1925) require notice and a hearing for contempt not committed in the court's presence, and Mayberry (1971) requires another judge where a defendant's insults embroil the trial judge. Alongside: prejudicial publicity, with Irvin (1961), Rideau (1963), Estes (1965) and Sheppard (1966) requiring an impartial jury and judicial control of the courtroom. The cluster splits in 1975-79.
rule: Due process requires the essentials of fair treatment in juvenile adjudications, including notice, counsel and proof beyond a reasonable doubt, and the Sixth Amendment jury right applies to the States for serious offenses, including serious criminal contempt, those punishable by more than six months.

history: Dominant rule: Maiden v. Rozwood (1999) anchors both slices: summary disposition is decided and reviewed on the evidence properly before the trial court at the motion, with the nonmovant required to show a genuine factual dispute; a causation theory just as possible as another is not enough (Skinner, 1994), and temporal proximity alone does not show retaliation (West, 2003). How it changed: the 2015-19 slice (1,555 cases) merges in a Michigan criminal unit and is led as well by child-protective cases. Trejo (2000) is a leading termination case; Mason (2010) bars termination of an incarcerated parent without evidence of future harm; Olive/Metts (2012) requires explicit findings on relative placement; Moss (2013) sets best interests at a preponderance; White (2014) treats service-plan noncompliance as evidence of harm; Frey (2012) on benefit from services. In 2020-24 those cases leave and premises liability leads: Lugo (2001) and Hoffner (2012) deny a duty for open and obvious dangers without special aspects, with Allison (2008) on snow in a parking lot. Also: insurance rescission for fraud (Bazzi 2018) and contractual uninsured-motorist coverage (Rory 2005).

name: New York Article 78 review of parole and agency decisions (Russo, Gramatan)
description: New York article 78 review in a single 2010-14 cluster anchored by Russo (1980): parole creates no expectancy of release before the maximum term, and the Board's weighing of statutory factors stands unless irrational (Travis, 2000). Agency findings need only a rational basis or substantial evidence (300 Gramatan, 1978). Mootness exceptions (Hearst v. Clyne, 1980) and organizational standing (Society of Plastics, 1991) ride along.
history: Dominant rule: limited judicial review of New York administrative decisions, especially parole. Russo (1980) anchors the only slice, 2010-14, formed from a New Jersey appellate-review unit and another 2005-09 unit: the parole statute gives no legitimate expectancy of release before the maximum of an indeterminate sentence, so due process demands little, and the Board's discretion is broad. Travis (2000) lets the Board weigh the statutory factors without giving each equal weight, and the leading Appellate Division cases of the period (Creighton, 2010; Kaur, 2010; Halper, 2009; Paulino, 2007; Lallmohamed, 2005) apply that deference. 300 Gramatan (1978) requires only a rational basis, or substantial evidence, for agency findings. Alongside: the exception to mootness for likely-repeated issues that evade review and raise significant questions (Hearst v. Clyne, 1980), associational standing (Society of Plastics, 1991) and an unrelated felony-murder causation case (Cable, 1984). No change of rule appears in the slice; the unit splits in 2015-19.
rule: New York courts review parole and other administrative determinations under CPLR article 78 only for a rational basis or substantial evidence, and the Parole Board's discretionary release decisions stand unless irrational, since an inmate has no legitimate expectation of release before the maximum term (Russo, Travis, 300 Gramatan).

name: State taxes and regulation in Indian country, 1975-89: McClanahan to Bracker
description: The family rule on state power over reservation activity, 1975-89: state law does not reach tribal members on the reservation absent congressional consent (Williams, 1959; McClanahan, 1973, anchor 1975-84), but nondiscriminatory state law applies off it (Jones, 1973). From 1985-89 Bracker (1980) anchors, weighing federal, tribal and state interests for non-Indians; Oliphant (1978) and Montana (1981) limited tribal power over nonmembers.
history: Dominant rule: the boundary between state and tribal authority over reservation activity. McClanahan (1973) anchors 1975-79 and 1980-84: Arizona could not tax a member's reservation income, building on Worcester (1832) and Williams v. Lee (1959). How it changed: Moe (1976) barred state property taxes on members and Bryan (1976) held Public Law 280 conferred no civil regulatory or taxing power. In 1978 Wheeler and Santa Clara Pueblo described retained inherent sovereignty while Oliphant denied criminal jurisdiction over non-Indians. Bracker (1980) set a particularized interest-balancing test for state regulation of non-Indians and anchors 1985-89; Colville (1980) allowed taxes on sales to non-members, and Montana (1981) limited tribal civil authority over nonmembers on fee land. Treaty fishing rights (Washington Passenger Fishing, 1979), trust-breach claims (Mitchell, 1983) and gaming (Cabazon, 1987) enter late. The lineage splits in 1990-94.
rule: State law does not reach tribes and tribal members within a reservation unless Congress authorizes it (McClanahan; Williams), and state regulation of non-Indians on the reservation is judged by a particularized inquiry weighing federal, tribal and state interests (Bracker), while off-reservation Indians are subject to nondiscriminatory state law (Mescalero/Jones).

changes.what: Tribes are distinct political communities within whose territory state law has no force.

name: New Mexico criminal appeals: right-for-any-reason affirmance and double jeopardy
description: New Mexico criminal appeals in the partial 2025-29 slice, anchored by Romero (1990): rulings are affirmed if right for any reason (Armendariz 2003), implicit findings are presumed (Ross 2000), and evidence is viewed for the ruling (Kniatt 2006); preservation requires record references (Rojo 1998). Double jeopardy turns on legislative intent (Swafford 1991, Blockburger 1931, unit of prosecution in Phillips 2024).
history: Dominant rule: Romero (1990) anchors this single partial 2025-29 slice, merged in part from a speedy-trial unit: New Mexico appellate courts may affirm a trial ruling on grounds not argued below if right for any reason (Romero; Armendariz, 2003, for suppression), assume implicit findings supporting the ruling where none were made (Ross, 2000), and review habeas and other rulings with evidence viewed in their favour (Kniatt, 2006, also fixing jurisdiction when the writ is filed). Preservation is enforced: the court will not search the record without transcript references (Rojo, 1998), though some issues may be raised first on appeal (Montoya, 2015). Double jeopardy: for multiple punishments the sole limit is legislative intent (Swafford, 1991), tested by Blockburger's elements test (1931); unit-of-prosecution cases begin with the statute (Phillips, 2024), and the Fifth Amendment alone is applied when no broader state claim is argued (Sena, 2020). Also: Pearce (1969) on harsher sentences after appeal, Armstrong (1996) on selective prosecution, Tollardo (2012) on confrontation, and cross-admissibility defeating severance prejudice (Martinez, 2020).
rule: New Mexico appellate courts affirm a trial ruling if it is right for any reason, presume implicit findings supporting it, view the evidence in the light most favourable to it, and decide multiple-punishment double jeopardy by legislative intent, applying Blockburger's elements test.

name: North Carolina appeals 2010-24: criminal plain error, then termination review
description: North Carolina appeals, 2010-24, in two phases. Odom (1983) anchors 2010-14 and Fritsch (2000) 2015-19 on criminal review: plain error for unobjected instructions and evidence, requiring probable impact on the verdict (Lawrence 2012), and substantial-evidence review of motions to dismiss (Smith 1980). From 2020-24 Montgomery (1984) anchors termination of parental rights, with the Supreme Court's 2019 decisions (T.N.H., E.H.P.) on review of findings.
history: Dominant rule: North Carolina's standards of appellate review. In 2010-14 Odom (1983) anchors, after merging with a capital-appeals lineage: unobjected-to instructional error gets plain-error review. Smith (1980) and Powell (1980) define the substantial evidence needed to survive a motion to dismiss, and Smith (2007) vacates habitual-felon judgments when the underlying conviction falls. How it changed: Lawrence (2012) restated plain error as requiring a fundamental error with probable impact on the guilty verdict, limited to instructions and evidence. In 2015-19 Fritsch (2000) anchors: the State's evidence is credited and the defendant's disregarded unless consistent; Pakulski (1987) and Sturdivant (1981) enter, along with civil summary-judgment cases (Will of Jones, 2008; Forbis, 2007). In 2020-24 the anchor moves to termination of parental rights: Montgomery (1984) judges neglect by the child's conditions and limits review of conclusions to the findings, Ballard (1984) and Young (1997) govern prior neglect and abandonment windows, and the Supreme Court's T.N.H. (2019), E.H.P. (2019) and D.L.W. (2016) define review of findings and willful abandonment. T.R.P. (2006) ties jurisdiction to a verified petition.
rule: North Carolina appellate courts review unobjected-to instructional and evidentiary error only for plain error, requiring a showing that the error probably affected the verdict (Odom, Lawrence), and test a motion to dismiss by whether substantial evidence supports each element, viewed for the State (Smith, Fritsch).

history: Dominant rule: changes with the anchor. In 1975-84 Taylor v. Louisiana (1975) anchors: venires must reflect a fair cross-section, with Duren (1979) and Castaneda (1977) on proof, and Swain (1965) demanding proof of systematic strikes; Wheeler (Cal. 1978) and Soares (Mass. 1979) barred group-based strikes under state law. How it changed: Batson (1986) anchors 1985-94, letting defendants prove racial strikes from their own trial; Griffith (1987) applied it to pending appeals, and Powers, Edmonson and Hernandez (1991) and McCollum (1992) extended it, while Young (Ill. 1989) defers to trial findings on race-neutral reasons. Albanese (1984) adopted Strickland and Collins (1985) adopted Jackson v. Virginia. From 1995-99 Enoch (1988) anchors: forfeiture without an objection and a written posttrial motion; Coleman (1998) on postconviction pleading anchors 2000-04. Herron (2005) and Piatkowski (2007) anchor 2010-14 with the two-prong plain-error test. In 2015-19 Outboard Marine (1992) and pension-reform cases show civil drift, and in 2020-24 Foutch (1984), requiring the appellant to supply a complete record, anchors with juvenile cases.
rule: The anchor shifts: first, juries must be drawn from a fair cross-section and peremptory strikes may not be race-based (Taylor, Batson); later, in Illinois an issue is preserved only by both a trial objection and a written posttrial motion (Enoch), and unpreserved error is reviewable as plain error only when the evidence is closely balanced or the error is so serious it undermined the trial's fairness (Herron, Piatkowski).

changes.case: Swain v. Alabama; Taylor v. Louisiana; Castaneda v. Partida; Duren v. Missouri
changes.what: Systematic exclusion from venires violates the Sixth Amendment fair-cross-section guarantee and equal protection, but Swain required proof of strikes over many cases; Taylor anchors 1975-84.

changes.case: People v. Wheeler (Cal.); Commonwealth v. Soares (Mass.)
changes.what: State courts barred group-based peremptory strikes under state constitutions before Batson.

changes.case: Batson v. Kentucky; Griffith v. Kentucky
changes.what: A defendant may make a prima facie case of racial strikes from his own trial, replacing Swain's evidentiary burden, and Batson applies to all cases on direct review; Batson anchors 1985-94.

changes.case: Powers v. Ohio; Hernandez v. New York; Edmonson; Georgia v. McCollum
changes.what: Batson protects excluded jurors whatever the defendant's race, covers civil litigants and criminal defendants, and accepts race-neutral explanations credited by the trial judge.
Preservation requires a trial objection and a written posttrial motion; Enoch anchors 1995-99 and 2005-09.

changes.case: People v. Herron; People v. Piatkowski
changes.what: Illinois keeps a two-prong plain-error test, declining to adopt Olano's four-part test; first-prong reversal for closely balanced evidence requires showing the error threatened to tip the scales; Herron anchors 2010-14.

name: Anders no-merit appeals, 1995-2009: New York, then Texas, with plea-bargain notice
description: The 1995-2009 no-merit family, anchored by Anders (1967): New York practice (Saunders, Paige, Gonzalez) and Penson (1988) lead 1995-99, then Texas, where High (1978) adopted the procedure, Stafford (1991) requires new counsel once arguable grounds are found and Bledsoe (2005) bars deciding pro se issues on the merits. Distinctively, Texas plea-bargain appeal limits under former Rule 40(b)(1) and Rule 25.2 (Lyon, Davis 1994; Cooper 2001).
history: Dominant rule: Anders v. California (1967) anchors all three slices, 1995-99 through 2005-09: appointed counsel who finds an appeal frivolous must file a brief evaluating the record and referring to anything arguable, and the court must review the record itself. How it changed: in 1995-99 New York no-merit practice (Saunders, Paige 1976; Gonzalez 1979) and Penson (1988) lead, after three earlier units merge. From 2000-04 the lineage turns Texan: High (1978) adopted Anders and required discussion of trial objections, Currie (1974) described the professional evaluation, and Stafford (1991) required new counsel if arguable grounds exist. Bledsoe (2005) held that a court of appeals may decide only whether arguable grounds exist, not their merits, and In re Schulman (2008) addressed counsel's duties. Texas notice-of-appeal rules for plea bargains recur: Lyon and Davis (1994) under former Rule 40(b)(1), Olivo (1996) on jurisdiction, and Cooper (2001) barring voluntariness claims under Rule 25.2(b) (with Vidaurri 2001). Also: proportionality under Solem (1983) and Harmelin (1991), and enforceable appeal waivers (Marin 1992). The cluster splits in 2010-14.
rule: Appointed counsel who finds an appeal frivolous must file an Anders brief that professionally evaluates the record and any arguable grounds; the appellate court independently reviews the record and, if it finds arguable grounds, must appoint new counsel rather than decide them (Stafford; Bledsoe).

changes.what: Counsel seeking to withdraw from a frivolous appeal must file a brief referring to anything arguable, and the court must examine the record.
Adopted the Anders procedure in Texas, requiring the brief to discuss trial objections and rulings and why they present no reversible error.
Allowing withdrawal without a proper Anders review leaves the appellant without counsel, and prejudice is presumed.
If the court finds arguable grounds, it must abate for new counsel to brief them.
The court of appeals may only decide whether arguable grounds exist; addressing the merits of issues raised in a pro se response is error.

changes.case: Lyon; Davis; Cooper v. State (Tex. Crim. App.)
changes.what: Under former Rule 40(b)(1) and Rule 25.2(b), a plea-bargaining defendant's general notice of appeal did not permit challenges to sufficiency or to the voluntariness of the plea.

written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, round 2 after the lineage re-link)

before_differentiation.name: Anders no-merit briefs in Texas appeals (High, Stafford, Bledsoe)
before_differentiation.description: Anders no-merit appeals, anchored by Anders (1967) in 1995-2009, mostly in Texas: High (1978) adopted the procedure, Stafford (1991) requires new counsel once arguable grounds are found, Bledsoe (2005) bars deciding pro se issues on the merits, and Penson (1988) presumes prejudice. Also Texas plea-bargain appeal limits under former Rule 40(b)(1) and Rule 25.2 (Lyon, Davis 1994; Cooper 2001).

distinct_from.how: The earlier family (1995-2009), New York then Texas with plea-bargain notice-of-appeal rules, not the 2015-29 Pennsylvania-led family with Turner/Finley and termination appeals.
A broader 1995-2009 family that also holds New York practice and Texas plea-bargain jurisdiction rules; that lineage is Texas Anders procedure alone, continuing to 2029 with Schulman, Kelly and P.M.

name: Double jeopardy: mistrial, retrial and issue preclusion (Arizona v. Washington, Ashe)
description: A 2010-14 cluster on double jeopardy, anchored by Arizona v. Washington (1978): retrial after a mistrial needs manifest necessity, judged with deference to the trial judge, and a defence-requested mistrial bars retrial only if the prosecutor goaded it (Oregon v. Kennedy, 1982). Ashe (1970) and Yeager (2009) bar relitigating facts an acquittal decided. Joinder and severance (Zafiro, 1993) and harmless error (Kotteakos, 1946) ride along.
history: Dominant rule: double jeopardy after an aborted or partly unsuccessful trial. Arizona v. Washington (1978) anchors the only slice, 2010-14, which merged in from a Washington state appellate-practice lineage: retrial after a mistrial is allowed when there was manifest necessity, and the trial judge's assessment, for example of prosecutorial misconduct or juror bias, gets great deference. Oregon v. Kennedy (1982) bars retrial after a defence-requested mistrial only where the prosecutor intended to goad the motion, and Richardson (1984) holds a hung jury does not end jeopardy. Ashe (1970) makes issue preclusion part of the guarantee; Dowling (1990) limits it to ultimate issues and allows other-acts evidence of acquitted conduct; Yeager (2009) disregards hung counts, so acquittals barred retrial on related counts. Brown (1977) treats greater and lesser included offenses as the same offense. Alongside: joint trials, where mutually antagonistic defences are not prejudicial per se and limiting instructions usually suffice (Zafiro, 1993; Whitfield, 2009); Kotteakos (1946) harmless error; suspicionless checkpoints (Martinez-Fuerte, 1976; Sitz, 1990); and Roe v. Flores-Ortega (2000) on counsel's failure to file an appeal.
rule: After a mistrial the Double Jeopardy Clause permits retrial if there was manifest necessity, judged with deference to the trial judge, or if the defendant moved for it, unless the prosecution goaded the motion; and an acquittal precludes relitigating any ultimate fact it necessarily decided (Arizona v. Washington, Oregon v. Kennedy, Ashe).

changes.what: Collateral estoppel is part of the double-jeopardy guarantee, barring relitigation of an ultimate fact decided by an acquittal.
A greater and lesser included offense are the same offense for successive prosecution and cumulative punishment.
Manifest necessity for a mistrial is reviewed with special deference to the trial judge's assessment.
A defendant who moves for a mistrial may invoke double jeopardy only if the prosecutor intended to goad the motion.
A hung-jury mistrial does not terminate jeopardy, so retrial is permitted.
Evidence of conduct underlying an acquittal may be admitted under a lower standard of proof; preclusion applies only to ultimate issues.
Hung counts are disregarded in the issue-preclusion analysis, so acquittals can bar retrial on hung counts.

name: Capital punishment: individualized sentencing (Lockett), Gregg guided discretion
description: Death-penalty law of 1980-94: after Furman (1972), Gregg (1976) upheld guided discretion and Woodson (1976) struck mandatory death; Lockett (1978) and Eddings (1982) require consideration of all mitigation and anchor 1980-84 and 1990-94; Zant (1983) requires narrowing aggravators. Strickland (1984) anchors 1985-89. Witt (1985) and Lockhart (1986) eased death qualification; Penry (1989) and Payne (1991, admitting victim impact) follow.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Capital punishment: Eighth Amendment and sentencing
previous.description: Death-penalty jurisprudence after Furman and Gregg: individualized sentencing and mitigation (Lockett, Eddings, Woodson), juror exclusion (Witherspoon, Witt), aggravating circumstances (Zant) and ineffective assistance at the penalty phase (Strickland).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: individualized capital sentencing within guided discretion. Lockett (1978) anchors 1980-84 and 1990-94: the sentencer must be free to consider any mitigating circumstance, building on Woodson (1976), which struck mandatory death statutes, and on Gregg, Proffitt and Jurek (1976), which upheld guided-discretion schemes after Furman (1972). How it changed: Eddings (1982) barred limits on mitigation, Zant (1983) required aggravators that narrow the class, and Caldwell (1985) barred diminishing the jury's sense of responsibility. In 1985-89 Strickland (1984) anchors as the cluster absorbs general criminal procedure: Chapman (1967) harmless error, Wainwright v. Sykes (1977) procedural default, Batson (1986) and Swain on jury strikes, and Anders. Witt (1985) loosened Witherspoon's (1968) standard for excluding jurors, and Lockhart (1986) upheld death-qualified juries. In 1990-94 Penry (1989) and Boyde (1990) on giving effect to mitigation, Coleman (1991) on default, Teague (1989) on retroactivity, and Payne (1991), allowing victim-impact evidence, enter alongside California capital appeals (Lang, Lewis). The cluster then splits into sentencing and habeas units.
rule: The death penalty is constitutional only under procedures that guide and narrow the sentencer's discretion (Gregg, Zant) while allowing individualized consideration of any mitigating aspect of the defendant's character, record or offense (Woodson, Lockett, Eddings); jurors may be excluded only if their views would substantially impair their duties (Witherspoon, Witt).

changes.case: Furman v. Georgia; Gregg v. Georgia; Proffitt; Jurek; Woodson v. North Carolina
changes.what: Arbitrary capital sentencing violates the Eighth Amendment, guided-discretion statutes are valid, and mandatory death sentences are not.

changes.case: Lockett v. Ohio; Eddings v. Oklahoma
changes.what: The sentencer may not be precluded from considering any relevant mitigating evidence; Lockett anchors 1980-84 and 1990-94.

changes.case: Zant v. Stephens; Caldwell v. Mississippi
changes.what: Aggravators must genuinely narrow the eligible class, and a jury may not be led to believe responsibility for the death sentence rests elsewhere.
Ineffective assistance requires deficient performance and a reasonable probability of a different result, including at a capital sentencing; Strickland anchors 1985-89.

changes.case: Wainwright v. Witt; Lockhart v. McCree
changes.what: Jurors may be excluded if their views would prevent or substantially impair their duties, displacing Witherspoon's stricter formulation, and death-qualified guilt juries do not violate the fair-cross-section requirement.

changes.case: Penry v. Lynaugh; Boyde v. California; Payne v. Tennessee
changes.what: Jurors must be able to give effect to mitigation such as mental retardation (though Penry allowed executing such offenders), and Payne admitted victim-impact evidence, overruling Booth and Gathers.

name: Guilty pleas in 1980-89: Boykin record, limits on collateral relief, Hill v. Lockhart
description: Guilty pleas in 1980-89, as attacked collaterally: the record must show a knowing, voluntary plea and waiver of trial rights (Boykin 1969, anchor of both slices; McCarthy 1969), but technical Rule 11 violations give no collateral relief (Timmreck 1979). Brady (1970), Alford and Santobello (1971) stand; Hill v. Lockhart (1985) applied Strickland to plea advice, and deportation was treated as a collateral consequence needing no warning.
history: Dominant rule: a guilty plea waives trial rights, so the record must affirmatively show it was knowing and voluntary (Boykin 1969, anchor in 1980-84 and 1985-89; In re Tahl 1969 required the three rights to be enumerated). McCarthy (1969) demanded strict Rule 11 compliance in federal court, but Timmreck (1979) and Hill v. United States (1962) denied collateral relief for technical violations. Brady, Parker and McMann (1970) held a plea to obtain a lesser penalty, or made on competent but mistaken advice, voluntary; Alford (1970) allowed pleas with protestations of innocence. Santobello (1971) bound the state to its promises, and Henderson v. Morgan (1976) required notice of an essential element. How it changed: in 1985-89 Hill v. Lockhart (1985) and Tollett (1973) enter; Hill applied Strickland to counsel's plea advice, and Tollett barred pre-plea constitutional claims. Also: courts held deportation a collateral consequence needing no warning (Edwards 1981, Campbell 1985), and Mauro (1978) on detainers.
rule: A guilty plea is valid only if the record affirmatively shows it was knowing, intelligent and voluntary, with the defendant aware of the rights waived and the plea's direct consequences; promises that induce a plea must be kept.

changes.case: Boykin v. Alabama; McCarthy v. United States
changes.what: Voluntariness must appear on the record; noncompliance with federal Rule 11 required automatic reversal.

changes.case: Brady v. United States; McMann v. Richardson; Parker v. North Carolina; North Carolina v. Alford
changes.what: A plea induced by fear of a heavier sentence is not coerced; competent counsel's misjudgment does not void it; a court may accept a plea from a defendant who maintains innocence given a strong factual basis.
The prosecution must keep a promise that induced the plea.

changes.case: Henderson v. Morgan; United States v. Timmreck
changes.what: A plea is involuntary without notice of an essential element; a technical Rule 11 violation does not support collateral relief.
Strickland's two-part test governs ineffective-assistance challenges to guilty pleas.

written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, round 2 after the lineage re-link)

before_differentiation.name: Guilty pleas must be knowing and voluntary on the record (Boykin, Brady)
before_differentiation.description: Validity of guilty pleas, 1980-89: the record must show a knowing, voluntary plea and waiver of trial rights (Boykin 1969, anchor of both slices; McCarthy 1969). A plea to avoid a harsher sentence is not coerced (Brady 1970), Alford pleas are allowed, and plea promises bind the prosecution (Santobello 1971). Hill v. Lockhart (1985) applied Strickland to plea advice; deportation was treated as a collateral consequence.

distinct_from.how: This 1980-89 cluster centres on collateral attacks (Timmreck, Hill v. Lockhart, deportation warnings); that 1970-74 cluster is the founding slice, when McCarthy, Halliday and the Brady trilogy were new.

This cluster stresses federal collateral relief and counsel's plea advice in the 1980s; that sub is the 1970-89 line on the plea colloquy itself, with In re Tahl, Wade v. Coiner and Henderson v. Morgan on notice of elements.

name: FOIA exemptions and disclosure: Mink, Rose, Vaughn and Reporters Committee
description: Freedom of Information Act litigation: exemptions are narrow and the agency must justify withholding (Mink, 1973; Vaughn, 1973; Rose, 1976, anchor 1980-89), Exemption 5 tracks civil-discovery privileges (Sears, 1975), and Reporters Committee (1989, anchor 1990-94) defined the privacy public interest. In 1995-99 the anchor moves to privileges and public access: Upjohn (1981), Nixon (1974), Richmond Newspapers (1980) and Press-Enterprise (1986).
history: Dominant rule: FOIA's presumption of disclosure and its narrowly read exemptions. How it changed: in 1975-79 Mink (1973) anchors, with Vaughn (1973) requiring an itemized index, Sears (1975) reading Exemption 5 to protect predecisional deliberations but not final opinions, and Soucie (1971) on which offices are agencies. Rose (1976) anchors 1980-84 and 1985-89, stressing that disclosure is the dominant objective; Robbins Tire (1978) allowed withholding of enforcement witness statements, Mead Data (1977) and Coastal States (1980) policed segregability and deliberative process, and Cox (1979) and Cuneo (1977) addressed fee awards. Reporters Committee (1989) anchors 1990-94, limiting the public interest to information about agency conduct. In 1995-99 the anchor shifts to Upjohn (1981), with Hickman (1947) work product, Nixon (1974) executive privilege, and the press access cases Richmond Newspapers (1980), Globe (1982) and Press-Enterprise (1986).
rule: FOIA makes disclosure the dominant objective, so its exemptions are narrowly construed, the agency bears the burden of justifying withholding with a detailed index (Vaughn) and segregating nonexempt material, Exemption 5 covers privileged predecisional deliberative material (Sears), and privacy exemptions weigh the public interest in revealing what the government is up to (Reporters Committee).

changes.case: EPA v. Mink; Vaughn v. Rosen (D.C. Cir.)
changes.what: In camera inspection is not automatic and factual material must be segregated; an agency must itemize and justify each withholding (the Vaughn index).

changes.case: NLRB v. Sears, Roebuck; Renegotiation Board v. Grumman
changes.what: Exemption 5 incorporates executive and deliberative-process privileges for predecisional material but not final opinions; FOIA does not require agencies to create documents.

changes.case: Department of the Air Force v. Rose
changes.what: Disclosure, not secrecy, is FOIA's dominant objective; Exemption 2 covers only internal housekeeping matters.
Witness statements in a pending enforcement proceeding may be withheld under Exemption 7(A) as a class.

changes.case: Coastal States Gas v. Department of Energy (D.C. Cir.)
changes.what: The deliberative-process privilege does not cover documents that apply established policy rather than recommend new policy.

changes.case: Department of Justice v. Reporters Committee
changes.what: Privacy interests in compiled rap sheets outweigh disclosure where the information does not shed light on the agency's performance of its duties.
Attorney-client privilege covers communications between corporate counsel and employees made to secure legal advice.

phases.rule: FOIA exemptions and the agency's burden
attorney-client, executive and work-product privileges and public access to criminal proceedings
