name: Personal jurisdiction, federal and Texas: minimum contacts (Shoe, Burger King)
description: The personal-jurisdiction family, joining the Supreme Court line with Texas special-appearance law: International Shoe (1945, anchor 1950-94) replaced Pennoyer's presence test with minimum contacts; Hanson, World-Wide Volkswagen (1980) and Burger King (1985, anchor from 1995-99) require purposeful availment; Goodyear and Daimler (2011-14) confined general jurisdiction; Bristol-Myers (2017) and Ford (2021) refined relatedness. Texas long-arm cases lead in 2000-14.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Personal jurisdiction (minimum contacts)
previous.description: Due-process limits on personal jurisdiction from International Shoe onward: minimum contacts, purposeful availment and foreseeability (Hanson, World-Wide Volkswagen, Burger King v. Rudzewicz, Asahi), general and specific jurisdiction (Helicopteros), and their Texas long-arm application.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: jurisdiction over a nonresident requires purposeful minimum contacts with the forum and must be fair and reasonable. How it changed: before 1945 the anchors are People's Tobacco (1918) and International Harvester (1914), asking whether a corporation was present by doing business, with Pennoyer (1878) behind them. International Shoe (1945) enters in 1945-49 and anchors 1950-94; the 1950s carry divorce-jurisdiction cases (Sherrer, Williams). McGee (1957) and Hanson (1958) set the purposeful-availment limit. Shaffer (1977) subjected quasi in rem jurisdiction to minimum contacts, and Woodson (1980), Hall (1984), Burger King (1985) and Asahi (1987) enter as the modern framework; Burger King anchors from 1995-99. Texas cases (Guardian Royal 1991, Marchand 2002, Holten 2005, Drugg 2007) lead 2000-14. Goodyear and Nicastro (2011), Daimler and Walden (2014) narrowed general and specific jurisdiction; Bristol-Myers (2017) and Ford (2021) lead 2015-29. Punitive-damages entrants (Gore, Campbell) in 2020-24 are drift.
rule: A court may exercise personal jurisdiction over a nonresident only if the defendant purposefully established minimum contacts with the forum, the claim arises out of or relates to those contacts (or the defendant is essentially at home there), and jurisdiction comports with fair play and substantial justice.

changes.case: Pennoyer v. Neff; International Harvester v. Kentucky; People's Tobacco v. American Tobacco
changes.what: Territorial presence: jurisdiction over a corporation required it to be 'doing business' in the state, and mere solicitation was not enough; these anchor 1920-49.
Minimum contacts and fair play and substantial justice replaced physical presence; anchor 1950-94.

changes.case: McGee v. International Life; Hanson v. Denckla
changes.what: A single contract can suffice, but the plaintiff's unilateral activity cannot; the defendant must purposefully avail itself of the forum.

changes.case: Shaffer v. Heitner; Rush v. Savchuk
changes.what: All assertions of jurisdiction, including quasi in rem, must meet International Shoe; Rush rejected Seider attachment of an insurer's obligation.

changes.case: World-Wide Volkswagen v. Woodson; Helicopteros v. Hall; Burger King v. Rudzewicz; Asahi
changes.what: Foreseeability means reasonably anticipating suit; purchases alone do not create general jurisdiction; a contract alone is not enough; reasonableness factors can defeat jurisdiction; Rudzewicz anchors from 1995-99.

changes.case: Guardian Royal (Tex.); BMC Software v. Marchand; Michiana v. Holten; Moki Mac v. Drugg
changes.what: Texas long-arm reaches as far as due process; directing a tort from afar is not purposeful availment; specific jurisdiction needs a substantial connection to the operative facts.

changes.case: Goodyear v. Brown; J. McIntyre v. Nicastro; Daimler AG v. Bauman; Walden v. Fiore
changes.what: General jurisdiction only where a corporation is essentially at home; contacts must be the defendant's own with the forum, not with the plaintiff.

changes.case: Bristol-Myers Squibb v. Superior Court; Ford Motor v. Montana Eighth Judicial District
changes.what: Nonresidents' claims need their own forum connection; 'relate to' does not require strict causation.

before_differentiation.name: Personal jurisdiction: minimum contacts (International Shoe, Burger King)
before_differentiation.description: Due-process limits on personal jurisdiction: International Shoe (1945, anchor 1950-94) replaced Pennoyer's presence test with minimum contacts; Hanson, World-Wide Volkswagen (1980) and Burger King (1985, anchor from 1995-99) require purposeful availment; Goodyear and Daimler (2011-14) confined general jurisdiction to where a defendant is at home; Bristol-Myers (2017) and Ford (2021) refined relatedness. Texas long-arm cases lead in the 2000s.

distinct_from.how: That sub-cluster is the Supreme Court and federal minimum-contacts line alone and shares most of this cluster's cases; this cluster also holds the Texas special-appearance cases that lead it in 2000-14.
That sub-cluster is Texas special-appearance law in 2000-14 only; this cluster is the whole family from before 1945.

name: Confrontation Clause (Crawford, Bruton) and juvenile sentencing appeals
description: A partial 2025-29 cluster of criminal appeals, mostly Fourth Circuit, combining the Confrontation Clause (Crawford 2004, Davis 2006, Bruton 1968, Marsh 1987) and joint-trial severance (Zafiro 1993) with the Eighth Amendment juvenile-sentencing line (Roper 2005, Graham 2010 as anchor, Miller 2012). Also Jardines (2013) on porch dog sniffs and routine sentencing review (within-Guidelines presumption, oral pronouncement of conditions).
history: Dominant rule: two lines lead this single partial 2025-29 slice. Confrontation: Crawford (2004) bars testimonial hearsay unless the declarant is unavailable and was cross-examined, and Davis (2006) defines testimonial by the primary purpose of the questioning. Joint trials: Bruton (1968) excludes a non-testifying codefendant's confession that incriminates the defendant, Richardson v. Marsh (1987) allows a redacted confession with a limiting instruction, and Zafiro (1993) holds antagonistic defences do not require severance. Eighth Amendment: Graham (2010) anchors the slice, with Roper (2005) and Miller (2012) restricting the harshest juvenile sentences. How it applies: Fourth Circuit cases supply the rest: within- or below-Guidelines sentences are presumed reasonable (Zelaya, 2018), discretionary supervised-release conditions must be orally pronounced (Rogers, 2020) and a PSR must be adopted (Smith, 2024), ineffectiveness is heard on direct appeal only if conclusive on the record (Kemp, 2023), and instructions and prosecutorial remarks are reviewed under set tests (Lighty 2010, Benson 2020). Also: Jardines (2013) treats a dog sniff on a porch as a search. No rule change appears within this one slice.
rule: Testimonial out-of-court statements are inadmissible unless the declarant is unavailable and the defendant had a prior chance to cross-examine (Crawford), and a non-testifying codefendant's confession naming the defendant cannot be admitted at a joint trial (Bruton) unless redacted with a limiting instruction (Marsh).

changes.case: Bruton v. United States; Richardson v. Marsh
changes.what: A non-testifying codefendant's incriminating confession violates confrontation; redaction plus a limiting instruction cures it.
Mutually antagonistic defences are not prejudicial per se and do not mandate severance.

changes.case: Crawford v. Washington; Davis v. Washington
changes.what: Testimonial statements require unavailability and prior cross-examination; statements are testimonial when their primary purpose is to establish past events for prosecution.

changes.case: Roper v. Simmons; Graham v. Florida; Miller v. Alabama
changes.what: The Eighth Amendment bars executing juveniles, life without parole for juvenile nonhomicide offenders, and mandatory LWOP for juvenile murderers; Graham anchors the slice.

name: Federal fee-shifting and sanctions 1980-2004: Hensley lodestar, Rule 11, Chambers
description: Federal fee-shifting under the American Rule (Alyeska 1975), 1980-2004, together with sanctions: a § 1988 prevailing party recovers a lodestar cut for limited success (Hensley 1983, anchor 1985-99; Blum 1984); Cooter & Gell (1990) set abuse-of-discretion review of Rule 11 rulings and Chambers (1991) confirmed inherent-power sanctions. In 2000-04 Browder (1978) on appeal deadlines anchors as class-certification cases (Amchem 1997) join.

previous.name: Attorney's fees and sanctions
previous.description: Fee-shifting and sanctions: the American Rule (Alyeska), § 1988 lodestar and prevailing-party status (Hensley, Blum, Farrar, Texas Teachers), Rule 11 (Cooter & Gell) and inherent-power sanctions (Chambers).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: under the American Rule (Alyeska, 1975) fees shift only by statute or the court's inherent power, and under § 1988 the court computes a lodestar of reasonable hours times the market rate (Blum, 1984), reduced for limited success (Hensley, 1983). How it changed: in 1980-84 Nadeau v. Helgemoe (1st Cir. 1978) anchors with Maher (1980), Christiansburg (1978) and the Johnson factors (1974), on who prevails. Hensley anchors 1985-89 through 1995-99; Delaware Valley (1986) enters, and Rule 11 cases such as Zaldivar (9th Cir.) appear. In 1990-94 Cooter & Gell (1990) made abuse of discretion the standard for all aspects of Rule 11 rulings, Texas Teachers (1989) required a change in the parties' legal relationship, Blanchard (1989) refused to cap fees at a contingency agreement, and Chambers (1991) confirmed inherent-power sanctions; Farrar (1992) made nominal damages enough to prevail but allowed a low or no fee. Browder (1978) and Robinson (1960), on mandatory appeal deadlines, rise from 1995-99, and Browder anchors 2000-04 as class-certification cases (Amchem 1997, Falcon 1982, Castano, and Texas cases such as Bernal 2000) enter beside Buckhannon (2001), which rejected the catalyst theory. That last slice is drift.
rule: Under the American Rule fees shift only by statute or inherent power; a § 1988 prevailing party recovers a lodestar fee reduced for limited success, and fee and sanction rulings are reviewed for abuse of discretion.

changes.case: Alyeska Pipeline Service Co. v. Wilderness Society
changes.what: Absent statute, courts may not shift fees on a private-attorney-general theory.

changes.case: Hensley v. Eckerhart; Blum v. Stenson
changes.what: The § 1988 fee is a lodestar at market rates, reduced for limited success.

changes.case: Texas State Teachers Ass'n v. Garland ISD; Farrar v. Hobby
changes.what: Prevailing requires a material change in the parties' legal relationship; nominal damages suffice but may warrant a low or no fee.
All aspects of a Rule 11 determination are reviewed for abuse of discretion.
Federal courts may award fees as a sanction under their inherent power for bad-faith conduct.

changes.case: Buckhannon Board & Care Home v. West Virginia DHHR
changes.what: A plaintiff whose suit merely caused a voluntary change is not a prevailing party; the catalyst theory is rejected.

before_differentiation.name: Federal fee-shifting: § 1988 lodestar and prevailing party (Hensley, Farrar)
before_differentiation.description: Fee-shifting under the American Rule (Alyeska, 1975): under § 1988 a prevailing party recovers a lodestar adjusted for success (Hensley, 1983, anchor throughout; Blum). Farrar (1992) made nominal damages enough to prevail; Buckhannon (2001) rejected the catalyst theory. Also Rule 11 review (Cooter & Gell, 1990) and inherent-power sanctions (Chambers, 1991).

distinct_from.how: Ends in 2004 and mixes § 1988 fees with Rule 11 and inherent-power sanctions, drifting to appeal deadlines and class certification; the sub-cluster stays on civil-rights fee awards from 1980 to 2024, through Buckhannon and Perdue.

name: Warren Court criminal procedure family, 1970-84: Miranda anchor and its limits
description: The 1970-84 criminal-procedure family built on the Warren Court, anchored on Miranda (1966) in every slice: custodial statements need warnings and waiver, with Chapman (1967) harmless error, Bruton (1968), Gideon and lineup cases (Wade, Stovall, Simmons). The 1970s limit and refine Miranda (Harris, 1971; Mosley, 1975; Doyle, 1976), add plea rules (Boykin, Brady) and in 1980-84 Innis and Edwards (1981). Splits from 1985-89.

history: Dominant rule: Miranda (1966), the anchor in all three slices, bars the prosecution's use of statements from custodial interrogation unless the suspect was warned and knowingly waived his rights, and Chapman (1967) requires reversal of constitutional error unless it was harmless beyond a reasonable doubt. How it changed: in 1970-74 the unit merges the late-1960s doctrines: Escobedo and Johnson v. New Jersey (Miranda applied only to later trials), Jackson v. Denno (1964) on a separate voluntariness hearing, Bruton (1968) on codefendant confessions, Wade, Gilbert and Stovall (1967) and Simmons (1968) on identifications, and Gideon and Zerbst on counsel. In 1975-79 the Burger Court limits enter: Harris (1971) allows impeachment with unwarned statements, Mosley (1975) lets police resume after honouring silence, and Doyle (1976) forbids using post-warning silence; Boykin, McCarthy and Brady v. United States set plea rules, and Faretta (1975) self-representation. In 1980-84 Biggers and Manson add reliability for identifications, Brewer (1977) fixes attachment of counsel, and Innis (1980), Edwards (1981) and Ohio v. Roberts (1980) appear, along with hypnosis and Frye cases. The unit splits in 1985-89.
rule: Statements from custodial interrogation are inadmissible in the prosecution's case unless the suspect was warned and validly waived his rights (Miranda), and constitutional trial errors require reversal unless harmless beyond a reasonable doubt (Chapman).

name: Oregon appellate method: PGE/Gaines statutory construction and Ailes plain error
description: Oregon appellate method, 2005-29: statutes construed by text and context with legislative history (PGE, 1993, anchor 2005-09; Gaines, 2009, anchor 2015-24), and unpreserved error corrected only as discretionary plain error (Ailes, 1991; Vanornum, 2013, anchor 2025-29). Search and seizure under Article I, section 9 runs alongside (Hall, 2005, anchor 2010-14; Rodgers, 2010), and Ramos (2020) ended nonunanimous verdicts.
history: Dominant rule: how the Oregon courts read statutes and review unpreserved error. PGE (1993) anchors 2005-09: text and context first, legislative history only if needed, then maxims (Stamper, 2005). How it changed: Gaines (2009) let courts consult legislative history at the first step whether or not the text is ambiguous; it anchors 2015-19 and 2020-24 (Cloutier, 2011). Ailes (1991) requires a stated discretionary decision to correct plain error, Wyatt (2000) and Peeples (2008) police preservation, and Vanornum (2013), which anchors 2025-29, requires error obvious and not reasonably in dispute; Chitwood (2022) applies it to prosecutorial statements. Davis (2003) sets the harmless-error test. Alongside: search and seizure under Article I, section 9: Hall (2005), anchor 2010-14, treats retaining identification for a warrant check as a seizure; Rodgers/Kirkeby (2010) bar extending a completed traffic stop with unrelated questions; Ashbaugh (2010) dropped the subjective-belief component of seizure; Ehly (1993) governs review of suppression findings. Ramos (2020) enters in 2020-24, requiring unanimous verdicts and unsettling Oregon convictions.
rule: Oregon courts discern legislative intent from text and context, with legislative history given the weight it deserves and maxims used only if intent remains unclear (PGE, Gaines), and review unpreserved error only if it is plain and the court chooses to exercise its discretion to correct it (Ailes).

changes.what: Even plain error is corrected only through a discretionary decision the court must explain.

name: Double jeopardy 1990-99: Grady/Dixon same offense, then Halper civil sanctions
description: Double jeopardy, 1990-99, in two phases. Grady (1990) anchors 1990-94 with a same-conduct bar on successive prosecutions that Dixon (1993) overruled, restoring Blockburger's same-elements test. Halper (1989) anchors 1995-99 as courts ask whether civil penalties, forfeitures (Austin 1993) and drug taxes (Kurth Ranch 1994) are punishment; Ursery (1996) exempted civil forfeiture and Hudson (1997) overruled Halper in part.
history: Dominant rule: when a second prosecution or sanction is for the 'same offence'. How it changed: in 1990-94 Grady v. Corbin (1990) anchors with Blockburger (1931), Brown (1977) on lesser included offenses, Vitale (1980) and Pearce (1969) on harsher sentences after retrial. Grady added a same-conduct test for successive prosecutions; Dixon (1993) overruled it, leaving same elements as the only test, and Felix (1992) held a crime and a conspiracy to commit it are not the same offense. Hunter (1983) and Garrett (1985) let clear legislative intent authorise cumulative punishment. The dominant question then shifts: Halper (1989) anchors 1995-99, where civil penalties, drug forfeitures (Austin 1993, $405,089.23 (9th Cir. 1994)) and Montana's drug tax (Kurth Ranch 1994) were treated as punishment, until Ursery (1996) held in rem civil forfeitures are not punishment and Hudson (1997) overruled Halper in part. Also: collateral estoppel (Ashe), implied acquittal (Green), and Ex Post Facto cases (Collins, Weaver).
rule: Two offenses are the same for double jeopardy only if they fail Blockburger's same-elements test, and a civil sanction counts as a second punishment only when it is punitive in purpose or effect.

changes.what: Offenses are distinct when each requires proof of an element the other does not.
Added a same-conduct bar to successive prosecutions; Grady anchors 1990-94.
Overruled Grady's same-conduct test; same-elements is the only test.
A civil penalty, a drug forfeiture (under the Excessive Fines Clause) or a drug tax can be punishment; Halper anchors 1995-99.
In rem civil forfeitures are neither punishment nor criminal for double jeopardy purposes.
Overruled Halper in part, returning to the Kennedy v. Mendoza-Martinez test of legislative intent and punitive effect.

description: Umbrella lineage, 1970-2004, whose anchor shifts: school-desegregation remedies (Green 1968, Swann 1971) in 1970-74; Griggs (1971) disparate impact in 1975-79; then from 1980 McDonnell Douglas (1973) burden-shifting, refined by Burdine (1981), Aikens (1983), Hicks (1993) and Reeves (2000), and decided under the 1986 summary-judgment trilogy, with harassment rules from Meritor, Harris and Faragher.

history: Dominant rule: across most of the span, the McDonnell Douglas (1973) framework for proving intentional discrimination, anchor in every slice from 1980-84 to 2000-04. How it changed: in 1970-74 Green (1968) anchors with Swann (1971), Alexander (1969) and Carter (1970), imposing an immediate duty to dismantle dual school systems. Griggs (1971) anchors 1975-79 as Title VII takes over: neutral practices with disparate effects need business necessity; Albemarle (1975) presumes back pay, Franks (1976) allows retroactive seniority, and Teamsters (1977) sets pattern-or-practice proof, while Washington v. Davis (1976) keeps intent for constitutional claims. From 1980-84 McDonnell Douglas anchors, with Burdine (1981) making the employer's burden one of production, Pullman-Standard (1982) and Anderson (1985) on clear-error review, and Aikens (1983). In 1990-94 an antitrust unit merges and the 1986 summary-judgment trilogy (Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Celotex, Matsushita) leads as Hicks (1993) holds that disbelief of the employer's reason permits but does not compel a finding of discrimination. In 1995-99 harassment law joins (Meritor 1986, Harris 1993, Faragher and Ellerth 1998). Reeves (2000) enters in 2000-04; Ohio's Dresher (1996) and patent claim-construction cases (Markman) are drift.
rule: A Title VII plaintiff without direct evidence makes a prima facie case, the employer articulates a legitimate nondiscriminatory reason, and the plaintiff must show that reason is a pretext for discrimination, decided under the summary-judgment standards of the 1986 trilogy.

name: West Virginia appellate review: summary judgment, then abuse-and-neglect cases
description: West Virginia's highest court. In 1995-2004 Painter (1994) anchors civil review: summary judgment viewed for the nonmovant, de novo review of law (Chrystal R.M. 1995, anchor 2005-09). From 2010-14 abuse-and-neglect cases dominate: clear-error review (Tiffany Marie S. 1996), discretionary improvement periods (Katie S.; Timber M. 2013), permanency first (Cecil T. 2011), and Edward Charles L. (1990), anchor 2015-24.
history: Dominant rule: the West Virginia Supreme Court of Appeals' standards of review, applied first to civil judgments and then, from 2010-14, chiefly to child abuse-and-neglect appeals. How it changed: Painter v. Peavy (1994) anchors 1995-99 and 2000-04, with Williams v. Precision Coil (1995) and Andrick (1992) on summary judgment and Burnside (1995) on family law masters. Chrystal R.M. (1995), setting de novo review for questions of law, anchors 2005-09. From 2010-14 the anchor moves to In Interest of Tiffany Marie S. (1996), clear-error review of abuse-and-neglect findings, and to State v. Edward Charles L. (1990), admitting other-acts evidence of lustful disposition in child sexual-abuse cases, in 2015-19 and 2020-24. The abuse-and-neglect rules: R.J.M. (1980) on least restrictive alternatives and termination; Katie S. (1996), Charity H. (2004), Timber M. (2013) and M.M. (2015) on discretionary improvement periods; Emily (2000) barring them after abandonment; Cecil T. (2011), anchor in 2025-29, making permanency paramount; Kristin Y. (2011) on termination; K.H. (2015) on psychological parents. Also: Guthrie (1995) on sufficiency of evidence and Miners (1941) on plain meaning.
rule: The West Virginia Supreme Court of Appeals reviews legal questions de novo and findings for clear error (Chrystal R.M.; Tiffany Marie S.); in abuse-and-neglect cases the child's welfare and permanency are paramount, improvement periods are discretionary, and parental rights may be terminated where conditions cannot be substantially corrected.

history: Dominant rule: the Appellate Division reviews both legal sufficiency (Contes, 1983) and, as a separate factual power, the weight of the evidence (Bleakley, 1987). How it changed: Pellegrino (1983) anchors 1985-89, and Contes anchors 1990-94 through 2000-04. Bleakley takes over in 2005-14, and Danielson (2007) anchors from 2015-19 to the partial 2025-29 slice, holding that a legally sufficient verdict may be against the weight of the evidence measured against the elements as charged. Preservation narrowed: Gray (1995) required a sufficiency motion specifically directed at the error, and Hawkins (2008) held a general motion insufficient. Appeal waivers became central: Seaberg (1989) and Callahan (1992) enforced knowing and voluntary waivers, Lopez (2006) accepted an oral colloquy, and Bradshaw (2011) rejected one where the defendant never showed he grasped the right. Also: meaningful representation under Baldi (1981) and Benevento (1998), harmless error under Crimmins (1975), and the Appellate Division's interest-of-justice sentence reduction under Suitte (1982).
rule: New York appellate courts test legal sufficiency by whether any rational juror could find the elements proved, viewing the evidence most favourably to the People (Contes), and separately review the weight of the evidence as an independent fact-finding power (Bleakley), with sufficiency claims preserved only by a specifically directed motion.

name: California search and seizure in the 1960s: probable cause and consent (Ingle)
description: California search-and-seizure law of the early 1960s, after the state's 1955 exclusionary rule. Ingle (1960) anchors both slices: reasonable cause to arrest may rest on information not admissible at trial. People v. Michael, Gorg, Martin and Simon (1955) set consent and cause standards; Blodgett (1956) on furtive conduct and Cruz (1964) on the scope of consent follow.
history: Dominant rule: a warrantless arrest or search in California needed reasonable cause known to the officer beforehand or a valid consent, and an arrest could not be justified by what the search turned up (Simon 1955). Ingle (1960) anchors both slices, 1960-64 and 1965-69, holding that reasonable cause is not limited to evidence admissible at trial. How it changed: the 1955 cases that followed California's adoption of the exclusionary rule lead in 1960-64: Michael and Gorg on consent and its voluntariness, Martin, and Fischer (1957). Willson (1956) and Blodgett (1956) assess cause from furtive movements in narcotics stops. In 1965-69 Mickelson (1963) and Torres (1961) join the core and Cockrell (1965), Reeves (1964), Cedeno (1963) and Cruz (1964) enter, refining consent, ruses to gain entry, and whose property a consent covers. The holdings evidence is thin for several leading cases. The lineage then rejoins the general Fourth Amendment cluster in 1970-74.
rule: Under California's judicially created exclusionary rule, a warrantless arrest or search was lawful only on reasonable cause known to the officer beforehand, which could rest on information not admissible at trial, or on a voluntary consent by a person apparently entitled to give it.

name: Pennsylvania Commonwealth Court: Election Code, RTKL and workers' compensation
description: Pennsylvania Commonwealth Court in 2020-24, anchored by Bowling (2013) on de novo Right-to-Know Law review: agencies must prove exemptions with more than conclusory affidavits. history: Dominant rule: Bowling (2013) anchors this single 2020-24 slice of Commonwealth Court administrative and election law. Under the 2008 Right-to-Know Law, which broadened access, courts review agency decisions de novo and may expand the record; an agency cannot meet its burden with a conclusory affidavit (2017), and trooper recordings on public roads are not 'oral communications' (2017). Election Code cases, many from the 2020 election litigation, revive older rules: courts construe election laws liberally so technicalities do not defeat voters (James, 1954; Ross, 1963), void ballots for irregularities only sparingly (Bauman, 1944), and do not invalidate ballots for ink colour without fraud (Wieskerger, 1972); but mandatory requirements such as in-person delivery of absentee ballots are enforced (2004). Workers' compensation: the WCJ is the exclusive arbiter of credibility (Daniels 2003; Dorsey 2006), substantial evidence means any supporting evidence (Hoffmaster, 1998), and Protz (2017) struck the AMA Guides delegation, with Whitfield (2018) on reinstatement. Also: Robinson Township (2013) and the single-subject rule (2003).
rule: The Pennsylvania Commonwealth Court construes the Election Code liberally to protect candidates' and voters' rights while enforcing mandatory requirements, reads the Right-to-Know Law to favour access with the agency bearing the burden of proving exemptions, and defers to the workers' compensation judge as exclusive arbiter of credibility.

name: Pennsylvania PCRA: Brady disclosure claims and Turner/Finley withdrawal
description: Pennsylvania PCRA appeals in the partial 2025-29 slice, anchored by Turner/Finley (1988) and led by Brady (1963): suppressing favourable, material evidence violates due process, including impeachment (Giglio 1972, Bagley 1985), police-held evidence (Kyles 1995) and perjury (Napue 1959); materiality is a reasonable probability (Strickler 1999). Untimely petitions fail, and unrelated misconduct reports are not new facts (2015, 2023).
history: Dominant rule: Turner and Finley (1988) anchor this single partial 2025-29 slice, which merged from the no-merit appeals cluster, and Brady v. Maryland (1963) is its heaviest case. Brady and Giglio (1972) require disclosure of evidence favourable to the defence, including impeachment of key witnesses; Bagley (1985) sets materiality as a reasonable probability of a different result, Kyles (1995) extends the duty to evidence held only by police and assesses materiality cumulatively, and Strickler (1999) restates the three components; Napue (1959) bars knowingly using perjured testimony. How it applies: these claims arrive through the PCRA, whose time-bar is jurisdictional (2010); newspaper accounts of detective misconduct in unrelated cases are not newly discovered facts (2015, 2023), and after-discovered evidence fails if credible evidence undermines it (2019). Ineffectiveness claims fail if any prong is unproven (2014, 2019), though misadvice about plea consequences is ineffective (2013) and failing to challenge novel expert science can have arguable merit (2020). Also: inevitable discovery via inventory search (2021) and Ohio leave requirements for new-trial motions (Bethel, 2022).
rule: The prosecution violates due process by suppressing evidence favourable to the accused, including impeachment evidence and evidence known only to police, when it is material, meaning a reasonable probability of a different result; in Pennsylvania such claims arise mostly on PCRA review, where timeliness is jurisdictional and counsel may withdraw by a Turner/Finley no-merit letter.

changes.case: Brady v. Maryland; Giglio v. United States; Napue v. Illinois (1959)
changes.what: Suppression of favourable, material evidence violates due process; impeachment evidence of a key witness counts; knowing use of perjury is a due-process violation.

name: Categorical approach to prior convictions under the ACCA (Taylor, Shepard, Descamps)
description: A 2010-14 cluster anchored by Taylor (1990): prior convictions qualify as ACCA violent felonies or immigration and Guidelines predicates by their elements, not conduct, with Shepard (2005) documents for divisible statutes and Descamps (2013) barring the modified approach for indivisible ones. The residual clause was read through James (2007), Begay (2008), Chambers (2009) and Sykes (2011); Johnson (2010) required violent force.
history: Dominant rule: the categorical approach. Taylor (1990) anchors the only slice, 2010-14, split from the federal sentencing and Apprendi/Booker lineage: a prior conviction counts only if its elements match the generic offense, and courts look to the statute rather than the facts. Shepard (2005) limits the modified categorical approach to charging documents, plea agreements and colloquies, and Descamps (2013) forbids it for indivisible statutes. How it changed: the residual clause of the ACCA was repeatedly reinterpreted. James (2007) brought attempted burglary within it under an ordinary-case risk inquiry; Begay (2008) confined it to purposeful, violent and aggressive crimes, excluding felony DUI; Chambers (2009) excluded failure to report; Sykes (2011) included vehicular flight. Johnson v. United States (2010) held that physical force in the elements clause means violent force, as a matter of federal law. Alongside: immigration uses of the same approach, with Duenas-Alvarez (2007) on generic theft and the realistic-probability test, Nijhawan (2009) allowing a circumstance-specific inquiry for loss amounts, Leocal (2004) and Estrada-Espinoza (2008); Woods (2009) excluded reckless involuntary manslaughter. The unit rejoins the sentencing lineage in 2015-19.
rule: Whether a prior conviction counts as a violent felony or other predicate offense is decided categorically, by comparing the statutory elements with the generic offense rather than the defendant's conduct, with the modified categorical approach and Shepard documents used only for divisible statutes (Taylor, Shepard, Descamps).

changes.what: Burglary under the ACCA means generic burglary, judged by a categorical rather than factual approach.
A crime of violence requires more than negligent conduct; DUI causing injury does not qualify, and dual-use statutes are read consistently.
For pleaded convictions courts may look only to the charging document, plea agreement, colloquy and similar records.

changes.what: Attempted burglary fits the residual clause, but it reaches only purposeful, violent and aggressive crimes, excluding felony DUI.

changes.what: Failure to report is not a violent felony; some statutory qualifiers call for a circumstance-specific rather than categorical inquiry.

changes.case: Johnson v. United States; Sykes v. United States
changes.what: Physical force means violent force, so simple battery does not qualify; vehicular flight is a violent felony under the residual clause.

name: Minnesota criminal appeals: plain error (Griller, Ramey) and circumstantial evidence
description: Minnesota criminal appeals. Plain-error review leads 2010-19: unobjected error is reversed only if plain and affecting substantial rights (Griller 1998, anchor 2010-14), with Ramey (2006, anchor 2015-19) governing unobjected prosecutorial misconduct. From 2020-24 Harris (2017) anchors and circumstantial-evidence sufficiency leads (Andersen 2010, Silvernail 2013), with deference to the factfinder on credibility (Al-Naseer 2010).
history: Dominant rule: Minnesota standards for appellate review of criminal convictions. Griller (1998) anchors 2010-14: unobjected error is reviewed for plain error and reversed only if it affected substantial rights. Ramey (2006) anchors 2015-19 and adapts the test for prosecutorial misconduct, balancing fair trials the first time around against obvious injustice; Carridine (2012) applies a modified plain-error test to jury selection, and Milton (2012) shows an error is not plain where the law was not yet clear. How it changed: from 2020-24 Harris (2017) anchors, and circumstantial-evidence review leads: courts defer to the jury on the circumstances proved (Andersen, 2010), review them as a whole (Silvernail, 2013), view evidence for the verdict (Webb, 1989) and leave credibility to the factfinder (Al-Naseer, 2010). Also: issues not raised below are not considered (Thiele, 1988), Spreigl (1965) other-crimes evidence, Amos (2003) unavailability, dispositional departures (Soto, 2014; Kindem, 1981), and a 2015-19 strand on termination of parental rights (J.R.B. 2011, T.R. 2008).
rule: Minnesota appellate courts reverse for unobjected-to error only if it is plain and affected substantial rights (Griller), shifting to the State the burden on prejudice for unobjected prosecutorial misconduct (Ramey), and test circumstantial-evidence convictions by deferring to the circumstances proved and then asking whether they are consistent only with guilt.

changes.what: Unobjected error is reversed only if it is plain error affecting substantial rights; anchors 2010-14.
For unobjected prosecutorial misconduct the defendant shows plain error and the State must then show no effect on substantial rights; anchors 2015-19.

changes.case: State v. Andersen; State v. Al-Naseer; State v. Silvernail
changes.what: Circumstantial evidence is reviewed as a whole, deferring to the jury's acceptance of the circumstances proved.

name: Speedy trial 2025-29 (partial): Barker, Brillon, Texas preservation (Henson)
description: Speedy-trial claims in the partial 2025-29 slice, after the New Mexico appeals split away, anchored by Barker v. Wingo (1972): balance delay, reasons, assertion and prejudice. Doggett (1992) presumes prejudice from long negligent delay; Brillon (2009) charges defence-caused delay to the defendant. Texas courts dominate: Shaw (2003) and Cantu (2008) on triggering delay and dismissal, Balderas (2016), Henson (2013) on preservation.
history: Dominant rule: Barker v. Wingo (1972) anchors this single partial 2025-29 slice, carried over from a 2020-24 speedy-trial unit: courts weigh the length of delay, the reason for it, the defendant's assertion of the right and the resulting prejudice, and the main burden to bring cases to trial is on courts and prosecutors. The right attaches only at accusation (Marion, 1971) and applies to the states through the Fourteenth Amendment. Doggett (1992) holds that long government negligence can violate it without bad intent; Brillon (2009) charges delay caused by the defence, or a defendant's disruption, against him, while a court's failure to replace counsel promptly counts against the State. How it applies in Texas, the bulk of the slice: delay approaching a year triggers analysis (Shaw, 2003), crowded dockets weigh against the State but not heavily, a 17-month delay is presumptively prejudicial and dismissal with prejudice follows only an actual violation (Cantu, 2008), good-faith plea talks do not count against the State (Munoz, 1999), the defendant's request for delay extenuates prejudice (Balderas, 2016), anxiety evidence can show prejudice (Zamorano, 2002), and the claim must be preserved (Henson 2013; Dragoo 2003).
rule: Whether the Sixth Amendment speedy-trial right was violated is decided by balancing the length of delay, the reason for it, the defendant's assertion of the right and prejudice (Barker), with delay approaching a year triggering the inquiry and dismissal with prejudice the remedy for a violation.

changes.what: The speedy-trial right attaches only on accusation; pre-indictment delay does not violate the Sixth Amendment.
Four-factor balancing test; the primary burden to bring cases to trial is on courts and prosecutors. Anchors the slice.
Long government negligence can violate the right without intent to harm, with prejudice presumed from excessive delay.
Delay caused by defence counsel or the defendant's disruption weighs against the defendant.
Preservation requirements apply to speedy-trial claims.

name: Massachusetts appeals family: Latimore sufficiency, then parental-unfitness appeals
description: The Massachusetts appellate family, 2010-29, shifting from criminal to family law: Latimore (1979, anchor 2015-19) sufficiency review leads 2010-19 alongside Saferian ineffectiveness; from 2020-24 care-and-protection and adoption appeals lead (Adoption of Ilona 2011, Adoption of Nancy 2005, Custody of Eleanor 1993: unfitness by clear and convincing evidence, deference to the judge, best interests), with Chace (2008) anchoring.
history: Dominant rule: Massachusetts appellate standards of review. In 2010-14 and 2015-19 the criminal cases lead: Latimore (1979) asks whether any rational factfinder could find every element beyond a reasonable doubt, Saferian (1974) sets the ordinary-fallible-lawyer test for ineffective assistance, and new-trial motions on newly discovered evidence require evidence unknown and not reasonably discoverable (1986). How it changed: from 2015-19 family cases enter, led by Adoption of Ilona (2011), which holds that the judge must rule in the child's best interests even when DCF failed to make reasonable efforts, and 2014 abuse-of-discretion review ('a clear error of judgment'). In 2020-24 the anchor moves to Chace (2008; unpublished decisions persuasive, not binding), with Adoption of Nancy (2005), Custody of Eleanor (1993: unfitness needs clear and convincing evidence) and sex-offender registry review (Doe, 2019); the partial 2025-29 slice drifts to mixed civil appeals (Iannacchino 2008, Curtis 2011).
rule: Massachusetts appellate courts test convictions for sufficiency under Latimore and ineffective assistance under Saferian, and in care-and-protection and adoption appeals defer to the judge's credibility findings while requiring parental unfitness by clear and convincing evidence and decisions in the child's best interests.

changes.what: Ineffective assistance requires conduct below that of an ordinary fallible lawyer that likely deprived the defendant of an available, substantial defence.
Sufficiency review asks whether any rational trier of fact could find each element beyond a reasonable doubt, conforming to Jackson v. Virginia.
Even where DCF failed to make reasonable efforts under G. L. c. 119, § 29C, the judge must rule in the child's best interests; enters 2015-19 and leads from 2020-24.

history: Dominant rule: speedy-trial claims are resolved by Barker v. Wingo's (1972) balancing of length of delay, reasons, assertion of the right and prejudice. Barker anchors 1990-94 and 2005-09 through 2020-24. How it changed: Mississippi capital cases (Neal, 1984) anchor 1985-89. Marion (1971) and Lovasco (1977) confine the Sixth Amendment right to post-accusation delay. Doggett (1992) held that long delay from government negligence can be presumptively prejudicial. The dominant rule shifts in 1995-99 and 2000-04, when Batson (1986) anchors after an Illinois jury-selection group merges in: Hernandez (1991) on deference to intent findings and disparate impact, Powers (1991), J.E.B. (1994) extending Batson to sex, and Purkett (1995) holding that a race-neutral reason need not be plausible at step two. name: Ohio summary judgment, 2005-09 cluster: open-and-obvious premises, Galatis
description: The one-slice 2005-09 Ohio cluster: the Dresher (1996) burdens and de novo review (Grafton 1996) applied mostly to premises liability, where owners owe no duty to warn of open and obvious dangers (Sidle 1968, unique here; Armstrong 2003), and to products duty to warn (Temple 1977), legal malpractice (Vahila 1997) and insurance coverage (Galatis 2003, overruling Ezawa).
history: Dominant rule: Ohio summary-judgment practice. Dresher v. Burt (1996) anchors the only slice, 2005-09, formed when Title VII and Ohio criminal-appeal units merged in: the movant bears an initial burden to identify record evidence showing no genuine issue on the elements of the nonmovant's claim, and the nonmovant then has a reciprocal burden to set out specific facts showing a triable issue. Harless (1978) states the three-part standard, Grafton (1996) sets de novo appellate review, Murphy (1992) requires the trial court to decide the motion itself, and Mitseff (1988) bars adding a ground for summary judgment on appeal. Alongside, the substantive settings: premises owners owe no duty to warn of open and obvious dangers (Sidle, 1968; Paschal, 1985; Armstrong, 2003); Temple (1977) adopted § 402A and limited the duty to warn about components; Vahila (1997) extended Krahn's malpractice-harm rule to civil cases; Brown (1993) addressed trespass by emissions; and Galatis (2003) overruled Ezawa on coverage of employees under corporate policies. The unit continues into 2010-14 as a separate lineage.
rule: Under Ohio Civ.R. 56 the movant must identify the parts of the record showing no genuine issue on the elements it challenges, the nonmovant must then set out specific facts showing a genuine issue for trial, and appellate courts review the ruling de novo (Dresher, Harless, Grafton).

changes.what: Summary judgment requires no genuine issue of material fact, entitlement to judgment as a matter of law, and that reasonable minds can reach only a conclusion adverse to the nonmovant.
A motion must specify its grounds; the nonmovant is not on notice that the whole claim is challenged.
The trial court must make the initial Civ.R. 56 determination; appellate review cannot replace it.

changes.case: Dresher v. Burt; Grafton v. Ohio Edison
changes.what: The movant bears an initial burden of pointing to record evidence, and the nonmovant has a reciprocal burden to show specific facts; review is de novo.

name: Labor law 1950-69: picketing, Garmon preemption, then § 301 and the Trilogy
description: Federal labor law in court. The cluster moves from picketing as speech (Giboney 1949, anchor 1950-54) to NLRA preemption (Garner 1954, Garmon 1959, anchor 1955-59) to its main phase, § 301 enforcement of collective agreements: Lincoln Mills (1957) and the Steelworkers Trilogy (1960, anchor 1960-69) presume arbitrability and bar courts from weighing the merits; Maddox (1965) and Vaca (1967) follow.
history: Dominant rule: from 1960 the cluster centers on § 301 of the LMRA. Lincoln Mills (1957) made collective agreements and arbitration promises enforceable under federal law, and the Steelworkers Trilogy (1960), anchoring 1960-69, presumes arbitrability, keeps courts out of the merits and enforces awards that draw their essence from the agreement. How it changed: the anchor moves across doctrines. In 1950-54 Giboney (1949) anchors with Thornhill (1940), Gazzam and Hughes (1950): picketing is partly speech but may be enjoined for unlawful objectives. In 1955-59 Garner (1954) anchors the preemption cases, Weber (1955), Guss (1957) and Garmon (1959), which bar state regulation of conduct arguably within §§ 7 or 8, with Laburnum (1954) allowing state tort damages. In 1960-69 Lucas Flour and Evening News (1962) require federal law in § 301 suits and let employees sue; Maddox (1965) requires exhaustion of grievance procedures; Steele (1944) and Vaca (1967) add the duty of fair representation. The cluster then passes into the general NLRA lineage.
rule: Collective bargaining agreements are enforced in court under § 301 of the LMRA by federal law; disputes are presumed arbitrable unless clearly excluded, and courts enforce awards that draw their essence from the agreement without weighing the merits.

changes.case: Thornhill v. Alabama; Giboney v. Empire Storage; Hughes v. Superior Court; Building Service Employees v. Gazzam
changes.what: Peaceful picketing is partly protected speech, but states may enjoin picketing aimed at an unlawful end or contrary to valid state policy.

changes.what: State regulation of conduct arguably protected or prohibited by §§ 7 or 8 of the NLRA is preempted, even where the Board declines jurisdiction.
Section 301 makes collective agreements, including promises to arbitrate, enforceable under federal law.

changes.case: Steelworkers v. American Mfg.; Steelworkers v. Warrior & Gulf; Steelworkers v. Enterprise Wheel
changes.what: Doubts are resolved in favor of arbitration, courts do not weigh the merits, and awards drawing their essence from the agreement are enforced.

history: Dominant rule: State v. Golding (1989) anchors every slice from 1990-94 to 2015-19: an unpreserved claim is reviewable only if the record is adequate, the claim is constitutional, the violation clearly exists and deprived the defendant of a fair trial, and it was not harmless. It built on State v. Evans (1973). How it changed: in 1990-94, after a merge with federal trial cases, the leaders are the federal rights such claims invoke: Brady (1963), Agurs (1976) and Bagley (1985) on disclosure, and Roberts (1980), Davis (1974) and Van Arsdall (1986) on confrontation. In 2000-04 a merge with double-jeopardy cases brings ex post facto and punishment rules (Collins, 1990, overruling Kring; Weaver, 1981; Hendricks and Hudson, 1997). From 2005-09 Connecticut cases lead: State v. Williams (1987) factors for prosecutorial impropriety, Stevenson (2004) and Fabricatore (2007) on waiver of instruction claims. Kitchens (2011) held that accepting instructions after a meaningful opportunity to review them waives Golding review, overruling Ebron in part. Salamon (2008) narrowed kidnapping to restraint beyond that incidental to another crime.
rule: A Connecticut defendant may obtain review of an unpreserved claim only if the record is adequate, the claim is of constitutional magnitude, the violation clearly exists and deprived the defendant of a fair trial, and the State cannot show it harmless (State v. Golding).

changes.what: Review of unpreserved claims in exceptional circumstances where the record shows a clear deprivation of a fundamental constitutional right.

name: Florida guidelines departures and ex post facto (Albritton, Miller v. Florida)
description: Florida's sentencing guidelines in 1985-89: departures need written, valid reasons not already scored (Hendrix, Jackson 1985), and Albritton (1985, anchor) requires resentencing unless the court would have departed on valid reasons alone; Mischler and Whitehead (1986) barred remorse and habitual-offender grounds. Miller v. Florida (1987), building on Weaver (1981), barred retroactive harsher guidelines as ex post facto.
history: Dominant rule: Albritton (Fla. 1985), anchor of the single slice (1985-89), governs appellate review of guidelines departures: when some reasons are invalid, the sentence is remanded unless the State shows beyond a reasonable doubt that the judge would have departed on the valid reasons alone. Hendrix (1985) barred departures on factors already weighed in the presumptive score, and State v. Jackson (1985) required written reasons. How it changed: the Florida Supreme Court policed departure reasons in 1986: Mischler barred inferring lack of remorse from exercising constitutional rights, Whitehead held habitual-offender status cannot support departure, and Scurry addressed other reasons. Florida (1987) held that applying amended guidelines raising the presumptive range to earlier crimes is ex post facto. Marks (1977) adds the due-process bar on retroactive judicial expansion. The cluster splits three ways in 1990-94.

name: New federalism: commerce power (Lopez) and state sovereign immunity (Seminole)
description: The Rehnquist Court's federalism revival, 1995-99 only: Lopez (1995, anchor) set limits on the commerce power; Seminole Tribe (1996) barred abrogation of state immunity under Article I; Boerne (1997) confined § 5 legislation. Eleventh Amendment basics (Hans, Ex parte Young, Edelman, Pennhurst, Scanlon) and anti-commandeering (New York 1992) anchor the rest. Circuits upheld the Hobbs Act after Lopez (Bolton 1995).
history: Dominant rule: the federal government is one of enumerated powers, and courts enforce limits on Congress in favour of the states. The lineage is a single 1995-99 cluster anchored by Lopez (1995), formed from merging units and later splitting into arbitration and public-law clusters. How it developed: the post-1937 view of the commerce power (Perez 1971; Hodel 1981; Garcia 1985) gave way when Lopez struck down the school-zone gun ban as beyond the commerce power. On sovereign immunity, Hans (1890) extended the Eleventh Amendment to suits by a state's own citizens; Ex parte Young (1908) allowed injunctions against state officers; Edelman (1974) barred retroactive monetary relief; Pennhurst (1984) barred state-law claims; Atascadero v. Scanlon (1985) required unequivocal waiver; Fitzpatrick (1976) allowed abrogation under § 5. Seminole Tribe (1996) then barred abrogation under Article I, and City of Boerne (1997) held RFRA beyond § 5 power. New York v. United States (1992) and Gregory v. Ashcroft (1991) protected state self-government. Circuit courts rejected Lopez challenges to the Hobbs Act and § 924(c) (Bolton 1995).

name: Guilty pleas, 1970-74: Boykin, McCarthy's Rule 11, the new Brady trilogy
description: Guilty pleas in 1970-74 (one slice), when the governing cases were new: Boykin (1969, anchor) requires a record showing a knowing, voluntary waiver of trial rights; McCarthy (1969) let Rule 11 noncompliance void a plea, prospectively (Halliday 1969). The Brady trilogy (1970) holds pleas to avoid harsher punishment or on competent advice voluntary; Alford (1970) allows pleas despite claimed innocence; Santobello (1971) enforces plea promises.
history: Dominant rule: a guilty plea is itself a conviction (Kercheval 1927) and waives trial rights, so it must be knowing and voluntary. Boykin v. Alabama (1969), the anchor, requires that the record affirmatively show a voluntary and understanding plea, and California's In re Tahl (1969) required express enumeration of the waived rights. McCarthy (1969) held that failure to comply with Rule 11 entitles a federal defendant to plead anew, but Halliday (1969) made that rule prospective only. How it changed: the 1970 Brady trilogy narrowed collateral attacks. Brady v. United States held that a plea entered to avoid a possible death sentence is not coerced; McMann v. Richardson held that a plea on reasonably competent advice cannot be attacked because counsel misjudged a confession's admissibility; Parker v. North Carolina applied both. North Carolina v. Alford (1970) let courts accept a plea from a defendant maintaining innocence where a strong factual basis exists. Santobello (1971) held the prosecution to promises that induced a plea. Machibroda (1962) required § 2255 hearings where allegations concern matters outside the record. The cluster merges into the general criminal-procedure cluster in 1975-79.
rule: A guilty plea is valid only if the record affirmatively shows it was knowing and voluntary, a plea induced by a lawful bargain or competent advice is not coerced, and in federal court noncompliance with Rule 11 allows withdrawal.

history: Dominant rule: after Booker, appellate courts review sentences for abuse of discretion, first for procedural error (a miscalculated range, ignoring § 3553(a), clearly erroneous facts, an inadequate explanation) and then for substantive reasonableness (Gall, 2007). Holguin-Hernandez (2020) settled preservation nationally and leads the 2020s with Chavez-Meza (2018) on the explanation needed.

history: Dominant rule: which constitutional errors require automatic reversal and which are reviewed for harmlessness, centred on the right to counsel. Gideon (1963) anchors the lineage's only slice, 2000-04, formed from a right-to-counsel lineage and a harmless-error lineage, and later continuing as a self-representation and conflicts lineage. How it changed: Chapman (1967) set the harmless-beyond-a-reasonable-doubt test while excepting rights such as counsel; Fulminante (1991) separated trial errors from structural defects; Vasquez (1986, grand-jury discrimination), Waller (1984, public trial), Tumey (1927, a biased judge) and Sullivan (1993, a deficient reasonable-doubt instruction) are structural; Rose (1986), Carella (1989), Roy (1996) and Neder (1999) apply harmless error to faulty presumptions, intent instructions and omitted elements, after Gaudin (1995) required juries to find every element. Custis (1994) limited collateral attacks on enhancing convictions to Gideon violations, and Daniels and Coss (2001) extended that limit to § 2255 and § 2254. Also: McKaskle (1984) on standby counsel and Shelton (2002) on suspended sentences.
rule: Most constitutional errors are subject to Chapman harmless-error review, but a narrow class of structural errors (denial of counsel, a biased judge, a defective reasonable-doubt instruction, grand-jury discrimination, closure of trial) requires automatic reversal; and only Gideon violations allow collateral attack on prior convictions used to enhance a sentence (Custis, Daniels, Coss).

changes.case: Gideon v. Wainwright; Chapman v. California
changes.what: Right to appointed counsel in state felony trials; constitutional errors may be harmless only if harmless beyond a reasonable doubt, though denial of counsel never is. Gideon anchors the slice.

changes.case: Arizona v. Fulminante; Sullivan v. Louisiana
changes.what: Distinguished trial errors from structural defects; a constitutionally deficient reasonable-doubt instruction is structural.
Omitting an uncontested element from the jury instructions can be harmless; structural errors arise only in a very limited class of cases.

changes.case: Custis v. United States; Daniels v. United States; Lackawanna County DA v. Coss
changes.what: A defendant may collaterally attack prior convictions used for enhancement at sentencing or under § 2255/§ 2254 only on the ground of a Gideon violation.

name: Who is a § 1983 defendant, 2025-29: Monell policy, Will, official capacity
description: Proper defendants under § 1983, in the partial 2025-29 slice only: municipalities answer only for their own policy or custom (Monell 1978), incl. a final policymaker's decision (Pembaur 1986) or deliberately indifferent failure to train (Canton 1989; Brown 1997, Connick 2011); States and official-capacity defendants are not persons (Will 1989; Graham 1985, Hafer 1991). Also Nieves (2019) on retaliatory arrest.
history: Dominant rule: Monell (1978), the anchor, made municipalities persons under § 1983 (overruling Monroe v. Pape in part) but barred respondeat superior; liability requires a policy or custom that is the moving force behind the violation (Piotrowski 2001). Pembaur (1986) allowed a single decision by a final policymaker to be policy; Canton (1989) allowed failure-to-train liability on deliberate indifference; Brown (1997) held negligent hiring insufficient; Connick (2011) required a pattern of similar violations for notice. Alongside: capacity and sovereign immunity. Official-capacity suits are suits against the entity (Graham 1985), States and state officials in official capacity are not persons (Will 1989), the Eleventh Amendment bars suits against States whatever the relief (Pennhurst/Halderman 1984) and in state court (Alden 1999), but individual-capacity suits are allowed (Hafer 1991). Also: First Amendment retaliatory arrest with probable cause (Nieves 2019; Gonzalez 2024 on comparators), conscience-shocking executive action (Lewis 1998), prosecutorial immunity (Imbler). The lineage exists only in the partial 2025-29 slice.
rule: A local government is liable under § 1983 only for its own policy or custom that is the moving force behind a violation, not on respondeat superior, while States and officials sued in official capacity are not "persons" for damages.

changes.case: Monell v. Department of Social Services
changes.what: Municipalities are persons under § 1983 but are liable only for their own policies or customs, overruling Monroe v. Pape on that point.
Deliberately indifferent failure to train can be a municipal policy.
Failure-to-train liability ordinarily needs notice from a pattern of similar violations.
Probable cause generally defeats a First Amendment retaliatory-arrest claim.
The Nieves exception does not demand virtually identical comparators.

name: State action 1960-2009: Burton-era expansion, then Jackson and Lugar limits
description: When private conduct is state action, traced 1960-2009: Shelley (1948, anchor 1960-64), Burton's (1961, anchor 1965-74) symbiotic relationship, public functions (Marsh, Evans, Terry) and joint action (Adickes 1970). From 1972 the Court narrowed it: regulation or licensing is not enough (Moose Lodge; Jackson 1974, anchor 1975-84 and 1990-2004; Flagg Bros. 1978), and Lugar (2005-09 anchor), Rendell-Baker and Blum (1982) rejected funding-based theories.

history: Dominant rule: private conduct violates the Fourteenth Amendment only when fairly attributable to the State. Shelley (1948) anchors 1960-64, alongside the bus-segregation cases (Gayle, Browder) and the Civil Rights Cases (1883). How it changed: Burton (1961) anchors 1965-74: a restaurant leasing space in a public garage was a state actor, and Evans (1966), Reitman (1967), the sit-in cases and the white-primary cases (Terry, Allwright) widened the reach, with Price and Guest (1966) on conspiracies with officials; Adickes (1970) recognised joint action. Moose Lodge (1972) and Jackson v. Metropolitan Edison (1974), the anchor of 1975-84, held regulation and licensing not enough, and Flagg Bros. (1978) found no state action in self-help repossession. Rendell-Baker anchors 1985-89 with the 1982 trilogy: Lugar treats color of law and state action as identical and finds joint action in prejudgment attachment, while Rendell-Baker and Blum reject funding and regulation theories; West v. Atkins (1988) enters. Jackson anchors again 1990-2004 as the restrictive cases settle, with Sullivan (1999) on acquiescence and Brentwood (2001) on entwinement entering, and Lugar anchors 2005-09.
rule: The Fourteenth Amendment and § 1983 reach private conduct only when it is fairly attributable to the State, through judicial enforcement, joint action or a symbiotic relationship, a traditionally exclusive public function, or state coercion; regulation, licensing or funding alone is not enough.

changes.what: Judicial enforcement of racially restrictive covenants is state action; Shelley anchors 1960-64.

changes.case: Burton v. Wilmington Parking Authority; Evans v. Newton; Reitman v. Mulkey
changes.what: A private lessee in a public building, a park with a tradition of municipal control, and a state constitutional provision authorizing private discrimination all involve state action; Burton anchors 1965-74.
A private party acts under color of law when it conspires with state officials or acts under a state-enforced custom.

changes.case: Moose Lodge v. Irvis; Jackson v. Metropolitan Edison; Flagg Bros. v. Brooks
changes.what: State licensing, regulation and monopoly status do not convert private conduct into state action, nor does statutorily authorized self-help.

changes.case: Lugar v. Edmondson Oil; Rendell-Baker v. Kohn; Blum v. Yaretsky
changes.what: Color of law equals state action; joint use of state attachment procedures qualifies, but near-total public funding and regulation of private schools and nursing homes do not; these anchor 1985-89.

Metropolitan Edison, 1974; Flagg Bros., 1978), and Lugar, Rendell-Baker and Blum (1982) tied § 1983 color of law to state action and rejected funding-based theories.

name: Juvenile de facto life terms 2025-29: California youth parole, Washington
description: State-court reach of the juvenile-sentencing cases in the partial 2025-29 slice, anchored by Graham (2010), led by California and Washington: de facto life terms (Caballero 2012, Contreras 2018), youth-offender parole as a cure (Franklin 2016) and youth considered for any juvenile sentence (Houston-Sconiers 2017). Federal base: Roper (2005), Graham, Miller (2012), Montgomery (2016); Jones (2021) required no incorrigibility finding.
history: Dominant rule: Graham v. Florida (2010) anchors this single partial 2025-29 slice, which merged several 2020-24 juvenile-sentencing units. Juveniles are constitutionally different: Roper (2005) barred the death penalty for offenders under 18, building on Atkins (2002); Graham barred life without parole for nonhomicide offences and required a meaningful opportunity for release; Miller (2012) barred mandatory LWOP for homicide; Montgomery (2016) made Miller retroactive on collateral review. How it changed: state courts extended the rule to term-of-years sentences: Caballero (Cal. 2012) struck a 110-year minimum, Franklin (Cal. 2016) let youth-offender parole cure the defect, Contreras (Cal. 2018) held parole at 66 or 74 inadequate, and Houston-Sconiers (Wash. 2017) required consideration of youth for any juvenile sentence, treated as a significant change in law (Ali, 2020); Colorado requires a forward-looking assessment (Delbosque, 2020) yet upheld felony-murder LWOP (Sellers, 2024). Jones v. Mississippi (2021) narrowed the federal rule, requiring no finding of permanent incorrigibility. For adults, proportionality review stays narrow (Solem 1983, Harmelin 1991, Ewing 2003).
rule: The Eighth Amendment treats juveniles as categorically less culpable: no death penalty (Roper), no life without parole for nonhomicide offences (Graham), no mandatory life without parole for homicide (Miller, retroactive under Montgomery), with youth considered before a discretionary life sentence but no separate finding of permanent incorrigibility required (Jones).

changes.what: Executing offenders under 18 at the time of the crime violates the Eighth Amendment.
Life without parole for juvenile nonhomicide offenders is barred; anchors the slice.

changes.case: Miller v. Alabama; People v. Caballero (Cal.)
changes.what: Mandatory LWOP for juvenile murderers is barred; Caballero applied Graham to a 110-years-to-life term.

changes.case: Montgomery v. Louisiana; People v. Franklin (Cal.)
changes.what: Miller is retroactive on state collateral review; California's youth-offender parole statute supplies the remedy without resentencing.

changes.case: State v. Houston-Sconiers (Wash.); People v. Contreras (Cal.); In re Ali (Wash.)
changes.what: Courts must consider youth for any juvenile sentence; parole at 66 or 74 is not a meaningful opportunity; Houston-Sconiers is a significant change in law.
No separate finding of permanent incorrigibility is required before a discretionary juvenile LWOP sentence.

Proportionality for adults remains narrow (Harmelin 1991, Ewing 2003).

name: Religion clauses: from the Lemon test to Smith's neutral-law rule
description: Religion clauses: the Lemon test governs Establishment Clause cases on school aid, prayer and displays through 2015-19; from 2020-24 the anchor is Employment Division v. Smith (neutral, generally applicable laws need no compelling interest), as RFRA and RLUIPA cases, Tandon and Kennedy v. Bremerton (2022, abandoning Lemon) enter.

previous.name: Religion clauses: Establishment and Free Exercise
previous.description: Government and religion: the Lemon test and Establishment Clause cases on aid, prayer and displays (Everson, Schempp, Walz, Lynch v. Donnelly, Allegheny, Lee v. Weisman, Wallace v. Jaffree), and free exercise from Sherbert and Yoder to Employment Division v. Smith.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: through 2015-19, the Lemon test (1971) for the Establishment Clause (secular purpose, primary effect, no excessive entanglement). It governed school aid (Nyquist, Meek, Wolman), school prayer and teaching (Wallace, Edwards, Lee v. Weisman) and holiday displays, where Lynch and Allegheny read it as an endorsement test. From 2020-24 the anchor is Employment Division v. Smith (1990): a neutral, generally applicable law needs no compelling interest. How it changed: Smith replaced Sherbert's test for neutral laws, and Lukumi (1993) kept strict scrutiny for laws that are not neutral. Congress answered Smith with RFRA and RLUIPA (Boerne, Cutter, and Hobby Lobby and Holt in 2015-19). Agostini (1997) overruled Aguilar and Ball, and Helms and Zelman upheld neutral aid. In 2020-24, Kennedy v. Bremerton (2022) abandoned Lemon for history and tradition, and Cuomo and Tandon widened what counts as non-neutral. Hosanna-Tabor and Morrissey-Berru set the ministerial exception.
rule: Establishment Clause review under Lemon (purpose, effect, entanglement) through 2015-19; from 2020-24 the free-exercise rule of Employment Division v. Smith (neutral, generally applicable laws need no compelling interest).

changes.what: Three-part Establishment Clause test.
Endorsement inquiry for holiday displays.
Neutral, generally applicable laws no longer need Sherbert's compelling interest.

changes.case: Lukumi; City of Boerne; Cutter; Burwell v. Hobby Lobby; Holt v. Hobbs
changes.what: Non-neutral laws still get strict scrutiny (Lukumi); RFRA and RLUIPA restore compelling-interest review by statute.
Agostini overruled Aguilar and Ball; neutral aid reaching religious schools upheld.

changes.case: Roman Catholic Diocese v. Cuomo; Tandon v. Newsom; Kennedy v. Bremerton
changes.what: Lemon abandoned for history and tradition (Kennedy); a law that treats comparable secular activity better is not neutral (Tandon).

name: Illinois section 2-615/2-619 dismissals in tort and defamation cases
description: Illinois pleading-stage dismissals in 2020-24, anchored by Marshall (2006) on a business's duty to invitees: section 2-615 dismissal only if no set of facts entitles relief (Blagojevich 2008), section 2-619 on an affirmative matter with a shifted burden (Hodge 1993, Van Meter 2003). Applied to defamation per se and the fair-report privilege (Bryson 1996, Solaia 2006, Green 2009), anti-SLAPP (Sandholm 2012), malpractice repose (DeLuna 2006).
history: Dominant rule: Marshall (2006) anchors this single 2020-24 slice, holding that a restaurant owes invitees a duty against a car losing control in its lot, which frames the slice's theme: pleading-stage dismissal of tort claims. Under section 2-615 dismissal is proper where no set of facts provable under the pleadings would entitle relief (Blagojevich, 2008). Under section 2-619 the defendant raises an affirmative matter, a defence other than negating essential allegations (Hodge, 1993), and the plaintiff's failure to carry the shifted burden justifies dismissal (Van Meter, 2003). Defamation is prominent: per se categories need no extrinsic facts (Bryson, 1996; Green, 2009, including imputations of adultery), claims accrue on publication, extrinsic facts can support per quod claims (Moon, 2016), and the fair-report privilege applies to reports of filed suits without a malice inquiry (Solaia, 2006); the Citizen Participation Act targets meritless SLAPPs (Sandholm, 2012). Also: misfeasance in supplying alcohol to a minor (Wakulich, 2003), substantial-factor causation (Young, 2004), IIED as a continuing tort in marriage (Feltmeier, 2003), and fraudulent concealment tolling repose (DeLuna, 2006).
rule: Illinois courts dismiss under section 2-615 only where no set of facts provable under the pleadings would entitle the plaintiff to relief, and under section 2-619 where an affirmative matter, a defence other than negating the plaintiff's essential allegations, defeats the claim and the plaintiff fails to carry the shifted burden.

changes.what: An 'affirmative matter' under section 2-619 is a defence other than negation of the plaintiff's essential allegations.
Defamation per se needs no extrinsic facts; a defamation claim accrues on publication to a third party.
A business owes invitees a duty against foreseeable harm from vehicles leaving the parking lot; anchors the slice.
The fair-report privilege covers reports of a filed complaint, and malice is not part of the inquiry.

description: Louisiana review of findings of fact and fault, not damages, 1990-2029: no reversal without manifest error (Arceneaux, 1978; Watson, 1985; Rosell, 1989; Stobart, 1993), with de novo review where legal error taints the findings. The standard stays stable; Rosell anchors 1990-99 and from 2010-14, Stobart 2000-09. Damages review (Coco, Youn) merges in from 2000-04; also tort presumptions (Mart; Sistler).

history: Dominant rule: a Louisiana appellate court may not disturb a factual finding of a judge or jury, including causation and the allocation of fault, unless it is manifestly erroneous or clearly wrong; where a reversible error of law interdicted the fact-finding, the court must redetermine the facts de novo from the record. How it changed: the rule stays stable and the anchors restate it. Rosell (1989) anchors 1990-94 and 1995-99, restating Arceneaux (1978) and adding deference even to findings based on documentary evidence (Virgil, 1987); Watson (1985) brought fault allocation under the same review. Stobart (1993) anchors 2000-04 and 2005-09, insisting that the appellate court may not reweigh reasonable evaluations of credibility, and Rosell anchors again from 2010-14 through the partial 2025-29 slice. General-damages review joins as the quantum lineage merges in from 2000-04 (Coco, 1977; Reck; Youn, 1993: prior awards only after an abuse is found). Also: the rear-end presumption (Mart, 1987), custodial liability for defects (Sistler, 1990; Loescher), causation presumed from good health before an accident (Housley, 1991) and workers' compensation findings (Bruno; Banks).
rule: A Louisiana court of appeal may not set aside a finding of fact, including causation and the allocation of fault, absent manifest error, but must decide the facts de novo where a reversible error of law tainted the findings.

name: Commerce power limits on federal crimes: Lopez, Morrison and jurisdictional elements
description: Commerce Clause limits on federal criminal statutes: Lopez (1995) struck down the Gun-Free School Zones Act and Morrison (2000) VAWA's civil remedy, barring regulation of noneconomic intrastate conduct by aggregate effect, against the broader Wickard, Heart of Atlanta and Perez line. Jones (2000) read the arson statute narrowly, and circuits upheld § 922(g) and the Hobbs Act because of their jurisdictional elements (Scarborough, 1977).

previous.name: Commerce power: Lopez, Morrison and federal crimes
previous.description: Commerce Clause limits on federal criminal statutes after Lopez and Morrison, measured against Wickard, Heart of Atlanta, McClung and Perez; Jones v. United States and Bass on the arson statute and jurisdictional nexus (1995-2004).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session subagents, from cocite evidence; second pass differentiated near-duplicates)

history: Dominant rule: Lopez (1995) anchors both slices. Congress may regulate the channels and instrumentalities of interstate commerce and activities that substantially affect it, but possessing a gun near a school is not economic activity and § 922(q) lacked a jurisdictional element, so it exceeded the commerce power. The earlier expansive line is cited as the baseline: Wickard (1942), Darby (1941), Heart of Atlanta and McClung (1964-65), Wirtz (1968), Perez (1971) and Hodel (1981). How it changed: in 1995-99 circuit cases test other federal crimes against Lopez and mostly uphold them: the Hobbs Act on an asset-depletion theory (Bolton, 1995) and § 922(g) because the firearm once moved in commerce (Bell, Hanna, following Scarborough, 1977). In 2000-04 Morrison (2000) extends Lopez to VAWA's civil remedy, and Jones (2000) construes § 844(i) narrowly to exclude private homes, following Bass (1971) on clear statements in criminal law. Rodia (1999) and Wang (2000) apply these to child-pornography production and residential Hobbs Act robberies. New York v. United States (1992) appears early on anti-commandeering.
rule: Congress may regulate the channels and instrumentalities of interstate commerce and activities that substantially affect it, but not noneconomic, intrastate conduct on an aggregate-effects theory (Lopez, Morrison); a statute with an express interstate-commerce element, such as § 922(g), survives.

changes.case: Wickard v. Filburn; Heart of Atlanta; Katzenbach v. McClung; Perez
changes.what: Aggregate effects of intrastate economic activity, including loansharking and discrimination in local businesses, bring it within the commerce power.
The felon-in-possession statute requires only that the firearm have once travelled in interstate commerce.
Struck down the Gun-Free School Zones Act, § 922(q), as beyond the commerce power: gun possession near schools is not economic activity and the statute had no jurisdictional element.
Circuits upheld the Hobbs Act and § 922(g) after Lopez because of their express jurisdictional elements and Scarborough's minimal nexus.
Invalidated VAWA's civil remedy under the Commerce Clause and § 5; Congress may not regulate noneconomic violent crime by its aggregate effect.
Read the federal arson statute, § 844(i), not to reach an owner-occupied private residence, avoiding the constitutional question.

name: Eyewitness identification: Wade lineup counsel to Biggers-Manson reliability
description: Eyewitness identification: Wade and Gilbert (1967) required counsel at post-indictment lineups (limited to post-charge by Kirby, 1972), and Stovall (1967), Simmons (1968) and Foster (1969) opened due-process review of suggestive procedures. Neil v. Biggers (1972) and Manson v. Brathwaite (1977) made reliability the linchpin and anchor from 1975-79 on; Texas cases (Barley, 1995) apply them, and Perry (2012) enters in 2010-14.

previous.name: Eyewitness identification and lineups
previous.description: Wade, Gilbert and Stovall on counsel at lineups and suggestive identifications, Simmons, Neil v. Biggers and Manson on reliability, and Kirby limiting the right to post-charge stages.

history: Dominant rule: identification evidence following a suggestive police procedure is excluded only if, under the totality of the circumstances, it creates a very substantial likelihood of irreparable misidentification; reliability, judged by the witness's opportunity to view, degree of attention, accuracy of prior description, certainty and the time elapsed, is the linchpin (Biggers, 1972; Manson, 1977). How it changed: Wade (1967) anchors 1965-69 and 1970-74, holding a post-indictment lineup a critical stage, with Gilbert (1967) and Schmerber (1966) on nontestimonial evidence; Stovall (1967) made Wade prospective and recognised due-process challenges. Simmons (1968) set the test for photo arrays, Foster (1969) excluded an identification, and Kirby (1972) confined the counsel right to after formal charge. Biggers anchors 1975-84 and Manson 1985-99, with Neil and Manson alternating to 2010-14. In 1985-89 retroactivity cases join (Linkletter, Desist, Johnson v. New Jersey). Later slices are state applications, especially Texas (Barley, 1995; Loserth, 1998; Ibarra, 1999), on the defendant's burden and on photo arrays. Perry v. New Hampshire (2012) enters in 2010-14. Also: cautionary identification instructions (Telfaire, 1972).
rule: An identification following an unnecessarily suggestive police procedure is admissible unless, judged by the Biggers factors under the totality of the circumstances, it creates a very substantial likelihood of misidentification (Simmons, Biggers, Manson).

changes.what: Very-substantial-likelihood-of-misidentification test for photo arrays; Foster excluded an identification made all but inevitable.

history: Dominant rule: a Tennessee summary-judgment movant must shift the burden of production before the nonmovant must produce specific facts showing a genuine issue (Byrd 1993), and negligence turns on duty as a question of law balancing foreseeability and gravity of harm against the burden of prevention. How it changed: Byrd anchors 1995-99 through 2010-14, joined by McCall (1995) on the duty balancing test, Bain (1997) on duty to warn of a roommate's HIV status, Carvell (1995) and Hunter (1997) on discovery-rule accrual, Robinson (1997) on negligent misrepresentation, and Staples (2000) treating duty as a legal question. McCarley (1998) and Blair (2004) required movants to affirmatively negate an element. Hannan (2008) enters in 2005-09 and leads 2010-14, requiring movants to negate an element or show the nonmovant cannot prove it at trial (with Martin 2008 and Giggers 2009). The Legislature reversed Hannan for suits filed from July 1, 2011 (§ 20-16-101), and Rye (2015), anchoring 2015-19 through the partial 2025-29 slice, overruled Hannan. Also: Webb (2011) on motions to dismiss and TWB Architects (2019) join as leading cases from 2015-19 and 2020-24.
rule: Tennessee summary judgment requires the movant to shift the burden of production, after which the nonmovant must set out specific facts showing a genuine dispute, with evidence viewed in its favor; in negligence, duty is a question of law decided by balancing the foreseeability and gravity of harm against the burden of preventing it.
