history: Dominant rule: how the Florida Supreme Court reviews death sentences and capital postconviction claims. How it changed: Urbin (1998) anchors 2000-04, restating that proportionality review compares the totality of circumstances with other capital cases (Porter, 1990, rejects counting aggravators against mitigators) and condemning golden-rule victim scripts; DiGuilio (1986) supplies harmless error. Ring v. Arizona (2002), which overruled Walton (1990) and required jury findings of aggravators, enters as the heaviest case; the unit merged in from Arizona capital review. Florida denied Ring relief in Bottoson and King (2002) and where a prior-violent-felony aggravator applied (Doorbal, 2003). Freeman (2000) anchors 2005-09 as postconviction cases dominate: Huff (1993) hearings, the bar on relitigating direct-appeal claims through ineffectiveness (Freeman; Rutherford, 2000), and strategy deference (Occhicone, 2000); Johnson (2005) held Ring not retroactive. Caldwell (1985) challenges to the standard instructions failed (Brown, 1998). The lineage splits in 2010-14.
rule: The Florida Supreme Court reviews death sentences for proportionality on the totality of the circumstances compared with other capital cases (Urbin; Porter), tests errors for harmlessness beyond a reasonable doubt (DiGuilio), rejected Ring v. Arizona challenges to its judge-sentencing scheme, and in postconviction bars relitigating direct-appeal claims as ineffective assistance (Freeman).

name: Illinois civil trials: Pedrick directed-verdict standard and Maple new trials
description: Illinois civil trials and appeals: directed verdict and judgment n.o.v. only when the evidence so overwhelmingly favours the movant that no contrary verdict could stand (Pedrick, 1967), and a new trial only against the manifest weight (Maple, 1992). Pedrick anchors 1990-2004, Maple from 2005-09. Applied to retaliatory discharge (Kelsay, 1978) early and medical-malpractice causation, instructions and apparent agency later (Holton, 1997; York, 2006).

previous.description: Illinois civil appeals: the Pedrick standard for directed verdicts and judgment n.o.v. (Maple, York), the appellant's duty to present a complete record (Foutch), jury instructions, and damages caps (Best v. Taylor Machine Works).

history: Dominant rule: Pedrick (1967) anchors 1990-94 to 2000-04. A court may direct a verdict or enter judgment n.o.v. only where all the evidence, viewed most favourably to the opponent, so overwhelmingly favours the movant that no contrary verdict could stand, so substantial factual disputes and credibility stay with the jury. How it changed: Maple (1992) enters in 1995-99 and anchors from 2005-09: a new trial is a discretionary remedy granted when the verdict is against the manifest weight of the evidence. The cases applying these standards shift. In 1990-94 they are retaliatory-discharge suits (Kelsay, 1978; Palmateer, 1981; Hinthorn, 1988) and punitive damages (Loitz, 1990). From 1995-99 they are mainly medical malpractice: Borowski (1975) and Holton (1997) reject a 'better result' requirement for causation, Leonardi (1995) allows a sole-proximate-cause defence, Snelson (2003), Simmons (2002) and Sullivan (2004) require expert causation and standard-of-care testimony, and York (2006) reaffirms Gilbert's apparent-agency test. Also: jury instructions (Schultz, 2002), Rule 213 disclosure (Copeland, Radfar, 2000) and Best (1997) striking damages caps. Insurance cases split off in 2015-19.
rule: A directed verdict or judgment n.o.v. is proper only where all the evidence, viewed most favourably to the opponent, so overwhelmingly favours the movant that no contrary verdict could ever stand (Pedrick); a new trial may be granted only when the verdict is against the manifest weight of the evidence (Maple).

changes.what: Set the overwhelmingly-favours standard for directed verdicts and judgments n.o.v., preserving jury resolution of substantial factual disputes.
Recognised the tort of retaliatory discharge for an at-will employee fired for filing a workers' compensation claim.
A new trial is within the trial court's discretion and is warranted when the verdict is against the manifest weight of the evidence, a lower bar than Pedrick's.
Reaffirmed Borowski: in malpractice the plaintiff proves causation by 'more probably than not', not by a 'better result' test, allowing recovery for lost chance.
Held the 1995 tort-reform cap on noneconomic damages unconstitutional.

changes.case: York v. Rush-Presbyterian-St. Luke's Medical Center
changes.what: Reaffirmed Gilbert's apparent-agency framework for hospitals, with reliance treated distinctively in health care.

name: Eleventh Circuit drug conspiracies, 1985-89: Bell sufficiency, Pinkerton liability
description: Eleventh Circuit drug-conspiracy appeals, 1985-89, on co-conspirator liability: Bell (1982, en banc, anchor) and Glasser (1942) sustain verdicts a reasonable trier could reach on evidence viewed for the government; Pinkerton (1946) makes conspirators liable for foreseeable acts. Bonner (1981) and Stein (1982) adopt former Fifth Circuit precedent. Also RICO conspiracy (Phillips 1981), severance (Carson 1983) and coconspirator statements (James 1979).
history: Dominant rule: United States v. Bell (11th Cir. en banc 1982), anchor of the single slice (1985-89), holds that a verdict must stand if a reasonable trier of fact could find guilt beyond a reasonable doubt, applying Glasser's (1942) rule that the evidence is viewed most favourably to the government. Pinkerton (1946) extends conspirators' liability to co-conspirators' foreseeable crimes, and Vergara (1982) infers agreement from meetings and activity. How it changed: the slice is built from the new Eleventh Circuit's early case law: Bonner (1981) adopted pre-split Fifth Circuit decisions as binding precedent and Stein (1982) did the same for Unit B. Phillips (1981) used a RICO conspiracy count as the common thread in a smuggling case, and Jefferson (1983) barred punishing both a drug conspiracy and the continuing criminal enterprise built on it. Alongside: joint trials and spillover prejudice cured by instructions (Carson 1983), James (1979) hearings on coconspirator statements, expert testimony on drug paraphernalia (Young 1984), questioning jurors about extrinsic influence (Brantley 1984), and the Bank Robbery Act's reach (Bell v. United States 1983). The unit splits into joint-trial and conspiracy lineages in 1990-94.
rule: A conviction stands if a reasonable trier of fact could find guilt beyond a reasonable doubt on the evidence viewed most favourably to the government, and conspirators answer for co-conspirators' foreseeable acts in furtherance.

changes.case: Glasser v. United States; Pinkerton v. United States
changes.what: Verdicts are sustained on substantial evidence viewed favourably to the government; conspirators are liable for co-conspirators' foreseeable substantive offenses.

changes.what: Former Fifth Circuit decisions through September 30, 1981, and later Unit B decisions, bind the Eleventh Circuit.

changes.what: Sufficiency review asks whether a reasonable trier of fact could find guilt beyond a reasonable doubt; the evidence need not exclude every reasonable hypothesis of innocence.

name: Union's duty of fair representation: Steele to Vaca and DelCostello
description: The duty of fair representation, 1945-94: Steele and Tunstall (1944-45) implied the duty under the Railway Labor Act against racial discrimination, and Huffman (1953) carried it to the NLRA; Steele anchors 1945-64, with Slocum (1950) on Adjustment Board jurisdiction. Vaca (1967) anchors 1970-84: arbitrary, discriminatory or bad-faith handling breaches the duty; Hines (1976) and Mitchell (1981) followed. DelCostello (1983), anchor 1985-94, set a six-month limit.

previous.name: Union duty of fair representation and NLRA preemption
previous.description: Vaca, Hines and DelCostello hybrid § 301/fair-representation suits and their limitations period, with Garmon and Garner on NLRA preemption of state law.

history: Dominant rule: an exclusive bargaining agent must represent all employees fairly. How it changed: Steele v. Louisville & Nashville (1944), the anchor through 1960-64, and Tunstall (1945) held that the Railway Labor Act implies a judicially enforceable duty barring a union from discriminating against Black employees; Trainmen v. Howard (1952) and Conley v. Gibson (1957, anchor 1965-69) applied it. In 1950-54 Slocum (1950) gave the National Railroad Adjustment Board exclusive jurisdiction over minor disputes (with Burley 1945 and Pitney 1946). Huffman (1953) extended the duty to NLRA unions, and Humphrey (1964) allowed good-faith choices among members. Vaca v. Sipes (1967) anchors 1970-84: perfunctory or bad-faith grievance handling breaches the duty, a meritorious grievance alone does not, and the employee may then sue the employer despite unexhausted procedures (Maddox 1965). Hines (1976) let a breach undo a final award, and Mitchell (1981) made it the indispensable predicate of the hybrid suit. DelCostello (1983), anchor 1985-94, replaced borrowed state periods (Hoosier Cardinal 1966) with § 10(b)'s six months. In 1990-94 limitations borrowing in other federal statutes (Wilson 1985, Malley-Duff 1987, Reed 1989, Owens 1989) joins the unit.
rule: A union that is the exclusive bargaining representative owes all members of the unit a duty of fair representation, breached by arbitrary, discriminatory or bad-faith conduct; that breach is the predicate of a hybrid § 301 suit against the employer, which must be brought within six months.

changes.case: Steele v. Louisville & Nashville R.R.; Tunstall v. Brotherhood of Locomotive Firemen
changes.what: The Railway Labor Act imposes a judicially enforceable duty on unions not to discriminate among those they represent.

changes.case: Slocum v. Delaware, Lackawanna & Western R.R.
changes.what: The Adjustment Board has exclusive jurisdiction over minor disputes under existing agreements.
The duty of fair representation applies to unions under the NLRA.
A union breaches the duty by arbitrary, discriminatory, bad-faith or perfunctory grievance handling.

changes.case: Hines v. Anchor Motor Freight; United Parcel Service v. Mitchell
changes.what: A breach can overturn a final award and is the indispensable predicate of the hybrid suit.

changes.case: DelCostello v. International Brotherhood of Teamsters
changes.what: Hybrid § 301 and fair-representation suits take the six-month NLRA § 10(b) period instead of state limitations periods.

round1.name: NLRA preemption (Garner, Garmon) and the union's duty of fair representation (Vaca)
round1.description: Labor preemption and fair representation (1950-94): through 1965-69, Garner (1954) and Garmon (1959) bar state regulation of conduct arguably protected or prohibited by the NLRA, except violence (Laburnum, Russell). From 1970-74 Vaca (1967) anchors: a union breaches its duty by arbitrary, discriminatory or bad-faith conduct (Steele, Huffman, Hines 1976), and DelCostello (1983), the anchor from 1985, set a six-month limit for hybrid suits.
round1.history: Dominant rule: the anchor doctrine changes. 1950-69: NLRA preemption. Bethlehem (1947) and Briggs-Stratton (1949) began the inquiry; Garner (1954) anchors 1955-64, holding state remedies displaced where the Board's remedies apply, and Guss (1957) extended this even where the Board declined jurisdiction. Laburnum (1954), Russell (1958) and Youngdahl (1957) left states free to address violence, and Garmon (1959), the 1965-69 anchor, gave the Board exclusive jurisdiction over conduct arguably within §§ 7 or 8. How it changed: from 1970-74 Vaca (1967) anchors the duty of fair representation, rooted in Steele (1944) and Huffman (1953) and limited by Humphrey (1964). Maddox (1965) requires exhaustion of grievance procedures. Hines (1976) lets a breach overturn an arbitral award, and Mitchell (1981) makes the breach a predicate of the hybrid claim. DelCostello (1983) replaced state limitations periods, drawn from Hoosier Cardinal (1966), with § 10(b)'s six months, and it anchors 1985-94 as the circuits apply it to railway and airline cases. In 1990-94 limitations borrowing in other federal statutes (Reed 1989, Malley-Duff 1987, Gilbertson 1991) joins the unit.
round1.rule: States may not regulate conduct that the NLRA arguably protects or prohibits, except to police violence and matters of deeply rooted local concern (Garner, Garmon); a union owes every employee it represents a duty of fair representation, breached by arbitrary, discriminatory or bad-faith conduct, and an employee's hybrid § 301/fair-representation suit against employer and union requires that breach and must be filed within six months (Vaca, Hines, DelCostello).

changes.what: A duty of fair representation under the Railway Labor Act, extended to the NLRA, with a wide range of reasonableness for unions.

name: Entrapment: predisposition test and outrageous government conduct
description: The federal entrapment defense turns on predisposition (Sorrells 1932, Sherman 1958, anchor 1965-74; Russell 1973, anchor 1975-99). Hampton (1976) narrowed outrageous-conduct claims, though Twigg (3d Cir. 1978) applied one; Mathews (1988) allowed entrapment with denial of the offense, and Jacobson (1992) required proof of predisposition before government contact.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Entrapment and outrageous government conduct
previous.description: The entrapment defense: predisposition as the central inquiry (Sorrells, Sherman, Russell, Jacobson), entitlement to an instruction while denying the offense (Mathews), and the due-process outrageous-conduct defense (Hampton, Twigg).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: entrapment depends on whether a defendant was predisposed, not on how aggressive the government was. How it changed: Sherman (1958) anchors 1965-74, with Sorrells (1932) and circuit cases on burdens and instructions (Notaro 1966, Riley 1966). Russell (1973) enters and anchors from 1975-79 on, rejecting the objective test urged by some courts (Turner 1973) while leaving room for a due-process defense. Hampton (1976) enters in 1975-79, holding that supplying contraband to a predisposed defendant is not a due-process violation. Twigg (3d Cir. 1978) enters in 1980-84, reversing where agents conceived and ran a drug laboratory, while Jannotti (1982) and Bogart (1986) confined outrageous-conduct claims. Mathews (1988) enters in 1985-89, allowing inconsistent defenses, and Jacobson (1992) enters in 1990-94, overturning a child-pornography conviction because predisposition was not shown to precede the government's campaign. Late circuit cases (Davis 1994) mix in sentencing issues before the unit splits.
rule: Entrapment is established where the government induced a person who was not otherwise predisposed to commit the crime, the focus being the defendant's predisposition rather than the officers' conduct (Sorrells, Sherman, Russell), with the government bearing the burden to prove predisposition existing before contact (Jacobson); a separate due-process defense for outrageous government conduct is recognized only in extreme cases.

changes.case: Sorrells v. United States; Sherman v. United States
changes.what: Entrapment bars conviction of an otherwise innocent person lured by government agents; Sherman found entrapment as a matter of law. Sherman anchors 1965-74.
Rejected an objective test and reaffirmed predisposition, while suggesting outrageous conduct could bar prosecution; anchors 1975-99.
Supplying and buying back contraband from a predisposed defendant did not violate due process.
Reversed a conviction for outrageous conduct where agents set up and ran a drug laboratory.

changes.case: United States v. Jannotti (3d Cir.); United States v. Bogart (9th Cir.)
changes.what: Courts refused to let the objective test reemerge as due process and rejected outrageous-conduct claims where the enterprise predated government involvement.
A defendant may deny the offense and still receive an entrapment instruction.
The government must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the defendant was predisposed before first contact with agents.

history: Dominant rule: neutral time, place and manner rules are allowed, but content-based restrictions face strict scrutiny outside historic categories. How it changed: 1945-64 is the Jehovah's Witness and street-literature era: Murdock (1943, overruling Jones v. Opelika) anchors 1945-49 and Cantwell (1940) 1950-64, with Lovell, Schneider, Thomas (1945) and Barnette (1943); religion-clause cases split off in 1960-64. Cox v. Louisiana (1965) anchors 1965-74 with Edwards and Adderley on protest. Grayned (1972) anchors 1975-89 with Mosley, Gooding, Cohen and Broadrick on vagueness and overbreadth; commercial speech (Virginia Pharmacy 1976, Central Hudson) joins, and forum and manner cases (Perry 1983, Vincent and Clark 1984, Renton 1986) enter. Ward (1989) anchors 1990-2014, with Texas v. Johnson (1989) and R.A.V. (1992); Citizens United (2010) leads 2010-14. Stevens (2010) anchors 2015-19 as public-employee speech (Pickering, Garcetti) merges in; R.A.V. anchors 2020-24, and Reed (2015) anchors 2025-29 with Moody v. NetChoice (2024).
rule: Government may regulate the time, place and manner of speech if the rule is content neutral, narrowly tailored to a significant interest and leaves ample alternatives, but content-based restrictions face strict scrutiny outside a few historic unprotected categories.

changes.what: Licensing and littering rationales cannot suppress leafleting and solicitation; Murdock overruled Jones v. Opelika and Barnette overruled Gobitis.

changes.what: Peaceful protest in traditional public places is protected, but not on non-public property such as jail grounds.

round1.history: Dominant rule: government may regulate the time, place and manner of speech neutrally, but content-based restrictions face strict scrutiny outside a few historic categories. How it changed: 1940-59 concerns street literature and Jehovah's Witness cases: Schneider (1939) anchors 1940-44, Murdock (1943, overruling Jones v. Opelika) 1945-49, and Cantwell (1940) 1950-64, with Barnette (1943) overruling Gobitis. Cox (1965) anchors 1965-74 with Edwards and Adderley on protest. Grayned (1972) anchors 1975-79 with Mosley, Gooding and Cohen; Virginia Pharmacy (1976) anchors 1980-84 as commercial speech (Bates, Central Hudson) joins. Grayned anchors again in 1985-89 alongside Perry (1983), Vincent and Clark (1984). Ward (1989) anchors 1990-2014, joined by Texas v. Johnson (1989), R.A.V. (1992), Renton (1986) and Hill (2000), and Citizens United (2010) leads 2010-14. Stevens (2010) anchors 2015-24 as public-employee speech (Pickering, Garcetti) merges in; Reed (2015) anchors 2025-29 with Moody v. NetChoice (2024) and free-exercise entrants.
round1.rule: Content-based restrictions on speech receive strict scrutiny, including laws that are content-based on their face (Reed), while content-neutral time, place and manner rules are valid if narrowly tailored to a significant interest, not necessarily the least restrictive means, and leave ample alternative channels (Ward); only historically recognized categories fall outside protection (Stevens).

name: Fugitive disentitlement: Molinaro, with Ortega-Rodriguez's nexus requirement
description: Courts may dismiss appeals and claims of fugitives from justice (Smith, 1876; Molinaro, 1970; Estelle, 1975). Ortega-Rodriguez (1993) required a nexus between the flight and the proceeding, so former fugitive status before appeal does not justify dismissal, and Degen (1996) barred automatic judgment against a fugitive civil-forfeiture claimant. Later cases apply it to civil litigants and aliens.

previous.description: Dismissal of appeals and claims by fugitives: Molinaro and Smith v. United States on disentitlement, Ortega-Rodriguez requiring a nexus between flight and the appellate process, and Degen limiting the doctrine in civil forfeiture. No Hague Convention cases appear in the evidence.

history: Dominant rule: the fugitive disentitlement doctrine. A party who flees forfeits the court's help in deciding his claims, a practice dating from Smith v. United States (1876), Bohanan (1887) and Eisler (1949), with Allen (1897) and Estelle (1975) upholding state escape rules against due-process attack. Molinaro (1970) anchors from 1985-89 through 1995-99; circuit cases dismiss appeals of defendants who fled before sentencing (Persico, Parrish, Puzzanghera) and FOIA or tax claims by fugitives (Doyle, Conforte). How it changed: Ortega-Rodriguez (1993) enters in 1990-94 and anchors from 2000-04: dismissal needs a connection between the flight and the appellate process, and a fugitive recaptured before appeal is not dismissed for that alone. Degen (1996) enters in 1995-99 and limited the doctrine in civil forfeiture. Also: application to civil litigants evading judgments (Barnette, Finkelstein, 1997), to a Hague Convention petition by a fugitive parent (Prevot, 1995), and in 2005-09 to aliens in immigration appeals (Antonio-Martinez, 2003; Sapoundjiev, 2004).
rule: A court may dismiss the appeal or claim of a party who is a fugitive from justice, but only where the party's fugitive status has a sufficient connection to the proceeding from which he is disentitled.

changes.case: Smith v. United States; Bohanan; Allen v. Georgia; Eisler
changes.what: The Supreme Court may refuse to hear, or strike from its docket, the case of a convicted party who has escaped; a state's dismissal of an escapee's appeal does not violate due process (Allen, 1897).

changes.case: Molinaro v. New Jersey; Estelle v. Dorrough
changes.what: A fugitive is disentitled to call on the court's resources; a state may by statute make escape during appeal a forfeiture of the appeal.

A court may not enter judgment against a civil-forfeiture claimant merely because he is a fugitive from a related criminal prosecution; ordinary case-management powers suffice.

name: California capital appeals 1995-99 (Hardy): special circumstances, penalty factors
description: California capital appeals in 1995-99 only, anchored by Hardy (1992), on the guilt-side special circumstances and the statutory penalty factors: Anderson (1987) limits the intent-to-kill requirement to accomplices; Tuilaepa (1994) upholds the penalty factors; Cox (1991) and Benson (1990) uphold the mitigating-factor wording; Balderas (1985) requires other crimes proved beyond a reasonable doubt. Also Morris (1991) on in-limine objections.
history: Dominant rule: the California Supreme Court's settled answers to recurring claims in death-penalty appeals. The lineage exists only in 1995-99, anchored by People v. Hardy (1992), continuing a 1980s California capital-appeals unit and splitting in 2000-04. How it developed: Anderson (1987) overruled Carlos and required intent to kill for the felony-murder special circumstance only when the defendant was not the actual killer (with Pinholster 1992 on aider-and-abettor instructions). In the penalty phase, Balderas (1985) required other violent crimes to be proved beyond a reasonable doubt; Benson (1990) and Cox (1991) upheld the "extreme" and "substantial" modifiers in the mitigating factors; and Tuilaepa (1994) held the statutory factors not unconstitutionally vague. Trial rulings recur: a motion in limine preserves an objection (Morris 1991); a defendant may not use hearsay to testify without cross-examination (Edwards 1991); a codefendant may stress that he testified (Hardy); unanimity is not required on the theory of felony murder (Pride 1992); voir dire on racial prejudice (Kelly 1992); and Mickey (1991) modified Bigelow on self-representation.
rule: California's death-penalty statute is applied on automatic appeal by upholding the statutory penalty factors and their wording against Eighth Amendment challenge (Tuilaepa) and requiring intent to kill for the felony-murder special circumstance only for accomplices (Anderson).

changes.what: Unadjudicated criminal activity offered in aggravation must be proved beyond a reasonable doubt.

changes.case: People v. Benson; People v. Cox
changes.what: Modifiers such as "extreme" and "substantial" in the mitigating factors do not unconstitutionally limit the jury's consideration of mitigation.

description: Texas Anders practice since 2020: counsel's brief and the court's full review of the record (Anders 1967, Penson 1988, High 1978, Stafford 1991), no merits ruling on pro se issues (Bledsoe, 2005), and counsel's duties to the client (Schulman 2008, Kelly 2014), extended to termination appeals (P.M., 2016). previous.description: Texas appellate handling of Anders briefs since 2020: Anders and Penson on counsel's duty and the court's full examination of the record, with Texas Court of Criminal Appeals cases In re Schulman, Bledsoe, Stafford, Kelly and High on procedure for frivolous appeals, extended to parental-termination appeals (In re P.M.).

history: Dominant rule: Anders v. California (1967) anchors both slices: appointed counsel may file a brief stating that the appeal is frivolous only after a conscientious examination of the record, and the court of appeals must review the record itself (Penson, 1988; Flores, 2011). How it changed: no change in the rule within the slices; the lineage forms in 2020-24 from the earlier Texas Anders unit and a federal sentencing unit (Feemster, 2009). Its Texas rules rest on High (1978), Stafford (1991, new counsel for arguable grounds), Bledsoe (2005, no merits ruling on pro se issues), In re Schulman (2008, informing the client about a pro se petition for discretionary review) and Kelly (2014, helping the client obtain the record), with Ex parte Owens (2006) on losing a discretionary-review proceeding. In re P.M. (2016) carries the procedure into parental-termination appeals, where counsel's duty lasts through Supreme Court review, and G.P. (2016) applies the § 263.307(b) factors. In the partial 2025-29 slice judgment-reformation cases enter (Asberry, 1991; French, 1992; Bigley, 1993), as courts affirm while correcting judgments, along with attorney-fee assessments (Riles, 2015).
rule: Texas courts accept an Anders brief only after confirming counsel's conscientious review and the client's access to the record and right to respond, independently review the whole record, and either affirm (reforming the judgment to correct errors where needed) or abate for new counsel if an arguable ground exists.

changes.case: Anders v. California; Penson v. Ohio
changes.what: Counsel's no-merit brief and the court's independent examination of the record; denial of appellate counsel is presumptively prejudicial.

changes.case: High v. State; Stafford v. State
changes.what: Texas adopted Anders and requires new counsel when the court finds arguable grounds.

changes.case: Asberry v. State; French v. State; Bigley v. State
changes.what: Appellate courts may reform a judgment to make the record speak the truth, such as adding a deadly-weapon finding or correcting clerical errors.

changes.case: Bledsoe v. State; In re Schulman; Kelly v. State
changes.what: Courts do not decide pro se issues on the merits; counsel must inform the client of pro se review rights and facilitate access to the record.

description: Hawaii Supreme Court criminal law in 1995-99, anchored by Arceo (1996): an election or a specific unanimity instruction is required when several acts could support a charge, and its absence is plain error. history: Dominant rule: Hawaii's protective rules on jury instructions and error review. Arceo (1996) anchors the lineage's only slice, 1995-99, which later splits into three 2000-04 units: unless the prosecution elects the act it relies on, the court must give a specific unanimity instruction, and failure is plain error. How it changed: Holbron (1995) overruled Tagaro and adopted harmless beyond a reasonable doubt under HRPP Rule 52(a). Toyomura (1995) treated an officer's improper lay opinion on intoxication as harmless; Gaylord (1995) limited restitution to what a defendant can pay; Hoey (1994) gave broader state right-to-counsel protection; Kelekolio (1993) rejected a bright-line bar on police use of false documents in interrogation. Alongside: statutory construction (Gray 1997, Camara 1996, In the Interest of Doe 1994), sufficiency on circumstantial evidence (Batson 1992), and some civil cases (Amfac 1992, Sullivan 1998).
rule: When several acts could support a single charge, the Hawaii prosecution must elect the act it relies on or the court must give a specific unanimity instruction, and failure to do so is plain error (Arceo); preserved errors are reviewed for harmlessness beyond a reasonable doubt (Holbron).

changes.what: The Hawaii Constitution gives broader right-to-counsel protection: police must stop questioning or seek only clarification after an equivocal request for counsel.
Overruled State v. Tagaro and read HRPP Rule 52(a) to impose a harmless-beyond-a-reasonable-doubt standard.
Restitution orders are limited to an amount the defendant can afford to pay.
A specific unanimity instruction is required unless the prosecution elects the specific act it relies on; failing to give it was plain error.

name: Minimum contacts in the Supreme Court, 1930-2029: International Shoe to Ford
description: The Supreme Court's minimum-contacts line: the pre-1945 'doing business' test (International Harvester, People's Tobacco) gave way to International Shoe (1945, anchor from 1950-54). Hanson, World-Wide Volkswagen (1980) and Burger King (1985, anchor from 1995-99) require purposeful availment; Goodyear (2011), Daimler and Walden (2014) narrowed jurisdiction; Bristol-Myers (2017) and Ford (2021) refined relatedness.

history: Dominant rule: a state may bind a nonresident only on the basis of the defendant's purposeful contacts with the forum, consistent with fair play and substantial justice. How it changed: in 1930-49 the anchors are McKibbin (1917), People's Tobacco (1918) and International Harvester (1914), asking whether a corporation was doing business in the state, with Cannon (1925) keeping subsidiaries separate and Davis (1923) barring suits that burdened interstate commerce. International Shoe (1945) enters in 1945-49 and anchors 1950-94, joined by McGee (1957) and Hanson (1958); the 1960s carry divorce-jurisdiction cases. Shaffer (1977) and Kulko (1978) enter in 1975-79, and Woodson (1980), Keeton and Calder (1984), Hall (1984), Burger King (1985) and Asahi (1987) build the modern test; Burger King anchors from 1995-99. Internet and effects cases (Panavision, Schwarzenegger) lead 2005-09. Goodyear, Nicastro, Daimler and Walden enter in 2010-14, and Bristol-Myers and Ford lead 2020-29.
rule: Due process permits jurisdiction over a nonresident only where the defendant's own purposeful contacts with the forum give rise or relate to the claim, or the defendant is essentially at home there, and the exercise of jurisdiction is reasonable.

changes.case: International Harvester v. Kentucky; People's Tobacco; Davis v. Farmers Co-op (1923); Cannon Manufacturing v. Cudahy
changes.what: A foreign corporation was suable only if doing business in the state; solicitation alone was not enough, a subsidiary's presence was not the parent's, and suits that unduly burdened interstate commerce were barred.
Minimum contacts and fair play and substantial justice replaced the presence test; anchor from 1950-54.

description: Alabama custody: a parent seeking to modify custody must show the change materially promotes the child's welfare and its good offsets the disruption (Ex parte McLendon, 1984, anchor 1985-2004); a parent beats a nonparent unless unfit (Terry, 1986). Termination requires statutory grounds and no viable alternative (Ex parte Beasley, 1990, anchor 2005-09). Fann (2001) overruled Fesmire on explicit abuse findings.

history: Dominant rule: an existing custody judgment is modified only if the petitioner shows the change will materially promote the child's best interests and that its positive good offsets its disruptive effect (Ex parte McLendon, 1984, the anchor from 1985-89 through 2000-04). How it changed: Terry (1986) and Mathews (1983) gave a natural parent a prima facie right to custody against a nonparent unless unfit, a presumption McLendon held lost after a judgment for a nonparent; W.B.Z. (1994) applied it to unwed fathers. Sims (1987) held McLendon inapplicable to initial determinations after a pendente lite order, and Couch (1988) applied best interest to joint-custody modification. Bryowsky (1996) entered in 1995-99, requiring appellate courts to presume the findings needed to support the judgment. In 2000-04 termination cases merge in, and Ex parte Beasley (1990) anchors 2005-09: termination needs clear and convincing grounds and consideration of viable alternatives (L.M., 2002, on abandonment; T.V., 2007). Ex parte Fann (2001) overruled Fesmire and stressed ore tenus deference. Also: property division and alimony (Parrish, 1993).
rule: A parent seeking to modify an existing custody judgment must show that the change will materially promote the child's welfare and that its positive good offsets the disruption (Ex parte McLendon), and parental rights may be terminated only on clear and convincing proof of statutory grounds with no viable alternative (Ex parte Beasley).

name: State school-finance litigation, 1990-99: education clauses (Rose, Abbott)
description: School funding under state education clauses, 1990-99, after Rodriguez (1973) closed the federal route: courts read education clauses as enforceable (Robinson 1973, Seattle 1978, Pauley 1979, Rose 1989, Kirby 1989, Helena 1989, Abbott 1990, McWherter 1993), while others upheld funding or found no fundamental right (Thompson 1975, Walter 1979, Lujan 1982, Hornbeck 1983). Rose anchors 1990-94 and Abbott 1995-99.

history: Dominant rule: state constitutions govern school funding. Robinson v. Cahill (1973) struck New Jersey's system under its thorough-and-efficient clause, with remedial Robinson decisions in 1975-76; Seattle School District (1978) and Pauley (1979) treated education clauses as enforceable duties and allowed higher state standards. Other courts deferred: Thompson (1975), Walter (1979), McDaniel (1981), Lujan (Colorado 1982), Nyquist (1982), Hornbeck (1983) and Fair School Finance (Okla. 1987) upheld funding systems or held equal funding not required. How it changed: Rose (1989) anchors 1990-94; Kentucky held its whole system unconstitutional and defined an efficient system by minimum characteristics and seven student capacities, and Kirby (Texas) and Helena (Montana) struck systems the same year, while Kukor (Wis. 1989) applied rational-basis review. Abbott v. Burke (1990) anchors 1995-99: a thorough and efficient education is a changing concept. McWherter (Tenn. 1993) found an enforceable qualitative component, and the Robinson line re-enters as precedent for judicial remedies. The unit dissolves in 2000-04.
rule: With education not a fundamental federal right, state constitutional education clauses govern school funding, and several state courts read them as enforceable duties to provide an adequate, thorough and efficient education.

changes.what: Financing with no relation to equal educational opportunity violates the state thorough-and-efficient clause.

changes.what: Education clauses impose enforceable duties beyond federal equal-protection standards.

changes.what: Whole funding systems struck, with Rose defining an efficient system by required student capacities.

changes.case: Abbott v. Burke; Tennessee Small School Systems v. McWherter

round1.name: State school-finance litigation: education clauses after Rodriguez (Robinson, Rose, Abbott)
round1.description: State school-finance litigation after Rodriguez (1973) closed the federal equal-protection route: state courts read 'thorough and efficient' and adequacy clauses as enforceable (Robinson, 1973; Seattle, 1978; Pauley, 1979; Rose, 1989; Kirby, 1989; Abbott, 1990; DeRolph, 1997), while others upheld funding or found no justiciable claim (Walter, 1979; Hornbeck, 1983; Sundlun, 1995). round1.history: Dominant rule: state constitutions, not the federal one, govern school funding. Rodriguez (1973) held education is not a fundamental right under the Equal Protection Clause. Robinson v. Cahill (1973) then struck New Jersey's system under its thorough-and-efficient clause, followed by remedial Robinson decisions (1975-76). Seattle School District (1978) and Pauley (1979) treat education clauses as enforceable duties requiring more than equal dollars. Other courts deferred: Walter (1979), Lujan (Colorado, 1982), Nyquist (1982) and Hornbeck (1983) upheld funding systems. How it changed: Rose (1989) anchors 1990-94. Kentucky held its whole system unconstitutional and defined an efficient system by seven student capacities, and Kirby (1989) and Helena (1989) struck systems in Texas and Montana. Abbott (1990) anchors 1995-99 and 2000-04: adequacy is a changing concept and the state bears full responsibility. McWherter (1993) found a qualitative component, and DeRolph (1997, 2000) and Burke (1997-98) struck Ohio and New Jersey funding. By 2005-09 Burke anchors, and Sundlun (1995) and Chiles (1996) represent the non-justiciability response.
round1.rule: Because Rodriguez held education is not a fundamental federal right, school-funding challenges proceed under state education clauses, which many state courts read to impose an enforceable duty to provide a thorough, efficient or adequate education, while others find the claims non-justiciable or satisfied by rational funding.

name: § 10(b) securities fraud: scienter, PSLRA strong inference (Tellabs), Basic reliance
description: Private § 10(b) and Rule 10b-5 actions: scienter beyond negligence (Hochfelder, 1976), total-mix materiality (TSC, Basic) and presumed reliance (Basic, 1988). After the 1995 PSLRA the circuits split over the strong-inference standard (Time Warner, Silicon Graphics, Greebel, Advanta) until Tellabs (2007) required an inference at least as compelling as any innocent one; Dura (2005) added loss causation and Central Bank (1994) barred aiding-and-abetting suits.

previous.name: Securities fraud: § 10(b) scienter and pleading
previous.description: Section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5 private actions: Hochfelder scienter, Basic and TSC materiality, Dura loss causation, and PSLRA strong-inference pleading (Tellabs, Silicon Graphics, Advanta, Greebel).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session subagents, from cocite evidence; second pass differentiated near-duplicates)

history: Dominant rule: the elements and pleading of a private Rule 10b-5 claim. Basic v. Levinson (1988) anchors 2000-09 for materiality and fraud-on-the-market reliance, with Hochfelder (1976) on scienter, TSC (1976) on materiality and Blue Chip Stamps (1975) on standing. How it changed: in 1995-99 the anchor is In re Time Warner (2d Cir. 1993), whose motive-and-opportunity or recklessness test governed Rule 9(b) pleading. The 1995 PSLRA required facts giving a strong inference of scienter, and in 2000-04 circuit decisions divided: Silicon Graphics (9th Cir. 1999) required deliberate recklessness, while Greebel (1st Cir.), Advanta (3d Cir.), Comshare and Helwig (6th Cir.) took case-by-case approaches. Central Bank (1994) barred aiding-and-abetting suits and Stoneridge (2008) limited scheme liability; Dabit (2006) read SLUSA broadly; Dura (2005) required loss causation. Tellabs (2007) settled the strong-inference standard and anchors 2010-14, with Matrixx (2011) on materiality and Second Circuit puffery cases (ECA, ATSI). The 2010-14 slice then splits into general pleading.
rule: A private Rule 10b-5 plaintiff must plead and prove a material misstatement or omission (TSC, Basic), scienter beyond negligence (Hochfelder) pleaded with facts giving a strong inference at least as compelling as any innocent one (PSLRA, Tellabs), reliance (presumed under fraud-on-the-market), and loss causation (Dura).

changes.case: Blue Chip Stamps; Ernst & Ernst v. Hochfelder; TSC Industries
changes.what: Only purchasers and sellers may sue, negligence is not enough, and a fact is material if it would alter the total mix of information.
Reliance may be presumed under the fraud-on-the-market theory, and the total-mix materiality test applies to 10b-5; Basic anchors 2000-09.
No private aiding-and-abetting liability under § 10(b).

changes.case: PSLRA; In re Time Warner (2d Cir.); In re Silicon Graphics (9th Cir.); Greebel (1st Cir.); Advanta (3d Cir.)
changes.what: Circuits divided on whether the PSLRA's strong-inference standard kept the Second Circuit's motive-and-opportunity test or required facts showing deliberate recklessness.
An inflated purchase price alone does not plead loss causation; the misrepresentation must proximately cause economic loss.
A strong inference is one at least as compelling as any opposing inference, judged holistically; Tellabs anchors 2010-14.
Materiality of adverse-event reports is not limited to statistical significance.

name: Copyright: originality, idea-expression and fair use (Harper & Row, Feist)
description: Copyright's scope and limits: protection reaches original expression, not ideas or facts (Baker 1880, Nichols 1930, Feist 1991 rejecting sweat of the brow), and fair use weighs the § 107 factors (Sony 1984, Harper & Row 1985, Campbell 1994 on transformative use). Harper & Row anchors most slices from 1985-89; Napster (2001) and Grokster (2005) lead 2005-09 on secondary liability.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Copyright: originality, infringement and fair use
previous.description: Copyright protection and its limits: Feist on originality, Baker v. Selden and Nichols on idea/expression, Harper & Row, Sony and Campbell on fair use, Stewart v. Abend, and Altai (Computer Associates) on software infringement.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session subagents, from cocite evidence; second pass differentiated near-duplicates)

history: Dominant rule: copyright protects original expression only, subject to fair use. How it changed: in 1975-84 Mazer (1954) and Reyher (2d Cir. 1976) anchor idea-expression and substantial-similarity law (Nichols, Peter Pan Fabrics, Hoehling on historical facts, scenes a faire). Harper & Row (1985) enters and anchors 1985-94: copying the heart of an unpublished work was not fair use, with Sony (1984) treating time-shifting as fair use; the Second Circuit's Salinger and New Era (1987-90) cases on unpublished letters follow. Feist (1991) enters in 1990-94, rejecting sweat of the brow, and anchors 2000-04 and 2015-19. Campbell (1994) enters in 1995-99, making transformative use central, with Altai (1992) and Lotus v. Borland (1995) on software. Napster (2001) and Grokster (2005) lead 2005-09, when Sony anchors, on secondary liability. Bill Graham Archives (2006), Perfect 10 (2007) and Authors Guild v. Google (2015) apply transformative use. Drift: in 2020-24 unrelated bankruptcy cases (Radlax) merge in.
rule: Copyright protects only original expression, not ideas, facts or utilitarian features, and a use is fair or infringing according to the four § 107 factors, weighed together with particular attention to whether the use is transformative or supersedes the original.

changes.case: Baker v. Selden; Nichols v. Universal; Mazer v. Stein
changes.what: Protection extends to expression, not ideas or systems, and not literally to text alone; applied art is copyrightable but not its utilitarian aspects.

changes.case: Sony Corp. v. Universal City Studios
changes.what: Home time-shifting was fair use, and selling a device capable of substantial noninfringing uses is not contributory infringement.
Taking the heart of unpublished memoirs was not fair use; unpublished status and market substitution weigh heavily. Anchors from 1985-89.
Rejected the sweat-of-the-brow doctrine; compilations of facts need a modicum of creative originality.
Abstraction-filtration-comparison test for nonliteral copying of software.
Commercial parody can be fair use; the central question is whether the use is transformative, and the factors are weighed together.

changes.case: A&M Records v. Napster; MGM v. Grokster
changes.what: Peer-to-peer services can be contributorily or vicariously liable, and inducing infringement creates liability despite Sony.

name: Pennsylvania standing (William Penn) and constitutional limits on legislation
description: Pennsylvania justiciability and legislative-process cases: standing needs a substantial, direct and immediate interest (William Penn Parking, 1975), legislators' standing is narrow (Fumo 2009, Markham 2016), and no advisory opinions issue. Single-subject and nondelegation challenges lead in 2005-14 (City of Philadelphia 2003, PAGE 2005, Stilp 2006); from 2015-19 Robinson Township (2013) anchors on the Environmental Rights Amendment.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Pennsylvania standing, ripeness and single-subject challenges
previous.description: Pennsylvania Supreme Court justiciability cases: William Penn Parking's substantial-direct-immediate standing test, advisory opinions and mootness, and single-subject challenges to legislation (Stilp, Jubelirer, Fumo).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session subagents, from cocite evidence; second pass differentiated near-duplicates)

history: Dominant rule: William Penn Parking (1975) anchors 2005-09 and leads throughout: a party is aggrieved only with an interest that is substantial, direct and immediate, not the common interest of all citizens in obedience to law; courts give no advisory opinions and dismiss moot cases (In re Gross, 1978). How it changed: in 2005-09 and 2010-14 the leading merits cases enforce Article III's process rules: City of Philadelphia (2003) rejected 'municipalities' as a single subject, Pennsylvanians Against Gambling Expansion Fund (2005) struck a Gaming Act provision for lack of standards, and Stilp (2006) allowed germane amendments. Fumo (2009) limited legislative standing to harms to legislative power, later followed in Markham (2016). Robinson Township (2013) anchors 2015-19 and 2020-24, invalidating Act 13's limits on local zoning of drilling and reviving Article I, § 27; Payne (1973, 1976) enters and leaves as the Court abandoned its test in 2017. Also: nondelegation (Chiropractic Examiners, 1971; Protz, 2017), Commonwealth Court jurisdiction over Right-to-Know disputes (Governor's Office v. OOR, 2014), and the rule that holdings are read against their facts (Maloney, 2009).
rule: A party has standing in Pennsylvania only with a substantial, direct and immediate interest in the outcome (William Penn Parking), and the Supreme Court enforces the Constitution's procedural and structural limits on legislation, including the single-subject and original-purpose rules, nondelegation, and the Environmental Rights Amendment.

changes.case: William Penn Parking Garage v. City of Pittsburgh
changes.what: Aggrievement requires an interest that is substantial (beyond the common interest of citizens), direct and immediate.

changes.case: City of Philadelphia v. Commonwealth (2003); Pennsylvanians Against Gambling Expansion Fund v. Commonwealth (2005); Stilp v. Commonwealth (2006)
changes.what: Single-subject review rejects overly broad unifying subjects such as 'municipalities'; Gaming Act § 1506 lacked adequate standards; germane amendments do not violate the three-day rule.

changes.case: Fumo v. City of Philadelphia; Markham v. Wolf
changes.what: Legislators have standing only for injury to their legislative authority, not for general disagreement with how the law is executed.
A plurality held Act 13 unconstitutionally limited municipal zoning of oil and gas operations, reading Article I, § 27 as a public trust.

changes.case: Pennsylvania Environmental Defense Foundation v. Commonwealth; Protz v. WCAB
changes.what: The Court rejected the Payne (1973, 1976) balancing test for Article I, § 27 in favour of trust principles, and Protz struck a delegation to the AMA Guides.

name: Fourth Circuit disability review: treating-physician weight and Hays (1990-94)
description: Fourth Circuit Social Security review, 1990-94: treating physicians' opinions get great weight unless persuasive contrary evidence exists (Foster 1986, Coffman 1987), and Hays (1990) leaves weighing to the ALJ under the Perales (1971, anchor), Consolidated Edison and Laws (1966) substantial-evidence test. The ALJ must show the evidence considered (Stephens 1985); vocational hypotheticals must include all impairments (Walker 1989).
history: Dominant rule: Richardson v. Perales (1971), anchor of the single slice (1990-94), with Consolidated Edison (1938) and Laws v. Celebrezze (4th Cir. 1966), defines substantial evidence as what a reasoning mind would accept as sufficient, and Consolo (1966) holds that two inconsistent conclusions do not defeat it. Hays v. Sullivan (4th Cir. 1990) confines review to substantial evidence and correct law, leaving the weight of evidence and conflicts to the ALJ. How it changed: the slice gathers circuit refinements of the late 1980s. Foster (1986) and Coffman (1987) gave treating physicians' opinions great weight, overcome only by persuasive contrary evidence. Walker v. Bowen (1987) let ALJs discount subjective discomfort not borne out by objective evidence, and Walker (1989) required vocational hypotheticals that fairly set out all impairments, with Shively (1984) reserving the disability decision to the ALJ. Stephens (7th Cir. 1985) required enough discussion to trace the ALJ's reasoning, and Delgado (1986) required the court to review the whole record. The unit merged from Sixth Circuit and other disability units and splits again in 1995-99.
rule: A disability denial stands if supported by substantial evidence, evidence a reasoning mind would accept as sufficient, and if the correct law was applied; the ALJ, not the court, weighs evidence and resolves conflicts, but must explain the evidence considered and give a treating physician's opinion great weight absent persuasive contrary evidence.

changes.case: Laws v. Celebrezze (4th Cir.); Consolo v. Federal Maritime Comm'n
changes.what: Substantial evidence is what a reasoning mind would accept as sufficient; the possibility of drawing inconsistent conclusions does not defeat it.
The ALJ's discussion must let the court trace the path of reasoning and show important evidence was considered.

changes.case: Foster v. Heckler; Coffman v. Bowen (4th Cir.)
changes.what: A treating physician's opinion is entitled to great weight and may be disregarded only on persuasive contrary evidence.

changes.case: Walker v. Bowen; Walker v. Bowen (4th Cir.)
changes.what: Subjective complaints may be discounted if unsupported by objective evidence; vocational hypotheticals must fairly set out all impairments.
Review asks only whether substantial evidence supports the findings and the correct law was applied; the ALJ resolves conflicts.

name: Ohio mootness: actual controversies (Fortner) and served sentences (Wilson, Golston)
description: Ohio mootness: courts decide only live, actual controversies (Fortner, 1970). A misdemeanor appeal is moot once a voluntarily served sentence leaves no collateral disability (Wilson, 1975; Berndt, 1987), but Golston (1994) held felony convictions always carry collateral consequences. Exceptions: capable of repetition yet evading review for the same parties, and great public interest. Fortner and Cyran (2018) lead the 2020s.

previous.name: Ohio mootness doctrine
previous.description: Ohio Supreme Court decisions (Fortner, Wilson, Golston, Cyran) refusing to decide abstract or moot controversies and their exceptions.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session subagents, from cocite evidence; second pass differentiated near-duplicates)

history: Dominant rule: Ohio courts refuse to decide moot or abstract questions; they decide actual controversies whose judgment can be given effect (Fortner, 1970; Tschantz, 1991). Wilson (1975) anchors from 1995-99 to 2015-19: an appeal from a misdemeanor conviction is moot once the sentence has been voluntarily served, unless the defendant offers evidence of some collateral disability apart from the sentence; Berndt (1987) held an enhanced penalty on a later offence is not such a disability. How it changed: Golston (1994) limited Wilson and Berndt to misdemeanors, since a felony conviction's collateral consequences are severe and obvious. Lewis (2011) and In re S.J.K. (2007) enter in 2010-14. In 2015-19 public-utilities appeals briefly merge in (Monongahela Power, Constellation NewEnergy), drawing on Fortner. From 2020-24 the anchor is Cyran (2018) with State v. Smith (2019), In re A.G. (2014) and Dibert (2018), applying mootness and its exceptions (capable of repetition for the same party, Flaherty, 1991; abatement on death, In re L.W., 2006). Fortner anchors 2025-29.
rule: Ohio courts decide only actual controversies whose judgments can be carried into effect; an appeal from a misdemeanor conviction whose sentence was voluntarily served is moot unless the defendant shows a collateral disability, while a felony conviction carries collateral consequences that keep the appeal alive.

changes.what: Every tribunal's duty is to decide actual controversies between parties legitimately affected by specific facts and to render judgments that can be carried into effect.

changes.case: State v. Wilson; State v. Berndt
changes.what: A misdemeanant who voluntarily completes the sentence has a moot appeal absent evidence of a collateral disability; an enhanced penalty on a later conviction is not one.
The Wilson and Berndt test applies only to misdemeanors; a felony conviction's collateral consequences are severe and obvious, so its appeal is not moot.
The capable-of-repetition exception needs a reasonable expectation that the same controversy will recur for the same complaining party.

Armbrister (2013) governs parenting-schedule changes. In 2005-09 termination-of-parental-rights cases lead (In re Valentine 2002), and Bogan (2001) anchors 2010-14.

history: Dominant rule: discretionary decisions on alimony, property and parenting, reviewed for abuse of discretion. How it changed: in 2005-09 the anchor is In re Valentine (2002), as termination-of-parental-rights cases merge in (C.W.W. 2000; M.J.B. 2004; Jones 2002), with Blair (2002) on superior parental rights after a valid custody transfer; that strand splits off in 2010-14. Bogan (2001), on modifying alimony when the obligor retires, anchors 2010-14, with Robertson (2002), which replaced lifelong support with a preference for rehabilitation, and Kendrick (2002) on custody modification. Lee Medical (2010) frames abuse-of-discretion review and Eldridge (2001) holds that applying incorrect legal principles is an abuse. Gonsewski (2011) anchors 2015-19 and 2020-24, telling appellate courts not to second-guess alimony and stressing need and ability to pay; Armbrister (2013), Kelly (2014) and Lovlace (2013) govern parenting-plan changes. General civil rules travel with the unit: prejudgment interest (Myint 1998), contempt (Konvalinka 2008), Rule 60.02 (Henderson 2010), fees (Wright 2011). Eldridge anchors the partial 2025-29 slice.
rule: Tennessee appellate courts review discretionary decisions on alimony, property division and parenting for abuse of discretion, which occurs when a court applies an incorrect legal standard or reaches an illogical result, viewing the evidence in favor of the decision (Eldridge; Lee Medical; Gonsewski).

changes.what: Division of marital property, including retirement benefits, need not be mathematically precise but must reflect essential fairness.
A trial court abuses its discretion when it applies incorrect legal principles; visitation is not limited without definite evidence of harm to the child.
Lifelong support was superseded by the legislature's preference for rehabilitative alimony, with property division used to meet need where feasible.
In termination cases substantial noncompliance is a question of law reviewed de novo, and one statutory ground suffices.
Appellate courts should not second-guess alimony decisions, reviewing the evidence in the light most favorable to them; need and ability to pay are the key factors.
Modifying a residential parenting schedule needs a lower showing of a material change than modifying custody; Kelly (2014) applied the standard to initial designations.

round1.description: Tennessee domestic-relations appeals: early slices on fault-neutral alimony (Fisher, 1983) and marital retirement accounts (Batson, 1988); Brown (1994) and Kinard (1998) on fair property division. Burlew (2001) and Robertson (2002) replaced lifelong support with a preference for rehabilitative alimony; Gonsewski (2011) anchors from 2015 on need, ability to pay and deferential review; Armbrister (2013) governs parenting changes.
round1.history: Dominant rule: discretionary decisions on alimony, property and parenting, reviewed for abuse of discretion. In 1985-94 small units anchor on Fisher (1983), which forbids punitive use of fault, and Batson (1988), which classifies marital-income growth in retirement accounts as marital. How it changed: Brown (1994) anchors 1995-2004 on separate gifts and fair, not equal, division, with Cohen (1996) treating vested and unvested pensions accrued during marriage as marital and Kinard (1998) requiring essential fairness. Burlew (2001) and Crabtree (2000) set the alimony factors and the threshold finding that rehabilitation is not feasible before alimony in futuro; Robertson (2002) declared lifelong support superseded by the legislative preference for rehabilitation. In 2005-09 the anchor is In re Valentine (2002), as termination-of-parental-rights cases merge in. Robertson anchors 2010-14 and Gonsewski (2011) 2015-24, holding the court should not second-guess alimony decisions and stressing need and ability to pay. Lee Medical (2010) frames abuse-of-discretion review, Eldridge (2001) anchors 2025-29, and Armbrister (2013) governs parenting-plan modifications.
round1.rule: Tennessee trial courts have broad discretion over property division, alimony and parenting, reviewed for abuse of discretion (Eldridge, Lee Medical, Gonsewski); alimony turns chiefly on the disadvantaged spouse's need and the obligor's ability to pay, with a statutory preference for rehabilitative or transitional over long-term alimony in futuro (Burlew, Robertson, Gonsewski).

changes.case: Fisher v. Fisher; Duncan v. Duncan; Batson v. Batson
changes.what: Fault may be considered but not punitively in alimony, punitive alimony is not allowed, and retirement-account growth funded with marital income is marital property; Fisher and Batson anchor 1985-94.

changes.case: Brown v. Brown; Aaron v. Aaron; Cohen v. Cohen; Kinard v. Kinard
changes.what: Property division need not be equal but must be fair, retirement benefits accrued during marriage are marital, and attorney's fees are reviewed for abuse of discretion; Brown anchors 1995-2004.

changes.case: Burlew v. Burlew; Robertson v. Robertson
changes.what: Lifelong support to maintain the marital standard of living was superseded by a legislative preference for rehabilitative alimony, with in futuro awarded only where rehabilitation is not feasible; Robertson anchors 2010-14.

previous.description: Texas trial-court discretion: discovery sanctions and death-penalty sanctions (TransAmerican v. Powell, Cire), adequacy of medical-malpractice expert reports (Palacios, Wright), and just-and-right division of the community estate (Murff, Jacobs).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: deference to the trial court under the abuse-of-discretion standard, chiefly in dividing marital property. Murff (1981) anchors 1995-2004 and 2010-24: the court may consider many factors, including fault and the size of separate estates, and its just and right division is presumed proper. Jacobs (1985) confines division to community property and requires remand of the entire estate for material error, and Penick (1990), Zieba (1996) and Boyd (2004) cover reimbursement, waste and tracing of separate property. Downer (1985) defines abuse of discretion, Worford (1991) and Gillespie (1982) apply it to support and conservatorship, and Schlueter (1998) bars an independent tort for wrongful disposal of community assets. How it changed: in 2005-09 the anchor moves to Palacios (2001). Medical-malpractice expert reports are reviewed within their four corners and must address standard of care, breach and causation (Wright 2002; Broders 1996 on qualifications). Chapter 74 (§ 74.351) replaced former § 13.01 in 2003, and Lewis (2008) allowed cure by a new expert. That strand splits off in 2010-14. Sanctions follow TransAmerican v. Powell (1991), Cire (2004) and Low (2007). 2015-24 returns to family-law division and modification.
rule: A Texas trial court abuses its discretion only when it acts arbitrarily or without reference to guiding rules and principles (Downer); under that standard it has wide latitude to make a just and right division of the community estate, considering factors such as fault and the size of separate estates (Murff), and to decide conservatorship, support and sanctions.

changes.what: The court may weigh disparity of earning capacity, fault, separate estates and other factors in a just and right division, and its division is presumed proper.

changes.case: Downer v. Aquamarine Operators; Jacobs v. Jacobs
changes.what: Abuse of discretion means acting without guiding rules or principles (Downer); a material error in part of the property division requires remanding the whole community estate (Jacobs).

changes.case: American Transitional Care Centers v. Palacios; Bowie Memorial Hospital v. Wright
changes.what: Adequacy of a medical-malpractice expert report under former § 13.01 is judged within its four corners, and a report must explain standard of care, breach and causation.

changes.case: Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code § 74.351; Walker v. Gutierrez; Lewis v. Funderburk
changes.what: Chapter 74 replaced § 13.01; a deficient report can be cured by an amended report or a new expert, and a motion to dismiss for an inadequate report is immediately appealable.
A death-penalty sanction requires the court to consider lesser sanctions and explain why the one imposed is appropriate.

name: Just and reasonable rates under the Natural Gas Act: Hope, Permian Basin
description: Federal ratemaking under the Natural Gas Act: a rate is just and reasonable if its end result balances investor and consumer interests (Hope, 1944), with producer regulation from Phillips (1954) and area rates upheld in Permian Basin (1968). Mobile-Sierra (1956) limits changes to contract rates. From 1990-94 the lineage turns to the filed-rate doctrine (Maislin, 1990).
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Natural gas and energy rate regulation
previous.description: Federal Power Commission ratemaking under the Natural Gas Act: just and reasonable rates and the end-result test (Hope Natural Gas, Natural Gas Pipeline), producer regulation (Phillips Petroleum, Permian Basin, Atlantic Refining 'CATCO'), the Mobile-Sierra doctrine and the filed-rate doctrine (Maislin).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: under the Natural Gas Act a commission may fix any rate within a zone of reasonableness (Natural Gas Pipeline, 1942), and what matters is the end result, balancing investor and consumer interests, not a 'fair value' formula (Hope, 1944). How it changed: the early slices (1960-69) concern producer certificates and pricing after Phillips (1954) extended jurisdiction to wellhead sales, with Atlantic Refining (CATCO, 1959) and Callery (1965) on certificate conditions. Permian Basin (1968) upheld area maximum rates and leads from 1970-74; Hope anchors 1970-84. Mobile-Sierra (1956) on contract rates joins the leaders in 1985-89. The dominant rule then shifts: from 1990-94 Maislin (1990) anchors and the lineage becomes about the filed-rate doctrine (Maxwell, 1915; Keogh, 1922; Western Pacific), under which a carrier must charge its filed tariff and privately negotiated rates are unenforceable.
rule: A rate is just and reasonable if its end result balances investor and consumer interests within a zone of reasonableness; the method used does not control.

changes.case: Natural Gas Pipeline (FPC 1942); FPC v. Hope Natural Gas
changes.what: The commission may fix any rate within the zone of reasonableness, and the end result rather than a 'fair value' method decides whether a rate is lawful.
FPC jurisdiction reaches independent producers' wellhead sales.

changes.case: United Gas Pipe Line v. Mobile Gas; FPC v. Sierra Pacific
changes.what: Contract rates may be modified only when the public interest requires (Mobile-Sierra).
Upheld area-wide maximum rates for producers instead of individual company ratemaking.
The filed-rate doctrine bars enforcing privately negotiated unfiled rates; the agency cannot override it as an 'unreasonable practice'.

name: California Prop. 36 resentencing: Apprendi does not apply (Kaulick, Osuna)
description: California Three Strikes Reform Act (Proposition 36, 2012) resentencing: prisoners already sentenced must petition under § 1170.126 (Yearwood, 2013), and because resentencing can only lower a term, Apprendi and Blakely do not apply: the court finds dangerousness (Kaulick, 2013) and arming disqualifiers (Osuna, Blakely, 2014) itself. Blakely, 2014; Elder; Brimmer). description: Apprendi (2000, anchor) and Blakely (2004) after Booker, 2005-09, centred on Fifth Circuit illegal-reentry appeals: Almendarez-Torres (1998) still lets judges find prior convictions (Pineda-Arrellano 2007), and unpreserved Booker error is reviewed for plain error (Mares 2005). name: Equal protection challenges to automobile guest statutes (Brown v. Merlo)
description: Whether automobile guest statutes, which bar a passenger's ordinary-negligence suit against the driver, deny equal protection. Older cases upheld them (Silver 1929, Shea 1936, Perozzi 1934). Brown v. Merlo (Cal. 1973) struck California's statute, and in 1974-75 Henry (Kan.), Thompson (Idaho), Laakonen (Mich.) and Primes (Ohio) followed, while Delaware and South Dakota courts upheld theirs.

previous.description: State-court equal protection challenges to automobile guest statutes barring passengers' negligence suits against drivers (Brown v. Merlo, Henry v. Bauder, Thompson v. Hagan, Silver v. Silver).

history: Dominant rule: guest statutes are tested against equal protection, and the answer turned over during the lineage. Hagan (Idaho 1974) as anchor: Henry v. Bauder (Kan.), Thompson (applied prospectively), Laakonen (Mich.) and Primes (Ohio) struck their statutes, while Justice (Del. 1974) and Behrns (S.D. 1975) deferred to the legislature and upheld theirs. name: Juvenile life sentences after Miller in Illinois: Holman, Buffer, Dorsey
description: Eighth Amendment limits on juvenile life sentences as applied in Illinois: Miller (2012) barred mandatory life without parole for under-18 offenders, retroactively (Montgomery, 2016). Holman (2017) extended Miller to discretionary life terms, Buffer (2019) treated sentences over 40 years as de facto life, and Dorsey (2021) held good-time credit can avoid that line; Jones (2021) needs no incorrigibility finding. Young-adult claims (Harris, Clark) lead 2025-29.

previous.name: Juvenile life sentences after Miller (Illinois)
previous.description: Eighth Amendment limits on life sentences for juveniles: Roper, Graham, Miller and its retroactivity (Montgomery), applied by Illinois courts to de facto life terms and young adults (Holman, Buffer, Harris).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: Miller v. Alabama (2012) anchors 2015-19 and 2020-24: mandatory life without parole for offenders under 18 violates the Eighth Amendment, building on Roper (2005) and Graham (2010). Montgomery (2016) made Miller retroactive. In 2015-19 the lead also includes Teague (1989) on retroactivity and out-of-state cases extending Miller to long term-of-years and aggregate sentences (Iowa's Null and Ragland, 2013; Wyoming's Bear Cloud, 2014). How it changed: Illinois decisions enter in 2020-24. Holman (2017) applied Miller to discretionary life sentences. Buffer (2019) set 40 years as the line for de facto life, near the juvenile sentencing statute effective January 1, 2016. Dorsey (2021) held day-for-day credit that allows release by 38 years avoids it. Jones v. Mississippi (2021) needs no incorrigibility finding. Pitsonbarger (2002) supplies the cause-and-prejudice test for successive petitions, and People v. Miller (2002) the state proportionate-penalties route. In 2025-29 the anchor is People v. Clark (2023), with Hilliard (2023), on young adults over 18 seeking Miller-based relief and on the youthful-offender parole statute.
rule: The Eighth Amendment bars mandatory life without parole for offenders under 18 (Miller), retroactively (Montgomery); Illinois extends this to discretionary and de facto life sentences, treating a term over 40 years as de facto life unless good-time credit makes earlier release possible.

name: Louisiana criminal appeals: excessive-sentence review (Sepulvado, Dorthey)
description: Louisiana criminal appeals on sentence and sufficiency: a sentence within the statutory range may still be constitutionally excessive (Sepulvado, 1979), judges have wide discretion under art. 894.1 (Lanclos, 1982), and Dorthey (1993) lets courts go below a habitual-offender minimum that is excessive as applied. Hearold (1992) decides sufficiency first. Sepulvado anchors 1980-94; Dorthey and State v. Smith (1995) lead later.

previous.name: Louisiana criminal appeals: sufficiency and sentencing
previous.description: Louisiana criminal appeals: errors-patent review, sufficiency raised with other errors (Hearold, Bonanno), retrial after insufficiency reversals (Hudson, Burks), and constitutional review of habitual-offender sentences (Dorthey).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: review of Louisiana sentences for constitutional excessiveness. Sepulvado (1979) anchors 1980-84 to 1990-94: a sentence within the statutory range can still violate the state constitution's bar on excessive punishment, and Bonanno (1980), Quebedeaux (1982, maximum sentences for the worst offenders) and Lanclos (1982, art. 894.1 guidelines are not mandatory formulas) apply it. How it changed: Dorthey (1993) enters in 1995-99 and leads from 2000-04: the Habitual Offender Law is a valid enhancement, its hearing is not a trial for double-jeopardy purposes, but a court may depart below its minimum when that minimum is constitutionally excessive. Hearold (1992) also enters, requiring sufficiency to be decided first when raised with trial errors. Anchors then change slice by slice (Hogan, 1985; Bradford, 1997; State v. Smith, 1995; Weaver, 2002), with Pigford (2006) and Tate (2003) leading later. In 2020-24 the Louisiana errors-patent and Anders unit merges in (Oliveaux, Weiland, Lynch). Dorthey anchors 2020-24 and State v. Smith (1995) 2025-29.

name: Separation of powers, 2015-19: Chadha's bicameralism and presentment, Youngstown
description: General structural separation of powers as cited in 2015-19 (one slice), anchored by Chadha (1983): legislative acts require bicameralism and presentment; Youngstown (1952) limits unilateral executive action; Freytag and Morrison govern appointments, and Stern (2011) limits non-Article III adjudication. Noel Canning (2014) voided recess appointments; Winter supplies the injunction standard in challenges like Washington v. Trump (2017).

previous.name: Separation of powers: legislative veto, appointments, Article III (2015)
previous.description: Structural separation-of-powers cases as cited in 2015-19: Chadha's legislative veto, the line-item veto (Clinton), recess and principal-officer appointments (Noel Canning, Freytag), Article III adjudication (Stern) and foreign affairs (Zivotofsky). Its 2020s successor (28392) shifts to the President's removal power.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, contrastive pass from family evidence)

history: Dominant rule: the Constitution's structure limits each branch. Chadha (1983) anchors the single 2015-19 slice: Congress acts only through bicameralism and presentment, so the one-House veto falls, and Clinton v. City of New York (1998) applied the same logic to the line-item veto. Youngstown (1952) denies the President inherent power to seize property without Congress. Marbury (1803) and McCulloch (1819) supply judicial review and the necessary-and-proper reading. Appointments: Freytag (1991) held Tax Court special trial judges inferior officers, Morrison (1988) upheld the independent counsel, and Noel Canning (2014) invalidated recess appointments and voided NLRB orders. Article III: Stern (2011) bars bankruptcy courts from final judgment on certain core claims. Mistretta (1989) upheld the Sentencing Commission's delegation, and Zivotofsky (2012) narrowed the political-question doctrine. Also: NFIB (2012) on taxing and spending, Din (2015) on consular nonreviewability, and Winter (2008), the heaviest case, as the preliminary-injunction test in challenges to executive orders (Washington v. Trump 2017). In 2020-24 the unit splits into agency review and a removal-power unit.
rule: Each branch must act within its constitutional grant: Congress legislates only through bicameralism and presentment (Chadha), the President's power is weakest when he acts against Congress's will (Youngstown), officers must be appointed as Article II directs, and Congress may not give Article III judicial power to non-Article III tribunals (Stern).

name: Johnson (2015) residual-clause vagueness on collateral review: Welch, Beckles
description: Vagueness challenges and § 2255 motions after Johnson (2015, anchor) voided the ACCA residual clause, 2015-19 only: Welch (2016) made Johnson retroactive, Beckles (2017) held the advisory Guidelines immune from vagueness challenges (as the Eleventh Circuit had in Matchett), Beeman (2017) put the burden on the § 2255 movant to show the residual clause was used, and Dimaya (2018) struck § 16(b).
history: Dominant rule: the ACCA's residual clause, which counted any crime presenting a serious potential risk of injury as a violent felony, is void for vagueness (Johnson, 2015, anchor of the only slice, 2015-19). How it changed: the lineage forms when ACCA categorical-approach and habeas time-bar units merge. Before Johnson, the Supreme Court had applied the residual clause case by case (James 2007, attempted burglary; Begay 2008, DUI not violent; Sykes 2011, vehicle flight). Welch (2016) made Johnson a substantive rule retroactive on collateral review, prompting waves of § 2255 motions. The Eleventh Circuit held the Guidelines immune from vagueness challenges (Matchett 2015), extended this to mandatory-Guidelines sentences (In re Griffin 2016), and required a movant to prove the residual clause actually affected the sentence (Beeman 2017); Beckles (2017) confirmed the advisory Guidelines cannot be challenged for vagueness. Sessions v. Dimaya (2018) struck the parallel § 16(b) clause. Also: elements-clause classifications such as aggravated battery (Turner 2013) and Hobbs Act robbery under § 924(c) (Saint Fleur 2016). The unit flows back into the ACCA cluster in 2020-24.

Chapter 74 (2003) carried the rule into § 74.351; Ogletree and Lewis (2007-08) allow cure by extension; Jelinek (2010) requires explained causation; Scoresby (2011) lets any deficiency be cured; Zamarripa (2017) and Abshire (2018) refine causation.

history: Dominant rule: a health care liability claimant must serve an expert report that, within its four corners, fairly summarizes the standard of care, the breach and the causal link, so the defendant knows the conduct challenged and the court can see the claim has merit (Palacios 2001, anchor from 2005-24). How it changed: Wright (2002) rejected possibility-of-better-outcome causation while requiring no magic words; Broders (1996) required expert qualification on the specific matter; Walker (2003) applied abuse-of-discretion review to extensions. The 2003 reform recodified the requirement in Chapter 74, and Rubio (2005), Marks and Yamada (2010) and Loaisiga (2012) held that claims cannot be artfully pleaded around it, while Ross (2015) limited the definition for a visitor's slip and fall. Jernigan (2006) and Gray (2006) rejected passing references and generic standards; Ogletree (2007), Lewis and Leland (2008) allowed thirty-day cures and new experts. Jelinek (2010) required explained causation, and Scoresby (2011), following the Samlowski plurality, made all deficiencies curable. Van Ness (2015), Zamarripa (2017) and Baty and Abshire (2018) refine causation; Abshire anchors the partial 2025-29 slice. Also: no loss-of-chance recovery (Kramer 1993).
rule: A health care liability claimant must timely serve an expert report that, within its four corners, represents a good-faith effort to summarize the standard of care, how the defendant breached it, and how the breach caused the injury, informing the defendant of the conduct at issue and giving the court a basis to find the claim has merit; the trial court's ruling is reviewed for abuse of discretion.

changes.case: American Transitional Care Centers v. Palacios
changes.what: Under former art. 4590i § 13.01 the court looks only to the four corners of the report, which must inform the defendant of the conduct at issue and show the claim has merit.
A report speaking only of the possibility of a better outcome is insufficient on causation, though no magic words such as 'reasonable medical probability' are required.

changes.case: Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code ch. 74; Diversicare v. Rubio (2005)
changes.what: Article 4590i was repealed and recodified in Chapter 74, and a health care liability claim cannot be recast as another cause of action to avoid it.
