changes.what: A deficient report is not 'no report'; a thirty-day extension to cure is available, including through a new expert, and dismissal orders are immediately appealable.
The report must explain how the breach caused the injury, not merely assert it.
A report by a qualified expert that the claim has merit and implicates the defendant's conduct may be cured of any deficiency, in opinion or qualifications.

changes.case: Columbia Valley Healthcare v. Zamarripa; Abshire v. Christus Health; Baty
changes.what: The report must explain proximate cause linking conclusions to facts (abrogating contrary holdings) and is read as a whole.

name: Ohio felony sentencing review and Crim.R. 11 pleas: Foster to Marcum and Jones
description: Ohio felony sentencing review and Crim.R. 11 pleas. Foster (2006) excised judicial fact-finding after Blakely; Kalish (2008) set two-step review; after Oregon v. Ice (2009) consecutive findings returned (Bonnell, 2014). Marcum (2016) made review clear-and-convincing under R.C. 2953.08(G)(2) and Jones (2020) barred re-weighing the § 2929.11-.12 factors. Pleas: Nero and Veney compliance, and Dangler's (2020) prejudice rule.

previous.name: Ohio criminal: pleas and felony sentencing review
previous.description: Ohio Supreme Court cases on Crim.R. 11 plea colloquies (Nero, Veney, Dangler) and felony sentencing review (Foster, Kalish, Marcum, Bonnell, Jones).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session subagents, from cocite evidence; second pass differentiated near-duplicates)

history: Dominant rule: how far an Ohio appellate court may disturb a felony sentence, with plea-colloquy review alongside. The anchor shifts as the law changed. Foster (2006) anchors 2005-09: Blakely invalidated Ohio's required findings for non-minimum, maximum and consecutive terms, which Foster severed, leaving full discretion within the range subject to considering R.C. 2929.11 and 2929.12 (Mathis, 2006). Kalish (2008) anchors 2010-14 with its plurality two-step review (contrary to law, then abuse of discretion), as Oregon v. Ice (2009) enters, holding juries need not find consecutive-sentence facts; Ohio then restored consecutive findings, and Bonnell (2014) requires them at the hearing and in the entry. Marcum (2016) anchors 2015-19 and 2020-24: review is under R.C. 2953.08(G)(2), reversing only on clear and convincing proof the record does not support the findings. Jones (2020) anchors 2025-29: courts may not re-weigh the § 2929.11-.12 factors. Also: Crim.R. 11 pleas, with strict compliance for constitutional rights and substantial compliance otherwise (Nero, 1990; Veney, 2008), and Dangler (2020) requiring prejudice except for a complete failure.
rule: An Ohio appellate court may vacate or modify a felony sentence only if it clearly and convincingly finds the record does not support the required findings or the sentence is contrary to law (Marcum), and a plea stands unless the Crim.R. 11 colloquy failed on a constitutional right or the defendant shows prejudice (Veney, Dangler).

changes.case: State v. Foster; State v. Mathis
changes.what: Held the statutory findings required for non-minimum, maximum and consecutive sentences violated Blakely and excised them; trial courts gained full discretion within the range but must still consider R.C. 2929.11 and 2929.12.
Plurality two-step review: is the sentence clearly and convincingly contrary to law, then was it an abuse of discretion.
Strict compliance is required for the constitutional rights in Crim.R. 11(C)(2)(c); substantial compliance suffices for nonconstitutional notices (Nero, 1990).
The Sixth Amendment does not require juries to find facts for consecutive sentences, which allowed Ohio to restore statutory consecutive-sentence findings.
Consecutive-sentence findings must be made at the hearing and in the entry, but no talismanic words are needed if the record shows the correct analysis.
Replaced Kalish's abuse-of-discretion step with the R.C. 2953.08(G)(2) clear-and-convincing standard.

changes.case: State v. Jones; State v. Dangler
changes.what: Jones: an appellate court may not independently weigh the R.C. 2929.11 and 2929.12 factors; Dangler: outside a complete failure on constitutional rights, a plea challenger must show prejudice on the record.

name: California CEQA review of EIRs: Laurel Heights, Vineyard, Sierra Club v. Fresno
description: California Environmental Quality Act review of EIRs, anchored by Laurel Heights (1988) in every slice from 1995-99 but 2010-14 (Vineyard 2007): an informative EIR and alternatives analysis reviewed for substantial evidence (Goleta Valley 1990), no extra-record evidence (Western States 1995). Later: water supply and programmatic EIRs (Vineyard; Bay-Delta 2008), baselines (CBE 2010; Smart Rail 2013), exemptions (Berkeley Hillside 2015), Sierra Club v. Fresno (2018).
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, round 2 after the lineage re-link)

previous.description: California Environmental Quality Act review of environmental impact reports (Laurel Heights, Vineyard Area Citizens, Citizens of Goleta Valley, Sierra Club v. Fresno, Neighbors for Smart Rail) together with California water rights and the public trust (Bay-Delta).

history: Dominant rule: CEQA requires an EIR that informs decision makers and the public of significant effects and feasible alternatives, and courts ask whether the agency proceeded as required by law and whether substantial evidence supports its findings. How it changed: Laurel Heights I (1988) anchors 1995-99 through 2005-09, joined by Goleta Valley (1990) on alternatives, Laurel Heights II (1993) on recirculation, and Western States (1995) limiting extra-record evidence; No Oil (1974) on the fair-argument test reappears in 2005-09. Water and land-use cases join from 2000-04 (Kings County Farm Bureau 1990; County of Amador 1999; Planning and Conservation League 2000; Napa Citizens 2001 on fee-based mitigation). Vineyard (2007) anchors 2010-14, with Bay-Delta (2008) on programmatic EIRs and the public trust and California Native Plant Society (2009) on alternatives. Laurel Heights anchors again from 2015-19, as baseline rules (CBE 2010; Smart Rail 2013), categorical exemptions (Berkeley Hillside 2015), CEQA in reverse (CBIA 2015) and later-activity review (San Mateo Gardens 2016) enter. Sierra Club v. Fresno (2018) on adequacy of impact discussion and South of Market (2019) lead 2020-24, and Laurel Heights anchors the partial 2025-29 slice.
rule: Under CEQA an EIR must inform decision makers and the public of a project's significant effects and feasible alternatives; courts ask whether the agency proceeded as the law requires and whether substantial evidence supports its findings, without resolving disagreements among experts (Laurel Heights I).

changes.case: Laurel Heights Improvement Ass'n v. Regents (Laurel Heights I)
changes.what: An EIR must analyze reasonably foreseeable future uses and feasible alternatives, and its conclusions are reviewed for substantial evidence; expert disagreement does not make it inadequate.

changes.case: Citizens of Goleta Valley v. Board of Supervisors
changes.what: The range of alternatives is governed by a rule of reason, focused on those that would feasibly attain the project's basic objectives.

changes.case: Laurel Heights Improvement Ass'n v. Regents (Laurel Heights II)
changes.what: A final EIR must be recirculated only when significant new information is added.

changes.case: Western States Petroleum Ass'n v. Superior Court
changes.what: Evidence outside the administrative record is generally inadmissible to challenge quasi-legislative CEQA decisions.

changes.case: Vineyard Area Citizens v. City of Rancho Cordova; In re Bay-Delta Programmatic EIR
changes.what: An EIR must reasonably identify long-term water supplies; a programmatic EIR may defer site-specific detail, and the state must weigh the public trust in allocating water.

changes.case: Communities for a Better Environment v. South Coast AQMD; Neighbors for Smart Rail
changes.what: The baseline is normally existing physical conditions, not permitted levels; a future baseline needs justification.

changes.case: Sierra Club v. County of Fresno
changes.what: Whether an EIR's discussion of impacts is adequate is reviewed de novo as a question of law, while factual findings get substantial-evidence review.

round1.history: Dominant rule: CEQA requires an EIR that informs decision makers and the public of significant effects and feasible alternatives. round1.rule: Under CEQA an agency must prepare an environmental impact report that adequately informs decision makers and the public of a project's significant effects and reasonable alternatives, and courts review whether the agency proceeded as the law requires and whether its determinations are supported by substantial evidence.

changes.case: Friends of Mammoth v. Board of Supervisors
changes.what: CEQA applies to private projects that need a government permit, and is read to give the fullest possible protection to the environment.

changes.case: No Oil, Inc. v. City of Los Angeles
changes.what: An EIR is required whenever it can be fairly argued on substantial evidence that the project may have a significant effect.

changes.case: Laurel Heights Improvement Ass'n v. Regents (Laurel Heights I)
changes.what: An EIR must analyze reasonably foreseeable future expansion and discuss alternatives; courts defer to the agency's factual conclusions, and disagreement among experts does not make an EIR inadequate. Anchors from 1990-94.

changes.case: Citizens of Goleta Valley v. Board of Supervisors
changes.what: The range of alternatives an EIR must discuss is governed by a rule of reason.

changes.case: Western States Petroleum Ass'n v. Superior Court

changes.what: The baseline is ordinarily existing physical conditions, not permitted levels; a future baseline alone is allowed only if substantial evidence shows an existing baseline would mislead.

changes.case: Sierra Club v. County of Fresno

name: Georgia murder appeals: Jackson v. Virginia sufficiency and capital review
description: Georgia Supreme Court murder and felony-murder appeals applying Jackson v. Virginia (1979): a verdict stands if any rational trier of fact could find guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. Alongside: Williams (1991) on similar-transaction evidence, Malcolm (1993) on merger and felony murder, and in 2000-04 death-penalty review (DeYoung, Jenkins, Gissendaner) on juror qualification and proportionality.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Georgia criminal: Jackson sufficiency (1990s)
previous.description: Georgia Supreme Court murder and felony-murder appeals applying the Jackson v. Virginia rational-trier-of-fact standard.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: Jackson v. Virginia (1979) anchors both slices. A conviction is upheld if, viewing the evidence for the prosecution, any rational trier of fact could have found the essential elements beyond a reasonable doubt. The Georgia Supreme Court recites this in nearly every murder and felony-murder appeal. How it changed: the standard itself is stable. In 1995-99 the unit is very large (about 1,600 cases) and mixed, with Texas and federal cases (Arambula-Ruiz, Lennick, Baker) beside Georgia's Williams (1991), the three-pronged similar-transaction test. In 2000-04 a Georgia capital lineage merges in and the leading cases become Georgia death-penalty appeals: DeYoung (1997), Jenkins (1998), Barnes (1998), Greene (1997), Pace (1999, a juror merely leaning toward death is not excusable for cause) and Gissendaner (2000, proportionality review). Malcolm (1993) governs merger of felony murder and its underlying felony, and Ford (1987) holds Georgia juries need not balance aggravating against mitigating circumstances. The lineage then splits into Texas sufficiency units in 2005-09.
rule: A conviction stands if, viewing the evidence in the light most favourable to the verdict, any rational trier of fact could find every element proved beyond a reasonable doubt (Jackson v. Virginia).

changes.what: Due process requires evidence from which a rational trier of fact could find guilt beyond a reasonable doubt; the Georgia Supreme Court applies it in every murder appeal.
Announced the three-pronged test for admitting similar-transaction evidence, with findings required before admission.
The underlying felony merges into a felony-murder conviction, and a felony-murder verdict is vacated by operation of law when the defendant is also convicted of malice murder.
Statutory proportionality review asks whether a death sentence is excessive per se or substantially out of line with sentences in similar cases.

name: Texas no-evidence points, 2015-19: equal inferences and conclusory experts
description: How Texas no-evidence review treats particular kinds of proof, one 2015-19 slice: evidence resting on equally probable inferences (Pitzner 2003) or on conclusory expert opinion, even unobjected (Coastal Transport 2004), is no evidence, and lost profits need a complete calculation (Heine 1992); reasonable minds must be able to differ (Kindred 1983). Exemplary-damage and defamation reviews ride along.
history: Dominant rule: Texas appellate courts sustain a no-evidence challenge when there is no more than a scintilla of evidence of a vital fact, applying Garza (1965) and Kindred (1983): the question is whether reasonable minds could differ, and circumstantial evidence must transcend suspicion. The single slice, 2015-19, is anchored by King (1985) and led by Crye (1995) and Martinez (1998). How it changed: the leading cases apply the rule to particular proofs. Pitzner (2003) held causation evidence insufficient where the circumstances support any number of equally probable inferences; Coastal Transport (2004) held that conclusory expert testimony is no evidence and may be challenged without an objection at trial; Heine (1992) required a complete lost-profits calculation; Martinez (1998) left alternative-design risk to the jury; and Cazarez (1997) applied heightened review to exemplary damages. McGalliard (1986) and Anderson (1991) leave credibility and findings of fact to the factfinder. Alongside: defamation sufficiency (Bentley 2002, Turner 2000) and tortious interference (Reyna 1994). The unit rejoins the main Texas sufficiency lineage in 2020-24.
rule: Evidence is legally insufficient in Texas when it amounts to no more than a scintilla, rests on inferences no more probable than others, or is conclusory expert opinion, which can be challenged as no evidence without a trial objection; credibility and conflicts remain for the factfinder.

changes.what: No-evidence test asks whether reasonable minds could differ on a vital fact; circumstantial evidence must transcend suspicion.
Lost profits require one complete calculation from objective facts; differing methods do not suffice.
Causation evidence permitting many equally probable inferences is legally insufficient.

changes.case: Coastal Transport v. Crown Central Petroleum
changes.what: No objection is needed to preserve a no-evidence challenge to conclusory or speculative expert testimony.

before_differentiation.name: Texas no-evidence review: more than a scintilla, inferences and conclusory proof
before_differentiation.description: Texas legal-sufficiency review in 2015-19: evidence is no evidence if reasonable minds could not differ (Kindred 1983) or if it rests on equally probable inferences (Pitzner 2003); the factfinder resolves credibility (McGalliard 1986). Conclusory expert opinion is no evidence even without objection (Coastal Transport 2004), and lost profits need a complete calculation (Heine 1992). Exemplary-damage (Cazarez) and defamation (Bentley, Turner) reviews ride along.

That one concerns the summary-judgment burden; this one reviews evidence after trial.
That parent cluster covers all Texas civil review standards; this is one 2015-19 slice on no-evidence review of specific proofs.

name: Batson: three-step test for discriminatory peremptory strikes
description: Batson (1986) bars race-based peremptory strikes through a three-step test, replacing Swain's systematic-exclusion proof. It was extended to any defendant (Powers, 1991), civil cases (Edmonson, 1991), defence strikes (McCollum, 1992) and gender (J.E.B., 1994); Hernandez (1991) and Purkett (1995) made step two easy and step three deferential; Johnson (2005) eased the prima facie step; Miller-El, Snyder and Flowers use comparative juror analysis.

previous.name: Batson: discriminatory jury strikes
previous.description: Peremptory challenges under the Equal Protection Clause: Batson's three-step test, Hernandez and Purkett on race-neutral reasons, Powers and McCollum on standing and defense strikes, J.E.B. on gender, and Miller-El and Snyder on comparative juror analysis.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session subagents, from cocite evidence; second pass differentiated near-duplicates)

history: Dominant rule: Batson v. Kentucky (1986) anchors every slice from 1985-89 to 2025-29. A party may not use peremptory strikes on account of race. The objector makes a prima facie showing, the striking party gives a neutral reason, and the court decides whether purposeful discrimination is proved. How it changed: Batson displaced Swain (1965), which demanded proof of exclusion across many cases. Allen (1986) and Griffith (1987) limited retroactivity. In 1990-94 Powers, Edmonson and McCollum (1991-92) extended Batson to defendants of any race, civil litigants and defence strikes, and Hernandez (1991) set clear-error review; jury-composition cases (Strauder, 1880; Taylor, 1975; Castaneda, 1977) join. In 1995-99 Purkett (1995) held any facially neutral reason suffices at step two, and J.E.B. (1994) added gender. In 2005-09 Johnson v. California (2005) lowered the prima facie burden and Miller-El (2005) and Snyder (2008) used side-by-side juror comparisons to find pretext; Foster (2016) and Flowers (2019) follow. Alabama capital Batson cases merge in 2015-19, and California's Wheeler (1978) leads the partial 2025-29 slice.
rule: The Equal Protection Clause forbids peremptory strikes based on race (or gender), tested in three steps: a prima facie inference of discrimination, a neutral explanation from the striking party, and the trial court's finding whether purposeful discrimination is proved, reviewed for clear error (Batson, Hernandez, Purkett).

changes.what: Replaced Swain's (1965) requirement of systematic exclusion over many cases with a three-step inquiry into strikes in the defendant's own case.

changes.case: Allen v. Hardy; Griffith v. Kentucky
changes.what: Batson applies to cases pending on direct review but not retroactively on collateral review.

changes.case: Powers v. Ohio; Edmonson v. Leesville Concrete; Georgia v. McCollum
changes.what: A defendant may object whatever his race, civil litigants are bound, and criminal defendants may not strike on race either.

changes.case: Hernandez v. New York; Purkett v. Elem
changes.what: A step-two reason need only be facially neutral, not persuasive; credibility is decided at step three and the trial court's finding gets clear-error deference.

changes.case: J.E.B. v. Alabama ex rel. T.B.
changes.what: Extended Batson to strikes based on gender.
A prima facie case requires only evidence permitting an inference of discrimination, rejecting California's more-likely-than-not standard.

changes.case: Miller-El v. Dretke; Snyder v. Louisiana; Foster v. Chatman; Flowers v. Mississippi
changes.what: Comparative juror analysis and all relevant circumstances can show pretext; the Court reversed convictions on that basis.

name: California ineffective assistance on direct appeal, 2020-24 (Mendoza Tello)
description: California ineffective-assistance claims on direct appeal, 2020-24 only, anchored by Fosselman (1983): claims fail unless the record rules out a tactical reason (Mendoza Tello 1997) and prejudice is shown (Bolin 1998). McCoy v. Louisiana (2018) treats conceding guilt over objection as an autonomy violation without prejudice inquiry. Also preservation of venue claims (Maury 2003; Posey 2004) and sufficiency of intent-to-kill evidence (Houston 2012).
history: Dominant rule: California appellate courts reject ineffective-assistance claims on direct appeal unless the record affirmatively shows counsel had no rational tactical purpose, and the defendant must show prejudice; claims depending on facts outside the record go to habeas (Mendoza Tello 1997). The lineage exists only in 2020-24, anchored by People v. Fosselman (1983), which lets trial courts hear such claims on a new-trial motion; it forms from two capital-appeal units and splits in 2025-29. How it developed: Johnson (1980) barred counsel from waiving speedy-trial rights for other clients' convenience. In re Bolin (1998) found no prejudice where no expert testimony was shown. McCoy v. Louisiana (2018) carved out conceding guilt over the client's objection as a structural autonomy violation. Recurring companions: renewing a change-of-venue motion after voir dire to preserve it (Maury 2003) and venue under state law (Posey 2004), probable cause for arrest (Kraft 2000), sufficiency of circumstantial evidence (Snow 2003) and of intent to kill from close-range shooting (Houston 2012), and serious bodily injury (Fosselman).
rule: On direct appeal in California an ineffective-assistance claim fails unless the record shows counsel had no rational tactical purpose or none could be imagined, and prejudice is required; claims needing facts outside the record belong in habeas (Mendoza Tello), though a trial court may hear them on a new-trial motion (Fosselman).

changes.what: Counsel may not waive a client's speedy-trial right to accommodate other clients rather than to benefit the defendant.
A trial court may grant a new trial on the ground that the defendant was denied effective assistance of counsel.
Where the record does not explain counsel's choices, an ineffective-assistance claim on appeal must be rejected and left to habeas.
No prejudice is shown absent evidence that an uncalled expert would have provided exculpatory testimony.
Counsel's concession of guilt over the client's objection violates the client's autonomy and is structural error, needing no Strickland prejudice.

name: Attorney-client privilege and work product: Upjohn and Hickman
description: Evidentiary privileges in federal and Illinois courts: corporate attorney-client privilege covers employees' communications with counsel (Upjohn 1981) and attorney work product is protected (Hickman 1947), construed narrowly. Trammel (1980) gave the adverse-spousal privilege to the witness spouse, Zolin (1989) allowed in camera review for crime-fraud, and Jaffee (1996) added a psychotherapist privilege. A single 2010-14 slice.

previous.description: Privilege and work-product doctrine: Upjohn, Hickman v. Taylor, in camera review and the crime-fraud exception (Zolin), spousal privilege (Trammel), reporter's privilege (Branzburg) and Nobles.

history: Dominant rule: Upjohn (1981) anchors the single 2010-14 slice. Communications from corporate employees to counsel made to obtain legal advice are privileged, though the underlying facts are not, and Hickman v. Taylor (1947) protects an attorney's notes and mental impressions absent necessity. How it changed: Nobles (1975) carried work product into criminal trials and to investigators working for counsel. Trammel (1980) overruled the rule that a defendant could bar adverse spousal testimony, leaving the privilege to the witness spouse while keeping the marital communications privilege. Zolin (1989) allowed in camera review to test the crime-fraud exception on a threshold showing. Under Rule 501, Jaffee (1996) recognised a psychotherapist-patient privilege, Swidler & Berlin (1998) held the privilege survives death, and University of Pennsylvania v. EEOC (1990) declined a peer-review privilege. Also: Illinois cases (Waste Management 1991, Decker 1992) confine privilege narrowly and define the crime-fraud exception, and Jicarilla Apache (2011) refused the fiduciary exception against the United States.
rule: Confidential communications between a client, including a corporation's employees, and counsel made to obtain legal advice are privileged, and an attorney's trial-preparation materials are protected work product, but privileges are narrowly construed and do not reach communications in furtherance of crime or fraud.

changes.what: Attorney notes and mental impressions from preparing for litigation are protected absent a showing of necessity.
Work-product protection applies in criminal trials and to work by agents such as investigators, but can be waived.
Overruled Hawkins in part: the witness spouse alone holds the adverse-testimony privilege; the confidential marital communications privilege remains.
The corporate privilege covers employees' communications to counsel for legal advice, rejecting the control-group test, but not the underlying facts.
Courts may review documents in camera to decide whether the crime-fraud exception applies, after a threshold showing.
Recognised a psychotherapist-patient privilege under Rule 501 and held the attorney-client privilege survives the client's death.

name: ERISA review after Bruch, 1990-94: express discretion and the de novo record
description: ERISA § 502(a)(1)(B) benefit denials in 1990-94, on when de novo review applies and on what record: Firestone v. Bruch (1989), the anchor, made review de novo unless the plan expressly grants discretion (Moon 1989, Masella 1991). Circuits split on limiting de novo review to the administrative record (Perry 1990 v. Moon) and construed ambiguities against the drafter (Kunin, Masella). Pre-Bruch severance-plan cases (Jung, Sly, Brooks) remain.
history: Dominant rule: Firestone Tire & Rubber v. Bruch (1989), anchor of the single slice (1990-94), replaced the general arbitrary-and-capricious standard: benefit denials are reviewed de novo unless the plan gives the administrator discretionary authority. How it changed: circuits worked out Bruch's consequences. Discretion must be granted expressly and cannot be implied from power to define coverage (Moon, 3d Cir. 1989; Masella, 2d Cir. 1991). Moon held that de novo review need not be confined to the record before the administrator, while Perry v. Simplicity Engineering (6th Cir. 1990) limited review to the administrative record. Under de novo review, ambiguities are construed against the drafter (Masella) and limitations must be clear to a layperson (Kunin, 9th Cir. 1990). For discretionary plans, courts still weigh inconsistent application (De Nobel, 4th Cir. 1989) and use a two-step correct-interpretation-then-reasonableness test (Batchelor 1989). Alongside: older Fifth Circuit severance-pay cases under arbitrary-and-capricious review (Jung 1985, Sly 1983, Brooks 1986) and who is a participant (Yancy 1985).
rule: A denial of ERISA benefits is reviewed de novo unless the plan expressly gives the administrator discretionary authority to determine eligibility or construe its terms, in which case review is for abuse of discretion.

changes.what: De novo review applies unless the plan grants the administrator discretionary authority.
Discretion must be expressly given and will not be implied from authority to define benefits.

changes.case: Moon (3d Cir.); Perry v. Simplicity Engineering (6th Cir.)
changes.what: Circuits divided on whether de novo review is confined to the administrative record.
Under de novo review, plan ambiguities are construed against the drafter.

distinct_from.how: That 1995-99 slice turns to how much deference a conflicted administrator gets (Brown sliding scale, Doe, Atwood); this 1990-94 slice concerns whether discretion was expressly granted and what record de novo review may use.

name: Fourth Amendment before 1985: from Boyd and Weeks to Mapp, Chimel and Terry
description: The Fourth Amendment line to 1985: Boyd (1886) and Counselman on compelled papers, Weeks's (1914) federal exclusionary rule, Carroll's (1925) automobile exception, Rabinowitz (1950) on searches incident to arrest, Mapp (1961) applying exclusion to the states, Aguilar-Spinelli on tips, Katz (1967) on privacy, Chimel (1969) narrowing searches incident to arrest, and Terry (1968), the anchor from 1970-74.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Fourth Amendment: warrants, exclusion and incident-to-arrest (to 1980)
previous.description: The earlier Fourth Amendment line from Boyd and Weeks through Carroll's automobile exception, Mapp's exclusionary rule, the Aguilar-Spinelli informant test, Chimel search incident to arrest, Coolidge and Katz; succeeded after 1980 by the modern search-and-seizure sub-clusters.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: unreasonable searches and seizures are barred and their fruits excluded; a warrant on probable cause is the norm, with defined exceptions. The anchor shifts over the lineage. How it changed: 1900-19 is about compelled testimony and papers under Boyd (1886) and Counselman (1892), with Brown v. Walker (1896) and Hale (1906) on immunity. Weeks (1914) anchors 1920-29 and created the federal exclusionary rule, extended to fruits by Silverthorne (1920) and applied in Gouled and Amos (1921). Carroll (1925) anchors 1930-34. Rabinowitz (1950) and Brinegar (1949) lead the 1950s. Mapp (1961) enters and anchors 1960-64, after Elkins (1960) ended the silver platter, and Wong Sun (1963) set fruit-of-the-poisonous-tree analysis. Katz (1967) replaced Olmstead's trespass test, Aguilar (1964) and Spinelli (1969) governed informant tips, and Chimel (1969) overruled Rabinowitz. Terry (1968) anchors 1970-84 as Coolidge, Chambers and Schneckloth join. In 1985-89 the unit splits into the modern privacy, warrant and stop sub-clusters.
rule: Evidence obtained by an unreasonable search or seizure is excluded, and searches generally need a warrant on probable cause, subject to exceptions for vehicles (Carroll), searches incident to arrest (as narrowed by Chimel) and brief stops on reasonable suspicion (Terry).

changes.case: Boyd v. United States; Counselman v. Hitchcock; Brown v. Walker; Hale v. Henkel
changes.what: Compelled production of private papers violates the Fourth and Fifth Amendments; immunity statutes must be coextensive with the privilege.

changes.case: Weeks v. United States; Silverthorne Lumber; Gouled; Amos
changes.what: Federal exclusionary rule, extended to derivative evidence; Weeks anchors 1920-29.
Automobile exception on probable cause; Carroll anchors 1930-34.
Broad search of premises incident to arrest, overruling Trupiano's practicability rule; Rabinowitz anchors 1965-69.

changes.case: Elkins v. United States; Mapp v. Ohio
changes.what: Ended the silver-platter doctrine and applied the exclusionary rule to the states, overruling Wolf (1949) on remedy; Mapp anchors 1960-64.

changes.case: Aguilar v. Texas; Spinelli v. United States
changes.what: Two-pronged test for informant tips in warrant affidavits.
Reasonable-expectation-of-privacy test; electronic eavesdropping is a search, abandoning Olmstead's trespass rule.

changes.case: Terry v. Ohio; Chimel v. California
changes.what: Stop and frisk on reasonable suspicion; Chimel limited search incident to arrest to the area within the arrestee's reach, overruling Rabinowitz; Terry anchors 1970-84.

name: State action tests for private actors under § 1983 (Lugar, Jackson, Brentwood)
description: State action for private actors under § 1983, 1995-2004: Jackson v. Metropolitan Edison (1974) anchors, with Lugar, Blum and Rendell-Baker (1982) and Flagg Bros. (1978): regulation, funding or acquiescence alone is not state action (Sullivan, 1999). West (1988) and Brentwood (2001, entwinement) found state action; circuit cases reject it for off-duty officers (Barna) and private accreditors. Section 1985(3) needs class-based animus (Griffin, Bray).
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: State action: private actors under § 1983 (1995-2004)
previous.description: Tests for when private parties act under color of law: Lugar, Jackson v. Metropolitan Edison, Blum, Rendell-Baker, Burton, West v. Atkins and American Manufacturers v. Sullivan.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session subagents, from cocite evidence; second pass differentiated near-duplicates)

history: Dominant rule: private conduct is state action only when fairly attributable to the State. Jackson v. Metropolitan Edison (1974) anchors both slices, with Lugar (1982) the heaviest: color of law under § 1983 and Fourteenth Amendment state action are identical, and joint participation with officials in state procedures suffices. Blum and Rendell-Baker (1982) deny state action for publicly funded and regulated nursing homes and schools, Flagg Bros. (1978) for statutory self-help, and San Francisco Arts (1987) and Tarkanian (1988) for the USOC and NCAA; West (1988) finds it for a contract prison doctor. How it changed: Lebron (1995) treated Amtrak as government; Sullivan (1999) held that state approval of private insurers' conduct is not state action; Brentwood (2001) adopted an entwinement theory for a state athletic association. In 1995-99 Third Circuit cases apply the tests to off-duty officers (Barna, Pitchell) and private accreditors (McKeesport). In 2000-04 § 1985(3) conspiracy cases (Griffin, 1971; Carpenters, 1983; Bray, 1993) and color-of-law classics (Screws, Girard College) join.
rule: A private party acts under color of state law only if the deprivation is fairly attributable to the State, through a close nexus or state coercion, joint action, delegation of a traditionally exclusive public function, or pervasive entwinement; mere regulation, funding, approval or acquiescence is not enough.

changes.case: Jackson v. Metropolitan Edison; Flagg Bros.; Lugar; Rendell-Baker; Blum
changes.what: The modern tests: regulation and funding are insufficient, and color of law equals state action; Jackson anchors both slices.

changes.case: West v. Atkins; NCAA v. Tarkanian
changes.what: A private doctor under contract to treat prisoners acts under color of law; the NCAA does not become a state actor when a state university follows its rules.

changes.case: Lebron v. National Railroad Passenger Corp.
changes.what: A corporation created and controlled by the government for governmental objectives is part of the government despite a charter disclaiming it.
Private insurers withholding workers' compensation payments under a state scheme are not state actors; mere approval or acquiescence is not state action.
A state athletic association pervasively entwined with public schools and officials is a state actor.

changes.case: Griffin v. Breckenridge; Carpenters v. Scott; Bray v. Alexandria Women's Health Clinic
changes.what: Section 1985(3) reaches private conspiracies only with class-based invidiously discriminatory animus, which economic groups and women seeking abortions did not show.

name: § 1983 municipal liability (Monell) and due-process torts, from civil commitment
description: Due process in § 1983 suits. Through 1985-89 the unit concerns civil commitment (Baxstrom, Jackson v. Indiana, Lessard, Addington, Youngberg). From 1990 it turns to due-process torts: Parratt (1981) and Daniels (1986) on negligent deprivations, DeShaney (1989) on no duty to protect. From 1995-99 Monell anchors: municipal liability only for policy or custom (Pembaur, Canton, Brown), with Lewis (1998) requiring conscience-shocking conduct.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Municipal liability and due-process torts under § 1983
previous.description: Monell custom-or-policy liability (Pembaur, Praprotnik, Canton failure to train, Brown) joined with substantive and procedural due-process torts: DeShaney, Daniels, Parratt/Hudson post-deprivation remedies, Collins, Lewis and Youngberg.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session subagents, from cocite evidence; second pass differentiated near-duplicates)

history: Dominant rule: the anchor shifts across slices. In 1965-89 it is due process in civil commitment: Baxstrom (1966) and Jackson v. Indiana (1972) on equal protections and indefinite incompetency holds, Lessard (1972) on counsel and standards, O'Connor (1975) and Addington (1979, clear and convincing proof), and Youngberg (1982) on committed patients' safety and freedom from restraint. In 1985-89 Bowers (1982) and Martinez (1980) bring in harm by released patients. How it changed: from 1990-94 Daniels anchors, with Parratt and Hudson on post-deprivation remedies, Daniels (1986) holding negligence insufficient, Zinermon (1990) limiting Parratt, and DeShaney (1989) denying a duty to protect, with state-created danger cases (Wood v. Ostrander) alongside. From 1995-99 Monell (1978) anchors every slice: municipalities answer only for policy or custom, including a final policymaker's single decision (Pembaur, Praprotnik) and deliberately indifferent failure to train (Canton, 1989; Brown, 1997; Connick, 2011). Collins (1992) and Lewis (1998) require conscience-shocking action. In 2005-09 state-action cases (Lugar, West, Brentwood) merge in.
rule: A municipality is liable under § 1983 only when its own policy or custom, including deliberately indifferent failure to train, is the moving force behind a violation, and the Due Process Clause is not offended by negligence or by a failure to protect against private violence; the lineage began with due process in civil commitment.

changes.case: Baxstrom; Jackson v. Indiana; Lessard; O'Connor v. Donaldson; Addington v. Texas
changes.what: Civil commitment requires equal procedural protections and proof by clear and convincing evidence, and a person incompetent to stand trial cannot be held indefinitely.
Involuntarily committed patients keep substantive due-process interests in safety and freedom from restraint.

changes.case: Parratt; Hudson v. Palmer; Daniels; Zinermon
changes.what: Random unauthorized deprivations are cured by post-deprivation remedies, negligence is not a deprivation (Daniels overruling Parratt on that point), but Parratt does not apply where predeprivation process was feasible (Zinermon).
The State has no due-process duty to protect against private violence; circuits recognised a state-created danger exception (Wood v. Ostrander).
A single decision by a final policymaker can be policy; failure to train counts if deliberately indifferent; hiring claims need deliberate action as the moving force.
Executive action violates substantive due process only if it shocks the conscience.

name: Eleventh Amendment and federal power over states: Edelman, Fitzpatrick, Usery
description: Federal power over states in 1970-89: the Eleventh Amendment bars retroactive money relief from a state treasury (Edelman, 1974) absent waiver (Parden, 1964, anchor 1970-79) or valid abrogation, which § 5 of the Fourteenth Amendment allows (Fitzpatrick, 1976). National League of Cities v. Usery (1976, anchor 1980-84) limited commerce-power regulation of states; 1985-89 drifts into intergovernmental tax immunity.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Eleventh Amendment and federal power over states (1970s)
previous.description: 1970s cases on how far federal law reaches state governments: Eleventh Amendment immunity and its waiver or abrogation (Edelman, Parden, Employees v. Missouri, Fitzpatrick, Ford Motor) together with federal wage regulation of state employees (Fry, National League of Cities v. Usery). Succeeded by the narrower immunity sub-cluster 21690.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, contrastive pass from family evidence)

history: Dominant rule: a state may not be sued in federal court by private parties for money from its treasury unless it consents or Congress validly abrogates its immunity (Hans, 1890; Ford Motor, 1945; Read, 1944), but officers may be enjoined prospectively (Ex parte Young, 1908). How it changed: Parden (1964) anchors 1970-74 and 1975-79, finding constructive consent where a state ran an interstate railroad; Employees (1973) refused to find a clear abrogation in the FLSA. Edelman (1974) entered in 1975-79, limiting relief to prospective injunctions and rejecting waiver by program participation, and Fitzpatrick (1976) allowed abrogation under § 5 of the Fourteenth Amendment; Hutto v. Finney allowed fee awards. In 1980-84 the anchor moves to National League of Cities v. Usery (1976), which overruled Maryland v. Wirtz and shielded traditional state functions from the FLSA, tested against Darby, Wickard and Hodel (1981) and narrowed in Long Island R.R. (1982) and EEOC v. Wyoming (1983). In 1985-89 the unit drifts into intergovernmental tax immunity under McCulloch (1819) and United States v. New Mexico (1982). Usery was overruled by Garcia in 1985 and Parden by College Savings Bank in 1999.
rule: The Eleventh Amendment bars private suits in federal court for retroactive money relief from a state treasury unless the state waives immunity or Congress validly abrogates it, while prospective relief against state officers remains available under Ex parte Young.

changes.what: A state operating a railroad in interstate commerce after FELA's enactment constructively consented to suit; anchors 1970-79.

changes.case: Employees v. Missouri Public Health Dep't
changes.what: Although the FLSA bound the state, Congress had not clearly lifted its immunity from private suit, though the federal government could sue.
Federal courts may enjoin state officials prospectively but may not award retroactive monetary relief payable from the treasury; participation in a federal program is not a waiver.
Congress may abrogate state immunity when legislating under § 5 of the Fourteenth Amendment.

changes.case: National League of Cities v. Usery
changes.what: Overruled Maryland v. Wirtz and barred applying FLSA wage rules to states' traditional governmental functions; anchors 1980-84 (itself overruled by Garcia in 1985).

changes.case: College Savings Bank v. Florida Prepaid
changes.what: Overruled Parden's constructive-waiver doctrine (after this lineage ends).

name: IDEA free appropriate public education: Rowley and Burlington-Carter reimbursement
description: Special education under the IDEA, 1995-2019: Rowley (1982) anchors every slice, asking whether the school followed the Act's procedures and offered an IEP reasonably calculated to confer benefit, with due weight to administrative findings. Burlington (1985) and Carter (1993) allow reimbursement for private placement; Schaffer (2005) puts the burden on the party seeking relief. Second Circuit cases (R.E., M.H. 2012; M.W. 2013) lead 2010-19.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, round 2 after the lineage re-link)

previous.name: Special education under the IDEA
previous.description: Free appropriate public education under the IDEA: the Rowley standard, reimbursement for private placement (Burlington, Carter), burden of proof (Schaffer), exhaustion (Fry), and Second Circuit IEP review (R.E., M.H., Walczak, Gagliardo).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, contrastive pass from family evidence)

history: Dominant rule: Rowley (1982) anchors every slice from 1995-99 to 2015-19. A school complies if it follows the IDEA's procedures and offers an IEP reasonably calculated to provide educational benefit, and courts give due weight to state administrative findings under modified de novo review (Roland M. 1990, Walczak 1998, Amanda J. 2001, Gagliardo 2007). Reimbursement: Burlington (1985) and Carter (1993) allow repayment when the IEP is inadequate and the private placement appropriate, even if unapproved, and Frank G. (2d Cir. 2006) did not require prior public special-education services. How it changed: 1995-99 adds discipline (Honig 1988) and services for privately enrolled children (K.R. 1996-97); 2000-04 adds exhaustion as non-jurisdictional (Charlie F. 1996) and compensatory education beyond the age limit (Pihl 1993). Schaffer (2005) put the burden of persuasion on the party seeking relief, applied to both Burlington prongs (Gagliardo 2007). From 2010-14 the Second Circuit leads: R.E. (2012) judges the IEP as written and bars retrospective testimony, M.H. (2012) explains deference between IHO and SRO decisions, and M.W. (2013) holds a missing behavioral assessment not fatal alone. The lineage splits before Endrew F. (2017) leads the 2020s.
rule: A school satisfies the IDEA if it follows the Act's procedures and offers an IEP reasonably calculated to provide educational benefit (Rowley), and parents who unilaterally place a child privately may be reimbursed if the IEP was inadequate and the placement appropriate (Burlington, Carter).

changes.what: A FAPE requires procedural compliance and an IEP reasonably calculated to provide educational benefit, with due weight to state proceedings.

changes.case: Burlington School Committee; Florence County v. Carter
changes.what: Reimbursement for private placement when the IEP is inadequate and the placement appropriate, even if not state-approved.
The party seeking relief bears the burden of persuasion, including on both reimbursement prongs.

changes.case: R.E. v. NYC Dept. of Education; M.H. (2d Cir.)
changes.what: The IEP is judged prospectively as written, and courts weigh IHO and SRO decisions by their reasoning.

round1.name: IDEA free appropriate public education: Rowley, Burlington-Carter, Endrew F.
round1.description: Special education under the IDEA: Rowley (1982) anchors throughout, asking whether the school followed the Act's procedures and offered an IEP reasonably calculated to confer benefit; Burlington (1985) and Carter (1993) allow reimbursement for private placement. Second Circuit cases (R.E., M.H. 2012) judge the IEP as written. Endrew F. (2017) raised the substantive bar, and Fry (2017) limited exhaustion to FAPE-based claims.
round1.history: Dominant rule: Rowley (1982) anchors every full slice from 2010-14. A school satisfies the IDEA if it complies with its procedures and offers an IEP reasonably calculated to enable the child to receive educational benefit, and courts give due weight to state administrative findings under modified de novo review (Walczak 1998, Gagliardo 2007). Reimbursement: Burlington (1985) and Carter (1993) let courts order repayment when the IEP is inadequate and the private placement appropriate, even unapproved; Forest Grove (2009) extended that to children never enrolled in public special education. Schaffer (2005) puts the burden of persuasion on the party seeking relief. How it changed: in 2015-19 the Second Circuit cases lead. R.E. (2012) evaluates the IEP prospectively, M.H. (2012) weighs IHO and SRO decisions, and M.W. (2013) holds a missing behavioral assessment not fatal by itself. In 2020-24 Fry and Endrew F. (both 2017) enter: exhaustion applies only to suits seeking relief for denial of a FAPE, and the IEP must enable progress appropriate in light of the child's circumstances, while the Fifth Circuit kept its Michael F. factors (E.R. 2018). Also: compensatory education (D.C. 2005) and parental participation (Doug C. 2013).
round1.rule: A school provides a free appropriate public education if it complies with the IDEA's procedures and offers an IEP reasonably calculated to enable the child to receive educational benefit (since Endrew F., progress appropriate in light of the child's circumstances); parents who unilaterally place a child privately may be reimbursed if the IEP was inadequate, the private placement appropriate, and equities favor them.

changes.what: Two-part FAPE inquiry (procedural compliance; IEP reasonably calculated to confer educational benefit), with due weight to state administrative findings.

changes.case: Burlington School Committee; Florence County v. Carter
changes.what: Courts may order reimbursement for a private placement when the IEP is inappropriate and the private placement appropriate, even if the school is not state-approved.
The party seeking relief bears the burden of persuasion at the administrative hearing.

changes.case: Forest Grove School District v. T.A.
changes.what: Reimbursement is available even if the child never received public special-education services.

changes.case: R.E. v. NYC Dept. of Education; M.H. (2d Cir.)
changes.what: An IEP is judged prospectively as written, so retrospective testimony cannot cure material gaps, and courts weigh the more careful of the IHO and SRO decisions.

changes.case: Fry v. Napoleon Community Schools; Endrew F. v. Douglas County
changes.what: IDEA exhaustion applies only when the gravamen of a suit is denial of a FAPE (Fry), and an IEP must enable progress appropriate in light of the child's circumstances, more than de minimis (Endrew F.).

name: First Step Act reductions: § 404 covered offenses and compassionate release
description: Sentence reductions under the First Step Act (2018). Section 404 eligibility turns on the statute of conviction (Shaw, S. Jones 2020) and is not a plenary resentencing (Hegwood 2019). For compassionate release, courts may define extraordinary and compelling reasons once § 1B1.13 does not apply (McCoy, M. Jones 2020) and may deny on § 3553(a) alone (Chambliss 2020, anchor; Elias 2021), with Chavez-Meza's (2018) modest explanation duty. A single slice, 2020-24.
history: Dominant rule: the First Step Act of 2018 opened two routes to reduce a final federal sentence: § 404, which made the Fair Sentencing Act's crack changes retroactive, and defendant-filed compassionate-release motions under § 3582(c)(1)(A). Both remain discretionary, limited proceedings in the mould of Dillon (2010) and Dorsey (2012). The lineage covers only 2020-24, anchored by Chambliss (5th Cir. 2020). How it developed: for § 404, Hegwood and Jackson (5th Cir. 2019) held a reduction is not a plenary resentencing and excludes other changes in law; Shaw (7th Cir. 2020) and Steven Jones (11th Cir. 2020) tied eligibility to the statute of conviction, not drug quantity or career-offender status; Denson (2020) denied any right to a hearing. For compassionate release, McCoy (4th Cir. 2020), Michael Jones (6th Cir. 2020) and Kibble (2021) held that § 1B1.13 does not bind defendant motions, letting courts treat § 924(c) stacking disparities as extraordinary and compelling; Chambliss and Elias (2021) allowed denial on the § 3553(a) factors or one missing prerequisite. Chavez-Meza (2018) and High (2021) require only an explanation adequate for review. The unit splits in three in 2025-29.
rule: Under the First Step Act a court may reduce a sentence for a covered crack offense under § 404 or for extraordinary and compelling reasons under § 3582(c)(1)(A), in its discretion and with an explanation adequate for appellate review, but neither is a plenary resentencing.

changes.case: Dillon v. United States; Dorsey v. United States
changes.what: Sentence modification is a limited adjustment, not a plenary resentencing, and the Fair Sentencing Act reached only pre-Act offenders sentenced after it.
A brief explanation, even a checked form, can suffice for a sentence-modification ruling when the record shows the court considered the arguments.

changes.case: United States v. Hegwood; United States v. Jackson (5th Cir.)
changes.what: A § 404 reduction is not a plenary resentencing, and the court may not apply other post-sentencing changes in the law.

changes.case: United States v. Shaw (7th Cir.); United States v. Steven Jones (11th Cir.)
changes.what: Eligibility turns on the statute of conviction: an offense is covered if its statutory penalty was modified by the Fair Sentencing Act, whatever the drug quantity or career-offender status.

changes.case: United States v. McCoy (4th Cir.); United States v. Michael Jones (6th Cir.); United States v. Kibble (4th Cir.)
changes.what: U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13 does not govern defendant-filed compassionate-release motions, so district courts may define extraordinary and compelling reasons, including § 924(c) stacking disparities.

changes.case: United States v. Chambliss (5th Cir.); United States v. Elias (6th Cir.); United States v. High (4th Cir.)
changes.what: A court may deny compassionate release on the § 3553(a) factors or any one missing prerequisite alone, and need not address every argument.

name: Illinois policy wording, 2020-24: Outboard Marine, plain meaning, COVID losses
description: Illinois reading of policy language in 2020-24, anchored by Outboard Marine (1992): policies read as a whole for the parties' intent (Eljer 2001), plain meaning with dictionaries (Munoz 2010), ambiguities and exclusions construed against the insurer (Hobbs 2005), a duty to defend that may look beyond the complaint (Wilson 2010), and indemnity limited to covered facts (Crum & Forster 1993). Sweet Berry (2022) rejected COVID-19 business-interruption claims.
history: Dominant rule: Outboard Marine (1992) anchors this single 2020-24 slice: ambiguous insurance provisions are construed in favour of the insured, and summary-judgment rulings are reviewed de novo. Courts read the policy to give effect to the parties' intent (Eljer, 2001), consult dictionaries for undefined terms (Munoz, 2010), construe exclusions liberally for the insured (Wilson, 2010) but enforce clear anti-stacking clauses (Hobbs, 2005), and presume different terms in different sections mean different things (Thompson, 2011). The duty to defend is broad and may consider facts beyond the complaint (Wilson, 2010), while indemnity requires facts actually within coverage (Crum & Forster, 1993). How it applied: Valley Forge (2006) found advertising-injury coverage for junk faxes, and Sweet Berry Cafe (2022) held that the pandemic and shutdown orders caused no direct physical loss. Also: implied waiver as a question of law where facts are undisputed (Home Insurance, 2004), speculation insufficient for summary judgment (Sorce, 1999), fiduciary duty between creditor and guarantor as a fact question (Schrager, 2002), tariffs as law (Adams, 2004) and discovery sanctions (Nedzvekas, 2007).
rule: Illinois courts construe an insurance policy as a whole to give effect to the parties' intent, applying plain meaning to unambiguous terms and construing ambiguous provisions, especially exclusions, against the insurer; the duty to defend may look beyond the complaint, while indemnity requires facts actually within coverage.

changes.what: Ambiguous policy provisions are construed for the insured, and summary judgment rulings are reviewed de novo; anchors the slice.
An insurer must indemnify only if the facts alleged actually fall within coverage; policies are not expanded beyond the bargain.

changes.case: Valley Forge Insurance v. Swiderski Electronics
changes.what: Unsolicited fax advertisements implicate the right of privacy, triggering advertising-injury coverage.
A trial court may look beyond the underlying complaint in deciding the duty to defend.

changes.case: Sweet Berry Cafe v. Society Insurance
changes.what: Neither COVID-19 nor shutdown orders caused direct physical loss of or damage to property.

written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, round 2 after the lineage re-link)

before_differentiation.name: Illinois insurance coverage: ambiguities for the insured, duty to defend
before_differentiation.description: Illinois insurance-coverage law in 2020-24, anchored by Outboard Marine (1992): policies read as a whole for the parties' intent (Eljer 2001), plain meaning with dictionaries (Munoz 2010), ambiguities and exclusions construed against the insurer (Hobbs 2005), a duty to defend that may look beyond the complaint (Wilson 2010), and indemnity limited to covered facts (Crum & Forster 1993). name: Rule 10b-5 elements: scienter (Hochfelder), standing, materiality, reliance (1960-99)
description: Rule 10b-5 elements: purchaser-seller standing (Birnbaum 1952, Blue Chip 1975), scienter (Hochfelder 1976, anchor 1975-94, with recklessness enough), materiality (TSC 1976, Basic 1988), reliance presumed for omissions (Affiliated Ute 1972) and fraud on the market (Basic). Santa Fe (1977) required deception; Chiarella and Dirks set insider-trading duties; Central Bank (1994) ended private aiding-and-abetting suits.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Securities fraud: Rule 10b-5 scienter and materiality (1960-99)
previous.description: Private and SEC actions under § 10(b) and Rule 10b-5: Birnbaum and Blue Chip Stamps standing, Hochfelder scienter, Santa Fe v. Green deception, TSC/Basic materiality, Affiliated Ute reliance, Chiarella insider trading and Central Bank aiding-and-abetting.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session subagents, from cocite evidence; second pass differentiated near-duplicates)

history: Dominant rule: a private Rule 10b-5 action needs a material deception made with scienter in connection with a purchase or sale, causing loss to an actual purchaser or seller who relied. How it changed: in 1960-74 circuit cases lead; Vine (1967) anchors 1965-69, letting forced sellers sue, and Birnbaum (1952) anchors 1970-74 with Bankers Life (1971) reading 'in connection with' broadly. Hochfelder (1976) enters in 1975-79 and anchors through 1990-94, requiring scienter, with Blue Chip (1975) adopting Birnbaum, Santa Fe (1977) excluding mere fiduciary unfairness, Affiliated Ute (1972) presuming reliance for omissions, and Sundstrand (1977) accepting recklessness. In 1980-84 Aaron and Chiarella (1980) enter, followed by Dirks and Huddleston (1983). Basic v. Levinson (1988) leads 1990-94, applying TSC's materiality to merger talks and adopting fraud-on-the-market reliance. Central Bank (1994) anchors 1995-99 and bars private aiding-and-abetting claims, while O'Hagan (1997) upheld misappropriation. The unit then splits into the PSLRA-era pleading lineage.
rule: A Rule 10b-5 claim requires a material misstatement or omission, or other deception, made with scienter in connection with the purchase or sale of a security by an actual purchaser or seller, with reliance that may be presumed for omissions or a fraud on the market.

changes.what: Only purchasers and sellers may sue under Rule 10b-5; Birnbaum anchors 1970-74.

changes.case: SEC v. Capital Gains Research; Vine v. Beneficial Finance (2d Cir.); Superintendent of Insurance v. Bankers Life
changes.what: Full disclosure replaces caveat emptor; a forced seller in a short-form merger may sue; 'in connection with' read flexibly; Vine anchors 1965-69.

changes.case: Affiliated Ute Citizens v. United States
changes.what: Reliance presumed where the claim is chiefly an omission.

changes.case: Blue Chip Stamps; Ernst & Ernst v. Hochfelder; TSC Industries v. Northway; Santa Fe Industries v. Green
changes.what: Purchaser-seller rule adopted; negligence not enough; materiality means a substantial likelihood a reasonable investor would consider it important; no claim for unfair dealing without deception; Hochfelder anchors 1975-94.

changes.case: Sundstrand Corp. v. Sun Chemical (7th Cir.)
changes.what: Recklessness, an extreme departure from ordinary care, satisfies scienter.

changes.case: Aaron v. SEC; Chiarella v. United States; Dirks v. SEC; Herman & MacLean v. Huddleston
changes.what: SEC actions under § 10(b) also need scienter; nondisclosure is fraud only where a duty to disclose exists; tippee liability turns on the insider's breach; 10b-5 coexists with § 11.
TSC materiality applies to preliminary merger talks; fraud-on-the-market presumption of reliance.

changes.case: Central Bank of Denver; United States v. O'Hagan
changes.what: No private aiding-and-abetting liability (Central Bank anchors 1995-99); the misappropriation theory of insider trading upheld.

name: Ohio capital and plain-error review: Jenkins, then Long and Barnes, Bradley
description: The capital and error-review strand of Ohio criminal appeals, 1985-2029: Jenkins (1984), upholding the death-penalty statute and describing independent sentence review, anchors 1985-2004; from 2010-14 Long (1978) plain error anchors, with Barnes (2002, anchor 2020-24) stating its limits and Bradley (1989) adopting Strickland. history: Dominant rule: the standards for reviewing Ohio criminal, and especially capital, convictions. The anchor shifts across the slices. From 1985-89 to 2000-04 it is State v. Jenkins (1984), which upheld Ohio's death-penalty statute and described the court's independent review of death sentences, with Maurer (1984), Steffen (1987), Buell (1986) and Lott (1990) leading on capital-trial issues such as hearsay, photographs, Miranda waivers and prosecutorial argument (State v. Smith, 1984). How it changed: in 2000-04 Long (1978, plain error only for unobjected-to instructions) and Smith v. Phillips (1982, a hearing to prove actual juror bias) enter, Thompkins (1997) anchors 2005-09, and from 2010-14 Long anchors, with Barnes (2002, anchor 2020-24) stating the three plain-error limits and Bradley (1989) adopting Strickland's two-part ineffectiveness test. Long or Barnes anchors every later slice as the unit grows to several hundred cases. Also: Buell (1986) admitted general expert testimony on eyewitness memory; Treesh (2001) and LaMar (2002) on capital sentencing instructions.
rule: On direct review of Ohio criminal and capital convictions, unobjected-to error is reviewed only for plain error that clearly affected the outcome (Long, Barnes), and ineffective assistance requires deficient performance plus a reasonable probability of a different outcome (Bradley).

changes.what: Failure to object to a jury instruction forecloses review absent plain error, noticed only in exceptional circumstances to prevent a manifest miscarriage of justice.

name: Betts special-circumstances counsel cases, 1945-64: Uveges, Bute, Gibbs, Moore

history: Dominant rule: under Betts v. Brady (1942), a state defendant in a non-capital case had a due-process right to appointed counsel only where special circumstances made a trial without counsel fundamentally unfair; waiver had to be intelligent and understanding (Zerbst 1938). How it changed: in 1945-49 Tomkins (1945) anchors with Kaiser, Rice and White (1945), where guilty pleas or hurried trials without counsel were reviewed on habeas and unrebutted allegations taken as true. Uveges (1948) anchors from 1950-54 through 1960-64, granting relief on special circumstances, while Bute (1948) refused relief where none appeared and Gibbs (1949) and Townsend (1948) applied the test. Massey (1954) and Fretag (1954) added capacity and opportunity to obtain counsel; Moore (1957) put the waiver burden on the petitioner, and Carnley (1962) barred presuming waiver from a silent record. In 1960-64 Zerbst and Powell rejoin the core before the unit splits as Gideon (1963) overruled Betts.
rule: Before Gideon, due process required appointed counsel in a state non-capital case only where special circumstances (youth, ignorance, complexity of the charge, trial conduct) made a trial without counsel unfair, and a waiver had to be intelligent and understanding.

changes.what: The Sixth Amendment's counsel guarantee did not bind the states; due process required counsel only on special circumstances.

changes.case: Tomkins v. Missouri; Rice v. Olson; White v. Ragen; Williams v. Kaiser
changes.what: Defendants who pleaded guilty to serious charges without counsel, or were rushed to trial, could be denied due process; habeas courts must take unrebutted allegations as true.

changes.case: Uveges v. Pennsylvania; Bute v. Illinois; Gibbs v. Burke; Townsend v. Burke
changes.what: Special circumstances turn on the defendant's age and understanding and the complexity of the case; Bute refused relief where none were shown.

changes.case: Massey v. Moore; Moore v. Michigan; Carnley v. Cochran
changes.what: Capacity to defend oneself and an intelligent waiver were required, and waiver could not be presumed from a silent record.

round1.name: Right to appointed counsel: Powell and Betts special circumstances to Gideon
round1.description: The right to counsel before and through Gideon: Powell (1932) and Johnson v. Zerbst (1938) required counsel and a knowing waiver; Betts v. Brady (1942) limited state cases to special circumstances (Uveges 1948, anchor 1950-59); Hamilton (1961) and Carnley (1962) widened protection, and Gideon (1963, anchor 1960-69) overruled Betts. Griffin (1956), Douglas and Pointer (1965) extended related rights.
round1.history: Dominant rule: an accused is entitled to counsel unless he knowingly and intelligently waives it, and from 1963 that right binds the states in all serious prosecutions. How it changed: Powell (1932) anchors 1935-39, finding a due-process violation in the Scottsboro defendants' lack of counsel, with Mooney (1935) on perjured testimony. Johnson v. Zerbst (1938) anchors 1940-44 and set the waiver standard for federal courts. Betts (1942) enters in 1940-44 and confined state-court appointment to special circumstances; Glasser (1942) addressed conflicted joint representation. Powell anchors again in 1945-49, and Uveges (1948) anchors 1950-59 as the special-circumstances cases (Rice, Bute, Gibbs, Moore 1957) multiplied. Hamilton (1961) and Carnley (1962) enter in 1960-64, treating arraignment as a critical stage and rejecting waiver on a silent record. Gideon (1963) enters and anchors 1960-69, overruling Betts; White (1963) extended the right to preliminary hearings. In 1965-69 Pointer and Douglas (1965) join before the unit splits into later counsel and confrontation lineages.
round1.rule: An accused facing a serious criminal charge has a right to counsel, appointed if indigent, unless he knowingly and intelligently waives it (Johnson v. Zerbst); for state trials that right was limited to special circumstances under Betts v. Brady until Gideon (1963) made it a fundamental right binding on the states.

changes.what: Failure to give capital defendants a real opportunity for counsel denies due process; Powell anchors 1935-39 and 1945-49.
The Sixth Amendment requires counsel in federal prosecutions absent an intelligent, competent waiver, the intentional relinquishment of a known right; Zerbst anchors 1940-44.

changes.case: Betts v. Brady; Glasser v. United States
changes.what: No universal right to appointed counsel in state trials, only where special circumstances make a trial unfair; joint representation with conflicting defenses violates the Sixth Amendment.

changes.case: Rice v. Olson; Uveges v. Pennsylvania; Moore v. Michigan
changes.what: Special circumstances such as youth, ignorance or complex charges required counsel, including for guilty pleas; Uveges anchors 1950-59.

changes.case: Hamilton v. Alabama; Carnley v. Cochran
changes.what: Arraignment is a critical stage; waiver of counsel cannot be presumed from a silent record.

changes.case: Gideon v. Wainwright; White v. Maryland
changes.what: Gideon overruled Betts: the right to appointed counsel applies to the states; a plea at a preliminary hearing without counsel is reversible; Gideon anchors 1960-69.

changes.case: Griffin v. Illinois; Douglas v. California; Pointer v. Texas
changes.what: Indigents get transcripts and counsel on first appeal; the Confrontation Clause binds the states.

name: Fifth Circuit drug conspiracies: plain error (Calverley), severance (Zafiro), Pinkerton
description: Fifth Circuit criminal appeals of 1995-99, mostly drug conspiracies: plain-error review under Calverley (en banc 1994), severance under Zafiro (1993) requiring specific and compelling prejudice (Faulkner 1994), Pinkerton (1946) co-conspirator liability, single-conspiracy and sufficiency review (Bell 1982, Bermea 1994, Morris 1995), and Beechum (1978) on extrinsic offenses. history: Dominant rule: in this single 1995-99 slice, anchored by Calverley (en banc 1994), the Fifth Circuit reviewed drug-conspiracy convictions deferentially: unpreserved errors needed to be clear or obvious and prejudicial, with correction discretionary; joint trials were the norm; and conspirators answered for co-conspirators' foreseeable acts. How it changed: little within the slice; the leading cases restate settled rules. Pinkerton (1946) supplied co-conspirator liability; Beechum (1978) governed extrinsic-offense evidence; Bell (en banc 1982) dropped the reasonable-hypothesis-of-innocence requirement for sufficiency; Rocha (1990) held that evidence admissible against only one defendant does not require severance. Zafiro (1993) rejected per se severance for antagonistic defenses, applied in Faulkner (1994), which demanded specific and compelling prejudice. Puig-Infante (1994) and Carreon (1994) let courts rely on the presentence report for drug quantity, and Morris (1995) inferred a single conspiracy from a common plan. Curtis (1995) distinguished waiver from forfeiture. The lineage continues in 2000-04 as unlabelled units.
rule: In the 1990s Fifth Circuit, unpreserved errors were reviewed for clear or obvious error affecting substantial rights with discretionary correction (Calverley), joint trials of conspirators stood absent specific and compelling prejudice (Zafiro), and each conspirator was liable for co-conspirators' foreseeable acts (Pinkerton).

changes.what: Conspirators are liable for reasonably foreseeable substantive offenses committed by co-conspirators in furtherance of the conspiracy.
Two-step test for admitting extrinsic-offense evidence under Rule 404(b).
A verdict stands if a reasonable trier of fact could find guilt beyond a reasonable doubt; the evidence need not exclude every reasonable hypothesis of innocence.
Mutually antagonistic defenses are not prejudicial per se; severance is required only for a serious risk of prejudice, and limiting instructions often cure it.
Plain error must be clear or obvious under current law and affect substantial rights, and correction is discretionary; anchors this slice.

changes.case: United States v. Faulkner; United States v. Bermea; United States v. Puig-Infante
changes.what: Severance requires specific and compelling prejudice; testimony and identifications can prove participation; drug quantity may rest on the PSR and trial testimony.
A single conspiracy may be inferred from a common plan even among competing purchasers.

name: Punitive damages after State Farm, 2005-19: ratios, nonparty harm, Exxon
description: Applying due-process limits on punitive damages after State Farm v. Campbell (2003, anchor 2010-14), 2005-19: Gore's (1996) guideposts (anchor 2005-09, 2015-19) with few awards beyond single-digit ratios; Philip Morris v. Williams (2007) barred punishing harm to nonparties and Exxon v. Baker (2008) capped maritime ratios at 1:1. Lower courts applied the ratios to employment and civil-rights awards and allowed higher ones for small harms (Mathias 2003).
history: Dominant rule: the Due Process Clause forbids grossly excessive punitive damages. Haslip (1991) upheld jury instructions confining discretion to deterrence and retribution, TXO (1993) allowed potential harm to count, and Oberg (1994) required judicial review of the amount. Gore (1996), anchor in 2005-09 and 2015-19, set three guideposts: the reprehensibility of the conduct, the ratio of punitive to actual or potential harm, and comparable civil penalties. Cooper Industries (2001) made appellate review de novo. How it changed: Campbell (2003), anchor in 2010-14, struck a 145-to-1 award, held that few awards beyond a single-digit ratio pass, and barred punishing dissimilar or out-of-state conduct. Philip Morris v. Williams (2007) barred punishment for injury to nonparties, and Exxon v. Baker (2008) set a 1:1 ceiling in maritime cases. Lower courts applied the guideposts to employment and civil-rights awards (Zhang 2003, Williams v. ConAgra 2004, Roby 2009), Title VII caps, and larger ratios where harm was small (Mathias 2003). Also: Browning-Ferris (1989) on the Excessive Fines Clause and the Engle tobacco findings (2006).
rule: Due process bars grossly excessive punitive damages, measured by the reprehensibility of the conduct, the ratio to the plaintiff's actual or potential harm (rarely beyond single digits) and comparable civil penalties, with de novo appellate review.

changes.case: Pacific Mutual v. Haslip; TXO Production v. Alliance Resources; Honda Motor v. Oberg
changes.what: Punitive awards are subject to due-process review; potential harm counts; states must provide judicial review of the amount.

changes.case: BMW of North America v. Gore
changes.what: Three guideposts: reprehensibility, ratio to harm, and comparable sanctions; a $2 million award on $4,000 harm was grossly excessive.

changes.case: Cooper Industries v. Leatherman Tool Group
changes.what: Appellate courts review the constitutionality of punitive awards de novo.
Few awards exceeding a single-digit ratio satisfy due process; out-of-state and dissimilar conduct cannot be punished.

changes.case: Philip Morris USA v. Williams; Exxon Shipping v. Baker
changes.what: Juries may not punish for harm to nonparties; in maritime cases a 1:1 ratio is the upper limit.

name: New York appeal-waiver colloquies, 2010-19: Lopez (2006) and Bradshaw
description: New York appeal waivers in 2010-19: Lopez (2006), anchor of both slices, upholds an oral waiver if the colloquy shows the defendant understood it as separate from the plea; Bradshaw (2011) invalidated a waiver lacking that understanding, and Sanders (2015) and Brown (2014) continue the scrutiny. Seaberg (1989) makes bargained waivers enforceable, and Hidalgo (1998) bars excessive-sentence claims after a valid waiver.
history: Dominant rule: People v. Lopez (2006) anchors 2010-14 and 2015-19: an appeal waiver need not be written, but the record must show that the defendant understood the right to appeal as separate and distinct from the trial rights forfeited by the plea. It rests on Seaberg (1989), which made bargained appeal waivers enforceable, Callahan (1992), which preserved a narrow set of non-waivable claims, Kemp (1999) and Hidalgo (1998), under which a valid waiver forecloses an excessive-sentence argument if the sentencing range was explained; Ramos (2006) and Lococo (1998) lead with them. How it changed: Bradshaw (2011) applied Lopez to invalidate a waiver where the defendant never orally confirmed that he grasped the concept, and Maracle (2012) and Brown (2014) continued checking colloquies. In 2015-19 Sanders (2015) enters, with Bryant (2016) and Santeramo (2017), as courts weigh written waivers against brief colloquies; Suitte (1982) frames the Appellate Division's sentence-reduction power that a valid waiver displaces. The lineage merged from and splits back into the main New York appeal-waiver lineage.

history: Dominant rule: a Texas court of appeals has jurisdiction over final judgments and statutorily authorized interlocutory orders, must find its jurisdiction timely invoked, and need not search the record or law for an appellant who briefs an issue inadequately. How it changed: Verburgt (1997) anchors 2010-19: a notice of appeal filed within the fifteen-day extension period implies a motion to extend (Jones 1998 applied it to other perfecting instruments). Lehmann (2001) leads every slice and anchors from 2020-24: without a conventional trial, a judgment is final only if it actually disposes of every claim and party or clearly says so, and courts may abate for clarification. Crowson (1995) and Mackie (2006) govern probate finality. Briefing waiver runs through Fredonia (1994), Valadez and Martinez (2007) and Bolling (2010), with Cohn (1978) holding pro se parties to the rules. In 2015-19 deemed admissions and good cause (Wheeler 2005, Marino 2011, Stelly 1996) and Rule 91a motions (Wooley 2014) enter; Perez (2011) and Sabre (2019) strictly construe interlocutory-appeal statutes. Also: Mex-Tex (2004) on insurance-code delay penalties.
rule: Texas appellate courts have jurisdiction only over final judgments, those that dispose of all claims and parties or clearly say so, and over interlocutory orders a statute expressly makes appealable, strictly construed; a notice of appeal filed within the fifteen-day grace period implies a motion to extend, and inadequately briefed issues are waived, for pro se litigants too.

changes.what: Pro se litigants must comply with the same procedural rules as licensed attorneys.
Test for when a phase of a probate proceeding is final and appealable.

name: Absolute immunity by function, 1990-2004: Imbler, Stump, Burns, Buckley
description: Absolute (not qualified) immunity from § 1983 damages, 1990-2004, turning on function: judges for judicial acts within jurisdiction (Bradley 1872; Stump 1978; Mireles 1991), prosecutors for advocacy (Imbler 1976, anchor throughout), witnesses for testimony (Briscoe 1983). history: Dominant rule: absolute immunity from damages under § 1983 depends on the function performed, not the office. Judges are immune for judicial acts within their jurisdiction, however erroneous or malicious (Bradley 1872, Pierson 1967, Stump 1978, Mireles 1991), and prosecutors for activities intimately associated with the judicial phase of the criminal process (Imbler 1976, the anchor in all three slices). How it changed: Butz (1978) extended immunity to agency adjudicators and Briscoe (1983) to trial witnesses, while Cleavinger (1985) gave prison hearing officers only qualified immunity. Forrester (1988) withheld it from a judge's employment decisions, and Burns (1991) protected a probable-cause hearing but not advice to police; both lead from 1990-94. Buckley (1993) joins the leaders in 1995-99, denying immunity for investigative work and press statements, and Kalina (1997) and circuit cases (Ireland v. Tunis 1997, Hill 1995) followed. In 2000-04 malicious-prosecution claims join (Albright 1994, Gallo 1998, Reed 1996) before the unit merges into the qualified-immunity lineage.

history: Dominant rule: because children are constitutionally different for sentencing, the Eighth Amendment forbids mandatory life without parole for juvenile homicide offenders and requires a sentencer to consider youth and its attendant characteristics before imposing life (Miller, 2012, the anchor in both slices). Jones v. Mississippi (2021) held that no separate finding of permanent incorrigibility is required, and Dorsey (2021) held that good-time eligibility can keep a long sentence from being de facto life. name: Due process limits on civil commitment: Jackson v. Indiana, O'Connor, Addington
description: Civil commitment and institutional rights, 1970-89 (not § 1983 defences): incompetent defendants cannot be held indefinitely (Jackson v. history: Dominant rule: involuntary commitment is a significant deprivation of liberty that requires due process: adversarial procedure with counsel, proof of mental illness and dangerousness by at least clear and convincing evidence, and confinement whose nature and length bear a reasonable relation to its purpose. Greaves (1984) on the right to refuse antipsychotic medication; Jones (1983) allowed commitment on an insanity acquittal.
