name: Texas defamation suits: false gist and implied facts (Turner, Bentley)
description: Texas state-court defamation, 2005-14, applying rather than making the federal limits: Turner (2000, anchor 2010-14) allowed liability for a publication's false gist though each statement is literally true; Bentley (2002) made implied verifiable facts actionable under Milkovich (1990), while Isaacks (2004) protected satire. history: Dominant rule: defamation claims in Texas courts are shaped by First Amendment limits. New York Times (1964) and Gertz (1974), the anchor in 2005-09, require actual malice from public officials and figures and fault from private plaintiffs; mere failure to investigate is not reckless disregard (St. Amant 1968), but purposeful avoidance of the truth can be (Connaughton 1989, Skeen 2005). Bose (1984) requires independent review of actual-malice findings. How it changed: Texas cases built on these rules. McLemore (1998) defined limited-purpose public figures and found no malice where a reporter explained his sources; Huckabee (2000) declined a clear-and-convincing standard at summary judgment and allowed liability for distorting omissions; Turner (2000), anchor in 2010-14, held that a broadcast's false gist may be actionable though each statement is literally true. Bentley (2002) held an accusation of corruption actionable because it implied verifiable facts, applying Milkovich (1990), while Isaacks (2004) protected satire. In 2010-14 cases on the context of a whole publication (Vice 2009, Neely 2013, Rehak 2013) enter and the lineage feeds into Texas anti-SLAPP litigation. name: Prejudgment creditor seizures: Fuentes, Sniadach, Mitchell v. W.T. Grant, Di-Chem
description: Creditor remedies under due process, 1975-79 only: replevin, garnishment and sequestration by state process need notice and a hearing (Sniadach 1969; Fuentes 1972, anchor), unless a judge issues the writ on a sworn showing with a prompt post-seizure hearing (Mitchell v. W.T. Grant 1974); Di-Chem (1975) struck a statute lacking those safeguards. Summary seizures for forfeiture, health or taxes (Calero-Toledo 1974) and Mullane notice sit alongside.
history: Dominant rule: before the state, or a creditor using state process, takes property, the owner is entitled to adequate notice and ordinarily a prior hearing. Fuentes (1972) anchors the single 1975-79 slice, striking replevin statutes that let creditors seize household goods without a hearing, following Sniadach (1969) on wage garnishment. How it changed: Mitchell v. W.T. Grant (1974) upheld Louisiana sequestration because a judge issued the writ on a sworn showing and the debtor could get an immediate hearing, while Di-Chem (1975) invalidated a Georgia garnishment scheme lacking those features. Alongside: the notice cases Mullane (1950), Walker (1956), Schroeder (1962) and Armstrong (1965) require notice reasonably calculated to reach known parties, and Boddie (1971) guaranteed indigents access to divorce courts. name: California negligence duty, 2020-24: Rowland factors, special relationships, Privette
description: The substantive duty question, in a single 2020-24 slice anchored by Kesner (2016): Civil Code § 1714's general duty of care, limited by the Rowland (1968) factors; no duty to protect from third parties without a special relationship (Delgado 2005; Castaneda 2007; Zelig 2002; Regents 2018); Privette (1993), Hooker (2002) and Kinsman (2005) on hirers of contractors; Southern California Gas (2019) against purely economic loss.
history: Dominant rule: California starts from the general duty of reasonable care in Civil Code § 1714 and recognizes exceptions only when the Rowland (1968) factors clearly support them. The lineage exists only in 2020-24, anchored by Kesner (2016). How it developed: Kesner extended duty to take-home asbestos exposure, and Vasilenko (2017) applied Rowland to adjacent-premises risks. For harm caused by third parties a special relationship is required: police generally have no duty to aid (Zelig 2002), a voluntary undertaking creates one (Delgado 2005), landlords must secure controlled areas against foreseeable crime (Castaneda 2007), and Regents (2018) found a university-student relationship for curricular activities. For hirers of independent contractors, Privette (1993) bars peculiar-risk liability to the contractor's employees, with exceptions for retained control affirmatively contributing to injury (Hooker 2002), concealed premises hazards (Kinsman 2005) and promises to fix known hazards (Gonzalez 2021), and SeaBright (2011) extends Privette to delegated safety duties. Biakanja (1958) and Southern California Gas (2019) limit duty for purely economic loss, applied in Goonewardene (2019).

name: Pendent jurisdiction and its limits 1980-89: Hagans, Gibbs, Aldinger, Kroger
description: Federal jurisdiction over pendent claims in civil-rights and welfare suits, 1980-89. King v. Smith (1968) anchors 1980-84 with Rosado (1970) and Hagans (1974): a substantial constitutional claim carries pendent Social Security Act claims; Chapman (1979) limited § 1343. Gibbs (1966) anchors 1985-89, with Aldinger (1976) and Kroger (1978) limiting pendent-party and ancillary jurisdiction.
history: Dominant rule: a federal court with a substantial federal claim may decide related state or statutory claims (Gibbs 1966), a discretionary power usually declined when federal claims are dismissed before trial. King v. Smith (1968) anchors 1980-84: welfare plaintiffs pairing constitutional and Social Security Act claims could have the statutory claims decided as pendent ones (Rosado 1970; Hagans 1974, under Bell v. Hood's 1946 insubstantiality test), and state AFDC rules were struck (Lewis 1970, Townsend 1971, Shea 1974, Hurley 1975). McNeese (1963) required no exhaustion of state remedies. How it changed: Chapman (1979) held that Supremacy Clause claims do not fall within § 1343(3). Gibbs anchors 1985-89 as the focus moves to limits on pendent jurisdiction: Aldinger (1976) refused pendent-party jurisdiction over a county, and Kroger (1978) barred ancillary claims that would defeat complete diversity. Seventh Circuit § 1983 cases enter (Moore and Llaguno 1985, Gramenos 1986), with Draper (1984) urging dismissal of state claims once federal claims fall. The unit then joins the supplemental-jurisdiction lineage.

history: Dominant rule: a party who had a full and fair opportunity to litigate is bound, and federal courts must give state judgments the preclusive effect the state would give them. How it changed: Blonder-Tongue (1971) ended the mutuality requirement for defensive estoppel, and Parklane v. Shore (1979), anchor of 1980-84, allowed offensive nonmutual estoppel at the court's discretion without a Seventh Amendment problem; Montana v. United States (1979), anchor of 1990-94, stated the full-and-fair-opportunity test and the change-in-law exception. Allen v. McCurry (1980), anchor of 1995-99 and the heaviest case, applied preclusion to § 1983 claims; Kremer (1982) extended it to Title VII after state-court review. Migra (1984) anchors 1985-89, holding that § 1738 imports state claim-preclusion law, and Marrese (1985) followed. Elliott (1986) gave preclusive effect to unreviewed state agency fact-finding in § 1983 cases but not Title VII, and Solimino (1991) refused it in ADEA cases. Grogan (1991) applied issue preclusion in bankruptcy dischargeability. Moitie (1981) held that unappealed judgments bind even after the law changes. The lineage splits in 2000-04 toward abstention and Rooker-Feldman.

history: Dominant rule: a single 2020-24 slice, anchored by Richards (1996) with Taylor v. Sturgell (2008) as the most cited case. A judgment binds parties and their privies, but due process forbids binding nonparties who lacked adequate representation (Hansberry, 1940; Richards, 1996). How it changed: the slice reflects rules settled earlier rather than change within it. Taylor (2008) rejected virtual representation and listed six exhaustive exceptions to the rule against nonparty preclusion, putting the burden on the party asserting it (applied in Duckett v. Fuller, 2016). Semtek (2001) held that a federal diversity judgment's preclusive effect follows the forum state's law. Montana (1979) bars relitigation of issues fully and fairly litigated unless controlling law has changed, and Parklane (Shore, 1979) allowed offensive nonmutual collateral estoppel at the court's discretion. Also: the law-of-the-case doctrine and narrow Rule 59(e) reconsideration (Oto, 2000; Cincinnati Life, 2013; Edmonds, 2019), Pullman-Standard (1982) on findings of fact, Currier (2018) on double jeopardy after severance, and Wisconsin products-liability cases (Morden, 2000; Godoy, 2009; Zimmer, 2018).
rule: A judgment generally binds only parties; nonparties are precluded only within the recognised exceptions, such as adequate representation in a properly conducted class or representative suit (Taylor, Hansberry, Richards), while parties who had a full and fair opportunity to litigate an issue may be precluded from relitigating it, including offensively (Montana, Parklane).

description: U.S. Supreme Court text-first construction, 1990-99, applied chiefly to the Bankruptcy Code: unambiguous text ends the inquiry (Ron Pair 1989, anchor of both slices; Germain 1992), save for absurd results (Griffin 1982), and differing language is presumed intentional (Russello 1983). history: Dominant rule: courts enforce unambiguous statutory text as written, reading it in its statutory context and grammar and departing only to avoid absurd results (Ron Pair 1989, the anchor in both slices). Older precedents supply the canon: Caminetti (1917), Reiter (1979), GTE Sylvania (1980), Rubin (1981), Griffin (1982) and Russello (1983, presuming that differing language in the same act is intentional). How it applied: in 1990-94 the unit forms from the agency-deference lineage, with Bankruptcy Code cases applying the method: Timbers and Ahlers (1988) on secured creditors and the absolute priority rule, Davenport (1990) holding restitution dischargeable in Chapter 13 because Congress did not except it, Wilson (1990) on the anti-modification clause, and Butner (1979) leaving property interests to state law. In 1995-99 Germain (1992) leads with Ron Pair: when the words are unambiguous, judicial inquiry is complete, even against legislative history. Dewsnup (1992) relied on pre-Code practice to bar Chapter 7 lien stripping, a counterpoint to pure textualism; Crandon (1990) read text with design and purpose. Longshore Act cases merge in (Caputo 1977, Estate of Cowart 1992). The unit splits in 2000-04.
rule: When statutory text is unambiguous, read in its context and grammatical structure, the judicial inquiry is complete, absent an absurd result or a clearly expressed contrary intent.

name: Confrontation as cross-examination and presence, 2005-09: Davis, Coy, Craig
description: A 2005-09 lineage, split off beside Crawford, on confrontation as cross-examination and physical presence: the defendant is guaranteed an opportunity for effective cross-examination, especially on bias (Davis v. Alaska, 1974, anchor), subject to reasonable limits (Van Arsdall, 1986; Fensterer, 1985; Owens, 1988). Coy (1988) secured face-to-face confrontation and Craig (1990) allowed closed-circuit child testimony on a finding of necessity.
history: Dominant rule: confrontation as the right to cross-examine. Davis v. Alaska (1974) anchors the only slice, 2005-09, split from a pre-Crawford confrontation lineage: denying effective cross-examination on bias is constitutional error. Van Arsdall (1986) gives trial judges latitude to limit repetitive or marginally relevant questioning and makes improper limits subject to harmless-error review, and Fensterer (1985) and Owens (1988) hold the clause satisfied by a full opportunity to probe a witness's memory and infirmities. Olden (1988) found error in excluding cross-examination crucial to a consent defence. Also: physical presence, with Coy (1988) requiring face-to-face confrontation and Craig (1990) allowing closed-circuit testimony by a child witness on a finding of necessity; the older foundations of Mattox (1895), Pointer (1965), Douglas (1965), Barber (1968) on unavailability and Green (1970) on prior statements of testifying witnesses. State courts applied these rules after Crawford to prior statements of testifying witnesses (Sharp, 2005; Price, 2006). The unit rejoins the post-Crawford lineage in 2010-14.
rule: The Confrontation Clause guarantees an opportunity for effective cross-examination, including on a witness's bias, though trial judges may impose reasonable limits on repetitive or marginally relevant questioning (Davis v. Alaska, Van Arsdall).

changes.what: Prior trial testimony is admissible on retrial if the witness has become unavailable; confrontation may yield to necessity.

changes.what: The clause binds the states; reading a silent witness's confession violates it; the state must show unavailability; prior statements of a witness cross-examined at trial are admissible.

name: California fines and probation conditions: Dueñas ability to pay and Lent
description: California fines, fees and probation conditions in 2020-24 only. Dueñas (2019) required an ability-to-pay hearing before assessments and fines; Kopp, Gutierrez, Frandsen and Castellano (2019) split on its basis and on forfeiture. Lent (1975, anchor) tests probation conditions for a reasonable relation to the crime or future criminality, applied to electronic searches in Ricardo P. (2019). Splits to a 2020s sentencing-reform unit in 2025-29.
history: Dominant rule: when a California court may impose monetary penalties and conditions as part of a sentence or probation. The lineage exists only in 2020-24, anchored by People v. Lent (1975), after Three Strikes and other units merge; it flows into a 2020s sentencing-reform unit in 2025-29. How it changed: Dueñas (2019) held that due process bars imposing court assessments, and requires staying a restitution fine, without a finding of ability to pay. Appellate courts quickly divided: Kopp (2019) and others treated fines under the excessive-fines clause and found Dueñas reasoning flawed, while Frandsen, Gutierrez and Castellano (2019) addressed forfeiture where no objection was made. Lent's three-part test for probation conditions was applied in Ricardo P. (2019), which struck an electronics-search condition as disproportionate to its rehabilitative purpose. Also: lesser-included instructions require substantial evidence (Avila 2009), sufficiency of evidence may be raised first on appeal (Beltran 2013), and the abstract of judgment cannot alter the oral pronouncement (Mitchell 2001).
rule: California courts split over whether due process requires an ability-to-pay determination before imposing assessments and fines (Dueñas), and a probation condition is invalid if it is unrelated to the crime, regulates noncriminal conduct, and is not reasonably related to future criminality (Lent).

changes.what: Three-part test for invalid probation conditions: no relation to the offense, conduct not itself criminal, and no reasonable relation to future criminality.
Due process requires an ability-to-pay determination before court assessments are imposed and execution of a restitution fine stayed for an indigent defendant.

name: Federal money laundering: concealment, tainted funds, and guideline choice (Smith)
description: Federal money-laundering and fraud prosecutions in a single 2000-04 slice anchored by Smith (3d Cir. 1999), which sentenced an atypical fraud-laundering case under the fraud guideline. Concealment intent (Powers 1999), partly tainted funds under § 1957 (Moore 1994), proceeds (Hemmingson 1998) and disproportionate forfeitures (Bajakajian 1998). Also severance (Faulkner 1994), business records (Sokolow 1996) and all-records warrants (Cherna 1999).
history: Dominant rule: the elements and sentencing of federal money laundering in fraud cases. Smith (3d Cir. 1999) anchors the lineage's only slice, 2000-04, which split from a plain-error lineage: where laundering is incidental to fraud, the sentence should follow the fraud guideline rather than the harsher money-laundering guideline, an approach the Commission later adopted. How it changed: within the span the leading cases define the offense. Powers (1999) requires intent to conceal or to create the appearance of legitimate wealth; Moore (1994) held that § 1957 does not require funds exclusively derived from unlawful activity; Hemmingson (1998) addressed what counts as proceeds; Bajakajian (1998) capped punitive forfeitures by gross disproportionality. Sharpe (1999) upheld a murder cross-reference. Alongside: severance requires specific and compelling prejudice (Faulkner 1994), business records received from others (Sokolow 1996), probable cause for all-records searches (Cherna 1999) and Franks omissions (Davis 2000), venue for aiding and abetting (Winship 1984), constructive possession (Mergerson 1993), and the scope of conspiracies to conceal (Grunewald 1957).
rule: Money laundering requires a financial transaction in proceeds of specified unlawful activity, with intent to conceal or create the appearance of legitimate wealth (§ 1956) or exceeding $10,000 (§ 1957, without proof that the funds were exclusively tainted); in an atypical fraud-laundering case the sentence may follow the fraud guideline, and punitive forfeitures must not be grossly disproportional (Bajakajian).

changes.what: The government need not prove that funds in a § 1957 transaction were exclusively derived from the unlawful activity.
A punitive forfeiture violates the Excessive Fines Clause if grossly disproportional to the gravity of the offense.

The government must show the defendant meant to create the appearance of legitimate wealth or to conceal the nature of the funds.

history: Dominant rule: an applicant for asylum must show past persecution or a well-founded fear of it on account of a protected ground, and the Ninth Circuit upholds the BIA's findings, credibility included, unless the evidence compels a contrary result. Elias-Zacarias (1992) anchors 1995-2004, requiring proof of the persecutor's motive and the compelling-evidence standard. Ventura (2002) entered in 2000-04 and requires remand to the agency, and Falcon Carriche (2003) upheld streamlined summary affirmances. Farah (2003) anchors 2005-09 on credible establishment of the elements. After the REAL ID Act of 2005, Shrestha (2010) holds that credibility rests on the totality of the circumstances and anchors from 2015-19 into the partial 2025-29 slice; Wakkary (2009) anchors 2010-14 on cumulative harm.

description: Unenumerated liberties under the Due Process Clause: parental rights (Meyer, Pierce, Stanley, Troxel), privacy and contraception (Griswold), and abortion (Roe 1973; Casey's undue-burden test 1992), screened from 1997 by Glucksberg's history-and-tradition test. Rational-basis cases (Cleburne, Romer, Beach) and Windsor (2013) mark 2010-14, Obergefell (2015) and Hellerstedt (2016) enter in 2015-19, and Dobbs (2022) enters in 2020-24 and overruled Roe and Casey. history: Dominant rule: deferential review of Virginia convictions. How it changed: there is no change within these two slices; the unit split off in 2020 from a multi-state sufficiency lineage. history: Dominant rule: the prosecution violates due process when it suppresses evidence favourable to the accused that is material to guilt or punishment, irrespective of good faith (Brady, 1963, the anchor from 1965-69 through 2025-29), or obtains a conviction through testimony it knows to be false. How it changed: the 1960-64 slice is the false-testimony line, Mooney (1935), Pyle (1942), Alcorta (1957) and Napue (1959), which anchors it. Brady added suppression. Giglio (1972) extended the duty to impeachment evidence and to promises known to any government lawyer. Agurs (1976) imposed a duty without a request but graded materiality by the type of request; Bagley (1985) unified the test as a reasonable probability of a different result. Trombetta (1984) and Youngblood (1989) treated lost evidence separately, requiring bad faith for merely potentially useful evidence. Kyles (1995) judged materiality cumulatively and charged prosecutors with what police knew; Strickler (1999) and Banks (2004) set the three elements and cause on habeas. Also: the right to present a defense (Chambers, 1973; Holmes, 2006) and actual-innocence gateways (Schlup, House) in some slices.

name: Removal on a preemption defense, 1995-99: well-pleaded complaint, complete preemption
description: Federal-question removal of state claims, 1995-99, not the merits of preemption: the well-pleaded-complaint rule (Mottley 1908, Gully 1936) bars removal on a federal defense, and Franchise Tax Board (1983, anchor) held ERISA § 514 preemption alone insufficient. Only complete preemption under ERISA § 502(a) (Taylor 1987) or LMRA § 301 (Avco 1968) supports removal; Caterpillar (1987) and Merrell Dow (1986) confined jurisdiction; Warner (1995) separated the doctrines.
history: Dominant rule: federal-question removal depends on the well-pleaded complaint, so a federal defense, including ordinary preemption, does not make a state claim removable (Mottley 1908; Gully 1936). Franchise Tax Board v. Construction Laborers (1983) anchors the single slice (1995-99): ERISA § 514 preemption does not by itself permit removal of claims outside the civil-enforcement provisions. The exception is complete preemption: Avco (1968) for LMRA § 301 and Metropolitan Life v. Taylor (1987) for claims within ERISA § 502(a). Caterpillar (1987) held that a plaintiff relying on individual contracts may stay in state court despite a preemption defense, and Merrell Dow v. Thompson (1986) denied jurisdiction over a state negligence claim built on a federal statute lacking a private remedy; Smith v. Kansas City Title (1921) marks the substantial-federal-question line. How it changed: circuits applied these limits to ERISA claims, insisting that complete-preemption removal and § 514 preemption be kept distinct (Warner v. Ford, 6th Cir. en banc 1995) and that non-enumerated parties' claims are not completely preempted (Harris 1994). Also: law of the case (Christianson 1988, Arizona v. California 1983) and concurrent state jurisdiction (Tafflin 1990).

How it changed: Haimes (1978) anchors 1980-84, and Zimmer (1985) anchors 1985-89 and 1990-94, making liability absolute despite the worker's negligence. Lombardi and Comes (1992-93) and later Ortega (2008) tie § 200 liability to supervisory control. Rizzuto (1998) made § 241(6) vicarious but open to comparative fault. Narducci (2001) limited falling-object claims, and Blake (2003) and Cahill (2004), leading from 2005-09, deny recovery where the worker's own conduct was the sole proximate cause. Runner (2009) leads from 2010-14 with its direct-consequence-of-gravity test, followed by Wilinski (2011). By 2020-24 the lineage merges toward general New York summary-judgment and premises law.
rule: New York Labor Law § 240(1) imposes absolute, nondelegable liability on owners and contractors for injuries proximately caused by the failure to provide proper protection against elevation-related (gravity) risks, while § 241(6) imposes a nondelegable duty enforceable only through a specific Industrial Code provision.

changes.case: Zimmer v. Chemung County Performing Arts
changes.what: Absolute § 240(1) liability where no proper safety device was furnished for the task; contributory negligence is no defense.
Section 240(1) covers only hazards related to the effects of gravity, not every construction-site risk.
Section 240(1) reaches only elevation-related risks, and § 241(6) requires violation of a specific Industrial Code regulation, not a general safety standard.
Section 241(6) makes owners and general contractors vicariously liable for a subcontractor's negligence without control, though comparative fault remains available.
Falling-object liability requires a hazard contemplated by § 240(1) and the absence or inadequacy of an enumerated safety device.

changes.case: Blake v. Neighborhood Housing Services; Cahill v. Triborough Bridge & Tunnel Auth.
changes.what: Liability requires a statutory violation that proximately caused the injury; none attaches where the worker's own conduct is the sole proximate cause.

changes.case: Runner v. New York Stock Exchange
changes.what: The test is whether harm flowed directly from the application of the force of gravity, covering a worker pulled into a device by a descending load.

changes.case: Wilinski v. 334 East 92nd Housing Development Fund Corp.
changes.what: Rejected a rule that objects at the same level as the worker are categorically outside § 240(1).

name: NLRB review: Universal Camera, Gissel orders, Wright Line mixed motive
description: Appellate review of NLRB orders (1970-2004): Universal Camera's (1951) whole-record substantial-evidence test anchors most slices. Gissel (1969) bargaining orders anchor 1970-74; mixed-motive discharge cases follow the Wright Line burden shift (1980-81), upheld in Transportation Management (1983); successor employers must bargain under Burns (1972) and Fall River Dyeing (1987). Lechmere (1992) and Curtin Matheson (1990) appear later.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: NLRB review: Universal Camera, Wright Line and successorship
previous.description: Appellate review of NLRB orders under Universal Camera's substantial-evidence standard, with Wright Line/Transportation Management mixed-motive discharges, Gissel bargaining orders and successorship (Burns, Fall River Dyeing, Fibreboard), cited 1970-2004.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session subagents, from cocite evidence; second pass differentiated near-duplicates)

history: Dominant rule: Universal Camera (1951) anchors every slice from 1975-79 except 1985-89. Board findings stand if supported by substantial evidence on the whole record, and Curtin Matheson (1990) adds deference to Board rules that are rational and consistent with the Act. How it changed: in 1970-74 Gissel (1969) anchors. Coercive interrogation, threats and promises can justify a bargaining order on a card majority, alongside Katz (1962) on unilateral changes and Fibreboard (1964) on contracting out; H.K. Porter (1970) bars compelled contract terms. In 1975-79 circuit cases on interrogation and discriminatory discharge lead (Varo, Camco, Fibers International). In 1980-84 Wright Line enters, the Board's adoption of Mt. Healthy burden-shifting, and the cert. denial in Wright Line (1982) anchors 1985-89. Transportation Management (1983) approved the test, displacing the First Circuit's view that the burden of persuasion stays on the Board. From 1990-94 successorship leads: Burns (1972) and Fall River Dyeing (1987) require a successor to bargain but not to adopt the old contract. Lechmere (1992) and Babcock & Wilcox (1956) return in 2000-04 on nonemployee access. The unit splits in 2005-09 into general agency review and arbitration.
rule: A court enforces an NLRB order if its findings rest on substantial evidence on the record as a whole and its legal standard is rational and consistent with the Act; in a discharge case the General Counsel must show antiunion animus was a motivating factor, after which the employer must prove it would have acted the same anyway (Wright Line, Transportation Management).

changes.what: Substantial evidence is assessed on the whole record, including an examiner's contrary findings.

changes.case: NLRB v. Katz; Fibreboard Paper Products
changes.what: Unilateral changes during bargaining violate § 8(a)(5) without proof of bad faith; contracting out unit work is a mandatory subject.
A bargaining order is an appropriate remedy when unfair practices undermine a card majority, and coercive employer threats are not protected speech.
The Board cannot compel agreement to a substantive contract term.

changes.case: Wright Line (NLRB 1980; 1st Cir. 1981); NLRB v. Transportation Management Corp.
changes.what: The Board adopted Mt. Healthy burden-shifting for mixed-motive discharges; the First Circuit had kept the burden of persuasion on the Board, and the Supreme Court upheld the Board's test in 1983.

changes.case: NLRB v. Burns International Security; Fall River Dyeing
changes.what: A successor that hires a majority of the predecessor's employees with substantial continuity must bargain with the union but is not bound by the old contract.
Courts defer to Board policies that are rational and consistent with the Act, such as refusing to presume replacements oppose the union.

name: Washington criminal sufficiency (Salinas, Green) and Petrich multiple-acts unanimity
description: Washington criminal appeals: sufficiency review admits the State's evidence and reasonable inferences and asks whether any rational juror could convict (Green, 1980; Salinas, 1992, anchoring both slices; Thomas, 2004; Homan, 2014), with circumstantial and direct evidence equally reliable. Multiple-acts unanimity requires election or a Petrich instruction (Petrich, 1984; Kitchen, 1988; Camarillo, 1990), but alternative means need not be unanimous if each is supported (Ortega-Martinez, 1994).
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Washington criminal appeals: sufficiency and unanimity
previous.description: Washington criminal precedent: the Salinas/Green sufficiency standard, jury unanimity and Petrich instructions for multiple acts (Kitchen, Camarillo), and refusal to review issues given only passing treatment.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: Salinas (1992) anchors both slices. A defendant challenging sufficiency admits the truth of the State's evidence and all reasonable inferences, and the conviction stands if any rational trier of fact could find guilt beyond a reasonable doubt, the standard Green (1980) adopted from Jackson v. Virginia. Courts defer to the trier of fact on credibility and conflicts (Thomas, 2004; Camarillo, 1990), may infer intent from conduct (Delmarter, 1980), and treat circumstantial and direct evidence as equally reliable (Homan, 2014). How it changed: no shift in the core rules within these two slices, which split from Washington personal-restraint units. Unanimity runs alongside: Petrich (1984) requires election or a unanimity instruction when several acts could support a count, Kitchen (1988; dated 2004 in the evidence) treats omission as constitutional error, Carson (2015) finds a clear election sufficient, and Ortega-Martinez (1994) and Owens (2014) apply the alternative-means rule. Also: Pirtle (1995) approving WPIC 4.01 on reasonable doubt, Levy (2006) on judicial comment, and Ramirez (2018) applying LFO amendments to pending appeals.
rule: A Washington sufficiency challenge admits the truth of the State's evidence and all reasonable inferences, and the conviction stands if any rational trier of fact could find the elements beyond a reasonable doubt (Green, Salinas); when the State alleges several distinct acts for one count, it must elect an act or the jury must be instructed to agree unanimously on one (Petrich, Kitchen).

changes.what: Adopted the Jackson v. Virginia rational-trier-of-fact standard.
Where several acts could constitute the charged crime, the State must elect or the court must give a unanimity instruction.
Failure to elect or instruct on unanimity in a multiple-acts case is constitutional error, harmless only if no rational juror could doubt any of the acts.
A sufficiency claim admits the State's evidence and every reasonable inference from it.
For alternative means of one crime, unanimity on the means is not required if substantial evidence supports each alternative.
Legislative amendments limiting legal financial obligations apply to cases pending on direct appeal.

name: Texas contract and policy construction: Coker ambiguity; eight-corners duty to defend
description: Texas contract and insurance construction (1995-2009): unambiguous contracts are construed as a matter of law, reading the whole instrument (Coker 1983, Forbau 1994, Columbia Gas 1996), and extrinsic evidence cannot create ambiguity (CBI 1995). Policy ambiguity favors the insured (Hudson Energy 1991, Balandran 1998). The duty to defend follows the eight-corners rule (Merchants Fast Motor Lines 1997, the 2005-09 anchor); indemnity follows the actual facts.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Texas contract and insurance interpretation
previous.description: Texas contract construction: unambiguous contracts enforced as written and ambiguity as a question of law (Coker v. Coker, Columbia Gas, Forbau), and insurance policies, the eight-corners duty to defend and indemnity (National Union v. Merchants Fast Motor Lines, Cowan).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: Coker v. Coker (1983) anchors 1995-2004. If a contract can be given a definite meaning it is unambiguous and the court construes it as a matter of law, considering the whole writing so that no provision is meaningless. Forbau (1994) gives the specific provision priority, Columbia Gas (1996) defines ambiguity as two reasonable readings after the rules of construction are applied, and CBI Industries (1995) bars using extrinsic evidence to create ambiguity and upheld the absolute pollution exclusion. Insurance: policies are contracts, but an insured's reasonable reading of an ambiguous exclusion wins (Hudson Energy 1991, Balandran 1998). How it developed: in 2005-09 the anchor becomes Merchants Fast Motor Lines (1997). The duty to defend turns on the factual allegations in the latest pleading and the policy (Heyden Newport 1965, St. Paul 1999), Cowan (1997) ties indemnity to the facts actually established and Gehan Homes (2004) found a possible occurrence in builder negligence. GuideOne (2006) addressed narrow exceptions to the eight-corners rule. Also: 'arising out of' causation (Utica 2004). The unit splits into arbitration in 2010-14.
rule: A Texas contract that can be given a definite legal meaning is unambiguous and construed by the court as a matter of law, reading the whole instrument to give effect to every provision (Coker); insurance policies follow the same rules, ambiguous coverage terms are construed for the insured, the duty to defend is decided by the eight corners of the pleading and policy, and the duty to indemnify by the facts actually established.

changes.case: Heyden Newport Chemical Corp. v. Southern General Insurance
changes.what: The duty to defend is judged from the allegations and the policy, construed liberally, while indemnity depends on the actual facts.
Unambiguous contracts are construed as a matter of law; ambiguity exists only if the contract is reasonably open to more than one meaning, even if both parties claim otherwise.

changes.case: National Union v. Hudson Energy; Balandran
changes.what: An insured's reasonable reading of an ambiguous exclusion controls, even if the insurer's is more reasonable.

changes.case: National Union v. CBI Industries; Columbia Gas v. New Ulm; National Union v. Merchants Fast Motor Lines; Trinity Universal v. Cowan
changes.what: Extrinsic evidence cannot create ambiguity in a clear contract (CBI, upholding the absolute pollution exclusion); eight-corners review looks at factual allegations, not legal theories (Merchants); 'bodily injury' excludes purely emotional harm (Cowan).

changes.case: Utica National v. American Indemnity; Gehan Homes; GuideOne Elite v. Fielder Road Baptist Church
changes.what: Policies are construed like other contracts; builder negligence can be an occurrence; and the court noted only a limited exception to the eight-corners rule for pure coverage questions.

name: Illinois duty: intended users and open-and-obvious dangers (Ward, Bucheleres)
description: Illinois duty analysis, 1990-2009. In 1990-94 Risner (1986) anchors municipal duty under Tort Immunity Act § 3-102, owed only to intended users (Di Domenico 1988, Wojdyla 1992). From 1995 Ward (1990) anchors: under Restatement § 343A an obvious danger does not bar a duty where distraction is foreseeable; Bucheleres (1996) reaffirmed the open-and-obvious doctrine, LaFever (1998) applied deliberate encounter, and Marshall (2006) restated the duty factors.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, round 2 after the lineage re-link)

previous.name: Illinois premises liability: open and obvious danger
previous.description: Illinois duty analysis for known or obvious hazards: Ward and Deibert on distraction exceptions, Bucheleres and Sollami on open-and-obvious risks, Marshall and Bruns on the four-factor duty test, and voluntary-undertaking duties.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session subagents, from cocite evidence; second pass differentiated near-duplicates)

history: Dominant rule: whether an Illinois landowner or public entity owes a duty, decided as a question of law by the four-factor test (Kirk 1987 on policy). How it changed: in 1990-94 Risner (1986) anchors with Mason, Di Domenico and Ross (1988): under § 3-102 of the Tort Immunity Act a municipality owes a duty only to permitted and intended users, so pedestrians outside crosswalks and drivers seeking median barriers lose. Ward (1990) anchors 1995-99 through 2005-09: following § 343A, a store may owe a duty to a customer distracted from an obvious post, and Deibert (1990) adopted the Restatement's definition of obvious. Vaughn (1995) and Curatola (1993) continue the intended-user line. Bucheleres (1996) reaffirmed the open-and-obvious doctrine for natural water hazards, Mt. Zion (1995) found no duty to a child near a pool, and LaFever (1998) applied the deliberate-encounter exception. In 2000-04 Espinoza (1995) on breach as a jury question, Rangel (1999) and Bokodi (2000) on contractor control, and Frye (1992) on voluntary undertakings enter. Marshall (2006) enters in 2005-09 with City of Chicago v. Beretta (2004).
rule: In Illinois, duty is a question of law decided on foreseeability, likelihood of injury, the burden of guarding against it and its consequences; a landowner may owe a duty despite an open and obvious danger where distraction or deliberate encounter is foreseeable (Ward, § 343A), and a municipality owes a duty only to permitted and intended users of its property (§ 3-102).

changes.case: Curtis v. County of Cook; Di Domenico v. Village of Romeoville; Wojdyla; Curatola
changes.what: A local entity's duty under § 3-102(a) extends only to intended users; a pedestrian outside a crosswalk is not one, save the narrow area around a legally parked car.

changes.case: Ward v. K mart; Deibert v. Bauer Brothers
changes.what: Adopted Restatement § 343A: an obvious danger does not bar a duty where the owner should anticipate harm, as when a customer may be distracted. Ward anchors 1995-2009.
Reaffirmed the open-and-obvious doctrine; Lake Michigan is an obvious danger to divers.
Applied the deliberate-encounter exception while still running the four-factor duty inquiry.
Restated the four-factor duty test and held a restaurant owed invitees a duty against a car that lost control in its lot.

round1.name: Illinois duty and open-and-obvious dangers: Ward, Bucheleres, Marshall, Bruns
round1.description: Illinois duty analysis for known or obvious hazards: Ward (1990) adopted Restatement § 343A, so an obvious danger does not bar a duty where distraction is foreseeable; Bucheleres (1996) reaffirmed the open-and-obvious doctrine and LaFever (1998) recognized deliberate encounter. Marshall (2006) restated the four-factor duty test, and Bruns (2014) limited the distraction exception. Earlier slices cover duty generally (Cunis, Curtis).
round1.history: Dominant rule: whether a landowner or business owes a duty against known or obvious dangers, decided by the four-factor duty test. In 1980-84 the anchor is Cunis (1974): duty is a question of law and foreseeability is but one consideration, with Pippin (1979) and Cross (1980) on voluntary undertakings to provide security. In 1985-89 Curtis (1983) anchors, with public-duty and Tort Immunity Act cases (Huey, Marvin). How it changed: in 1990-94 Rowe (1988) anchors on a landlord's limited duty against third-party crime, Genaust (1976) on § 343, and Kirk (1987) on policy in duty. Ward (1990) anchors 1995-2009: following § 343A, a store may owe a duty to a customer distracted from an obvious post, and Deibert (1990) applied the distraction idea. Bucheleres (1996) reaffirmed the open-and-obvious doctrine for natural water hazards; LaFever (1998) and Sollami (2002) addressed the deliberate-encounter exception. Marshall (2006) anchors 2010-14 and restates the four factors for § 314A duties; Simpkins (2012) and Krywin (2010) follow. Bruns (2014) anchors 2015-24, confining the distraction exception to distractions the defendant should foresee.
round1.rule: In Illinois, duty is a question of law decided by weighing foreseeability and likelihood of injury against the burden and consequences of guarding against it (the four-factor test of Ward and Marshall); an open and obvious danger weighs against a duty but does not end the inquiry where the possessor should anticipate harm, as under the distraction and deliberate-encounter exceptions (Restatement § 343A).

changes.case: Cunis v. Brennan; Pippin v. Chicago Housing Authority
changes.what: Duty is a question of law in which foreseeability is only one factor, and a voluntary undertaking creates a duty limited to its scope; Cunis anchors 1980-84.
Public-duty and Tort Immunity Act limits on governmental duties to particular users; Curtis anchors 1985-89.

changes.case: Ward v. K mart; Deibert v. Bauer Brothers
changes.what: Illinois adopted Restatement § 343A: a possessor may owe a duty despite an obvious risk if it should anticipate that invitees will be distracted; Ward anchors 1995-2009.

changes.case: Bucheleres v. Chicago Park District; LaFever v. Kemlite; Sollami v. Eaton
changes.what: The open-and-obvious doctrine remains viable (Lake Michigan diving, trampoline double-jumping), with a deliberate-encounter exception, and courts still run the four-factor duty analysis.
A business owes invitees a duty of reasonable care against foreseeable harm under § 314A, decided by the four factors, not fact-specific breach; Marshall anchors 2010-14.
The distraction exception applies only where the defendant should reasonably anticipate the distraction, not where the plaintiff was simply looking elsewhere; Bruns anchors 2015-24.

phases.rule: municipal duty under Tort Immunity Act § 3-102: only intended and permitted users of streets (Risner, Di Domenico, Ross)
open-and-obvious dangers and the distraction and deliberate-encounter exceptions (Ward, Bucheleres, LaFever)

name: Expert admissibility: Daubert gatekeeping, Kumho, Joiner and Frye states
description: Expert evidence: Daubert (1993) replaced Frye in federal court with judicial gatekeeping of reliability; Joiner (1997) set abuse-of-discretion review and Kumho Tire (1999) extended gatekeeping to all experts. States split: Massachusetts (1994), Mississippi (2003) and Maryland (Rochkind, 2020) moved to Daubert; Pennsylvania (Grady, 2003) and Illinois kept Frye. Differential diagnosis can show causation (Westberry, 1999).
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Expert testimony: Daubert, Kumho and Frye
previous.description: Admissibility of expert evidence: Daubert's reliability gatekeeping, its extension to all expert testimony (Kumho Tire), abuse-of-discretion review (Joiner), differential diagnosis (Paoli, Westberry) and states keeping the Frye general-acceptance test.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: Daubert (1993) anchors most slices: Rule 702, not Frye's general-acceptance test, governs federal admissibility, and the judge screens expert testimony for reliability and fit. How it changed: Joiner (1997) made the ruling reviewable only for abuse of discretion and allowed exclusion where there is too great an analytical gap; Kumho Tire (Carmichael, 1999), which anchors 2005-09 and 2010-14, applied gatekeeping to technical and experience-based testimony. Paoli (1994), Westberry and Heller (1999) treated reliability as a lower bar than correctness and accepted differential diagnosis for causation. In state courts, Frye survives and competes: Washington (Cauthron, 1993) and Illinois (Donaldson, 2002) reaffirmed it, Pennsylvania (Grady, 2003, reading Topa, 1977) applies it to methodology only, while Massachusetts (Lanigan, 1994), Ohio (Miller, 1998) and Mississippi (McLemore, 2003) adopted Daubert, and in 2020-24 Maryland abandoned Frye-Reed in Rochkind (2020). Also: actuarial risk tools in sex-offender commitments (Taylor, 2002; Simons, 2004) and, in the partial 2025-29 slice, product-design expert cases such as Sardis (2021).
rule: Under Rule 702 and Daubert the trial judge must ensure that all expert testimony rests on reliable methods reliably applied and fits the case, a gatekeeping decision reviewed for abuse of discretion, while some states keep Frye's general-acceptance test for novel scientific evidence.

changes.what: Scientific evidence is admissible only if its principle has gained general acceptance in its field.
Rule 702 displaced Frye in federal court; judges assess reliability through factors such as testing, peer review, error rate and acceptance.

changes.case: General Electric v. Joiner; Kumho Tire v. Carmichael; Weisgram v. Marley
changes.what: Admissibility rulings are reviewed for abuse of discretion, gatekeeping covers all expert testimony, and appellate courts may direct judgment after excising inadmissible expert evidence.

changes.case: Westberry v. Gislaved Gummi; Heller v. Shaw Industries
changes.what: A reliable differential diagnosis can support specific causation without epidemiology, and need not rule out every alternative cause.

changes.case: Commonwealth v. Lanigan (Mass. 1994); McLemore (Miss. 2003); Grady (Pa. 2003); Donaldson (Ill. 2002); Rochkind v. Stevenson (Md. 2020)
changes.what: States divided: Massachusetts, Mississippi and later Maryland adopted Daubert, while Pennsylvania and Illinois retained Frye.

name: Review of reinstated removal orders: finality and the 30-day petition deadline
description: A single 2020-24 slice on judicial review of reinstated removal orders: courts presume review (Abbott Labs 1967, Block 1984) and read bars narrowly (Kucana 2010), while jurisdictional deadlines are enforced (Bowles 2007; Arbaugh 2006 on what is jurisdictional). Luna-Garcia (2015, anchor) and Ortiz-Alfaro (2012) treat reinstated orders as not final during reasonable-fear proceedings; Bhaktibhai-Patel (2022) counts the 30 days from reinstatement.

history: Dominant rule: courts presume Congress intends judicial review of agency action (Abbott Laboratories 1967, Califano v. Sanders 1977), though a statute may preclude it for some parties (Block 1984), and Kucana (2010) limited § 1252(a)(2)(B)(ii) to decisions made discretionary by statute. Requirements count as jurisdictional only if Congress clearly says so (Arbaugh 2006), but statutory appeal deadlines are jurisdictional (Bowles 2007). How it applied: the lineage exists only in 2020-24, merged from a 2015-19 unit on jurisdictional versus claim-processing rules, and centers on reinstated removal orders under § 1231(a)(5), which bar relitigation of the prior order (Garcia-Villeda 2008). Luna-Garcia (10th Cir. 2015), the anchor, and Ortiz-Alfaro (9th Cir. 2012) held a reinstated order not final while reasonable-fear or withholding-only proceedings continue, so the petition clock runs from their end; Bhaktibhai-Patel (3d Cir. 2022) held the court lacks jurisdiction over a petition filed more than 30 days after reinstatement. Related cases address the reasonable-fear process (Sorto Bonilla 2018, Tomas-Ramos 2022) and § 1231 detention (Martinez v. LaRose 2020). Clear-error review of findings (Anderson 1985) runs alongside. The unit splits in 2025-29.

changes.case: Abbott Laboratories v. Gardner; Block v. Community Nutrition Institute
changes.what: A presumption of reviewability of agency action, overcome only by clear statutory preclusion.

changes.case: Arbaugh v. Y&H Corp.; Bowles v. Russell
changes.what: Only clearly stated limits are jurisdictional, but statutory appeal deadlines are.
The § 1252(a)(2)(B)(ii) bar covers only determinations made discretionary by statute, not by regulation.

round1.name: Review of removal orders: presumption of review, Guerrero-Lasprilla, Nasrallah
round1.description: A single 2020-24 slice on review of immigration decisions: jurisdiction-stripping provisions are read narrowly (Abbott Labs, Bowen; Kucana, 2010), mixed questions are reviewable questions of law (Guerrero-Lasprilla, 2020), and CAT orders fall outside the criminal-alien bar (Nasrallah, 2020). round1.history: Dominant rule: courts presume Congress intends judicial review of agency action and read immigration review bars narrowly, while enforcing the statutory deadline and finality requirements for petitions for review. round1.rule: Statutes limiting judicial review of immigration decisions are read narrowly under a presumption favouring review, so courts of appeals may review questions of law including mixed questions and CAT orders, but a petition must be filed within the time limit running from an administratively final removal order.

name: SORNA challenges: commerce power, retroactivity and delegation (Guzman, Reynolds)
description: Challenges to the Sex Offender Registration and Notification Act (one slice, 2010-14): courts upheld it under the commerce power as limited by Lopez (1995) and Morrison (2000) and broadened by Raich (2005), rejected due process and ex post facto claims (Guzman 2010, anchor; Gould, Ambert 2009), and upheld the delegation to the Attorney General (Whaley 2009). Carr (2010) limited § 2250 to post-enactment travel; Reynolds (2012) tied pre-Act offenders to the AG's rule.

previous.name: SORNA: commerce power and ex post facto challenges (2010)

Doe, Hendricks, Carr). It shares the commerce-power core with 24410 but is defined by registration cases (Guzman, Gould, Ambert).

history: Dominant rule: SORNA (Adam Walsh Act, 2006) is a valid exercise of the commerce power, judged against Lopez (1995, the heaviest case) and Morrison (2000), with Raich (2005) allowing regulation of economic activity in the aggregate and McCulloch (1819) the necessary-and-proper reading; registration duties do not commandeer states (New York v. United States 1992). How it applied: Guzman (2d Cir. 2010), the anchor, found no ex post facto problem where travel and failure to register follow SORNA; Gould (4th Cir. 2009) held the duty not conditioned on state implementation and gave adequate notice; Ambert (11th Cir. 2009) rejected due process claims; Whaley (2009) upheld the delegation to the Attorney General to decide retroactivity. How it changed: the circuits disagreed on when SORNA reached pre-Act offenders (May and Hinckley 2008, Shenandoah 2010); Carr (2010) held § 2250 does not reach travel before enactment, and Reynolds (2012) held the registration requirements do not apply to pre-Act offenders until the Attorney General so specifies. The unit splits in 2015-19, partly into separation-of-powers cases (where Gundy, 2019, later rejected the nondelegation challenge).
rule: SORNA's registration requirement and § 2250 failure-to-register offense are valid under the commerce and necessary-and-proper powers, but they reach only post-enactment travel and apply to pre-Act offenders only as the Attorney General specifies.

changes.what: Circuits upheld SORNA against commerce, due process, ex post facto and delegation challenges.

name: Utah agency review under UAPA: Morton's grant-of-discretion test

name: Biased adjudicator as structural error: Tumey, Caperton, Williams; Weaver limit
description: Judicial bias as structural error, one 2020-24 slice anchored by Tumey (1927): a judge with a stake or prior prosecutorial role denies due process (Murchison 1955; Caperton 2009 objective test; Williams 2016; Rippo 2017), alongside other structural rights (Gideon, Gonzalez-Lopez 2006, Waller, Sullivan). history: Dominant rule: most constitutional errors are reviewed for harmlessness, but structural errors that affect the framework of the trial require automatic reversal (Fulminante 1991; Neder 1999). name: PLRA termination of prison consent decrees and separation of powers (Plaut, Plyler)
description: Separation-of-powers challenges to the Prison Litigation Reform Act's termination of consent decrees, 1995-99: Congress cannot reopen final judgments (Plaut 1995, Wheeling Bridge 1856) or prescribe rules of decision (Klein 1872), but may change the underlying law (Robertson 1992). history: Dominant rule: Article III protects final judgments from legislative revision, but prospective relief remains subject to changes in law. Plaut (1995) struck a statute reopening final judgments dismissed as time-barred; Klein (1872) bars Congress from prescribing rules of decision in pending cases; Wheeling Bridge (1856) holds that a decree enforcing a public right becomes unenforceable once Congress changes that right; Robertson (1992) upheld a statute that changed the law rather than directing results. Equity's power to modify injunctions for changed conditions comes from Swift (1932) and Wright (1961), made flexible for institutional-reform decrees in Rufo (1992). How it applied: the PLRA (1996) allowed defendants to terminate prison consent decrees lacking findings of a federal-law violation. Plyler v. Moore (4th Cir. 1996), the anchor, held that plaintiffs had no vested right in continued prospective relief, followed by Rouse and Dougan (1997, consent decrees are not the last word of the judicial department) and Hadix (6th Cir. 1998). Alongside: Article III limits on non-Article III adjudication and delegation (Northern Pipeline 1982, Schor 1986, Mistretta 1989). Single slice; Miller v. French (2000) later upheld the automatic-stay provision.

description: A single 2005-09 slice: deadlines are jurisdictional only where Congress clearly says so (Kontrick, 2004; Eberhart, 2005; Arbaugh, 2006), and limits against the government may be equitably tolled (Irwin, 1991), but statutory appeal periods stay jurisdictional (Robinson, 1960, anchor; Browder; Bowles, 2007). previous.description: Two threads cited together around 2005: whether filing deadlines are jurisdictional or claim-processing rules (Kontrick, Eberhart, Bowles, Arbaugh, Browder, Houston v. history: Dominant rule: whether a time limit is jurisdictional depends on whether Congress clearly made it so. Statutory deadlines to appeal are jurisdictional and cannot be excused, while court rules and most other limits are claim-processing rules subject to forfeiture and, against the government, to equitable tolling. How it changed: the lineage exists only in 2005-09, merged from three 2000-04 units including one on the timeliness of appeals, and Robinson (1960) anchors it with Browder (1978) and Houston v. Lack (1988). Zipes (1982) and Irwin (1991) had already treated Title VII and government-suit limits as non-jurisdictional, while Brockamp (1997) refused tolling for tax refund claims. Kontrick (2004), Scarborough (2004) and Eberhart (2005) recast bankruptcy, EAJA and criminal-rule deadlines as claim-processing rules, and Arbaugh (2006) required a clear statement. Bowles (2007) held statutory appeal limits jurisdictional and ended equitable excuses, and John R. Sand & Gravel (2008) kept the Tucker Act limit jurisdictional on stare decisis. Alongside: the FTCA discretionary-function exception (Varig, 1984; Berkovitz, 1988; Gaubert, 1991) and strict construction of sovereign-immunity waivers (Lane v. Peña, 1996).
rule: A filing deadline is jurisdictional only if Congress clearly ranks it so, as with statutory appeal periods (Bowles); court-made rules and most limits are claim-processing rules that can be forfeited and, against the government, are presumptively subject to equitable tolling (Kontrick, Eberhart, Irwin).

history: Dominant rule: Murphy v. Carron (1976) anchors every slice from 2005-09 through 2020-24: a court-tried judgment stands unless unsupported by substantial evidence, against the weight of the evidence, or legally erroneous. How it changed: in 2005-09 the standard is applied mostly in driver's-license revocation and implied-consent appeals (Hinnah 2002, Verdoorn 2003, Brown 2002, York 2006). In 2010-14 the Missouri Supreme Court refined it: White (2010) confined factual review to the existence of substantial evidence and deferred to credibility findings; Crider (2010) set out the steps an against-the-weight challenge must follow, including identifying evidence favourable to the judgment; Pearson (2012) viewed facts favourably to the judgment where no findings were made. Ivie (2014) and D.G.R. (2014) required substantial-evidence and misapplication-of-law claims to be raised in separate points under Rule 84.04(d). In 2015-19 parental-rights cases enter (S.M. 2011, S.S.S. 2017, J.P.B. 2017 on incarcerated parents). In 2020-24 summary-judgment review (ITT Commercial Finance 1993), briefing rules (Thummel 1978) and Goerlitz (2011) join the lineage.
rule: A Missouri court-tried judgment is affirmed unless no substantial evidence supports it, it is against the weight of the evidence, or it erroneously declares or applies the law (Murphy v. Carron), with each challenge raised in a separate point and argued under its own framework.

history: Dominant rule: Mississippi appellate courts test legal sufficiency by asking whether a rational juror could find every element proved beyond a reasonable doubt, and weight by asking whether the verdict works an unconscionable injustice. How it changed: May (1984) anchors 1985-94, with Edwards (1985) rejecting convictions resting on speculation and Fisher (1985) on circumstantial evidence excluding every reasonable hypothesis. Wetz (1987) anchors 1995-99 and McClain (1993) 2000-04, both standard weight-of-evidence citations. Bush (2005) enters and anchors 2005-09 through 2015-19, clarifying that sufficiency and weight are distinct inquiries and stating that Wetz had misstated the weight standard. Little v. State (2017) overruled Bush in part on other grounds. Alongside: waiver for want of objection (Billiot 1984), lesser-included instructions available to either side (Harveston 1986), prosecutorial misconduct requiring a mistrial (McFee 1987), and Barker speedy-trial balancing (Herring 1997). Ambrose (2018) anchors 2020-24.
rule: In Mississippi a conviction is legally sufficient if, viewing the evidence most favorably to the State, any rational juror could find every element beyond a reasonable doubt, and a new trial for weight of the evidence is warranted only where the verdict is so contrary to the overwhelming weight of the evidence that letting it stand would sanction an unconscionable injustice.

changes.case: May v. State; Edwards v. State
changes.what: Standards for directed verdict and sufficiency: all elements must be proved beyond a reasonable doubt, and proof that the defendant 'might have' committed the crime is insufficient.

name: MSPB jurisdiction over involuntary resignations: Christie, Staats, Garcia
description: Federal Circuit review of MSPB jurisdiction over constructive removals: a resignation or retirement is presumed voluntary unless coerced, induced by misinformation or forced by intolerable conditions, judged objectively (Christie 1975, Covington 1984). Staats (1996) called the doctrine narrow and tied hearings to nonfrivolous allegations; Garcia (en banc 2006) anchors from 2010-14 and requires proof by preponderant evidence.

previous.name: Federal employee appeals to the MSPB
previous.description: Federal Circuit review of Merit Systems Protection Board jurisdiction, chiefly involuntary resignation or retirement claims (Christie, Covington, Scharf, Staats, Shoaf, Garcia) and the nonfrivolous-allegation standard for hearings and IRA appeals.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session subagents, from cocite evidence; second pass differentiated near-duplicates)

history: Dominant rule: because the MSPB hears only appealable adverse actions, a resignation or retirement comes within its jurisdiction only if it was involuntary and so a constructive removal. How it changed: Covington (1984) anchors the small 1985-89 and 1990-94 slices, with Christie (1975), Scharf (1983) and Schultz (1987): the test is objective, two unattractive options are not coercion, but misleading information or an agency threat without reasonable grounds can make the choice involuntary. Burgess (1985) required explicit notice of the jurisdictional burden. Staats (1996) anchors 2000-04 and 2005-09, calling coercive involuntariness narrow and requiring a hearing only on a nonfrivolous allegation. Shoaf (2001) added intolerable conditions judged by the totality of circumstances. Garcia (en banc 2006) anchors 2010-14 and 2015-19: a nonfrivolous allegation earns a hearing at which jurisdiction must be proved by preponderant evidence, and discrimination claims cannot be reached without it. Alongside: nonfrivolous-allegation rules in IRA whistleblower appeals (Yunus, 2001; Kahn and Johnston, 2008), waiver of filing deadlines (Mendoza, Walls), and Federal Circuit jurisdiction over Board jurisdictional dismissals (2013).
rule: A federal employee's resignation or retirement is presumed voluntary and outside MSPB jurisdiction unless it was obtained by coercion, misinformation or intolerable conditions judged objectively, and a nonfrivolous allegation of involuntariness entitles the employee to a jurisdictional hearing at which jurisdiction must be proved by preponderant evidence.

history: Dominant rule: the Confrontation Clause read as a guarantee of cross-examination and reliability. A nontestifying codefendant's confession naming the defendant could not be used at a joint trial (Bruton, 1968), and hearsay of an unavailable declarant needed indicia of reliability (Roberts, 1980). How it changed: the 1970-74 slice, anchored by Bruton, builds on Pointer (1965), Douglas (1965) and Barber (1968, unavailability requires a good-faith effort), with Chapman and Harrington (1969) allowing harmless-error review. Green (1970), the 1975-79 anchor, admitted prior statements of a witness cross-examined at trial, and Dutton (1970) allowed reliable coconspirator hearsay. Davis v. Alaska (1974) protected cross-examination on bias, and Chambers (1973) limited mechanistic evidence rules against the defense. Roberts anchors 1980-84, with Parker v. Randolph (1979) on interlocking confessions. The lineage splits in 1985-89; Crawford (2004) later overruled Roberts.
rule: The Confrontation Clause bars a nontestifying codefendant's confession naming the defendant at a joint trial (Bruton), admits prior statements of a witness cross-examined at trial (Green), and admits an unavailable declarant's hearsay only with adequate indicia of reliability (Roberts), with violations subject to harmless-error review.

How it changed: the 1970-74 slice, anchored by Bruton, builds on Pointer (1965), Douglas (1965) and Barber (1968, unavailability requires a good-faith effort), with Chapman and Harrington (1969) allowing harmless-error review. description: 1980s § 1983 law: Monell (1978) made municipalities liable only for policy or custom, with no good-faith immunity (Owen, 1980); Tuttle (1985) and Pembaur (1986) defined policy. previous.description: 1980s § 1983 cases on municipal liability (Monroe, Monell, Owen, Tuttle, Pembaur) and on whether negligent or random deprivations violate due process given postdeprivation remedies (Parratt, Hudson v. Palmer, Daniels, Davidson).
