history: Dominant rule: two limits on § 1983 suits in the 1980s. First, municipal liability: Monell (1978) anchors 1980-84, overruling Monroe (1961) to make municipalities persons but rejecting respondeat superior; Owen (1980) denied them good-faith immunity; Tuttle (1985) held a single excessive-force incident cannot by itself prove an inadequate-training policy; Pembaur (1986) allowed liability for one decision of a final policymaker. Rizzo (1976) required an affirmative link for supervisors. Second, due process: Parratt (1981) anchors 1985-89, holding a negligent loss of an inmate's property is not a due-process violation if the State offers an adequate post-deprivation remedy; Logan (1982) excluded deprivations under established procedure, and Hudson (1984) extended Parratt to intentional random acts. How it changed: Daniels and Davidson (1986) held that negligence does not trigger due process, overruling Parratt on that point. Alongside: Baker v. McCollan (1979), Carey (1978) nominal damages, Glick (2d Cir. 1973) and Rochin (1952) on conscience-shocking force, with Garner (1985) and Whitley (1986) preparing the move of force claims to specific amendments.
rule: Municipalities are § 1983 persons liable only for their own policy or custom, without good-faith immunity (Monell, Owen); random and unauthorized deprivations satisfy due process if the State provides an adequate post-deprivation remedy (Parratt, Hudson), and negligence is not a deprivation at all (Daniels).

changes.case: Monell v. Department of Social Services
changes.what: Overruled Monroe v. Pape (1961) in part: municipalities are persons, but not vicariously liable; Monell anchors 1980-84.
Municipalities have no qualified immunity for good-faith constitutional violations.

changes.case: Parratt v. Taylor; Logan v. Zimmerman Brush; Hudson v. Palmer
changes.what: A post-deprivation remedy satisfies due process for random, unauthorized negligent or intentional deprivations, but not for deprivations under established state procedure; Parratt anchors 1985-89.

changes.case: City of Oklahoma City v. Tuttle; Pembaur v. Cincinnati
changes.what: A single incident by a subordinate does not prove a municipal policy, but a single decision by a final policymaker can.

changes.case: Daniels v. Williams; Davidson v. Cannon
changes.what: Negligence does not trigger the Due Process Clause, overruling Parratt to the extent it held otherwise.

name: Under color of law and the white primary: Classic, Screws, Monroe v. Pape
description: Federal civil-rights enforcement before 1965: officials who misuse state authority act under color of law even when breaking state law (Classic, 1941; Screws, 1945), and party primaries are state action (Nixon v. Herndon, Smith v. Allwright, Terry). Collins v. Hardyman (1951, anchor 1955-59) kept private conduct outside; Monroe v. Pape (1961) opened § 1983 to suits against police, overruling contrary circuit law.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Civil-rights enforcement and the white primary (1955-60)
previous.description: Federal protection of voting and civil rights before 1960: 'under color of law' for officials acting illegally (Classic, Screws, later Monroe v. Pape), the white-primary cases (Nixon v. Herndon, Smith v. Allwright), and Snowden v. Hughes.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, contrastive pass from family evidence)

history: Dominant rule: an official who abuses power held by virtue of state law acts under color of law even if the act is unlawful under state law, and racial exclusion from primaries integral to elections is state action. How it changed: the 1955-59 slice, merged from school desegregation and other units, is anchored by Collins v. Hardyman (1951), which held the civil-rights conspiracy statute did not reach purely private conduct, alongside Classic (1941), Screws (1945) on willfulness under § 242, Snowden (1944) on unequal administration of election law and Williams (1951) on coerced confessions. In 1960-64 Classic anchors and Monroe v. Pape (1961) enters, holding that § 1983 reaches police who violate state law and needs no specific intent; Cohen v. Norris (9th Cir. 1962) then overruled Agnew v. Compton. The white-primary line (Nixon v. Herndon, 1927; Nixon v. Condon, 1932; Allwright, 1944; Terry, 1953) and Lane v. Wilson (1939) join, with Gomillion (1960) opening racial gerrymanders to challenge. The unit then splits into state action, qualified immunity and apportionment lineages.
rule: Officials who misuse power possessed by virtue of state law act under color of law even when they violate state law, and primary elections integral to choosing officials are state action subject to the Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments.

changes.case: Nixon v. Herndon; Nixon v. Condon; Smith v. Allwright; Terry v. Adams
changes.what: Racial exclusion from party primaries is state action barred by the Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments, whether imposed by statute, party committee or private association.

changes.case: United States v. Classic; Screws v. United States
changes.what: Misuse of power possessed by virtue of state law is action under color of law; § 242 survives vagueness because it requires willfulness. Classic anchors 1960-64.
The civil-rights conspiracy statute and the Fourteenth Amendment do not reach merely private conduct; anchors 1955-59.
§ 1983 reaches officers who violate state law in abusing their authority and requires no specific intent to deprive a federal right.
Following Monroe, overruled Agnew v. City of Compton and allowed § 1983 suits against police for unreasonable searches.

name: Public-employee speech: Pickering-Connick balance, Garcetti, patronage (Elrod)
description: First Amendment rights of public employees: Pickering (1968) balancing, limited by Connick (1983) to speech on matters of public concern and by Garcetti (2006) to speech outside official duties, with Mt. Healthy (1977) causation. Patronage dismissals are barred unless affiliation suits the job (Elrod, Branti), extended by Rutan (1990) and to contractors in Umbehr and O'Hare (1996). From 2010-14 Garcetti anchors, with Engquist and Guarnieri.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Public-employee speech and patronage
previous.description: First Amendment rights of government employees: the Pickering balance and public concern (Connick, Rankin, Waters), official-duties speech (Garcetti), mixed-motive causation (Mt. Healthy), and political patronage dismissals (Elrod, Branti, Rutan).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: the Pickering-Connick test. Pickering (1968) anchors 1980-84 and 2000-04 and Connick (1983) the other slices to 2009: speech is protected if it addresses a matter of public concern and the employee's interest outweighs the employer's interest in efficiency, with Mt. Healthy (1977) letting the employer show it would have acted anyway and Givhan (1979) protecting private complaints. How it changed: Connick narrowed Pickering to public-concern speech; Rankin (1987) protected a private remark about a presidential assassination attempt; Waters (1994) let employers act on reasonable beliefs; NTEU (1995) struck the honoraria ban. In patronage, Elrod (1976) and Branti (1980) bar party-based dismissals unless affiliation is appropriate for the post, with First Circuit Puerto Rico cases (Jimenez Fuentes, Mendez-Palou) defining policymaking posts in 1985-89; Rutan (1990) reached promotions and transfers, and Umbehr and O'Hare (1996) contractors. Garcetti (2006) excluded official-duties speech and anchors 2010-14, as Olech, Engquist (2008) and Guarnieri (2011) enter and patronage cases leave.
rule: A public employee's speech is protected if made as a citizen on a matter of public concern and the employee's interest outweighs the employer's interest in efficient operations (Pickering, Connick), unless made pursuant to official duties (Garcetti); dismissal for political affiliation is barred except where affiliation is an appropriate job requirement (Elrod, Branti).

changes.case: Pickering; Mt. Healthy v. Doyle; Givhan
changes.what: Balancing of employee speech against employer interests, a same-decision defense for mixed motives, and protection for private complaints to supervisors.

changes.case: Elrod v. Burns; Branti v. Finkel
changes.what: Patronage dismissals violate the First Amendment unless party affiliation is an appropriate requirement for the job.
Only speech on a matter of public concern, judged by content, form and context, triggers Pickering balancing; Connick anchors 1985-99 and 2005-09.
Patronage limits reach promotions and transfers, and speech and association protections reach independent contractors.
The employer may act on its reasonable belief about what was said after an adequate investigation, and predicted disruption can outweigh the speech.
Statements made pursuant to official duties are not citizen speech and are unprotected; Garcetti anchors 2010-14.

changes.case: Engquist v. Oregon Dept. of Agriculture; Borough of Duryea v. Guarnieri
changes.what: Class-of-one equal protection does not apply to public employment, and Petition Clause claims by employees also require a matter of public concern.

name: Texas factual-sufficiency era and after, 2000-29: Johnson, Watson, Brooks, Hooper
description: The 2000-29 strand of Texas sufficiency review: Johnson (2000, anchor 2000-04) read Clewis as adopting the full civil factual-insufficiency test, Sims (2003) required discussing the evidence against the verdict, and Watson (2006) overruled Zuniga in part; Brooks (2010) then abolished factual sufficiency, leaving Jackson as measured by the hypothetically correct charge (Malik 1997), with Hooper (2007, anchor 2020-24) separating inference from speculation.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Texas criminal: sufficiency after Brooks
previous.description: Texas review of criminal convictions for sufficiency: Jackson v. Virginia as the single standard after Brooks (2010) abolished factual-sufficiency review (Clewis, Johnson, Watson), measured against the hypothetically correct jury charge (Malik).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: a conviction is legally sufficient if any rational juror, viewing all the evidence for the verdict, could find each element beyond a reasonable doubt (Jackson 1979, Winship 1970), measured by the hypothetically correct jury charge (Malik 1997), with weight and credibility for the jury (Cain 1997, Williams 2007). How it changed: Johnson (2000) anchors 2000-04, reading Clewis (1996) as adopting the full civil factual-insufficiency test, and Sims (2003) required courts to discuss the evidence against the verdict. In 2005-09 Jackson anchors while Zuniga (2004) and Watson (2006), which reclarified Clewis and overruled Zuniga in part, lead; Brown (1995) had already dropped the reasonable-hypothesis rule for affirmative links. Brooks (2010) held that Jackson is the only standard and leads from 2010-14, with Hooper (2007) on inferences versus speculation, Clayton (2007) on considering all evidence, and Isassi (2010) on deference to inferences from basic to ultimate facts. Hooper anchors 2020-24 and Brooks the partial 2025-29 slice. Also: variance between pleading and proof (Byrd 2011) and inadequate briefing (Lucio 2011).
rule: Evidence is reviewed under Jackson v. Virginia: viewing all the evidence in the light most favorable to the verdict, measured against the hypothetically correct jury charge, could any rational juror find each element beyond a reasonable doubt; from 2000 to 2010 Texas also applied a separate neutral-light factual-sufficiency review.

changes.what: Sufficiency is measured against the elements as defined by the hypothetically correct jury charge.
Clewis read as adopting the complete civil factual-insufficiency formulation, including evidence so outweighed by contrary proof as to be manifestly unjust.
A court rejecting a factual-sufficiency claim must discuss the most important evidence the appellant says undermines the verdict.
Reclarified Clewis and overruled Zuniga v. State (2004) to the extent of conflict.

changes.case: Hooper v. State; Clayton v. State
changes.what: Juries may draw reasonable inferences but not speculate; circumstantial evidence is as probative as direct, and all evidence, properly or improperly admitted, is considered.
Jackson legal sufficiency is the only standard; separate factual-sufficiency review is abolished.

before_differentiation.name: Texas sufficiency review: factual sufficiency (Johnson, Watson) to Brooks
before_differentiation.description: Texas sufficiency review under Jackson v. Virginia, measured against the hypothetically correct charge (Malik 1997). Johnson (2000) anchors 2000-04 with full factual-sufficiency review, reclarified by Watson (2006, overruling Zuniga in part). Brooks (2010) abolished factual sufficiency and leads from 2010-14, with Hooper and Clayton (2007) on inferences and circumstantial evidence; Hooper and Brooks anchor the 2020s.

distinct_from.how: That cluster is the whole family since the 1980s (Geesa, Clewis's adoption, Almanza charge error); this sub-cluster is only the 2000-29 working-out of factual sufficiency and its replacement by Brooks.

name: Tennessee criminal: sufficiency review (Cabbage, Tuggle, Dorantes) and plain error
description: Tennessee criminal sufficiency review: the State gets the strongest legitimate view of the evidence and the jury weighs credibility (Cabbage, 1978; Tuggle, 1982). Dorantes (2011, anchor from 2020-24) put circumstantial and direct evidence on one standard. Plain-error review follows the Adkisson factors adopted in Smith (2000), and Adkisson anchors 2015-19. The early slices are capital appeals on aggravators.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Tennessee criminal: circumstantial evidence and plain error
previous.description: Tennessee criminal appeals: sufficiency and circumstantial evidence (Cabbage, Tuggle, Dorantes), and plain-error review under the Adkisson factors adopted in State v. Smith.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: on appeal the State receives the strongest legitimate view of the evidence and all reasonable inferences. A guilty verdict accredits the State's witnesses and credibility is for the jury (Grace, 1973; Cabbage, 1978; Tuggle, 1982). How it changed: in 1985-89 and 1990-94 the lineage is Tennessee capital review, anchored by State v. Williams (1985) and Barber (1988). Thompson (1989) and Middlebrooks (1992) narrowed the heinous-atrocious-cruel and felony-murder aggravators. Cabbage anchors 1995-99, alongside Ashby's (1991) sentencing review. Tuggle anchors 2000-04 and 2005-09, with Matthews (1990) on issues not preserved and Bland (1997), the anchor in 2010-14. Smith (2000) adopted the Adkisson plain-error factors, and Adkisson (1994) anchors 2015-19 as plain-error and waiver cases lead. Dorantes (2011) enters in 2010-14 and anchors 2020-24 and the partial 2025-29 slice: circumstantial evidence is reviewed under the same standard as direct evidence. Hanson (2009) and Bise (2012) join the final slices.
rule: A Tennessee appellate court views the evidence in the light most favorable to the State, leaves credibility and weight to the jury, and sustains a conviction resting on direct or circumstantial evidence alike; unpreserved errors get relief only if every Adkisson plain-error factor is shown.

changes.case: State v. Williams; State v. Thompson; State v. Middlebrooks
changes.what: The heinous-atrocious-cruel aggravator requires torture or depravity of mind, and the felony-murder aggravator cannot support death for a felony-murder conviction because it does not narrow the class.

changes.case: Grace v. State; State v. Cabbage; State v. Tuggle
changes.what: A guilty verdict accredits the State's witnesses, and the State gets the strongest legitimate view of the evidence and all reasonable inferences.

changes.case: State v. Adkisson; State v. Smith
changes.what: Five factors govern plain error, including breach of a clear and unequivocal rule and no tactical waiver; Smith adopted them and lets courts stop when one fails.
Comparative proportionality review of death sentences and a restatement that credibility and weight belong to the trier of fact; anchors 2010-14.
Circumstantial evidence alone may sustain a conviction under the same standard as direct evidence, dropping the rule that it must exclude every reasonable hypothesis but guilt.

name: California fee awards, 2020-24: proving fees, limited success, related contracts
description: California fee awards in 2020-24 only, anchored by Drexler (2000), stressing limits on recovery: the claimant must prove the litigation warranted fees and the hours were reasonable (SOURCE 2015), awards drop for limited success (Chavez 2010), § 1717 contract fees reach related agreements (Mountain Air 2017), and anti-SLAPP fees cover only the motion (Alnor 2008). Lodestar follows Ketchum (2001) and Serrano (1977).
history: Dominant rule: California courts compute fee awards by lodestar and leave the amount to the experienced trial judge (Drexler 2000, anchor of the only slice, 2020-24). The lineage forms in 2020-24 from a 2015-19 California civil-appeals unit and splits in 2025-29; it continues the earlier California fee lineage. How it applies: Ketchum (2001) bars multipliers based on factors already in the lodestar and allows fees for enforcing the fee right; Serrano (1977) grounds private-attorney-general fees, Graham (2005) keeps the catalyst theory, and the claimant bears the burden of proving the litigation warranted fees and the hours were reasonable (Save Our Uniquely Rural Community Environment 2015), even with a boilerplate prayer (Sweetwater 2019). Chavez (2010) allows reduction for limited success, Gorman (2009) excludes meals from costs, and Alnor (2008) limits anti-SLAPP fees to the motion. For contract fees, § 1717 makes one-sided clauses reciprocal (Alperson 1979); Hsu (1995) and Santisas (1998) define the prevailing party and clause scope; Mountain Air (2017) reads related agreements together; DisputeSuite (2017) denies fees where the dispute continues elsewhere. North Bay v. Maldonado (2010) avoids absurd literal readings.
rule: California fee awards start from a lodestar of reasonable hours at market rates, adjusted only for factors not already reflected (Ketchum; Drexler), may be reduced for limited success (Chavez), and contract fee clauses are made reciprocal by § 1717 and read with related agreements (Santisas; Mountain Air).

changes.what: Private attorney general fees, later codified in Code Civ. Proc. § 1021.5, computed by lodestar.

changes.case: Hsu v. Abbara; Santisas v. Goodin
changes.what: A party with an unqualified win on the contract must be found prevailing; broad clauses covering disputes arising out of the agreement reach tort claims.

changes.case: PLCM Group v. Drexler; Ketchum v. Moses
changes.what: The trial judge sets the value of services, including in-house counsel's at market rates; multipliers may not double-count lodestar factors, and fees on fees are recoverable.

changes.case: Chavez v. City of Los Angeles
changes.what: A reduced fee is appropriate where the claimant achieves only limited success, though not for losing intertwined claims.

changes.case: Mountain Air Enterprises v. Sundowner Towers
changes.what: Related agreements may be read together, so a fee clause in one can reach a dispute under another it superseded; an affirmative defense can be an action on the contract.

written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, round 2 after the lineage re-link)

before_differentiation.name: California attorney's fees in the 2020s: lodestar, § 1717 and fee clauses
before_differentiation.description: California fee awards in 2020-24 only, anchored by Drexler (2000): the lodestar and multipliers (Ketchum 2001; Serrano 1977), reductions for limited success (Chavez 2010), § 1021.5 private-attorney-general fees and the catalyst theory (Graham 2005; SOURCE 2015), and contract fees under § 1717 (Alperson, Hsu, Santisas) read with related agreements (Mountain Air 2017). Anti-SLAPP fees cover only the motion (Alnor 2008).

distinct_from.how: This 2020-24 slice applies the settled lodestar rules to proof, limited success, anti-SLAPP and related-contract fees; that 1995-2014 lineage built the rules themselves, from Xuereb's contract clauses through Serrano III and IV, Woodland Hills and Ketchum to Drexler.

name: Sexually violent predator commitment as civil, not punitive: Hendricks, Crane
description: Civil commitment of sexually violent predators: allowed on clear and convincing proof (Addington, 1979; Foucha, 1992) of a mental abnormality making the person dangerous (Hendricks, 1997), with serious difficulty controlling behaviour (Crane, 2002, anchor 2000-04). Such schemes are civil, so double jeopardy and ex post facto do not apply; in 2005-09 the intent-effects test (Mendoza-Martinez, Hudson) extends to registration (Smith v. Doe, 2003).
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Civil commitment of sexually violent predators
previous.description: Civil commitment and sex-offender statutes: mental abnormality and dangerousness (Hendricks, Crane), clear and convincing proof (Addington, Foucha, Jones v. United States), whether the statute is punitive for double jeopardy and ex post facto (Mendoza-Martinez, Hudson, Smith v. Doe), and state SVP acts.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: a state may confine a person civilly if it proves by clear and convincing evidence a mental abnormality or disorder that makes him dangerous and gives him serious difficulty controlling his behaviour; because such a scheme is civil and nonpunitive, it raises no double jeopardy or ex post facto problem. How it changed: the background rules come from Addington (1979, clear and convincing proof), Jones v. United States (1983) and Foucha (1992, release when no longer mentally ill), and Allen v. Illinois (1986), which held sexually-dangerous-person proceedings not criminal for the privilege. Hendricks (1997) upheld the Kansas SVP Act as civil, and Washington's Young (1993) and California's Hubbart (1999) did the same. Crane (2002), the 2000-04 anchor, required a lack-of-control finding, and state courts read it into their statutes (Thorell, 2003; People v. Williams, 2003). Seling (2001) barred as-applied punitive challenges. In 2005-09 Hendricks anchors as the unit turns to the civil-punitive test of Mendoza-Martinez (1963), Ward (1980), Ursery (1996) and Hudson (1997), applied to sex-offender registration in Smith v. Doe (2003). It splits into SVP and SORNA units in 2010-14.
rule: A state may civilly commit a sexually violent predator on clear and convincing proof of a mental abnormality making him dangerous and causing serious difficulty controlling his behaviour; such a civil, nonpunitive scheme does not violate double jeopardy or the Ex Post Facto Clause.

changes.case: Addington v. Texas; Jones v. United States; Foucha v. Louisiana
changes.what: Civil commitment needs clear and convincing proof of mental illness and dangerousness; an acquittee who is no longer mentally ill must be released.
Kansas's SVP Act is civil, not criminal, so commitment under it is not punishment for double jeopardy or ex post facto purposes.
A statute found civil cannot be held punitive as applied to a single person.

Commitment requires proof of serious difficulty controlling behaviour, though not total lack of control; Crane anchors 2000-04, and state courts held their statutes already satisfied it (Thorell; People v. Williams).

changes.case: Hudson v. United States; Smith v. Doe
changes.what: The intent-effects test (Mendoza-Martinez factors) governs whether a sanction is punitive; Alaska's sex-offender registration law is civil.

name: Federal summary judgment after the 1986 trilogy: Anderson, Celotex, Matsushita
description: The federal summary-judgment standard as circuits applied it in 1985-94: Celotex (1986) anchors 1985-89 and Anderson v. Liberty Lobby (1986) 1990-94, with Matsushita (1986). The trilogy built on Diebold (1962) and Cities Service (1968) but moved away from Poller's (1962) caution: the nonmovant must show specific, admissible facts on which a reasonable jury could find for it (Garside 1990, Street 1989).
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Summary judgment trilogy (early 1990s)
previous.description: Federal summary-judgment standard built on the 1986 trilogy, Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Celotex and Matsushita, with antecedents Diebold, Cities Service and Poller, as cited in circuit decisions of 1985-94.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session subagents, from cocite evidence; second pass differentiated near-duplicates)

history: Dominant rule: the 1986 trilogy. Celotex anchors 1985-89 and Anderson v. Liberty Lobby anchors 1990-94, with Matsushita as the third leading case. Anderson asks whether a reasonable jury could find for the nonmovant under the governing standard of proof, Celotex lets a movant without the trial burden point to the absence of evidence, and Matsushita bars implausible inferences in antitrust conspiracy cases. How it changed: the earlier law, still cited, drew every inference for the nonmovant (Diebold 1962) and warned that summary judgment is often inappropriate where motive and intent are central (Poller 1962), though Cities Service (1968) already held that evidence without probative force cannot defeat the motion. Circuit decisions in 1988-91 put the trilogy to work. Street v. J.C. Bradford (1989) said the court no longer has to search the record, Garside v. Osco Drug (1990) required admissible evidence of expected expert testimony, Mack v. A&P (1989) rejected exploratory discovery, and International Shortstop (1991) addressed Rule 56(f) requests, now Rule 56(d). Intent cases still caution against summary judgment (Waltman 1989 on harassment). Also: shareholder standing (Canderm 1988) and authentication in Japanese Electronic Products (1983). The unit splits after 1990-94.
rule: Summary judgment is proper when, viewing the evidence and justifiable inferences in the nonmovant's favor through the lens of the substantive burden of proof, no reasonable jury could find for the nonmovant; a movant may meet its burden by pointing to the absence of evidence on an element the nonmovant must prove, and the nonmovant must then come forward with specific, admissible evidence, not metaphysical doubt or implausible inferences.

changes.case: United States v. Diebold; Poller v. CBS; First National Bank of Arizona v. Cities Service
changes.what: Inferences are drawn for the nonmovant and summary judgment is used sparingly where motive is at issue (Poller), but unsupported allegations lacking probative force do not create a genuine issue (Cities Service).

changes.case: Anderson v. Liberty Lobby; Celotex Corp. v. Catrett; Matsushita v. Zenith
changes.what: The trilogy recast summary judgment as a tool to dispose of claims without evidentiary support: the substantive burden governs, a movant may point to missing evidence, and implausible inferences do not defeat the motion.

changes.case: Street v. J.C. Bradford (6th Cir. 1989); Garside v. Osco Drug (1st Cir. 1990); International Shortstop (5th Cir. 1991)
changes.what: Courts need not search the record for a dispute, opponents must show admissible evidence, and Rule 56(f) discovery requests must be specific.

name: Texas sentence proportionality, 2005-09: Solem test, forfeiture and void sentences
description: Texas Eighth Amendment challenges to prison terms in 2005-09: a sentence within the statutory range is generally not excessive (Jordan 1973); only a grossly disproportionate sentence violates the Eighth Amendment (Solem 1983, anchor; narrowed by Harmelin 1991 and McGruder 1992; Ewing 2003). The complaint is forfeited if first raised on appeal (Curry, Rhoades, Trevino), unlike a void sentence (Nicholas 2001).
history: Dominant rule: in Texas criminal appeals, punishment within the range set by a valid statute is not excessive, cruel or unusual (Jordan 1973, Davis 1995), and the only federal check is the narrow gross-disproportionality principle. Solem (1983) anchors the single slice, 2005-09: the Eighth Amendment forbids sentences disproportionate to the crime. Harmelin (1991) left the Court without clear standards for terms of years and, per McGruder v. Puckett (5th Cir. 1992), modified Solem's test so that a court first asks whether the sentence is grossly disproportionate before any comparison. Rummel (1980) and Ewing (2003) confirm such challenges succeed only in exceedingly rare cases. Alongside: preservation. Curry (1995), Rhoades (1996) and Trevino (2005) hold that a cruel-and-unusual or disproportionality complaint is forfeited if first raised on appeal; Nicholas (2001) separates void, unauthorized sentences, which can be raised at any time.
rule: A sentence within the statutory range is generally not cruel and unusual; only a grossly disproportionate noncapital sentence violates the Eighth Amendment, and the complaint is forfeited unless raised in the trial court.

changes.what: The Eighth Amendment bars noncapital sentences disproportionate to the crime.

changes.case: Harmelin v. Michigan; McGruder v. Puckett (5th Cir.)
changes.what: Harmelin modified Solem to a narrow gross-disproportionality test; McGruder applies a threshold comparison of gravity and sentence first.
A narrow proportionality principle applies to noncapital sentences only in exceedingly rare cases.
Texas courts hold a disproportionate-sentence complaint forfeited unless made by timely objection or motion for new trial.

written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, round 2 after the lineage re-link)

before_differentiation.name: Texas Eighth Amendment proportionality: Solem, Harmelin, McGruder
before_differentiation.description: Texas appeals raising Eighth Amendment challenges to prison terms (2005-09). A sentence within the statutory range is generally not excessive (Jordan 1973); only a grossly disproportionate sentence violates the Eighth Amendment (Solem 1983, narrowed by Harmelin 1991 and McGruder 1992; Ewing 2003). The complaint must be preserved in the trial court (Curry, Rhoades, Trevino).

distinct_from.how: Same Texas proportionality rule; this is the earlier 2005-09 slice, with Nicholas on void sentences, while that one covers 2015-24, ends anchored by Jordan, and adds community-supervision revocation review.

name: Federal habeas gateways 2010-14: Holland tolling, Schlup actual innocence
description: Ways past federal collateral-review bars, 2010-14 only: AEDPA's one-year limit is tolled while a properly filed state application is pending (Pace 2005) and equitably on diligence and extraordinary circumstances (Holland 2010, anchor); Schlup's (1995) actual-innocence gateway reaches the time bar (McQuiggin 2013); and the § 2255(e) savings clause covers convictions an intervening decision negates (Dorsainvil 1997; Bousley 1998).
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, round 2 after the lineage re-link)

previous.name: Habeas time bar: equitable tolling and actual innocence
previous.description: AEDPA limitations and procedural default: Pace and Holland on equitable tolling (diligence and extraordinary circumstances), Carey and Lawrence on statutory tolling, and Schlup, Sawyer and Murray v. Carrier on the actual-innocence gateway.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session subagents, from cocite evidence; second pass differentiated near-duplicates)

history: Dominant rule: the limits on federal collateral review and the exceptions that let a prisoner past them. In the single 2010-14 slice Holland v. Florida (2010) anchors: AEDPA's limitations period is not jurisdictional and can be equitably tolled for diligence and an extraordinary circumstance such as serious attorney misconduct. Pace (2005) held untimely state petitions not properly filed, and Lawrence (2007) excluded certiorari time. How it changed: the actual-innocence gateway leads, from Murray v. Carrier (1986) and Sawyer (1992) through Schlup (1995), Calderon v. Thompson (1998) and House (2006), with Herrera (1993) denying freestanding innocence claims and McQuiggin (2013) carrying Schlup to the time bar. Federal prisoners' savings-clause cases also lead: Dorsainvil (1997), Bousley (1998), Wofford (1999), Reyes-Requena (2001) and Gilbert (2011), which refused § 2241 for sentencing errors within the statutory maximum. McCleskey (1991) supplies abuse-of-the-writ limits. The lineage splits in 2015-19 into COA and successive-petition units.
rule: AEDPA's one-year limit is tolled only while a properly filed state application is pending (Pace) and equitably only for diligence plus an extraordinary circumstance (Holland), while a credible showing of actual innocence on new reliable evidence opens a gateway past default and the time bar (Schlup; McQuiggin), and federal prisoners may use § 2241 only where § 2255 is inadequate.

changes.case: Murray v. Carrier; Sawyer v. Whitley; Schlup v. Delo
changes.what: A fundamental miscarriage of justice excuses default where new reliable evidence makes it more likely than not that no reasonable juror would convict (Schlup), or by clear and convincing evidence for the death sentence (Sawyer).
A freestanding claim of actual innocence does not itself warrant federal habeas relief.

changes.case: In re Dorsainvil (3d Cir.); Wofford v. Scott (11th Cir.); Reyes-Requena v. United States (5th Cir.)
changes.what: The § 2255(e) savings clause allows a § 2241 petition when an intervening decision negates the crime of conviction, not merely because § 2255's gatekeeping bars relief.
Actual innocence can excuse default of a claim based on a new substantive interpretation, such as Bailey's reading of 'use' of a firearm.

changes.case: Pace v. DiGuglielmo; Lawrence v. Florida
changes.what: An untimely state petition is not properly filed and does not toll; a certiorari petition from state collateral review does not toll.

round1.name: AEDPA time bar: statutory and equitable tolling (Pace, Holland), Schlup
round1.description: AEDPA's one-year limit: tolled only while a properly filed state application is pending (Artuz, 2000; Carey, 2002; Pace, 2005, the 2005-09 anchor; Lawrence, 2007), and equitably only for diligence plus an extraordinary circumstance, a rule the circuits adopted around 1998-2003 and Holland (2010, the 2010-14 anchor) confirmed. In 2010-14 the Schlup (1995) actual-innocence gateway joins, extended to the time bar by McQuiggin (2013).
round1.history: Dominant rule: a state prisoner has one year to seek federal habeas relief; the period stops only while a properly filed state post-conviction application is pending, and equitable tolling requires diligence and an extraordinary circumstance that prevented timely filing. How it changed: the 2000-04 slice, anchored by Harris v. Hutchinson (4th Cir. 2000), is the circuits' first reading of § 2244(d): Davis (5th Cir. 1998) and Miles v. Prunty (9th Cir. 1999) allowed equitable tolling only in rare and exceptional cases, Taliani (1999) rejected a lawyer's miscalculation. In 2005-09 the Supreme Court's tolling cases dominate, with Pace (2005) as anchor: Artuz (2000) and Pace on 'properly filed', Duncan (2001) excluding federal petitions, Carey (2002) and Evans (2006) on gaps between state levels, Lawrence (2007) excluding certiorari petitions, and Rhines (2005) on stay and abeyance of mixed petitions. Holland (2010), the 2010-14 anchor, confirmed equitable tolling for serious attorney misconduct (anticipated by Spitsyn, 2003). In 2010-14 the Brady unit merges in and the actual-innocence gateway joins: Murray v. Carrier (1986), Sawyer (1992), Schlup (1995), House (2006), and McQuiggin (2013) applying Schlup to the time bar.
round1.rule: AEDPA's one-year limit is tolled only while a properly filed state application is pending (§ 2244(d)(2)), and equitably only for a petitioner who pursued his rights diligently and was blocked by an extraordinary circumstance (Pace, Holland); a credible Schlup showing of actual innocence opens a gateway past default and, after McQuiggin, the time bar.

changes.case: Davis v. Johnson (5th Cir.); Miles v. Prunty (9th Cir.); Harris v. Hutchinson (4th Cir.); Spitsyn v. Moore (9th Cir.)
changes.what: Circuits held the limit non-jurisdictional and open to equitable tolling in rare cases, but not for ordinary attorney miscalculation; egregious misconduct may qualify. Harris anchors 2000-04.

changes.case: Artuz v. Bennett; Duncan v. Walker; Carey v. Saffold; Pace v. DiGuglielmo; Lawrence v. Florida
changes.what: Defined 'properly filed' and 'pending': untimely state petitions do not toll, federal petitions and certiorari petitions do not toll, intervals between state levels do. Pace anchors 2005-09.
District courts may stay mixed petitions, modifying Rose v. Lundy's dismissal rule.
Equitable tolling is available; serious attorney misconduct beyond garden-variety neglect can be extraordinary. Holland anchors 2010-14.

changes.what: Actual innocence, shown by new reliable evidence that no reasonable juror would convict, is a gateway past default and the limitations period, though not a freestanding claim (Herrera).

before_differentiation.name: Habeas time bar and actual-innocence gateways: Holland, Pace, Schlup
before_differentiation.description: Gateways around habeas bars in 2010-14: AEDPA's one-year limit is tolled while a properly filed state application is pending (Pace, 2005) and equitably on diligence and extraordinary circumstances (Holland, 2010, anchor); Schlup's (1995) actual-innocence gateway was extended to the time bar by McQuiggin (2013); and the § 2241 savings clause reaches convictions an intervening decision negates (Dorsainvil, 1997; Bousley, 1998).

name: Missouri capital appeals: statutory proportionality review and post-conviction rules
description: Missouri Supreme Court death-penalty review: from 1980-84 Newlon (1982), Mercer and Baker apply statutory aggravator and proportionality review; Antwine (1987) set deferential Batson review; Day (1989) made Rule 24.035 and 29.15 time limits mandatory and anchors 1990-94; Ervin (1992) barred claims against post-conviction counsel; Ramsey (1993) anchors 2000-04 on death-qualification voir dire. Pre-1980 slices are small non-capital units.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Missouri capital appeals
previous.description: Missouri Supreme Court death-penalty review: statutory aggravators and proportionality (Newlon), voir dire on death-penalty views (Ramsey), and Batson and post-conviction claims (Antwine, Griffin, Day).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: Missouri's independent review of death sentences and the procedural rules around it. In 1970-79 small units anchor on Holbert (1967) and Reese (1954) on prejudicial evidence and corpus delicti, unrelated to capital review. How it changed: in 1980-84 the unit becomes capital: Newlon (1982) anchors, with Mercer (1981) on voir dire language, Turner, Royal and Baker (1981-82) applying statutory aggravators and comparing similar cases, and McIlvoy (1982) vacating a disproportionate sentence. In 1985-89 Guinan (1984) anchors, with Bottoson and other cases on effective assistance. In 1990-94 Day (1989) anchors: Rule 24.035 and 29.15 time limits are mandatory; Antwine (1987) governs Batson with clearly erroneous review, Sanders (1987) ineffective assistance, McMillin (1990) successive motions and Ervin (1992) the unreviewability of post-conviction counsel's performance. Griffin (1988) and Feltrop (1991) address depravity of mind. Mease (1992) anchors 1995-99 and Ramsey (1993) 2000-04, holding that jurors leaning toward death can serve if they can follow the law, with Kinder and Tokar (1996). The evidence here is thin on case names, so later rule changes are not traced.
rule: The Missouri Supreme Court independently reviews each death sentence for the evidence supporting the statutory aggravators and for proportionality to sentences in similar cases, defers to trial findings on Batson and death-qualification voir dire unless clearly erroneous, and enforces strict post-conviction rules, including mandatory time limits under Rules 24.035 and 29.15.

changes.case: State v. Mercer; State v. Newlon; State v. Baker; State v. McIlvoy
changes.what: Post-1977 capital review compared each death sentence with similar death and life cases, generally finding no disproportion, though McIlvoy vacated one for a follower of limited intelligence; Newlon anchors 1980-84.
A death sentence was upheld though a co-defendant received life; Guinan anchors 1985-89.
Missouri's Batson procedure, with great deference to the trial court's finding on the prosecutor's race-neutral reasons, reversed only if clearly erroneous.
The time limits of Rules 24.035 and 29.15 for post-conviction motions are valid and mandatory; Day anchors 1990-94.

changes.case: State v. McMillin; State v. Ervin
changes.what: Successive post-conviction motions are barred, and claims that post-conviction counsel was ineffective are not reviewable.
A venireperson leaning toward death need not be struck where he can follow instructions, and proportionality review is a legislative safeguard against arbitrary sentences; Ramsey anchors 2000-04.

name: Seventh Circuit drug conspiracies: proof of agreement and Pinkerton (Townsend)
description: Seventh Circuit drug-conspiracy appeals, 1985-94: agreement may be inferred from circumstances but mere knowledge is not enough, and Pinkerton (1946) makes conspirators liable for foreseeable acts in furtherance. Whaley (1987) anchors 1985-89; Durrive (1990) anchors 1990-94, when Townsend (1991) and Edwards (1991) tied conspiracy scope to Guidelines drug quantities. Also multiple-conspiracy instructions (Briscoe 1990).
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Pinkerton liability in drug conspiracies (late 1980s)
previous.description: Late-1980s federal drug-conspiracy appeals: Pinkerton liability for co-conspirators' reasonably foreseeable substantive offenses, mainly in the Seventh and Eleventh Circuits (Durrive, Townsend, Moya-Gomez).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: to convict of a drug conspiracy the government must prove that the defendant knowingly agreed to join it, which may be inferred from circumstantial evidence and the parties' relationship (Redwine 1984, Noble 1985: a conspirator need not take part in every facet), and each conspirator answers for co-conspirators' reasonably foreseeable acts in furtherance (Pinkerton, 1946). How it changed: in 1985-89 Whaley (1987, vindictive prosecution) anchors a mixed group of Seventh Circuit trial issues: Franks challenges (Pritchard 1984), Brady timing (Xheka 1983), identification of taped speakers (Vega 1988), self-representation when assets are frozen (Moya-Gomez 1988). In 1990-94 Durrive (1990) anchors and Pinkerton enters as a leading case. Townsend (1991) held that mere knowledge of illegality is not agreement and linked the limits of conspiracy law to Guidelines relevant conduct; Edwards (1991) declined to attribute co-conspirators' amounts to a limited participant. Briscoe (1990) rejected multiple-conspiracy instructions unsupported by the record, and Beverly (1990) upheld dual-object conspiracy verdicts if one object is proved. The lineage splits into an unlabelled group in 1995-99.
rule: A drug-conspiracy conviction requires proof that the defendant knowingly agreed to join the conspiracy, which may be inferred from circumstantial evidence but not from mere knowledge of illegality, and each conspirator is liable for co-conspirators' reasonably foreseeable acts in furtherance of it.

changes.what: Conspirators are liable for reasonably foreseeable substantive offenses committed by co-conspirators within the scope and in furtherance of the conspiracy.
A Pinkerton instruction is adequate where the beyond-reasonable-doubt phrase follows the doctrine's three elements.

Mere knowledge of illegality is not agreement to join it; conspiracy law and Guidelines relevant conduct share one limiting principle, so defendants answer only for transactions within the conspiracies they joined.
Drug amounts distributed by co-conspirators are not attributable to a defendant whose role was more limited.

name: Texas final-judgment rule 1995-2004: Mafrige overruled by Lehmann v. Har-Con
description: The Texas final-judgment rule in transition, 1995-2004: only final judgments are appealable absent statute (Aldridge 1966). Mafrige (1994, anchor 1995-99) treated summary judgments with Mother Hubbard clauses as final; Lehmann v. Har-Con (2001, anchor 2000-04) overruled it in part, requiring disposal of all claims and parties or an unequivocal finality statement. Verburgt (1997) implies extension motions.
history: Dominant rule: Texas appellate courts have jurisdiction only over final judgments unless a statute authorises an interlocutory appeal (Aldridge 1966), and a judgment after a trial on the merits is presumed to dispose of all claims. How it changed: Mafrige v. Ross (1994), anchor in 1995-99, held that a summary judgment stating that the plaintiff take nothing was final, so an order granting more relief than requested had to be reversed rather than dismissed (Inglish 1997; Teer 1984). Lehmann v. Har-Con (2001) anchors 2000-04: it overruled Mafrige in part, so a judgment rendered without a conventional trial is final only if it actually disposes of every pending claim and party or clearly and unequivocally states that it finally disposes of them, and appellate courts may abate for clarification. Garcia (2003) and Sanchez (1990) dismissed appeals from orders leaving claims pending; Martinez (1994) allowed finality by severance. Verburgt (1997) implied a motion to extend the time to appeal for a notice filed within the grace period (Jones 1998). Alongside: what counts as an appealable temporary injunction (Qwest 2000) and a contractor's retained control (Welch 1994).
rule: A Texas appeal lies only from a final judgment, one that disposes of all parties and claims or clearly and unequivocally states that it does, unless a statute makes the interlocutory order appealable.

changes.what: Only final judgments are appealable absent a statute, and a judgment after a conventional trial on the merits is presumed final.
A summary judgment with a Mother Hubbard clause ('take nothing') was treated as final, to be reversed if it granted more relief than requested.
A motion to extend time is implied when a notice of appeal is filed within the fifteen-day grace period.

Overruled Mafrige in part: a Mother Hubbard clause does not make a judgment without a conventional trial final; finality requires disposing of all claims and parties or an unequivocal statement of finality.

name: Warrantless home entry, 1975-89: Payton's warrant rule and exigency
description: Entry into the home, 1975-89: Payton (1980, anchor from 1980-84) requires a warrant to enter a home for a routine arrest and Steagald (1981) a search warrant for a third party's home; exigencies such as hot pursuit (Hayden, Santana) are narrow, Mincey (1978) rejected a murder-scene exception, and Welsh (1984) weighed the offense's gravity. Coolidge (1971) anchors 1975-79.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Warrantless home entry and exigent circumstances (1975-89)
previous.description: Fourth Amendment limits on warrantless entry of the home: Payton's warrant requirement for home arrests, exigent circumstances (Hayden, Santana, Vale, Mincey), plain view (Coolidge) and consent (Schneckloth, Bumper).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session subagents, from cocite evidence; second pass differentiated near-duplicates)

history: Dominant rule: the home is the core of Fourth Amendment protection, and without consent or exigent circumstances police need a warrant to enter it to search or arrest. How it changed: in 1975-79 the anchor is Coolidge (1971), with Johnson and McDonald (1948) on neutral magistrates, Chimel and Vale on search incident to arrest, and Hayden (1967) and Santana (1976) on hot pursuit; Watson (1975) allowed public arrests on probable cause. Payton (1980) enters in 1980-84 and becomes the anchor, striking New York's statutes authorizing warrantless home arrests, and Steagald (1981) required a search warrant to arrest someone in another person's home. Mincey (1978) and Tyler (1978) mark the limits of crime-scene and fire exigencies, and Dorman's factors guide what counts as exigent. In 1985-89 Welsh (1984) and circuit cases such as McConney (1984) on destruction of evidence lead, and Hicks (1987) required probable cause for plain-view seizures. Also: consent under Schneckloth, Bumper and Matlock. The unit merges into the general privacy lineage in 1990-94.
rule: Absent consent or exigent circumstances, police may not enter a home without a warrant to search or to make an arrest (Payton), and exigencies such as hot pursuit, danger or imminent destruction of evidence are narrowly construed.

changes.case: Johnson v. United States; McDonald v. United States
changes.what: Probable cause must be judged by a neutral magistrate; warrantless home entry without exigency is unreasonable.

changes.case: Warden v. Hayden; United States v. Santana
changes.what: Hot pursuit of a fleeing suspect justifies warrantless entry, even when the suspect retreats from a doorway into the house.

changes.case: Vale v. Louisiana; Mincey v. Arizona; Michigan v. Tyler
changes.what: No search of a house incident to an arrest outside it; no murder-scene exception; a burning building is an exigency.
A warrant from a prosecutor is invalid; plain view and exception limits; Coolidge anchors 1975-79.
A warrantless arrest in a public place on probable cause is valid.

changes.case: Payton v. New York; Steagald v. United States
changes.what: A warrant is needed to enter a home for a routine felony arrest, and a search warrant to enter a third party's home; Payton anchors 1980-89.
The gravity of the offense bears on exigency; warrantless home entry for a minor offense is rarely justified.
Seizing or moving an item in plain view requires probable cause.

name: Pennsylvania termination of parental rights: McCray, William L., Santosky
description: Pennsylvania termination of parental rights: grounds require more than a desire to parent, and parents, including incarcerated ones, must show reasonable firmness against obstacles (Diane B., 1974; McCray, 1975, anchor 1975-79). William L. (1978) refused to keep children in foster-care limbo. Santosky (1982, anchor 1980-84) then required clear and convincing evidence; Massachusetts unfitness cases join.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Pennsylvania termination of parental rights (1970s)
previous.description: 1970s Pennsylvania Supreme Court decisions on terminating parental rights (In re William L., Adoption of McCray, Burns) and the clear-and-convincing standard later required by Santosky.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, contrastive pass from family evidence)

history: Dominant rule: involuntary termination requires proof of a statutory ground such as abandonment or continued failure to perform parental duties, with the child's needs considered only after the ground is established, and from 1982 that proof must be clear and convincing. How it changed: the 1975-79 slice is Pennsylvania Supreme Court law under the 1970 Adoption Act, anchored by McCray (1975), which applied an abandonment analysis and held that an incarcerated parent who yields to obstacles may forfeit rights; Diane B. (1974) held a mere desire to parent insufficient, while M.T.T. (1976) and Farabelli (1975) excused parents who used available resources or were blocked. R.I. (1976) put statutory grounds before needs and welfare. Burns (1977) limited petitions to cases where adoption is contemplated, and William L. (1978) refused to preserve a nonexistent relationship. In 1980-84, after merging with other units, Santosky (1982) anchors, requiring clear and convincing evidence as a matter of due process, alongside Marshall (1978) on clearly necessary removal, B.D.S. (1981) on obstruction, and Massachusetts cases requiring unfitness (Custody of a Minor, 1979; Little Wanderers, 1975). The unit then splits toward substantive due process and other state termination lineages.
rule: Parental rights may be involuntarily terminated only on proof of statutory grounds, such as a settled purpose to relinquish or failure to perform parental duties despite reasonable firmness against obstacles, and, after Santosky (1982), only by clear and convincing evidence; the child's needs are weighed after the grounds are found.

changes.case: Appeal of Diane B.; In re Adoption of McCray; In re Adoption of M.T.T.; In re Adoption of R.I.
changes.what: A mere desire to parent is not enough; a parent, including an incarcerated one, must use available resources and show reasonable firmness against obstacles, and needs and welfare are considered only after statutory grounds are met. McCray anchors 1975-79.

changes.case: In re Burns; In re William L.
changes.what: Termination petitions lie only where adoption is contemplated, and the state need not preserve a nonexistent family relationship by leaving children in foster-care limbo.

changes.case: In re Marshall; Custody of a Minor (Mass.); In re Adoption of B.D.S.
changes.what: Removal requires clear and convincing proof that it is clearly necessary, Massachusetts required a finding of unfitness, and obstruction by the custodial parent excuses a parent's failure to maintain contact.
Due process requires at least clear and convincing evidence before a state terminates parental rights; anchors 1980-84.

name: Removal, appointments and Article III private rights: Granfinanciera, Seila Law
description: Structural separation of powers in the 2020s, centred on who may adjudicate and who controls officers: non-Article III adjudication of private rights (Granfinanciera 1989, anchor; Stern 2011; Oil States 2018), appointments (Lucia 2018, Arthrex 2021), and removal (Myers 1926, Humphrey's Executor 1935, Bowsher 1986, Morrison 1988, Seila Law 2020). Chadha (1983) and Youngstown (1952) supply the general framework.

previous.name: Separation of powers: removal power and non-Article III adjudication (2020s)
previous.description: Successor to the 2015 separation-of-powers sub-cluster (27702), now centred on the President's power to remove officers (Myers, Humphrey's Executor line, Bowsher, Morrison v. Olson, Seila Law) and on public-rights adjudication outside Article III courts and its Seventh Amendment limits (Granfinanciera v. Nordberg, Tull, Stern).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, contrastive pass from family evidence)

history: Dominant rule: this single 2020-24 slice, anchored by Granfinanciera v. Nordberg (1989), joins three structural lines. Adjudication: Congress may not withdraw from Article III courts or juries matters of private right such as fraudulent-conveyance suits (Granfinanciera), and Stern (2011) barred bankruptcy courts from finally deciding a state-law counterclaim, though Oil States (2018) allowed agency inter partes review as a public right. Appointments: Lucia (2018) held SEC ALJs are officers, and Arthrex (2021) held APJs' unreviewable decisions inconsistent with inferior-officer appointment. Removal: Myers (1926) recognises presidential removal power, Humphrey's Executor (1935) permits limits for multi-member commissions, Bowsher (1986) bars congressional removal of executing officers, Morrison (1988) upheld the independent counsel, and Seila Law (2020) struck the single-director CFPB's protection. Also: Chadha (1983), Youngstown (1952) and United States v. Nixon (1974). The slice formed from the 2015-19 federal-powers unit and splits into emergency-relief units in 2025-29.
rule: Congress may not vest the judicial power over private-right claims of the kind tried at common law in non-Article III tribunals (Stern, Granfinanciera), officers wielding significant federal authority must be properly appointed (Lucia, Arthrex), and the President's removal power may be restricted only within the Humphrey's Executor and Morrison exceptions (Seila Law).

changes.case: Myers v. United States; Humphrey's Executor v. United States
changes.what: The President has inherent power to remove executive officers, but Congress may limit removal of members of independent multi-member commissions.

changes.case: INS v. Chadha; Bowsher v. Synar; Morrison v. Olson
changes.what: Legislative vetoes violate bicameralism and presentment; Congress cannot retain removal power over officers executing the law; an inferior independent counsel may have for-cause protection.
A fraudulent-conveyance defendant who has not filed a claim has a Seventh Amendment jury right that Congress cannot assign to a non-Article III court; anchors the slice.

name: Departures under the mandatory Guidelines: Diaz-Villafane to Koon
description: Departures from the mandatory federal Guidelines: a court may depart in an unusual case on a factor not forbidden, reviewed for reasonableness. Diaz-Villafane (1st Cir. 1989) anchors 1990-94; Burns (1991) required notice of upward departure and Williams (1992) made policy statements binding guides. Koon (1996) anchors from 1995-99, setting abuse-of-discretion review; the lineage splits into Booker-era review in 2005-09.

previous.name: Guidelines departures (1990s)
previous.description: Departures under the mandatory federal Sentencing Guidelines: abuse-of-discretion review of departure decisions (Koon), notice of upward departure (Burns), invalid departure grounds (Williams), and substantial-assistance motions under § 5K1.1 (Wade v. United States); First Circuit heavy (Diaz-Villafane).

history: Dominant rule: under the mandatory Guidelines a sentencing court may depart in an unusual case that falls outside the heartland, on a factor the Commission has not forbidden, and the decision and its extent are reviewed deferentially. How it changed: Diaz-Villafane (1st Cir. 1989) anchors 1990-94 with circuit tests for unusualness and reasonableness (Lira-Barraza, Jackson on criminal-history departures, Lambert 1993 on intermediate categories). Burns (1991) required notice before an upward departure; Williams (1992) treated policy statements as authoritative and split review into two inquiries; Wade (1992) allowed review of a refusal to file a § 5K1.1 motion only for unconstitutional motive. Koon (1996) anchors 1995-2004, holding that departures are reviewed for abuse of discretion and that the Guidelines do not limit the factors that may warrant departure; circuits then abandoned stricter rules (Collins 1997; Brock 1997, overruling Van Dyke on rehabilitation). Buford (2001) extended deferential review to fact-bound guideline applications. In 2005-09 the lineage splits into post-Booker reasonableness review.
rule: A sentencing court may depart from the Guidelines range in an unusual case outside the heartland on a factor the Commission has not forbidden, and an appellate court reviews the departure decision and its extent for abuse of discretion.

changes.what: Circuit framework for reviewing departures: whether circumstances are unusual enough, whether they are supported, and whether the extent is reasonable, without reducing departures to mechanistic arithmetic.
Rule 32 requires notice to the parties before a court departs upward on a ground not identified in the presentence report or by the government.
A policy statement is an authoritative guide to a guideline; a departure on an expressly rejected factor is a misapplication, and review proceeds in two separate inquiries.
A court may review the government's refusal to file a substantial-assistance motion only for an unconstitutional motive.
Departure decisions are reviewed for abuse of discretion, and the Guidelines do not limit the factors that may warrant departure unless forbidden.
Van Dyke's bar on post-offense rehabilitation as a departure ground was effectively overruled by Koon.

name: § 3582(c)(2) sentence reductions (Dillon) and Fifth Circuit prisoner appeals
description: Two Fifth Circuit dockets: § 3582(c)(2) reductions after crack amendments, held to be limited adjustments rather than resentencings (Dillon, 2010, anchor 2010-14), with Freeman (2011) and Dorsey (2012) on plea-based sentences and the Fair Sentencing Act. history: Dominant rule: through 2010-14 the lineage is about § 3582(c)(2): a court may reduce a sentence only when a retroactive Guidelines amendment lowers the range the sentence was based on, and the proceeding is a limited adjustment rather than a resentencing (Dillon, 2010, anchor in 2010-14). How it changed: the Fifth Circuit's early cases (Shaw, 1994, anchor 1995-2004; Whitebird, 1995; Bravo, 2000) confined the remedy to retroactive amendments and refused to reopen other issues. After the 2007 crack amendments, Moore (2008) excluded career offenders whose range was unaffected and Melvin (2009) held that Booker does not let courts go below the amended range, which Dillon confirmed. Freeman (2011) extended reductions to some plea-agreement sentences, and Dorsey (2012) applied the Fair Sentencing Act to pre-Act offenders sentenced afterwards. The dominant rule then shifts: from 2015-19 Baugh (1997) anchors and the lineage covers prisoner appeals, where IFP status requires a good-faith, non-frivolous appeal, pro se filings are liberally construed (Howard, 1983; Haines, 1972), unbriefed arguments are abandoned (Yohey, 1993; Brinkmann, 1987) and dismissals count as § 1915(g) strikes even on appeal (Coleman, 2015). Howard anchors the partial 2025-29 slice.

Contra non valentem suspends prescription only in the four Corsey (1979) situations, including concealment and the discovery rule (Plaquemines, 1987; Wimberly, 1994), and a plaintiff is charged with what diligence would reveal. name: Texas trial-error review in the 1990s: Montgomery and Almanza before the split
description: Texas Court of Criminal Appeals review of trial error, 1990-99 only, before it split into evidence and charge-error lineages: Montgomery (1991, anchor 1990-94) on abuse-of-discretion review and Rule 403; Almanza (1985, anchor 1995-99) on egregious harm from unobjected-to charge error; Royster (1981) and Rousseau (1993) on lesser-included instructions; cure by instruction to disregard (Harris 1989); capital issues (Keeton 1987, McFarland 1996).
history: Dominant rule: the standards for reviewing trial error in Texas criminal appeals. How it changed: in 1990-94 Montgomery (1991) anchors: evidentiary rulings, especially extraneous offenses, are reviewed for abuse of discretion with Rule 403 balancing; Harris (1989) holds most errors cured by an instruction to disregard; Royster (1981), Aguilar (1985) and Kinnamon (1990) govern lesser-included-offense instructions. In 1995-99 Almanza (1985) anchors: unobjected-to charge error requires egregious harm. Rousseau (1993) restated the lesser-included test, Bignall (1994) applied it, Dinkins (1995) treated statements explaining how a defendant became a suspect as non-hearsay, and McFarland (1992, 1996) addressed excited utterances and capital mitigation. Preservation rules continue: Narvaiz (1992) and Barnes (1994) require record citations and objections matching the appellate complaint. Also: Long (1991) on restraints, Keeton (1987) on future dangerousness and Smith (1995) on plea-offer evidence. The lineage splits in 2000-04 into evidentiary-harm and charge-error units.
rule: In the Texas Court of Criminal Appeals of the 1990s, unobjected-to jury-charge error requires reversal only for egregious harm (Almanza), evidentiary rulings are reviewed for abuse of discretion within the zone of reasonable disagreement and Rule 403 balancing (Montgomery), and a lesser-included-offense instruction is required when the lesser offense is within the proof of the charged offense and some evidence would permit a rational jury to find guilt only of the lesser (Royster; Rousseau).

changes.what: Two-step test for a lesser-included-offense instruction, which may require aggravated assault as a lesser of aggravated robbery on the proof.
Charge error preserved by objection needs only some harm, while unobjected-to error requires egregious harm that denied a fair and impartial trial.
Admission of extraneous-offense and other evidence is reviewed for abuse of discretion, with Rule 403 weighing of probative value against unfair prejudice.
The lesser offense must be included within the proof necessary for the charged offense, and some evidence must show the defendant guilty only of the lesser.
Article 37.071's definition of mitigating evidence is not too narrow under the Eighth Amendment, and the capital scheme is not unconstitutional for combining mitigation and structured discretion.

history: Dominant rule: this single-slice lineage (2000-04) gathers Georgia capital appeals on qualifying jurors and on sentencing-phase evidence, anchored by Palmer v. State (1999). A juror may be excused for cause only when his views would substantially impair his duties, and leaning for or against death is not enough (Pace, 1999; Isaacs, 1989, on reverse-Witherspoon challenges). Heidler (2000) holds that erroneously qualifying a juror is harmless if the juror was not among those from whom the deliberating jury was drawn. Morrow (2000) treats under-representation below ten percentage points as usually constitutional. At sentencing the State may introduce specific bad acts to show character (McMichen, 1995), the jury need not balance aggravating against mitigating circumstances (Ford, 1987), and defense witnesses may plead for mercy but may not testify merely to their views on the death penalty (Childs, 1987). Also: Raulerson (1997) on confessions and juror bias, and Romine (1986) on Allen charges. No rule change appears within the slice.
rule: In Georgia capital trials a prospective juror is excusable for cause only if his views on the death penalty would substantially impair his duties, not for merely leaning toward or against death, and at the sentencing phase the State may prove the defendant's character with evidence of specific bad acts, without the jury having to weigh aggravating against mitigating circumstances.

changes.what: Georgia juries need not balance aggravating against mitigating circumstances; sentencing considers the defendant's character and the circumstances of the crime.
Evidence of a defendant's specific bad acts is admissible at the sentencing phase to show character.
A prospective juror is not excusable for cause for merely leaning for or against a death sentence.

changes.case: Morrow v. State; Heidler v. State
changes.what: Under-representation of less than ten percentage points in the jury pool is usually constitutional, and erroneously qualifying a juror is harmless if that juror was not in the pool from which the deliberating jury was drawn.

name: Texas limitations: discovery rule and open-courts challenges (Altai, S.V., Sax)
description: Texas limitations and accrual, 1990-2004: a claim accrues when the wrong causes injury (Moreno 1990), with a discovery rule for undiscoverable injuries (Gaddis 1967; Willis 1988, anchor 1990-94), narrowed in Altai and S.V. (1996, S.V. anchors 2000-04) to injuries inherently undiscoverable and objectively verifiable. Open-courts rulings (Sax 1983, Krusen 1984, Neagle 1985) protect common-law malpractice claims.
history: Dominant rule: a Texas cause of action accrues when the wrongful act causes injury, whether or not the plaintiff knows of it (Moreno 1990, anchor 1995-99), subject to the discovery rule and fraudulent concealment, and to the open-courts guarantee. How it changed: Gaddis (1967) began the discovery rule for foreign-object malpractice; Sax (1983), Krusen (1984) and Neagle (1985) struck limitations under the open-courts provision as applied to minors and to patients unable to discover the wrong, though Kimball (1987) ran § 10.01 from the date of treatment and Bala (1995) and Moreno denied open-courts protection to statutory claims. Willis v. Maverick (1988), anchor in 1990-94, extended the discovery rule to fiduciaries who fail to disclose; Woods (1988) made it a pleaded defense, and Burns (1990) put the burden of negating it on a summary-judgment movant. Altai (1996) and S.V. (1996), the anchor in 2000-04, confined the rule to injuries inherently undiscoverable and objectively verifiable. In 2000-04 Shah v. Moss (2002) and other medical-malpractice cases (Husain 1998, Earle 1999) lead. Alongside: fraudulent concealment (Borderlon 1983, Nichols 1974).
rule: A Texas claim generally accrues when the wrongful act causes injury, deferred by the discovery rule only for injuries inherently undiscoverable and objectively verifiable or by fraudulent concealment, while the open-courts guarantee bars limitations that cut off common-law claims before they could be discovered.

history: Dominant rule: to win under the Lanham Act a plaintiff needs a protectable mark or trade dress and a likelihood of confusion. Sorensen v. WD-40 (7th Cir. 2015) anchors the single partial 2025-29 slice and treats actual confusion as an especially important factor, affirming summary judgment where no reasonable jury could find confusion. Two Pesos (1992) holds inherently distinctive trade dress protectable without secondary meaning. Uncommon v. Spigen (7th Cir. 2019) explains the spectrum of distinctiveness, the role of surveys and that registration gives only one presumption of distinctiveness. LSU v. Smack Apparel (5th Cir. 2008) and Scandia Down (9th Cir. 1985) apply the confusion factors. Booking.com (2020) rejected a per se rule that 'generic.com' terms are generic. Arla (2018). Also personal jurisdiction over online sellers (Hanwjh 2022). Unrelated criminal and First Amendment cases in the slice are drift. No change in the governing rule is visible.

history: Dominant rule: a temporary injunction preserves the status quo pending trial and issues only on a pleaded cause of action, a probable right to the relief sought and a probable, imminent and irreparable injury; appellate courts review it for abuse of discretion without deciding the merits (Davis 1978, Butnaru 2002). name: Bivens and congressional remedial schemes, 1985-99: Bush v. Lucas, Chilicky
description: Bivens limits from congressional remedial schemes, 1985-99: Bivens (1971), Davis (1979) and Carlson (1980) recognized remedies, but Bush v. history: Dominant rule: courts will not imply a Bivens remedy where special factors counsel hesitation, especially a comprehensive remedial scheme crafted by Congress. name: Unpreserved Booker error, 2005-09: the circuit split on plain-error prejudice
description: The cross-circuit split over unpreserved Booker (2005, anchor) error in 2005-09: all treated mandatory-Guidelines sentencing as plain error, but Mares (5th Cir.), Antonakopoulos (1st Cir.) and Gonzalez-Huerta (10th Cir.) required a reasonable probability of a lower sentence; Crosby (2d Cir.) and Ameline (9th Cir.) ordered limited remands; Hughes (4th Cir.) found prejudice from judge-found facts. Appeal waivers survived Booker (Cardenas).
history: Dominant rule: how appellate courts handled sentences imposed under the mandatory Guidelines once Booker (2005) made them advisory and applied its holding to all cases on direct review. Booker anchors the lineage's only slice, 2005-09, formed from the Apprendi, Olano plain-error and Guidelines-departure lineages and splitting in 2010-14 into reasonableness review and Fifth Circuit plain-error lineages. How it changed: the circuits split over unpreserved Booker error. All treated mandatory application as plain error (Valenzuela-Quevedo, Antonakopoulos), and constitutional (Booker) and statutory (Fanfan) errors were analysed alike (Martinez-Lugo). The Fifth (Mares), First (Antonakopoulos) and Tenth (Gonzalez-Huerta) Circuits required the defendant to show a reasonable probability of a different sentence; the Second (Crosby) and Ninth (Ameline) remanded for the district court to say whether it would have sentenced differently; the Fourth (Hughes) found prejudice from judge-found enhancements and disregarded the chance of the same sentence on remand. Dazey and Villegas found the fourth prong met where the defendant contested the facts. Also: Booker does not undo appeal waivers (Cardenas), and preservation requires the Sixth Amendment objection itself (White).

history: Dominant rule: statements from custodial interrogation are admissible in the case in chief only after Miranda warnings and a knowing, voluntary waiver; Miranda anchors every slice from 1965-69. history: Dominant rule: Brill v. Guardian Life (1995) anchors every slice from 2010-14: summary judgment is proper when the competent evidence, viewed for the nonmovant, allows a rational factfinder only one conclusion, and appellate review applies the same standard (Bhagat, 2014; Templo Fuente, 2016) with no deference to legal conclusions (Manalapan, 1995). How it changed: the 2005-09 slice is a duty-of-care unit anchored by Hopkins (1993); Olivo (2006) recognised a premises owner's duty to a spouse exposed to asbestos on work clothes, while New York (2005) and Georgia (CSX, 2005) refused that duty on policy grounds. From 2015-19 the slice grows fivefold and the net-opinion rule becomes central: Polzo (2008) and Pomerantz Paper (2011) bar conclusions without factual or methodological support, and Davis v. Brickman (2014) and Townsend v. Pierre (2015) apply it at summary judgment; Nicholas (2013) requires equivalently credentialed experts in malpractice cases. Also: Globe Motor (2016) on enforcing contracts as written, new-trial motions (Risko, 2011) in 2020-24, and CEPA and LAD claims. Celotex (1986) is cited alongside Brill in the partial 2025-29 slice.
rule: New Jersey summary judgment is granted when the competent evidence, viewed for the nonmovant, permits only one rational result (Brill), reviewed de novo with no deference to the trial court's legal conclusions (Manalapan), and an expert's unsupported net opinion cannot create a genuine issue.

history: Dominant rule: punitive damages must not be grossly excessive, under procedures and guideposts that tightened over the slices. How it changed: Haslip (1991) anchors 1990-94, upholding Alabama's system with instructions and post-verdict review under Hammond (1986) and Hornsby (1989); Browning-Ferris (1989) had held the Excessive Fines Clause inapplicable, and Eichenseer (5th Cir. 1991) stressed instructions. Gore (1996) enters and anchors 1995-2004, striking a 500-to-1 award and announcing three guideposts after TXO (1993) and Oberg (1994); on remand Alabama reduced the award (Gore 1997). Erie, Hanna, Guaranty Trust and Gasperini (1996) join in 1995-99 as federal diversity review of verdicts comes in. In 2000-04 Cooper Industries (2001) required de novo review, Campbell (2003) found a 145-to-1 ratio excessive, and Kolstad (1999) set the Title VII malice standard, with Lowery (2000) on managerial agents. The unit splits toward Texas defamation and punitive damages in 2005-09.
rule: The Due Process Clause forbids grossly excessive punitive damages, judged by the reprehensibility of the conduct, the ratio to actual or potential harm, and comparable civil penalties (BMW v. Gore), with single-digit ratios ordinarily the limit (State Farm v. Campbell) and de novo appellate review of excessiveness (Cooper Industries).

history: Dominant rule: the lineage carries two strands of criminal-appeal law, and its anchor shifts. From 1985-89 through 1990-94 Anders v. California (1967) anchors: appointed counsel who finds an appeal frivolous must file a brief referring to anything arguable, and the court must search the record; New York's no-merit practice (Saunders 1976, Paige 1976, Gonzalez 1979) and Penson (1988), which presumes prejudice when counsel withdraws without that process, lead. A Missouri capital strand runs alongside (Newlon 1982, Guinan 1984, Nash 1985). The Arizona capital strand grows and takes over in 1995-99, anchored by Atwood (1992): the supreme court independently reviews aggravation and mitigation; Gretzler (1983) defined the (F)(6) heinous-or-depraved aggravator and Gillies (1983) the (F)(5) pecuniary motive; Correll (1986) barred retroactive new aggravators; Walton (1989; U.S. 1990) upheld judge sentencing and a defendant's burden on mitigation; Fierro (1990) and White (1991) weighed premeditation; Bible (1993) limited review of unobjected error to fundamental error. The Anders strand splits off to Texas units in 1990-94 and 1995-99.
rule: Appointed appellate counsel may withdraw from a frivolous appeal only after filing a brief referring to anything arguable, with the court examining the record (Anders); in Arizona capital cases the supreme court independently reviews aggravators, such as Gretzler's heinous-or-depraved factors, and mitigation.

history: Dominant rule: whether a Washington local charge is a valid regulatory fee or an unauthorized tax. The lineage exists only in 2000-04, anchored by Covell v. City of Seattle (1995), after two 1995-99 units merge; it splits in 2005-09. How it developed: Teter (1985) held storm-water charges were fees; Margola (1993) remanded on whether rental-housing registration revenues were fees under RCW 82.02.020; King County Fire Protection District No. 16 (1994) held an ambulance charge was not a tax because it paid for a specific service. Covell (1995) then set the test, asking whether the primary purpose is to raise revenue or to regulate, whether the money is allocated to the regulatory purpose, and whether there is a direct relationship between the charge and the service received or burden produced, and held Seattle's street utility charge a tax. Hillis Homes (2002) struck a county impact fee as an illegal tax. Alongside: Weden (1998) upheld a ban on personal watercraft under the police power; High Tide Seafoods (1986) and Collins (2001) applied standing and justiciability limits under the Uniform Declaratory Judgments Act; Belas (1998) requires clear statutory intent for tax exemptions; Samis Land (2001) on taxing undeveloped lots.
rule: A Washington municipal charge is a regulatory fee rather than a tax only if its primary purpose is to regulate or to pay for a service or burden tied to the payer, the money is allocated to that purpose, and there is a direct relationship between the charge and the service or burden (Covell).
