round1.name: Washington vagueness of penal ordinances (Maciolek, Huff); then fees versus taxes
round1.description: Washington Supreme Court constitutional challenges: through 1995-99, vagueness and overbreadth of penal ordinances, under which a law is valid if the general area of prohibited conduct is plain (Maciolek 1984, Eze 1988, Huff 1989, Luvene 1992). In 2000-04 the anchor becomes Teter (1985) and the unit turns to whether municipal charges are regulatory fees or taxes (Covell 1995, Hillis Homes 2002).
round1.history: Dominant rule: through 1995-99, vagueness review of Washington penal laws. A statute gives fair notice if the general area of prohibited conduct is plain and it does not leave officers and juries to decide subjectively what is covered (Maciolek 1984, the 1985-89 anchor). Earlier cases tested particular phrases: 'unlawful purpose' (Bellevue v. Miller 1975), 'lawful order' (Rice 1980), and 'without lawful excuse', which Richmond (1984) held vague. Eze (1988) held that a law is not vague merely because one cannot predict the exact line, Douglass (1990) let citizens rely on statutes and case law, and Worrell (1988) required as-applied review outside speech. Huff (1989) anchors 1990-94 and upheld a harassing-call ordinance, and Luvene (1992) anchors 1995-99 and upheld a drug-loitering ordinance. O'Day (1988) read article I, § 5 more broadly than the First Amendment on prior restraints. How it changed: in 2000-04 an unlabelled unit merges in and Teter (1985) anchors. The dominant question becomes whether a charge is a regulatory fee or a tax: Teter upheld storm-water charges, Covell (1995) held Seattle's street utility charge a tax, and Hillis Homes (2002) struck an impact fee. Also: Weden (1998) on the police power and the public trust doctrine.
round1.rule: Through 1995-99: a Washington penal statute or ordinance is not void for vagueness if the general area of prohibited conduct is made plain and enforcement is not left to subjective judgment, even if the exact line cannot be predicted (Maciolek, Eze); from 2000-04 the anchor shifts to whether a municipal charge is a regulatory fee or a tax under the Covell factors.

name: Virginia criminal evidence review: abuse of discretion and harmless error
description: Virginia criminal appeals in 2015-24 on evidence: admissibility reviewed for abuse of discretion (Blankenship 2019), relevance (Thomas 2005, anchor 2015-19), Kotteakos harmless error and victim-fear statements (Clay 2001), expert basis evidence (Campos 2017), credibility for the fact finder (Grattan 2009), and decision on the best and narrowest grounds (Commonwealth 2015, anchor 2020-24). Rules of Evidence keep prior case law (Creamer 2015).
history: Dominant rule: Virginia appellate courts defer to trial courts on evidence and decide appeals narrowly. The lineage forms in 2015-19 from three units, including Virginia Court of Appeals criminal review, and splits three ways in 2025-29. How it developed: Thomas (en banc 2005), anchor of 2015-19, defines relevance broadly; Clay (2001) adopted Kotteakos for nonconstitutional harmless error and admitted victims' statements of fear; Michels (2006) reviews testimonial status de novo. Grattan (2009) and Anderson (2011) leave credibility, including experts', to the fact finder; Campos (2017) explains the Cartera rule as a nonhearsay basis for expert opinion. Commonwealth (2015), anchor of 2020-24, and Commonwealth (2017) require deciding cases on the best and narrowest grounds. Creamer (2015) reads the codified Rules of Evidence consistently with prior case law, and Blankenship (2019) restates abuse-of-discretion review. Also: preservation (Ohree 1998; Ortiz 2008), non-jurisdictional venue defects (Porter 2008), premeditation from brutality (Avent 2010), remote prior violence (Carter 2017) and the rape shield law (Fahringer 2019).
rule: Virginia appellate courts review evidentiary rulings for abuse of discretion, deem nonconstitutional error harmless under the Kotteakos standard (Clay), and decide cases on the best and narrowest grounds available.

description: Prisoners' procedural due process: a liberty interest exists only for restraints imposing atypical and significant hardship relative to ordinary prison life (Sandin, 1995, anchor 2005-09), replacing Hewitt's (1983) mandatory-language test; where it exists, Wolff (1974) procedures apply and some evidence suffices (Hill, 1985). history: Dominant rule: prisoners keep due-process protection, but a state creates a protected liberty interest only when a restraint imposes atypical and significant hardship in relation to the ordinary incidents of prison life (Sandin, 1995), or extends the sentence, as loss of good-time credit does. Where an interest exists, Wolff (1974), the 2000-04 anchor, requires advance written notice, a written statement of reasons and a limited right to call witnesses, and Hill (1985) upholds a decision supported by some evidence; circuits held a conduct report alone may be enough (McPherson, 1999; Webb, 2000). How it changed: Meachum (1976) denied an interest in transfers, Greenholtz (1979) found only a qualified interest in parole, and Hewitt (1983) and Olim (1983) located interests in regulations that limit official discretion. Sandin rejected that method, and it anchors 2005-09, when Wilkinson v. Austin (2005) found a supermax interest but approved informal procedures. Alongside: Turner (1987), O'Lone and Abbott on reasonable restrictions of rights, Wolfish (1979) on detainees, Lewis v. Casey (1996) requiring actual injury for access-to-courts claims, Harper (1990) on forced medication, and California parole suitability (Rosenkrantz; Dannenberg).
rule: A prisoner has a due-process liberty interest only in freedom from restraint that imposes atypical and significant hardship relative to ordinary prison life (Sandin), and where one exists a disciplinary hearing needs Wolff's notice, statement and limited witness rights, with the decision supported by some evidence (Hill).

name: Void for vagueness: fair notice and arbitrary enforcement (Grayned, Morales)
description: Void-for-vagueness doctrine in a single 2005-09 slice: criminal laws must give fair notice and set enforcement guidelines (Connally 1926, Papachristou 1972, Grayned 1972, anchor; Kolender 1983; Morales 1999), with limiting constructions considered and less rigor for economic regulation (Hoffman Estates 1982). history: Dominant rule: Grayned (1972) anchors this single 2005-09 slice. Connally (1926) supplies the common-intelligence test; Papachristou (1972) struck a vagrancy ordinance, and Goguen (1974) a flag-contempt law for its standardless sweep. Hoffman Estates (1982) directs courts to consider limiting constructions and permits greater leeway for business regulation; Kolender (1983) struck a stop-and-identify statute, emphasizing enforcement guidelines; Morales (1999) struck Chicago's gang-loitering ordinance. State applications: the Texas Court of Criminal Appeals in Ely (1979), Bynum (1989, as-applied review absent speech) and Long (1996, former stalking statute), and Rodriguez (2002) on sex-offender registration as civil; Washington courts in Douglass (1990), Lorang (2000), Williams (2001, harassment statute limited to true threats) and Holcombe (2006). No rule change within the slice.
rule: A criminal law is void for vagueness if it fails to give a person of ordinary intelligence fair notice of what is prohibited or lacks minimal guidelines to prevent arbitrary enforcement, with stricter review where First Amendment freedoms are affected and as-applied review otherwise (Grayned, Hoffman Estates, Kolender, Morales).

history: Dominant rule: a single 1970-74 slice of 1,573 cases, anchored by Aguilar v. Texas (1964), that gathers the Warren Court's search-and-seizure rules. Probable cause for a warrant based on an informant required the two Aguilar-Spinelli prongs (Spinelli, 1969), read in a commonsense way (Ventresca, 1965) and allowing hearsay with a substantial basis (Jones, 1960). Chimel (1969) limited search incident to arrest to the arrestee's person and reach; Terry (1968) allowed stops and frisks on reasonable suspicion; Carroll (1925), Brinegar (1949) and Chambers (1970) permitted warrantless vehicle searches on probable cause, while Preston (1964) barred searching a car after the arrestees were in custody; Coolidge (1971) required a neutral magistrate and particular description; Katz (1967) protected reasonable expectations of privacy; and Wong Sun (1963) excluded fruits of an illegal arrest. How it changed: later decisions abandoned parts of this core. Illinois v. Gates (1983) replaced Aguilar-Spinelli in federal law, and Jones's automatic standing rule was later abandoned. The slice splits in 1975-79 into separate stop, exclusion, vehicle and home-entry lineages.

changes.case: Aguilar v. Texas; Spinelli v. United States

history: Dominant rule: under the APA's arbitrary-and-capricious standard, a court asks whether the agency considered the relevant factors and rationally explained its choice, judged only on the grounds the agency invoked (State Farm 1983, Chenery 1947, Burlington Truck Lines 1962), without substituting its own policy judgment (FCC v. history: Dominant rule: the FAA requires enforcing arbitration agreements, including for federal statutory claims, as other contracts. How it changed: in 1995-99 the anchor is Cole (D.C. name: Union agency fees and dissenters: Abood, Ellis, Hudson procedures
description: Union agency fees: nonmembers may be charged for collective bargaining but not political spending (Street, 1961; Abood, 1977), with chargeability set by Ellis (1984) and Lehnert (1991). Chicago Teachers Union v. Hudson (1986, anchor 1990-2004) requires notice, an impartial hearing and escrow. Beck (1988) carried the rule to private-sector NLRA fees; Keller (1990) to bar dues. Abood was overruled by Janus in 2018.

previous.name: Compelled speech and union agency fees
previous.description: Compelled subsidies and speech: union agency fees and political spending (Machinists v. Street, Abood, Ellis, Hudson, Lehnert, Beck) and compelled messages (Wooley v. Maynard).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, contrastive pass from family evidence)

history: Dominant rule: compelled fees may fund a union's collective-bargaining activity but not, over objection, its political or ideological work, and the union must offer procedures adequate to protect objectors. How it changed: the RLA cases Hanson (1956), Street (1961) and Allen (1963) upheld union shops while barring political use of objectors' dues. Abood (1977) applied this to public employees under the First Amendment. Ellis (1984) anchors 1985-89, merged from a public-employee speech unit, separating chargeable from nonchargeable expenses and rejecting rebate-only schemes. Hudson (1986) anchors 1990-94 onward, requiring an adequate explanation of the fee, a prompt hearing before an impartial decisionmaker and escrow; Tierney (1987, 1990), Andrews (1987) and Hohe (1992) tested notices. In 1990-94 Beck (1988) extended the rule to private-sector NLRA agreements, Keller (1990) to bar dues and Lehnert (1991) set the germaneness test; Wooley (1977) brings compelled-message doctrine. In 1995-2004 NLRB notice duties (Bloom, Abrams, Wegscheid), compelled marketing fees (Glickman, 1997) and remedies (Prescott, 1999, rejecting full restitution) follow. Abood itself was later overruled by Janus (2018).
rule: Nonmembers may be required to pay their share of a union's collective-bargaining costs but not its political or ideological spending, and the union must give them adequate notice of the fee's basis, a prompt impartial decision on objections, and an escrow for disputed amounts (Abood, Ellis, Hudson).

changes.what: Union-shop agreements are valid, but the RLA bars spending an objecting employee's compelled dues on political causes, and dissent must be made known.

changes.what: Extended the line to public employees under the First Amendment: agency fees may fund collective bargaining but not ideological activity.

Davis (1975) read the 1972 privacy amendment to reach improper collection and use of information, Valley Bank (1975) extended it to confidential financial affairs, Britt (1978) protected association membership and contributors, and Gherardini (1979) medical and bank records. name: Immigration review: plenary power (Fiallo), then St. Cyr habeas and retroactivity
description: Judicial review in immigration: Fiallo (1977) anchors 1980-94 on Congress's plenary power over admission (Mezei, Mandel), with Jean v. Nelson (1984-85) on Mariel and Haitian detainees. history: Dominant rule: the anchor doctrine changes. 1980-94: the plenary power. Fiallo (1977) anchors 1980-84 and 1990-94, and Jean v. Nelson (1984) anchors 1985-89. Congress's power over admission leaves little room for review (Mezei 1953, Mandel 1972, Mathews v. Diaz 1976), and the Mariel and Haitian detention cases (Fernandez-Roque, Garcia-Mir, Jean) applied that to excludable aliens, while Landon (1982) gave returning residents due process and Lopez-Mendoza (1984) denied the exclusionary rule in deportation. How it changed: in 1995-99 Yang (1997) anchors as AEDPA and IIRIRA (1996) cut review for criminal aliens and repealed § 212(c). Landgraf (1994) and Hughes Aircraft (1997) supply the presumption against retroactivity, Felker (1996) upheld habeas limits, and the circuits split, Goncalves (1998) preserving § 2241 habeas and Laguerre (1999) finding it divested. Reno v. AADC (1999) read § 1252(g) narrowly. St. Cyr (2001) anchors 2000-09 and settled the split. name: Michigan governmental immunity and strict statutory notice (Odom, Rowland)
description: Michigan governmental tort immunity in 2015-19, anchored by Odom (2008): employees must plead and prove immunity, with Ross (1985) good-faith immunity for intentional torts and gross negligence that is the proximate cause (Robinson 2000) for negligence. Notice requirements are enforced as written (Rowland 2007, overruling Hobbs and Brown; McCahan 2012); exceptions are narrow (Nawrocki 2000, sidewalks in Moraccini 2012).
history: Dominant rule: Odom (2008) anchors this single 2015-19 slice: governmental immunity is an affirmative defense; for intentional torts the employee is immune if acting in good faith within the scope of authority on discretionary acts (from Ross, 1985), while negligence is governed by MCL 691.1407(2), which requires gross negligence, 'almost a willful disregard' (Tarlea, 2004), that is the proximate cause, meaning the one most immediate cause (Robinson, 2000). How it changed: the Michigan Supreme Court enforced the statutory text strictly: Nawrocki (2000) overruled decisions straying from the highway exception's language; Rowland (2007) overruled Hobbs and Brown and enforced the 120-day notice rule without a prejudice requirement, and McCahan (2012) extended that to other notice provisions; Plunkett (2009) allows substantial compliance in describing a defect. Also: sidewalk liability under MCL 691.1402a (Moraccini, 2012), the motor-vehicle exception (Stanton, 2002), wrongful-death limitations without a discovery rule (Trentadue, 2007), and tort liability defined broadly (Bradley Estate, 2013).
rule: Michigan governmental immunity extends to all tort liability except under the narrowly construed statutory exceptions; individual employees are immune from negligence unless grossly negligent and from intentional torts if acting in good faith within their authority (Odom), and statutory notice requirements are enforced as written (Rowland).

name: States' and tribes' immunity in 2020-24: Ex parte Young limits, Bay Mills, McGirt
description: Immunity of States and tribes with Indian-country status, one 2020-24 slice: the Eleventh Amendment bars suits against States (Halderman 1984, Seminole Tribe 1996, Alden 1999) except prospective Ex parte Young relief, which the Fifth Circuit limits to officials connected to enforcement (City of Austin 2019). Tribal immunity extends to off-reservation commerce (Bay Mills 2014). McGirt (2020, anchor) held the Creek reservation never disestablished.
history: Dominant rule: sovereign immunity of States and tribes. States are immune from private suits whatever the relief (Pennhurst/Halderman 1984), Congress cannot abrogate that immunity under Article I (Seminole Tribe 1996) or force States into their own courts (Alden 1999), and Franchise Tax Board v. Hyatt (2019) extended immunity to suits in other States' courts. Ex parte Young (1908) allows prospective relief against state officers, but not retroactive monetary relief (Edelman 1974); the Fifth Circuit requires that the official have a real connection to enforcing the challenged law (City of Austin v. Paxton 2019, Texas Democratic Party v. Abbott 2020). Tribes keep immunity for off-reservation commercial activity (Bay Mills 2014), though tribal officers do not share it (Santa Clara Pueblo 1978); federal immunity is waived only by statute (Mitchell 1983). Alongside: Indian-country jurisdiction: Williams (1959), McClanahan (1973), Bracker (1980) and Montana (1981) on state and tribal authority, Solem (1984) and Parker (2016) on diminishment, and McGirt (2020), the anchor, holding that the Creek reservation remains Indian country for Major Crimes Act purposes. Single slice; it splits in 2025-29.

changes.what: Congress cannot use Article I powers to abrogate state sovereign immunity.

history: Dominant rule: Monell (1978), the anchor in all three slices, overruled Monroe v. Pape in part: municipalities are persons under § 1983 but answer only for their own policies or customs, not on respondeat superior. name: Probation and parole revocation: Morrissey, Gagnon, and search conditions
description: Probation and parole revocation in 1980-84, anchored by Gagnon (1973) with Morrissey (1972): revocation requires notice and a hearing but not full criminal process. history: Dominant rule: probation and parole revocation require basic due process, and conditions of release must be reasonably related to the offense and rehabilitation. Fitzharris and Consuelo-Gonzalez (9th Cir. 1975) held parole and probation searches still subject to reasonableness, and Grubbs (1979) struck a blanket consent-to-search condition. history: Dominant rule: discretion and eligibility under California's Three Strikes law. Romero (1996) anchors 2010-14: trial courts may dismiss strike priors under § 1385 in furtherance of justice. Williams (1998) asks whether the defendant falls outside the law's spirit, Carmony (2004) reviews refusals for abuse of discretion, and Scott (1994) forfeits unobjected-to discretionary sentencing claims. Brown (2012) and Neal (1960, § 654) also lead. How it changed: Proposition 36 (2012) restricted life terms to serious or violent third strikes and created § 1170.126 petitions for resentencing. In re Lawrence (2008) supplies the current-dangerousness standard from parole cases, and In re Lynch (1972) the state disproportionality test. The lineage then merges into the broader ameliorative-sentencing unit in 2020-24.

history: Dominant rule: federal courts generally decline to interfere with pending state proceedings or to review state judgments. The anchor shifts doctrine in 2000-04. How it changed: in 1965-69 the anchor is Douglas (1943), with Dombrowski (1965) allowing relief against bad-faith prosecutions and Zwickler (1967) limiting Pullman. Younger (1971) and its companions (Samuels, Perez, Dyson, Boyle) enter in 1970-74 and Younger anchors through 1995-99, except 1975-79 when Huffman (1975) anchors as Younger reaches quasi-criminal civil proceedings, Colorado River (1976) and Juidice (1977) enter, and Steffel (1974) and Gibson (1973) mark exceptions. Moore (1979), Middlesex (1982) and Pennzoil (1987) extended Younger; NOPSI (1989) limited it. Burford and Quackenbush (1996) and Wilton (1995) lead 1995-99. Rooker (1924) and Feldman (1983) enter in 1990-94, and Feldman anchors 2000-14; Exxon Mobil (2005) confined the doctrine to state losers challenging earlier judgments. FELA entrants in 2010-14 are drift.
rule: Absent bad faith, harassment or other extraordinary circumstances, a federal court may not enjoin or declare against pending state criminal proceedings or comparable civil and administrative proceedings implicating important state interests (Younger), and lower federal courts may not review state-court judgments (Rooker-Feldman), a bar confined to state losers complaining of judgments entered before the federal suit (Exxon Mobil).

name: Ohio summary judgment 1990-2004: from the Harless/Temple test to Dresher
description: The Ohio sub-cluster that spans the arrival of Dresher, 1990-2004: Temple (1977, anchor 1990-94) and Harless (1978) state the three-part Civ.R. 56 test; Dresher v. history: Dominant rule: Ohio Civ.R. 56. Harless v. Willis Day Warehousing (1978) and Temple v. Wean United (1977), the anchor in 1990-94, require that no genuine issue of material fact remain, that the movant be entitled to judgment as a matter of law, and that reasonable minds construing the evidence most strongly for the nonmovant reach only one adverse conclusion. How it changed: Dresher v. Burt (1996) anchors 1995-99 and 2000-04: a movant may not rest on conclusory assertions that the nonmovant lacks evidence but must point to Civ.R. 56(C) materials, after which the nonmovant has a reciprocal burden to set forth specific facts (Mootispaw 1996). Mitseff (1988) requires the motion to state its grounds; Murphy (1992) keeps the initial determination with the trial court; Grafton (1996) sets de novo review; Turner (1993) bars resolving credibility conflicts. name: Bias cross-examination and the right to present a defense, 1985-94
description: The accused's right to cross-examine for bias and to present a defense, 1985-94: Davis v. Alaska (1974), anchor of both slices, made denial of bias cross-examination constitutional error; Chambers (1973) and Washington v. Texas (1967) protect defense evidence. Van Arsdall (1986) allowed reasonable limits with harmless-error review; Olden (1988) protected consent-related bias questioning, while Taylor (1988) and Lucas (1991) upheld discovery and rape-shield limits.
history: Dominant rule: Davis v. Alaska (1974), anchor of 1985-89 and 1990-94, holds that cross-examination to expose a witness's bias is central to confrontation, building on Alford (1931), Pointer (1965), Douglas (1965) and Smith v. Illinois (1968). Washington v. Texas (1967) incorporated compulsory process, Webb (1972) barred driving a defense witness off the stand, and Chambers (1973) held that evidence rules may not be applied mechanistically to defeat a defense. Abel (1984) confirmed impeachment for bias under the Federal Rules. How it changed: Delaware v. Van Arsdall (1986) enters as a leading case in 1990-94: trial judges keep wide latitude to limit repetitive or marginally relevant questioning, and wrongful limits are reviewed for harmlessness; Crane (1986) protected evidence on how a confession was obtained. Olden (1988) found a violation where a court barred cross-examination on a complainant's relationship that was crucial to consent. On the other side, Taylor (1988) upheld exclusion of a defense witness as a discovery sanction and Lucas (1991) upheld rape-shield notice requirements. State cases apply rape-shield exceptions (Howard 1981) and relevance limits (Arenda 1982, Springer 1978).
rule: The Sixth Amendment guarantees an accused effective cross-examination, especially to expose a witness's bias, and due process and compulsory process guarantee the right to present a defense, subject to reasonable limits on repetitive or marginally relevant questioning and legitimate procedural rules.

history: Dominant rule: courts uphold disability denials supported by substantial evidence, but in the Seventh Circuit the ALJ must articulate enough to let a court trace the reasoning. How it changed: Clifford (2000) anchors 2000-04 and 2005-09: ALJs must minimally articulate reasons and may not substitute their judgment for a physician's; Zurawski (2001) and Steele (2002) required specific credibility reasons. Parker (2010) anchors 2010-14 on rejecting boilerplate credibility findings and the Chenery bar; Craft (2008) required hypotheticals and RFCs to address mental limitations and the reasons for missed care, Villano (2009) required considering non-severe impairments, Terry (2009) allowed Reasoning Level 3 jobs for simple work, and Bjornson (2012) faulted unexplained skepticism of pain. name: Habeas appeal deadlines 2005-09: jurisdictional (Bowles) v. claim-processing
description: Federal habeas appellate procedure, 2005-09 only (anchor Rose v. Lee, 4th Cir. 2001), distinguished by timeliness: Browder (1978) and Bowles (2007) make statutory appeal deadlines jurisdictional, while Kontrick (2004) and Eberhart (2005) treat rule-based limits as forfeitable claim-processing rules; Pace (2005) limits AEDPA tolling. history: Dominant rule: Rose v. Lee (4th Cir. 2001), on when a state court's use of the wrong burden for Strickland prejudice is 'contrary to' federal law, anchors this single 2005-09 slice, but the leading cases concern how habeas appeals reach the court. Slack (2000) applies § 2253(c) to procedural dismissals and holds that refiling claims dismissed as unexhausted is not successive; Miller-El (2003) requires only that the claim be debatable among jurists. In the Fourth Circuit, Winestock (2003) treats Rule 60(b) motions attacking the conviction as successive petitions and Reid (2004) requires a COA to appeal a 60(b) denial. How it changed: timeliness doctrine sharpened. Browder (1978) and Robinson (1960) held appeal periods mandatory and jurisdictional; Kontrick (2004) and Eberhart (2005) then classed rule-based limits as forfeitable claim-processing rules; Bowles (2007) held statutory notice-of-appeal deadlines jurisdictional, with no unique-circumstances exception. Pace (2005) denied AEDPA tolling to untimely state petitions, while Irwin (1991) supports equitable tolling. Also: de novo review of objected-to magistrate findings (Thomas v. Arn, 1986). The slice splits in 2010-14 into tolling, standing and COA units.

name: Ohio abuse-of-discretion review (Blakemore, AAAA): plea withdrawal and Civ.R. 60(B)
description: Ohio abuse-of-discretion review, 2020-29: a decision is reversed only if unreasonable, arbitrary or unconscionable (Blakemore, 1983, anchor) or lacking a sound reasoning process (AAAA Enterprises, 1990), restated in Johnson v. Abdullah (2021). Common settings: plea withdrawal before (Xie, 1992) and after sentencing (Smith, 1977), Civ.R. 60(B) relief (GTE, 1976; Adams, 1988), custody allocation (Booth, 1989) and plain error in instructions (Adams, 1980).
history: Dominant rule: Ohio's abuse-of-discretion standard. Blakemore (1983) anchors both slices, 2020-24 and the partial 2025-29 slice, after a split from a lineage on Ohio civil appeals and family law: an abuse of discretion connotes a decision that is unreasonable, arbitrary or unconscionable, and AAAA Enterprises (1990) treats a decision as unreasonable when no sound reasoning process supports it. How it changed: the standard is stable; Johnson v. Abdullah (2021) enters in 2025-29 as the Ohio Supreme Court's restatement, and Weaver (2022) describes discretion as a choice among competing considerations. The settings: pre-sentence plea withdrawal, which is not an absolute right (Xie, 1992), and post-sentence withdrawal only for manifest injustice (Smith, 1977); Civ.R. 60(B) motions under the three-part GTE (1976) test, overruled if any element fails (Adams, 1988), with void judgments vacated under inherent authority (Patton, 1988); allocation of parental rights (Booth, 1989); same-day rulings that deny a party a chance to respond (Pons, 1993); and jury instructions, where omitting an element is not per se plain error (Adams, 1980). Also substitution of counsel (Jones, 2001) and capital-sentence review (Jenkins, 1984).

name: Sixth Circuit summary judgment in discrimination cases: Manzer pretext, Ercegovich
description: The 1986 summary-judgment trilogy (Anderson, Celotex, Matsushita) as the Sixth Circuit applies it to employment-discrimination claims (one slice, 2005-09): pretext is shown by proof that the employer's reason had no basis in fact, did not motivate it or was insufficient (Manzer 1994), comparators must be similar in relevant respects (Ercegovich 1998, Mitchell 1992), and temporal proximity can show retaliatory causation (DiCarlo 2004, Singfield 2004).

previous.description: Summary-judgment trilogy (Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Celotex, Matsushita) as applied by the Sixth Circuit in employment-discrimination pretext cases (Manzer, Wexler, Ercegovich, Mitchell v. Toledo Hospital) and prisoner medical-need claims.

history: Dominant rule: Anderson v. Liberty Lobby (1986) anchors the single 2005-09 slice with Celotex and Matsushita. A court asks whether a reasonable jury, applying the substantive burden of proof, could find for the nonmovant; a movant may point to the absence of evidence on an essential element; and the nonmovant must offer more than metaphysical doubt. How the Sixth Circuit applied it: Mitchell v. Toledo Hospital (1992) required comparators similarly situated and rejected subjective beliefs as evidence of pretext. Manzer (1994) set the three ways to show pretext and once required additional evidence of discrimination for the third; after Reeves (2000) a prima facie case and evidence of falsity can be enough. Ercegovich (1998) relaxed comparator rules to relevant aspects, and Smith v. Chrysler (1998) required an employer's honest belief to rest on particularized facts. Wexler (2003) focused the qualification prong on objective criteria. For retaliation, Nguyen (2000) left open causation from proximity alone, while DiCarlo (2004, 21 days) and Singfield (2004, three months) found it sufficient. Also: Jacklyn (1999) on materially adverse actions. The unit rejoins the McDonnell Douglas unit in 2010-14.
rule: Summary judgment is proper only if, viewing the evidence and justifiable inferences for the nonmovant, no reasonable jury could find for him (Anderson, Celotex, Matsushita); in Sixth Circuit discrimination cases a plaintiff shows pretext by evidence that the employer's reason had no basis in fact, did not actually motivate the action or was insufficient to warrant it (Manzer), using comparators similar in all relevant respects (Ercegovich).

changes.case: Mitchell v. Toledo Hospital; Manzer v. Diamond Shamrock

description: Federal Circuit review of MSPB jurisdiction, 2010-19: resignations and retirements are presumed voluntary unless objectively coerced, as by threatened unwarranted action or intolerable conditions (Shoaf, 2001; Staats, 1996, calling the doctrine narrow), and a jurisdictional hearing requires nonfrivolous allegations (Garcia en banc, 2006, anchoring both slices). history: Dominant rule: the MSPB hears appeals only from appealable actions, so a resignation or retirement is presumed voluntary and outside its jurisdiction unless the employee shows coercion, intolerable conditions or reasonable reliance on agency misinformation. Garcia (en banc 2006) anchors 2010-14 and 2015-19: nonfrivolous allegations entitle the employee to a jurisdictional hearing, jurisdiction must then be proved by preponderant evidence, and the Board does not reach discrimination claims without it. Staats (1996) calls involuntariness narrow, Terban (2000) holds that two unpleasant options do not make a choice involuntary, Shoaf (2001) recognises coercion by threatened adverse action, and Schultz (1987) found an immediate-resignation demand coercive. How it changed: in 2015-19 whistleblower and coverage cases weigh more. Johnston (2008) separates the nonfrivolous-allegation test for IRA jurisdiction from the merits, and Kahn (2008) bars allegations resting on speculation; Bolton (1998) defines supervisory status, and Forest (1995) limits excepted-service coverage. Kloeckner (2012) enters in 2010-14 on mixed-case review. Also: good cause for late filing (Mendoza, 1992) and the coverage limits of 5 U.S.C. § 6323 (Welshans, 2008).

name: New Jersey suppression review: deference to findings (Elders, Johnson)
description: New Jersey's appellate standard for suppression rulings (a review rule, not a search doctrine): findings stand if supported by sufficient credible evidence unless clearly mistaken (State v. Johnson 1964; Elders 2007, anchor of every slice); legal conclusions are de novo (Gamble 2014). S.S. (2017) extended deference to video-based findings; Witt (2015) dropped exigency from the automobile exception, Gonzales (2016) plain-view inadvertence.

history: Dominant rule: an appellate court defers to a suppression judge's findings supported by sufficient credible evidence and disturbs them only when so clearly mistaken that justice demands it (State v. Johnson, 1964; Locurto, 1999; Elders, 2007, the anchor in all four slices); the law and its application are reviewed de novo (Gamble, 2014). How it changed: S.S. (2017) applied that deference to findings based on video recordings, and Hubbard (2015) to custody findings. On the merits, Carty (2002) required reasonable suspicion before asking for consent to search a stopped car; Witt (2015) returned to an automobile exception without an exigency requirement; Gonzales (2016) removed inadvertence from plain view. Stops rest on reasonable, articulable suspicion judged on the totality (Davis 1986, Stovall 2002, Pineiro 2004), and the odor of marijuana supplied probable cause (Nishina 2003). Also: juvenile and Miranda waivers (Presha, A.M.), emergency aid (Edmonds) and detentions after a completed stop (Chisum, Rosario).
rule: On review of a suppression ruling, a New Jersey appellate court upholds the trial judge's findings if sufficient credible evidence in the record supports them and reverses only if they are so clearly mistaken that justice demands correction, while reviewing legal conclusions de novo (Elders; State v. name: Uncounseled convictions and actual imprisonment, 1980-84: Scott, Baldasar, Lewis
description: Limits on the indigent right to counsel and on uncounseled convictions, a single 1980-84 slice anchored by Gideon (1963): Scott (1979) confined Argersinger (1972) to cases of actual imprisonment, and Baldasar and Lewis (1980) split on whether an uncounseled or invalid prior may enhance a later sentence or serve as a predicate, against Burgett (1967) and Tucker (1972). history: Dominant rule: the Sixth Amendment, applied to the states by Gideon (1963), guarantees appointed counsel to an indigent who is actually imprisoned, and convictions obtained without counsel have limited further use. Gideon anchors the single 1980-84 slice, with Powell (1932), Hamilton (1961), and the equal-access cases Griffin (1956) and Douglas (1963). How it changed: Argersinger (1972) extended the right to misdemeanors carrying jail, and Scott (1979) held that only actual imprisonment, not authorized imprisonment, triggers it. Burgett (1967), Tucker (1972) and Loper (1972) barred the use of uncounseled convictions to convict, sentence or impeach; Baldasar (1980) barred using an uncounseled misdemeanor to enhance a later sentence, while Lewis (1980) allowed an invalid felony conviction as a firearms-statute predicate. Herring (1975) and Geders (1976) treated denial of closing argument and of overnight consultation as reversible without prejudice, while Morrison (1981) required tailored remedies. The unit then splits into the 1980-99 counsel and waiver lineage.
rule: An indigent defendant may not be sentenced to imprisonment without appointed counsel or a valid waiver (actual imprisonment, not the authorized penalty, triggers the right), and convictions obtained in violation of that right have limited later use.

name: Texas multiple-punishment double jeopardy: Blockburger and legislative intent (Ervin)
description: Texas multiple-punishment double jeopardy: Blockburger's elements test (1931) and Brown's greater/lesser rule (1977) yield to legislative intent (Hunter, 1983), which Texas measures by the Ervin factors (1999) and the allowable unit of prosecution (Cavazos, 2006: one burglary per entry). Dixon (1993) ended same-conduct analysis; Bigon (2008) keeps the most serious conviction. Later slices add retrial and mistrial rules (Pearce, Arizona v. Washington).

previous.name: Double jeopardy in Texas (2005-2025)
previous.description: Multiple-punishment double jeopardy in Texas courts: Blockburger elements analysis, legislative intent and allowable units of prosecution (Ex parte Cavazos, Ervin, Bigon, Langs), and Brown v. Ohio greater/lesser offenses.

history: Dominant rule: whether two Texas convictions punish the same offense. Blockburger (1931) anchors every slice but 2015-19, when Brown (1977) does: offenses are different if each requires proof of an element the other does not, and a lesser included offense is the same as the greater. Hunter (1983) and Whalen (1980) make that a rule of construction that yields to clear legislative intent. How it changed: Dixon (1993) overruled Grady's same-conduct test. The Court of Criminal Appeals then put legislative intent first: Ervin (1999) set the factors, Gonzalez (2000) limited first-time appellate claims to violations clear on the record, Ex parte Cavazos (2006) held the unit of burglary is the entry and overruled Landers on choosing the most serious offense, and Bigon (2008) set the remedy. Units of prosecution in sexual-assault statutes follow (Vick, 1999; Patterson, 2004; Aekins, 2014), with Benson (2015) and Shelby (2014) on intoxication offenses. Also: from 2010-14, successive-prosecution, implied-acquittal and mistrial rules (Green, 1957; Arizona v. Washington, 1978; Ashe, 1970) and Pearce (1969) on harsher sentences after retrial.
rule: Two convictions for the same conduct violate double jeopardy only if the legislature did not intend multiple punishments, judged first by Blockburger's elements test and then by the Ervin factors and the allowable unit of prosecution; the remedy is to keep the most serious conviction and vacate the other.

changes.what: In a single trial Blockburger is a rule of statutory construction that yields to clearly expressed legislative intent to punish cumulatively.
Overruled Grady v. Corbin's same-conduct test; the same-elements test alone governs.

Legislative intent is the ultimate question, so Blockburger cannot authorise two punishments where the legislature intended one; manslaughter and intoxication manslaughter of one victim are the same offense.
A multiple-punishment claim must be raised at trial unless the violation is clearly apparent on the face of the record and default serves no legitimate interest.

changes.case: Ex parte Cavazos; Langs v. State
changes.what: One burglary conviction per unlawful entry, not per complainant; the most serious offense is the one with the greatest sentence assessed, overruling Landers' wider factors.
The remedy for a multiple-punishment violation is to affirm the most serious conviction and vacate the others, and the claim may be raised first on appeal when apparent on the record.

history: Dominant rule: a case may be removed on a federal question only when federal law appears in the well-pleaded complaint. history: Dominant rule: the reasonable-doubt requirement as enforced through jury-instruction claims, filtered by harmless-error review. Sandstrom (1979) anchors both slices, with Chapman (1967) the most-cited case. Winship (1970) and Mullaney (1975) require proof of every element, while Patterson (1977) allows States to assign affirmative defenses that do not negate elements. How it changed: in 1985-89 Sandstrom held that a presumption of intent from ordinary consequences shifts the burden; Connecticut v. Johnson (1983) split on harmlessness; Francis v. Franklin (1985) reaffirmed Sandstrom; Rose v. Clark (1986) applied Chapman review; Hasting (1983) treated comment on silence (Griffin, 1965) as subject to harmless error. In 1990-94 Fulminante (1991) separated trial error from structural defects, Cage (1990) and Sullivan (1993) treated a defective reasonable-doubt instruction as structural, Yates (1991) and Estelle v. McGuire (1991) refined instruction review, and Brecht (1993) brought Kotteakos's (1946) standard to habeas. Also: Doyle (1976) on post-Miranda silence and Van Arsdall (1986) on cross-examination.
rule: A jury instruction that shifts to the defendant the burden on an element, such as a presumption that a person intends the ordinary consequences of his acts, violates the reasonable-doubt requirement (Winship; Sandstrom), but most such constitutional errors are reviewed for harmlessness (Chapman; Rose v. Clark), under Brecht's substantial-and-injurious-effect standard on habeas.

description: Compelled union fees: nonmembers may be charged for collective bargaining but not over objection for political activity (Street 1961; Abood 1977), with Hudson (1986) procedures of notice, impartial review and escrow, extended to the NLRA (Beck 1988) and bar dues (Keller 1990). history: Dominant rule: objecting nonmembers can be made to pay only for a union's collective-bargaining functions, not its ideological activities, under procedures that protect their objection. Ellis classified chargeable expenses and Hudson required adequate notice, an impartial decision-maker and escrow. Sipes (1967) anchors and the unit becomes duty of fair representation and § 1981 limitations law (DelCostello, O'Neill, Wilson v. Garcia). Janus (2018) overruled Abood after the lineage ends.

description: Federal habeas review of state convictions: procedural defaults bar review absent cause and prejudice (Wainwright v. Sykes, 1977, anchor 1980-89; Murray, 1986; Coleman, 1991, finishing off Fay v. Noia). After AEDPA (1996), § 2254(d) deference dominates: Williams v. history: Dominant rule: the gatekeeping of federal habeas. Through the 1990s it is procedural default: Wainwright v. Sykes (1977), anchoring 1980-84 and 1985-89, replaced Fay v. Noia's (1963) deliberate-bypass test with cause and prejudice. Engle (1982) denied cause for novel claims, Rose v. Lundy (1982) required total exhaustion, Frady (1982) extended the rules to § 2255, and Murray v. Carrier (1986), the 1990-94 anchor, required an external cause. Coleman (1991), the 1995-99 anchor, overruled Fay's remaining rule and denied cause for collateral-counsel error, and Schlup (1995) set the actual-innocence gateway. How it changed: AEDPA (1996), applied to post-enactment petitions by Lindh (1997), made deference the rule. Williams v. Taylor (2000) anchors 2000-04 through 2010-14: relief only if the state decision was contrary to or an unreasonable application of Supreme Court holdings; Lockyer (2003) stressed objective unreasonableness, and Brecht (1993) set habeas harmless error. Harrington and Cullen (2011) tightened review to fairminded disagreement on the state record; Harrington anchors 2015-19. In 2020-24 the anchor is Slack (2000), as COA and Rule 60(b) cases (Gonzalez, 2005; Buck, 2017) merge in.
rule: A federal court may not grant habeas relief on a claim the state courts rejected on an adequate procedural ground absent cause and prejudice or a miscarriage of justice (Sykes, Coleman), and on a claim adjudicated on the merits only if the decision was contrary to, or an objectively unreasonable application of, clearly established Supreme Court law (§ 2254(d); Williams v. Taylor; Harrington).

description: Delaware contract interpretation from 2020-24, after small mixed pleading slices in 2010-19 (Savor 2002, Central Mortgage 2011, Spence 1978): Kemp (2010) anchors objective interpretation: plain meaning in the context of the whole agreement, every term given effect, ambiguity only when fairly susceptible of different meanings (Rhone-Poulenc 1992), and a narrow implied covenant (Nemec 2010).

history: Dominant rule: Delaware follows the objective theory of contracts. How it changed: in 2010-14 Savor (2002) anchors a small slice of pleading cases, with Central Mortgage (2011) and Price (2011: conclusory allegations need not be accepted); in 2015-19 Spence (1978, defamation damages) anchors and Nemec (2010) and Abry Partners (2006) enter. From 2020-24 contract interpretation takes over and Kemp (2010) anchors through 2025-29: every term must be given effect and absurd readings rejected. A contract is ambiguous only if fairly susceptible of different meanings (Rhone-Poulenc, 1992), extrinsic evidence cannot create ambiguity (Eagle, 1997), courts are bound by the words and their plain meaning (Lorillard, 2006), give priority to the four corners (GMG Capital, 2012) and read the overall structure (Salamone, 2014). The implied covenant is narrow (Nemec 2010) and cannot avoid plain language (Allied Capital, 2006); a duty not to minimize earn-outs implies none to maximize them (Winshall, 2013). Also: pleading breach (VLIW 2003) and fraud's duty to disclose (Abry Partners 2006).
rule: Delaware courts read a contract objectively by the plain meaning of its words in the context of the whole agreement, giving every term effect, finding ambiguity only where provisions are fairly susceptible of different meanings, and using the implied covenant only narrowly to fill gaps.

round1.history: Dominant rule: Delaware follows the objective theory of contracts. round1.rule: Delaware courts enforce an unambiguous contract by the plain meaning of its terms read as a whole, giving every term effect and admitting extrinsic evidence only if the language is reasonably susceptible of more than one meaning, and the implied covenant of good faith fills only true gaps and never overrides express terms.

name: Fifth Circuit conspiracy trials, 1975-79: Glasser, Falcone, joint representation
description: Fifth Circuit (and other federal) multi-defendant conspiracy trials in 1975-79, on proof of knowing membership and counsel conflicts: the verdict stands on substantial evidence viewed for the Government (Glasser, 1942, anchor), but mere knowledge or association does not prove conspiracy (Falcone, 1940). Severance needs compelling prejudice (Perez, 1974), and joint representation with a conflict denies counsel (Foster, 1972; Holloway, 1978).
history: Dominant rule: in multi-defendant conspiracy trials a conviction stands if substantial evidence, taken most favourably to the Government, supports a reasonable inference of the defendant's knowing participation (Glasser, 1942, the anchor of the single 1975-79 slice), while mere knowledge, presence or casual meetings are not enough (Falcone, 1940; Apollo, 1973). How it changed: no change within the one slice. The cases address severance, which requires compelling prejudice (Perez, 1974), coconspirator statements that need independent proof of membership (Oliva, 1974), juror influence (Tillman, 1969), and conflicts of interest in joint representation: Foster (1972) put the burden on the government where no inquiry was made, and Holloway (1978) presumed prejudice when counsel was made to represent conflicting clients over objection. Also: single versus multiple conspiracies (Marionneaux, 1975). The lineage splits in 1980-84, partly into an Eleventh Circuit unit adopting former Fifth Circuit precedent.
rule: A conspiracy conviction stands if substantial evidence, viewed most favourably to the Government, supports a reasonable inference of the defendant's knowing participation (Glasser), mere knowledge or presence not being enough (Falcone), and a conflict from joint representation violates the right to counsel.

name: Texas negligence: existence of a duty as a question of law (Phillips, Otis)
description: Texas negligence law, 1990-99: the plaintiff must prove a duty, breach and proximate cause, and duty is a question of law (Poole 1987, anchor 1990-94; Phillips 1991, anchor 1995-99). Duties turn on control and foreseeability (Otis 1983 employer control; Redinger 1985 contractors). Doe and Allbritton (1995) rejected speculative causation; premises claims require knowledge of the condition (Corbin 1983, Keetch 1992).
history: Dominant rule: a Texas negligence plaintiff must establish a duty, its breach and damages proximately caused, and the existence of a duty is a question of law. Poole (1987), the anchor in 1990-94, states the burden and lets a penal statute set the standard of care. Otis Engineering (1983) recognised a duty arising from an employer's control over an incapacitated employee, and Redinger (1985) imposed a duty on a general contractor that retains control over a subcontractor's work. How it changed: Phillips (1991) anchors 1995-99, weighing foreseeability of third-party crime as part of duty; Walker (1996) found an apartment stabbing unforeseeable. Doe v. Boys Clubs (1995) and Allbritton (1995) tightened proximate cause against speculation and mere furnishing of a condition, and Bird (1994) denied a psychologist's duty to a third party. Premises liability requires knowledge of the condition (Corbin 1983) and is distinct from negligent activity (Keetch 1992); Tidwell (1993) addresses workplace safety. Alongside: summary-judgment burdens (Siegler 1995) and preservation, limiting review to grounds presented below (Travis 1992, Bushell 1991).
rule: A Texas negligence plaintiff must prove a duty owed by the defendant, a breach and proximate cause; whether a duty exists is a question of law turning on foreseeability, control and the relationship of the parties.

changes.what: An employer that exercises control over an incapacitated employee owes a duty to others on the road.

changes.case: Corbin v. Safeway; Keetch v. Kroger
changes.what: Premises liability requires actual or constructive knowledge of the condition; a slip on a condition, rather than ongoing activity, is a premises claim.
A general contractor who retains control over a subcontractor's work owes a duty of reasonable care in exercising it.

changes.case: Greater Houston Transportation Co. v. Phillips
changes.what: Duty is a question of law; one prior incident in twenty years did not make an employee's criminal act foreseeable.

changes.case: Doe v. Boys Clubs of Greater Dallas; Union Pump v. Allbritton
changes.what: Proximate cause cannot rest on conjecture, and conduct that merely furnishes the condition for the injury is not a legal cause.

description: Fifth Circuit Rule 52(b) review of unpreserved sentencing and plea errors, 2010-24, with Puckett (2009) the anchor in every slice. history: Dominant rule: Puckett (2009), which anchors every slice from 2010-14 to 2020-24, restated Olano's (1993) four-prong test for forfeited error. How it changed: the unit forms from 2005-09 Booker plain-error groups. Peltier (2007) held that failure to object to a sentence's reasonableness triggers plain-error review, Mondragon-Santiago (2009) required a showing that more explanation would have changed a within-range sentence, and Duarte and Cooks (2009) kept the presumption of reasonableness after Kimbrough and narrowed substantive challenges; Gomez-Herrera (2008) rejected benign-motive reentry arguments. In 2015-19 Molina-Martinez (2016) held that a miscalculated range ordinarily shows a reasonable probability of prejudice, and Rosales-Mireles (2018) held that such errors ordinarily satisfy the fourth prong, rejecting the Fifth Circuit's more demanding standards. Holguin-Hernandez (2020) held that arguing for a lower sentence preserves a reasonableness claim (knowledge, abrogating Peltier). In 2020-24 Rehaif (2019) made knowledge of status an element of § 922(g), and Greer (2021) required defendants on plain error to show they would have disputed that knowledge.
rule: An unpreserved error is corrected under Rule 52(b) only if there is an error that is clear or obvious, that affected substantial rights (a reasonable probability of a different outcome), and that seriously affects the fairness, integrity or public reputation of judicial proceedings, the last prong being discretionary.

name: Title VII disparate impact and pattern-or-practice: Griggs, Albemarle, Teamsters
description: Systemic Title VII litigation in 1980-89: Albemarle (1975) anchors both slices, requiring validated, job-related selection devices and presumptive back pay under Griggs's (1971) disparate-impact rule. Teamsters and Hazelwood (1977) govern statistical pattern-or-practice proof and Franks (1976) classwide seniority relief. history: Dominant rule: Albemarle Paper v. Moody (1975) anchors both slices. Under Griggs (1971), a neutral practice with disparate impact needs business necessity; Albemarle demands validation that the test predicts job performance and makes back pay presumptive. How it developed: Teamsters (1977) and Hazelwood (1977) let plaintiffs prove a pattern or practice through gross statistical disparities measured against the qualified labor pool, and Franks (1976) presumes class members were victims and allows retroactive seniority. Pettway (1974) allows classwide back-pay formulas. Dothard (1977) applied disparate impact to height and weight rules and read the BFOQ narrowly, Manhart (1978) barred sex-based pension contributions, and Teal (1982) rejected the bottom-line defense. Congress reversed Gilbert's (1976) pregnancy ruling in 1978. In 1985-89 Teamsters leads, and statistical proof is refined: Segar (1984) requires comparison of similarly qualified workers and Griffin v. Carlin (1985) applies impact analysis to a multicomponent process, and Bazemore (1986) treats omitted regression variables as going to weight. The unit merges into the McDonnell Douglas unit in 1990-94.

name: Mississippi heinousness aggravator after Shell and Clemons (2005-09 slice)
description: A one-slice (2005-09) Mississippi capital sub-cluster on a single question, the 'heinous, atrocious or cruel' aggravator: Shell v. Mississippi (1990) held the limiting instruction too vague, Clemons (1990) let appellate courts reweigh or find harmlessness, and on remand Shell and Clemons (1992) required new sentencing. Willie (1991) barred double-counting aggravators. Also mercy instructions (Goodin 2001), Batson and prosecutorial argument (Flowers 2003).
history: Dominant rule: the Eighth Amendment requires that Mississippi juries considering the 'heinous, atrocious or cruel' aggravator receive a limiting instruction that actually narrows it. Shell v. State (1989), anchor of the single slice (2005-09), approved photographs on heinousness, but Shell v. Mississippi (1990) held the limiting instruction used, defining the terms in equally vague words, unconstitutional. Pinkney (1988) had required a concrete instruction, and Pinkney (1992) treated the Coleman formulation as approved. How it changed: Clemons v. Mississippi (1990) allowed state appellate courts to reweigh or apply harmless-error review after striking an aggravator. On remand, Clemons (1992) sent the case to a jury because the court lacked authority to resentence, later superseded by statute; Shell (1992) and Jones (1992) found the error not harmless and remanded. Willie (1991) barred doubly weighing the underlying felony and its motive and overruled Jones (1987) in part. Manning (1999) held sufficiency review of aggravators is statutory and not procedurally barred. Alongside: mercy instructions (Goodin 2001, King 2001), Batson review (Walker 2002, Berry 2001, Snow 2001), confrontation (Balfour 1992) and plain-error review of argument (Flowers 2003).

changes.what: A limiting instruction defining heinousness in equally vague terms is insufficient; state appellate courts may reweigh or conduct harmless-error review after invalidating an aggravator.

name: Heck favorable-termination bar, 2005-09, with Bivens limits alongside
description: Anchored on Heck v. name: Multistate Jackson v. Virginia sufficiency, 2020-24 (La., Ga., Tex.; Davenport)
description: A one-slice (2020-24) multistate mix applying the federal Jackson v. Louisiana adds Captville and Hearold (1992, review all evidence); Georgia's Davenport (2020) ended routine sua sponte sufficiency review and Lane (2020) required cumulative error review; Texas adds Queeman (2017). history: Dominant rule: Jackson v. Louisiana cases supply the circumstantial-evidence gloss (Captville 1984: once the jury rejects the defendant's hypothesis of innocence, guilt follows unless another reasonable hypothesis remains; Mussall 1988) and Hearold (1992: sufficiency is judged on all the evidence). Texas adds Queeman (2017) on criminal negligence. How it changed: Georgia's Davenport (2020) ended routine sua sponte sufficiency review in non-capital cases, and Lane (2020) required cumulative assessment of trial errors. Alongside: Georgia harmless-error and other-acts rulings (Kirby 2018, Olds 2016, Jackson 2019). The lineage splits back into Texas sufficiency in 2025-29.

name: Multistate IAC procedure, 2025-29: Machner hearings, Arizona Rule 32, Cronic
description: State procedure for ineffective-assistance claims across several states in the partial 2025-29 slice, not one state's law: Strickland (1984, anchor) applied with Wisconsin's Machner (1979) hearing requirement, Arizona Rule 32 waiver and findings (Bennett, 2006; Pandeli, 2017), Illinois postconviction and forfeiture rules, and Braswell (N.C. 1985); Cronic (1984) and McCoy (2018) mark when prejudice is presumed or not required.

name: Early post-Booker reasonableness review and limits on extraordinary variances (2005-06)
description: Circuit reasonableness review in 2005-06, led by the Eighth Circuit (Haack, the anchor of this one-slice 2005-09 lineage; Mashek, Dalton, Saenz) with the Seventh (Mykytiuk, Dean) and Fourth (Moreland, Green): correct Guidelines first, within-range sentences presumed reasonable, and extraordinary variances rejected as unreasonable. history: Dominant rule: right after Booker, circuits built reasonableness review on the old departure standard. Haack (8th Cir. 2005) anchors this single 2005-09 slice, defining abuse of discretion and adopting Crosby's account of post-Booker fact-finding; Mashek (2005) and Green (4th Cir. 2006) required remand for any Guidelines miscalculation regardless of reasonableness. How it changed: the Seventh Circuit in Mykytiuk (2005) and the Eighth in Lincoln (2005) presumed within-range sentences reasonable, and Montes-Pineda (2006) put the burden on the defendant to show unreasonableness. Dean and Cunningham (7th Cir. 2005) set a moderate duty of explanation, and Johnson (2006) held that courts need not tick through every factor. The Eighth Circuit then tested variances by their size: Dalton (2005) and Saenz (2005) struck departures of 75% and 68% as extraordinary and unjustified, and Moreland (4th Cir. 2006) allowed substantive review for improper factors or rejection of Commission policy. Martinez-Martinez (2006) treated fast-track disparity as one non-controlling factor. Gall (2007) rejected the proportionality approach, and the lineage splits in 2010-14 into reasonableness review and Seventh Circuit plea-error lines.
rule: In the first post-Booker years, circuits reviewed sentences for reasonableness under an abuse-of-discretion standard after a correct Guidelines calculation, presumed within-range sentences reasonable, and required that the further a sentence varied from the range, the more compelling the justification, rejecting extraordinary variances or departures as unreasonable.

changes.case: United States v. Dean; United States v. Cunningham (7th Cir.)
changes.what: No mechanical recital of every § 3553(a) factor is required, but the judge must state adequate reasons and address principal mitigation arguments.

changes.case: United States v. Dalton; United States v. Saenz (8th Cir.)
changes.what: Very large downward departures or variances (75%, 68%) were held extraordinary and unreasonable absent extraordinary justification.

changes.case: United States v. Moreland; United States v. Green (4th Cir.)
changes.what: A sentence based on misapplied Guidelines is unreasonable, and one may be substantively unreasonable if it rests on improper factors or rejects congressional or Commission policy.
Rejected appellate rules requiring extraordinary circumstances or proportional justification for variances, displacing the Dalton and Saenz approach.

name: Tax substance over form: economic substance, shelters and penalties
description: Substance over form in federal tax: transactions without economic substance are disregarded (Gregory v. Helvering 1935; Frank Lyon 1978, anchor 2005-14; Coltec 2006; Klamath 2009). history: Dominant rule: the economic reality of a transaction, not its form, determines its tax treatment. How it changed: Frank Lyon (1978) anchors 2005-14 with Gregory v. name: Sex-offender registration as punishment: Smith v. Doe's intent-effects test
description: Whether sex-offender registration and related restrictions are punishment: a scheme the legislature labelled civil stays civil unless its effects are so punitive as to override that intent, under the Mendoza-Martinez factors (Smith v. history: Dominant rule: the intent-effects test for whether a civil regulatory scheme is criminal punishment. Smith v. How it changed: within the slice, state courts departed from Smith under their own constitutions: the Ohio Supreme Court in Williams (2011) held that the amended registration scheme was punitive as applied to earlier offenders, and Starkey (Okla. 2013) held a retroactive extension of the registration period invalid. Illinois cases, including In re J.W. (2003) on juvenile registration and residence restrictions, and Malchow (2000), upheld their scheme. Also: Illinois Second Amendment cases on the aggravated unlawful use of a weapon statute (Aguilar, 2014; Mosley, 2015) merged in from a 2010-14 unit.
rule: A sex-offender registration or commitment law is civil, and so escapes ex post facto and other punishment limits, unless the legislature meant it to punish or its effects are so punitive as to negate the civil intent, judged by the Mendoza-Martinez factors (Smith v. Doe; Hendricks).

changes.case: Strauder v. West Virginia; Ex parte Virginia; Virginia v. Rives; Neal v. Delaware
changes.what: A statute limiting jury service to white men violates equal protection, and officials who exclude Black jurors act for the State; Strauder anchors 1925-34.

changes.case: Norris v. Alabama; Pierre v. Louisiana; Smith v. Texas; Hill v. Texas
changes.what: Long-continued total exclusion establishes a prima facie case whatever the mechanism, and grand-jury discrimination voids an indictment; Norris anchors 1935-49 and 1955-59.

changes.case: Cassell v. Texas; Avery v. Georgia; Hernandez v. Texas
changes.what: Token limits on Black jurors and racially marked selection violate equal protection without a harmless-error inquiry, and Mexican-Americans are a protected class.

changes.case: Swain v. Alabama; Whitus v. Georgia; Alexander v. Louisiana; Peters v. Kiff
changes.what: Swain demanded proof of strikes over many cases, while Whitus and Alexander found prima facie cases from statistical disparity plus opportunity to discriminate; Peters let a white defendant challenge exclusion of Black jurors.

changes.case: Taylor v. Louisiana; Castaneda v. Partida; Duren v. Missouri
changes.what: The Sixth Amendment fair-cross-section requirement bars systematic exclusion of women, Duren sets a three-part prima facie test, and Castaneda accepts standard-deviation proof; Duren anchors 1980-89.

distinct_from.how: Spans 1925-84 and ends in the Sixth Amendment fair-cross-section test (Taylor, Duren); the cluster is a 1965-74 snapshot anchored by Smith v. Texas and Glasser.

history: Dominant rule: termination requires a § 2511(a) ground proved by clear and convincing evidence and, separately, a § 2511(b) finding that termination best serves the child's needs and welfare (C.L.G., 2008). How it changed: B.L.W. (2004) anchors 2010-14 and 2015-19: affirmance on any one (a) subsection plus (b). Leading cases refine each step: K.Z.S. (2008) on missed visits and addiction, Z.P. (2010) allowing caseworker evidence of bonds, S.P. rule: Involuntary termination under 23 Pa.C.S. § 2511 requires a § 2511(a) ground proved by clear and convincing evidence and then a separate § 2511(b) finding, weighing any parent-child bond, that termination best serves the child's needs and welfare.

changes.what: The Superior Court may affirm on any one § 2511(a) subsection together with § 2511(b); anchors 2010-14 and 2015-19.
Needs and welfare under § 2511(a)(8) and § 2511(b) are separate inquiries, addressed in turn.
Section 2511(b) does not require a formal bonding evaluation; caseworkers may give opinions on the bond.
Incarceration is relevant to parental incapacity under § 2511(a)(2).
Courts weigh the bond against the child's need for permanence and stability; anchors from 2020-24.
A child has a statutory right to counsel in contested involuntary termination proceedings.

How it changed: the small 2000-04 and 2005-09 slices, anchored by Atencio (1994) and R.J.S. round1.rule: Involuntary termination under 23 Pa.C.S. § 2511 requires clear and convincing proof of a ground under subsection (a), after which the court considers under subsection (b) the child's developmental, physical and emotional needs and welfare, including the parent-child bond, with affirmance if any one (a) ground and (b) are supported.

changes.case: In re Julissa O.; In re B.L.L.
changes.what: A parent must work affirmatively toward reunification, and under the Adoption and Safe Families Act a child's needs are not held in abeyance indefinitely.
The appellate court need agree with the orphans' court on only one subsection of § 2511(a), plus § 2511(b), to affirm.
Section 2511(b) does not require a formal bonding evaluation; caseworkers may assess the bond.
Incarceration is relevant to, and can be determinative of, incapacity under § 2511(a)(2); abandonment case law under (a)(1) does not control.
The (b) inquiry weighs the bond's character and the harm of severing it, together with the child's bond with foster parents and need for permanence.

name: Jurisdictional vs claim-processing time limits (Kontrick, Arbaugh, Bowles)
description: Single-slice (2005-09) unit on when deadlines are jurisdictional. Kontrick (2004), Eberhart (2005) and Arbaugh (2006) treat rule-based and non-clearly-stated limits as forfeitable claim-processing rules; Bowles (2007) held statutory appeal deadlines jurisdictional and ended the unique-circumstances exception. Irwin (1991) presumes equitable tolling against the government, limited by Brockamp, Beggerly and John R. Sand (2008).
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Claim-processing rules and tolling against the government (2005-09)
previous.description: Mid-2000s cases sorting jurisdictional limits from claim-processing rules (Kontrick, Eberhart, Arbaugh, Bowles, Zipes, John R. Sand & Gravel) and deciding when time limits allow equitable tolling against the government (Irwin, Brockamp, Beggerly, Kubrick).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session subagents, from cocite evidence; second pass differentiated near-duplicates)

history: Dominant rule: a time or filing requirement is jurisdictional only if Congress clearly ranks it so; other limits are claim-processing rules that a party forfeits by not raising them. The unit exists only in 2005-09, anchored by Kontrick (2004). How it changed: Zipes (1982) had held Title VII's charge deadline non-jurisdictional, and Kontrick (2004), Scarborough (2004), Eberhart (2005) and Arbaugh (2006, the clear-statement test) generalised the point. Bowles (2007) carved out statutory deadlines for taking an appeal, relying on their long treatment as jurisdictional, and overruled the unique-circumstances doctrine of Thompson (1964) and Harris Truck Lines (1962). Also: equitable tolling against the government. Irwin (1991) presumed tolling is available, but Brockamp (1997) and Beggerly (1998) refused it for § 6511 and the Quiet Title Act, and John R. Sand & Gravel (2008) held the Tucker Act limit jurisdictional. Kubrick (1979) on FTCA accrual rounds out the set. The unit splits in 2010-14 toward PLRA exhaustion and jurisdictional rules.
rule: A filing or time requirement limits a court's jurisdiction only when Congress clearly says so (or long statutory treatment makes it so); otherwise it is a forfeitable claim-processing rule, and limitations periods against the government are presumptively subject to equitable tolling unless the statute shows otherwise.

changes.case: Irwin v. Department of Veterans Affairs
changes.what: Rebuttable presumption that equitable tolling applies to suits against the United States as to private defendants.

changes.case: United States v. Brockamp; United States v. Beggerly
changes.what: No equitable tolling for tax-refund limits under § 6511 or the Quiet Title Act's 12-year period.

changes.case: Kontrick v. Ryan; Eberhart v. United States; Arbaugh v. Y & H Corp.
changes.what: Court-made rule deadlines are claim-processing rules subject to forfeiture, and a statutory element is jurisdictional only if Congress clearly states it.
Statutory appeal deadlines are jurisdictional; the 'unique circumstances' exception of Thompson and Harris Truck Lines was overruled.

changes.case: John R. Sand & Gravel Co. v. United States
changes.what: The Tucker Act's six-year limit (28 U.S.C. § 2501) is jurisdictional and not subject to waiver or tolling.

name: Mandamus over discovery and privilege orders, 2000-04 (Kerr, Allied Chemical)
description: Mandamus as the route to interlocutory review of discovery and privilege orders, in a single 2000-04 slice: Kerr (1976, anchor) and Allied Chemical (1980) confine the writ to clear and indisputable rights; the collateral-order cases (Cohen 1949, Livesay 1978, Digital Equipment 1994, Swint 1995, Cunningham 1999) mark the narrow alternative, and privilege cases (Nixon 1974, Upjohn 1981, Jaffee 1996) supply the rulings at issue.
history: Dominant rule: discovery and privilege rulings are ordinarily reviewed after final judgment (Catlin 1945); immediate review comes only through Cohen's (1949) collateral-order doctrine or mandamus. Kerr (1976) anchors the single 2000-04 slice: mandamus is drastic, reserved for extraordinary cases, and a petitioner must show a clear and indisputable right (Allied Chemical 1980), so that it cannot substitute for appeal (Steelworkers 1979). How it changed: the slice merges the 1995-99 collateral-order unit, bringing Livesay (1978), Abney (1977), Digital Equipment (1994) and Swint (1995), and Cunningham (1999), which denied immediate appeal of attorney sanctions. Privilege cases join as the rulings for which mandamus is sought: Nixon (1974) on executive privilege, Upjohn (1981) on corporate attorney-client communications, Jaffee (1996) recognizing a psychotherapist privilege, and Ford Motor (8th Cir. 1997) allowing mandamus for compelled disclosure of privileged documents. Also: presidential immunity (Nixon v. Fitzgerald 1982, Clinton v. Jones 1997) and recusal for personal bias (Beard 1987). The unit splits in 2005-09; Mohawk (2009) later denied collateral-order appeal of privilege orders.
rule: Interlocutory orders, including discovery and privilege rulings, are reviewable before final judgment only under Cohen's narrow collateral-order doctrine or by mandamus, a drastic remedy requiring a clear and indisputable right and no other adequate means of relief.

changes.case: Catlin v. United States; Cohen v. Beneficial Industrial Loan
changes.what: Only decisions ending the litigation are final, save a small class of collateral orders.

changes.case: Kerr v. U.S. District Court; Allied Chemical v. Daiflon
changes.what: Mandamus is reserved for extraordinary situations; a discretionary ruling cannot give a clear and indisputable right, and privilege claims can usually await in camera review.

changes.case: United States v. Nixon; Upjohn Co. v. United States
changes.what: Executive privilege yields to a specific need for evidence in a criminal trial; the attorney-client privilege covers corporate employees' communications with counsel.

changes.case: Digital Equipment v. Desktop Direct; Swint v. Chambers County; Cunningham v. Hamilton County
changes.what: The collateral-order exception is read narrowly, pendent appellate jurisdiction is limited, and Rule 37 sanctions on attorneys are not immediately appealable.

changes.case: Jaffee v. Redmond; In re Ford Motor Co. (8th Cir.)
changes.what: Federal courts recognized a psychotherapist privilege, and orders compelling production of privileged documents may support mandamus.

written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, round 2 after the lineage re-link)

V. 1996, B. D. 1999).

previous.description: Georgia Court of Appeals juvenile deprivation and termination cases: binding effect of earlier unappealed deprivation findings and the rational-trier standard after Santosky (Blackburn).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, contrastive pass from family evidence)

history: Dominant rule: termination requires clear and convincing evidence of present parental misconduct or inability causing deprivation that is likely to continue, reviewed under Blackburn (1982), which in light of Santosky asks whether a rational trier of fact could find the standard met. How it changed: R. N. (1997) anchors 1995-99, approving a juvenile court's concern for the stability of children bounced between foster and parental homes, with T. B. R. (1997, credibility and abandonment), J. M. C. (1991, recent progress against a long history of incarceration), D. I. W. (1994) and G. K. J. (1988, no bare recitals of misconduct). V. S. (1997) anchors 2000-04, construing the prior Juvenile Code's procedures for disposition orders, as N. J. W. (1998), B. D. (1999, evidence a year or two old is pertinent) and J. J. W. (2001, no search for relative placement) enter. Also: J. L. Y. (1987, promises versus past fact), A. M. V. (1996, past conduct predicts continued deprivation), E. C. (1997, unappealed deprivation findings bind) and L. F. (1992, imprisonment with aggravating circumstances).
rule: Georgia termination requires clear and convincing evidence of present parental misconduct or inability causing deprivation that is likely to continue, reviewed by asking whether a rational trier of fact could so find (Blackburn); past conduct, unappealed deprivation findings and the children's need for stability weigh heavily against recent promises of improvement.

changes.what: In light of Santosky, appellate review asks whether a rational trier of fact could find clear and convincing evidence for termination.

changes.case: In the Interest of J. L. Y.; G. K. J.; J. M. C.; L. F.
changes.what: A child's future must rest on more than promises contrary to past fact; findings cannot be bare recitals; recent progress may not overcome a long history; imprisonment with aggravating circumstances can support termination.

changes.case: In the Interest of R. N.; T. B. R.; E. C.
changes.what: Courts may weigh the children's need for stability, disregard self-serving testimony, and bind parents to unappealed deprivation findings; R. N. anchors 1995-99.

changes.case: In the Interest of V. S.
changes.what: Construed the prior Juvenile Code's procedures for disposition orders removing a child from the home; V. S. anchors 2000-04.

round1.name: Georgia deprivation and termination of parental rights: Blackburn review
round1.description: Georgia juvenile deprivation and termination: parental rights may be ended only on clear and convincing proof of present misconduct or inability causing continuing deprivation, not poverty (Shover 1980, Carvalho 1981). N. 1997) weigh past conduct and children's need for stability.
round1.history: Dominant rule: termination requires clear and convincing evidence of present parental misconduct or inability causing deprivation that is likely to continue. Chancey (1980) anchors 1980-84, with Shover (1980) reversing a termination based only on poverty and Carvalho (1981) requiring unfitness or compelling circumstances. Blackburn (1982) enters and anchors 1985-89: in light of Santosky, the Georgia Supreme Court reexamined appellate review and asked whether a rational trier of fact could find the clear-and-convincing standard met; In re Suggs (1982) required clear and convincing evidence for deprivation. (1997) anchors 2000-04 on disposition procedures under the prior Juvenile Code.
round1.rule: Georgia may terminate parental rights only on clear and convincing evidence of present parental misconduct or inability causing deprivation likely to continue and harm the child, not on poverty or a better home elsewhere; on appeal the question is whether a rational trier of fact could so find (Blackburn).

changes.what: Termination requires unfitness or compelling circumstances; poverty alone, or the prospect of a better home, does not suffice.
After Santosky v. Kramer, Georgia reexamined appellate review and adopted the rational-trier-of-fact test under the clear-and-convincing standard.

changes.case: In the Interest of J. L. Y.; G. K. J.; J. M. C.
changes.what: Positive promises cannot outweigh a negative past; the court must make specific findings, and may weigh repeated incarceration and the harm of prolonged foster care.

changes.case: In the Interest of R. N.; In the Interest of V. S.
changes.what: The need for stability for children shifted between foster homes supports termination; prior disposition procedures under the old Juvenile Code construed.

name: NLRA bargaining duties and Wright Line motive test: Fibreboard, Katz (1975-2004)
description: NLRA bargaining duties and mixed-motive discharges, 1975-2004: unilateral changes and bargaining over mandatory subjects (Katz 1962, Fibreboard 1964, anchor 1975-84, First National Maintenance 1981), inherently destructive conduct (Erie Resistor, Great Dane), successorship (Burns 1972, Fall River 1987), and the Wright Line test (Transportation Management 1983). Universal Camera's substantial-evidence review anchors 1985-2004.
