previous.name: NLRB unfair labor practices
previous.description: Unfair labor practices under NLRA §§ 8(a)(1), (3) and (5): mixed-motive discharges (Wright Line, Transportation Management), employer threats and bargaining orders (Gissel), unilateral changes (NLRB v. Katz), bargaining subjects (Fibreboard), successorship (Fall River Dyeing), and substantial-evidence review (Universal Camera).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: the NLRA forbids coercion, discrimination for union activity and refusals to bargain over mandatory subjects, and courts enforce Board orders resting on substantial evidence and reasonable readings of the Act. How it changed: in 1975-84 the anchor is Fibreboard (1964), with Katz (1962), Erie Resistor (1963), Great Dane (1967), Allied Chemical (1971) and Acme (1967) on information requests. H.K. Porter (1970) limited Board remedies, Weingarten (1975) created interview representation rights, and Ford Motor (1979) and First National Maintenance (1981) marked the edges of mandatory bargaining. From 1985-89 the NLRB review unit merges in and Universal Camera (1951) anchors through 2000-04, with Wright Line (1981) and Transportation Management (1983) setting the mixed-motive test and Gissel (1969) bargaining orders. Burns (1972) and Fall River (1987) govern successors. Curtin Matheson (1990), Health Care & Retirement (1994), Holly Farms (1996) and Allentown Mack (1998) enter in 1990-99. Telecommunications zoning entrants in 2000-04 are drift before the unit merges into general agency-review law.
rule: Under NLRA § 8(a), an employer must bargain in good faith over mandatory subjects and may not change them unilaterally, coerce employees or discriminate for union activity; in mixed-motive cases the employer must show it would have acted anyway (Wright Line; Transportation Management), and Board findings stand if supported by substantial evidence.

changes.case: NLRB v. Katz; NLRB v. Erie Resistor; Fibreboard v. NLRB
changes.what: Unilateral changes violate § 8(a)(5); superseniority for strike replacements is inherently destructive; contracting out unit work is a mandatory subject; Fibreboard anchors 1975-84.

changes.case: H.K. Porter v. NLRB; Allied Chemical Workers v. Pittsburgh Plate Glass; NLRB v. Burns International Security
changes.what: The Board cannot compel agreement to substantive terms; retirees' benefits are permissive subjects; a successor must bargain with the union but is not bound by the old contract.

changes.case: NLRB v. J. Weingarten; Ford Motor v. NLRB; Beth Israel Hospital v. NLRB
changes.what: Right to a union representative at investigatory interviews; in-plant food prices are mandatory subjects; reasonably defensible Board constructions get deference.
No duty to bargain over a decision to close part of a business for economic reasons, though effects must be bargained.

changes.case: NLRB v. Wright Line (1st Cir.); NLRB v. Transportation Management
changes.what: Mixed-motive burden-shifting test upheld; Universal Camera with Transportation Management anchors 1985-2004.
A successor with substantial continuity and a majority of predecessor employees must bargain; the duty attaches at a substantial and representative complement.

changes.case: NLRB v. Curtin Matheson Scientific; NLRB v. Health Care & Retirement Corp.; Holly Farms v. NLRB; Allentown Mack v. NLRB
changes.what: No presumption that replacements oppose the union; charge nurses directing others for the employer are supervisors; Board rules upheld if reasonable but findings must rest on substantial evidence.

name: Michigan no-fault insurance act: Shavers due process and benefit set-offs
description: Michigan's no-fault automobile insurance act in 1980-84: compulsory coverage gives motorists a due process interest in fair access to insurance (Shavers 1978); duplicative government benefits are set off against benefits (O'Donnell 1979, anchor); the act and workers' compensation are separate schemes (Mathis 1980); and 'resident of a household' is fact-dependent (Workman 1979).
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Michigan no-fault insurance
previous.description: Constitutional and statutory questions under Michigan's no-fault automobile insurance act (Shavers, O'Donnell, Kostamo, Workman).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, contrastive pass from family evidence)

history: Dominant rule: the Michigan no-fault act is a valid, self-contained compulsory insurance scheme. This is a single 1980-84 slice anchored by O'Donnell (1979), which split from the automobile guest-statute unit. The 1973 Advisory Opinion held the act complete in itself under the state constitution's title-object rule. Shavers (1978) held that because the Legislature made no-fault insurance compulsory, motorists have a protected interest in obtaining it on fair and equitable terms, so the rate and availability provisions must satisfy due process. O'Donnell (1979) upheld the set-off of duplicative governmental benefits, including Social Security survivors' benefits. Mathis (1980) treated the WDCA and the no-fault act as complete and separate schemes. Workman (1979) held that 'resident of a household' varies with circumstances, and Miller (1981) used rejected bills to discern legislative intent. No rule change within the slice.
rule: Because Michigan made no-fault insurance compulsory, motorists have a protected interest in obtaining it on fair and equitable terms (Shavers), while the act's set-off of duplicative government benefits is valid and read as a self-contained scheme alongside workers' compensation (O'Donnell, Mathis).

changes.case: Advisory Opinion re Constitutionality of 1972 PA 294
changes.what: The no-fault act was complete in itself and did not violate the Michigan Constitution's art 4, § 25.
Compulsory no-fault insurance makes driving dependent on insurance, so rate and availability regulation must satisfy due process.
Upheld the required set-off of duplicative government benefits such as Social Security survivors' benefits.

changes.case: Workman v. DAIIE; Mathis v. Interstate Motor Freight
changes.what: 'Resident of a household' depends on the circumstances (Workman), and the WDCA and no-fault act are separate self-contained schemes (Mathis).

name: Voter qualifications and durational residency: strict scrutiny (Kramer, Dunn)
description: Strict scrutiny of limits on who may vote, 1970-79: franchise restrictions on otherwise qualified residents must be necessary to a compelling interest (Carrington 1965; Harper 1966; Kramer 1969, anchor 1970-74; Cipriano 1969), and Dunn (1972, anchor 1975-79) struck durational residency for voting, drawing on Shapiro (1969) on travel. In 1975-79 ballot access (Bullock, Storer) and mootness of election and class claims (Sosna 1975) join.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Ballot access and mootness (1975)
previous.description: 1975 election-law cases: ballot access and party affiliation (Storer, Bullock, Williams v. Rhodes, Rosario), and the capable-of-repetition-yet-evading-review exception to mootness (Southern Pacific Terminal, Sosna, Weinstein v. Bradford, DeFunis). Predecessor of 21778.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, contrastive pass from family evidence)

history: Dominant rule: a state law that denies the vote to otherwise qualified residents, or conditions it on property, payment or length of residence, must be necessary to a compelling state interest. How it changed: Kramer (1969) anchors 1970-74, striking a school-district vote limited to property owners and parents, with Cipriano (1969) and Kolodziejski (1970) on bond elections, Carrington (1965) on servicemen, Harper (1966) on the poll tax and Evans v. Cornman (1970) on residents of a federal enclave; Shapiro (1969) and Guest (1966) supply the right to travel, and Oregon v. Mitchell (1970) appears. Dunn v. Blumstein (1972) anchors 1975-79, striking a one-year residency requirement for voting, and Memorial Hospital v. Maricopa County (1974) applied Shapiro to nonemergency medical care. Alongside, in 1975-79: ballot-access cases (Williams v. Rhodes 1968, Bullock 1972, Storer 1974) and mootness, where election challenges survive under the capable-of-repetition exception (Southern Pacific 1911, Moore v. Ogilvie 1969) and Sosna (1975) held that a certified class survives the named plaintiff's mootness. The unit splits toward Article III standing in 1980-84.
rule: Restrictions on the franchise among otherwise qualified residents, including property, payment and durational-residency conditions, are invalid unless necessary to a compelling state interest.

changes.case: Harper v. Virginia Board of Elections
changes.what: Conditioning the vote on payment of a poll tax violates equal protection.

changes.case: Kramer v. Union Free School District; Cipriano v. City of Houma

name: Florida capital appeals: Williams collateral-crime rule, CCP and harmless error
description: Florida death-penalty appeals built on the Williams rule (1959, later codified in § 90.404(2)): collateral-crime evidence is admissible if relevant to a material issue, not to show propensity. history: Dominant rule: Florida's Williams rule (1959) admits evidence of other crimes when relevant to a material fact such as identity, intent or plan, but not to show bad character, and it anchors 1980-84 and 1985-89; it was later codified in § 90.404(2), Florida Statutes. name: Texas Citizens Participation Act dismissals and defamation: In re Lipsky
description: Texas Citizens Participation Act: claims based on protected speech, petition or association are dismissed unless the plaintiff shows clear and specific evidence of each element, which In re Lipsky (2015), the anchor from 2015-19, held may be circumstantial. Dallas Morning News and Scripps (2019) apply defamation privileges. A 2019 amendment narrowed the Act.

name: Who decides arbitrability, 2005-14: clear delegation by AAA rules (AT&T, Kaplan)
description: Who decides arbitrability, 2005-14. AT&T Technologies (1986, anchor) and First Options v. Kaplan (1995) leave arbitrability to courts absent clear and unmistakable delegation; Howsam (2002) gives procedural questions to arbitrators. Circuits treated incorporation of AAA rules as clear delegation (Contec, Terminix 2005; Qualcomm 2006), kept litigation waiver for courts, and Carlisle (2009) applied state law to nonsignatories.
history: Dominant rule: whether an arbitrability question goes to the court or the arbitrator. AT&T Technologies (1986) anchors both slices: courts decide arbitrability, with a presumption of coverage drawn from the Steelworkers Trilogy (1960) and Wiley v. Livingston (1964). Kaplan (1995) reverses the presumption on the 'who decides' question, requiring clear and unmistakable evidence of delegation. How it changed: Howsam (2002) made procedural questions such as time limits presumptively for arbitrators, and the Bazzle plurality (2003) sent class-arbitration questions to them. In 2005-09 circuits held that incorporating AAA rules delegates arbitrability (Contec, Terminix, Qualcomm), and that waiver by litigation conduct stays with courts (Marie 2005, Ehleiter 2007). In 2010-14 Carlisle (2009) applied state law to nonsignatories (with estoppel cases such as Thomson-CSF 1995 and Sunkist 1993), and Fallo (2009) joined the AAA-rules line. Litton (1991) limits the presumption for expired labor agreements. The unit splits in 2015-19.

changes.case: AT&T Technologies v. CWA; First Options v. Kaplan
changes.what: Courts decide whether a dispute is arbitrable unless the parties clearly and unmistakably provided otherwise.

name: Patent validity: invention, combination patents and Graham nonobviousness
description: Patent validity in the regional circuits before the Federal Circuit. A&P Tea (1951, anchor 1950-64) required combination patents of old elements to show more than the sum of their parts; § 103 (1952) and Graham v. John Deere (1966, anchor 1965-84) replaced 'invention' with nonobviousness under factual inquiries. Anderson's-Black Rock (1969) and Sakraida (1976) held combinations without new results obvious.

previous.name: Patent validity: invention and obviousness (1945-80)

history: Dominant rule: patentability requires more than the ordinary skill of the art, framed first as 'invention' and then as nonobviousness. How it changed: A&P Tea (1951) anchors 1950-64, requiring careful scrutiny of combination patents, with Cuno (1941) and Lincoln Engineering (1938) on invention and new function, Graver Tank (1949-50) on equivalents and the deference owed to validity findings, and Jungersen (1949) and Goodyear v. Ray-O-Vac (1944) on commercial success; Kwikset (1954) and Lyon v. Bausch & Lomb (1955) enter in 1955-59. Graham (1966) enters and anchors 1965-84, reading § 103 to drop the flash-of-genius test and setting the factual inquiries with secondary considerations; Adams (1966), Stiffel and Compco (1964) join. Anderson's-Black Rock (1969) enters in 1970-74 and Sakraida and Dann (1976) in 1975-79, holding combinations without new results obvious. In 1980-84 regional-circuit decisions applying these cases lead before the unit splits as the Federal Circuit's own obviousness law takes over.
rule: A patent is valid only if the claimed advance would not have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the art, at first framed as 'invention' and, after § 103 (1952) and Graham (1966), as nonobviousness, with combinations of old elements scrutinized closely.

changes.what: An improvement needing no more than ordinary mechanical skill is not patentable.

changes.case: Lincoln Engineering v. Stewart-Warner; Cuno Engineering v. Automatic Devices
changes.what: A combination that produces no new function is not patentable, and invention requires more than skill in the art.

changes.case: Great Atlantic & Pacific Tea Co. v. Supermarket Equipment; Graver Tank v. Linde Air Products
changes.what: Combination patents of old elements get careful scrutiny; Graver Tank set the function-way-result test for equivalents.

changes.case: 35 U.S.C. § 103; Graham v. John Deere; United States v. Adams
changes.what: Section 103 replaced 'invention' with nonobviousness, determined through Graham's factual inquiries and secondary considerations, without a flash-of-genius requirement.

changes.case: Anderson's-Black Rock v. Pavement Salvage; Sakraida v. Ag Pro; Dann v. Johnston
changes.what: Combinations of old elements without a new or synergistic result are obvious despite commercial success.

name: Tennessee sentencing review: from Ashby's presumption of correctness to Bise
description: Tennessee sentencing review: Ashby (1991, anchor 2000-14) reviewed de novo with a presumption of correctness if the record showed the court weighed the sentencing principles. After Gomez (2007) and the 2005 amendments (Carter, 2008), Bise (2012) adopted abuse-of-discretion review with a presumption of reasonableness, extended to probation (Caudle, 2012) and consecutive sentences (Pollard, 2013).

previous.name: Tennessee sentencing review
previous.description: Tennessee appellate review of sentences after State v. Bise: abuse of discretion with a presumption of reasonableness for within-range sentences, extended to alternative sentencing and probation (Caudle) and consecutive sentences.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: the standard of appellate review for Tennessee sentences, and the findings a trial court must make. How it changed: Ashby (1991) anchors 2000-04 through 2010-14: review was de novo with a presumption of correctness that held only if the record showed the court considered the sentencing principles. Fletcher (1991) and Hooper (2000) govern deterrence-based denials of probation, and Hooper overruled cases requiring proof that incarceration would deter. Wilkerson (1995) requires extra findings for dangerous-offender consecutive sentences, limited by Lane (1999). In 2005-09 Gomez (2005, 2007) addresses Blakely, and the 2005 amendments made enhancement factors advisory and dropped the presumption of probation eligibility (Carter, 2008). Bise (2012) enters in 2010-14 and replaced Ashby with abuse-of-discretion review and a presumption of reasonableness. Caudle (2012) extended it to alternative sentencing and Pollard (2013) to consecutive sentences. Bise anchors from 2020-24, after Shaffer (2001) on probation revocation anchors 2015-19.
rule: Tennessee appellate courts review a within-range sentence, including length, alternative sentencing and consecutive terms, for abuse of discretion with a presumption of reasonableness when the trial court states reasons consistent with the purposes and principles of the Sentencing Act (Bise, Caudle, Pollard), replacing Ashby's de novo review with a conditional presumption of correctness.

changes.what: De novo review with a presumption of correctness, conditioned on an affirmative showing that the trial court considered the sentencing principles and relevant facts; anchors 2000-14.

changes.case: State v. Wilkerson; State v. Lane
changes.what: Consecutive sentences for a dangerous offender need findings that they protect the public and reasonably relate to the offenses, a requirement limited to that category.

changes.case: State v. Gomez (2005, 2007); 2005 Sentencing Act amendments
changes.what: Gomez II held that under the 1989 Act only prior convictions or admitted facts may enhance a sentence without a jury; the 2005 amendments made enhancement factors advisory and removed the presumption of probation eligibility (Carter, 2008).

changes.case: State v. Caudle; State v. Pollard
changes.what: Extended Bise review to alternative sentencing and probation (Caudle) and to consecutive sentencing, with the Wilkerson findings still required for dangerous offenders (Pollard).

history: Dominant rule: termination is a two-step proceeding, unfitness proved by clear and convincing evidence and then best interest, with deference to the trial court's findings. In re D.L. (2000) enters and anchors 2000-04: § 1(D)(m) unfitness evidence is confined to the statutory period, later conduct can be considered on best interest, and Santosky does not require clear and convincing proof of best interest. In re M.S. (1999, one ground suffices), Sheltanya S. (1999), C.M. (2001) and B.S. (2000, no adoptive parents needed) lead with it.

history: Dominant rule: Olano (1993) anchors this single 2005-09 slice: forfeited errors are corrected only if they are plain, affect substantial rights and seriously affect the fairness, integrity or public reputation of the proceedings (Atkinson 1936). How it changed: Johnson (1997) held that an error is plain if it is plain when the appeal is decided, which brought pre-Booker sentences within reach. Cotton (2002) held indictment defects non-jurisdictional, Vonn (2002) allowed review of the whole record on Rule 11 errors, and Dominguez Benitez (2004) required a reasonable probability of a different outcome. After Booker, the en banc Eighth Circuit in Pirani (2005) applied that test to unpreserved Booker claims: only an objection invoking Apprendi, Blakely or the Sixth Amendment preserves the error, and a sentence at the bottom of the range does not by itself show prejudice. Neder (1999) frames the harmlessness side, and Syme (2002) presumes prejudice from constructive amendment. Also: honest-services and mail fraud (McNally 1987, Rybicki 2003), Pinkerton liability, Old Chief (1997) stipulations and Jones (1999). The lineage splits in 2010-14 into Fifth Circuit plain-error review and post-Booker fact-finding lineages.

name: Erie and the Alien Tort Statute, 2010-14: Shady Grove, Sosa, Kiobel
description: Limits on federal law, 2010-14 only, in two strands: Erie (1938, anchor), Hanna (1965) and Shady Grove (2010: Rule 23 governs over a state class bar) on state versus federal rules in diversity; and the Alien Tort Statute, confined to specific, universal norms (Filartiga 1980, Sosa 2004) and, under the presumption against extraterritoriality (Morrison 2010), denied reach into another sovereign's territory (Kiobel 2013).
history: Dominant rule: the anchor is Erie (1938): no general federal common law, so diversity courts apply state substantive law, statutes of limitations included (Guaranty Trust 1945), while a valid Federal Rule controls (Hanna 1965). Alongside, with nearly equal weight: the Alien Tort Statute. Filartiga (1980) allowed suit for official torture; Tel-Oren (1984) and Sosa (2004) confined ATS claims to a narrow class of specific, universal and obligatory norms; Khulumani (2007) and Kiobel (2d Cir. 2010) addressed aiding-and-abetting and corporate liability, with the burden on the party invoking a norm; Sinaltrainal (2009) applied Iqbal pleading. The presumption against extraterritoriality (Aramco 1991; Morrison 2010 for § 10(b)) culminated in Kiobel (2013), holding that the ATS does not reach violations within another sovereign's territory. Single slice, 2010-14.

history: Dominant rule: review of Social Security and Medicare decisions runs through the statute. Weinberger v. Salfi (1975), the heaviest case, holds that § 405(h) channels claims into § 405(g) and that its final-decision requirement is more than judicial exhaustion doctrine, so futility cannot excuse it. Johnson v. Robison (1974) reads a preclusion clause to leave constitutional challenges to the statute itself open. How it changed: in the mid-1970s the circuits disagreed over whether the APA supplied independent jurisdiction. Sanders v. Weinberger (3d Cir. 1975) found APA review of refusals to reopen; Whitecliff (1976) and Adams Nursing Home (1977) found it for provider-reimbursement disputes; St. Louis University (1976) limited review to § 1331 constitutional challenges; South Windsor (1976), the anchor, sent pre-amendment reimbursement disputes to the Court of Claims. Califano v. Sanders (1977) resolved the split: the APA is not a jurisdictional grant and § 1331 is subject to preclusion statutes. Also: Medicaid review not barred by § 405(h) (Springdale 1977), mandamus unavailable where § 1395oo provides review (AAMC 1977), and due process claims about pretermination hearings (Ryan 1975, Elliott 1977).

history: Dominant rule: classifications not involving suspect classes or fundamental rights are presumed valid and upheld if any conceivable rational basis supports them. How it changed: McGowan (1961) anchors 1965-69 with Sunday-closing and school-prayer cases, before the religion cases split off. Reed (1971) anchors 1970-74, as sex and illegitimacy cases briefly join. Dandridge (1970) anchors 1975-89: welfare caps survive, Rodriguez (1973) denies education fundamental status, Murgia and Dukes (1976) apply deference (Dukes overruling Morey v. Doud), and Vance (1979) and Fritz (1981) uphold imperfect lines. Cleburne (1985) enters with Plyler (1982) and anchors 1990-94, striking a law resting on prejudice. Nordlinger (1992) and Allegheny Pittsburgh (1989) apply the test to taxation. FCC v. Beach Communications (1993) and Heller (1993) enter and anchor 1995-2004: no stated reasons are needed and challengers must negate every basis. Romer (1996) and military-policy cases (Steffan, Thomasson) join, and Olech (2000) recognised class-of-one claims.
rule: Economic and social classifications that burden no suspect class or fundamental right are upheld if any reasonably conceivable state of facts provides a rational basis for them, and the legislature need not state its reasons or address a problem all at once.

Paul (1963) anchors 1970-74 and 1980-84 on impossibility, with Hines (1941), Perez (1971, overruling Kesler) and Jones (1977). Rice anchors 1975-79 and 1985-94, with de la Cuesta (1982) on agency preemption, Silkwood (1984) and Hillsborough (1985) against implied preemption, and English (1990). Cipollone (1992) anchors 1995-2004: express clauses govern and can reach common-law claims; Lohr (1996) spared parallel device claims, Myrick (1995) and Geier (2000) addressed vehicle standards, Crosby (2000) and Buckman (2001) obstacle preemption. United States (2012) anchors 2015-19 and the partial 2025-29 slice, with Whiting (2011). The 2020s absorb ERISA and drug-pricing cases (2024): drift.
rule: Federal law preempts state law where Congress says so expressly, where federal regulation occupies the field, or where compliance with both is impossible or state law stands as an obstacle to federal objectives, starting from the presumption that historic state police powers are not superseded absent clear and manifest congressional purpose.

name: Teague and Apprendi on collateral review 2000-04: Sanders, Moss, Tyler
description: Teague (1989) retroactivity applied to Apprendi, in the single 2000-04 slice: new procedural rules do not reach final convictions unless they fit two narrow exceptions (Saffle, Sawyer 1990; Graham 1993; O'Dell 1997). history: Dominant rule: Teague (1989) bars applying new rules of constitutional criminal procedure to convictions that were final when the rule was announced, unless the rule places conduct beyond the power to punish or is a watershed rule implicit in ordered liberty. Teague anchors the lineage's only slice, 2000-04, formed from habeas and harmless-error units. How it changed: the main question in the span is Apprendi (2000). The circuits held it a new procedural rule that is not a watershed rule: Sanders (4th Cir. 2001), Moss (8th Cir. 2001) and McCoy (11th Cir. 2001). Tyler (2001) held that Cage's reasonable-doubt rule could not support a successive petition because the Court had not made it retroactive. Earlier cases set the method: Saffle and Sawyer (1990) defined new rules, Graham (1993) and O'Dell (1997, Simmons) confined the watershed exception, and Caspari (1994) applied Teague to state prisoners. Bousley (1998) applied Bailey's substantive reading of § 924(c) retroactively with an actual-innocence gateway. Also: Winship (1970) and Cage (1990) on the reasonable-doubt standard and Mackey (1971) on retroactivity's rationale.
rule: New rules of constitutional criminal procedure do not apply to convictions already final on collateral review unless they place conduct beyond the power to punish or are watershed rules implicit in ordered liberty (Teague); circuits held Apprendi is a new procedural rule that fits neither exception, while new substantive readings of statutes apply retroactively (Bousley).

history: Dominant rule: Padilla (2010), the anchor in both slices, holds that the Sixth Amendment requires defence counsel to tell a noncitizen client whether a guilty plea carries a risk of deportation, and to say so clearly when the consequence is presumptively mandatory. How it changed: earlier law, represented by Ex parte Morrow (1997) and Ford (1995), treated deportation as a collateral consequence outside counsel's duty. Lafler and Frye (2012) extended effective-assistance review to plea negotiations: counsel must communicate formal offers, and a rejected offer can establish prejudice. The Third Circuit in Orocio (2011) held Padilla retroactive, but Chaidez (2013) held it a new rule unavailable to convictions final before March 31, 2010, which De Los Reyes (2013) applied. In 2015-19 Jae Lee (2017) let a defendant show prejudice by a rational choice to risk trial to avoid deportation. Alongside: Texas habeas procedure, with the applicant's preponderance burden (Richardson, 2002) and deference to the habeas court's findings (Peterson, 2003; Kniatt, 2006).
rule: Counsel must advise a noncitizen client whether a guilty plea carries a risk of deportation, clearly when removal is presumptively mandatory (Padilla), and must give effective assistance in plea negotiations (Lafler, Frye); Padilla announced a new rule that does not apply retroactively on collateral review (Chaidez).

changes.case: Ex parte Morrow (Tex. Crim. App.); State v. Ford
changes.what: Before Padilla, deportation was a collateral consequence outside the Sixth Amendment duty of counsel.
Counsel must inform a noncitizen whether a plea carries a risk of deportation; Padilla anchors both slices.

changes.case: United States v. Orocio (3d Cir.); Chaidez v. United States
changes.what: Orocio treated Padilla as an old rule applying retroactively; Chaidez held it a new rule not available to convictions final before 2010 (De Los Reyes, 2013).

changes.case: Lafler v. Cooper; Missouri v. Frye
changes.what: Counsel must communicate formal plea offers, and a defendant who rejects an offer on bad advice can show prejudice if the plea would have been accepted and the result less severe.
Prejudice turns on whether a rational defendant who prized avoiding deportation would have gone to trial, even with poor odds of acquittal.

history: Dominant rule: motions to reopen are disfavored; the BIA may deny them for lack of a prima facie case, lack of new material evidence or in its discretion, and courts review only for abuse of discretion. Matter of Marin (1978) anchors 1990-94 as § 212(c) waiver cases (Francis, Cordoba-Chaves) and Abudu (1988) join. Wang anchors again in 1995-99 as Doherty (1992) settles the review standard. name: Rooker-Feldman and Heck bars to § 1983 suits, with absolute immunity, 2015-24
description: Threshold bars to civil-rights suits, 2015-24, anchored on Rooker-Feldman: lower federal courts may not review state judgments, but the bar is narrow (Exxon Mobil 2005, Lance 2006, Skinner 2011); Heck (1994) requires favorable termination, with accrual under Wallace (2007) and McDonough (2019); judges and prosecutors acting as advocates are absolutely immune (Stump, Imbler; not Burns, Buckley). Manuel (2017) put pretrial detention in the Fourth Amendment.
history: Dominant rule: Rooker (1924) and Feldman (1983), the anchors, bar lower federal courts from reviewing state-court judgments or claims inextricably intertwined with them. Exxon Mobil (2005) confined the doctrine to state-court losers complaining of injuries caused by judgments rendered before the federal suit began; Lance (2006) called it narrow, and Skinner (2011) let a prisoner challenge state DNA-testing procedures because he did not attack an adverse decision. Alongside: Heck (1994), Preiser and Wilkinson channel attacks on convictions into habeas; Wallace (2007) fixed accrual of false-imprisonment claims at legal process. Absolute immunity covers judges acting within jurisdiction (Stump 1978, Mireles 1991), prosecutors in advocacy (Imbler 1976) but not advising police (Burns 1991) or investigating (Buckley 1993), and grand-jury witnesses (Rehberg 2012). How it changed: Manuel (2017) held that pretrial detention without probable cause is a Fourth Amendment claim, and McDonough (2019), entering in 2020-24, held a fabricated-evidence claim accrues on favorable termination.

description: Oregon's method for construing statutes: text and context first, then legislative history, then general maxims. history: Dominant rule: Oregon courts discern legislative intent by examining text and context, then legislative history, and, if intent is still unclear, general maxims of construction. How it changed: PGE v. BOLI (1993) anchors 1995-99 through 2005-09 with a strict sequence in which legislative history came in only when text and context left doubt; Springfield Education Ass'n (1980) supplies the exact, inexact and delegative terms framework for agency interpretation (Coast Security, 2000). Stull (1997) held that the court must reach the correct interpretation whether or not argued. After the legislature amended ORS 174.020 in 2001, State v. Gaines (2009) refined PGE: text and context remain first, but history may be considered when useful and can show that seemingly plain text is not plain. Gaines enters in 2005-09 and anchors every slice from 2010-14. Also: Cloutier (2011) on redundancy, Comcast (2014) and Gonzalez-Valenzuela (2015) on dictionaries and legal terms of art, Mowry (2011) on stare decisis for prior constructions.
rule: Oregon courts construe a statute by examining its text and context, then any useful legislative history, and only if intent remains unclear the general maxims of construction, with the court bound to reach the correct interpretation whether or not argued.

changes.case: PGE v. Bureau of Labor and Industries
changes.what: Three-level template: text and context first, legislative history only if the text is unclear, then general maxims.
The court must identify the correct interpretation whether or not the parties assert it.
Parties may offer legislative history and the court may consult it without first finding the text ambiguous.
Text and context remain the first step, but legislative history may be consulted when useful and may confirm or undercut a seemingly plain meaning; maxims apply only if intent remains unclear.

changes.case: Comcast Corp. v. Department of Revenue; Gonzalez-Valenzuela

name: Guilty pleas: knowing and voluntary on the record (Boykin, Brady, Santobello)
description: Validity of guilty pleas: the record must affirmatively show a knowing, voluntary plea (McCarthy 1969 under Rule 11; Boykin 1969, anchor 1975-94). The 1970 Brady trilogy and Alford upheld bargained pleas and pleas with claimed innocence; Santobello (1971) enforces plea promises; Henderson v. history: Dominant rule: a guilty plea waives trial rights and stands only if knowing, intelligent and voluntary on the record. How it changed: before 1965 the lineage rests on Kercheval (1927), the anchor 1955-64, and circuit cases on withdrawing pleas induced by misunderstood promises. Machibroda (1962) anchors 1965-69, requiring hearings on off-record inducement claims, as McCarthy (1969) entered with automatic reversal for Rule 11 violations. In 1970-74 the anchor is Brady (1970), decided with McMann and Parker, upholding pleas made to avoid harsher punishment and on reasonable advice, and Alford (1970) and Santobello (1971) enter. Boykin (1969) becomes the anchor in 1975-79 and holds it through 1990-94, joined by Henderson v. Morgan (1976), California's Tahl rule and Tollett (1973). Blackledge (1977) and Mabry (1984) shaped collateral attacks and plea-offer claims. In 1985-89 competency cases (Pate, Drope, Dusky) join, and in 1990-94 Parke (1993) and Broce (1989) narrowed attacks on prior pleas.
rule: A guilty plea is valid only if the record affirmatively shows it was knowing, intelligent and voluntary, with an understanding of the charge and its direct consequences (Boykin; McCarthy); fear of a harsher sentence does not make it involuntary (Brady), and a promise by the prosecutor that induced the plea must be kept (Santobello).

changes.what: A guilty plea is itself a conviction; a withdrawn plea cannot be used as evidence of guilt; Kercheval anchors 1955-64.

round1.name: New Jersey relief from judgments and reconsideration (Guillaume, D'Atria)
round1.description: A lineage whose doctrine changes: California social-host and dram-shop liability in the 1980s (Bernhard, Vesely, Coulter, abrogated in 1978), New Jersey's social-host rule (Kelly, 1984) and duty cases in the 1990s, Consumer Fraud Act ascertainable loss (Cox, Furst, Bosland) to 2014, and from 2015-19 Guillaume (2012) on vacating judgments and D'Atria (1990) on narrow reconsideration.
round1.history: Dominant rule: the anchor changes doctrine across the slices. In 1980-84 and 1985-89 Bernhard (1976) anchors California cases on liability for serving alcohol and choice of law (Vesely, 1971; Coulter, 1978), later abrogated by the 1978 legislation noted in Cory (1981). In 1995-99 Hopkins (1993) anchors duty-of-care cases decided on fairness and policy (Dunphy, Carter Lincoln-Mercury, Carvalho), and Brill (1995) anchors 2000-04. name: Washington collateral estoppel from administrative rulings: Williams, Reninger
description: Washington issue preclusion (1995-2004): an issue decided in a prior final judgment, including an administrative one, binds the same party or its privy unless applying preclusion would work an injustice. State v. Williams (1997) anchors both slices, refusing on public-policy grounds to let a DSHS finding bar a criminal prosecution, following Dupard (1980); Reninger and Nielson (1998) gave preclusive effect to agency findings and judgments.

previous.name: Washington collateral estoppel
previous.description: Washington Supreme Court preclusion law: issue preclusion from administrative and prior proceedings (Reninger, Nielson, Dupard, State v. Williams), with malicious prosecution and false arrest claims.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, contrastive pass from family evidence)

history: Dominant rule: Washington applies collateral estoppel when the issues are identical, the earlier proceeding ended in a final judgment on the merits, the party to be bound was a party or in privity, and preclusion works no injustice. State v. Williams (1997) anchors both slices. DSHS, which had found in an administrative hearing that Williams did not intentionally take overpayments, was in privity with the prosecutor, yet public policy kept that finding from barring a fraud prosecution. That follows Dupard (1980), where a parole board's not-guilty finding did not bar prosecution because new crimes belong in the criminal system. How it applied: Reninger (1998) gave Personnel Appeals Board findings preclusive effect against later tort claims because the hearing resembled a trial, and made the injustice test a fundamental part of the doctrine. Nielson (1998) held that an appeal or settlement pending appeal does not undo a judgment's preclusive effect. Cleveland (1990) and Thompson (1999) treated different state offices as the same party. Also: probable cause as a complete defense to malicious prosecution and false arrest (Hanson 1993), and qualified privilege in defamation (Bender 1983, Moe 1999). The unit splits after 2000-04.
rule: In Washington, collateral estoppel bars relitigation of an issue identical to one decided by a final judgment on the merits against the same party or its privy, if applying it works no injustice; administrative findings can qualify, but the doctrine yields where public policy, such as keeping crimes in the criminal process, weighs against it.

changes.what: A parole board's finding did not estop a later prosecution for the same new crime, because preclusion may be rejected when it contravenes public policy.
DSHS was in privity with the prosecutor, but for policy reasons its administrative finding did not bar a welfare-fraud prosecution.

changes.case: Reninger v. Department of Corrections; Nielson v. Spanaway
changes.what: Personnel Appeals Board findings precluded later tort claims where the hearing resembled a trial (Reninger), and a judgment stays preclusive despite a later settlement pending appeal (Nielson).
Different state agencies or offices represented by different counsel can be the same party for preclusion.

name: South Dakota termination of parental rights, 1985-89: D.H. best interests
description: South Dakota Supreme Court termination cases, single 1985-89 slice, centred on best interests and reunification efforts: termination requires clear and convincing evidence that it serves the child's best interests (In re D.H. 1984, quoting Santosky 1982), with the State's parens patriae interest outweighing a parent's limited progress (N.J.W. 1978). history: Dominant rule: In re D.H. (1984) anchors the single 1985-89 slice. A trial court must find by clear and convincing evidence that terminating parental rights is in the child's best interests, the standard drawn from Santosky v. Kramer (1982). Earlier South Dakota cases (N.J.W. 1978, R.Z.F. 1979, M.S.M. 1982, S.L.H. 1983, S.S. 1983) stress the State's parens patriae interest and put the child's best interests above a parent's limited capacity or slow improvement. How it applied: People in Interest of P.B. (1985), including in an Indian Child Welfare Act case, held that the department need not persist in efforts destined to fail and need not try every conceivable form of help before termination is justified. Later cases (J.S.N. 1985, A.M.L. 1985, T.H. 1986, S.M. 1986, K.C. 1987) apply these rules to the adequacy of reunification efforts. The evidence shows no change in the governing rule within the slice. The unit absorbs a 1980-84 Pennsylvania termination unit when it forms.

changes.what: Termination findings must be made by clear and convincing evidence.

name: Georgia death-sentence review under the 1973 statute: Gregg, Jarrell, Fleming

history: Dominant rule: under the 1973 death-penalty statute the Georgia Supreme Court reviews each death sentence for passion or prejudice, for evidence supporting a statutory aggravating circumstance, and for proportionality, and reviews the evidence even when not argued (Gregg, 1974; Coley, 1974). How it changed: Floyd (1974) anchors 1975-79, with Jarrell and Moore (1975) setting the proportionality test (whether juries generally impose death for similar crimes). Hawes and Fleming (1977) anchor 1980-84 and require setting aside a death sentence for prosecutorial argument that risks corrupting sentencing, even without objection; Hance (1980) defined the (b)(7) aggravator. Allen (1984) added co-defendant sentences to proportionality review. From 1985-89 Spivey (1984) anchors and the cases turn to trial issues in capital cases: voir dire on parole, courtroom security, admissibility of statements and waiver by psychiatric testimony (Ingram, 1984). Todd (1991) anchors 1995-99 before the lineage splits toward Georgia sufficiency review.
rule: The Georgia Supreme Court reviews every death sentence for passion or prejudice, for evidence supporting a statutory aggravating circumstance, and for proportionality against similar cases, and reviews the whole record even on grounds not argued.

changes.what: Mandatory sentence review under the 1973 statute; death held disproportionate for armed robbery (Gregg) and rape (Coley), and evidence reviewed even when not argued.

name: Pennsylvania PCRA ineffectiveness: Pierce test, Grant deferral, Turner/Finley
description: Pennsylvania ineffectiveness and PCRA review, 2000-24: Albrecht (1998, anchor 2000-04) ended relaxed waiver in PCRA appeals; Grant (2002, anchor 2005-14) deferred ineffectiveness claims to collateral review; Pierce's (1987) Strickland-equivalent three-prong test governs throughout. history: Dominant rule: how Pennsylvania courts review claims of ineffective counsel on collateral review. Pierce (1987) equates the state test with Strickland, framed as arguable merit, no reasonable basis and prejudice, and a failure on any prong defeats the claim. How it changed: Albrecht (1998) anchors 2000-04, ending relaxed waiver in PCRA appeals, while claims not raised in the petition are waived and PCRA courts must give specific reasons for dismissal. Grant (2002) anchors 2005-09 and 2010-14, deferring ineffectiveness claims to collateral review. Pitts (2009) and Superior Court cases required PCRA counsel's ineffectiveness to be raised before appeal, treating claims first made in Rule 1925(b) statements as waived. From 2015-19 Turner and Finley (1988) anchor as no-merit withdrawal practice dominates, with deferential review of PCRA rulings supported by the record. Bradley (2021) later relaxed Pitts. The lineage splits in 2025-29.
rule: Pennsylvania reviews ineffectiveness claims under Pierce's Strickland-equivalent test (arguable merit, no reasonable basis, prejudice), generally deferred to collateral review under the PCRA (Grant), where unraised claims are waived and appointed counsel may withdraw on a Turner/Finley no-merit letter.

changes.what: Pennsylvania's ineffectiveness test is the same rule as Strickland, framed as arguable merit, lack of a reasonable basis and prejudice.

changes.case: Commonwealth v. Turner; Commonwealth v. Finley
changes.what: Appointed post-conviction counsel may withdraw on a no-merit letter explaining why the issues lack merit.
The relaxed waiver doctrine no longer applies in PCRA appeals, including capital cases.

changes.case: Commonwealth v. Pitts; Superior Court Rule 1925(b) cases
changes.what: A petitioner may not obtain remand to raise PCRA counsel's omissions, nor raise PCRA counsel's ineffectiveness for the first time in a Rule 1925(b) statement.
A PCRA petitioner may raise PCRA counsel's ineffectiveness at the first opportunity, including on appeal, relaxing Pitts.

round1.history: Dominant rule: how Pennsylvania courts review claims of ineffective counsel. In 1975-89 Maroney (1967) anchors: counsel's strategy needs only some reasonable basis, and Hubbard (1977) requires the claim at the earliest stage at which the challenged lawyer no longer represents the defendant. How it changed: Pierce (1987) anchors 1990-94 and equates the state test with Strickland, framed as arguable merit, no reasonable basis and prejudice. Turner and Finley (1988) let PCRA counsel withdraw on a no-merit letter. name: Ohio mootness: actual controversies and collateral disability (Fortner, Wilson)
description: Ohio courts decide only actual controversies and refuse moot or abstract questions (Fortner, 1970; Tschantz, 1991, anchor 2015-19). From 2020-24, with Cyran (2018) anchoring, criminal mootness joins: a completed misdemeanor sentence moots an appeal absent a collateral disability (Wilson, 1975; Berndt, 1987), but not a felony (Golston, 1994). Exceptions cover issues capable of repetition yet evading review. The rule is stable.

previous.name: Ohio mootness doctrine
previous.description: Ohio courts declining to decide moot or abstract questions (Fortner, Tschantz, Cyran, Lewis), with the capable-of-repetition exception.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, contrastive pass from family evidence)

history: Dominant rule: Ohio courts confine themselves to live controversies and decline to decide moot or abstract questions, applying exceptions only for issues capable of repetition yet evading review. How it changed: the lineage runs from 2015-19 to the partial 2025-29 slice and rests on older Ohio decisions. Tschantz (1991) anchors 2015-19 with Fortner (1970): no actual controversy exists once an outside event moots the case. Flaherty (1991), Barnes (1988) and Huffer (1989) define the capable-of-repetition exception, requiring a reasonable expectation that the same party will face the same controversy, and Pewitt (1992) and Russo (2000) allow extrinsic proof of mootness. In 2020-24 Cyran (2018) anchors as criminal-appeal mootness enters: Wilson (1975) holds a misdemeanant who voluntarily served the sentence has a moot appeal unless he shows a collateral disability, Berndt (1987) held a possible enhanced penalty on a later conviction is not enough, and Golston (1994) confined that test to misdemeanors, since felony convictions carry obvious collateral consequences. State v. Smith (2019), In re A.G. (2014) and Lewis (2011) also lead. Fortner anchors the partial 2025-29 slice. Also: standing (Ford v. Ruehlman, 2016). The evidence shows a stable rule rather than a change.
rule: Ohio courts decide only actual controversies and will not rule on moot or abstract questions, so a criminal appeal is moot once the sentence is served unless the defendant shows a collateral disability, subject to an exception for issues capable of repetition yet evading review.

changes.what: Courts must decide actual controversies between parties affected by specific facts and not give opinions on moot questions.

changes.case: State v. Wilson; State v. Berndt
changes.what: A misdemeanant who voluntarily completes the sentence moots the appeal unless evidence shows a collateral disability apart from the sentence, and a possible enhanced penalty on reoffending is not one; both enter in 2020-24.

changes.case: Barnes (1988); In re Suspension of Huffer (1989); Flaherty (1991)
changes.what: Courts may hear issues capable of repetition yet evading review, but only on a reasonable expectation that the same party will face the same controversy again.
The Wilson-Berndt test applies only to misdemeanors; felony convictions carry obvious collateral consequences, so serving the sentence does not moot the appeal.
The event that moots a case may be proved by extrinsic evidence outside the record.

history: Dominant rule: Kentucky's standards of criminal review. How it changed: the early slices are capital appeals: Grooms (1988) anchors 1990-94, Epperson (1991) 1995-99 and Tamme (1998) 2000-04, on juror qualification, the defendant's absence from instruction conferences, closing argument and aggravating factors (Sanders 1990; Bowling 1994, 1997; Mills 1999). Benham (1991) anchors 2005-09 and 2010-14: denial of a directed verdict stands unless a guilty finding would be clearly unreasonable on the whole evidence. In 2010-14 Winstead (2009) adopted the Kotteakos fair-assurance test, which leads with Kotteakos (1946) and Shane (2007). English (1999) anchors from 2015-19 through 2025-29, with abuse-of-discretion review and strict limits on common-scheme evidence under KRE 404(b), and Bell (1994) requiring cautious application. Thompson (2000) adopted Kumho Tire; Martin (2006) defined palpable error as manifest injustice; Brown (2010) held that jurors' knowledge of a retrial did not violate the defendant's rights; Brewer (2006) on forfeiture; Padgett (2010) and Ordway (2013) on wanton and intentional murder enter later. In 2025-29 Gross (1983) and McQueen (1997) enter.

name: Celotex and the 1986 summary-judgment trilogy, 1990-99
description: The 1986 summary-judgment trilogy itself, 1990-99, with Celotex (anchor of both slices) letting a movant point to missing evidence, Anderson v. Liberty Lobby asking whether a reasonable jury could find for the nonmovant under the governing burden, and Matsushita requiring more than metaphysical doubt; Diebold (1962) and Cities Service (1968) persist. history: Dominant rule: Celotex (1986) anchors both slices. The trilogy transformed summary judgment from a disfavored device into a routine test of whether the nonmovant has evidence for each element. Celotex held a movant without the trial burden may discharge its burden by pointing to an absence of evidence; Anderson v. Liberty Lobby (1986) asked whether a reasonable jury could find for the nonmovant under the applicable standard of proof; Matsushita (1986) held that implausible inferences and metaphysical doubt are not enough. Older cases persist: Diebold (1962) on inferences and First National Bank v. Cities Service (1968) on nonmovant evidence. In 1990-94 the applications are mixed civil appeals (Reid v. State Farm 1986, Waltman 1989, Ross 1985). In 1995-99 Fifth Circuit en banc Little v. Liquid Air (1994) and other circuit cases (Gallo 1994, Hedberg 1995, Chambers 1994) apply the standard in employment and commercial disputes. The rule is stable across the lineage.
rule: Summary judgment is proper where the movant shows the absence of evidence on an element the nonmovant must prove at trial (Celotex), and the nonmovant must then come forward with specific facts on which a reasonable jury could return a verdict under the applicable evidentiary standard (Anderson), more than metaphysical doubt (Matsushita), with inferences drawn in the nonmovant's favor (Diebold).

changes.what: Inferences are viewed most favorably to the nonmovant, but summary judgment is proper where the nonmovant's evidence lacks probative force.

changes.case: Little v. Liquid Air Corp. (5th Cir. en banc)

name: New Mexico appellate briefing and preservation: In re Adoption of Doe, Headley
description: New Mexico appellate practice, 2010-24: issues need argument and authority (In re Adoption of Doe, 1984), record citations and preservation (Crutchfield, 2004; Headley, 2005; Muse, 2008), and summary-calendar responses must point out specific errors (Mondragon, 1988). Self (1998) anchors 2010-14, Hennessy (1998) 2015-19 and Corona (2014) 2020-24. Also summary-judgment burdens (Romero, 2010).

previous.name: New Mexico civil appeals: briefing and preservation
previous.description: New Mexico appellate rules: issues unsupported by cited authority are not reviewed (In re Adoption of Doe), summary-calendar responses must point out specific errors (Mondragon), and preservation (Self).

history: Dominant rule: a New Mexico appellate court reviews only issues preserved below and adequately briefed with argument, authority and citations to the record. The rule rests on In re Adoption of Doe (1984). Self (1998) anchors 2010-14, when the unit forms from three 2005-09 units, with Headley (2005) declining cursory arguments lacking record citations, Sims (1996) on reading statutes against background law, and Woolwine (1987). Crutchfield (2004) and Muse (2008) refuse to search the record for facts or rulings. How it changed: in 2015-19, after merging with New Mexico criminal appeals, Hennessy (1998) anchors, with Mondragon (1988) requiring summary-calendar responses to point out specific errors and Franklin (1967) and Boyer (1985) letting counsel advance a client's contentions; Harris (2013) also leads. Corona v. Corona (2014) anchors 2020-24, with Willock (2013), Britton (2018) and Freeman (2018) on dismissal as a sanction for fault. Alongside: summary-judgment burdens (Romero, 2010), viable docketing-statement amendments (Moore, 1989; Salgado, 1991) and the duty to defend (BPLW, 2009). No change of substance appears; the lineage restates settled briefing rules.
