name: Jurisdictional versus claim-processing rules after Arbaugh: Henderson, Auburn, Wong
description: A single 2015-19 slice on the clear-statement rule for jurisdiction: requirements are jurisdictional only if Congress clearly says so (Arbaugh, 2006), so registration (Muchnick, 2010), veterans' and Medicare appeal deadlines (Henderson, 2011; Auburn, 2013) and FTCA limits (Kwai Fun Wong, 2015) are claim-processing rules. Bowles (2007, anchor) keeps statutory appeal periods jurisdictional; immigration notice cases (Pereira) also join.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Jurisdictional versus claim-processing rules (2015)
previous.description: The Supreme Court's sorting of deadlines and prerequisites into jurisdictional rules and nonjurisdictional claim-processing rules (Bowles, Arbaugh, Henderson v. Shinseki, Auburn Regional, Reed Elsevier v. Muchnick, Kwai Fun Wong, Gonzalez v. Thaler), with equitable tolling. Successor to the deadline thread of 26305.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, contrastive pass from family evidence)

history: Dominant rule: courts treat a statutory requirement as jurisdictional only when Congress clearly ranks it so, and otherwise as a claim-processing rule that can be waived, forfeited or tolled; statutory periods for appeal between courts remain jurisdictional. How it changed: the lineage exists only in 2015-19, merged from an Article III standing unit and the fugitive-disentitlement and Hague unit of 2010-14, and Bowles (2007) anchors it. Its foundations are Zipes (1982) and Irwin (1991) on non-jurisdictional, tollable limits, Kontrick (2004) on court-made rules, and Arbaugh (2006) on the clear-statement test, set against John R. Sand & Gravel (2008), which kept the Tucker Act limit jurisdictional by precedent. After Bowles the Court kept narrowing the category: Muchnick (2010) for copyright registration, Henderson (2011) for the veterans' appeal deadline, Gonzalez (2012) for COA defects and finality under § 2244, Auburn (2013) for an administrative appeal deadline, and Kwai Fun Wong (2015) for FTCA limits. Alongside: immigration cases on whether a defective notice to appear deprives the immigration court of jurisdiction (Pereira, 2018). The unit splits into removal-review and appeal-deadline lineages in 2020-24.
rule: A statutory prerequisite or deadline is jurisdictional only if Congress clearly states that it is; otherwise it is a nonjurisdictional claim-processing rule, though statutory deadlines for appealing from one Article III court to another remain jurisdictional (Bowles).

changes.what: Absent a clear statement from Congress, a statutory limitation on coverage is treated as nonjurisdictional.
The statutory time to file a civil notice of appeal is jurisdictional; anchor of the slice.

changes.case: Reed Elsevier v. Muchnick; Henderson v. Shinseki; Gonzalez v. Thaler; Sebelius v. Auburn Regional Medical Center
changes.what: The copyright registration requirement, the 120-day veterans' appeal deadline and a 180-day administrative-appeal limit are claim-processing rules, and a COA's defects are not jurisdictional.

changes.case: United States v. Kwai Fun Wong
changes.what: The FTCA's time limits are nonjurisdictional and subject to equitable tolling.
Brought into the lineage because courts asked whether a defective notice to appear deprives immigration courts of jurisdiction; Pereira was confined to the stop-time rule.

name: California arbitration unconscionability (Armendariz) and limits after Concepcion
description: California arbitration enforcement: Armendariz (2000) requires procedural and substantive unconscionability on a sliding scale and sets minimum terms for employment arbitration; Moncharsh (1992) limits review of awards. Discover Bank (2005) and Gentry (2007) barred class waivers until Concepcion (2011) abrogated them (Iskanian, 2014); Pinnacle, Sanchez and Baltazar (2012-16) restated unconscionability, McGill (2017) and Kho (2019) followed.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: California arbitration unconscionability
previous.description: Enforcing arbitration agreements in California: procedural and substantive unconscionability (Armendariz, Pinnacle, Sanchez, Baltazar), limited judicial review of awards (Moncharsh), class waivers after Concepcion (Discover Bank, Iskanian on PAGA) and fraud in the inducement (Engalla).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: Armendariz (2000) anchors every slice from 2010-14: an arbitration agreement fails if procedurally and substantively unconscionable, the more of one the less of the other, and employer-imposed arbitration of unwaivable statutory claims needs a neutral arbitrator, adequate discovery, a written award, all statutory remedies and no unusual costs for the employee. How it changed: in 2005-09 the unit is about review of awards: Moncharsh (1992) bars review for errors of fact or law, with Buckner (2002) anchoring and Coutee (2003) on manifest disregard. Discover Bank (2005) and Gentry (2007) invalidated many class-action waivers; Concepcion (2011) abrogated them, as Iskanian (2014) recognised while exempting representative PAGA claims. Pinnacle (2012) bound homeowners to CC&R clauses, Moreno (2013) confirmed that general unconscionability rules survive Concepcion, Sanchez (2015) and Baltazar (2016) restated the standard, McGill (2017) invalidated waivers of public injunctive relief, and Kho (2019) leads 2020-29 on oppression and surprise. Also: waiver of the right to arbitrate (Engalla, 1997; PacifiCare, 2003).
rule: In California an arbitration agreement is unenforceable if both procedurally and substantively unconscionable, on a sliding scale, and a mandatory employment agreement covering unwaivable statutory claims must meet Armendariz's minimum requirements (neutral arbitrator, adequate discovery, written award, full remedies, employer-paid forum costs); arbitral awards are otherwise reviewable only on narrow grounds (Moncharsh).

changes.what: An arbitrator's errors of fact or law generally cannot be reviewed; Moncharsh leads 2005-09, when the anchor is Buckner (2002) on limited review.

changes.case: Armendariz v. Foundation Health Psychcare Services
changes.what: Procedural and substantive unconscionability on a sliding scale, a modicum of bilaterality, and minimum requirements for arbitration of FEHA claims; Armendariz anchors from 2010-14.

changes.case: Discover Bank v. Superior Court; Gentry v. Superior Court
changes.what: Class-action waivers in adhesive consumer and some employment contracts were unenforceable.

changes.case: AT&T Mobility v. Concepcion; Iskanian v. CLS Transportation
changes.what: Concepcion abrogated Discover Bank and, by extension, Gentry; Iskanian (2014) so held but kept representative PAGA claims outside individual arbitration waivers.

changes.case: Pinnacle Museum Tower; Sonic-Calabasas v. Moreno; Sanchez v. Valencia Holding; Baltazar v. Forever 21
changes.what: State unconscionability rules survive if they do not disfavor arbitration; adhesion alone shows some procedural unconscionability, and substantive terms must be unreasonably one-sided.

changes.case: McGill v. Citibank; OTO v. Kho
changes.what: Waivers of public injunctive relief are invalid, and oppressive circumstances and surprise in presenting an agreement can carry high procedural unconscionability.

name: Civil forfeiture as punishment: Calero-Toledo, One Assortment, Halper to Ursery
description: Whether civil in rem forfeiture and penalties are punishment, 1980-99. Through the 1980s forfeiture is civil and remedial (Calero-Toledo 1974, Emerald Cut Stones 1972, One Assortment of 89 Firearms 1984). Halper (1989) let disproportionate civil penalties trigger double jeopardy and anchors 1995-99; Austin (1993) applied the Excessive Fines Clause to forfeiture; Ursery (1996) held civil forfeiture is not punishment, and Hudson (1997) retreated from Halper.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Civil forfeiture, double jeopardy and excessive fines
previous.description: Whether civil sanctions are punishment: Halper and Kurth Ranch on double jeopardy, Austin applying the Excessive Fines Clause to forfeiture, Ursery and Hudson retreating to the Ward/Mendoza-Martinez civil-versus-criminal test.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session subagents, from cocite evidence; second pass differentiated near-duplicates)

history: Dominant rule: a civil in rem forfeiture or civil penalty is not criminal punishment unless the statute is so punitive in purpose or effect as to override the legislature's civil label (Ward 1980; One Assortment of 89 Firearms 1984). How it changed: in 1980-84 (Ivers anchor) and 1985-89 (Calero-Toledo anchor) the lineage is the law of federal civil forfeiture: Calero-Toledo (1974) allowed seizure without pre-seizure notice and hearing and forfeiture of an innocent owner's property, Emerald Cut Stones (1972) held a criminal acquittal does not bar a later forfeiture, and One Assortment of 89 Firearms (1984) treated forfeiture as civil. In 1990-94 real-property forfeitures enter (4492 South Livonia Road anchors) alongside Halper (1989) and Austin (1993). In 1995-99 Halper anchors as Kurth Ranch (1994) treats a drug tax as punishment and two circuits bar forfeiture after conviction until Ursery (1996) reverses, and Hudson (1997) overruled Halper in part.
rule: A civil in rem forfeiture or civil penalty is not criminal punishment for double jeopardy purposes unless its purpose or effect is so punitive as to override the legislature's civil label.

changes.case: One Lot Emerald Cut Stones; Calero-Toledo v. Pearson Yacht Leasing; United States v. One Assortment of 89 Firearms
changes.what: Civil forfeiture is a remedial in rem sanction, unaffected by an acquittal and available without pre-seizure hearing in limited circumstances.
A civil penalty can be punishment for double jeopardy when it serves retribution and deterrence rather than remedial ends.

changes.case: Austin v. United States; Department of Revenue v. Kurth Ranch
changes.what: Civil forfeiture is subject to the Excessive Fines Clause, and a punitive drug tax is punishment that must be imposed in the first prosecution.

changes.case: United States v. $405,089.23 (9th Cir.); United States v. Ursery (6th Cir.)
changes.what: Read Halper and Austin to bar civil forfeiture after a criminal conviction for the same conduct.
In rem civil forfeitures are neither punishment nor criminal for double jeopardy purposes.
Disavowed Halper's approach and returned to the Ward/Mendoza-Martinez test of the statute on its face.

before_differentiation.name: Civil sanctions as punishment: Halper and Austin, then Ursery and Hudson
before_differentiation.description: Whether civil sanctions are punishment. Halper (1989) let disproportionate civil penalties trigger double jeopardy and anchors 1990-99; Austin (1993) applied the Excessive Fines Clause to forfeiture and Kurth Ranch (1994) treated a drug tax as punishment. Ursery (1996) held civil forfeiture is not punishment, and Hudson (1997, anchor 2000-04) abandoned Halper for the Ward/Mendoza-Martinez test, later applied to sex-offender registration (Smith v. Doe 2003).

distinct_from.how: Asks whether civil forfeiture is punishment at all, not when a criminal retrial or resentencing is barred.
Civil forfeiture and penalties, not multiple criminal punishments and sufficiency review in 1985-89.
The civil-forfeiture strand of its parent, reaching back to the 1980s forfeiture cases, without the Grady/Dixon same-offense phase.
Civil sanctions as punishment, not retrial after mistrial or acquittal.

name: Illinois civil appeals: de novo summary judgment and policy construction (Outboard Marine)
description: A mixed Illinois civil lineage held together by de novo review and contract construction. Outboard Marine (1992), anchoring from 2010-14, made summary judgment review de novo and construes ambiguous insurance terms for the insured, with the duty to defend measured by the complaint. Ward (1990), on duty despite open and obvious hazards, anchors 2005-09 with Marshall (2006). In 2015-19 civil trial rules (Pedrick, Maple, Foutch) merge in.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Illinois insurance coverage: duty to defend
previous.description: Illinois insurance law: the insurer's duty to defend measured against the underlying complaint, ambiguities construed for the insured (Outboard Marine), and reading policies so no provision is meaningless.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: there is no single doctrine here; the anchor changes. In 2005-09 the anchor is Ward (1990): a landowner can owe a duty despite an open and obvious danger when an invitee's distraction is foreseeable. Marshall (2006, duty to protect invitees from a third party's car), Bucheleres (1996) and Sollami (2002) on obvious risks, and Beretta (2004, no public nuisance for gun sales) lead. How it changed: from 2010-14 the anchor becomes Outboard Marine (1992), as an insurance-coverage lineage merges in. Outboard Marine held summary judgments are reviewed de novo, ambiguous policy terms are construed for the insured, and the duty to defend turns on the complaint's allegations. Crum & Forster (1993) limits indemnity to facts actually covered, Home Insurance (2004) addresses waiver and equitable contribution, Valley Forge (2006) finds advertising-injury coverage for TCPA fax claims, and Wilson (2010) lets courts look beyond the complaint. Khan (2011) and DeLuna (2006, fraudulent concealment tolls legal-malpractice repose) also lead. In 2015-19 the Illinois civil-trial unit merges in (Pedrick, Maple, Foutch's complete-record rule, Hodge on § 2-619 motions), and the lineage splits in 2020-24.
rule: Summary judgment is reviewed de novo and an insurance policy is construed as a whole, with ambiguous provisions read in favour of the insured; an insurer must defend if the underlying complaint alleges facts potentially within coverage (Outboard Marine).

changes.what: A landowner may owe a duty of reasonable care despite an open and obvious risk where it is foreseeable that the invitee will be distracted.

changes.case: Outboard Marine Corp. v. Liberty Mutual Insurance
changes.what: Reviewing courts review summary judgment de novo; ambiguous policy terms are construed for the insured and the duty to defend is measured by the complaint's allegations.

changes.case: Crum & Forster Managers Corp. v. Resolution Trust Corp.
changes.what: The duty to indemnify arises only if the facts actually fall within coverage, and policies are read in light of the insured subject matter and the whole contract.
A business owes invitees a duty under Restatement § 314A to protect against a third party's vehicle crashing into the premises; the complaint stated a duty.
A court may look beyond the underlying complaint to determine the duty to defend.

name: Categorical approach to prior convictions: Taylor, Shepard, Descamps, Mathis
description: The categorical approach to prior convictions in sentencing and immigration: compare statutory elements to the generic offense (Taylor 1990), using only Shepard (2005) documents for divisible statutes (Descamps 2013, Mathis 2016). The ACCA residual clause, read in James, Begay and Chambers, was struck as vague by Johnson (2015), which anchors 2015-19; Dimaya (2018) and Davis (2019) followed, and Borden (2021) excluded reckless crimes.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: ACCA and the categorical approach
previous.description: Classifying prior convictions for sentencing and immigration: the categorical and modified categorical approaches (Taylor, Shepard, Descamps, Mathis), violent felonies under the Armed Career Criminal Act and its void residual clause (Begay, James, Johnson 2015), and generic offenses (Duenas-Alvarez, Moncrieffe).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: courts classify prior convictions by the elements of the statute, not the underlying facts, under Taylor (1990), which anchors 1995-2014. How it changed: in 2000-04 the approach spread to immigration aggravated felonies (Corona-Sanchez, Ye), and Leocal (2004) excluded negligent DUI from § 16. Shepard (2005) limited the documents courts may consult, and Duenas-Alvarez (2007) required a realistic probability of nongeneric prosecution. The residual clause produced James (2007), Begay (2008, purposeful, violent and aggressive), Chambers (2009) and Sykes (2011); Johnson I (2010) required violent force. Descamps (2013) barred the modified approach for indivisible statutes. Johnson II (2015) voided the residual clause, overruled James and Sykes, and anchors 2015-19; Welch (2016) made it retroactive and Beckles (2017) left the Guidelines outside vagueness review. Mathis (2016) distinguished means from elements and anchors 2020-24, with Dimaya (2018), Davis (2019), Shular (2020) and Borden (2021).
rule: Whether a prior conviction counts as a predicate (an ACCA violent felony, a crime of violence, an aggravated felony) is decided by comparing the elements of the statute of conviction with the generic offense, not the defendant's conduct; only for divisible statutes listing alternative elements may a court consult a limited set of record documents to identify the offense.

changes.what: Categorical approach with a generic definition of burglary for ACCA enhancement.
DUI requiring no more than negligence is not a crime of violence under 18 U.S.C. § 16.
The modified categorical approach is limited to charging documents, plea agreements and colloquies, and comparable judicial records, not police reports.
The ACCA residual clause reached attempted burglary but not DUI or failure to report, which were not purposeful, violent and aggressive.
'Physical force' in the elements clause means violent force; simple battery by touching does not qualify.

changes.case: Descamps v. United States; Moncrieffe v. Holder
changes.what: The modified categorical approach does not apply to indivisible statutes; a realistic probability of prosecution governs overbreadth.

changes.case: Johnson v. United States (Johnson II); Welch v. United States
changes.what: The ACCA residual clause is void for vagueness, overruling James and Sykes, and the rule applies retroactively.
Statutes listing alternative means rather than elements are indivisible; courts may not use the modified approach for them.

changes.case: Sessions v. Dimaya; United States v. Davis; Borden v. United States
changes.what: Vagueness holding extended to § 16(b) and § 924(c)'s residual clause; reckless offenses do not satisfy the elements clause.

name: Texas arbitration by mandamus: Jack B. Anglin v. Tipps, FirstMerit, waiver
description: Texas arbitration by mandamus: under Tipps (1992), the FAA governs and preempts contrary state rules, and the movant must prove a valid agreement covering the dispute (Webster 2003; Kellogg Brown & Root 2005), after which a strong presumption favors arbitration. Waiver needs substantial invocation of litigation plus prejudice (Marshall 1995, Vesta 2006, Perry Homes v. Cull 2008). From 2010 it also takes in contract construction (Coker 1983).
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Texas arbitration mandamus
previous.description: Compelling arbitration in Texas by mandamus: the FAA and Texas Arbitration Act (Jack B. Anglin v. Tipps), scope and validity of the agreement (In re FirstMerit, Kellogg Brown & Root, Halliburton), and waiver by litigation conduct (In re Vesta, Bruce Terminix).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: Jack B. Anglin Co. v. Tipps (1992) anchors 1995-99 and 2005-09. The FAA preempts the DTPA's nonwaiver provision, a refusal to compel arbitration under the FAA is corrected by mandamus, and disputed facts on a motion to compel need an evidentiary hearing. How it changed: Oakwood Mobile Homes (1999) anchors 2000-04, placing the burden on the movant to prove the agreement and rejecting unconscionability for unequal bargaining power. FirstMerit (2001) and Halliburton (2002) narrowed unconscionability and illusoriness defenses, while J.M. Davidson v. Webster (2003) held an agreement the employer could end without notice illusory. Kellogg Brown & Root (2005) said the pro-arbitration presumption applies only once a valid agreement exists, and Weekley Homes (2005), Palm Harbor (2006) and Labatt (2009) set when nonsignatories are bound. Waiver stayed hard to prove (Marshall 1995, Bruce Terminix 1998, Vesta 2006), with Perry Homes v. Cull (2008) applying a totality test. From 2010-14 Webster anchors as a contract-interpretation unit merges in, adding Coker (1983) on ambiguity. In 2020-24 Henry (2018), G.T. Leach (2015) and Jody James Farms (2018) lead on waiver and nonsignatories.
rule: In Texas a party seeking to compel arbitration must first prove a valid agreement, under ordinary state contract law, that covers the dispute; the presumption favoring arbitration then applies, mandamus corrects a refusal to compel under the FAA, and waiver by litigation requires substantial invocation of the judicial process plus prejudice, against a strong presumption.

changes.case: Jack B. Anglin Co. v. Tipps
changes.what: The FAA preempts the DTPA's nonwaiver rule, mandamus is the remedy for denial of arbitration under the FAA, and disputed facts require an evidentiary hearing.

changes.case: Prudential Securities v. Marshall; EZ Pawn v. Mancias; In re Bruce Terminix
changes.what: Delay or discovery does not waive arbitration unless the opponent proves prejudice from substantial invocation of the judicial process.

changes.case: In re FirstMerit Bank; In re Halliburton Co.
changes.what: Unconscionability requires proof of actual costs or unfairness, and an employer's limited right to amend does not make an arbitration agreement illusory.
An agreement the employer can modify or end without notice is illusory, and a party must prove a valid agreement covering the dispute.

changes.case: In re Kellogg Brown & Root; In re Weekley Homes; In re Labatt Food Service
changes.what: The presumption favoring arbitration arises only after a valid agreement is shown; nonsignatories are bound only under contract and estoppel principles, and wrongful-death beneficiaries can be bound.
Waiver is judged on the totality of the circumstances, and orders compelling arbitration are reviewable after final judgment.

name: Plain error for unpreserved Booker claims: the circuit split on prejudice (2005)
description: The 2005 circuit split over plain-error review of unpreserved Booker claims, in a one-slice 2005-09 lineage anchored by Olano (1993): all agreed mandatory-Guidelines sentencing was plain error, but the Sixth Circuit presumed prejudice (Barnett, Oliver) while the First, Eighth and Tenth required a showing of a likely lower sentence (Antonakopoulos, Pirani, Gonzalez-Huerta), under Dominguez Benitez (2004). Hahn (2004) on appeal waivers.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Booker plain error across circuits: the prejudice-prong split (2005)
previous.description: Circuit decisions in 2005 applying Olano, Johnson and Cotton plain-error review to unpreserved Booker claims, with Dominguez Benitez and Vonn on substantial rights; Gonzalez-Huerta, Barnett, Pirani and Oliver show how circuits split on the prejudice prong.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session subagents, from cocite evidence; second pass differentiated near-duplicates)

history: Dominant rule: Olano (1993) anchors this single 2005-09 slice: forfeited errors are corrected only if plain, affecting substantial rights and seriously affecting the fairness, integrity or public reputation of proceedings. Johnson (1997) judged plainness at the time of appeal, which brought pre-Booker sentences within the test, and Cotton (2002), Vonn (2002) and Dominguez Benitez (2004) defined the substantial-rights inquiry as a reasonable probability of a different result shown on the whole record. How it changed: after Booker (2005), every circuit treated sentencing under mandatory Guidelines as plain error, but they split on prejudice. The Sixth Circuit in Barnett (2005) presumed prejudice, so a middle-of-the-range sentence did not rebut it, and Oliver (2005) remanded where the Guidelines were treated as mandatory. The First Circuit (Antonakopoulos), the Eighth (Pirani, en banc) and the Tenth (Gonzalez-Huerta, en banc) put the burden on the defendant, and a bottom-of-range sentence alone was not enough; Dazey (2005) found the fourth prong met where enhancement facts were contested. Hahn (2004) governs enforcement of appeal waivers. The split was never resolved by the Supreme Court and the lineage dissolves into plain-error review by 2010-14.
rule: Unpreserved Booker error is reviewed under Olano's four-part plain-error test; sentencing under mandatory Guidelines is error that is plain, but circuits divided on the third prong, some presuming prejudice and others requiring the defendant to show a reasonable probability of a lower sentence under advisory Guidelines.

changes.case: United States v. Olano; Johnson v. United States
changes.what: Four-part plain-error test, with plainness judged at the time of appeal. Olano anchors this one-slice lineage.

changes.case: United States v. Cotton; United States v. Vonn; United States v. Dominguez Benitez
changes.what: Plain-error review uses the whole record, and the defendant must show a reasonable probability of a different outcome.

changes.case: United States v. Hahn (10th Cir. en banc)
changes.what: Appeal waivers are enforced if the issue falls within the waiver, the waiver was knowing and voluntary, and enforcement would not cause a miscarriage of justice.

changes.case: United States v. Barnett; United States v. Oliver (6th Cir.)
changes.what: The Sixth Circuit presumed prejudice from mandatory-Guidelines sentencing, so a middle-of-range sentence did not rebut it, and remanded for resentencing.

changes.case: United States v. Pirani (8th Cir. en banc); United States v. Gonzalez-Huerta (10th Cir. en banc); United States v. Antonakopoulos (1st Cir.)
changes.what: Other circuits required the defendant to show a reasonable probability of a lighter sentence, and a bottom-of-range sentence alone did not suffice.

name: New Jersey summary judgment (Brill) and the net-opinion rule (Townsend)
description: New Jersey summary judgment under Brill (1995): judgment is proper when a rational factfinder could reach only one result on the competent evidence, reviewed de novo (Templo Fuente, 2016). From 2015-19 the net-opinion rule leads: an expert must give the why and wherefore, or the opinion is inadmissible and cannot defeat the motion (Polzo 2008, Davis 2014, Townsend 2015).
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: New Jersey civil: summary judgment and net opinions
previous.description: New Jersey summary judgment under Brill v. Guardian Life, and the net-opinion rule excluding expert conclusions without factual or methodological support (Townsend v. Pierre, Pomerantz Paper).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: Brill v. Guardian Life (1995) anchors every slice from 2010-14: a court grants summary judgment when the competent evidence, viewed for the nonmovant, would allow a rational factfinder only one conclusion, and the nonmovant cannot defeat the motion by pointing to immaterial or insubstantial disputes. The 2005-09 slice starts from the plain-language statutory unit (DiProspero, O'Connell). How it changed: from 2015-19 the slice grows fivefold and the net-opinion rule becomes its second pillar. Polzo (2008) and Pomerantz Paper (2011) excluded expert conclusions without factual foundation or a recognised standard; Davis v. Brickman (2014) and Townsend v. Pierre (2015) applied the rule at summary judgment, requiring the expert to explain the why and wherefore and to base the opinion on N.J.R.E. 703 facts. Templo Fuente (2016) and Bhagat (2014) restated de novo review. Also: Globe Motor (2016) on contract enforcement as written, LAD pretext and limitations (Zive, Henry), CEPA prima facie case (Dzwonar), and Celotex (1986) cited alongside Brill in the partial 2025-29 slice.
rule: New Jersey summary judgment is proper when the competent evidence, viewed most favourably to the nonmovant, would let a rational factfinder reach only one result (Brill), and an expert opinion without factual support or reasoning is an inadmissible net opinion that cannot create a genuine issue.

changes.case: Brill v. Guardian Life Insurance Co.

name: Alabama capital appeals 1990-94: unobjected plain error (Kennedy, Kuenzel)
description: Alabama death-case review in a single 1990-94 slice anchored by Kuenzel (1990-91): the court searches the record for plain error, and a failure to object weighs against prejudice but does not bar review (Ex parte Kennedy 1985); the heinous-atrocious-cruel aggravator turns on the manner of killing (Bankhead 1991); confessions and custody (Magwood, Hooks) and reasonable-doubt instructions (Ex parte White 1991) lead.

history: Dominant rule: Alabama appellate courts review death sentences for plain error, treating a failure to object as weighing against prejudice rather than barring review (Ex parte Kennedy, 1985), and review the aggravating circumstances found. Kuenzel (1990) and Ex parte Kuenzel (1991) anchor the lineage's only slice, 1990-94, which formed from three 1985-89 units and splits three ways in 1995-99. How it changed: no change within the span. Ex parte Bankhead (1991) upheld the heinous-atrocious-cruel aggravator on the manner of the killing. Alongside: voluntariness of statements and custody (Ex parte Magwood 1986, Hooks 1987), complicity and intent in robbery-murders (Ex parte Womack 1983, Hallford 1988), Ex parte Harrell (1985), and reasonable-doubt instructions without 'moral certainty' (Ex parte White 1991). McComb (1949), a civil-contempt case, appears among the leading cases as a citation artifact.
rule: Alabama appellate courts search the record of a death case for plain error, with a failure to object weighing against any claim of prejudice (Ex parte Kennedy), and review the guilt and sentencing phases, including aggravating circumstances such as heinous, atrocious or cruel, for error.

changes.what: Failure to object does not preclude plain-error review in a capital case but weighs against a claim of prejudice.

round1.description: Alabama capital-case review: plain-error search of the record with failure to object weighing against prejudice (Ex parte Kennedy 1985), the heinous-atrocious-cruel aggravator (Kyzer 1981, Bankhead 1991), and prosecutorial argument judged in context (Young 1985). Kuenzel (1990) anchors 1990-2004 and Bankhead 2005-09; earlier slices center on pretrial publicity (Irvin v. Dowd, Murphy v. Florida) and Beck (1981).
round1.history: Dominant rule: Alabama appellate courts review death sentences for plain error and apply a limited heinous-atrocious-cruel aggravator. Florida (1975) holding that exposure to news does not alone show juror bias. After merging with death-penalty material, Beck (1981), the Alabama Supreme Court's response to Beck v. Alabama, anchors 1985-89, with Ex parte Kyzer (1981) narrowing the heinous-atrocious-cruel aggravator. Ex parte Kennedy (1985) held that failure to object does not bar plain-error review but weighs against prejudice, and Baldwin (1985) adopted Strickland. Kuenzel (1990) enters and anchors 1990-2004 with Ex parte Bankhead (1991) and Taylor (1994-95), applying these rules to aggravators, photographs and argument. Haney (1991-92) upheld aggravators for a defendant who hired the killer under Tison. United States v. Young (1985) and Frady (1982) lead 2000-09, and Bankhead anchors 2005-09. The current label notes some civil-contempt material mixed into the parentheticals.
round1.rule: In Alabama capital appeals the courts search the record for plain error even without objection, though a failure to object weighs against a claim of prejudice; the 'heinous, atrocious or cruel' aggravator is limited to conscienceless or pitiless killings that are unnecessarily torturous, and prosecutorial argument is judged in context of the whole trial (Young).

name: New York summary judgment: prima facie showing first (Zuckerman, Winegrad, Alvarez)
description: New York summary judgment: the movant must make a prima facie showing with admissible evidence or the motion fails regardless of the opposition (Winegrad, 1985); the opponent must then show a triable issue in admissible form (Zuckerman, 1980; Alvarez, 1986). Gordon (1986) anchors 1990-99 on constructive notice in slip-and-fall cases; Zuckerman anchors 2000-04 and Alvarez from 2005-09, applied mostly to premises liability.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, round 2 after the lineage re-link)

previous.name: New York summary judgment and premises liability
previous.description: New York summary-judgment burdens under Zuckerman, Winegrad and Alvarez, most often applied in premises-liability cases on actual or constructive notice of a dangerous condition (Gordon, Basso).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session subagents, from cocite evidence; second pass differentiated near-duplicates)

history: Dominant rule: the two-step New York summary-judgment burden. How it changed: the lineage begins in 1990-94 and 1995-99 as a premises-liability unit anchored by Gordon (1986): constructive notice needs a visible and apparent defect present long enough to be discovered and remedied, and a general awareness of a hazard is not enough (Piacquadio, 1994; Bykofsky, 1994; Anderson, 1988). In 2000-04 Zuckerman (1980), Winegrad (1985) and Alvarez (1986) enter and Zuckerman anchors: the movant must first make a prima facie showing with admissible proof, failing which the motion is denied whatever the opposition, and the opponent must then lay bare admissible evidence of a triable issue. Alvarez anchors from 2005-09 through 2020-24 as the unit grows past 200 cases. The burden rule itself does not change. Its settings remain mostly premises liability: Basso (1976) and its single reasonable-care duty, trivial sidewalk defects (Trincere, 1997; Hutchinson, 2015) and liability for foreseeable injuries (Cupo, 2003). Stukas (2011) leads from 2010-14. Winegrad anchors the partial 2025-29 slice, which absorbs Labor Law cases (Ross, 1993).
rule: A New York summary-judgment movant must make a prima facie showing of entitlement with admissible evidence, or the motion fails regardless of the opposing papers; only then must the opponent produce admissible proof of a triable issue.

changes.what: Replaced the status categories of entrants with a single duty of reasonable care for landowners.

changes.case: Zuckerman v. City of New York
changes.what: Once the movant makes its showing, the opponent must lay bare admissible proof of a triable issue, not conclusions.

changes.case: Winegrad v. NYU Medical Center; Alvarez v. Prospect Hospital
changes.what: A movant's failure to make a prima facie showing requires denial regardless of the opposition.

changes.case: Gordon v. American Museum of Natural History; Piacquadio v. Recine Realty
changes.what: Constructive notice requires a visible, apparent defect existing long enough to be discovered; general awareness of a hazard is not notice of the particular condition.

changes.case: Trincere v. County of Suffolk; Hutchinson v. Sheridan Hill House
changes.what: Whether a sidewalk defect is trivial depends on all the circumstances, not a minimum dimension.

Winegrad (1985) and Alvarez (1986) join in 1990-94: a movant's failure to make a prima facie showing requires denial regardless of the opposing papers, and Alvarez anchors from 2005-09 as the lineage grows to over 200 cases. How it changed: no change to the burden rule itself; from 2005-09 the cases applying it are mostly premises liability, bringing in Basso (1976, a single reasonable-care duty for landowners), Gordon (1986, constructive notice needs a visible defect present long enough to be found) and Trincere (1997) and Hutchinson (2015) on trivial sidewalk defects. name: New York SEQRA review and standing: Jackson v. UDC hard look, Society of Plastics
description: New York SEQRA challenges: courts ask only whether the agency took a hard look at relevant environmental concerns and gave a reasoned elaboration (Aldrich, 1985; Jackson v. UDC, 1986, the usual anchor). Chinese Staff (1986) read SEQRA more broadly than NEPA; Society of Plastics (1991) set the special-injury and zone-of-interests test for standing; Riverkeeper (2007) anchors 2010-14.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: New York land use, SEQRA and standing
previous.description: New York challenges to land-use and agency action: SEQRA environmental-impact review (Jackson v. UDC, Chinese Staff, Riverkeeper), standing to sue (Society of Plastics, Sun-Brite), and Article 78 procedure (Solnick).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session subagents, from cocite evidence; second pass differentiated near-duplicates)

history: Dominant rule: judicial review of a SEQRA determination is limited to whether the agency identified the relevant areas of environmental concern, took a hard look at them and made a reasoned elaboration of its decision; courts do not substitute their judgment. How it changed: the small 1980-84 slice is Article 78 review of Medicaid nursing-home rates (Whalen, Solnick), drift from the later topic. From 1985-89 SEQRA cases take over: Aldrich (1985) anchors and Jackson v. UDC (1986) entered, which anchors 1995-99 and 2005-09; H.O.M.E.S. (1979) drew the review standard from NEPA cases. Chinese Staff (1986) required an EIS whenever there may be a significant effect, including on neighbourhood character. Akpan (1990) anchors 1990-94 with Sun-Brite (1987) on property-owner standing in zoning. Society of Plastics (1991) anchors 2000-04 and requires a special injury within SEQRA's zone of interests. Riverkeeper (2007) anchors 2010-14, applying the hard-look standard to supplemental review, alongside land-use challenges (Aspen Creek, Troy Sand & Gravel).
rule: A court reviewing an agency's SEQRA determination asks only whether it identified the relevant areas of environmental concern, took a hard look at them and made a reasoned elaboration of its decision, and a challenger must show an environmental injury different from the public at large within SEQRA's zone of interests.

changes.case: Aldrich v. Pattison; Jackson v. New York State UDC
changes.what: Review of SEQRA findings is limited to whether the agency followed lawful procedure and took a hard look with a reasoned elaboration; courts may not weigh new evidence or substitute their judgment.

changes.case: Chinese Staff & Workers Ass'n v. City of New York
changes.what: Unlike NEPA, SEQRA requires an EIS whenever an action may have a significant effect on the environment, including effects on population and neighbourhood character.

changes.case: Sun-Brite Car Wash v. Board of Zoning & Appeals
changes.what: A nearby owner or leaseholder may challenge zoning action, but zoning laws do not exist to protect business competition.

changes.case: Society of Plastics Industry v. County of Suffolk
changes.what: SEQRA standing requires an injury different in kind from the public at large and within the statute's zone of interests; associations must meet the federal-style associational test. Anchors 2000-04.

name: Rule 23 class certification: rigorous analysis from Amchem to Wal-Mart
description: Rule 23 class certification. The proponent must prove each requirement after rigorous analysis (Falcon 1982), even for settlement classes (Amchem 1997, anchor 2000-09; Ortiz 1999); Castano (1996) made state-law variation and reliance central to predominance. Wal-Mart v. Dukes (2011) tightened commonality and anchors from 2010-14, and Comcast (2013) required classwide damages models while Amgen (2013) and Tyson Foods (2016) limited that demand.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Class certification under Rule 23
previous.description: Rule 23 class certification: Falcon's rigorous analysis, Amchem and Ortiz on settlement classes, Castano and GM Pick-Up on mass torts, Wal-Mart v. Dukes on commonality, and Comcast v. Behrend and Amgen on predominance, plus Shutts and Hansberry on due process.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session subagents, from cocite evidence; second pass differentiated near-duplicates)

history: Dominant rule: certification depends on the proponent proving every Rule 23 requirement after rigorous analysis that may reach the merits (Falcon 1982). How it changed: Shutts (1985) anchors 1995-99 with due-process limits on binding absent members and on applying one state's law nationwide, alongside Castano (1996) and GM Pick-Up (1995) on predominance and settlement classes. Amchem (1997) anchors 2000-09: settlement classes must meet Rule 23 apart from trial manageability, and Ortiz (1999) restricted limited-fund classes. In 2000-04 Texas cases enter, led by Bernal (2000), which rejected 'certify now and worry later'. In 2005-09 IPO (2d Cir. 2006), Gariety (4th Cir. 2004) and Unger require evidentiary findings on contested facts. Wal-Mart (2011) enters and anchors from 2010-14, requiring a common question whose answer drives resolution. Comcast (2013) required a damages model matching the liability theory; Amgen (2013) and Tyson Foods (2016) held not every element must be proved classwide. Also: American Pipe tolling and Olean (9th Cir. en banc 2022) enter in 2020-24.
rule: The party seeking certification must affirmatively prove, after rigorous analysis that may overlap the merits, each Rule 23(a) requirement and one Rule 23(b) category, including for settlement classes, with predominance requiring that common issues, including damages, be provable classwide.

changes.what: Certification requires rigorous analysis of every Rule 23 requirement, even where it overlaps the merits.
Due process requires adequate representation, notice and opt-out for absent members in damages classes, and limits applying one state's law to all claims.
Courts must consider how variations in state law and individual reliance affect predominance and superiority.

changes.case: Amchem Products v. Windsor; Ortiz v. Fibreboard
changes.what: Settlement classes must satisfy Rule 23(a) and (b) apart from manageability; mandatory limited-fund classes require strict conditions.
Texas rejected 'certify now and worry later' and required a trial plan showing how claims would be tried.

changes.case: In re Initial Public Offering Securities Litigation (2d Cir.)
changes.what: A court must find each requirement met on the evidence, resolving factual disputes even when they overlap the merits.
Commonality requires a common answer that drives resolution; Rule 23 cannot abridge substantive rights.

changes.case: Comcast v. Behrend; Amgen; Tyson Foods v. Bouaphakeo
changes.what: Damages must be measurable classwide under the plaintiffs' theory (Comcast), but each element need not be proved classwide at certification (Amgen); representative statistical evidence can be used (Tyson).

name: Ninth Circuit asylum: particular social group (M-E-V-G-) and nexus (Zetino)
description: Ninth Circuit review of asylum and withholding denials: a particular social group must be immutable, particular and socially distinct (M-E-V-G-, W-G-R-, 2014, anchor 2015-19), and random crime bears no nexus (Zetino, 2010, anchor 2020-24). Barajas-Romero (2017) set a looser 'a reason' nexus for withholding; after Santos-Zacaria (2023) exhaustion became a mandatory claim-processing rule.

previous.name: Ninth Circuit asylum: particular social group and nexus
previous.description: Ninth Circuit review of asylum and withholding denials: particular-social-group definitions (Matter of M-E-V-G-, Henriquez-Rivas, Reyes, Delgado-Ortiz), nexus to a protected ground (Zetino, Barajas-Romero), corroboration (Aden) and substantial-evidence review.

history: Dominant rule: an applicant for asylum or withholding must show harm rising to persecution on account of a protected ground, and the agency's findings are upheld unless the evidence compels a contrary conclusion (Elias-Zacarias, 1992). How it changed: the lineage forms in 2015-19 from merged Ninth Circuit asylum units, anchored by Matter of M-E-V-G- (2014), which with W-G-R- requires a particular social group to share an immutable characteristic and be particular and socially distinct; Henriquez-Rivas (en banc 2013) had rejected an on-sight visibility reading. Reyes (2016), Delgado-Ortiz (2010) and Conde Quevedo (2020) rejected deportee, returnee and crime-witness groups. Zetino (2010) anchors 2020-24: random theft or violence bears no nexus. Barajas-Romero (2017) held that withholding needs only 'a reason' rather than 'one central reason'. In 2025-29 Duran-Rodriguez (2019) anchors on the extreme nature of persecution, and Umana-Escobar (2023) and Suate-Orellana (2024) apply Santos-Zacaria's holding that exhaustion is a non-jurisdictional but mandatory rule. changes.what: A desire to be free from random theft or criminal violence bears no nexus to a protected ground.

history: Dominant rule: entrapment turns on the defendant's predisposition. How it changed: in 1965-69 Lopez (1963) anchors a unit on undercover agents and electronic recording, with On Lee (1952), Hoffa (1966), Lewis (1967), Osborn (1967), Silverman (1961), Olmstead (1928) and Katz (1967). Those Fourth Amendment cases leave and Sherman (1958) anchors 1970-74 with Sorrells (1932), as Russell (1972 circuit, 1973 Supreme Court) enters. Russell anchors from 1975-79 to 1990-94, rejecting the objective test some courts had adopted (Turner 1973). Hampton (1976) enters in 1975-79, rejecting a due-process bar where a predisposed defendant bought contraband from agents. Twigg (3d Cir. 1978) enters in 1980-84 with the Abscam appeals, which rejected the objective test in due-process form. Mathews (1988) enters in 1985-89 and Jacobson (1992) in 1990-94, along with decoy cases such as Cruz (1985). The rule is otherwise stable.
rule: Entrapment bars conviction where government agents induced a crime that the defendant was not predisposed to commit, the inquiry focusing on predisposition rather than police conduct (Sorrells, Sherman, Russell), with predisposition required before government contact (Jacobson) and only extreme government involvement violating due process (Hampton, Twigg).

description: Texas review of evidentiary rulings and non-constitutional error, 2000-29: abuse of discretion within the zone of reasonable disagreement (Montgomery 1991, anchor 2000-24), Rule 403 balancing (Gigliobianco 2006), and correctness on any theory (De La Paz 2009, anchor 2025-29). previous.description: Texas Court of Criminal Appeals evidence law: abuse-of-discretion review and Rule 403 balancing (Montgomery, Gigliobianco), extraneous offenses (De La Paz), and harm analysis for non-constitutional error under Rule 44.2(b) (King, Motilla).

history: Dominant rule: evidentiary rulings are reviewed for abuse of discretion and stand if within the zone of reasonable disagreement or correct on any theory (Montgomery, 1991), and non-constitutional error is disregarded unless it affected substantial rights. Montgomery anchors every full slice from 2000-04 to 2020-24. How it changed: the 1997 Rules of Appellate Procedure brought Rule 44.2(b), and in 2000-04 King (1997) leads with Kotteakos (1946), adopting the substantial-and-injurious-effect test, while Johnson and Mosley (1998) classed evidentiary and argument errors as non-constitutional. In 2005-09 capital cases join on preservation (Santellan, 1997; Mendez, 2004), juror challenges (Ladd, 1999) and testimonial statements at punishment (Russeau, 2005). In 2010-14 jury argument (Wesbrook, 2000) and cures by instruction (Hawkins, 2004) lead. Motilla (2002) treated overwhelming evidence as one harm factor; Gigliobianco (2006) restated Rule 403 factors. De La Paz (2009) leads from 2015-19 and anchors the partial 2025-29 slice. Also: expert testimony (Weatherred, Wyatt, 2000) and extraneous-offense review (Moses, 2003).
rule: Texas evidentiary rulings are reviewed for abuse of discretion and stand if within the zone of reasonable disagreement or correct on any applicable theory (Montgomery; De La Paz), and non-constitutional error is disregarded under Rule 44.2(b) unless it had a substantial and injurious effect on the verdict (King; Kotteakos).

changes.what: Abuse-of-discretion review of evidentiary rulings, with Rule 403 weighing of probative value against unfair prejudice.

round1.description: Texas Court of Criminal Appeals evidence review: rulings are reviewed for abuse of discretion under Montgomery (1991), anchor from 2000-04, with Rule 403 balancing (Gigliobianco 2006) and extraneous-offense rebuttal (De La Paz 2009). Non-constitutional error is harmless under Rule 44.2(b) unless it had a substantial and injurious effect (King 1997, Kotteakos), applied to argument (Mosley 1998) and weighed with other factors (Motilla 2002).
round1.history: Dominant rule: evidentiary rulings are reviewed for abuse of discretion and stand if within the zone of reasonable disagreement or correct on any theory (Montgomery 1991; Romero 1990; De La Paz 2009), and non-constitutional error is disregarded unless it affected substantial rights. How it changed: in 1990-94 McQuillen (1988) anchors a capital-trial group (warrantless arrests, extraneous offenses, Strickland). Almanza (1985) anchors 1995-99, with preservation rules (Narvaiz, Barnes) and capital-sentencing challenges (McFarland 1996, Rousseau 1993). The new Rules of Appellate Procedure (1997) brought Rule 44.2(b): King (1997) adopted Kotteakos's substantial-and-injurious-effect test, Johnson and Mosley (1998) classed evidentiary and argument errors as non-constitutional, and Montgomery anchors from 2000-04 on. Motilla (2002) treated overwhelming evidence as one harm factor; Hawkins (2004) applied Mosley to mistrial rulings. Gigliobianco (2006) restated Rule 403 factors, and De La Paz (2009) leads from 2015-19 and anchors the partial 2025-29 slice. Also: same-transaction contextual evidence (Wesbrook, Wyatt 2000) and juror challenges (Ladd 1999).
round1.rule: A Texas trial court's evidentiary ruling is reviewed for abuse of discretion and upheld if within the zone of reasonable disagreement or correct on any applicable theory, and non-constitutional error is disregarded under Rule 44.2(b) unless it had a substantial and injurious effect on the verdict.

changes.what: Abuse-of-discretion review of evidentiary rulings and the Rule 403 balancing framework; a separate Rule 403 objection is needed after a Rule 404(b) objection is overruled.
Adopted the Kotteakos substantial-and-injurious-effect test for whether error affects a substantial right under new Rule 44.2(b).

changes.case: Mosley v. State; Johnson v. State
changes.what: Improper jury argument and erroneous admission of evidence are non-constitutional errors under Rule 44.2(b); Mosley adopted a three-factor test for argument.
Overwhelming evidence of guilt is one factor, not the only one, in Rule 44.2(b) harm analysis.
Restated the Rule 403 factors; unfair prejudice means a tendency to suggest decision on an improper basis.
Extraneous misconduct may be admitted to rebut a defensive theory, and a ruling correct on any theory stands.

before_differentiation.name: Texas evidentiary rulings: Montgomery abuse of discretion and Rule 44.2(b) harm
before_differentiation.description: Texas Court of Criminal Appeals evidence review, 2000-29: abuse of discretion under Montgomery (1991, anchor 2000-24), Rule 403 balancing (Gigliobianco, 2006) and correctness on any theory (De La Paz, 2009, anchor of the partial 2025-29 slice). Non-constitutional error is harmless under Rule 44.2(b) unless it had a substantial and injurious effect (King, 1997), applied to argument (Mosley, 1998) and weighed with other factors (Motilla, 2002).

distinct_from.how: That is the 1990-99 parent unit holding both evidence and charge error; this is the post-1997 evidence strand built on Rule 44.2(b) harm.
This reviews admission of evidence and argument for abuse of discretion and Rule 44.2(b) harm; that reviews the jury charge under Almanza's some-harm and egregious-harm tests.

name: What is a search and who may object: Katz privacy, Rakas, Jones trespass
description: The threshold of the Fourth Amendment: a search invades a reasonable expectation of privacy (Katz, 1967) and only the person whose own privacy was invaded may object (Rakas, 1979). Payton's (1980) home-entry rule anchors 2005-09; Jones (2012) and Jardines (2013) added a trespass test, and Riley and Carpenter (2014-18) limited the third-party doctrine. From 2020-24 the anchor drifts to Leon and warrant practice.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Fourth Amendment: privacy, homes and vehicle searches
previous.description: Expectation of privacy and standing to object (Katz, Rakas), home entry (Payton), consent (Schneckloth), the automobile exception and search incident to arrest of a vehicle (Carroll, Ross, Belton, Chimel) and the good-faith exception (Leon).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: a search is an intrusion on a reasonable expectation of privacy (Katz, 1967, the anchor in most slices), and only a person whose own expectation was invaded may seek suppression. How it changed: Rakas (1979) anchors 1980-89 and replaced separate standing analysis with the privacy inquiry; Salvucci (1980) ended Jones's automatic standing. Miller (1976) and Smith (1979) denied privacy in information given to third parties, and Oliver, Ciraolo and Dunn (1984-87) left open fields and aerial views unprotected. Payton (1980) enters in 1990-94 and anchors 2005-09: no warrantless home entry for a routine arrest, with Stuart (2006) on emergency entry. Horton (1990) dropped inadvertence from plain view; vehicle-search cases (Belton, Ross, Gant 2009) merge in from 1995-99. Kyllo (2001), Jones (2012) and Jardines (2013) restored a trespass test for homes and cars, and Riley (2014) and Carpenter (2018) lead 2015-24. From 2020-24 a merger makes Leon and Gates the anchors, which is drift toward warrants and exclusion.
rule: A search occurs when the government intrudes on a subjective expectation of privacy that society accepts as reasonable (Katz), or physically intrudes on a protected area, and only a person whose own legitimate expectation was invaded may seek suppression (Rakas).

changes.what: The Fourth Amendment protects people, not places: a reasonable expectation of privacy test.

changes.case: Rakas v. Illinois; United States v. Salvucci; Rawlings v. Kentucky
changes.what: Standing folded into the merits question of a legitimate expectation of privacy; Salvucci abandoned Jones's (1960) automatic standing; Rakas anchors 1980-89.

changes.case: United States v. Miller; Smith v. Maryland
changes.what: No reasonable expectation of privacy in bank records or dialed numbers conveyed to third parties.
Police may not make a warrantless, nonconsensual entry into a home for a routine felony arrest.
Plain-view seizure no longer requires inadvertent discovery.
Thermal imaging of a home is a search.
Vehicle search incident to arrest only if the arrestee can reach the car or it may hold evidence of the offense, narrowing Belton.

changes.case: United States v. Jones; Florida v. Jardines
changes.what: Physical intrusion on a protected area (GPS on a car, a dog sniff on the porch) is a search alongside the Katz test.

changes.case: Riley v. California; Carpenter v. United States
changes.what: Warrant needed to search a cell phone incident to arrest and to obtain historical cell-site records, limiting the third-party doctrine.

before_differentiation.name: Fourth Amendment search and standing: Katz expectation of privacy, Rakas, Payton
before_differentiation.description: What counts as a Fourth Amendment search and who may object: Katz's (1967) reasonable expectation of privacy, Rakas (1979) folding standing into that test, and Payton's (1980) warrant rule for home entry. Jones (2012) and Jardines (2013) added a trespass test; Riley and Carpenter (2014-18) limited the third-party doctrine. From 2020-24 the anchor drifts to Leon and warrant practice.

distinct_from.how: Asks what counts as a search and who has standing over the whole period, whereas that lineage is home entry and exigency, 1975-89.
Federal threshold search doctrine, not New Jersey's review standard.
The general privacy test that absorbed that unit in 1995-99, not the automobile exception and container rules themselves.
Katz privacy and standing, not vehicle searches incident to arrest (Belton, Gant).

name: Limits on changing sentences: § 3582(c)(2) (Dillon), FSA (Dorsey), ex post facto
description: Limits on changing a federal sentence after the fact. In 2010-14 the FSA's reach (Dorsey 2012, anchor; savings-statute cases such as Carradine) and § 3582(c)(2) as a limited reduction, not resentencing (Dillon 2010; Freeman 2011; no counsel right, Whitebird). In 2015-19 Dillon anchors and ex post facto cases enter: Peugh (2013) bars retroactive harsher Guidelines, with Weaver, Morales and Calder.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, round 2 after the lineage re-link)

previous.name: Sentence reductions and prisoner litigation (Fifth Circuit)
previous.description: Fifth Circuit review of § 3582(c)(2) reductions (Dillon, Freeman) and the Fair Sentencing Act (Dorsey), together with prisoner civil-rights screening, the three-strikes rule of § 1915(g) (Adepegba, Coleman v. Tollefson) and frivolousness (Baugh).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: once imposed, a federal sentence can be changed only within narrow statutory limits, and changes in sentencing law reach earlier conduct only as the savings statute and the Ex Post Facto Clause allow. How it changed: in 2010-14 Dorsey (2012) anchors. Circuit cases had held that § 109 preserved pre-Fair Sentencing Act penalties for pre-Act conduct (Carradine, Bell, Lewis, 2010); Dorsey held the Act's lower penalties apply to pre-Act offenders sentenced after it. Alongside, Dillon (2010) held that a § 3582(c)(2) motion permits only a limited adjustment within the amended range, not a plenary resentencing, so original findings stand (Bravo 2000; Doublin 2009); there is no right to appointed counsel (Whitebird 1995); career offenders were excluded from the crack amendment (Moore 2008); and Freeman (2011) allowed reductions for some plea-agreement sentences. In 2015-19 Dillon anchors and an ex post facto strand enters: Peugh (2013) bars retroactive use of harsher Guidelines, read with Calder (1798), Weaver (1981), Collins (1990), Morales (1995) and Garner (2000). Also: plain error where no circuit precedent supports the claim (Evans 2009).
rule: A § 3582(c)(2) motion permits only a limited reduction within an amended Guidelines range, not a plenary resentencing, and whether a new, more lenient or harsher sentencing rule reaches earlier conduct turns on the savings statute and the Ex Post Facto Clause.

changes.what: Amendment 706 (crack) does not reduce sentences of defendants sentenced as career offenders.
§ 3582(c)(2) authorizes only a limited adjustment to a final sentence, not a plenary resentencing, so Booker does not apply and original findings stand.
A defendant whose plea-agreement sentence was based on the Guidelines range may seek a § 3582(c)(2) reduction.
The Fair Sentencing Act's lower penalties apply to pre-Act offenders sentenced after its effective date, overriding the general savings statute (1 U.S.C. § 109) in that situation only.
Applying a harsher Guidelines amendment to an earlier offense violates the Ex Post Facto Clause even though the Guidelines are advisory.

round1.name: Fifth Circuit: § 3582(c)(2) limits (Dillon), then IFP prisoner appeals (Baugh)
round1.description: Fifth Circuit post-judgment and prisoner appeals. In 2010-14 the anchor is Dillon (2010): § 3582(c)(2) allows only a limited reduction, not resentencing, with Freeman (2011) and Dorsey (2012). From 2015-19 the dominant rule shifts to IFP prisoner appeals: good-faith review (Baugh, 1997), liberal reading of pro se filings (Howard, 1983) but abandonment of unbriefed issues (Yohey; Brinkmann), and § 1915(g) strikes (Coleman, 2015).
round1.history: Dominant rule: this lineage changes subject. In 2010-14, formed from a Booker-remand unit, Dillon (2010) anchors: a § 3582(c)(2) motion permits only a limited adjustment to an otherwise final sentence within the amended Guidelines range, not a plenary resentencing, so Booker does not apply and original findings stand (Bravo, 2000); there is no right to counsel (Whitebird, 1995). Freeman (2011) allowed reductions for some plea-agreement sentences, Moore (2008) excluded career offenders, and Dorsey (2012) applied the Fair Sentencing Act to pre-Act offenders sentenced after it. How it changed: from 2015-19 a Fifth Circuit prisoner-litigation unit merges in and Baugh v. Taylor (1997) anchors through 2025-29. An IFP appeal must raise nonfrivolous points (McGarrah, 2015); pro se filings are read liberally and later filings treated as amendments (Howard v. King, 1983; Haines), but a litigant who fails to brief arguments or identify the district court's error abandons them (Yohey, 1993; Brinkmann, 1987). Under § 1915(g) reversal nullifies a strike (Adepegba, 1996) but a pending appeal does not (Coleman v. Tollefson, 2015). In 2025-29 compassionate-release appeals enter (Chambliss, 2020).
round1.rule: In 2010-14, § 3582(c)(2) permits only a limited adjustment of a final sentence to an amended Guidelines range, not a plenary resentencing (Dillon); from 2015-19, a Fifth Circuit IFP appeal must be taken in good faith, and a pro se appellant who fails to brief or identify error abandons the claim (Baugh, Yohey, Brinkmann).

changes.case: Dillon v. United States; Freeman v. United States
changes.what: § 3582(c)(2) is a limited, two-step proceeding to which Booker does not apply; Freeman (via its concurrence) allowed reductions for some plea-agreement sentences. Dillon anchors 2010-14.
The Fair Sentencing Act's lower crack penalties apply to pre-Act offenders sentenced after its effective date.

changes.case: Baugh v. Taylor (1997); Howard v. King (1983); Yohey v. Collins (1993); Brinkmann (1987)
changes.what: The anchor moves to prisoner IFP appeals: the court may reach the merits on a good-faith certification challenge, read pro se filings liberally, but treat unbriefed arguments as abandoned.

changes.case: Adepegba v. Hammons; Coleman v. Tollefson
changes.what: Under § 1915(g), reversal nullifies a strike, but a dismissal counts as a strike while its appeal is pending.

name: Illinois administrative review standards: Belvidere, AFM Messenger, Cinkus
description: Illinois review of agency decisions: manifest-weight review of facts (Abrahamson, 1992), de novo review of law, and clear-error review of mixed questions adopted in Belvidere (1998) and defined in AFM Messenger (2001) from U.S. Gypsum (1948) and Anderson (1985). Carpetland (2002) kept de novo review for law, and Cinkus (2008) reaffirmed the scheme and forfeiture of issues not raised below. Applied to pensions, tax exemptions and utility rates.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Illinois administrative review
previous.description: Illinois standards for reviewing agency decisions: City of Belvidere, AFM Messenger, Cinkus and Abrahamson on de novo, clearly-erroneous and manifest-weight review of mixed and factual questions, borrowing the federal clearly-erroneous test of U.S. Gypsum, Anderson and Pullman-Standard.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session subagents, from cocite evidence; second pass differentiated near-duplicates)

history: Dominant rule: the three Illinois standards for reviewing administrative decisions. City of Belvidere (1998) anchors 2000-04: mixed questions of law and fact get clearly erroneous review, borrowed from the federal standard of U.S. Gypsum (1948), Anderson v. Bessemer City (1985) and Pullman-Standard (1982). Abrahamson (1992) and Zehnder (1999) supply manifest-weight deference to findings of fact. How it changed: AFM Messenger (2001) anchors 2005-09 and defines a mixed question as whether established facts satisfy an undisputed legal rule, finding clear error only on a definite and firm conviction of mistake; Carpetland (2002) confirmed de novo review for pure legal questions and that issues not raised before the agency are forfeited (McGaw, 1998). Cinkus (2008) anchors 2010-14 and reaffirms AFM. The standards stay stable and are applied to police and fire pension disability (Marconi, Wade, Kouzoukas, Jones v. Board of Trustees), unemployment insurance, property-tax charitable exemptions (Eden, Provena) and Illinois Commerce Commission utility rate orders (Commonwealth Edison, Business and Professional People).
rule: On Illinois administrative review, an agency's factual findings are upheld unless against the manifest weight of the evidence, questions of law are reviewed de novo, and mixed questions of law and fact are reviewed for clear error, meaning the court is left with a definite and firm conviction that a mistake has been made (Belvidere, AFM Messenger, borrowing U.S. Gypsum).

changes.case: Abrahamson v. Illinois Department of Professional Regulation
changes.what: Agency findings of fact are prima facie correct and reversed only if against the manifest weight of the evidence.

changes.case: City of Belvidere v. Illinois State Labor Relations Board
changes.what: Mixed questions of fact and law are reviewed under a clearly erroneous standard; Belvidere anchors 2000-04.

changes.case: AFM Messenger Service v. Department of Employment Security
changes.what: Defined a mixed question (settled facts, undisputed rule, whether the facts meet the standard) and adopted the U.S. Gypsum definition of clear error; AFM anchors 2005-09.

changes.case: Carpetland U.S.A. v. Illinois Department of Employment Security
changes.what: The clearly erroneous standard did not abandon de novo review of pure questions of law, and issues not raised before the agency are forfeited.

changes.case: Cinkus v. Village of Stickney Municipal Officers Electoral Board
changes.what: Reaffirmed AFM Messenger's standards and held that issues not raised at the administrative hearing are forfeited; Cinkus anchors 2010-14.

name: First Circuit sentencing review: Martin plausibility and Zannino waiver
description: First Circuit review of federal sentences, mostly from Puerto Rico: Martin (2008, anchor 2015-24) asks for a plausible rationale and defensible result; Clogston (2011) and Flores-Machicote (2013) leave factor-weighing and community-deterrence variances to the judge; Duarte (2001) sets plain error; Zannino (1990) waives undeveloped arguments and anchors 2010-14 and 2025-29. Ruiz-Huertas (2015) left preservation of substantive claims open.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: First Circuit criminal appeals: waiver and sentencing
previous.description: Sub-cluster form of the First Circuit's Zannino waiver rule for undeveloped arguments, applied with Alleyne mandatory-minimum challenges and reasonableness review of sentences (Martin, Flores-Machicote, Ruiz-Huertas).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: preserved sentencing challenges are reviewed for abuse of discretion, and a sentence stands if it rests on a plausible rationale and reaches a defensible result. How it changed: Zannino (1990) anchors 2010-14, with Duarte (2001) on plain error and Turbides-Leonardo (2006) allowing reasons to be inferred from the record. Martin (2008), decided after Gall and Kimbrough, upheld a below-range sentence for a crack career offender and anchors 2015-19 and 2020-24. Clogston (2011) left factor-weighing to the judge, and Flores-Machicote (2013) allowed upward variances based on community deterrence if the court also considers the individual. Ruiz-Huertas (2015) noted uncertainty over whether unpreserved substantive challenges are reviewed for plain error. In 2015-24 entrants mostly affirm upward variances in firearms cases (Del Valle-Rodriguez 2014, Rivera-Gonzalez 2015, Vargas-Garcia 2015, Diaz-Lugo 2020, Polaco-Hance 2024 on ammunition and magazines), while Rivera-Berrios (2020) vacated an unexplained variance. Zannino again anchors the partial 2025-29 slice.
rule: The First Circuit reviews preserved sentencing claims for abuse of discretion (legal questions de novo, facts for clear error), upholding a sentence, including a variance, if it rests on a plausible rationale and reaches a defensible result, while unpreserved claims get plain-error review and undeveloped arguments are waived under Zannino.

changes.what: Issues adverted to perfunctorily without developed argument are waived; Zannino anchors 2010-14 and the partial 2025-29 slice.
Four-part plain-error test for unpreserved sentencing claims.
A sentencing court need not address every argument frontally; the reasons can be inferred from the record.
After Gall and Kimbrough, a below-Guidelines sentence for a crack career offender was upheld; review asks for a plausible sentencing rationale and a defensible result. Martin anchors 2015-24.

changes.case: United States v. Clogston; United States v. Flores-Machicote
changes.what: Weighing the § 3553(a) factors is largely within the court's discretion; community-based deterrence can support an upward variance if the court does not neglect the individual defendant.
Left open whether an unpreserved substantive-reasonableness claim gets abuse-of-discretion or plain-error review.

A variance needs a plausible and coherent explanation tied to the case; factors already in the Guidelines may support it if the range does not capture the case's specifics; on remand a court may be limited to the range when nothing justifies a variance.

name: Tennessee-led post-conviction IAC with Missouri and others, 2020-24: Goad
description: Post-conviction review of counsel in 2020-24, Tennessee-led but merged with other states: Goad (1996, anchor) and Henley (1997) let a court deny on either Strickland prong; Baxter v. Rose (1975) sets competence; Fields (2001) leaves credibility to the post-conviction court; pleas follow Hill (1985) and Boykin (1969); Lockhart v. Fretwell (1993) frames prejudice. Missouri abandonment (Moore, 2015), Delaware and other state rules join.
history: Dominant rule: Strickland's (1984) two-pronged test for ineffective assistance as state post-conviction courts apply it, chiefly in Tennessee under Baxter v. Rose's (1975) range-of-competence standard. Goad (1996) anchors the single 2020-24 slice, formed by merging the Tennessee post-conviction unit with a broader state ineffective-assistance unit. How it changed: no change within the slice. Goad and Henley (1997) let courts deny on either prong and defer to strategy; Hellard (1982) rejects hindsight; Fields (2001) leaves credibility to the post-conviction court; Black (1990) requires uncalled witnesses to testify at the hearing. Hill (1985), Boykin (1969) and Alford (1970) govern plea claims; Cronic (1984) presumes prejudice for complete failures; Lockhart v. Fretwell (1993) frames prejudice as unreliability or unfairness. Other states' post-conviction rules appear: Missouri's abandonment inquiry for untimely amended motions (Moore, 2015), cumulative error (Starling, 2015), actual innocence (Beauclair, 2018) and cause for default (Younger, 1990). Burns (1999) on lesser-included offenses also leads. The lineage splits in 2025-29.
rule: A post-conviction petitioner alleging ineffective assistance must show both that counsel's performance fell below the range of competence demanded in criminal cases (Baxter; Strickland) and resulting prejudice, failure on either prong being enough to deny relief (Goad; Henley), with credibility left to the post-conviction court (Fields).

changes.what: Counsel's representation must be within the range of competence demanded of attorneys in criminal cases.

changes.case: Strickland v. Washington; United States v. Cronic; Hill v. Lockhart
changes.what: Deficient performance and prejudice are required, prejudice is presumed only for complete failures of counsel, and for pleas the question is whether the defendant would have gone to trial.
Prejudice requires that the deficiency made the result unreliable or the proceeding fundamentally unfair, not merely outcome-different under since-overruled law.

changes.case: Goad v. State; Henley v. State (Tenn.)
changes.what: Courts may deny on either prong without reaching the other, and give counsel latitude in strategy.
Credibility and factual findings belong to the post-conviction court.

name: Tennessee post-conviction IAC, 2005-09, with conflict-of-interest prejudice
description: Tennessee post-conviction review of counsel in 2005-09, merged with Texas IAC and conflict-of-interest units: Strickland (1984, anchor) with Baxter v. Rose (1975); Hill (1985) for pleas; Goad (1996) and Henley (1997) allow denial on either prong; Fields (2001) and Nichols (2002) defer to the court's credibility findings; Cronic (1984), Cuyler (1980) and Mickens (2002) on presumed prejudice. Also Boykin, Alford and Burns (1999).
history: Dominant rule: Strickland's (1984) deficient-performance and prejudice test, applied by Tennessee courts with Baxter v. Rose's (1975) range-of-competence standard. Strickland anchors the single 2005-09 slice, formed by merging a Tennessee post-conviction unit, a Texas ineffective-assistance unit and a conflict-of-interest unit. How it changed: no change within the slice. Hill (1985) asks whether a petitioner would have gone to trial; Goad (1996) and Henley (1997) allow a court to stop at either prong and defer to informed strategy; Hellard (1982) and House (2001) reject hindsight; Fields (2001) and Nichols (2002) defer to the post-conviction court's credibility findings; Black (1990) requires petitioners to present uncalled witnesses at the hearing. Plea voluntariness follows Boykin (1969) and Alford (1970); Cronic (1984), Cuyler (1980) and Mickens (2002) cover presumed prejudice; Momon (2000) the right to testify; Burns (1999) lesser-included offenses. The lineage splits in 2010-14, partly into a Tennessee post-conviction unit.
rule: A Tennessee post-conviction petitioner must prove by clear and convincing evidence that counsel's performance fell below the range of competence demanded of criminal attorneys (Baxter) and that it prejudiced the outcome (Strickland), or for a plea that he would have gone to trial (Hill), with the post-conviction court's credibility findings given deference and failure on either prong fatal.

changes.what: Counsel's representation must be within the range of competence demanded of attorneys in criminal cases.

changes.case: Strickland v. Washington; Hill v. Lockhart
changes.what: Deficient performance and a reasonable probability of a different result are required; for a plea, a reasonable probability the defendant would have insisted on trial.

changes.case: Goad v. State; Henley v. State
changes.what: A court need not address both prongs if either is not shown, and informed strategic choices receive deference.
Credibility issues are for the post-conviction court, whose factual findings are conclusive unless the evidence preponderates against them, while the application of law is reviewed de novo.
Model Penal Code-based test for lesser-included offenses, with instructions required where the evidence supports them.
