name: Pennsylvania weight v. sufficiency of the evidence: Widmer shocks-the-conscience
description: The merits of Pennsylvania evidence challenges in criminal appeals, 2015-29: a weight claim must be raised in the trial court (Brown 1994) and succeeds only if the verdict shocks the conscience, reviewed for abuse of discretion (Widmer 2000, the anchor in every slice; Champney 2003; Clay 2013); sufficiency is a question of law, applied to recurring elements such as constructive possession. Rule 1925(b) waiver rides along.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Pennsylvania Rule 1925(b) waiver
previous.description: Pennsylvania appellate waiver for issues not identified, or identified too vaguely, in a Rule 1925(b) concise statement (Lord, Castillo), with weight-of-the-evidence review.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: Commonwealth v. Widmer (2000) anchors every slice: weight and sufficiency differ, and a new trial for weight is proper only when the verdict is so contrary to the evidence as to shock one's sense of justice. Brown (1994) requires that the claim be raised first in the trial court and limits appellate review to the trial judge's discretion; Champney (2003) and Clay (2013) restate that the factfinder may believe all, part or none of the evidence and that an appellate court may not reweigh it. How it changed: no change in the governing rule. The 2015-19 slice forms from a PCRA and ineffectiveness unit and carries Rule 1925(b) waiver for issues not specified in the concise statement (2009, 2011). Later slices add sufficiency rulings on recurring elements: constructive possession requiring more than proximity or association (2013, 2018), the sufficiency of a single witness's uncorroborated testimony (2015, 2018), self-defence disproved by a failure to retreat (2018), and Rule 404(b) common-scheme and history-of-the-case evidence with limiting instructions (2002, 2014, 2015). Also: prima facie standards at the preliminary hearing (2005, 2016).
rule: A Pennsylvania weight-of-the-evidence claim, which must first be raised in the trial court, is granted only when the verdict is so contrary to the evidence as to shock the conscience, and the appellate court reviews only whether the trial court abused its discretion, while sufficiency is a question of law judged on the evidence viewed for the Commonwealth.

changes.what: A weight claim must be presented to the trial court first, and appellate review is limited to that court's exercise of discretion, without reassessing credibility.
Weight and sufficiency are distinct: on a weight claim the trial judge does not view the evidence for the verdict winner, and a new trial issues only if the verdict shocks the sense of justice.
The factfinder may believe all, part or none of the evidence, and appellate review of a weight ruling is for abuse of discretion.
The appellate court asks whether the trial court exceeded its discretion or invaded the jury's province, and may not reweigh the evidence.
Sufficiency and weight claims not specified in the concise statement, or not raised below, are waived.

description: Delaware pleading-stage review, 2020-29, anchored by Central Mortgage (2011): well-pleaded allegations, even vague ones giving notice, are accepted and dismissal is improper unless recovery is not reasonably conceivable; conclusory allegations (Price 2011) and strained readings (General Motors 2006) need not be credited. history: Dominant rule: the Fifth Circuit applies Olano plain-error review with a demanding prejudice prong. How it changed: in 2005-09, anchored by Llerena (2005), Mares (2005) held that sentencing under mandatory Guidelines is plain error but that the defendant must show a likely different sentence, and Valenzuela-Quevedo and Martinez-Lugo (2005) applied the same test to constitutional Booker error and nonconstitutional Fanfan error; Bringier (2005) held that a bottom-of-range sentence alone is not enough and that objections had to invoke Blakely or the Sixth Amendment. By contrast, Garza-Lopez and Villegas (2005) found that misapplied enhancements producing a substantially different range affect substantial rights and the fairness of proceedings; Garza-Lopez required Shepard documents. Smith (2006) made the Guidelines the frame of reference for non-Guidelines sentences. In 2010-14 the anchor becomes Beechum (en banc 1978), on extrinsic-offense evidence, as the lineage turns to plain error in trial issues: prosecutorial comments (Fields 2007, Gracia 2008) and, in Delgado (en banc 2012), unpreserved sufficiency claims. It then merges into Fifth Circuit plain-error review.
rule: In the Fifth Circuit an unpreserved Booker or Fanfan error is plain, but the defendant must show from the record that the judge would likely have imposed a different sentence under advisory Guidelines (Mares); an erroneous enhancement that substantially raises the range affects substantial rights and the fairness of the proceedings (Garza-Lopez, Villegas).

name: Ex Post Facto Clause: retroactive increases in punishment (Weaver, Collins, Morales)
description: Ex post facto doctrine: retroactive laws that increase punishment violate the Clause (Weaver 1981, anchor 1985-99; Miller v. Florida 1987; Lynce 1997), while procedural changes do not (Beazell, Dobbert 1977). history: Dominant rule: Weaver v. Graham (1981) anchors every slice: a retroactive law that disadvantages an offender by increasing punishment, as by cutting good-time credits, violates the Clause. How it changed: in 1985-89 the unit is drawn from Florida capital appeals, with Dobbert (1977) allowing procedural changes in the death-penalty statute and Beazell (1925) and Hopt (1884) on procedure. Miller v. Florida (1987) enters, striking retroactive guideline increases, and in 1990-94 Collins v. Youngblood (1990) enters, reaffirming Calder (1798) and overruling Kring; circuit parole cases (Rodriguez 1979, Fender 1989, Akins 1991) test parole rule changes. Poritz 1995, Ward 1994, Artway 1996) and Hendricks (1997), treating those measures as civil under Flemming v. Nestor (1960). It then splits into civil-sanction units in 2000-04.

Oliveaux (1975) anchors from 1995-99 to 2010-14, with Weiland (1990) anchoring 2015-19: a Louisiana court of appeal examines the record for errors visible on the face of the pleadings and proceedings, such as illegal sentences, whether or not the defendant raised them; Lynch (1983) settles conflicts by preferring the transcript to the minutes. How it changed: no shift in the rule. Early slices also carry trial issues in murder appeals (Prieur, 1973, other-crimes notice; Kilgore, 1998; Juluke, 1999). In 2005-09 Crosby (1976) enters: a guilty plea may reserve review of pre-plea rulings. In 2010-14 the Anders line enters and leads through 2015-19: Benjamin (1990) and Jyles (1997) set the procedure for appointed counsel's no-merit brief and the court's independent review, drawing on Anders and McCoy (1988). Several heavy cases dated 1925-1929 at 'La. App. 5' (Giliberti, Copenhaver, Hall, Canovsky) are probably misresolved Fifth Circuit citations and should not be read as old precedent. The lineage merges into the Louisiana sufficiency and sentencing unit in 2020-24.
rule: A Louisiana appellate court reviews every criminal record for errors patent on the face of the pleadings and proceedings (Oliveaux, Weiland), and when appointed counsel files a no-merit brief it independently reviews the record under Anders (Benjamin, Jyles).

name: Virginia sufficiency review: rational factfinder and hypotheses of innocence
description: Virginia sufficiency review: a conviction stands unless plainly wrong or unsupported, asking whether any rational factfinder could convict (Kelly, en banc 2003). Rejecting a hypothesis of innocence is a factual finding reviewed deferentially (Archer 1997, Haskins 2004), limited to theories advanced at trial (Hudson, 265 Va. 505, 2003), and the factfinder may infer lying to conceal guilt (Marable 1998). Chavez (2018) and Pijor (2017) anchor the 2020s.

previous.name: Virginia criminal: sufficiency review and rejected defense theories

history: Dominant rule: Virginia appellate courts affirm a conviction unless it is plainly wrong or without supporting evidence, asking whether any rational trier of fact could find the elements beyond a reasonable doubt; credibility and inferences are for the factfinder, who may reject the accused's account and treat it as lying to conceal guilt (Parks 1980, Marable 1998, Pease 2002). How it changed: Watkins (1998) anchors 2000-04, with Archer (1997) holding that a rejected hypothesis of innocence stands unless no rational factfinder would reject it and Dowden (2000) limiting it to hypotheses that flow from the evidence. Kelly (en banc 2003) anchors 2005-09 and 2015-19 and Hudson (265 Va. 505, 2003) anchors 2010-14, limiting the inquiry to theories advanced at trial; Haskins (2004) called reasonableness a question of fact. Bolden (2008) and Sullivan (2010) widened the record and deference to video. Vasquez (2016) restated the plainly-wrong test, and Chavez (2018) anchors 2020-24 and Pijor (2017) the partial 2025-29 slice. Also: constructive possession (Powers 1984, Maxwell 2008), preservation and assignments of error (Muhammad 2005, Banks 2017), and Vasquez's Eighth Amendment holding on aggregate term-of-years sentences.
rule: A Virginia conviction is affirmed unless plainly wrong or without evidence to support it: the question is whether any rational trier of fact could find the elements beyond a reasonable doubt, and whether a hypothesis of innocence is reasonable is itself a question of fact for the factfinder, who may reject the accused's account and infer he is lying to conceal guilt.

changes.case: Marable v. Commonwealth; Archer v. Commonwealth (1997)
changes.what: The factfinder may disbelieve the accused's self-serving testimony and conclude he is lying to conceal guilt; rejection of a hypothesis of innocence stands unless no rational factfinder would reach it.

changes.case: Hudson v. Commonwealth, 265 Va. 505; Kelly v. Commonwealth (en banc)
changes.what: Exclusion of reasonable theories of innocence is limited to theories the accused advanced at trial, and review asks whether a reasonable factfinder could reject them; Kelly restated the rational-trier test.

history: Dominant rule: the Illinois duty to defend and the construction of liability policies. In 1975-79 a small unit (Sims, 1963) concerns related insurance and procedure cases. How it changed: Thornton (1978) anchors 1980-94: an insurer that breaches its duty to defend is estopped from raising policy defenses in later garnishment or coverage suits, and Peppers (1976) holds the duty arises from allegations potentially within coverage, with declaratory judgments on ultimate facts premature while the tort suit is pending. Associated Indemnity (1979) and La Rotunda (1980) add true but unpleaded facts; Conway (1982) bars escape by tendering limits; Zurich v. Raymark (1987) addresses asbestos triggers; Wilkin (1991) applies the intended-or-expected test. Outboard Marine (1992) anchors 1995-2019: ambiguous terms favor the insured, and summary judgment is reviewed de novo. Crum & Forster (1993) limits indemnity to actual coverage, Koloms (1997) confines the pollution exclusion, Ehlco (1999) limits estoppel to breaches, and Eljer (2001) applies contract construction. Also: from 2010-14 premises-liability cases merge in (Ward, 1990; Marshall, 2006; Bruns, 2014), with Khan (2011) cited for de novo review.
rule: An Illinois liability insurer must defend if the complaint alleges facts potentially within coverage, is estopped from coverage defenses if it wrongly refuses (Thornton), and ambiguous policy terms are construed for the insured (Outboard Marine), while indemnity depends on facts actually within coverage (Crum & Forster).

Intentionally installing asbestos does not trigger the intended-or-expected exclusion unless the insured intended or expected the resulting damage.

The pollution exclusion is limited to traditional environmental pollution and does not reach a carbon monoxide leak.

name: Railway Labor Act: minor disputes to the Adjustment Board, status quo in major ones
description: Railway Labor Act disputes, 1960-89: Burley (1945, anchor in most slices) separates minor disputes under existing agreements, which the Adjustment Board decides exclusively (Slocum 1950, Gunther 1966; Andrews 1972, anchor 1975-79, for discharge claims), from major disputes. Courts may enjoin strikes over minor disputes (Chicago River 1957) and status-quo changes in major ones (Shore Line 1969; Chicago & North Western 1971). Sheehan (1979) narrowed award review.
history: Dominant rule: the Railway Labor Act's channeling of disputes. Elgin, Joliet & Eastern v. Burley (1945), the anchor in all but one slice, distinguishes minor disputes, which arise from the application of an existing agreement, from major disputes over new terms. Texas & New Orleans (1930) and Virginian Railway v. System Federation (1937) made RLA duties judicially enforceable. How it changed: Slocum (1950) gave the National Railroad Adjustment Board exclusive jurisdiction over minor disputes, and Brotherhood of Railroad Trainmen v. Chicago River (1957) allowed injunctions against strikes over them notwithstanding Norris-LaGuardia; Railroad Telegraphers (1960) held that a job-security demand was a labor dispute under Norris-LaGuardia. Gunther (1966) stressed the finality of Board awards. Detroit & Toledo Shore Line (1969) required the status quo during major-dispute procedures, and Chicago & North Western (1971) made the duty to treat enforceable by injunction. Andrews v. Louisville & Nashville (1972), anchor in 1975-79, sent wrongful-discharge claims grounded in the agreement to the Board, overruling Moore (1941). Union Pacific v. Sheehan (1979) called review of Board awards among the narrowest known. The unit merges into labor preemption units in 1990-94.
rule: Under the Railway Labor Act, minor disputes over the application of an existing agreement go exclusively to the National Railroad Adjustment Board, whose awards get very narrow review, while in major disputes over new terms the parties must maintain the status quo, enforceable by injunction despite Norris-LaGuardia.

history: Dominant rule: persecution requires more than harassment, threats or minor beatings, and the agency's findings are conclusive unless a reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to disagree. How it changed: in 2000-04 and 2005-09 Eighth Circuit cases lead. Perinpanathan (2002) defers to credibility findings with specific, cogent reasons, Regalado-Garcia (2002) rejects persecution without physical harm, and Ngure (2004) puts affirmance without opinion beyond review. From 2010-14 Uanreroro (2006) anchors Tenth Circuit law: the court reviews the BIA's decision and looks to the IJ only as far as the BIA relies on it (Sarr, 2007). Sidabutar (2007) and Tulengkey (2005) apply a high persecution threshold, and Dallakoti (2010) reads one central reason strictly. Rodas-Orellana (2015) adopted social distinction for gang-resistance groups. In 2020-24 the lineage turns to removal procedure: Pereira (2018) anchors on notices to appear that omit the hearing time and the stop-time rule, with Pierre-Paul (2019) and Ortiz-Santiago (2019) on whether such notices defeat jurisdiction, and Monreal (2001) and Recinas (2002) on hardship.

How it changed: in 1980-84 the anchor is Strahl (1979) and relocation cases lead: Weiss (1981) and Daghir (1981-82) required exceptional circumstances before a child could be moved away, and Nehra (1977) addressed deterring child abduction. (1989) and De Losh (1997) applying it. In 2000-04 Bennett v. Jeffreys (1976), requiring extraordinary circumstances before a nonparent can seek custody, and termination-of-parental-rights cases (In re Star and In re Sheila G., 1984) join the leading cases.

history: Dominant rule: Greenlaw (2008) anchors this single 2020-24 slice. Courts rely on the parties to frame issues, so an appellate court may not enlarge a judgment for a nonappealing party, and Sineneng-Smith (2020) reversed the Ninth Circuit for reframing a case, while allowing a modest initiating role in pro se and habeas cases. Castro (2003) requires notice before recharacterizing a pro se motion as § 2255, and Wood (2012) and Day (2006) govern raising forfeited limitations defenses; Kamen (1991) and Independent Insurance Agents (1993) allow courts to decide antecedent questions. Alongside: Erie (1938) and Hanna (1965) on state substantive law in diversity, and the presumption against extraterritoriality in Morrison (2010, § 10(b)), Kiobel (2013, ATS), RJR Nabisco (2016, RICO) and WesternGeco (2018, patent damages). Also: the American rule on fees from Alyeska (1975) and Peter v. NantKwest (2019), from a merged civil-rights fee unit. No rule change within the slice.
rule: Courts decide the questions the parties present and may not reframe a case or benefit a nonappealing party (Greenlaw, Sineneng-Smith), apply state substantive law in diversity while federal rules govern procedure (Erie, Hanna), and presume federal statutes do not apply abroad absent clear indication (Morrison, Kiobel, RJR Nabisco).

changes.case: Erie R. Co. v. Tompkins; Hanna v. Plumer
changes.what: No general federal common law; diversity courts apply state substantive law, but a valid Federal Rule governs over conflicting state procedure.

changes.case: Castro v. United States; Day v. McDonough; Wood v. Milyard
changes.what: Courts must warn pro se litigants before recharacterizing motions, and may raise a limitations defense sua sponte but not override a state's deliberate waiver.
Under the cross-appeal rule an appellate court cannot increase a sentence absent a government appeal.

changes.case: Morrison v. National Australia Bank; Kiobel v. Royal Dutch Petroleum; RJR Nabisco v. European Community; WesternGeco v. ION
changes.what: The presumption against extraterritoriality limits § 10(b) to domestic transactions and the ATS to domestic claims, applies a two-step focus test, and allows lost foreign profits for domestic patent infringement.
The Ninth Circuit erred by reframing the appeal around issues the parties had not raised; party presentation is supple but binding.

name: Special-needs and administrative searches: Camara, Skinner, Von Raab
description: Searches without a warrant or individualized suspicion: administrative inspections (Camara 1967, Marshall 1978, Burger 1987), school and workplace searches (T.L.O. 1985), drug testing (Skinner and Von Raab 1989, Acton 1995) and probation and DNA searches (Griffin 1987, Knights 2001, Kincade 2004). Edmond (2000) and Ferguson (2001) bar programs whose primary purpose is ordinary crime control.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Special-needs and administrative searches
previous.description: Fourth Amendment searches without individualized suspicion: administrative inspections (Camara), school searches (T.L.O.), drug testing (Skinner, Von Raab, Vernonia v. Acton), checkpoints (Martinez-Fuerte, Edmond), probationers (Griffin, Knights), and DNA collection (Kincade).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: where a search serves special needs beyond normal law enforcement, reasonableness is a balance of government interest against privacy, and a warrant, probable cause or individualized suspicion may be unnecessary. How it changed: the lineage begins in 1980-84 with administrative inspections, anchored by Marshall (1978), which required administrative warrants for OSHA inspections, while Biswell (1972), Donovan (1981) and Burger (1987) allowed warrantless inspection of closely regulated businesses. T.L.O. (1985), O'Connor (1987) and Griffin (1987) enter in 1985-89 and extend the doctrine to schools, public workplaces and probation. Skinner and Von Raab (1989) anchor 1990-2004 and uphold suspicionless drug testing; circuit cases apply them to federal employees. Acton (1995) added student athletes, while Chandler (1997) set a limit. Edmond (2000) and Ferguson (2001) enter in 2000-04 and exclude crime-control purposes. Knights (2001), Samson (2006) and the DNA-collection cases led by Kincade (2004) dominate 2005-09, after which the unit merges into the privacy lineage.
rule: When a search serves special needs beyond ordinary law enforcement, courts dispense with a warrant, probable cause or individualized suspicion if the government interest outweighs the reduced privacy interest, but not when the primary purpose is to detect ordinary crime (Edmond).

changes.case: Camara v. Municipal Court; See v. Seattle
changes.what: Administrative inspections need a warrant, but on area-wide standards rather than criminal probable cause.

changes.case: Colonnade; Biswell; Donovan v. Dewey; New York v. Burger
changes.what: Warrantless inspections of closely regulated businesses are permitted when a statute limits inspectors' discretion in time, place and scope.
OSHA's general regulation is not a closely regulated industry; nonconsensual inspections need an administrative warrant; Marshall anchors 1980-84.

changes.case: New Jersey v. T.L.O.; O'Connor v. Ortega; Griffin v. Wisconsin
changes.what: Reasonable-suspicion searches by school officials and public employers, and probation searches, justified by special needs.

changes.case: Skinner v. Railway Labor Executives; NTEU v. Von Raab
changes.what: Suspicionless drug testing of safety-sensitive employees and customs officers is reasonable; Von Raab and Skinner anchor 1990-2004.

changes.case: Vernonia v. Acton; Chandler v. Miller
changes.what: Random testing of student athletes upheld; Chandler struck testing of political candidates lacking a concrete special need.

changes.case: Indianapolis v. Edmond; Ferguson v. Charleston
changes.what: A checkpoint or testing program whose primary purpose is ordinary crime control is not a special need.

changes.case: United States v. Knights; United States v. Kincade (9th Cir. en banc); Samson v. California
changes.what: Probationer and parolee searches and compelled DNA collection from offenders upheld under the totality of the circumstances; Kincade anchors 2005-09.

name: Michigan contracts enforced as written (Rory) and summary disposition (Maiden)
description: Michigan civil appeals: unambiguous contracts and policies are enforced as written, every word given effect, with no reasonable-expectations or reasonableness review (Wilkie 2003, Klapp 2003, Rory 2005). Summary disposition follows Maiden (1999) and Quinto (1996). Titan v. Hyten (2012) allowed rescission for fraud even if discoverable, and Bazzi (2018) made rescission equitable.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Michigan civil: summary disposition and contract
previous.description: Michigan contract and insurance precedent: summary disposition under MCR 2.116(C)(10) (Maiden, Quinto), contracts enforced as written (Rory, Titan v. Hyten) and every word given effect (Klapp), with preservation rules.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: Michigan enforces contracts as written. Maiden (1999) anchors the large 2015-19 slice: under MCR 2.116(C)(10) the court reviews the evidence submitted at the motion, and the nonmovant must present more than conclusory allegations (Quinto, 1996; Gorman, 2013; Barnard, 2009). Rory (2005) anchors 2020-24: unambiguous terms, including a shortened contractual limitations period, are enforced unless they violate law or a traditional defence applies. How it changed: Wilkie (2003) rejected the reasonable-expectations doctrine and Klapp (2003) required that every word be given effect with ambiguity going to the jury. Titan v. Hyten (2012) let insurers rescind for fraud whether or not it was easily ascertainable, and Bazzi (2018) held that this abrogated the innocent-third-party rule while making rescission discretionary; Zufelt (2016) applied policy terms permitting rescission for misstatements. Joseph (2012) limited no-fault recovery to the year before suit. Also: retroactivity of statutes (Hughes, 1979; Frank W. Lynch, 2001; LaFontaine, 2014), retaliation causation (West, 2003), and retiree healthcare in collective bargaining agreements (Kendzierski, 2019).
rule: Michigan courts enforce unambiguous contracts, including insurance policies, as written, giving effect to every word and refusing to rewrite terms for reasonableness or expectations (Rory, Wilkie, Klapp), and grant summary disposition under MCR 2.116(C)(10) when the evidence before the court shows no genuine issue of material fact (Maiden, Quinto).

changes.case: Quinto v. Cross & Peters; Maiden v. Rozwood
changes.what: Once the movant supports its motion, the nonmovant must present admissible evidence, not conclusory affidavits, of a genuine issue; only evidence before the court at the motion counts.

changes.case: Wilkie v. Auto-Owners; Klapp v. United Insurance Group
changes.what: Rejected the reasonable-expectations doctrine; every word is given effect, and an ambiguous term becomes a jury question.
Unambiguous contract terms, including shortened limitations periods, are enforced as written absent a traditional contract defence; courts do not review them for reasonableness.

changes.case: Titan Insurance v. Hyten; Joseph v. Auto Club
changes.what: An insurer may rescind for fraud even if the misrepresentation was easily ascertainable; Joseph held the no-fault one-year-back rule is not tolled by minority or insanity.
Titan abrogated the innocent-third-party rule, but rescission is equitable and left to the trial court's discretion.

name: Ohio civil standards of review: Blakemore abuse of discretion, C.E. Morris, GTE
description: Ohio civil appeals: abuse of discretion means an unreasonable, arbitrary or unconscionable attitude (Blakemore, 1983, anchor in every slice), judgments resting on competent, credible evidence are not against the manifest weight (C.E. Morris 1978, Seasons Coal 1984), and Civ.R. 60(B) relief needs GTE's (1976) three elements. Applied heavily to custody and property division (Cherry, Booth, Davis). Johnson v. Abdullah (2021) leads in 2020-24.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Ohio civil appeals: abuse of discretion and family law
previous.description: Ohio civil standards of review: abuse of discretion (Blakemore), competent credible evidence (C.E. Morris, Seasons Coal), Civ.R. 60(b) relief (GTE), and custody and property division in domestic-relations appeals.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: Blakemore (1983), which anchors every slice from 1990-94 to 2025-29, defines abuse of discretion as an unreasonable, arbitrary or unconscionable attitude, and C.E. Morris (1978) and Seasons Coal (1984) make competent, credible evidence enough to defeat a manifest-weight challenge. How it changed: the standard is stable, but the cases applying it shift. GTE (1976), with Adams (1988) and Griffey (1987), sets the three-part Civ.R. 60(B) test and imputes counsel's neglect to the party. Domestic-relations review dominates the 1990s and 2000s: Cherry (1981) on property division, Booth (1989) and Miller (1988) on custody, Kunkle (1990) on spousal support and Davis (1997) on what change in circumstances permits modification; In re Jane Doe 1 (1991) applies the standard to judicial bypass. Pons (1993) brings administrative-appeal review. From 2015-19 custody cases split off, AAAA Enterprises (1990) adds the 'unreasonable' prong, and Johnson v. Abdullah (2021) leads in 2020-24, restating the standard. Criminal cases (Bethel 2022, Hackett 2020) join in the 2020s.
rule: Ohio appellate courts review discretionary civil rulings, including custody, property division and Civ.R. 60(B) motions, for abuse of discretion, meaning an unreasonable, arbitrary or unconscionable attitude, and will not reverse as against the manifest weight a judgment supported by some competent, credible evidence.

changes.case: GTE Automatic Electric v. ARC Industries
changes.what: A Civ.R. 60(B) movant must show a meritorious claim or defence, a ground under 60(B)(1)-(5) and timeliness; failing any one is fatal, and counsel's neglect is imputed to the party.

changes.case: C.E. Morris Co. v. Foley Construction; Seasons Coal Co. v. City of Cleveland
changes.what: Judgments supported by some competent, credible evidence are not against the manifest weight, with deference to the trial judge's view of witnesses.
Abuse of discretion connotes more than an error of law or judgment; it implies an unreasonable, arbitrary or unconscionable attitude.

changes.case: Cherry v. Cherry; Booth v. Booth; Miller v. Miller
changes.what: Property division and allocation of parental rights are reviewed for abuse of discretion, without flat division rules, guided by R.C. 3109.04.
A change in circumstances for custody modification must be a change of substance but need not be substantial.
Restated the abuse-of-discretion standard and confirmed that a court has no discretion to commit an error of law.

name: Texas criminal appeals 1985-89: Russell sufficiency and preservation rules
description: Texas Court of Criminal Appeals cases of 1985-89, many capital: sufficiency on the cumulative force of incriminating circumstances (Russell, 1983, anchor) and strict preservation, where a general or unbriefed objection preserves nothing (Smith, 1984; Hawkins, 1983; Fierro, 1986). Also accomplice corroboration (Mitchell), polygraph exclusion (Nethery), post-arrest silence (Franklin) and voir dire on the burden of proof (Phillips).
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, round 2 after the lineage re-link)

previous.name: Texas capital appeals (1970s-80s): voir dire and preservation
previous.description: Texas Court of Criminal Appeals capital cases after 1976: excusing jurors opposed to the death penalty (Witherspoon, Adams v. Texas) and preservation (a general objection preserves nothing).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: the review standards of the Texas Court of Criminal Appeals in the 1980s, in a single 1985-89 slice merged from two 1980-84 units. Russell (1983) anchors: the evidence is sufficient if guilt follows from the combined and cumulative force of the incriminating circumstances. How it changed: no change within the slice; the cases restate preservation rules. Smith (1984) holds that a point without authority or argument preserves nothing and that continuance motions must be written and sworn; Hawkins (1983) requires a timely objection to jury-communication errors; Fierro (1986) rejects general objections; Vanderbilt (1981) disregards brief assertions outside the record. Capital-trial issues run alongside: voir dire of jurors who would demand proof beyond all doubt (Phillips, 1985), prosecutorial comment on uncalled witnesses (O'Bryan, 1979), party liability for a foreseeable murder during a robbery (Green, 1984), accomplice corroboration (Mitchell, 1983), post-arrest silence under art. 38.22 (Franklin, 1985) and polygraphs (Nethery, 1985). The lineage splits in 1990-94, partly into federal habeas.
rule: In the Texas Court of Criminal Appeals of the 1980s, evidence is sufficient if guilt is warranted by the combined and cumulative force of all the incriminating circumstances (Russell), and a complaint is preserved only by a timely, specific objection and is waived on appeal if briefed without authority or argument (Smith; Hawkins; Fierro).

changes.what: Circumstantial evidence is sufficient when guilt is warranted by the combined and cumulative force of all the incriminating circumstances.
Noncompliance with art. 36.27 on jury communications cannot be reviewed without a timely objection.
A point of error presented without authority or argument preserves nothing; a motion for continuance must be written and sworn.
Polygraph results are inadmissible for any purpose, whether offered by the State or the defendant.
A general objection does not apprise the trial court of the complaint and preserves nothing.

round1.name: Texas capital appeals (1975-89): Witherspoon juror exclusion, Adams, preservation
round1.description: Texas Court of Criminal Appeals capital cases after 1976: jurors may not be excused merely for general scruples about the death penalty (Witherspoon 1968; Davis 1976), and Adams v. Texas (1980) applied that to the Texas punishment questions. By 1985-89 the anchor shifts to Russell (1983) on circumstantial sufficiency and to preservation rules: a general or unbriefed objection preserves nothing (Smith 1984, Fierro 1986).
round1.history: Dominant rule: in a capital trial, a venireperson may be excused for cause only if his views on the death penalty would keep him from following the law, not for general reservations (Witherspoon, 1968; Boulden, 1969), and an improper exclusion voids the death sentence (Davis v. Georgia, 1976). Moore (1976) anchors 1975-84, with Burns, Bodde and Livingston on cause challenges, argument and capital-murder pleading. How it changed: Adams v. Texas (1980) enters in 1980-84 and extends Witherspoon to the Texas punishment-phase procedure, so jurors cannot be excused because the death penalty might 'affect' their deliberations. In 1985-89 Witherspoon, Adams and Davis leave and the anchor becomes Russell (1983): evidence is sufficient on the cumulative force of the incriminating circumstances. Also: preservation, where a general objection or an issue without authority or argument preserves nothing (Smith 1984, Hawkins 1983, Fierro 1986), and future dangerousness at punishment (O'Bryan, Granviel).
round1.rule: A venireperson may not be excused for cause merely for general reservations about the death penalty; only one whose views would prevent following the law and the oath may be excluded, and an improper exclusion voids a death sentence.

changes.what: Jurors may not be excluded merely for voicing general objections to the death penalty.
The improper exclusion of even one qualified venireman means a later death sentence cannot stand.
Applied Witherspoon to the Texas punishment-phase procedure; jurors may not be excluded because the death penalty might 'affect' their deliberations.

changes.case: Russell; Smith v. State (1984); Hawkins; Fierro
changes.what: By 1985-89 the anchor is Russell (sufficiency by cumulative force of the circumstances), and general or unbriefed objections are held to preserve nothing.

name: Illinois nonparent custody standing (Peterson, Menconi); D.C. best interests
description: Nonparent custody: in Illinois a fit parent's right is superior, and a grandparent or other nonparent may seek custody only if the child is not in a parent's physical custody, judged by voluntary and indefinite relinquishment (Peterson, 1986, anchor 1985-94; Menconi, 1983; Kirchner, 1995). In 1995-99 D.C. adoption and termination cases merge in and In re L.L. (1995) anchors, applying the best interests of the child.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Nonparent custody (Illinois, D.C.)
previous.description: Custody claims by grandparents and other nonparents: standing when a parent has relinquished physical custody (Peterson, Harne, Townsend, Carey), and the superior right of fit parents.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, contrastive pass from family evidence)

history: Dominant rule: a fit parent has the superior right to custody, and a nonparent may contest it only after the parent has relinquished physical custody or been found unfit. How it changed: the small early slices are anchored by Marcus (1974) in 1975-79 and Livingston (1969) in 1980-84, with Giacopelli (1959), Eaton (1977) and Cebrzynski (1978) weighing parental fitness against a stepparent's long physical custody, and Townsend (1981) treating the natural parent's superior right as a presumption. Peterson (1986) anchors 1985-89 and 1990-94, holding that standing does not turn on who had the child when the petition was filed; Menconi (1983) held a father's four-day possession did not defeat grandparents' standing, Barokas (1982) required a hearing on standing, and McCuan (1988) read Peterson to require relinquishment of legal custody. In 1995-99 D.C. adoption and termination cases merge in and In re L.L. (1995) anchors, with In re L.W. (1992), Petition of DIS (1985) and In re D.R.M. (1990) on best interests and review of findings, while Kirchner (Ill. 1995, Baby Richard) restated Illinois nonparent standing. Also: Peoples Drug Stores (D.C. 1983) on statutory construction enters in 1995-99, drift from the custody topic.
rule: A fit parent has a superior right to custody, so a grandparent or other nonparent has standing to seek custody under Illinois law only if the child is not in the physical custody of a parent, as where the parent has voluntarily and indefinitely relinquished it (Peterson, Kirchner).

changes.what: A third party must show good cause to overcome the presumption that the natural parent has the first and superior right to custody.

changes.case: In re Custody of Menconi (Ill. App.)
changes.what: A parent's brief possession does not restore physical custody or defeat grandparents' standing.
Standing does not turn on who held the child when the petition was filed but on whether the parent voluntarily and indefinitely relinquished custody; anchors 1985-94.

changes.case: In re Custody of McCuan (Ill. App.)
changes.what: Read Peterson to require a nonparent to show the parent relinquished legal custody, not just physical possession.
Restated that a nonparent has standing only if the parent voluntarily and indefinitely relinquished custody or is found unfit, and that physical possession is not physical custody.

before_differentiation.name: Illinois nonparent custody standing (Harne, Peterson); D.C. parental preference
before_differentiation.description: Nonparent custody: in Illinois a fit parent's right is superior (Nye, 1952, anchor 1965-79), and a grandparent or other nonparent may petition only if the child is not in a parent's physical custody, judged by voluntary and indefinite relinquishment (Harne, 1979; Peterson, 1986, anchor 1985-94). D.C. cases add a parental preference in adoption (Appeal of H.R., 1990; In re L.L., 1995); from 2000-04 the unit drifts into D.C. statutory construction.

name: Duty of fair representation and hybrid § 301 suits: Vaca to DelCostello
description: Union duty of fair representation and hybrid § 301 suits: arbitrary, discriminatory or bad-faith handling breaches the duty (Vaca 1967, anchor 1975-84; Hines 1976; Mitchell 1981), and DelCostello (1983), anchor 1985-94, applied the six-month § 10(b) period. The anchor then shifts doctrine: Lingle (1988) on § 301 preemption in 1995-99, Caterpillar (1987) on removal in 2000-09, and Grable (2005) on embedded federal issues in 2010-14.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Labor preemption: § 301 and fair representation
previous.description: LMRA § 301 preemption of state-law claims (Allis-Chalmers v. Lueck, Lingle), complete preemption and removal (Caterpillar, Franchise Tax Board), hybrid § 301/fair-representation suits and their limitations period (Vaca, Hines, DelCostello), and federal-question jurisdiction (Merrell Dow).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: in 1975-94 the lineage is about the duty of fair representation: a union acts unlawfully when its conduct toward a member is arbitrary, discriminatory or in bad faith (Vaca 1967; Huffman 1953), and an employee suing the employer for breach of a CBA after an unfavorable grievance outcome must show that breach (Hines 1976, Mitchell 1981). How it changed: Vaca anchors 1975-84, with Humphrey (1964) and Maddox (1965) on exhausting contractual remedies, Czosek (1970) apportioning damages, Foust (1979) barring punitive damages and Clayton (1981) on internal union remedies. DelCostello (1983) anchors 1985-94, replacing borrowed state periods (Hoosier Cardinal 1966) with the six-month § 10(b) period; circuits applied it retroactively and to RLA claims (Perez 1983, Sisco 1984) and fixed accrual (Howard 1984). The dominant doctrine then shifts: Lingle (1988) anchors 1995-99 with Lueck (1985) on § 301 preemption; Caterpillar (1987) anchors 2000-09 with Franchise Tax Board (1983), Taylor (1987) and Anderson (2003) on complete preemption and removal; and Grable (2005) anchors 2010-14 as securities and jurisdiction cases (Dabit 2006, Kokkonen 1994) merge in: drift.
rule: A union breaches its duty of fair representation by arbitrary, discriminatory or bad-faith conduct, including perfunctory grievance handling; an employee suing the employer under § 301 despite a final grievance result must prove that breach, and the hybrid suit is governed by the six-month § 10(b) limitations period; later slices shift to § 301 preemption and well-pleaded-complaint removal.

changes.case: Ford Motor Co. v. Huffman; Vaca v. Sipes
changes.what: The duty of fair representation applies under the NLRA; it is breached by arbitrary, discriminatory or bad-faith conduct, not merely by declining a meritorious grievance.
A union's breach that seriously undermines the arbitral process lifts the finality of an arbitration award against the employer.

changes.case: IBEW v. Foust; Clayton v. UAW; United Parcel Service v. Mitchell
changes.what: No punitive damages against unions; internal union remedies must ordinarily be exhausted; the union's breach is an indispensable predicate to the hybrid suit, which resembles an action to vacate an award.
Hybrid § 301/fair-representation suits take the six-month § 10(b) period rather than borrowed state limitations periods (displacing the Hoosier Cardinal approach for these suits).

changes.case: Sisco v. Consolidated Rail (and other circuits)
changes.what: Circuits applied the § 10(b) period to fair-representation claims under the Railway Labor Act.

changes.case: Allis-Chalmers v. Lueck; Lingle v. Norge
changes.what: Section 301 preempts state claims only where they depend on interpreting the CBA.
A federal defense, including preemption, does not support removal unless complete preemption applies.

name: Federal tax substance over form: Gregory v. Helvering, Frank Lyon, Lucas v. Earl
description: Federal tax substance over form: transactions are taxed by economic substance, not form (Gregory 1935, Frank Lyon 1978), and income is taxed to the earner (Lucas v. Earl 1930). The 2000-04 slice turns on whether contingent attorney fees are the client's income (Cotnam v. Coady, Baylin); later slices on tax-shelter economic substance and penalties (Coltec 2006, Stobie Creek 2010) and § 6901 transferee liability (Starnes, Diebold, 2012-14).
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Tax: economic substance and assignment of income
previous.description: Federal tax doctrines of substance over form: economic substance and sham transactions (Gregory v. Helvering, Frank Lyon, Coltec, Stobie Creek), assignment of income (Lucas v. Earl), and deductions (Welch).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, contrastive pass from family evidence)

history: Dominant rule: substance controls form in federal taxation. Gregory v. Helvering (1935) disregards a reorganization done only to avoid tax, and Frank Lyon (1978) respects a sale-leaseback with real economic substance; Frank Lyon anchors 2005-14 and Gregory anchors 2015-19. Alongside, Lucas v. Earl (1930), Horst (1940) and Glenshaw Glass (1955) tax income to the earner and treat accessions to wealth broadly. How it applied: in 2000-04, Cotnam (5th Cir. 1959) anchors the split over contingent attorney fees, which Baylin (1995) and Coady (2000) included in the client's income where state law gave lawyers no ownership interest; settlement-income cases (Burke, Schleier, O'Gilvie) sit with them, and Cotnam leaves after 2000-04. From 2010-14, tax-shelter cases lead. Coltec (2006) analyzes the transaction that gives the benefit, Klamath (2009) holds lack of substance sufficient, and penalty cases address valuation-misstatement penalties (Todd, Heasley v. Gilman, Zfass) and reasonable cause (Boyle 1985, Stobie Creek 2010). In 2015-19 the focus moves to transferee liability under § 6901, where Commissioner v. Stern (1958) makes state law govern and Starnes (2012) and Diebold (2013) differ on federal recasting.
rule: Tax consequences follow the economic substance of a transaction rather than its form, so a transaction without real economic effect or business purpose apart from tax savings is disregarded (Gregory, Frank Lyon), and income is taxed to the one who earns it despite anticipatory assignments (Lucas v. Earl, Horst).

changes.case: Lucas v. Earl; Gregory v. Helvering; Helvering v. Horst
changes.what: Income is taxed to the earner despite assignment, and transactions are judged by substance rather than form.

changes.case: Cotnam v. Commissioner (5th Cir.); Baylin (Fed. Cir. 1995); Coady (9th Cir. 2000)
changes.what: Circuits divided over whether a contingent fee paid to the plaintiff's lawyer is the plaintiff's gross income, turning on state attorney-lien law.

changes.case: Frank Lyon Co. v. United States
changes.what: A sale-leaseback with genuine multiparty substance and nontax purpose is respected.

changes.case: Coltec Industries (Fed. Cir.); Klamath Strategic Investment Fund (5th Cir.)
changes.what: Economic substance is tested on the transaction producing the tax benefit, and lack of substance alone invalidates it whatever the taxpayer's other motives.

changes.case: United States v. Boyle; Stobie Creek (Fed. Cir. 2010)
changes.what: Reasonable-cause defenses to penalties require reasonable reliance on objective advice; reliance on an agent to meet a deadline is not enough.
Whether a transferee's liability under § 6901 is decided under state law without first recasting the transaction under federal substance-over-form law.

name: Federal equitable remedies, contempt and post-judgment limits (2020-24)
description: A 2020-24 grouping on limits to federal courts' remedial powers: laches cannot cut short a statutory limitations period (Petrella 2014), disgorgement is a penalty under § 2462 (Kokesh 2017), contempt requires no fair ground of doubt (Taggart 2019), and appeal and Rule 59(e) deadlines are strict (Browder 1978, Banister 2020). FTC enforcement cases (On Point, E.M.A. Nationwide) anchor it.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Appeal deadlines, Rule 59(e) and remedies (2020)
previous.description: 2020 sub-cluster on post-judgment procedure and equitable remedies: jurisdictional appeal deadlines and Rule 59(e) motions (Bowles, Banister, Browder, Houston v. Lack), default judgments, laches (Petrella), disgorgement as a penalty (Kokesh) and civil contempt for violating a discharge (Taggart).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, contrastive pass from family evidence)

history: Dominant rule: federal courts' equitable and contempt powers operate within statutory and procedural limits. This is a single 2020-24 slice anchored by an FTC enforcement case (On Point Capital Partners, 11th Cir. 2021, common-enterprise liability), so the grouping is mixed. How it changed: Browder (1978) treats the appeal deadline as mandatory and jurisdictional. Petrella (2014) bars laches against a claim filed within a congressional limitations period. Kokesh (2017) held SEC disgorgement is a penalty subject to § 2462's five-year limit, following circuit cases like Graham (2016). Taggart (2019) set an objective no-fair-ground-of-doubt standard for contempt of a discharge order, against the older Cooke (1925) and Shillitani (1966) contempt cases. Banister (2020) held a timely Rule 59(e) motion is not a successive habeas petition but cannot raise new arguments. Alongside: Rule 60(b)(6) cannot evade time limits (Aikens 2011), and FTC deception and summary-judgment cases (Novartis, E.M.A. Nationwide).
rule: Federal courts' equitable and contempt powers are bounded by statute and by fixed procedural limits: laches cannot shorten a statutory limitations period, disgorgement is a penalty subject to § 2462, civil contempt needs no fair ground of doubt, and appeal and Rule 59(e) deadlines are strictly enforced.

changes.case: Browder v. Director, Dep't of Corrections
changes.what: The time to appeal is mandatory and jurisdictional, and an untimely reconsideration motion does not bring up the judgment.
Laches cannot bar legal relief on a claim brought within a statute of limitations enacted by Congress.
SEC disgorgement is a penalty, so § 2462's five-year limitations period applies.
Civil contempt for violating a discharge order is proper only if there is no fair ground of doubt that the creditor's conduct was barred (an objective standard).
A timely Rule 59(e) motion in habeas is not a second or successive petition, and it may not raise new arguments that could have been raised earlier.

history: Dominant rule: under Civ.R. 56(C), summary judgment is proper only when no genuine issue of material fact remains, the movant is entitled to judgment as a matter of law, and reasonable minds viewing the evidence most strongly for the nonmovant can reach only one conclusion (Harless, 1978; Temple, 1977). history: Dominant rule: substantial-evidence review of asylum denials, with findings overturned only if the evidence compels a different result (Balogun 2004). How it was applied: the Seventh Circuit repeatedly limited weak credibility findings: a minor inconsistency alone is not enough (Korniejew 2004), unsupported skepticism is insufficient (Xia Lin 2004), and failure to explore explanations casts doubt (Uwase 2003); IJs must develop the record and not interrupt testimony (Kerciku 2003), may not exclude evidence merely because it was obtained after arrival (Gjerazi 2006), and may not assume a refugee can bribe his way out of persecution (Giday, 2d Cir. 2006). Single slice; it splits in 2010-14, when the REAL ID Act's credibility rules take over.

round1.rule: Under 28 U.S.C. § 1291 only final decisions are appealable, save a small class of orders that conclusively resolve an important issue separate from the merits and would be effectively unreviewable after final judgment (Cohen); mandamus is a drastic remedy for extraordinary cases.

Bland (1997) set proportionality review. The 1985-89 slice is federal death-qualification law (Witherspoon, Witt).

history: Dominant rule: in Tennessee murder appeals the trial court has broad discretion to admit victim photographs and other graphic exhibits after Rule 403 balancing (Banks, 1978; Harris, 1992; Cazes, 1994, the heaviest case). name: Kansas appellate preservation: new issues, waiver by inadequate briefing
description: Kansas preservation rules in the partial 2025-29 slice, anchored by Mendez (2024): issues raised first on appeal are not heard unless an exception is invoked and explained (Allen 2021; Ervin 2025 on a question of law on admitted facts); evidentiary claims need a specific objection under K.S.A. 60-404 (Keys 2022); arguments without authority are waived (Meggerson 2020; Gallegos 2021). Ward (2011) supplies harmlessness.
history: Dominant rule: Kansas appellate courts decide only issues properly preserved and briefed. The lineage is a single partial slice, 2025-29, anchored by State v. Mendez (2024), formed when three 2020-24 Kansas criminal units, including one on jury instructions and clear error, merge. How it developed: an issue may not be raised first on appeal unless the appellant explains why an exception applies, such as a question of law on admitted facts or the need to prevent a denial of fundamental rights (Allen 2021); Mendez declined a first-time challenge to the premeditated-murder statute, while Ervin (2025) reached jail credit under the legal-question exception. K.S.A. 60-404 requires a timely and specific objection to evidence (Keys 2022). Points without supporting authority, or that ignore contrary authority, are waived or abandoned (Meggerson 2020; Gallegos 2021). Ward (2011) sets harmlessness standards, applied in Holley (2021). Hopkins (2023) overruled Campbell (1978). Also: statutory interpretation reviewed de novo (Daniels 2024), ex post facto questions about amended statutes (Patton 2022), probation-revocation departures (Tafolla 2022), and invited error on lesser offenses (Peters 2024).
rule: Kansas appellate courts generally refuse issues raised for the first time on appeal, including constitutional challenges, unless the appellant invokes and explains an exception (such as a pure question of law on admitted facts), and treat inadequately briefed points as waived or abandoned.

changes.what: Set the harmlessness framework for Kansas trial errors and treated issues not raised in the petition for review as abandoned.
Failing to show why an argument is sound in the face of contrary authority is akin to inadequate briefing, and the point may be deemed waived.
K.S.A. 60-404 bars appellate review of an evidentiary challenge without a timely and specific objection on the record.

name: Expert testimony under Rule 702: Daubert, Joiner and Kumho Tire
description: Admissibility of expert testimony: the trial judge screens it for reliability and relevance under Rule 702 (Daubert, 1993, anchor 1995-2029), displacing Frye's general-acceptance test, for all expert testimony (Kumho Tire, 1999), reviewed for abuse of discretion (Joiner, 1997). Before Daubert the 1990-94 anchor is Brock (5th Cir. 1989) on epidemiological proof of causation; state courts keep Frye or Kelly.
history: Dominant rule: the trial judge's gatekeeping role over expert testimony. How it changed: in 1990-94 the Bendectin causation case Brock v. Merrell Dow (5th Cir. 1989) anchors, with Frye (1923) and Lynch (1987) on whether animal and statistical studies can prove causation. Daubert (1993) held Frye superseded by Rule 702 and anchors every slice from 1995-99. Paoli (3d Cir. 1994) treated reliability as less than correctness; Joiner (1997) set abuse-of-discretion review; Kumho Tire (1999) extended gatekeeping to all specialized knowledge. Westberry (1999) accepted differential diagnosis for specific causation, and Downing (1985) eyewitness-memory experts. State courts appear throughout: California's Kelly test, Louisiana's Foret (1993) on child-abuse experts, Texas's Robinson line. Also: in 2020-24 Hobbs Act crime-of-violence cases (Mathis, Taylor, 2022) drift in; the 2025-29 slice is partial.
rule: Under Federal Rule of Evidence 702 the trial judge must act as gatekeeper and admit expert testimony only if it is relevant and rests on a reliable methodology, replacing Frye's general-acceptance test (Daubert), for all expert testimony (Kumho Tire), with rulings reviewed for abuse of discretion (Joiner).

changes.what: Scientific evidence is admissible only if its principle has gained general acceptance in its field.
Frye's general-acceptance test was not part of the Federal Rules of Evidence; the judge screens expert testimony for reliability and fit.

changes.case: In re Paoli Railroad Yard PCB Litigation (3d Cir.)
changes.what: Reliability is a lower burden than the merits standard of correctness, and qualifications are read liberally.
Rulings admitting or excluding expert testimony are reviewed for abuse of discretion.
The gatekeeping duty applies to all expert testimony, not only scientific testimony.
A reliable differential diagnosis can establish specific causation in toxic-tort cases.

name: Title VII procedure: timely EEOC charges, accrual and equitable tolling
description: Title VII's procedural prerequisites. Early circuits read them liberally (Choate 1968, anchor 1965-74); Love (1972, anchor 1975-84) allowed EEOC referral to state agencies. Evans (1977) and Ricks (1980, anchor 1990-94) fixed accrual at the discriminatory decision, while Zipes (1982, anchor 1985-89, 1995-99) made the filing period non-jurisdictional and tollable, extended by Irwin (1991). American Pipe tolling joins in 1995-99.

previous.name: Title VII procedure: EEOC charges and limitations
previous.description: Procedural prerequisites to Title VII suits: timely EEOC charges and when discrimination accrues (Ricks, Evans), equitable tolling (Zipes, Baldwin County v. Brown), deferral to state agencies (Love, Mohasco v. Silver), § 1981 limitations (Johnson v. REA), and arbitration's non-preclusive effect (Alexander v. Gardner-Denver).

history: Dominant rule: timely EEOC filing is required but read flexibly. Mayer (1968) and Sullivan (1969) opened § 1981/§ 1982 remedies. Love (1972) anchors 1975-84; Alexander (1974) refused to let arbitration bar suit, Johnson (1975) held an EEOC charge does not toll § 1981, Robbins & Myers (1976) refused tolling for grievances, and Brown v. GSA (1976) made Title VII exclusive for federal employees. Evans (1977) and Ricks (1980) narrowed continuing-violation and accrual theories, and Mohasco v. Silver (1980) applied deferral timing strictly. Zipes (1982) enters and anchors 1985-89, making time limits non-jurisdictional. Ricks anchors 1990-94 as Irwin (1991), Cada (1991) and Lorance (1989) join. Zipes anchors 1995-99 with American Pipe (1974) class tolling and Holmberg (1946) on equitable tolling.
rule: A Title VII plaintiff must file a timely EEOC charge, measured from the date the discriminatory decision is made and communicated (Ricks), but the filing period is not jurisdictional and is subject to waiver, estoppel and equitable tolling (Zipes), and courts reject procedural technicalities serving no substantive purpose (Love).

changes.case: Choate v. Caterpillar Tractor (7th Cir.); Oatis v. Crown Zellerbach (5th Cir.); Caldwell v. National Brewing (5th Cir.)
changes.what: Early circuits read Title VII's prerequisites liberally: unsworn charges, class members not filing charges, and bypassing EEOC for § 1981 claims. Choate anchors 1965-74.

changes.case: Alexander v. Gardner-Denver; Johnson v. Railway Express Agency; Electrical Workers v. Robbins & Myers; Brown v. GSA

changes.case: Irwin v. Department of Veterans Affairs; Cada v. Baxter Healthcare (7th Cir.)

name: Washington insurance bad faith: duty to defend, coverage by estoppel (Butler, Kirk, Woo)
description: Washington insurance bad faith: an insurer owes an enhanced duty of fairness (Butler, 1992) and must defend whenever claims are conceivably covered (VanPort, 2002; Woo, 2007). Bad-faith breach brings a presumption of harm and coverage by estoppel (Kirk, 1998), with reasonable covenant judgments as the measure (Besel, 2002); refusal on a questionable legal reading is bad faith (American Best Food, 2010). history: Dominant rule: the liability insurer's duty to defend and the remedies for its bad-faith breach. Butler (1992) set the enhanced duty of fairness and made harm an element of bad faith. How it changed: Kirk (1998) anchors 2000-04: bad faith under a reservation of rights creates a rebuttable presumption of harm and coverage by estoppel; Hayden (2000) requires bad faith or prejudice to estop a new ground of denial, and Ellwein (2001) calls the UIM relationship adversarial. Besel (2002) anchors 2005-09: a covenant judgment reasonable under the Chaussee factors is the presumptive measure of harm, and VanPort Homes (2002) relieves the insurer of the duty to defend only if the claim is clearly not covered. Woo (2007) anchors 2010-14: the duty arises when claims are conceivably covered, and American Best Food (2010) and Dan Paulson (2007) apply bad-faith liability and its near-impossible rebuttal burden. In 2015-19 Quadrant (2005) anchors on policy construction and exclusions, with Weyerhaeuser (2000) on construction from the average purchaser's view and Queen City Farms (1995). Also: Olympic Steamship (1991) fees and Coventry (1998) bad-faith investigation.
rule: A Washington liability insurer must defend whenever the complaint's claims are conceivably covered (Woo, VanPort Homes); an insurer owes an enhanced duty of fairness (Butler), and a bad-faith breach of the duty to defend raises a rebuttable presumption of harm and estops the insurer from denying coverage (Kirk), with a reasonable covenant judgment as the presumptive measure of damages (Besel).

changes.case: Olympic Steamship Co. v. Centennial Insurance
changes.what: An insured compelled to litigate to obtain coverage may recover its attorney fees.

changes.what: Insurers owe an enhanced obligation of fairness; harm is an element of bad faith, and bad-faith refusal to defend can make the insurer liable beyond the contract.

changes.what: A bad-faith investigation is actionable even if coverage was properly denied, though harm must still be shown.

name: Mandamus to district courts and inherent-power sanctions (Kerr, Cheney, Chambers)
description: A single 2005-09 slice merged from sanctions and collateral-order units: mandamus issues only in extraordinary cases, to confine a court to its jurisdiction or compel a clear duty, with no adequate alternative and a clear and indisputable right (Roche, 1943; Kerr, 1976, anchor; Allied Chemical, 1980; Cheney, 2004). previous.description: Mandamus to federal district courts (Kerr, Cheney, Roche) and whether courts may compel lawyers to represent indigent civil litigants under § 1915 (Mallard), with inherent-power sanctions (Chambers) and excusable neglect (Pioneer).

history: Dominant rule: courts of appeals issue mandamus to district courts only in extraordinary situations, where the petitioner lacks other adequate means of relief, shows a clear and indisputable right to the writ, and the court finds the writ appropriate; it is not a substitute for appeal. How it changed: the lineage exists only in 2005-09, merged from 2000-04 units on Rule 11 and inherent-power sanctions and on the collateral-order doctrine, and Kerr (1976) anchors it. Roche (1943) confined the writ to jurisdictional and clear-duty cases, United Steelworkers (1979) refused it as a substitute for appeal, Allied Chemical (1980) held discretionary rulings rarely reachable, and Baker (1988) required a clear duty. Mallard (1989) held that § 1915 does not permit coercive appointments of counsel. Cheney (2004) restated the three-part test. Alongside: recusal for personal bias (In re Beard, 1987), inherent-power and Rule 11 sanctions (Chambers, 1991; Cooter & Gell, 1990), dismissal for failure to prosecute (Link, 1962; Poulis, 1984) and excusable neglect (Pioneer, 1993). No rule change appears within the slice.
rule: Mandamus is a drastic remedy available only to confine a lower court to its lawful jurisdiction or compel a clear duty, where the petitioner has no other adequate means of relief, a clear and indisputable right to the writ, and the court is satisfied the writ is appropriate (Kerr, Cheney).

changes.what: Mandamus lies only to confine an inferior court to the lawful exercise of its jurisdiction or compel it to act when it must.

changes.case: Kerr v. United States District Court; Allied Chemical v. Daiflon
changes.what: Mandamus is reserved for extraordinary situations; where a matter is committed to discretion, the right to a particular result cannot be clear and indisputable. Kerr anchors the slice.
§ 1915 does not authorise courts to compel unwilling lawyers to represent indigent civil litigants, and mandamus issued to correct such an order.
District courts retain inherent power to sanction bad-faith litigation conduct, including by fee awards, alongside Rule 11.

history: Dominant rule: in 2015-19, Iowa ineffective-assistance doctrine, the route by which unpreserved errors reach review: a claimant must prove by a preponderance that counsel failed to perform an essential duty and that prejudice resulted, a reasonable probability of a different result (Ledezma, 2001; Graves, 2003; Straw, 2006; Maxwell, 2008), with review de novo. Counsel does not breach a duty by omitting a meritless objection, but does when no reasonable strategy explains the omission (Graves). Straw refused a per se prejudice rule for defective plea colloquies, and Clay (2012), the 2015-19 anchor, allowed cumulative assessment of prejudice. Preservation requires that an issue be raised and decided below (Meier v. Senecaut, 2002; Lamasters, 2012). How it changed: in 2020-24 the anchor is State v. Williams (2005), and the leading cases are recent Iowa Supreme Court decisions on jury pools and trial management: Plain (2017) overruled the absolute-disparity test of State v. Jones (1992) and gave defendants access to jury-pool data, Veal and Lilly (2019) applied the fair-cross-section standard, and Tipton (2017), Benson (2018) and Alcala (2016) addressed instructional error.
rule: An Iowa defendant claiming ineffective assistance must prove by a preponderance that counsel failed to perform an essential duty and that prejudice resulted (Ledezma, Straw, Clay), and an issue is preserved for appeal only if it was both raised and decided below (Meier v. Senecaut).

changes.what: Essential-duty and prejudice elements, reviewed de novo; no per se prejudice for defective plea advice (Straw); no duty breached by failing to raise a meritless objection.
Issues must be raised and decided by the district court; a motion to enlarge is needed if the court fails to rule.
Prejudice from multiple deficiencies is assessed cumulatively; Clay anchors 2015-19.

name: Vehicle search incident to arrest, 2005-09: Belton, Thornton, Gant
description: Vehicle searches incident to an occupant's arrest, in the single 2005-09 slice: Belton (1981, anchor) let officers search the passenger compartment, Thornton (2004) extended that to recent occupants, and Gant (2009) narrowed it to an arrestee within reach or reason to believe evidence of the offense is inside. Alongside: the automobile exception on probable cause (Carroll, Ross, Acevedo 1991, Dyson 1999) and inventory searches.
history: Dominant rule: police may search a vehicle without a warrant incident to arresting an occupant, or on probable cause under the automobile exception. Belton (1981) anchors the 2005-09 slice, with Chimel (1969) and Robinson (1973) on searches incident to arrest. How it changed: Thornton (2004) extended Belton to recent occupants, and Gant (2009), arriving at the end of the slice, limited such searches to an arrestee within reach or a reasonable belief that evidence of the offense is in the car. The automobile exception runs from Carroll (1925) and Chambers (1970) through Ross (1982), Carney (1985), Acevedo (1991), Labron (1996) and Dyson (1999), which need no exigency beyond probable cause. Also: inventory searches of impounded cars (Opperman 1976, Bertine 1987), and state decisions adopting Belton under a state constitution (Murrell 2002) or departing from federal law (New Jersey: Carty 2002 on consent, Eckel 2006 rejecting Thornton-style searches). The unit splits in 2010-14.
rule: Police may search a vehicle without a warrant incident to an occupant's arrest (Belton, limited by Gant to reach or evidence of the offense) or on probable cause that it holds contraband (Carroll, Ross).

changes.what: A vehicle may be searched without a warrant on probable cause that it carries contraband.
After a custodial arrest of an occupant, police may search the passenger compartment incident to the arrest.

changes.case: California v. Acevedo; Pennsylvania v. Labron; Maryland v. Dyson
changes.what: Probable cause allows a warrantless search of a car and containers in it with no separate exigency.
Belton applies when the arrestee was a recent occupant, even if first contacted outside the car.
A vehicle search incident to arrest is allowed only if the arrestee is within reaching distance or it is reasonable to believe evidence of the offense is inside.

history: Dominant rule: under Golding (1989), which anchors every slice, an unpreserved constitutional claim is reviewable if the record is adequate, the claim is constitutional, the violation clearly exists and deprived the defendant of a fair trial, and the State cannot show harmlessness; the party seeking review bears the burden. How it changed: in 2000-04 the leaders are prosecutorial-impropriety cases applying State v. Williams (1987): Brown and Gallo (2000) ask whether misconduct denied a fair trial, Alexander (2000) bars a prosecutor's personal opinion on guilt and Singh (2002) bars asking a witness whether another lied. From 2005-09 waiver becomes central: Fabricatore (2007) held that counsel who expressly approved an instruction and adopted it in summation waived the claim, failing Golding's third prong. Ebron (2009) took a narrower view, but Kitchens (2011), which leads from 2010-14, held that waiver may be implied when counsel had a meaningful opportunity to review the instructions and accepted them, overruling Ebron in part and leaving prejudice from such waivers to habeas. McClain (2017) and Davis (2017) lead 2015-19. Also: Whelan (1986) on substantive use of prior inconsistent statements and Hines (1998) on reasonable-doubt language.

previous.description: Ohio felony sentencing after State v. Foster struck judicial fact-finding, appellate review of sentences (Kalish, then Marcum), allied offenses (Rance, Johnson), and knowing, intelligent and voluntary guilty pleas under Crim.R. 11 (Veney, Clark).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: the standard for reviewing Ohio felony sentences, which shifts over the lineage. How it changed: Foster (2006) anchors 2005-09: under Blakely it severed the statutes requiring findings for non-minimum, maximum and consecutive terms (Comer, 2003, had required them), and Mathis (2006) kept the duty to consider R.C. 2929.11 and 2929.12. Kalish (2008) anchors 2010-14 with a two-step test. Johnson (2010) leads the same slice, overruling Rance (1999) and moving allied-offense analysis to the defendant's conduct. Oregon v. Ice (2009) prompted the legislature to restore consecutive-sentence findings, and Bonnell (2014) required them at the hearing (knowledge on H.B. 86). Marcum (2016) anchors from 2015-19, replacing Kalish with R.C. 2953.08(G)(2)'s clear-and-convincing test, and Jones (2020), anchor of the partial 2025-29 slice, held that appellate courts cannot vacate a sentence for lack of record support under 2929.11 and 2929.12. Alongside, from 2015-19 plea law joins: Nero (1990) and Veney and Clark (2008) set Crim.R. 11 compliance, Xie (1992) presentence withdrawal, and Dangler (2020) a prejudice requirement.
rule: Ohio appellate courts may modify or vacate a felony sentence only if they clearly and convincingly find the record does not support required statutory findings or the sentence is contrary to law (R.C. 2953.08(G)(2), Marcum), consecutive sentences require findings made at the hearing (Bonnell), and a guilty plea must be knowing, intelligent and voluntary under Crim.R. 11.

changes.case: State v. Nero; State v. Veney; State v. Clark
changes.what: Substantial compliance with nonconstitutional Crim.R. 11 advisements suffices if the defendant understood, but omission of constitutional advisements invalidates the plea.

changes.what: Severed the statutes requiring judicial fact-finding for non-minimum, maximum and consecutive sentences as violating Blakely; courts must still consider R.C. 2929.11 and 2929.12.
Plurality two-step review: whether the sentence is contrary to law, then abuse of discretion.

changes.case: Oregon v. Ice; State v. Bonnell
changes.what: Ice allowed judicial findings for consecutive sentences, the General Assembly restored them (H.B. 86, 2011), and Bonnell required the findings at the hearing and in the entry.
Allied-offense analysis under R.C. 2941.25 looks to the defendant's conduct, overruling Rance's abstract-elements comparison.
R.C. 2953.08(G)(2)'s clear-and-convincing standard, not Kalish's abuse-of-discretion step, governs felony sentence review.

changes.case: State v. Jones; State v. Dangler
changes.what: Jones bars appellate courts from vacating a sentence because the record does not support findings under R.C. 2929.11 and 2929.12; Dangler requires prejudice for most Crim.R. 11 defects.

before_differentiation.description: Ohio felony sentencing and pleas: Foster (2006) struck judicial fact-finding statutes under Blakely; Kalish (2008) set two-step review until Marcum (2016) adopted R.C. 2953.08(G)(2)'s clear-and-convincing standard; Bonnell (2014) requires consecutive-sentence findings; Johnson (2010) overruled Rance on allied offenses; Jones (2020) limited review of R.C. 2929.11-.12 factors. name: Zoning power and exclusionary zoning, 1975-79: Euclid, Belle Terre, Mount Laurel
description: Land use, not school funding: the zoning power and its limits in the single 1975-79 slice. Euclid (1926) upholds zoning under a fairly debatable standard and Belle Terre (1974) applies rational-basis review, but Pennsylvania and New Jersey courts struck exclusionary zoning (National Land 1965, Girsh 1970) and Mount Laurel (1975) required a realistic opportunity for lower-income housing. Robinson v. Cahill (1973) appears alongside as New Jersey precedent.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, round 2 after the lineage re-link)

previous.name: Zoning power and exclusionary zoning (1970s)
previous.description: The police power to zone and its limits: Euclid and Belle Terre v. Boraas, and state-court challenges to exclusionary zoning (Mount Laurel, Girsh Appeal, National Land v. Easttown) and rent control (Inganamort). Unlike the takings sub-clusters, these ask whether zoning is valid at all.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, contrastive pass from family evidence)

history: Dominant rule: zoning is within the police power and stands if its validity is fairly debatable (Euclid 1926), and under the federal Equal Protection Clause a non-suspect zoning classification needs only a rational basis (Belle Terre 1974, upholding limits on unrelated occupants). Berman v. Parker (1954) gives broad deference on public purpose. How it was limited: state courts developed doctrines against exclusionary zoning. National Land (Pa. 1965) held that zoning may plan for the future but not deny it; Girsh and Concord Township (Pa. 1970) struck towns' failure to allow apartments or their large-lot minimums; and Mount Laurel (N.J. 1975) held that developing municipalities must provide a realistic opportunity for low- and moderate-income housing, announcing the duty under the state constitution; Golden (N.Y. 1972) had upheld a timed-growth plan. The 1975-79 slice is anchored by a 1975 case on the same municipal housing obligation (cited as Mathews). Inganamort (N.J. 1973) let municipalities adopt rent control. Alongside: Robinson v. Cahill (N.J. 1973), the heaviest case, held New Jersey's school-finance system unconstitutional under the state education clause. The unit splits in 1980-84.
rule: Zoning is a valid exercise of the police power if its validity is fairly debatable and, absent a suspect class or fundamental right, needs only a rational basis, but state courts held that municipalities may not zone to exclude lower-income housing.

changes.case: Village of Euclid v. Ambler Realty Co.
changes.what: Comprehensive zoning is a valid exercise of the police power.

changes.case: National Land & Investment Co. v. Easttown; Girsh Appeal (Pa.)
changes.what: Zoning may not be used to exclude growth, such as by failing to provide for apartments.
School financing with no relation to equal educational opportunity violates the state constitution.

changes.case: Village of Belle Terre v. Boraas
changes.what: Rational-basis review for zoning classifications not involving a suspect class or fundamental right.

changes.case: Southern Burlington County NAACP v. Township of Mount Laurel (N.J.)
changes.what: Developing municipalities must provide a realistic opportunity for low- and moderate-income housing.
