name: Colorado equal protection for overlapping criminal statutes: Calvarest, Marcy
description: Colorado criminal law: a statute punishing conduct more harshly than an indistinguishable lesser offense violates equal protection (Calvarest 1975, felony manslaughter; Marcy 1981, extreme-indifference murder; Mumaugh 1982), but reasonable distinctions or greater specificity defeat the claim (Czajkowski 1977, Westrum 1981). The 1975-79 slice centres on Bennett (1973), which dropped the special circumstantial-evidence rule.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Colorado criminal: equal protection and overlapping statutes
previous.description: Colorado Supreme Court cases holding that a statute imposing harsher punishment for conduct not sufficiently distinguishable from a lesser offense violates equal protection (Calvarest, Marcy, Bramlett), with deadly-weapon definitions.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session subagents, from cocite evidence; second pass differentiated near-duplicates)

history: Dominant rule: Colorado reads equal protection, implicit in its due process clause (Max 1921), to bar harsher penalties for conduct indistinguishable from a lesser offense. How it changed: in 1975-79 the small unit is anchored by People v. Bennett (1973), which abandoned the requirement that circumstantial evidence exclude every reasonable hypothesis of innocence, with Calvarest (1975) already leading. Calvarest struck the felony manslaughter statute as indistinguishable from criminally negligent homicide. Czajkowski (1977) limited the doctrine where one offense is more specific, and Bramlett (1977) defined a deadly weapon by its manner of use. Heninger (1980), on license revocation and the right to travel, anchors 1980-84. Marcy (1981) enters and anchors 1985-89: the extreme-indifference murder definition was indistinguishable from second-degree murder. Mumaugh (1982) applied the rule to traffic offenses, and Westrum (1981) confirmed there is no violation where reasonable distinctions exist.
rule: Under Colorado's equal protection guarantee, a statute that punishes conduct more harshly than another statute punishing conduct that is not reasonably distinguishable from it is invalid; if reasonable distinctions can be drawn between the statutes, there is no violation.

changes.what: Abandoned the rule that wholly circumstantial evidence must exclude every reasonable hypothesis of innocence; one sufficiency test applies to all evidence.
Felony manslaughter violated equal protection because it was not sufficiently distinguishable from misdemeanor criminally negligent homicide.

changes.case: People v. Czajkowski; People v. Bramlett
changes.what: A more specific offense may carry a greater penalty (Czajkowski), and the deadly-weapon definition by manner of use was left to the legislature (Bramlett).

changes.case: People v. Marcy; People v. Westrum; People v. Mumaugh
changes.what: Extreme-indifference murder was held indistinguishable from second-degree murder (Marcy), and leaving the scene offenses likewise (Mumaugh); Westrum restated that only identical conduct raises the problem.

name: Contract Clause: Blaisdell's police-power exception and the Spannaus test
description: State laws impairing contracts are valid if a substantial impairment serves a significant and legitimate public purpose by reasonable means (Blaisdell, 1934). U.S. Trust (1977) applied stricter review to a state's own bond covenants; Spannaus (1978) struck a narrow-class pension law; Energy Reserves (1983) settled the three-step test. In 1980-84 federal retroactive pension legislation (Nachman, PBGC cases) joined.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Contract Clause
previous.description: State laws impairing contracts: Blaisdell's emergency exception, U.S. Trust Co., Allied Structural Steel v. Spannaus, Energy Reserves Group, and federal retroactive legislation (Nachman v. PBGC).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, contrastive pass from family evidence)

history: Dominant rule: the Contract Clause is not read literally; a state may impair contracts under its police power if the impairment is reasonable and appropriate to a legitimate public purpose. Blaisdell (1934) anchors 1970-79, with Simmons (1965), Veix (1940) and the Depression-era cases (Kavanaugh, Thomas, Treigle) marking the limits. How it changed: U.S. Trust (1977) and Spannaus (1978) entered in 1975-79; U.S. Trust held New Jersey and New York to their Port Authority bond pledge with less deference to self-interested impairments, and Spannaus, the 1980-84 anchor, struck a law serving a narrow class. Energy Reserves Group (1983), the 1985-89 anchor, with Eagerton (1983), settled the three-step inquiry and gave weight to pervasive regulation. Alongside: in 1980-84 the unit drew in due-process challenges to retroactive federal pension legislation (Nachman, 1980; Peick and Shelter Framing on MPPAA withdrawal liability), which left by 1985-89.
rule: A state law that substantially impairs a contract is valid if it serves a significant and legitimate public purpose through reasonable means appropriate to that purpose, with less deference when the state impairs its own contracts.

changes.case: Home Building & Loan Ass'n v. Blaisdell
changes.what: The Contract Clause is not absolute; a state may reasonably modify contracts under its police power in an emergency.

changes.case: United States Trust Co. v. New Jersey
changes.what: Impairment of a state's own financial obligations (the Port Authority bond covenant) is reviewed with less deference and must be reasonable and necessary.

changes.case: Allied Structural Steel Co. v. Spannaus
changes.what: A severe impairment aimed at a narrow class, not a broad societal interest, violates the clause.

changes.case: Energy Reserves Group v. Kansas Power & Light; Exxon v. Eagerton
changes.what: Three-step test: substantial impairment, a significant and legitimate public purpose, and reasonable conditions appropriate to that purpose; pervasive regulation lowers expectations.

name: Illinois insurance: duty to defend potentially covered suits (Outboard Marine, Ehlco)
description: Illinois liability insurance: the insurer must defend if the complaint alleges facts potentially within coverage (Peppers, 1976), with ambiguities construed for the insured (Outboard Marine, 1992, anchoring every slice). Ehlco (1999) estops an insurer that fails to defend; Koloms (1997) confined the pollution exclusion to traditional pollution; General Agents (2005) barred recouping defense costs; defective workmanship is not an occurrence (Wil-Freds, Viking).

previous.name: Illinois insurance: duty to defend and pollution
previous.description: Illinois insurance coverage: duty to defend when the complaint alleges facts potentially within coverage (Wilkin Insulation, Outboard Marine), estoppel for insurers who fail to defend (Ehlco), pollution exclusions (Koloms) and excess coverage.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: Outboard Marine (1992) anchors all three slices. An insurer's duty to defend is broader than its duty to indemnify: it must defend whenever the complaint alleges facts within or potentially within coverage (Peppers, 1976), and ambiguous policy words are read for the insured. Crum & Forster (1993) holds indemnity arises only if the facts actually fall within coverage. How it changed: Wilkin Insulation (1991) treated asbestos removal as an occurrence; Lapham-Hickey (1995) limited the duty to formal suits; Koloms (1997) read the absolute pollution exclusion as limited to traditional environmental pollution. In 2000-04 Ehlco (1999) enters: an insurer that neither defends under a reservation of rights nor seeks a declaratory judgment is estopped from raising coverage defenses. Eljer (2001) restates intent-based construction. In 2005-09 the construction-defect line leads (Hydra, 1993; Wil-Freds, 1996; Tillerson, 2002; Viking, 2005: faulty workmanship is not an occurrence), with CILCO (2004) on environmental cleanup and General Agents (2005) denying reimbursement of defense costs. Also: Ward (1990) and Bucheleres (1996) on open-and-obvious premises duty, which briefly join in 2000-04.
rule: An Illinois liability insurer must defend if the underlying complaint alleges facts within or potentially within coverage, construing the complaint and ambiguous policy terms for the insured; an insurer that neither defends under reservation nor seeks a declaratory judgment is estopped from raising coverage defenses.

changes.what: The duty to defend arises if the complaint alleges facts potentially within coverage, even if only one of several counts is covered; a declaratory action may not decide ultimate facts of the underlying suit.

changes.case: USF&G v. Wilkin Insulation; Outboard Marine v. Liberty Mutual
changes.what: Asbestos removal costs are an occurrence and damage is excluded only if the insured expected it; ambiguous terms such as 'damages' are construed for the insured.
The duty to defend extends only to suits embodied in a complaint, not to claims or accusations short of suit.
The absolute pollution exclusion covers only traditional environmental pollution, not a carbon-monoxide leak from a furnace.

changes.case: Employers Insurance of Wausau v. Ehlco Liquidating Trust
changes.what: An insurer that breaches the duty to defend is estopped from raising policy defenses, without any showing of prejudice.

changes.case: General Agents Insurance v. Midwest Sporting Goods
changes.what: An insurer that defends under a reservation of rights cannot recover defense costs if coverage is later found lacking.

changes.case: Indiana Insurance v. Hydra; Monticello v. Wil-Freds; Viking Construction
changes.what: Natural results of defective workmanship are not an 'occurrence' or 'property damage' under a CGL policy.

name: Prisoner Eighth Amendment deliberate indifference: Estelle, Farmer (main line)
description: The main prisoner civil-rights line, 1970-2029, led from 1990 by the Eighth Amendment rule: deliberate indifference to serious medical needs or a substantial risk of harm (Estelle 1976, anchor 1990-94; Farmer 1994, anchor 1995-2029), with Wilson (1991) adding a state-of-mind element. Earlier phases center on revocation due process (Gagnon, Morrissey, 1970-79) and prison due process and conditions (Wolff, Wolfish, 1980-89).

history: Dominant rule: from 1990-94 on, Eighth Amendment deliberate indifference. Estelle (1976) held that deliberate indifference to serious medical needs is cruel and unusual punishment, and Farmer (1994) defined it as subjective recklessness. How it changed: in 1970-74 Gagnon (1973) anchors and in 1975-79 Morrissey (1972): parole and probation revocation require due process. Wolff (1974) anchors 1980-84 and Wolfish (1979) 1985-89 as prison due-process and conditions cases grow (Meachum, Greenholtz, Procunier, Pell, Bounds, Turner 1987). Estelle anchors 1990-94, with Wilson (1991) requiring a culpable state of mind and Hudson (1992) on force. Farmer anchors from 1995-99 on, with Neitzke (1989), Denton (1992) and Haines (1972) on frivolous and pro se suits; Sandin (1995) joins in 2005-09; PLRA exhaustion (Woodford 2006, Jones 2007) leads 2010-14; Monell (1978) and Canton (1989) join from 2015-19, and Kingsley (2015) and detainee cases (Brawner 2021) in 2020-24. The partial 2025-29 slice returns to Wilson, Rhodes and Hudson.
rule: A prison official violates the Eighth Amendment by deliberate indifference to an inmate's serious medical needs or to a substantial risk of serious harm, meaning the official knew of and disregarded the risk.

changes.case: Morrissey v. Brewer; Gagnon v. Scarpelli
changes.what: Parole and probation revocation require notice, a hearing and other basic due process, though not the full rights of a criminal trial.

Deliberate indifference is subjective recklessness: the official must know of and disregard a substantial risk of serious harm.
Liberty interests arise only from atypical and significant hardship, not from mandatory regulatory language.

name: Anderson-Burdick balancing of election and ballot-access burdens
description: Election regulation under Anderson-Burdick: courts balance the burden on voting and association against the state's interests, with strict scrutiny only for severe burdens (Anderson 1983, Burdick 1992). Earlier ballot-access cases (Williams v. Rhodes, Jenness, Bullock, Storer) feed in; Tashjian (1986) and Timmons (1997) cover party association; Buckley campaign-finance cases dominate 2000-04, and districting cases (Rucho, Gill) join in 2020-24.

previous.name: Ballot access and election regulation: Anderson-Burdick
previous.description: Anderson v. Celebrezze and Burdick balancing of election burdens, with Storer, Jenness, Bullock and Williams v. Rhodes on ballot access and Tashjian and Timmons on party association. Small through the 1990s, largest in 2020-24.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session subagents, from cocite evidence; second pass differentiated near-duplicates)

history: Dominant rule: Anderson v. Celebrezze (1983) anchors most slices from 1985-89 and Burdick v. Takushi (1992) from 2005-09. A court weighs the character and magnitude of the burden on voting and association rights against the state's precise interests, applying strict scrutiny only to severe burdens. How it changed: in 1980-84 the unit is pre-Anderson ballot-access law anchored by Jenness (1971), with Storer (1974), Bullock (1972) and Williams v. Rhodes (1968). Anderson replaced that approach with flexible balancing, and Tashjian (1986) extended association rights to party primaries. Burdick (1992) enters in 1990-94 and upheld a write-in ban as a reasonable, nondiscriminatory restriction; Timmons (1997) upheld a fusion ban. Drift: in 1995-2004 Buckley v. Valeo leads and anchors 2000-04 as campaign-finance cases (Nixon v. Shrink 2000, Colorado Republican) merge in. In 2010-19 Crawford (2008) and voting-rights cases join, and in 2020-24 the unit absorbs districting and justiciability cases (Baker v. Carr, Rucho 2019, Gill 2018).
rule: A court weighs the character and magnitude of an election law's burden on voting and association rights against the state's justifications: severe burdens need narrow tailoring to a compelling interest, while reasonable, nondiscriminatory restrictions are usually justified by important regulatory interests (Anderson v. Celebrezze; Burdick v. Takushi).

changes.what: Ballot-access limits burden voting and association rights; states may require a significant modicum of support, but exclusionary fees and barriers get close scrutiny.

description: A single 2010-14 slice joining two doctrines: mandamus requires extraordinary circumstances and a clear and indisputable right (Kerr, 1976, anchor; Cheney, 2004), and federal crimes presume mens rea (Morissette, 1952; U.S. Gypsum, 1978; Staples, 1994). Linking them are § 2259 restitution cases requiring proximate cause (Monzel, Kennedy, 2011) and CVRA victim petitions, where circuits split on the mandamus standard (Kenna, 2006; Antrobus, 2008).

name: Ninth Circuit REAL ID adverse credibility: totality test (Shrestha, Alam)
description: Ninth Circuit review of adverse credibility findings, 2015-29: Shrestha (2010, anchor throughout) holds that the REAL ID Act lets IJs rely on any inconsistency, judged on the totality of the circumstances, abrogating the heart-of-the-claim test (Ren 2011). name: ERISA plan amendment, vesting and fiduciary misrepresentation (Varity v. Howe)
description: ERISA retiree and welfare benefits, 1995-2004: employers may amend or end unvested welfare benefits under a reservation-of-rights clause (Schoonejongen 1995; Sprague 1998; Unisys 1995), and amendment is not fiduciary action (Spink 1996). But fiduciaries may not mislead participants, with individual equitable relief under § 502(a)(3) (Varity v. Howe 1996, anchor 2000-04), limited by Mertens (1993, anchor 1995-99) and Russell (1985).
history: Dominant rule: welfare benefits do not vest unless the plan says so, and an employer may amend or terminate them under a reservation-of-rights clause (Schoonejongen 1995; Musto 1988; Wise 1993; Sprague, 6th Cir. en banc 1998), so 'lifetime' language in informal communications does not override the plan (Gable 1994, Unisys 1995). Plan changes must follow the written amendment procedure (Hozier 1990). Remedies frame the claims: Mertens (1993), anchor in 1995-99, confines § 502(a)(3) to traditional equitable relief, and Russell (1985) confines § 502(a)(2) to plan-wide relief. How it changed: Varity v. Howe (1996) anchors 2000-04, holding that misleading participants about plan prospects is a fiduciary breach remediable by individuals under § 502(a)(3), while Spink (1996) held plan design and amendment are settlor, not fiduciary, acts. Courts applied misrepresentation claims with a 'serious consideration' materiality test (Hockett 1997) and recognised breaches by affirmative misstatements (Drennan 1992, Krohn 1999). Also: class certification of retiree claims (Sprague, Frahm 1998) and party anonymity (Doe v. Frank 1992, James v. Jacobson 1993) in 2000-04.

name: Blakely and Booker on jury-found sentencing facts: remedies and retroactivity (2005)
description: The 2005 wave applying Apprendi, Blakely (2004, anchor of this one-slice 2005-09 lineage) and Booker (2005): judge-found facts may not raise the sentence above the verdict-based maximum, and Booker made the Guidelines advisory. history: Dominant rule: Blakely (2004), anchor of this single 2005-09 slice, defined the statutory maximum as what the jury's verdict or the defendant's admissions authorize, building on Jones (1999) and Apprendi (2000); Almendarez-Torres (1998) still excepts prior convictions, and Harris (2002) still allowed judge-found mandatory minimums. How it changed: Booker (2005) applied Blakely to the federal Guidelines and remedied the violation by making them advisory, applying both holdings to all cases on direct review under Griffith (1987). The circuits then divided on how to handle unpreserved Booker error: the Fourth Circuit in Hughes (2005) found plain error where enhancements rested on judge-found facts, while the Ninth Circuit en banc in Ameline (2005) ordered limited remands to ask whether the district court would have sentenced differently; White (2005) distinguished statutory from constitutional error for preservation. On collateral review, Schriro v. Summerlin (2004) held Ring not retroactive, and courts such as McReynolds (2005) held Booker unavailable in successive § 2255 motions. Cunningham (2007) struck California's determinate sentencing law.
rule: Under Blakely and Booker, a sentence may not exceed the maximum authorized by facts the jury found or the defendant admitted (prior convictions excepted), so mandatory Guidelines enhancements based on judge-found facts violate the Sixth Amendment; Booker applies to all cases on direct review but not retroactively on collateral review.

history: Dominant rule: civil RICO reaches any person injured by a § 1962 violation, but the plaintiff must plead a pattern of racketeering with particularity. (1989) settled it and anchors 1990-94: the predicates must be related and amount to or threaten continued criminal activity. Holmes (1992) required proximate cause. In 1995-99 Reves (1993) limits § 1962(c) to those who operate or manage the enterprise, and criminal enterprise prosecutions lead (Locascio, Thai and VICAR under Concepcion). Salinas (1997) anchors 2000-04 on RICO conspiracy, alongside § 666 federal-program bribery cases (Zwick 1999, Fischer 2000).
round1.rule: RICO liability requires a person, distinct from an enterprise (legitimate or not), who conducts or participates in operating or managing the enterprise's affairs through a pattern of racketeering, meaning related predicate acts that amount to or threaten continued criminal activity; civil plaintiffs need no prior conviction or special racketeering injury but must show injury proximately caused by the predicates.

changes.what: Circuits required an enterprise structure distinct from the racketeering, applied Rule 9(b) to fraud predicates and rejected a racketeering-injury requirement.

changes.what: Circuits divided on pattern: a multifactor test rejecting a multiple-scheme rule (Morgan) versus holding a single scheme insufficient (Fulmer).

name: Brady disclosure: materiality of suppressed exculpatory and impeachment evidence
description: The prosecution's disclosure duty under Brady (1963), extended to impeachment evidence (Giglio, 1972; Bagley, 1985) and to evidence known only to police (Kyles, 1995). Materiality means a reasonable probability of a different result, judged cumulatively (Kyles; Strickler, 1999; Wearry, 2016). Lost evidence violates due process only with bad faith (Youngblood, 1989). The rule was stable across 2010-19.

history: Dominant rule: suppression of favorable, material evidence violates due process (Brady, 1963, the anchor in 2010-14). Favorable evidence includes impeachment evidence (Giglio, 1972; Bagley, 1985, the anchor in 2015-19), and materiality means a reasonable probability of a different result. How it changed: this lineage covers only 2010-14 and 2015-19 and restates settled law rather than changing it. Napue (1959) and Giglio govern false testimony. Agurs (1976) dropped any request requirement. Kyles (1995) made materiality cumulative and imputed police knowledge to the prosecution, and Strickler (1999) restated the three elements. Trombetta (1984) and Youngblood (1989) require bad faith for lost potentially useful evidence. In 2015-19 Smith v. Cain (2012) and Wearry (2016) reaffirm cumulative review, Cone (2009) and Banks (2004) govern Brady claims in habeas, and Texas and Arkansas state habeas and coram nobis decisions apply the rule (Chabot, 2009; Larimore, 2000; Howard, 2012). Confrontation cases (Van Arsdall, Davis) drop out after 2010-14.
rule: Due process is violated when the prosecution suppresses, willfully or inadvertently, evidence favorable to the accused, whether exculpatory or impeaching, that is material, meaning there is a reasonable probability of a different result when the suppressed evidence is assessed cumulatively.

changes.case: Napue v. Illinois; Brady v. Maryland
changes.what: Knowing use of false testimony violates due process, and suppression of favorable evidence material to guilt or punishment does too, whatever the prosecutor's good faith.

changes.case: Giglio v. United States; United States v. Agurs
changes.what: The duty covers impeachment of key witnesses and knowledge anywhere in the prosecution, and applies without a defense request.
Impeachment and exculpatory evidence are treated alike, and evidence is material if there is a reasonable probability of a different result; Bagley anchors 2015-19.

changes.case: California v. Trombetta; Arizona v. Youngblood
changes.what: Failure to preserve merely potentially useful evidence violates due process only on a showing of police bad faith.
Materiality is judged cumulatively, the duty reaches evidence known only to police, and no separate harmless-error review follows a Brady violation.
A Brady claim requires favorable evidence, suppressed by the State willfully or inadvertently, and resulting prejudice.

changes.case: Smith v. Cain; Wearry v. Cain
changes.what: Evidence is material when there is any reasonable likelihood it could have affected the jury, and courts may not assess items in isolation.

history: Dominant rule: Mississippi appellate courts enforce a contemporaneous-objection rule, so unobjected-to errors and grounds not presented at trial are procedurally barred. How it changed: May (1984) anchors 1985-89 and Neal (1984) 1990-94, on confessions and sufficiency, with Billiot (1984) and Cole (1987) warning that counsel may not sit silent and raise errors later. McFee (1987) anchors 1995-99: prosecutorial misconduct that substantially impairs a fair trial requires reversal if a mistrial is wrongly refused. In capital cases, Pinkney (1988) and Shell v. Mississippi (1990) required an adequate limiting definition of the heinousness aggravator, Willie (1991) barred doubly weighing the underlying felony and its motive, and Hansen (1991) limited prior convictions and co-defendant statements. Chase (1994), Conner (1994) and Carr (1995) hardened the waiver rules; Conner was overruled on other grounds by Weatherspoon (1999). Walker (1995) anchors 2000-04 before the lineage continues as Mississippi criminal appeals of the 2000s.

history: Dominant rule: on review of a suppression ruling, a Pennsylvania appellate court considers only the suppression record, accepts findings it supports and reviews the law de novo (In re L.J., 2013, the anchor in both slices). How it changed: the lineage forms in 2015-19, so its rules come from earlier decisions. In re D.M. (2001), following Wardlow, held that unprovoked flight in a high-crime area gives reasonable suspicion, but suspicion must exist when police first seize the person, so nervousness or furtive movements alone are a hunch. Strickler (2000) governs consent after a stop. Chase (2008) and Feczko (2010) set the reasonable-suspicion and probable-cause thresholds for Vehicle Code stops. Gary (2014) adopted the federal automobile exception; Alexander (2020) later overruled it, and the evidence notes Alexander claims only as waived. Hicks (2019) enters in 2020-24 and holds that possessing a concealed gun is not enough by itself. Also: mere encounters, plain view, rental-car standing and Terry frisks of passengers. In 2025-29 the unit returns to the national stops lineage.

name: Ohio sufficiency v. manifest weight, 2010-29: Thompkins anchor (Jenks, Martin)
description: The evidence-review strand of the 2010-29 Ohio cluster, anchored throughout by Thompkins (1997): sufficiency asks whether any rational trier of fact could convict (Jenks 1991), manifest weight whether the jury clearly lost its way (Martin 1983). DeHass (1967) leaves credibility to the factfinder; under Tibbs (1982) only a sufficiency reversal bars retrial. The rule is stable; Eastley (2012) extended weight review to civil cases.
history: Dominant rule: Ohio's two evidence-review standards. Thompkins (1997) anchors all four slices, 2010-14 through 2025-29. Sufficiency is a test of adequacy: viewing the evidence most favourably to the prosecution, could any rational trier of fact find the elements proved beyond a reasonable doubt (Jenks, 1991, which also gave circumstantial evidence the same probative value as direct evidence; Berry, 2013). Manifest weight is a test of persuasiveness: the appellate court reviews the whole record, weighs the evidence and credibility, and orders a new trial only where the jury clearly lost its way (Martin, 1983; Otten, 1986). Credibility remains primarily for the factfinder (DeHass, 1967), and under Tibbs (1982) a sufficiency reversal bars retrial while a weight reversal does not. How it changed: the rule is stable; Eastley (2012) extended the weight standard to civil cases. Alongside: prosecutorial references to legal concepts (Smith, 1997), mere presence not proving complicity (Johnson, 2001), hearsay in police reports (Leonard, 2004), instructions on preliminary matters (Comen, 1990) and on provocation for voluntary manslaughter (Shane, 1992), and the duty to repeat vital instructions. The lineage is a sub-unit of the Ohio capital and criminal appeals cluster.
rule: Sufficiency asks whether, viewing the evidence most favourably to the prosecution, any rational trier of fact could find each element beyond a reasonable doubt (Jenks); manifest weight asks whether the jury clearly lost its way and created a manifest miscarriage of justice requiring a new trial (Thompkins, Martin).

changes.what: The weight of evidence and credibility of witnesses are primarily for the trier of fact.
Reversal for insufficient evidence bars retrial, but reversal on the weight of the evidence does not.

changes.case: State v. Martin; State v. Otten (Ohio App.)
changes.what: Set the manifest-weight standard: the court weighs the evidence and credibility as a thirteenth juror and reverses only in exceptional cases.
Adopted the rational-trier-of-fact sufficiency test and gave circumstantial and direct evidence equal probative value.
Sufficiency and weight are qualitatively different tests with different consequences on reversal.
The manifest-weight standard applies in civil cases too.

name: NLRB remedies in the 1970s: Gissel card-based bargaining orders, H.K. Porter
description: NLRB remedies and their review, 1970-79: Gissel (1969) anchors 1970-74, approving bargaining orders based on authorization cards when employer misconduct undermines an election, and Universal Camera (1951) anchors 1975-79 on substantial-evidence review. Katz (1962) bars unilateral changes; Fibreboard (1964) makes contracting out bargainable; broad Board remedies (Phelps Dodge 1941, Seven-Up 1953) are limited by H.K. Porter (1970) and Allied Chemical (1971).

history: Dominant rule: deferential review of Board unfair-labor-practice orders. How it changed: NLRB v. Gissel Packing (1969) anchors 1970-74, holding that authorization cards may support a bargaining order where the employer's unfair labor practices make a fair election unlikely, and that employer threats of retaliation are not protected speech; circuit cases enforced such orders on threats and interrogation (L.B. Foster 1969, Varo 1970). Universal Camera (1951) anchors 1975-79: Board findings stand on substantial evidence on the whole record, examiner disagreements included. Alongside: duties to bargain, with Katz (1962) forbidding unilateral changes during negotiations, Fibreboard (1964) on contracting out (read narrowly in Westinghouse 1967), American National Insurance (1952), and Allied Chemical (1971) excluding retirees' benefits as mandatory subjects. Remedies are broad (Phelps Dodge 1941, Virginia Electric 1943, Franks Bros. 1944, Seven-Up 1953 on backpay, Rutter-Rex 1970 on delay) but H.K. Porter (1970) bars ordering substantive contract terms; unit determinations get informed discretion (Packard 1947). In 1975-79 interrogation cases (Camco 1965, Mueller Brass 1977) enter before the unit splits in 1980-84.
rule: Courts enforce NLRB orders supported by substantial evidence on the whole record and defer to the Board's broad remedial discretion, including bargaining orders where unfair labor practices make a fair election unlikely, but the Board may not compel agreement on substantive terms.

changes.what: Substantial-evidence review on the whole record, including an examiner's contrary findings.

changes.what: Unilateral changes during bargaining are unlawful, and contracting out unit work is a mandatory subject.
Card-based bargaining orders may remedy unfair labor practices that undermine a fair election.
The Board may not compel a party to agree to a substantive contract provision.

changes.case: Allied Chemical & Alkali Workers v. Pittsburgh Plate Glass
changes.what: Retirees are not employees, so their benefits are not a mandatory subject; mid-term changes give a contract remedy.

round1.name: NLRB orders on review: Universal Camera substantial evidence, Gissel orders
round1.description: NLRB orders reviewed for substantial evidence on the whole record (Universal Camera 1951, anchor of every slice), with deference to examiner credibility (Walton 1962). Substantive rules: Katz (1962) on unilateral changes, Fibreboard and Exchange Parts (1964), Great Dane (1967) on motive, Gissel (1969) bargaining orders, and Wright Line (1981) and Transportation Management (1983) for mixed-motive discharges.
round1.history: Dominant rule: courts enforce Board orders supported by substantial evidence on the whole record and do not reweigh the Board's choice between fairly conflicting views (Universal Camera, 1951, anchor in every slice from 1955-59 to 1980-84). How it changed: Consolidated Edison (1938) defined substantial evidence, and Phelps Dodge (1941) and Franks Bros. (1944) framed Board remedies. In the 1960s, Walton (1962) stressed deference to examiners who saw the witnesses, and circuit enforcement cases (Camco, Griggs) applied it to coercive interrogation and discharges. In 1970-74 Supreme Court substantive cases join: Katz (1962) on unilateral changes, Fibreboard (1964) on contracting out, Exchange Parts (1964) on election benefits, Great Dane and Fleetwood (1967) on discriminatory motive and strikers, and Gissel (1969) on card-based bargaining orders. In 1975-79 Savair (1973) and Armcor (1976) tightened election and bargaining-order review. Wright Line (1981) and Transportation Management (1983) enter in 1980-84 with the mixed-motive test before the unit merges into the general NLRB lineage.
round1.rule: A court enforces an NLRB order if substantial evidence on the record as a whole, including the trial examiner's contrary findings, supports it, and may not displace the Board's choice between two fairly conflicting views of the evidence (Universal Camera).

changes.case: Consolidated Edison v. NLRB; Phelps Dodge v. NLRB; Franks Bros. v. NLRB
changes.what: Substantial evidence is what a reasonable mind might accept as adequate; refusal to hire union members is discrimination; Board remedies include reinstatement and bargaining orders.
Review on the whole record, giving weight to examiner findings the Board rejects; anchor of every slice.

changes.what: Credibility findings of the examiner deserve deference; unilateral changes during bargaining violate § 8(a)(5) without proof of bad faith.

changes.what: Contracting out unit work is a mandatory subject; benefits timed to affect an election violate § 8(a)(1).

A bargaining order based on authorization cards is an appropriate remedy where unfair labor practices undermined the majority; anchor-adjacent from 1970-74.

name: Ninth Circuit monopolization and predatory pricing: Janich, Inglis
description: Ninth Circuit monopolization and predatory pricing: monopoly power plus exclusionary conduct (Grinnell, 1966), with average variable cost as the proxy for the predatory-price floor (Janich, 1978). California Computer Products (1979) protected product innovation; Inglis (1982) rejected a rigid marginal-cost rule. Alongside: summary judgment in antitrust cases, sparing under Poller (1962) but proper where evidence lacks force (Cities Service, 1968).
history: Dominant rule: a § 2 claim needs monopoly power and willful acquisition or maintenance of it, not growth through a superior product or skill (Grinnell, 1966, the anchor in 1975-79; du Pont, 1956, on market definition). How it changed: by 1980-84 Ninth Circuit predatory-pricing cases lead. Janich Bros. (1978) took average variable cost as the proxy for marginal cost and anchors 1980-84; California Computer Products (1979) held that integrating a disk controller was lawful innovation and that lawful acts do not combine into a violation; Inglis (1982) declined a rigid marginal-cost rule, over a dissent from denial of rehearing en banc. Alongside: summary judgment in antitrust cases, disfavoured where motive and intent matter (Poller, 1962) but proper where the nonmovant's evidence lacks probative force (Cities Service, 1968); dealer terminations and resale-price coercion (Bushie, Hanson, Rea).
rule: A § 2 monopolization or predatory-pricing claim requires monopoly power plus exclusionary conduct, with pricing below an appropriate cost measure (average variable cost as a proxy for marginal cost) as the test for predation; summary judgment in such cases is used sparingly (Poller) but is proper where the plaintiff's evidence lacks probative force (Cities Service).

changes.what: Monopolization requires monopoly power plus its willful acquisition or maintenance, as distinct from growth by superior product, business acumen or historic accident.
Average variable cost accepted as the proxy for marginal cost, the floor below which prices may be considered predatory.
Integrating a product design was a useful innovation, not an attempt to monopolize, and a pattern of individually lawful acts does not add up to a § 2 violation.

changes.what: The Ninth Circuit declined to make marginal-cost pricing a rigid rule for predation, drawing a dissent from denial of rehearing en banc.

history: Dominant rule: sex classifications are tested by heightened scrutiny that rejects archaic and overbroad generalizations. (1981) upheld a male-only statutory rape law. The unit merges back into general equal protection review in 1985-89.

name: Defamation and the First Amendment: actual malice (Sullivan, Gertz)
description: Constitutional defamation law: New York Times v. Sullivan (1964) requires actual malice for public officials, extended to public figures (Butts 1967); Gertz (1974, anchor 1975-99) replaced Rosenbloom's public-interest test and let states set fault for private figures. Bose (1984) requires independent review, Hepps (1986) puts the burden of falsity on plaintiffs, and Milkovich (1990) protects only statements that cannot be read as fact.

history: Dominant rule: the First Amendment limits defamation liability, requiring public officials and public figures to prove actual malice and limiting what private figures may recover. How it changed: in 1950-64 the unit concerns contempt by publication, anchored by Pennekamp (1946) and Craig (1947) under Bridges' (1941) clear-and-present-danger test. New York Times (1964) enters in 1965-69 and anchors that slice with Garrison (1964), Rosenblatt (1966), Butts and Hill (1967) and St. Amant (1968). Butts anchors 1970-74, as Rosenbloom (1971) briefly extended actual malice to matters of public interest and Bresler (1970) protected hyperbole. Gertz (1974) enters in 1975-79 and anchors through 1995-99, replacing Rosenbloom; Firestone (1976) and Hutchinson (1979) narrowed public-figure status. Bose (1984), Dun & Bradstreet (1985) and Hepps (1986) enter in 1985-89, and Milkovich (1990), Connaughton (1989) and Masson (1991) in 1990-94. New York Times anchors 2000-04 and Milkovich 2005-09, as Illinois cases on innocent construction (Chapski, Bryson) signal a drift toward state defamation law.
rule: A public official or public figure may recover for defamation only by proving with convincing clarity that a false statement was made with actual malice, knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard (New York Times; Butts), while states may let private figures recover on a lesser fault standard but not presumed or punitive damages without actual malice (Gertz).

changes.case: Bridges v. California; Pennekamp v. Florida; Craig v. Harney
changes.what: Publications criticizing courts can be punished as contempt only on a clear and present danger to the administration of justice; these anchor 1950-64.

changes.case: New York Times v. Sullivan; Garrison v. Louisiana
changes.what: Actual-malice rule for public officials, applied to criminal libel; New York Times anchors 1965-69 and 2000-04.

changes.case: Rosenblatt v. Baer; Curtis Publishing v. Butts; Time v. Hill; St. Amant v. Thompson
changes.what: Public official defined by federal standards; actual malice extended to public figures and false-light claims; reckless disregard requires serious doubts about truth; Butts anchors 1970-74.

changes.case: Greenbelt Cooperative v. Bresler; Rosenbloom v. Metromedia
changes.what: Rhetorical hyperbole is not actionable; a plurality extended actual malice to private persons in matters of public interest.

changes.case: Gertz v. Robert Welch; Time v. Firestone; Hutchinson v. Proxmire
changes.what: Gertz rejected Rosenbloom's public-interest test: private figures may recover on fault short of actual malice, with presumed and punitive damages limited; narrow limited-purpose public figures; Gertz anchors 1975-99.

changes.case: Bose v. Consumers Union; Dun & Bradstreet v. Greenmoss; Philadelphia Newspapers v. Hepps
changes.what: Independent appellate review of actual malice; Gertz damages limits do not apply to private-concern speech; private plaintiffs bear the burden of proving falsity on matters of public concern.

changes.what: No separate opinion privilege: statements are protected unless they imply provably false facts; altered quotations are actionable only if they materially change meaning; Milkovich anchors 2005-09.

name: Fugitive disentitlement (Molinaro, Ortega-Rodriguez), then Hague child-return cases
description: Two rules in one lineage. Through 1995-99, fugitive disentitlement: courts may dismiss a fugitive's appeal (Molinaro, 1970, anchor 1975-94; Estelle, 1975), but only where flight is connected to the proceeding (Ortega-Rodriguez, 1993; Degen, 1996). From 2000-04, Hague Convention child return: habitual residence and narrow exceptions (Feder, 1995; Friedrich, 1996; Blondin), with ne exeat rights as custody rights (Abbott, 2010).
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Fugitive disentitlement and the Hague Abduction Convention
previous.description: Two lines of cases on international and absconding parties: the fugitive disentitlement doctrine (Molinaro, Ortega-Rodriguez) and Hague Convention child-return cases on habitual residence, grave risk and ne exeat rights (Friedrich, Mozes, Abbott v. Abbott).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, contrastive pass from family evidence)

history: Dominant rule: the anchor changes doctrine. Through 1995-99 the lineage is fugitive disentitlement: Smith (1876), Bohanan (1887) and Eisler (1949) removed escaped defendants' cases, and Molinaro (1970) anchors 1975-79 to 1995-99, holding that a fugitive is disentitled from calling on the court. Estelle v. Dorrough (1975) upheld state dismissal rules, and circuits extended disentitlement to habeas (Joensen, 1980), tax (Conforte, 1982), forfeiture and FOIA claims. Ortega-Rodriguez (1993) required a connection between the flight and the appellate proceeding, and Degen (1996) barred automatic forfeiture judgments against fugitive claimants, later reversed for forfeiture by § 2466 (2000). From 2000-04, after a merger, the lineage is Hague Abduction Convention cases: Feder (1995) anchors on habitual residence, Friedrich (1996) narrows the grave-risk exception, and Blondin (1999, 2001), anchoring 2005-09, applies grave risk and the mature-child objection. In 2010-14 Mozes (2001) anchors on shared parental intent, Abbott (2010) treats a ne exeat right as a right of custody, and Chafin (2013) holds a returned child's appeal not moot. The unit then splits toward jurisdictional versus claim-processing rules.
rule: Through 1995-99: a court may dismiss the appeal or claims of a litigant who has fled its jurisdiction, provided the flight has a connection to the proceeding (Molinaro, Ortega-Rodriguez); from 2000-04 the lineage turns to the Hague Abduction Convention rule that a wrongfully removed child must be returned to the place of habitual residence unless a narrow exception applies.

changes.case: Smith v. United States; Bohanan; Eisler; Molinaro v. New Jersey
changes.what: An escaped or fugitive defendant is disentitled to call on the court to review his conviction; Molinaro anchors 1975-94.
A state may constitutionally dismiss the appeal of a prisoner who escapes while it is pending.
An appellate court may not dismiss an appeal for flight that occurred before the appeal and was recaptured beforehand, absent a connection between the flight and the appellate process.

A court may not enter judgment against a forfeiture claimant merely because he is a fugitive from a related prosecution; Congress later authorised disentitlement in civil forfeiture in 28 U.S.C. § 2466 (2000).

changes.case: Feder v. Evans-Feder; Friedrich v. Friedrich; Blondin v. Dubois; Mozes v. Mozes
changes.what: Habitual residence turns on the child's settled presence and the parents' shared intent, and the grave-risk and other exceptions are narrow; Feder anchors 2000-04.

changes.case: Abbott v. Abbott; Chafin v. Chafin
changes.what: A ne exeat right is a right of custody under the Convention, and a child's return does not moot the appeal.

name: Washington subject-matter jurisdiction versus venue (Marley, Young); preclusion
description: Washington courts on what counts as subject-matter jurisdiction (2010-14): only the type of controversy, so filing-county rules are venue (Dougherty, Young 2003, overruling earlier cases) and an unappealed agency order is final (Marley 1994). In 2015-19 the anchor becomes Hadley (2001) on collateral estoppel elements (Christensen 2004), and in 2020-24 Loveridge (1995) on privity and claim splitting in res judicata.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Washington subject-matter jurisdiction and finality of agency orders
previous.description: Washington decisions distinguishing subject-matter jurisdiction from venue and other errors (Marley, Dougherty, Young), and the preclusive effect of unappealed agency orders.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, contrastive pass from family evidence)

history: Dominant rule: in 2010-14, Young (2003) anchors. Subject-matter jurisdiction depends on the type of controversy, and article IV, § 6 bars the legislature from dividing it among superior courts, so Young overruled earlier cases and read RCW 4.12.020(3) as venue. Dougherty (2003) treated RCW 51.52.110's county designation as venue, and Marley (1994) held that errors in a Department order do not void it, so an unappealed order binds. Cole (2011), Bin (2011), Posey (2012) and ZDI Gaming (2012) continue the move away from labelling ordinary errors jurisdictional. How it changed: the anchor shifts with the slices. In 2015-19 Hadley (2001) anchors with Christensen (2004): collateral estoppel requires identical issues, a final judgment on the merits, the same parties or privies and no injustice, judged by whether the first hearing was full and fair, and an unemployment-benefits ruling has no preclusive effect by statute. In 2020-24 Loveridge (1995) anchors on claim preclusion: privity requires control of or substantial participation in the earlier case, and claim splitting is barred (Ensley 2009, Eugster 2017). Also: Rains (1983) on identity of causes of action, and Hisle (2004) on wages.
rule: In Washington, subject-matter jurisdiction turns only on the type of controversy, so county-filing requirements and other errors go to venue or the merits, and an unappealed agency order becomes a binding final adjudication (Marley); from 2015 the unit centres on preclusion, requiring identity of issues or claims, a final judgment and the same parties or their privies.

changes.case: Marley v. Department of Labor & Industries
changes.what: Errors in an agency decision do not defeat its subject-matter jurisdiction, and an unappealed order becomes final and binding.

changes.case: Dougherty v. Department of Labor & Industries; Shoop v. Kittitas County
changes.what: RCW 51.52.110's county designation is venue, not jurisdiction.
Overruled earlier cases and held that article IV, § 6 bars the legislature from limiting subject-matter jurisdiction as among superior courts, so RCW 4.12.020(3) concerns venue.

changes.case: Cole v. Harveyland; Bin v. Coloma; ZDI Gaming v. State; In re Marriage of Buecking/Posey
changes.what: Rejected 'drive-by' jurisdictional rulings: unlawful-detainer defects and single-county filing limits are not jurisdictional, and a statute restricting jurisdiction to one county is unconstitutional.

changes.case: Hadley v. Maxwell; Christensen v. Grant County Hospital District
changes.what: Collateral estoppel requires identical issues, a final judgment, the same parties or privies and no injustice, assessed by whether the earlier hearing was full and fair.

name: Natural Gas Act ratemaking: Hope's end-result test and Permian Basin area rates
description: Natural Gas Act ratemaking: a rate is just and reasonable if its end result balances investor and consumer interests within a zone of reasonableness (Hope Natural Gas, 1944, anchor from 1970-74). Phillips (1954) brought wellhead producers under FPC rate control, Mobile-Sierra (1956) protected filed contracts, Permian Basin (1968) upheld area rates, and Duquesne v. Barasch (1989) reaffirmed Hope over Smyth v. Ames.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Natural gas and energy rate regulation
previous.description: Federal Power Commission ratemaking under the Natural Gas Act (1960s-80s): Hope Natural Gas end-result test and return on equity, Phillips Petroleum producer regulation, Permian Basin area rates, Mobile-Sierra contract rates and Louisiana Power curtailment.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session subagents, from cocite evidence; second pass differentiated near-duplicates)

history: Dominant rule: under the Natural Gas Act a rate is just and reasonable if, taken as a whole, it balances investor and consumer interests and lets the company maintain its credit and attract capital; the commission may choose any method within a zone of reasonableness (Natural Gas Pipeline, 1942; Hope, 1944; Bluefield, 1923). How it changed: the 1960-64 slice is anchored by Phillips Petroleum (1954), which extended FPC jurisdiction to independent producers at the wellhead, and turns on certificates under § 7 (Atlantic Refining, 1959). Mobile-Sierra (1956) held filed contract rates binding unless the commission finds the public interest requires change. Hope becomes the anchor from 1970-74 as Permian Basin (1968) and Southern Louisiana (1970) upheld area-wide producer rates instead of company-by-company cost of service. In 1980-84 state utility-commission cases from the District of Columbia appear, and 1985-89 adds nondelegation cases (Schechter, Yakus). Duquesne Light v. Barasch (1989) leads 1990-94, confirming that Hope's end-result test, not Smyth v. Ames (1898), governs.
rule: A rate is just and reasonable, and not confiscatory, if its total effect balances investor and consumer interests within a zone of reasonableness, whatever method the commission uses (Hope Natural Gas).

changes.case: FPC v. Natural Gas Pipeline Co.; FPC v. Hope Natural Gas
changes.what: The commission may fix any rate within a zone of reasonableness, and it is the end result, not the method, that counts.
Independent producers selling gas at the wellhead for resale in interstate commerce are natural-gas companies subject to FPC rate regulation.

changes.case: United Gas Pipe Line Co. v. Mobile Gas Service Corp.; FPC v. Sierra Pacific Power
changes.what: A seller may not unilaterally change a filed contract rate; the commission may modify contracts only when the public interest requires.
Upheld area-wide maximum rates for producers in place of individual company cost-of-service rates.
The Constitution requires no particular ratemaking method; Hope's end-result test controls, displacing the fair-value approach of Smyth v. Ames.

name: California harmless error: Watson for state-law error, Chapman for federal
description: California's two harmlessness standards: Watson's (1956) reasonable-probability test for state-law error and Chapman's (1967) beyond-a-reasonable-doubt test for federal constitutional error. Breverman (1998) put lesser-included-offense instruction errors under Watson; from 2020-24 Neder (1999) and Aledamat (2019) lead on Chapman review of omitted-element and alternative-theory instructions. Also Auto Equity Sales (1962) on stare decisis.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: California criminal: Watson and Chapman harmless error
previous.description: California's two harmlessness standards: Watson's reasonable-probability test for state-law error and Chapman's beyond-a-reasonable-doubt test for federal constitutional error, with Auto Equity Sales on stare decisis among California courts.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: Watson (1956) anchors every slice: an error of California law is reversible only if it is reasonably probable the defendant would have obtained a more favorable result without it; the test asks what a jury is likely to have done, not what it could have done. Federal constitutional error requires reversal unless harmless beyond a reasonable doubt (Chapman, 1967). How it changed: Breverman (1998) held that failing to instruct sua sponte on a lesser included offense in a noncapital case is state-law error under Watson, and Barton (1995) set the duty to instruct on unreasonable self-defense. In 2020-24 Neder (1999), Fulminante (1991), Sullivan (1993) and Aledamat (2019) enter, shifting weight to Chapman review: omitted-element and alternative-theory instructional errors are reviewed for harmlessness, while structural errors are few. Also: Auto Equity Sales (1962) binding lower courts to Court of Appeal decisions (2015-19), gang-enhancement cases (Gardeley, Albillar) in 2010-14, and heat-of-passion instructions (Moye, Gutierrez). The lineage merges into the capital-appeals unit in 2025-29.
rule: California courts reverse for state-law error only if it is reasonably probable the result would have been more favorable without it (Watson), and for federal constitutional error unless it is harmless beyond a reasonable doubt (Chapman).

changes.what: State-law error is reversible only on a reasonable probability of a more favorable result.
Federal constitutional error requires reversal unless the state proves it harmless beyond a reasonable doubt.
Failure to instruct sua sponte on a lesser included offense in a noncapital case is state-law error reviewed under Watson.
Omitting an element from the jury instructions is subject to Chapman harmless-error review rather than automatic reversal.
Instructing on both a valid and an invalid theory is reviewed under Chapman, asking whether the error was harmless beyond a reasonable doubt.

name: Foreign affairs in U.S. courts: Sosa's ATS norms, political question, act of state
description: International and foreign-affairs claims in U.S. courts, 2005-09: Sosa (2004, anchor) confines ATS suits to narrow, well-defined norms (after Filartiga 1980 and Kadic 1995); Baker v. Carr (1962) and Alperin (2005) frame political-question dismissals; Sabbatino (1964) and Altmann (2004) address act of state and FSIA reach; Hamdi (2004), Zadvydas (2001), Eisentrager and Verdugo-Urquidez define rights of detainees and aliens abroad.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, round 2 after the lineage re-link)

previous.name: Foreign sovereign immunity and international law in U.S. courts
previous.description: Suits involving foreign states and international law: the FSIA (Amerada Hess, Weltover, Nelson, Altmann), the Alien Tort Statute (Filartiga, Tel-Oren, Sosa, Kiobel), treaties and consular rights (Breard), extraterritoriality (Morrison) and the act-of-state doctrine.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: courts' limited role in foreign affairs. Sosa v. Alvarez-Machain (2004), the anchor, holds that the Alien Tort Statute supports federal common-law claims only for a narrow class of specific, universal and obligatory international norms, building on Filartiga (1980, official torture) and the Second Circuit's 1995 Kadic v. Karadzic decision (genocide and war crimes, no immunity for an unrecognized state's leader). Baker v. Carr (1962), the heaviest case, supplies the political-question test, applied in Alperin (9th Cir. 2005) to bar claims requiring review of foreign-policy judgments, though Japan Whaling (1986) found statutory claims justiciable. Sabbatino (1964) makes the act-of-state doctrine federal law; Altmann (2004) applied the FSIA to pre-enactment conduct; Garamendi (2003) let executive agreements preempt state law. Alongside: constitutional rights of aliens and detainees: Eisentrager (1950) and Verdugo-Urquidez (1990) deny rights abroad, Zadvydas (2001) limits post-removal detention, and Hamdi (2004) requires due process for citizen enemy combatants. Single slice; it splits in 2010-14 among ATS, Erie and immigration-habeas units.
rule: Federal courts hear international-law tort claims under the Alien Tort Statute only for specific, universal and obligatory norms, and decline cases that present political questions or require judging the official acts of foreign sovereigns.

changes.what: Official torture violates a clear international norm actionable under the ATS.
ATS claims are limited to a narrow class of specific, universal and obligatory international-law norms.
The FSIA codifies sovereign-immunity standards and applies to conduct before its enactment.
A citizen detained as an enemy combatant is entitled to due process to contest the factual basis for detention.
War-crimes claims requiring review of foreign-policy judgments are nonjusticiable political questions.

round1.name: Foreign states and international law in U.S. courts: FSIA, Alien Tort Statute (Sosa)
round1.description: Foreign states and international law in U.S. courts: the FSIA is the sole basis for suing a foreign state (Amerada Hess 1989, anchor 2000-04; Weltover, Nelson, Altmann 2004). The Alien Tort Statute, from Filartiga (1980), was narrowed by Sosa (2004, anchor 2005-14) and Kiobel (2013, anchor 2015-19), following Morrison's (2010) presumption against extraterritoriality. Also Vienna Convention claims (Breard 1998) and Guantanamo detention cases.
round1.history: Dominant rule: courts hear suits against foreign states only under the FSIA's exceptions, and international-law claims under the ATS only for well-defined, universally accepted norms with sufficient connection to the United States. How it changed: the unit forms in 2000-04 with Amerada Hess (1989) as anchor, alongside Weltover (1992) and Nelson (1993) on the commercial-activity exception, Filartiga (1980) and Tel-Oren (1984) on the ATS, and Breard (1998) and circuit cases refusing suppression for Vienna Convention violations. Sosa (2004) enters and anchors 2005-14, confining ATS claims to specific, universal and obligatory norms; Altmann (2004) applied the FSIA retroactively and Sanchez-Llamas (2006) and Medellin limited treaty remedies. In 2010-14 war-on-terror detention cases (Hamdi, Boumediene, Al-Bihani) and Morrison (2010) lead. Kiobel (2013) anchors 2015-19, extending the presumption against extraterritoriality to the ATS, with RJR Nabisco (2016) and circuit ATS cases (Nestle, Drummond) following.
round1.rule: The FSIA is the sole basis for jurisdiction over a foreign state, subject to its exceptions such as commercial activity (Amerada Hess), and the Alien Tort Statute supports only claims for violations of specific, universal and obligatory international norms (Sosa), limited by the presumption against extraterritoriality (Kiobel).

changes.case: Filartiga v. Pena-Irala (2d Cir.); Tel-Oren v. Libyan Arab Republic (D.C. Cir.)
changes.what: Official torture violates the law of nations and is actionable under the ATS; Tel-Oren's divided court questioned private ATS causes of action.

changes.case: Verlinden v. Central Bank of Nigeria; Argentine Republic v. Amerada Hess; Republic of Argentina v. Weltover; Saudi Arabia v. Nelson
changes.what: FSIA codifies restrictive immunity and is the exclusive basis of jurisdiction; bond refinancing is commercial activity, but police torture is sovereign; Amerada Hess anchors 2000-04.

changes.case: Breard v. Greene; Sanchez-Llamas v. Oregon; Medellin v. Dretke
changes.what: Vienna Convention consular-notification claims are subject to state procedural default and do not require suppression.

changes.case: Sosa v. Alvarez-Machain; Republic of Austria v. Altmann
changes.what: ATS claims limited to norms as definite and accepted as the 18th-century paradigms; FSIA applies to pre-enactment conduct; Sosa anchors 2005-14.

changes.case: Hamdi v. Rumsfeld; Boumediene v. Bush; Al-Bihani v. Obama (D.C. Cir.)
changes.what: Detainees may challenge enemy-combatant classification; habeas reaches Guantanamo; AUMF detention covers those 'part of' al Qaeda forces.
A statute with no clear indication of extraterritorial application has none; § 10(b) reaches only domestic transactions.

changes.case: Kiobel v. Royal Dutch Petroleum; RJR Nabisco v. European Community
changes.what: The presumption against extraterritoriality applies to ATS claims, which must touch and concern the United States; two-step extraterritoriality analysis; Kiobel anchors 2015-19.

name: Antitrust 2010-24: Leegin, Noerr petitioning immunity, Amex two-sided markets
description: Modern antitrust litigation, 2010-24, after per se rules receded: Leegin (2007, anchor 2010-14) put minimum resale prices under the rule of reason; private plaintiffs need antitrust injury (Brunswick 1977, Atlantic Richfield 1990); § 2 requires monopoly power (Grinnell, Trinko 2004). Noerr-Pennington petitioning immunity anchors 2015-19, and Ohio v. American Express (2018) anchors 2020-24, requiring net harm across both sides of a two-sided market.
history: Dominant rule: the rule of reason governs most restraints. Continental TV (1977) applied it to vertical non-price limits, Khan (1997) to maximum resale prices, and Leegin (2007, the anchor in 2010-14) overruled Dr. Miles' per se rule for minimum resale prices; NCAA (1984) and Dagher (2006) kept joint ventures out of per se treatment, and a parent and subsidiary cannot conspire (Copperweld 1984). Private plaintiffs must prove antitrust injury (Brunswick 1977, Atlantic Richfield 1990), and § 2 requires monopoly power in a relevant market (Grinnell 1966, Kodak 1992, Trinko 2004). How it changed: in 2010-14 RICO proximate cause sits alongside (Holmes 1992, Anza 2006, Bridge 2008, Hemi 2010). In 2015-19 Noerr (1961) and Pennington (1965) petitioning immunity and its sham exception (Professional Real Estate Investors 1993), with Parker state-action immunity, anchor. From 2020-24 Ohio v. American Express (2018) anchors: in two-sided transaction markets the plaintiff must show net harm across both sides, with direct or indirect proof of anticompetitive effects; Microsoft (2001) and Novell (2013) on monopolization.
rule: Most restraints of trade, including vertical price restraints, are judged under the rule of reason, a private plaintiff must show antitrust injury flowing from the anticompetitive aspect of the conduct, and § 2 liability requires monopoly power in a properly defined market.

changes.what: Vertical non-price restraints are judged under the rule of reason.

changes.case: Copperweld Corp. v. Independence Tube Corp.
changes.what: A parent and its wholly owned subsidiary cannot conspire under § 1.
Vertical maximum price-fixing moved to the rule of reason.

changes.case: Leegin Creative Leather Products v. PSKS
changes.what: Vertical minimum resale price maintenance is no longer per se unlawful; it is judged under the rule of reason.
In two-sided transaction markets, anticompetitive effects are assessed across both sides, by direct or indirect evidence.

before_differentiation.name: Antitrust: rule of reason, antitrust injury and monopoly power (Leegin, Amex)
before_differentiation.description: Antitrust litigation, 2010-24: vertical price restraints moved from per se illegality to the rule of reason (Continental TV 1977, Khan 1997, Leegin 2007); private plaintiffs need antitrust injury (Brunswick 1977, Atlantic Richfield 1990); § 2 requires monopoly power (Grinnell, Trinko 2004). Noerr-Pennington petitioning immunity anchors 2015-19, and Ohio v. American Express (2018) anchors 2020-24 on two-sided markets and proof of effects.

name: Seventh Circuit drug sentencing: quantity estimates, relevant conduct, acceptance
description: Seventh Circuit drug sentencing under the mandatory Guidelines, a single 1995-99 slice anchored by Beler (1994): drug quantity may be estimated from purchase rates and duration if nebulous eyeballing is avoided (Duarte 1992, Taylor 1995); relevant conduct follows similarity, regularity and timing (Cedano-Rojas 1993); continued drug use or other crimes can defeat acceptance of responsibility (Watkins 1990, Pace 1994, Byrd 1996).
history: Dominant rule: how a federal sentencing court finds the facts that drive a drug sentence under the mandatory Guidelines. Beler (7th Cir. 1994) anchors the lineage's only slice, 1995-99, which formed from a Pinkerton drug-conspiracy unit and Guidelines units. How it changed: no change within the span; the leading circuit cases settle the methods. Quantity may be estimated by multiplying approximate weekly or monthly purchases by the period of involvement (Beler), and findings need not reach the precision of Newtonian physics so long as they avoid nebulous eyeballing (Duarte 1992, Taylor 1995). Relevant conduct turns on similarity, regularity and temporal proximity (Cedano-Rojas 1993). Acceptance of responsibility includes refraining from further violations (Watkins 1990), so post-offense drug use (O'Neil 1991, Pace 1994) and unrelated criminal conduct (McDonald 1994, Byrd 1996) can justify denial. Also: foreseeable gun possession in drug deals (Gutierrez 1992), the aggravating-role adjustment (Mustread 1994), the crack penalty scheme upheld (Lawrence 1991, Galloway 1992), and verdicts on alternative grounds (Townsend 1991).
rule: A sentencing court may estimate drug quantity from reliable evidence, such as typical purchases multiplied by the period of involvement, so long as it avoids nebulous eyeballing (Beler, Duarte); relevant conduct includes transactions in the same course of conduct (Cedano-Rojas); and continued drug use or other criminal conduct may justify denying acceptance of responsibility (Watkins, Pace, Byrd).

changes.case: United States v. Watkins; O'Neil; Pace; McDonald; Byrd (7th Cir.)
changes.what: Acceptance of responsibility includes refraining from further violations, so post-offense drug use and even unrelated criminal conduct may justify denying the § 3E1.1 reduction.

changes.case: United States v. Duarte; Beler; Taylor (7th Cir.)
changes.what: Drug-quantity findings need not be precise; multiplying an approximate purchase rate by the period of involvement is acceptable if nebulous eyeballing is avoided. Beler anchors the slice.
Whether other transactions are the same course of conduct turns on similarity, regularity and temporal proximity.
The crack penalty scheme survives due process and equal protection challenges; no discriminatory intent shown.

name: Ballot access for candidates and parties: Anderson-Burdick balancing, 1985-99
description: Burdens on candidates, parties and ballot access, 1985-99, under Anderson-Burdick balancing: the injury to voting and association is weighed against the state's interests (Anderson, 1983, anchor 1985-94), with strict scrutiny only for severe burdens (Burdick, 1992). Built on Williams v. Rhodes, Bullock and Storer; Tashjian (1986) protected party association; by 1995-99 campaign-finance cases (Buckley, Bellotti) join and Timmons (1997) upheld a fusion ban.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Ballot access and election regulation (1985-95)
previous.description: Constitutional challenges to election rules under the Anderson v. Celebrezze/Burdick balancing test: ballot access for independents and minor parties (Storer, Bullock, Williams v. Rhodes, Jenness, Munro), party primaries (Tashjian, Eu, La Follette) and candidate qualifications (Clements). Successor to the 1975 sub-cluster 19103.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, contrastive pass from family evidence)

history: Dominant rule: election regulations are reviewed by weighing the character and magnitude of the injury to voting and associational rights against the precise interests the state offers, so that severe burdens need narrow tailoring to a compelling interest and reasonable, nondiscriminatory rules need only important regulatory interests. How it changed: the lineage builds on ballot-access cases, Williams v. Rhodes (1968), Jenness (1971), Bullock (1972), Storer and White (1974) and Lubin (1974), which allowed states to require a modicum of support but not prohibitive fees. Anderson (1983) anchors 1985-89 and 1990-94, rejecting an early deadline that protected major parties from independents. Tashjian (1986) and Eu (1989) protected party association, while Munro (1986) let states demand more support. Burdick (1992) entered in 1990-94, confirming that only severe burdens draw strict scrutiny, and Norman (1992) applied it to signature thresholds. In 1995-99 Storer anchors, Buckley (1976) and Bellotti (1978) bring in campaign-finance speech, Thornton (1995) bars state term limits on congressional candidates, and Timmons (1997) upholds a fusion ban; the unit then splits toward First Amendment defamation.
rule: A court weighs the character and magnitude of an election rule's burden on voting and associational rights against the state's justifications; severe burdens must be narrowly drawn to a compelling interest, while reasonable, nondiscriminatory restrictions are justified by important regulatory interests (Anderson, Burdick).

changes.case: Williams v. Rhodes; Jenness v. Fortson; Bullock v. Carter; Storer v. Brown; Lubin v. Panish
changes.what: Ballot-access laws burden voting and association; states may demand a modicum of support but not exclusionary fees or unequal paths to the ballot.
Struck an early filing deadline for independents under a balancing of burden against state interests; anchors 1985-94.

changes.case: Tashjian v. Republican Party of Connecticut; Munro v. Socialist Workers Party
changes.what: A closed-primary law violated the party's associational rights, while states may require a substantial showing of support for ballot access.

history: Dominant rule: certification requires proof, after rigorous analysis, that Rule 23 is satisfied. history: Dominant rule: Alabama's review of capital convictions and death sentences, focusing on the elements of the capital offense, the aggravating circumstances and the sentencing procedure. Alabama (1995) held the Constitution does not require Tedder-style weight for a jury's life recommendation. history: Dominant rule: courts distinguish trial errors, which are reviewed for harmlessness, from structural defects in the trial mechanism, which require automatic reversal (Fulminante, 1991). Clark (1986), Carella (1989) and Yates (1991) applied it to burden-shifting presumption instructions. Sullivan (1993) held that a deficient reasonable-doubt instruction is structural because there is no jury verdict to test; Victor (1994) upheld instructions read as a whole. O'Neal (1995) resolved grave doubt in the petitioner's favour. The unit splits into several units in 2000-04.

history: Dominant rule: before CAFRA, the government had to show probable cause of a substantial connection between seized property and drug trafficking, after which the burden shifted to the claimant; sheer quantity of cash, its packaging or a canine alert were weak evidence on their own. history: Dominant rule: State v. Ward (2011) anchors every slice: an error not of constitutional magnitude is harmless unless there is a reasonable probability it affected the outcome, and a constitutional error requires the State to show beyond a reasonable doubt that it did not. How it changed: in 2010-14 Tosh (2004) still governs prosecutorial misconduct, with Inkelaar (2011), Bridges (2013) and Holt (2014) on gross and flagrant conduct, and Herbel (2013) approves a nonpattern reasonable-doubt instruction. Plummer (2012) and Williams (2012) lead from 2015-19, setting the four-step instruction analysis and a clear-error test for unobjected instructions (Smith-Parker, 2014, found 'must' and 'will' language error). Gunby (2006) had ended res gestae as a basis for admitting other crimes. Sherman (2016) replaced the Tosh test with a prosecutorial-error inquiry measured by Ward, and Chandler (2018) applied it to unobjected comments. In 2020-24 leading cases are Butler, Chandler, Miller and Lowery (2018) on preservation, record designation and abandonment of inadequately briefed issues. Also: King (2009) on the contemporaneous-objection rule and Brown (2012) on alternative means.
rule: Kansas appellate courts reverse for nonconstitutional error only if there is a reasonable probability it affected the outcome, and for constitutional error unless the State shows beyond a reasonable doubt it did not (Ward), and they review instruction claims in four steps, with unpreserved instruction errors reversible only if clearly erroneous.

changes.what: Prosecutorial misconduct was judged by a three-factor test of gross and flagrant conduct, ill will and the weight of the evidence.
Res gestae is no longer an independent basis to admit other-crimes evidence outside K.S.A. 60-455; failure to give a limiting instruction is reviewed for clear error.
Unified harmless-error standard: reasonable probability for statutory error, Chapman's beyond-a-reasonable-doubt test for constitutional error.

changes.case: State v. Plummer; State v. Williams
changes.what: Four-step instruction review (reviewability, legal appropriateness, factual appropriateness, harmlessness); unpreserved error is clearly erroneous only if the court is firmly convinced the verdict would differ.
Replaced Tosh's misconduct test with a prosecutorial-error inquiry followed by Ward's harmlessness test.

before_differentiation.name: Kansas criminal appeals: Ward harmless error and Plummer instruction review
before_differentiation.description: Kansas Supreme Court criminal appeals: Ward (2011) harmless-error standards anchor every slice, and Plummer and Williams (2012) set four-step review of jury instructions with clear-error review of unobjected ones. Tosh (2004) governed prosecutorial misconduct until Sherman (2016) recast it as prosecutorial error judged under Ward; the 2020-24 slice is led by 2018 cases on preservation and record designation.

distinct_from.how: The merits-review strand of its parent: harmless error, instruction review and the Tosh-to-Sherman change on prosecutorial error, rather than preservation, briefing waiver and sentencing rules.

name: Clear-error review of findings under Rule 52(a): Anderson v. Bessemer City
description: Appellate review of trial findings in 1985-89 (one slice): a finding is clearly erroneous only on a firm and definite conviction of mistake (U.S. Gypsum 1948, anchor; Yellow Cab 1949); discriminatory intent is a question of fact (Pullman-Standard 1982); and the factfinder's choice between two permissible views stands, even when based on documents or adopted findings (Anderson 1985). Applied to constructive discharge, negligence and trademark confusion (Inwood 1982).
history: Dominant rule: Rule 52(a) clear-error review. United States v. United States Gypsum (1948), the anchor, defines a clearly erroneous finding as one leaving the reviewing court with a definite and firm conviction that a mistake has been made; Yellow Cab (1949) and McAllister (1954) bar reweighing evidence that supports either conclusion; Duberstein (1960) applied the standard to whether a transfer was a gift. How it applied: Pullman-Standard v. Swint (1982) held that discriminatory intent under Title VII is a pure question of fact subject to Rule 52(a), and courts must remand rather than find facts themselves (also Worthington 1986). Anderson v. Bessemer City (1985) held that the standard applies even to findings based on documents or adopted from a party's proposals, and that where two permissible views exist the factfinder's choice cannot be clearly erroneous. Inwood Laboratories (1982) applied the same deference to trademark findings, including contributory infringement, with Scandia Down (1985) on likelihood of confusion; Mucha v. King (1986) treated legal characterizations as facts. Discrimination cases applied the standard to constructive discharge (1982, 1985) and other employment findings (Craft 1985). Single slice; it splits in 1990-94.
rule: Under Rule 52(a), an appellate court may set aside a trial court's findings of fact, including findings of discriminatory intent and findings drawn from documents, only if clearly erroneous, and where two permissible views of the evidence exist the factfinder's choice cannot be clearly erroneous.

changes.case: United States v. United States Gypsum Co.
changes.what: A finding is clearly erroneous when the reviewing court is left with a definite and firm conviction that a mistake was made.
Discriminatory intent is a question of fact reviewed for clear error, and appellate courts should remand rather than find facts.
Applied clear-error deference to trademark findings and set the standard for contributory infringement by inducement.

changes.case: Anderson v. City of Bessemer City
changes.what: Clear-error review applies to all findings, including those based on documents or adopted from a party, and a choice between two permissible views cannot be clearly erroneous.

written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, round 2 after the lineage re-link)

name: Ohio S.B. 2 sentencing findings and sexual-predator hearings (Edmonson, Cook)
description: Ohio felony sentencing and sex-offender classification, a single 2000-04 slice anchored by Edmonson (1999): S.B. 2 required findings and reasons on the record for non-minimum, maximum and consecutive terms, made at the hearing (Comer 2003). Cook (1998) held H.B. 180's sexual-predator scheme civil, and Eppinger (2001) set hearing procedures. Also Rance (1999) on allied offenses.
history: Dominant rule: Ohio's S.B. 2 sentencing statutes required a trial court to make specific findings, with reasons, before imposing more than the minimum, the maximum, or consecutive terms. Edmonson (1999) anchors the lineage's only slice, 2000-04, which split from the Ohio sufficiency/manifest-weight lineage. How it changed: Comer (2003) required those findings to be made at the sentencing hearing, and Jones (2001) told appellate courts to vacate and remand rather than modify a sentence contrary to law. Alongside: sexual-predator classification under R.C. Chapter 2950 (H.B. 180): Cook (1998) held it civil, so retroactive application is permitted, and Williams (2000) held double jeopardy inoperative; Eppinger (2001) set hearing procedures, including an appointed expert when reasonably necessary. Also: Rance (1999) on cumulative punishment for allied offenses, and Woods (2000) upholding post-release control against a separation-of-powers challenge.
rule: Under Ohio's S.B. 2 felony-sentencing statutes a trial court must make the required findings, with reasons, on the record before imposing more than the minimum or a maximum term (Edmonson, Comer); sexual-predator classification under R.C. Chapter 2950 is civil and remedial, not punishment (Cook).

changes.what: R.C. Chapter 2950 as enacted by 1996 H.B. 180 is civil in nature, so applying it retroactively is not an ex post facto violation; State v. Williams (2000) held double jeopardy inoperative for the same reason.
A court must record its findings before imposing a sentence that departs from the minimum or reaches the maximum.
An indigent offender is entitled to an appointed expert at a sexual-predator hearing when reasonably necessary, and the hearing has model procedures.
The statutory findings for non-minimum and consecutive sentences must be made at the sentencing hearing.
