name: Roberts reliability gives way to Crawford, 2005-09: hearsay and retroactivity
description: The 2005-09 hearsay-reliability strand: Ohio v. Roberts (1980) and Wright (1990) admitted firmly rooted or trustworthy hearsay, with accomplice statements suspect (Lee, Williamson, Lilly); Crawford (2004, anchor) replaced that test for testimonial statements. Lower courts sorted testimonial from nontestimonial statements (Saget, Cromer, Horton, 2004), Davis (2006) set the primary-purpose test, and Whorton (2007) held Crawford not retroactive.
history: Dominant rule: Crawford v. Washington (2004), anchoring the only slice, 2005-09, which merged in a lineage built on Ohio v. Roberts. How it changed: under Roberts (1980) and Wright (1990) an unavailable declarant's hearsay was admissible if firmly rooted or particularly trustworthy, White (1992) dropped the unavailability showing for spontaneous declarations, and Lee (1986), Williamson (1994) and Lilly (1999) treated accomplice statements as suspect; Bourjaily (1987) let courts find co-conspirator foundations by a preponderance, and Street (1985) allowed nonhearsay use of a confession. Crawford replaced that reliability test for testimonial statements. Lower courts then held that private remarks and statements to unwitting informants are not testimonial (Horton, 2004; Saget, 2004), while accusations to police are (Cromer, 2004). Davis v. Washington (2006) defined testimonial statements by the primary purpose of the interrogation, and Whorton v. Bockting (2007) refused retroactive application on collateral review. The unit continues into 2010-14 as the Confrontation Clause after Crawford.
rule: Testimonial out-of-court statements are inadmissible against the accused unless the declarant is unavailable and the defendant had a prior opportunity to cross-examine (Crawford); nontestimonial hearsay falls outside the clause's core.

changes.case: Ohio v. Roberts; Idaho v. Wright
changes.what: An unavailable declarant's hearsay was admissible if it fell within a firmly rooted exception or bore particularized guarantees of trustworthiness.

changes.case: Lee v. Illinois; Williamson v. United States; Lilly v. Virginia
changes.what: A codefendant's statements implicating the accused are presumptively unreliable, and only truly self-inculpatory portions of a statement are admissible.
Abandoned Roberts' reliability test for testimonial statements in favor of unavailability plus prior cross-examination.

changes.case: United States v. Saget; United States v. Cromer; Horton v. Allen
changes.what: Statements in private conversations or to unwitting informants are not testimonial; accusations made to police are.
Statements are testimonial when the primary purpose of the questioning is to prove past events for prosecution.
Crawford is not a watershed rule and does not apply retroactively on collateral review.

written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, round 2 after the lineage re-link)

before_differentiation.name: Crawford replaces Roberts: testimonial hearsay under the Confrontation Clause
before_differentiation.description: The 2005-09 transition from Ohio v. Roberts (1980) to Crawford (2004), which anchors: testimonial hearsay needs unavailability and a prior chance to cross-examine, replacing the reliability test of Roberts and Wright (1990). Lower courts sorted testimonial from nontestimonial statements (Saget, Cromer, Horton, 2004), Davis (2006) set the primary-purpose test, and Whorton (2007) held Crawford not retroactive on collateral review.

distinct_from.how: The parent cluster covers the whole 2005-09 Confrontation Clause, including Bruton, cross-examination limits and Golding; this sub-cluster is the Roberts-to-Crawford hearsay strand with co-conspirator rules (Bourjaily) and Whorton.
This is the 2005-09 transition from Roberts; that sibling is the 2010-29 post-Crawford law on forensic reports and expert basis evidence.

name: Second Circuit sentencing review after Booker: Crosby remands, Cavera reasonableness
description: Second Circuit sentencing review after Booker: Crosby (2005) remands to ask whether the sentence would differ, Fernandez (2006) declined a reasonableness presumption, Villafuerte (2007) applied plain error to unpreserved procedural claims, and Cavera (en banc 2008), the anchor from 2010-14 to 2025-29, with Rigas (2009) limited substantive-reasonableness reversal to rare cases. Dorvee (2010) and Broxmeyer (2012) refine it.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Second Circuit sentencing review
previous.description: Second Circuit review of federal sentences after Booker: Crosby remands, procedural and substantive reasonableness (Cavera en banc, Rigas, Dorvee), plain error for unpreserved sentencing objections (Villafuerte) and clear error in fact-finding.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: sentences are reviewed for reasonableness, akin to abuse of discretion, and are substantively unreasonable only in exceptional cases. How it changed: Crosby (2005) anchors 2005-09, creating the limited remand by which district courts decided whether they would have sentenced differently under advisory Guidelines; Fleming (2005) applied reasonableness review to revocation sentences, and Fernandez (2006) declined to presume within-range sentences reasonable but presumed the judge considered § 3553(a). Kimbrough (2007) abrogated Rattoballi (2006) in part. Villafuerte (2007) applied plain-error review to unpreserved procedural objections, as did Verkhoglyad (2008). Cavera (en banc 2008) anchors every later slice: fact-finding is reviewed for clear error, and substantive reversal is reserved for sentences outside the range of permissible decisions; Jones (2008) rejected heightened scrutiny, and Rigas (2009) compared the standard to manifest injustice. Dorvee (2010) reversed a child-pornography sentence for over-reliance on an unempirical Guideline, while Broxmeyer (2012) stressed deference on weighing factors. Also: Marcus (2010) on plain error, and white-collar cases (Coplan, Binday) in 2015-19.
rule: The Second Circuit reviews federal sentences for reasonableness akin to abuse of discretion, setting aside a sentence as substantively unreasonable only in exceptional cases where it falls outside the range of permissible decisions, reviewing sentencing fact-finding for clear error and unpreserved procedural objections for plain error.

changes.case: United States v. Crosby; United States v. Fleming
changes.what: Booker errors remanded for the district court to decide whether it would have imposed a materially different sentence; reasonableness review extends to all sentences, with no required verbal formula for considering § 3553(a).
No presumption of reasonableness for within-Guidelines sentences, but a presumption that the judge considered the statutory factors.
Plain-error review in full rigor applies to unpreserved claims of procedural sentencing error.
Abrogated Rattoballi (2006) in part, confirming discretion to vary on policy grounds.

changes.case: United States v. Cavera (en banc); United States v. Rigas
changes.what: Substantive reasonableness is reviewed deferentially, with reversal only in the rare case akin to manifest injustice or shocks-the-conscience standards.

changes.case: United States v. Dorvee; United States v. Broxmeyer
changes.what: Deference to a Guideline depends on the Commission's empirical analysis (child-pornography Guideline criticised), while the weight given to factors remains with the sentencing judge.

name: Tennessee civil appellate review: abuse of discretion (Lee Medical), Rye, Sneed
description: Tennessee Court of Appeals civil review in the 2020s: discretionary rulings are tested by Lee Medical's (2010) three-part framework and reviewed deferentially in family cases (Eldridge 2001, Gonsewski 2011, Armbrister 2013); undeveloped arguments are waived (Sneed 2010); summary judgment follows Rye (2015), the 2020-24 anchor. Eldridge anchors the partial 2025-29 slice as criminal evidence cases enter.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Tennessee civil appeals (2020s)
previous.description: Recent Tennessee Court of Appeals civil precedent: waiver of skeletal, undeveloped arguments (Sneed), abuse-of-discretion review in family cases (Gonsewski, Armbrister), summary judgment after Rye, and statutory construction (Lee Medical v. Beecher).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: Tennessee appellate courts defer to discretionary trial-court decisions unless the court applied an incorrect legal standard, reached an illogical result, or rested on a clearly erroneous assessment of the evidence, using Lee Medical's (2010) three questions: evidentiary support, correct law, and a choice within the acceptable range. How it changed: the lineage forms in 2020-24 from earlier groups on Tennessee summary judgment and divorce. Rye (2015) anchors 2020-24, restoring a Celotex-style burden shift for summary judgment; Gonsewski (2011) on alimony, Armbrister (2013) and Kelly (2014) on parenting designations, Lovlace (2013) on material change, Eldridge (2001) on limiting visitation, Kinard (1998) on dividing retirement benefits, and Trezevant (2018) on dividing property before alimony lead with it. Sneed (2010) waives skeletal arguments, Young (2003) gives pro se litigants limited leeway, and Konvalinka (2008) sets the elements of contempt. Myint (1998) allowed prejudgment interest despite reasonable disputes. Eldridge anchors the partial 2025-29 slice, where criminal-evidence cases (Cannon 2008, Gilliland 2000, Shirley 1999) enter: drift.
rule: Tennessee appellate courts review discretionary decisions, especially in family cases, by asking whether the factual basis is supported by evidence, the trial court identified and applied the correct legal principles, and the decision is within the range of acceptable alternatives, viewing the evidence in its favor; questions of law are reviewed de novo, undeveloped arguments are waived, and summary judgment follows Rye.

changes.what: Overruled cases denying prejudgment interest whenever an obligation is disputed on reasonable grounds.
A court abuses its discretion by applying incorrect legal principles; visitation is limited only on definite evidence of harm to the child.

changes.case: Lee Medical v. Beecher; Sneed v. Board of Professional Responsibility
changes.what: Three-part framework for reviewing discretionary decisions; issues not developed with argument and authority are waived.

changes.case: Gonsewski v. Gonsewski; Armbrister v. Armbrister
changes.what: Alimony and parenting decisions get deferential abuse-of-discretion review, with evidence viewed in favor of the decision.

changes.case: Rye v. Women's Care Center of Memphis
changes.what: A movant shifts the summary-judgment burden by showing the nonmovant's evidence is insufficient, and the nonmovant must then show more than metaphysical doubt.

name: Pennsylvania suppression review and vehicle stops: In re L.J., Feczko
description: Pennsylvania suppression appeals: review is limited to the suppression-hearing record (In re L.J., 2013, anchor from 2020-24), with supported findings binding. Vehicle stops need reasonable suspicion where investigation could follow and probable cause otherwise (Chase 2008, Feczko 2010). Gary (2014) adopted the federal automobile exception until Alexander (2020) overruled it; Hicks (2019) held a firearm alone is not suspicious.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Pennsylvania suppression review and investigative stops
previous.description: Pennsylvania appellate cases on scope of suppression review (In re L.J.) and the reasonable-suspicion/probable-cause line for vehicle stops under the Fourth Amendment and Article I, § 8.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session subagents, from cocite evidence; second pass differentiated near-duplicates)

history: Dominant rule: on review of a suppression ruling the appellate court looks only at the suppression record, is bound by findings the record supports, and reviews the law de novo (In re L.J., 2013). How it changed: the 2015-19 anchor is Feczko (Pa. Super. 2010), which, applying Chase (2008), required probable cause for a stop based on a violation that further investigation could not confirm, such as weaving out of a lane, and reasonable suspicion otherwise. L.J., which barred looking past the suppression record, becomes the anchor in 2020-24. On the merits, Strickler (2000) addressed consent after a stop, Gary (2014) adopted the federal automobile exception, and Hicks (2019) enters in 2020-24 holding that carrying a concealed gun is not reasonable suspicion by itself. Alexander (2020) overruled Gary and restored warrant and exigency requirements under Article I, § 8; it appears only as a waived claim in the evidence. Also: mere encounters versus detentions, plain view, officer experience in the probable-cause mix, and rental-car standing. In 2025-29 the unit folds back into the national stops lineage.
rule: Pennsylvania appellate review of a suppression ruling is confined to the suppression-hearing record, accepts supported findings and reviews legal conclusions de novo; a vehicle stop needs reasonable suspicion when further investigation is possible and probable cause when it is not.

changes.what: Consent after a completed traffic stop may be voluntary even without a clear endpoint; consent after an illegal stop faces a heightened standard.
Investigative detention is coterminous under the Fourth Amendment and Article I, § 8; stops on reasonable suspicion of a Vehicle Code violation are permitted.

changes.case: Commonwealth v. Feczko (Pa. Super. en banc)
changes.what: A stop for a violation that needs no further investigation, such as failing to drive in a single lane, requires probable cause; Feczko anchors 2015-19.
Appellate scope of review is limited to the record developed at the suppression hearing, not the trial record; L.J. anchors 2020-24.
The federal automobile exception: probable cause alone justifies a warrantless car search.
Possession of a concealed firearm alone does not give reasonable suspicion.
Overruled Gary; Article I, § 8 requires a warrant and exigency for a car search.

name: Judicial estoppel (New Hampshire v. Maine) and nonparty preclusion (Taylor)
description: Judicial estoppel and preclusion: a party who succeeded on one position may be barred from a clearly inconsistent one for unfair advantage (New Hampshire v. Maine, 2001, anchor from 2000-04), applied often to debtors who hid claims in bankruptcy (Oneida, 1988; Coastal Plains, 1999). From 2010-14 nonparty preclusion joins: Taylor v. Sturgell (2008) rejected virtual representation, with Montana (1979), Parklane, Richards, Semtek and Hansberry.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Judicial estoppel and preclusion
previous.description: Barring inconsistent positions and relitigation: judicial estoppel (New Hampshire v. Maine), including in bankruptcy nondisclosure, nonparty preclusion and privity (Taylor v. Sturgell, Richards, Hansberry), federal-judgment preclusion (Semtek), and law of the case (Christianson).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: judicial estoppel prevents a party who persuaded a court to adopt a position from later taking a clearly inconsistent one that would give it an unfair advantage; it is equitable and not applied to inadvertence or mistake. How it changed: the 1990-94 and 1995-99 slices are circuit cases adopting the doctrine (Edwards v. Aetna and Allen v. Zurich, 1982; Patriot Cinemas, 1987), with bankruptcy nondisclosure as the main setting: Oneida (3d Cir. 1988) estopped a debtor who omitted a lender-liability claim, and Ryan Operations (1996) required bad faith; bankruptcy related-to jurisdiction (Pacor; Celotex v. Edwards, 1995) also appears. Coastal Plains (5th Cir. 1999) applied estoppel to a concealed claim. New Hampshire v. Maine (2001) set the national factors and anchors every slice from 2000-04. In 2010-14 claim and issue preclusion join: Taylor v. Sturgell (2008) confined nonparty preclusion to recognised exceptions and placed the burden on the party asserting it, with Montana v. United States (1979), Parklane v. Shore (1979) on offensive collateral estoppel, Richards (1996) and Hansberry (1940) on due process, and Semtek (2001) on federal-judgment preclusion. Also: the law of the case (Christianson, 1988).
rule: A party who persuaded a court to accept one position may be estopped from taking a clearly inconsistent position for unfair advantage (New Hampshire v. Maine), and a judgment binds nonparties only within narrow, due-process-limited exceptions (Taylor v. Sturgell).

changes.case: Edwards v. Aetna; Allen v. Zurich; Oneida Motor Freight; Ryan Operations v. Santiam-Midwest (3d Cir. 1996)
changes.what: Circuits adopted judicial estoppel, including against debtors who failed to disclose claims in bankruptcy, but required more than inadvertence (no bad faith in Ryan Operations).
Barred a debtor's officer from benefiting from the debtor's failure to disclose a claim; declined to limit estoppel to factual positions.
Set the factors: clearly inconsistent positions, success in persuading a court, and unfair advantage; anchors from 2000-04 to the end.
Rejected virtual representation; nonparty preclusion is limited to recognised categories, with federal common law governing federal judgments.

name: Michigan criminal appeals: Unger evidence, then Carines plain error and Ginther
description: The criminal strand of Michigan appeals, 2010-29, criminal throughout: Unger (2008) anchors 2010-14 on evidence of motive, intent and other acts (MRE 404(b)); from 2015-19 Carines (1999) plain-error review anchors, with ineffectiveness needing deficient performance and outcome-determinative prejudice shown at a Ginther (1973) hearing (Trakhtenberg, 2012). Lockridge (2015) made the guidelines advisory, and Hardy (2013) set review of scoring facts.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, round 2 after the lineage re-link)

previous.name: Michigan criminal: plain error and ineffective assistance
previous.description: Sub-cluster form of the Michigan criminal line: Carines plain error, Ginther hearings on ineffective assistance, futile objections, and other-acts evidence under MRE 404(b).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: plain-error review and ineffectiveness claims in Michigan criminal appeals. In 2010-14 Unger (2008) anchors, with Carines, Ginther, Ericksen (2010) and Dobek (2007) leading: motive and consciousness of guilt are relevant evidence, intent to kill may be inferred from the wounds, other acts of abuse of the complainant are admissible under MRE 404(b), and cumulative error may be raised on appeal. How it changed: Carines (1999) anchors from 2015-19 through 2025-29 as the unit merges with two other 2010-14 units. Unpreserved errors, constitutional or not, need a clear or obvious error affecting substantial rights, and Vaughn (2012) treats structural error as meeting that prong. Trakhtenberg (2012) enters and requires deficient performance that was outcome-determinative, with Ginther hearings for facts outside the record and the factual predicate on the defendant (Solloway, 2016). Sentencing joins in 2015-19: Milbourn (1990) proportionality, Francisco (2006) resentencing for scoring errors, Hardy (2013) on scoring facts, and Lockridge (2015) making the guidelines advisory. Also: prosecutorial argument on the evidence (Bahoda, 1995), police explaining investigative steps (Heft, 2012) and joinder (Gaines, 2014).
rule: Michigan appellate courts review unpreserved error, including constitutional error, for plain error affecting substantial rights (Carines), and an ineffectiveness claim needs deficient performance and outcome-determinative prejudice, with any facts outside the record developed at a Ginther hearing (Trakhtenberg).

changes.what: Evidentiary hearing for ineffective-assistance claims based on matters not of record.
Abandoned the shock-the-conscience test for a principle of proportionality.
Plain-error review extends to unpreserved claims of constitutional error.

changes.case: People v. Francisco; People v. Dobek
changes.what: A sentence based on a miscalculated guidelines range requires resentencing; prior acts of sexual abuse of the complainant may be admitted under MRE 404(b).

changes.case: People v. Vaughn; People v. Trakhtenberg
changes.what: Structural errors satisfy the third Carines prong, and ineffectiveness requires outcome-determinative deficiency.
Michigan's mandatory sentencing guidelines violated the Sixth Amendment and became advisory, with departures reviewed for reasonableness.

round1.name: Michigan criminal: other-acts evidence (VanderVliet), then Carines plain error and Ginther
round1.description: Michigan criminal appeals: early slices center on MRE 404(b) other-acts evidence (Golochowicz, 1982; VanderVliet, 1993, adopting a Huddleston-style test; Sabin, 2000). From 2000-04 Carines (1999) anchors: plain error for unpreserved errors, including constitutional ones, after Grant (1994) adopted Olano; Lukity (1999) governs preserved error. Ginther (1973) hearings and Trakhtenberg (2012) on ineffectiveness and Lockridge (2015) on advisory guidelines follow.
round1.history: Dominant rule: the anchor changes once. In 1990-94 and 1995-99 Golochowicz (1982) anchors other-acts evidence; VanderVliet (1993) replaced its four-part test with a proper-purpose, relevance and Rule 403 inquiry, and Starr (1998), Crawford (1998) and Sabin (2000) apply it. Grant (1994) adopted Olano plain error for nonconstitutional errors, and Mateo (1996) and Gearns (1998) addressed harmless error. How it changed: Carines (1999) anchors 2000-04, 2005-09 and 2015-29. It extended plain-error review to unpreserved constitutional claims, putting the burden of prejudice on the defendant. Lukity (1999) overruled Gearns and requires preserved nonconstitutional error to be more probably than not outcome-determinative. In 2005-09 Babcock (2003) on guidelines departures and Cornell and Mendoza (2002-03) on lesser-included instructions lead. Unger (2008) anchors 2010-14 as Ginther (1973), Ericksen (2010, futile objections), Dobek (2007) and Payne (2009) enter. In 2015-19 the unit merges with the parent cluster and Trakhtenberg (2012) and Lockridge (2015) enter.
round1.rule: Unpreserved errors in Michigan criminal trials are reviewed under Carines's plain-error test and preserved nonconstitutional errors reverse only if more probably than not outcome-determinative (Lukity); other-acts evidence is admissible under MRE 404(b) when offered for a proper non-character purpose, relevant, and not substantially more prejudicial than probative (VanderVliet).

changes.what: Four-part test for admitting other-acts evidence, including substantial evidence that the defendant committed the act.

Replaced Golochowicz with a Huddleston-style inquiry: proper purpose, relevance, Rule 403 balancing and a limiting instruction; Rule 404(b) applies only when the evidence is relevant solely through character.
Adopted Olano's plain-error test for unpreserved nonconstitutional errors.

changes.case: People v. Carines; People v. Lukity
changes.what: Carines applied plain error to unpreserved constitutional errors; Lukity overruled Gearns and set the more-probable-than-not standard for preserved nonconstitutional error.
Lesser-offense instructions are limited to necessarily included offenses supported by a rational view of the evidence.
An abuse of discretion is an outcome outside the range of principled outcomes; guidelines departures require reasons for the specific departure.

changes.case: People v. Trakhtenberg; People v. Lockridge
changes.what: Ineffectiveness requires deficient, outcome-determinative performance (Trakhtenberg); the sentencing guidelines became advisory (Lockridge).

before_differentiation.name: Michigan criminal appeals: Carines plain error, Ginther ineffectiveness, Lockridge
before_differentiation.description: Michigan criminal appeals, 2010-29: unpreserved error, including constitutional error, gets Carines (1999) plain-error review; ineffectiveness needs deficient performance and outcome-determinative prejudice, developed at a Ginther (1973) hearing (Trakhtenberg, 2012). Unger (2008) anchors 2010-14 and Carines from 2015-19. Lockridge (2015) made the sentencing guidelines advisory, and Hardy (2013) set review of scoring facts.

distinct_from.how: The criminal sub-cluster, anchored on Unger's evidence rulings in 2010-14 rather than the parent's civil Boodt unit; from 2015 both are the same Carines-anchored criminal body.

name: Qualified immunity, 2025-29 only: particularized precedent after Pearson
description: The partial 2025-29 qualified-immunity slice, anchored on Pearson (2009): courts may take the two prongs in either order, and clearly established law must be particularized (Brosseau 2004, Mullenix 2015, White 2017, Wesby and Kisela 2018, Rivas-Villegas and Bond 2021), save obvious cases (Hope 2002, Taylor 2020); Harlow (1982) and Anderson (1987) state the test and denials are immediately appealable (Mitchell v. Forsyth 1985).
history: Dominant rule: qualified immunity shields officials whose conduct does not violate clearly established rights a reasonable person would have known (Harlow 1982), judged objectively (Anderson 1987), protecting all but the plainly incompetent (Malley 1986); denials turning on law are immediately appealable (Forsyth 1985). How it changed: Pearson (2009), the anchor, made Saucier's two-step order optional, letting courts decide only the clearly-established prong (Reichle 2012). The Court then insisted the right be defined with specificity in the factual context: Brosseau (2004), Plumhoff (2014), Mullenix (2015), White v. Pauly (2017), Kisela and Wesby (2018, requiring controlling authority or a robust consensus), and the 2021 summary reversals Rivas-Villegas and Bond, which put the burden on the plaintiff to identify a closely analogous case. Hope (2002) and Taylor v. Riojas (2020) preserve an obvious-case exception. Circuit cases add that factual disputes can preclude summary judgment and that video may be credited (2021). Circuit led: Calvert Cliffs (1971) held that every federal agency must consider the environmental impact of its actions, and NRDC v. Morton (1972), the anchor in both slices, required the statement to discuss all reasonably available alternatives, including those the agency itself could not adopt. Committee for Nuclear Responsibility (1971) required meaningful reference to opposing views; Environmental Defense Fund (1972) required objective evaluation; Arlington Coalition (1972) and Hanly v. Mitchell (1972) applied NEPA to highways and urban projects; Scientists' Institute (1973) required program statements and recognized organizational standing; Jones v. Lynn (1973) disfavored laches; Overton Park (1971) supplied record review. How it changed: in 1975-79 the courts began to limit the duty. Morton (1974) confined alternatives to those reasonably related to a project's purposes; NRDC (1975) limited the area of cumulative review; and Kleppe (1976) entered, holding that Interior need not prepare a regional statement absent a regional proposal and that agencies may set a statement's scope. Aberdeen & Rockfish (1975) addressed injunctions. The unit splits in 1980-84.
rule: NEPA requires every federal agency to consider the environmental impact of major federal actions and to discuss reasonable alternatives in an impact statement, with courts enforcing the procedure on the administrative record.

changes.case: Scientists' Institute for Public Information v. AEC (D.C. Cir.)

round1.name: NEPA's procedural duty: Calvert Cliffs, NRDC v. Morton, Kleppe, Vermont Yankee
round1.description: NEPA requires agencies to consider environmental impact and reasonable alternatives (Calvert Cliffs, 1971; NRDC v. Morton, 1972, anchor 1970-79), but the duty is procedural: Kleppe (1976) let agencies fix an EIS's scope, Vermont Yankee (1978) barred courts from adding procedures, and Karlen (1980) held NEPA requires no more than consideration. By 1985-89 the lineage turns to injunctive relief (Weinberger, 1982; Gambell).
round1.history: Dominant rule: NEPA's duties are procedural. An agency must take environmental consequences and reasonable alternatives into account in an impact statement, and courts enforce the procedure rather than the result. How it changed: in 1970-79 the D.C. Circuit decisions lead and NRDC v. Morton (1972) anchors: Calvert Cliffs (1971) made every agency consider environmental impact, NRDC v. Morton required discussion of alternatives beyond the agency's own authority, and Scientists' Institute (1973) addressed program-level statements, with Overton Park (1971) supplying record review. The Supreme Court then narrowed review. Kleppe (1976) entered in 1975-79 and anchors from 1980-84, letting the agency define a statement's scope absent a regional proposal; Vermont Yankee (1978) barred courts from imposing procedures beyond § 553; Karlen (1980) held that NEPA requires only consideration of consequences; Andrus (1979) gave CEQ's interpretation weight. In 1985-89 the lineage turns to relief and assessments: Weinberger v. Romero-Barcelo (1982) made injunctions discretionary, and Save Our Ecosystems (1984) treated an EA functioning as an EIS alike.
round1.rule: NEPA imposes procedural duties to consider environmental consequences and reasonable alternatives in an impact statement, and courts enforce that procedure without second-guessing the agency's substantive choice or adding procedures of their own.

changes.case: Calvert Cliffs' Coordinating Comm. v. AEC; NRDC v. Morton
changes.what: Every federal agency must consider environmental impact, and an EIS must discuss all reasonable alternatives, including ones outside the agency's authority.
No regionwide EIS was required absent a regional proposal; the agency may define the scope of its statement unless arbitrary. Kleppe anchors from 1980-84.
Courts may not impose procedural requirements beyond those in § 553 and the statute.

changes.case: Strycker's Bay Neighborhood Council v. Karlen
changes.what: NEPA requires only that the agency consider environmental consequences; it need not elevate them over other concerns.
An injunction for a statutory violation is discretionary unless Congress clearly says otherwise.

before_differentiation.name: NEPA's impact-statement duty: Calvert Cliffs, NRDC v. Morton, Kleppe (1970s)
before_differentiation.description: NEPA in the 1970s: every agency must consider environmental impact (Calvert Cliffs 1971), and the impact statement must discuss reasonable alternatives, even beyond the agency's authority (NRDC v. Morton 1972, anchor throughout). Program-level statements (Scientists' Institute 1973) and objective evaluation (EDF 1972) followed. Kleppe (1976) let agencies define the scope of a statement absent a regional proposal; Morton (1974) tied alternatives to project purposes.

distinct_from.how: The 1970s expansion of NEPA in the D.C. Circuit, anchored by NRDC v. Morton; the 1980s sibling is anchored by Kleppe and records the Supreme Court's procedural narrowing and Ninth Circuit practice.

name: Michigan contract interpretation: unambiguous contracts enforced as written (Rory)
description: Michigan contract and insurance-policy interpretation, 2015-24, anchored by Rory (2005): unambiguous contracts are enforced as written, so optional coverage is purely contractual and shortened limitations periods stand. Klapp (2003) sends ambiguous terms to the jury; Wilkie (2003) reads terms in context; Quality Products (2003) lets parties modify despite anti-waiver clauses; Titan v. Hyten (2012) permits rescission for fraud.
history: Dominant rule: Rory (2005) anchors both slices: Michigan courts enforce unambiguous contracts as written, reject judicial reasonableness review, and treat optional insurance coverage as purely contractual, so a shortened contractual limitations period is valid. A term is ambiguous only if it fairly admits two meanings, read in context (Wilkie, 2003), using ordinary contemporary meaning (Henderson, 1999); if ambiguous, intent is a jury question (Klapp, 2003). Parol evidence may show whether a writing is integrated (UAW-GM, 1998), parties may waive or modify despite anti-waiver clauses (Quality Products, 2003), and exclusions such as 'expected or intended' injury are applied as written (Churchman 1992; Hunt 2014). How it changed: Titan v. Hyten (2012) let insurers rescind uncertified policies for fraud. In 2020-24 the slice adds settlement enforcement (Kloian 2007), rights of first refusal (Smith Trust 2008), breach-of-contract elements (Miller-Davis 2014), retiree benefits under CBAs (Kendzierski 2019), and review of combined (C)(8)/(C)(10) motions (Innovation Ventures 2016).
rule: Michigan courts enforce unambiguous contracts, including insurance policies, as written according to their plain meaning without judicial reasonableness review, and treat the meaning of a genuinely ambiguous term as a question of fact for the jury.

changes.case: UAW-GM Human Resource Center v. KSL Recreation
changes.what: Parol evidence of prior or contemporaneous negotiations is admissible on the threshold question whether a writing is fully integrated.

changes.case: Klapp v. United Insurance Group; Wilkie v. Auto-Owners; Quality Products v. Nagel Precision
changes.what: Ambiguity makes intent a jury question; contract terms are read in context; parties may waive or modify despite anti-modification clauses.
Optional insurance coverage is purely contractual, and shortened contractual limitations periods are enforced as written; anchors both slices.
An insurer may rescind an uncertified policy for fraud: the limit in MCL 257.520(f)(1) applies only to certified policies.

name: Pennsylvania discretionary sentencing review: substantial question (Devers, Walls)
description: Pennsylvania Superior Court review of the discretionary aspects of a sentence: a four-part threshold of timely appeal, preservation at sentencing or in a post-sentence motion, a Rule 2119(f) statement and a substantial question. Devers (1988) presumes a court with a presentence report weighed mitigation; Mouzon (2002) and Walls (2007) set the substantial-question and deference rules.

previous.name: Pennsylvania discretionary aspects of sentencing
previous.description: Pennsylvania Superior Court review of the discretionary aspects of a sentence: the substantial-question requirement, presumption that a court with a presentence report weighed mitigating factors, and excessiveness claims.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: a 2010 Superior Court decision anchors every slice, restating that a challenge to the discretionary aspects of a sentence is a petition for permission to appeal, reached only if timely, preserved at sentencing or in a motion to modify, presented in a Rule 2119(f) statement, and raising a substantial question. Unpreserved objections are waived (2006, 2013). How it changed: no change in the framework within the slices; the precedents that shape it predate them. Devers (1988) presumes that a court with a presentence report considered character and mitigating factors and rejected a requirement of extended explanation; Mouzon (2002) let excessiveness claims within statutory limits raise a substantial question when plausibly argued; and Walls (2007) cautioned that reversal for unreasonableness should be rare. Later decisions define which claims qualify: excessiveness plus failure to consider mitigating factors (2013, 2014, 2015, 2019), total confinement for a technical probation violation (2000, 2010), and double counting of guideline factors (2020) raise substantial questions; bald consecutive-sentence claims (2013) and standard-range mitigation complaints (2021) do not. Also: Santiago (2009) Anders brief requirements, carried from the merged no-merit unit.
rule: A Pennsylvania appellant has no automatic right to review of the discretionary aspects of a sentence; the Superior Court reaches the claim only if it is timely, preserved at sentencing or in a post-sentence motion, set out in a Rule 2119(f) statement, and raises a substantial question, and then reverses only for an abuse of discretion.

changes.what: Where the court had a presentence report, it is presumed to have weighed the defendant's character and mitigating factors; Superior Court decisions demanding extended explanations were disapproved.
An excessiveness claim can raise a substantial question even for a sentence within statutory limits, if the appellant gives plausible reasons the sentence violates the Code or fundamental norms.
Appellate courts may not usurp the sentencing court's discretion; reversal for unreasonableness under § 9781 should occur infrequently, above or below the guidelines.

changes.case: Superior Court decisions on substantial questions
changes.what: Excessiveness combined with failure to consider mitigating factors raises a substantial question, but a bald claim about consecutive sentences does not.

name: Wrongful birth recognized, wrongful life mostly rejected: Becker, Harbeson, Turpin
description: Wrongful birth and wrongful life (1985-99): parents may recover when negligent genetic counselling or prenatal diagnosis denied them the choice to avoid or end a pregnancy, at least for extraordinary costs (Becker 1978, Berman 1979, Harbeson 1983, James 1985), while most courts reject the child's wrongful-life claim, with Turpin (1982) and Procanik allowing medical expenses. In 1995-99, wrongful-pregnancy cases on child-rearing costs anchor (Johnson 1989).

previous.name: Wrongful birth and wrongful life
previous.description: Tort claims by parents and children after negligent genetic counselling or prenatal diagnosis: wrongful birth recognized, wrongful life mostly rejected (Becker, Harbeson, Turpin, Berman, Procanik, Cillo, James). Successor to the wrongful-pregnancy sub-cluster 19109.

history: Dominant rule: Becker v. Schwartz (N.Y. 1978) anchors 1985-94. Parents can sue for the wrongful birth of an impaired child when a physician negligently fails to warn them, recovering pecuniary costs of care, but the child has no claim for being born. How it changed: Jacobs (1975) and Dumer (1975) first allowed limited recovery after rubella misdiagnosis. New Jersey moved from Gleitman (1967) to Berman (1979, emotional distress for parents) to Schroeder (1981, overruling Berman in part to allow extraordinary expenses) and Procanik and Cillo (1984), letting the child recover extraordinary medical expenses where the parents could not. Turpin (Cal. 1982) and Harbeson (Wash. 1983) also allowed the child special damages, and Harbeson set proximate cause for wrongful birth. Others refused wrongful life (James 1985, Azzolino 1985, Lininger 1988, Arche 1990), and some limited damages to minority. Haymon (1987) required proof the mother would have ended the pregnancy. In 1995-99, as wrongful-pregnancy units merge in, Johnson v. University Hospitals (1989) anchors: after a failed sterilization producing a healthy child, only pregnancy costs are recoverable, against Hartke (1983) allowing child-rearing costs.
rule: Parents may sue for wrongful birth when negligent prenatal diagnosis or genetic counselling denies them the choice to avoid or end a pregnancy, recovering at least the extraordinary costs of the child's impairment, but most courts deny the child a wrongful-life claim for general damages because life, even impaired, is not a legal injury; a few allow the child the extraordinary medical expenses.

changes.what: Recognized parents' claims after a missed rubella diagnosis, limited to the costs of treating the child's impairment.

changes.case: Becker v. Schwartz (N.Y.); Berman v. Allan (N.J.)
changes.what: Wrongful birth was recognized (Becker for pecuniary expenses; Berman for emotional distress after failure to offer amniocentesis) while the child's wrongful-life claim was rejected.
Overruled Berman in part to allow parents the extraordinary medical expenses.

changes.case: Turpin v. Sortini (Cal.); Harbeson v. Parke-Davis (Wash. 1983); Procanik; Cillo (N.J. 1984)

Declined to recognize wrongful birth or wrongful life, leaving the question to the legislature.
For failed sterilization producing a healthy child, recovery is limited to the costs of the pregnancy.

description: Title VII sexual harassment. Meritor (1986, anchor 1990-99) recognized hostile-environment claims; Harris (1993) required severe or pervasive conduct without psychological injury; Faragher and Ellerth (1998, Faragher anchor 2000-04) set vicarious liability and an affirmative defense; Oncale (1998) reached same-sex harassment; Morgan (2002) set timeliness for hostile-environment claims. history: Dominant rule: harassment that is severe or pervasive is sex discrimination, with employer liability depending on who harassed and how. How it changed: Meritor (1986) anchors 1990-94 with circuit cases building the doctrine: Henson (1982) on elements, Hall (1988) and Hicks (1987) treating non-sexual hostility as relevant, Rabidue (1986) and Ellison (1991) dividing over the reasonable-person or reasonable-woman standard, and Andrews (1990) on pervasive derogatory language. Meritor still anchors 1995-99 as Harris (1993) and the 1998 cases enter: Faragher and Ellerth on vicarious liability and the affirmative defense, and Oncale on same-sex harassment; Franklin (1992) and Cannon (1979) bring Title IX remedies. Faragher anchors 2000-04, Morgan (2002) addresses continuing-violation timing, and Seventh Circuit cases (Hilt-Dyson 2002, Haugerud 2001, Smart 1996) apply severity and adverse-action limits. The unit then splits toward McDonnell Douglas pretext in 2005-09.
rule: Sexual harassment violates Title VII when it is quid pro quo or creates a hostile environment that is severe or pervasive, judged objectively and subjectively under the totality of the circumstances (Meritor, Harris), whether same-sex or not (Oncale); employers are vicariously liable for supervisor harassment, subject to an affirmative defense where no tangible employment action occurred (Faragher, Ellerth).

changes.case: Henson v. City of Dundee (11th Cir.)
changes.what: Set elements for hostile-environment and quid pro quo harassment and inferred employer knowledge from pervasiveness.
Hostile-environment sexual harassment is sex discrimination; voluntariness is no defense if advances were unwelcome. Anchors 1990-99.

changes.case: Rabidue v. Osceola Refining (6th Cir.); Ellison v. Brady (9th Cir.); Andrews v. Philadelphia (3d Cir. 1990)
changes.what: Circuits divided over the reasonable-person versus reasonable-woman perspective and the role of non-sexual hostility.
No concrete psychological harm is required; conduct must be severe or pervasive enough to alter conditions, viewed in all circumstances.

changes.case: Faragher v. City of Boca Raton; Burlington Industries v. Ellerth
changes.what: Employers are vicariously liable for supervisor harassment, with an affirmative defense of reasonable care and the employee's unreasonable failure to use complaint procedures; Faragher anchors 2000-04.
Same-sex harassment is actionable, though Title VII is not a general civility code.

changes.case: National Railroad Passenger Corp. v. Morgan
changes.what: A hostile-environment claim is timely if one contributing act falls within the filing period, while discrete acts must each be timely.

history: Dominant rule: the IRS's summons power is broad and enforced on a Powell showing, subject to defenses of improper purpose or privilege. Powell (1964) anchors 1965-69 with Reisman (1964), Morton Salt (1950) and Walling (1946) on agency subpoenas, and Boren (1957) on summonses after indictment. How it changed: Donaldson (1971) anchors 1970-79, limiting taxpayer intervention and allowing summonses with possible criminal use made in good faith; Roundtree (1969) voided a summons used solely to build a prosecution, Kordel (1970) allowed parallel civil and criminal proceedings, and Couch (1973) narrowed the Fifth Amendment defense. Bisceglia (1975) approved John Doe summonses, McCarthy (1975) addressed proof of the Powell elements, and LaSalle (1978) set an institutional good-faith test, displaced by the 1982 amendments to § 7602. Powell anchors again from 1980-84 to 1995-99 as Euge (1980) and Arthur Young (1984) enter and attorney-client privilege claims against summonses appear. In 1995-99 Gertner (1995) and RTC v. Walde (1994) lead before the unit joins administrative-search law.
rule: A court enforces an IRS summons or agency subpoena when the government shows a legitimate purpose, relevance, that the information is not already in its possession, and compliance with required procedures, without probable cause; the respondent must then show bad faith or abuse of process.

changes.case: Oklahoma Press v. Walling; United States v. Morton Salt

changes.case: United States v. Powell; Reisman v. Caplin
changes.what: The IRS needs no probable cause; Powell's four elements make a prima facie case, and challenges are raised in court enforcement proceedings.

changes.case: United States v. Roundtree (5th Cir.); Donaldson v. United States
changes.what: A summons used solely to build a criminal prosecution fails, but one issued in good faith before a criminal referral is valid; taxpayer intervention is limited.
The Fifth Amendment privilege is personal and no accountant-client privilege defeats a summons to the taxpayer's accountant.

changes.case: United States v. Bisceglia; United States v. LaSalle National Bank
changes.what: John Doe summonses are permitted, and good faith is measured by the IRS's institutional posture before a recommendation to prosecute.

changes.case: United States v. Euge; United States v. Arthur Young & Co.
changes.what: The IRS may compel handwriting exemplars and accountants' tax accrual workpapers; no accountant work-product protection applies.

changes.case: Tax Equity and Fiscal Responsibility Act (26 U.S.C. § 7602(b), (d))
changes.what: Summonses may serve criminal investigation purposes but not after a Justice Department referral, displacing LaSalle's institutional test.

How it changed: Reisman (1964) anchors 1965-69, with Morton Salt (1950) and Walling (1946) on agency subpoenas. Couch (1973) and Fisher (1976) narrowed the Fifth Amendment defense, Bisceglia (1975) approved John Doe summonses, and LaSalle (1978) set an institutional good-faith test, displaced by the 1982 amendments to § 7602. history: Dominant rule: private relators may sue for fraud on the government only within the limits Congress set in 1986, chiefly the public-disclosure bar and its original-source exception, and must plead actual false claims with particularity. How it changed: Hess (1943) upheld qui tam suits and set damages rules. The unit forms in 1995-99 with Wang (9th Cir. 1992) as anchor, joined by Stinson (1991), Springfield Terminal (1994) and Cooper (1994), which defined public disclosure and direct and independent knowledge. In 2000-04 Harrison (1999) anchors with Thompson (1998) on Rule 9(b) and false certification, Hopper v. Anton (1996) tying liability to claims rather than regulatory violations, and Vermont Agency (2000), which excluded states from qui tam liability. In 2005-09 Springfield Terminal anchors as first-to-file cases (Lujan 2001, Hampton 2003, Grynberg 2004), Clausen's (2002) requirement to identify submitted claims, Karvelas (2004) on retaliation, and Rockwell (2007) on original sources enter. The 2010 amendments, noted only as 'pre-PPACA' in the evidence, later changed the bar.
rule: A qui tam relator may not sue on allegations based on publicly disclosed information unless he is an original source with direct and independent knowledge he voluntarily gave the government, must plead the false claims themselves with Rule 9(b) particularity, and liability attaches to knowingly false claims for payment, not to regulatory violations or innocent mistakes.

changes.case: United States ex rel. Marcus v. Hess
changes.what: Qui tam suits upheld; double damages are compensatory, and a forfeiture applies to each claim tainted by collusive bidding.
Strengthened relator incentives while adding the public-disclosure jurisdictional bar and the original-source exception.

changes.case: Stinson (3d Cir.); Wang v. FMC (9th Cir.); Kreindler (2d Cir.); Springfield Terminal (D.C. Cir.); Cooper v. Blue Cross (11th Cir.)
changes.what: Discovery material can be publicly disclosed; 'based upon' does not mean 'solely'; an original source must have direct knowledge and have voluntarily informed the government before suing; Wang anchors 1995-99 and Springfield Terminal 2005-09.

changes.case: Hagood v. Sonoma County (9th Cir.); Hopper v. Anton (9th Cir.); Thompson v. Columbia/HCA (5th Cir.); Harrison v. Westinghouse Savannah River (4th Cir.)

history: Dominant rule: the standards the Oklahoma Court of Criminal Appeals applies in death-penalty appeals. In 1990-94 Fox (1989) anchors, upholding blood-spatter testimony and resolving evidentiary and jury issues, with Walker (1986) on the heat-of-passion manslaughter instruction, Boltz (1991) on refusing that instruction where design to kill is shown, Nguyen (1988) and Sellers (1991) on evidence. How it changed: Romano (1993) anchors 1995-99, holding that Oklahoma law adequately guides the decision to seek death; Pickens (1993) treats lack of remorse as pertinent to continuing threat; Stouffer (1987) limits the heinous, atrocious or cruel aggravator to conscious suffering, which Neill (1994) found in a victim's extreme mental anguish; Mayes and Bryson (1994) refuse instructions defining life without parole or the option of life after an aggravator is found; Romano v. Oklahoma (1994) rejects a diminished-responsibility claim. Cargle (1995) limits victim-impact evidence. The lineage splits in 2000-04.
rule: In capital appeals the Oklahoma Court of Criminal Appeals upholds a death sentence where the statutory aggravators, read narrowly (heinous, atrocious or cruel requiring conscious suffering; continuing threat), are supported by the evidence, the jury was not misled about its sentencing role, and penalty-phase evidence and instructions stayed within statutory limits.

changes.what: Oklahoma law adequately guides prosecutorial discretion to seek death; lack of remorse is pertinent to the continuing-threat aggravator.

Victim-impact evidence must be limited to the circumstances of the death and its effects, as noticed before trial, not general praise of the victim.

name: Ohio sufficiency versus manifest weight: Thompkins, Jenks, Martin and Tibbs
description: Ohio review of the evidence behind a conviction: sufficiency, a question of law under Jenks (1991, which adopted Jackson v. Virginia and dropped the reasonable-theory-of-innocence rule), against manifest weight, where the court as thirteenth juror reverses only if the jury clearly lost its way (Martin, 1983). Thompkins (1997), anchoring from 1995-99, separated the two; Tibbs (1982) explains why only a sufficiency reversal bars retrial.

previous.name: Ohio sufficiency vs manifest weight: Thompkins/Jenks core and Tibbs
previous.description: Ohio appellate review distinguishing legal sufficiency (Jenks) from manifest weight of the evidence (State v. Thompkins, State v. Martin), with Tibbs v. Florida on why a weight reversal does not bar retrial.

history: Dominant rule: two distinct standards. Sufficiency asks whether, viewing the evidence for the prosecution, any rational trier of fact could find each element beyond a reasonable doubt (Jenks, 1991); credibility belongs to the trier of fact (Dehass, 1967). Manifest weight lets the court of appeals weigh the evidence as a thirteenth juror and reverse only where the jury clearly lost its way (Martin, 1983; Otten, 1986). How it changed: in 1990-94 the anchor is Jordan (1978) with Dehass, Long and Eley, and Jenks (1991) enters, overturning the requirement that circumstantial evidence exclude every reasonable theory of innocence. Thompkins (1997) enters in 1995-99 and anchors every slice after that: it set the tests apart, limited the thirteenth-juror power, and relied on Tibbs (1982), which also enters then, for the rule that a sufficiency reversal bars retrial but a weight reversal does not. Wilson (2007) applied civil weight review to classification proceedings, and Eastley (2012) briefly appears in 2010-14. Also: lesser-included instructions and rejection of acquittal-first charges (Thomas, 1988), constructive possession (Hankerson, 1982) and plain error (Barnes, 2002).
rule: Sufficiency is a question of law (could any rational trier of fact find the elements proved beyond a reasonable doubt, Jenks); manifest weight lets the court of appeals, as thirteenth juror, reverse only where the jury clearly lost its way (Martin, Thompkins), and a weight reversal, unlike a sufficiency reversal, does not bar retrial (Tibbs).

changes.what: Double jeopardy bars retrial after reversal for insufficient evidence but not after reversal on the weight of the evidence.

Sufficiency and weight are qualitatively different; the thirteenth-juror power is limited to preserve the jury's role, and a weight reversal requires a unanimous panel.
Sex-offender classification proceedings are civil and reviewed under the civil manifest-weight standard, unlike criminal convictions.

name: Right to counsel takes hold, 1965-69: Gideon, Douglas, critical stages, habeas
description: The founding of the indigent right to counsel, one 1965-69 slice anchored by Gideon (1963): the Sixth Amendment right binds the states, with Douglas (1963) requiring counsel on a first appeal, Griffin (1956) transcripts for indigents, Hamilton (1961) and White (1963) counsel at critical stages, and Carnley (1962) barring presumed waiver. Fay and Townsend (1963) opened federal habeas to enforce it, and Gault (1967) reached juveniles.
history: Dominant rule: Gideon v. Wainwright (1963) anchors this single 1965-69 slice, which merged the pre-Gideon right-to-counsel units: an indigent felony defendant in state court is entitled to appointed counsel under the Sixth and Fourteenth Amendments. Its antecedents lead too: Powell (1932) on effective counsel in capital cases and Johnson v. Zerbst (1938), which required counsel in federal courts and defined waiver as an intentional relinquishment of a known right; Carnley (1962) forbids presuming waiver from a silent record. How it changed: the right moved outward from trial. Hamilton (1961) and White (1963) made arraignment and preliminary hearings critical stages with no harmless-error inquiry. On appeal, Griffin (1956) and Lane (1963) required transcripts for indigents and Douglas (1963) required counsel on a first appeal as of right. Federal habeas became the enforcement route: Fay v. Noia (1963) read the 1867 Act broadly and Townsend v. Sain (1963) required evidentiary hearings in set circumstances. Pointer (1965) incorporated the Confrontation Clause, and In re Gault (1967) extended notice and counsel to juvenile delinquency proceedings.

changes.what: Due process required effective counsel in the capital Scottsboro trials; the Sixth Amendment requires counsel in federal courts, and waiver must be an intentional relinquishment of a known right.

name: Timing of agency review: exhaustion (Myers, McKart), Leedom v. Kyne, Abbott ripeness
description: When agency action can be challenged in court (1960-94): through 1979, NLRB review cases lead, as Leedom v. Kyne (1958) allows suits against action in excess of statutory power and Boire (1964) narrows it, with exhaustion under Myers (1938) and McKart (1969). previous.name: Exhaustion and ripeness for judicial review
previous.description: When review of agency action is available: exhaustion of administrative remedies (Myers v. Bethlehem Shipbuilding, McKart, Weinberger v. Salfi), review despite statutory preclusion (Leedom v. Kyne, Boire, McCulloch), ripeness of rules (Abbott Laboratories, Toilet Goods) and final agency action (FTC v. Standard Oil).

history: Dominant rule: courts intervene in agency proceedings only at the right time. In 1960-69 the unit is about NLRB representation cases. Certification orders are not directly reviewable (AFL v. NLRB 1940), but Leedom v. Kyne (1958), the 1960-64 anchor, allows district courts to strike Board action that violates a clear statutory command. McCulloch (1963) used that route for foreign-flag crews, and Boire v. Greyhound (1964), the 1965-69 anchor, restricted it to extraordinary cases. How it changed: in 1970-79 Myers (1938) and McKart (1969) lead on exhaustion. The rule bars premature suits, but McKart applies it according to its purposes, while McGee (1971) enforced it, and Hirsch (1947) weighed irreparable injury from delay. Abbott Laboratories (1967) anchors 1980-94: pre-enforcement challenges are ripe if the issues are fit and the hardship real, as against Toilet Goods (1967), and the APA presumes review. FTC v. Standard Oil (1980) holds an FTC complaint not final agency action. In 1990-94 benefits cases merge in. Salfi (1975) makes § 405(g) exhaustion jurisdictional, Califano v. Sanders (1977) and Heckler v. Ringer (1984) channel claims, and Bowen v. Michigan Academy (1986) and McNary (1991) preserve review of regulations and patterns of practice.
rule: A party must exhaust prescribed administrative remedies and await final agency action before seeking judicial relief (Myers, FTC v. Standard Oil), save narrow exceptions for agency action in plain excess of statutory power (Leedom v. name: Connecticut motions to strike: legal sufficiency on the pleaded facts
description: Connecticut's motion-to-strike standard, 1990-2004: a motion to strike tests legal sufficiency on the facts pleaded, construed favourably to the pleader (Mingachos, 1985; Gordon, 1988; Grigsby, 1990), but conclusions unsupported by facts fall (Novametrix, 1992, anchor 1995-99; Faulkner, 1997; Peter-Michael, 1998, anchor 2000-04). history: Dominant rule: a Connecticut motion to strike tests only whether the facts alleged, taken as true and construed broadly in the pleader's favour, state a legally sufficient claim; it cannot be used to decide facts (Mingachos, 1985) or rest on facts outside the pleading (Grigsby, 1990). How it changed: the rule stayed stable while the anchor moved. Gordon (1988), which also declined to abolish the public duty doctrine, anchors 1990-94. Novametrix (1992) anchors 1995-99 and held that bare legal conclusions may be stricken. Peter-Michael (1998) anchors 2000-04, finding a right-of-first-refusal claim sufficient. name: Erie and CAFA removal, 2005-09: Hanna, Gasperini; Brill burden of proof
description: Federal jurisdiction in diversity cases, 2005-09 only: Erie (1938, anchor), Guaranty Trust (1945), Hanna (1965) and Gasperini (1996) on when state substantive law governs, paired with removal: amount in controversy fixed at removal (St. Paul Mercury 1938); after CAFA (2005) the proponent keeps the jurisdictional burden (Brill 2005, Abrego 2006), and CAFA reaches pre-2005 suits only through amendments that do not relate back.

Alongside, and nearly as heavy: removal jurisdiction. Post-removal reductions cannot defeat jurisdiction (St. Paul Mercury 1938). After the Class Action Fairness Act took effect in 2005, the circuits held that CAFA did not shift the burden from the proponent of federal jurisdiction (Brill 2005, Abrego 2006), that the objector must prove a CAFA exception (Evans 2006), and that whether CAFA reaches a pre-2005 suit depends on whether an amendment adding parties relates back (Knudsen 2005, Plubell 2006, Braud 2006, Prime Care 2006). Allapattah (2005) allowed supplemental jurisdiction over additional plaintiffs below the amount. Single slice, 2005-09.

name: Timely notice of appeal as mandatory and jurisdictional: Browder, Lack, Torres
description: Federal appellate timeliness: the notice-of-appeal deadline is mandatory and jurisdictional (Robinson 1960; Browder 1978, anchor 1980-2004), with a narrow unique-circumstances exception (Thompson 1964). Griggs (1982) and Osterneck (1989) voided notices filed while Rule 59(e) motions pend, a rule relaxed by the 1993 amendments; Houston v. Lack (1988) adopted the prison mailbox rule; Torres (1988) made unnamed parties a jurisdictional defect.

previous.name: Timeliness of appeals and post-judgment motions
previous.description: When a notice of appeal is effective: timeliness as mandatory and jurisdictional (Browder, Robinson, Griggs v. Provident Consumer Discount), the prison mailbox rule (Houston v. Lack), naming parties (Torres v. Oakland Scavenger), and the effect of Rule 59(e) and 60(b) motions (Osterneck).

history: Dominant rule: Browder (1978) anchors every slice: the time to appeal is mandatory and jurisdictional (Robinson 1960, Griggs 1982), courts cannot enlarge it, an untimely post-judgment motion neither tolls the time nor brings up the judgment, and Rule 60(b) motions do not affect finality (Peake 1983). In 1995-2004 the mailbox rule extends to service and other filings (Faile 1993). The lineage moves into jurisdictional time limits in 2005-09.

name: Pennsylvania PCRA time-bar and Alleyne retroactivity
description: Pennsylvania post-conviction practice in 2015-19: the PCRA time-bar is jurisdictional (1999 anchor), so untimely petitions fail unless a statutory exception applies, whatever the claim, and relabelling as habeas does not help (2013). Alleyne (2013) mandatory-minimum challenges dominate: applied on direct appeal and to strike § 6317 (2015), but not retroactive on collateral review (2014, 2016).
history: Dominant rule: a 1999 Pennsylvania decision anchors this single 2015-19 slice: if a petitioner misses the PCRA's time requirements, the courts have no jurisdiction, and legality-of-sentence claims must still meet the time limits. The bar holds regardless of the constitutional nature of the claim (2000), cannot be escaped by claiming counsel's ineffectiveness (2000, 2001) or by calling the filing habeas corpus (2013), and the newly-discovered-facts exception requires due diligence (2010); a 2007 case held the bar may be unconstitutional as applied to an abandoned petitioner without access to records. How it changed: Alleyne (2013) leads the slice. Pennsylvania courts applied it to cases pending on direct appeal (2014), found no violation when prior convictions raised the minimum (2014), struck mandatory-minimum statutes such as § 6317 without rewriting them (2015), and held it non-retroactive on collateral review (2014, 2016). Miller v. Alabama was not extended to offenders 18 or older (2013).
rule: The PCRA's one-year time limit is jurisdictional: an untimely petition, even one raising legality of sentence, ineffectiveness or a constitutional claim, can be heard only if a statutory exception is pleaded and proved, and Alleyne (2013) does not supply one because it applies only to cases pending on direct review.

changes.case: Commonwealth v. Fahy; Pennsylvania Supreme Court decisions (2000)
changes.what: The PCRA time-bar is jurisdictional and applies to legality-of-sentence and constitutional claims; ineffectiveness of prior counsel does not excuse untimeliness.
Facts that raise a mandatory minimum must be found by a jury beyond a reasonable doubt.

name: Fourth Circuit: revocation sentences (Crudup, Slappy) and appeal waivers (Blick)
description: Fourth Circuit criminal appeals, 2005-29. Through 2010-14 the rule is enforcement of plea-agreement appeal waivers (Wessells 1991, Marin 1992), which bar Booker claims (Blick 2005, anchor 2005-09) but not sentences above the statutory maximum (Johnson 2005). From 2015-19 the lineage turns to supervised-release revocation sentences, reversed only if plainly unreasonable (Crudup 2006), with a duty to address nonfrivolous arguments (Thompson 2010, Slappy 2017).
history: Dominant rule: shifts within the span. In 2005-09 Blick (2005) anchors: appeal waivers questioned in the Rule 11 colloquy are enforced (Wessells 1991, Marin 1992, Khattak 2001), Booker claims fall within them (Blick, Bradley and Rubbo 2005), and Hahn (10th Cir. 2004) sets the enforcement procedure. In 2010-14 Johnson (2005) anchors, preserving review of sentences above the statutory maximum, with General (2002, Apprendi challenges), Martinez (2002, prejudice from Rule 11 errors) and DeFusco (1991, plea voluntariness); Poindexter (2007) on the government's choices in Anders cases and Tollett (1973) on counselled pleas enter. How it changed: from 2015-19 the lineage centres on revocation of supervised release. Crudup (2006) anchors, reviewing revocation sentences only for plain unreasonableness; Webb (2013) makes breach of trust the main concern; Thompson (2010) requires attention to nonfrivolous arguments; Moulden (2007) and Padgett (2015) apply the deferential standard. Slappy (2017) anchors 2020-24 and the partial 2025-29 slice, treating failure to address arguments for a within-range revocation sentence as procedural error, with Coston and Patterson (2020) and Setser (2012).
rule: In the Fourth Circuit a knowing and voluntary appeal waiver in a plea agreement is enforced, including against Booker claims, except for a narrow class such as sentences above the statutory maximum (Marin, Blick); and a supervised-release revocation sentence is reversed only if plainly unreasonable, though the court must address the defendant's nonfrivolous arguments (Crudup, Thompson, Slappy).

changes.case: United States v. Wessells; United States v. Marin (4th Cir.)
changes.what: An appeal waiver questioned in the Rule 11 colloquy is valid and enforceable if knowing and voluntary.

changes.case: United States v. Blick; United States v. Johnson; United States v. Rubbo (11th Cir.)
changes.what: A Booker claim concerns the manner of sentencing and is barred by a valid waiver; a sentence above the statutory maximum stays reviewable. Blick anchors 2005-09.
Revocation sentences are reviewed for whether they are plainly unreasonable, a more deferential inquiry than reasonableness; Crudup anchors 2015-19.
The court's reasons may be clear from context, but failure to address nonfrivolous arguments for leniency is not harmless if a lower sentence was conceivable.

changes.case: United States v. Webb; United States v. Padgett; United States v. Slappy (4th Cir.)
changes.what: A revocation sentence sanctions mainly the breach of trust; ignoring arguments for a within-policy-statement sentence is procedural error. Slappy anchors 2020-29.

phases.rule: enforcing appeal waivers in plea agreements and their narrow exceptions (Wessells, Marin, Blick, Johnson)
review of supervised-release revocation sentences: plainly unreasonable standard and the duty to explain (Crudup, Webb, Slappy)

name: Arizona severance: clear-and-convincing grounds, best interests (Kent K.)
description: Arizona termination of parental rights: a statutory ground by clear and convincing evidence and best interests by a preponderance (Kent K., 2005), with affirmance if reasonable evidence supports any one ground (Michael J., Jesus M.). Best interests mean a benefit from termination or a detriment from continuing, such as adoptability (Mary Lou C.); Demetrius L. (2016) made the child's stability the primary concern.

previous.name: Arizona termination of parental rights
previous.description: Arizona severance proceedings: statutory grounds proved by clear and convincing evidence and best interests by a preponderance (Kent K. v. Bobby M.), appellate deference to the juvenile court (Jesus M., Mary Lou C.), and Department of Child Safety reunification efforts.

history: Dominant rule: severance requires a statutory ground under A.R.S. § 8-533(B) proved by clear and convincing evidence and a best-interests finding by a preponderance (Kent K. v. Bobby M., 2005, applying Santosky). Michael J. (2000) and Jesus M. (2002) anchor the early slices: the appellate court affirms if reasonable evidence supports any one ground and defers to the juvenile court on credibility. How it changed: Jesus M., Mary Lou C. and Oscar O. (2002-2004) defined best interests as a benefit from termination or a detriment from continuing the relationship, which adoptability or an available adoptive placement can show. Demetrius L. (2016) enters in 2015-19 and anchors the partial 2025-29 slice: the test is disjunctive and the child's stability and security are the primary concern. Also: the duty to make diligent reunification efforts (Mary Ellen C., 1999) and its exception for abandonment (Toni W., 1999), and waiver of unraised objections to services or findings (Christy C., 2007; a 2014 ADES case).
rule: Arizona courts may terminate parental rights only on a statutory ground proved by clear and convincing evidence and a finding, by a preponderance, that termination is in the child's best interests, and the appellate court affirms if reasonable evidence supports any one ground.

changes.what: If reasonable evidence supports termination on any one statutory ground, the appellate court need not consider the others, and it defers to the juvenile court's credibility findings.

changes.case: Jesus M.; Mary Lou C.; Oscar O.
changes.what: Best interests require an affirmative benefit from termination or a detriment from continuing the relationship; adoptability or an adoptive placement can suffice.
Due process requires statutory grounds by clear and convincing evidence (Santosky) and best interests only by a preponderance.
At the best-interests stage the child's interest in stability and security is the primary concern, and the benefit or detriment test is disjunctive.

name: Rule 10b-5 elements: Hochfelder scienter, Basic reliance, Tellabs pleading
description: Private Rule 10b-5 actions: plaintiffs must be purchasers or sellers (Blue Chip Stamps, 1975) and prove scienter, not negligence (Hochfelder, 1976), a material misstatement (TSC, Basic) and reliance, presumed for omissions (Affiliated Ute) and under Basic (1988). After the PSLRA (1995), pleading scienter dominates: Silicon Graphics (1999) and Tellabs (2007, anchor from 2005-09) on the strong inference.

previous.description: Sub-cluster form of Rule 10b-5 doctrine: scienter (Hochfelder, Aaron, then Tellabs on pleading), materiality (TSC, Basic), deception (Santa Fe v. Green), insider trading (Chiarella), and private standing (Blue Chip Stamps, Huddleston).

history: Dominant rule: a private § 10(b)/Rule 10b-5 action requires a purchase or sale, a material misstatement or omission, scienter and reliance. How it changed: the 1960s slices rest on early implied-action cases (Kardon, Kohler, Capital Gains). Affiliated Ute (1972) excused proof of reliance in omission cases, and Bankers Life (1971) read 'in connection with' flexibly. Blue Chip Stamps (1975) limited standing to purchasers and sellers; Hochfelder (1976), the anchor from 1975-79 through 1985-89, required scienter and excluded negligence; Santa Fe v. Green (1977) excluded mere breaches of fiduciary duty; TSC (1976) defined materiality by the total mix. Basic v. Levinson (1988) anchors from 1990-94 through 2000-04, applying TSC materiality and a presumption of reliance. After the PSLRA (1995), the slices turn to pleading scienter: Silicon Graphics (9th Cir. 1999) required deliberate recklessness and held motive and opportunity insufficient, and Tellabs (2007), the 2005-09 anchor, set the comparative strong-inference test, alongside Dura v. Broudo (2005) on loss causation. The last slice splits into a Twombly/Iqbal pleading unit.
rule: A private Rule 10b-5 plaintiff must be a purchaser or seller and prove a material misstatement or omission made with scienter, on which it relied; negligence is not enough.

name: Inherent power to sanction bad faith and discipline lawyers (Chambers v. NASCO)
description: Federal courts' inherent power to sanction bad-faith litigation and to discipline lawyers. Chambers (1991), building on Roadway Express v. Piper (1980) and Link (1962), anchors both slices (1995-2004): inherent power reaches all bad-faith abuse. Rule 11 after 1993 requires the safe-harbor period (Ridder 1997). By 2000-04 bar discipline and reciprocal discipline (Theard, Selling, Ruffalo, Snyder) gain weight.
history: Dominant rule: federal courts possess inherent power, a limited power implied from the need to function, to sanction bad-faith conduct and to control admission to and discipline of their bar. Chambers v. NASCO (1991) anchors 1995-99 and 2000-04: that power extends to a full range of litigation abuses, including fee awards. It builds on Link (1962, dismissal for failure to prosecute), Roadway Express v. Piper (1980, fees against counsel in narrow circumstances), and old limits on federal courts' powers (Hudson and Goodwin 1812, Ex parte Robinson 1874, Ex parte Burr 1824, Eash 1985). Cooter & Gell (1990) supplies abuse-of-discretion review. How it changed: after the 1993 amendment, Ridder (6th Cir. 1997) treated Rule 11's 21-day safe harbor as an absolute requirement, and Cox (1998) approved dismissal for fraud. In 2000-04 attorney discipline grows: district courts' power to discipline and disbar (Theard 1957, Snyder 1985), reciprocal discipline subject to due process (Selling 1917), and fair notice of charges (Ruffalo 1968).
rule: Federal courts have inherent power, used with restraint and on a finding of bad faith, to sanction abusive litigation conduct and to regulate and discipline the attorneys who practise before them.

changes.what: Courts may assess fees against counsel for abusive litigation practices in narrowly defined circumstances, on a bad-faith finding.
Inherent power to sanction bad faith reaches the full range of litigation abuses and survives the Rules and statutes on sanctions.

changes.case: 1993 amendment of Fed. R. Civ. P. 11; Ridder v. City of Springfield (6th Cir. 1997)
changes.what: Rule 11 sanctions are unavailable unless the motion was served for the full 21-day safe-harbor period before filing.

name: Jurisdictional versus claim-processing rules; immigration judicial review
description: Whether statutory limits are jurisdictional: only if Congress clearly says so (Arbaugh 2006), so most deadlines are claim-processing rules open to tolling (Henderson 2011, Auburn 2013, Kwai Fun Wong 2015), though appeal deadlines stay jurisdictional (Bowles 2007, anchor 2015-19). In 2020-24 the unit turns to immigration review: Kucana (2010), Guerrero-Lasprilla and Nasrallah (2020), and reinstated-order finality (Luna-Garcia 2015, Guzman Chavez 2021).
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Jurisdictional vs claim-processing rules in immigration cases (2015-24)
previous.description: Supreme Court cases separating jurisdictional limits from claim-processing rules (Arbaugh, Bowles, Henderson v. Shinseki, Sebelius v. Auburn, Muchnick) and equitable tolling, applied to immigration review (Kucana, Nasrallah, Guerrero-Lasprilla) and filing deadlines.

history: Dominant rule: courts treat a statutory requirement as jurisdictional only if Congress clearly states it is. How it changed: in 2015-19 Bowles (2007) anchors after PLRA-exhaustion and related units merge in. Arbaugh (2006) set the clear-statement rule; Bowles kept statutory appeal deadlines jurisdictional; Muchnick (2010), Henderson v. Shinseki (2011), Sebelius v. Auburn (2013) and Kwai Fun Wong (2015) held other limits nonjurisdictional and tollable. Karingithi (9th Cir. 2019) held a defective notice to appear does not strip an immigration court of jurisdiction. In 2020-24 the anchor becomes Luna-Garcia (10th Cir. 2015) and the unit centres on review of removal orders: Kucana (2010) limits the discretionary-decision bar to statutory discretion; Guerrero-Lasprilla (2020) treats application of law to settled facts as a reviewable question of law; Nasrallah (2020) allows review of CAT orders; Guzman Chavez (2021) and Bhaktibhai-Patel (2022) fix when reinstated orders become final and when the 30-day petition period runs. It splits into standing and injunction units in 2025-29.
rule: A statutory limit is jurisdictional only if Congress clearly states that it is; otherwise filing deadlines and preconditions are claim-processing rules subject to waiver, forfeiture and equitable tolling, though statutory appeal deadlines remain jurisdictional (Bowles).

changes.what: Title VII's employee-numerosity requirement is an element of the claim, not jurisdictional; only clearly stated thresholds are jurisdictional.
The statutory time limit to file a civil notice of appeal is jurisdictional and admits no equitable exception.

changes.case: Reed Elsevier v. Muchnick; Henderson v. Shinseki; Sebelius v. Auburn Regional; United States v. Kwai Fun Wong
changes.what: Copyright registration, the veterans' 120-day appeal limit, the Medicare 180-day limit and the FTCA time limits are nonjurisdictional; Kwai Fun Wong allowed equitable tolling.
§ 1252(a)(2)(B)(ii) bars review only of decisions made discretionary by statute, not by regulation.

name: California SVPA commitments: civil, indeterminate terms upheld (Hubbart, McKee)
description: California SVPA commitments, a single 2010-14 slice: commitment is civil, not punitive (Hubbart, 1999), and indeterminate terms after Proposition 83 survive due process (McKee I, 2010, anchor). McKee I remanded equal protection; McKee II (2012) held SVPs may be treated differently because they are more dangerous, which McKnight and McDonald then applied. Also Ghilotti (2002) on dangerousness evaluations.
