history: Dominant rule: SVPA commitment is a civil measure, and indeterminate commitment of sexually violent predators is constitutional because the state may treat those reasonably found more dangerous differently from other civil committees. How it changed: the lineage appears only in 2010-14, merged from a 2005-09 unit on civil commitment of sexually violent predators. Hubbart (1999) held the Act civil and consistent with Hendricks; Ghilotti (2002), Williams (2003) and Cooley (2003) defined the dangerousness and volitional-control findings and the probable-cause hearing. McKee I (2010), the anchor, upheld the indeterminate term against due-process and ex post facto attack but sent the equal-protection claim back for an evidentiary hearing. McKee II (2012) held on remand that the state had justified the disparate treatment, and McKnight (2012) and McDonald (2013) treated that as dispositive. Also: stale evaluations (Landau, 2013). The unit then splits toward California sentencing reform in 2015-19.
rule: Commitment under California's Sexually Violent Predators Act is civil rather than punitive, and indeterminate commitment of persons found to be SVPs is consistent with due process and equal protection where they are shown to pose a greater danger than other civil committees.

changes.what: The SVPA is civil, not punitive, and its link between a diagnosed mental disorder and dangerousness satisfies Hendricks.

changes.case: People v. Superior Court (Ghilotti); People v. Williams; Cooley v. Superior Court
changes.what: Defined the likelihood of reoffending and the serious difficulty in controlling behaviour required by Crane, and the probable-cause standard for pretrial detention.
Upheld the indeterminate term against due-process and ex post facto challenges but remanded the equal-protection claim for the state to justify treating SVPs differently from other committees.
On remand the Court of Appeal held the state had shown SVPs pose a greater danger, defeating the equal-protection challenge; later cases (McKnight, McDonald) follow it.

name: Illinois two-prong plain-error test 1990-2029: Herron, Piatkowski, Sebby
description: How Illinois reviews forfeited error, 1990-2029: an issue is preserved only by a trial objection plus a written post-trial motion (Enoch, 1988; for sentences, Hillier, 2010); Herron (2005) set the two-prong plain-error test, rejecting Olano, and Piatkowski (2007) placed the prejudice burdens; Thompson (2010) held Rule 431(b) errors are not structural, and Sebby (2017) made them first-prong error in close cases. Krankel inquiries lead from 2020-24.

previous.name: Illinois criminal: forfeiture and plain error
previous.description: Illinois preservation rules (Enoch's contemporaneous objection plus written post-trial motion) and the two-prong plain-error doctrine for closely balanced evidence or structural error (Herron, Piatkowski, Thompson, Sebby), including jury-admonishment error under Rule 431(b) (Zehr).

history: Dominant rule: forfeiture and plain error in Illinois criminal appeals. Enoch (1988) anchors from 1990-94 to 2005-09: preservation requires both a contemporaneous objection and a written post-trial motion, and without a motion review is limited to constitutional issues raised at trial, sufficiency and plain error. Collins (1985, Jackson v. Virginia) and Albanese (1984, Strickland) lead early, with capital-era trial issues (Steidl, Childs, Enis). How it changed: Herron (2005) enters in 2005-09 and anchors 2010-14 and 2015-19: it kept a disjunctive two-prong test rather than Olano's. Piatkowski (2007) anchors from 2020-24: the first prong requires the error alone to threaten to tip the scales; the second presumes prejudice. Glasper (2009) and Thompson (2010), on Rule 431(b) juror admonitions under Zehr (1984), held such errors are not structural; Sebby (2017, reported 2018) enters in 2015-19 and treats them as first-prong error when evidence is close. Hillier (2010) extends Enoch to sentencing. Krankel (1984) inquiries into pro se ineffectiveness claims lead from 2020-24. Sufficiency cases (Cunningham, Siguenza-Brito) merge back in 2025-29.
rule: An Illinois defendant preserves an issue only by a contemporaneous objection and a written post-trial (or post-sentencing) motion; otherwise the reviewing court corrects only clear or obvious error that occurred where the evidence was closely balanced or that was so serious it affected the fairness of the trial.

changes.what: A trial court must inquire into a defendant's pro se post-trial claims of ineffective assistance and may appoint new counsel to investigate them.
Both a trial objection and a written post-trial motion are required to preserve an issue.

Under the first prong the defendant must show the error alone threatened to tip the scales; under the second prong prejudice is presumed.

changes.what: A Rule 431(b) (Zehr) admonition error is not structural and does not automatically satisfy the second prong without evidence of jury bias.
Sentencing issues are preserved only by objection at the hearing and a written motion to reconsider sentence.
A Rule 431(b) error in a case with closely balanced evidence is reversible first-prong plain error.

name: Ohio Civ.R. 12(B)(6) dismissal under notice pleading (Hanson, York) and writs
description: Ohio pleading-stage dismissal, 2015-29, anchored in every slice by Hanson (1992): a Civ.R. 12(B)(6) motion tests the complaint's sufficiency, taking its allegations as admitted (Kiger 1989), and brief, sketchy allegations suffice under notice pleading (York 1991). Applied to employer intentional torts (Mitchell 1988), emotional distress (Morrow 2009), public-policy discharge (Greeley 1990), and mandamus and procedendo actions against courts.
history: Dominant rule: State ex rel. Hanson (1992) anchors all three slices: a Civ.R. 12(B)(6) motion tests only the sufficiency of the complaint. The material allegations are taken as admitted with reasonable inferences for the plaintiff (Kiger, 1989), and under notice pleading brief and sketchy allegations of fact suffice (York, 1991). Courts apply it to claims whose elements are hard to plead: employer intentional tort requiring substantial certainty of injury (Mitchell, 1988), outrageous conduct for emotional distress (Morrow, 2009), attorneys' qualified immunity to third parties (LeRoy, 2007), wrongful discharge in violation of a clear statutory public policy (Greeley 1990; Dohme 2011), and OCSPA class claims (Volbers-Klarich 2010). Statutory text is applied as written (Perrysburg, 2004). How it changed: from 2020-24 original actions grow: mandamus and procedendo compel a court to proceed but not how to rule (Levin 1994, Sutula 1995, Nadel 1998), courts may take judicial notice in writ cases without converting the motion (O'Donnell 2021), and FitzGerald (2015) enters; standing to challenge statutes appears in 2025-29 (Cool 2022). O'Brien (1975) on enjoining libel recurs throughout.
rule: An Ohio Civ.R. 12(B)(6) motion tests only the sufficiency of the complaint: material allegations are taken as true with reasonable inferences for the plaintiff, brief and sketchy allegations suffice under notice pleading, and dismissal is proper only if the plaintiff can prove no set of facts entitling relief.

name: Timely notice of appeal as mandatory and jurisdictional (Browder, Griggs)
description: Federal appellate deadlines, 1985-94: a timely notice of appeal is mandatory and jurisdictional (Robinson 1960; Browder 1978, anchor of both slices). Griggs (1982) made a notice filed during a pending Rule 59 motion a nullity; Harcon Barge (1986) and Osterneck (1989) treat any motion attacking the judgment's correctness as Rule 59(e). Houston v. history: Dominant rule: the time limit for a notice of appeal is mandatory and jurisdictional (Robinson, 1960; Browder, 1978, the anchor in 1985-89 and 1990-94), and only a timely post-judgment motion that attacks the correctness of the judgment suspends it. How it changed: Mallis (1978) tied the start of the period to Rule 58's separate document. Griggs (1982) treated a notice filed while a Rule 59 motion pended as a nullity, and Acosta (1986) held a motion is disposed of only on entry of the order. Harcon Barge (5th Cir. en banc 1986) set a bright line that any motion questioning the judgment, filed within the Rule 59(e) time, is a Rule 59(e) motion; a Rule 60(b) motion does not affect finality (Peake, 1983, leading from 1990-94). Osterneck (1989) applied Rule 59(e) to prejudgment-interest motions. Houston v. Lack (1988) adopted the prison mailbox rule. The unique-circumstances doctrine of Harris Truck Lines (1962) and Thompson (1964) allowed narrow relief. Also: a busy lawyer is not excusable neglect (Baker v. Raulie, 1989), and Rule 60(b) relief limits (Ackermann, Klapprott, Liljeberg).

description: Capital Eighth Amendment law: Gregg (1976) upheld guided discretion and Woodson (1976) barred mandatory death, Zant (1983) required narrowing, and Lockett (1978) and Eddings (1982) let the sentencer weigh any mitigation; Penry (1989) required a vehicle for it. previous.name: Double jeopardy: mistrials and retrial
previous.description: When the Double Jeopardy Clause bars a second trial: manifest necessity for mistrials (Perez, Arizona v. Washington, Somerville, Downum), defense-requested mistrials (Dinitz, Jorn), retrial after reversal for insufficiency (Burks) and government appeals (Scott).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: retrial after a mistrial without the defendant's consent requires manifest necessity, and acquittals are final. How it changed: Perez (1824) anchors 1960-64 and Wade v. Hunter (1949) 1965-69, with Gori (1961) allowing retrial after a mistrial in the defendant's interest and Downum (1963) barring it where the prosecution proceeded without its witness. Jorn (1971) enters and anchors 1970-84, barring retrial after an abrupt mistrial; Somerville (1973) allowed retrial for an incurable indictment defect. Dinitz (1976) and Arizona v. Washington (1978) enter in 1975-79, on defense-requested mistrials and deference for misconduct-based ones. Scott, Martin Linen and Wilson join in 1980-84 on government appeals. Burks (1978) anchors 1985-89 with Bullington (1981) and Rumsey (1984) applying jeopardy to capital sentencing and Richardson (1984) to hung juries. Arizona v. Washington anchors 1990-99 with Oregon v. Kennedy's goading test. Martin Linen anchors 2010-14 as Smith v. Massachusetts (2005) and Evans (2013) stress acquittal finality.
rule: Once jeopardy attaches, a mistrial declared without the defendant's consent bars retrial unless there was manifest necessity, to which deference depends on the reason (Perez, Jorn, Arizona v. Washington); a defense-requested mistrial permits retrial unless the prosecution intended to goad the motion (Dinitz, Oregon v. Kennedy); and an acquittal, or a reversal for insufficient evidence, bars retrial (Ball, Burks).

changes.what: A deadlocked jury is manifest necessity; trial courts have broad discretion to discharge a jury.

changes.case: Wade v. Hunter; Gori v. United States; Downum v. United States
changes.what: Retrial allowed after mistrials serving the ends of public justice, but not where the prosecution gambled on proceeding without a witness; jeopardy attaches when the jury is sworn.
An abrupt sua sponte mistrial without considering alternatives barred retrial; the judge's label does not control. Anchors 1970-84.

changes.case: United States v. Dinitz; Arizona v. Washington
changes.what: Defense-requested mistrials generally permit retrial; mistrials for prosecutorial or defense misconduct get great deference to the trial judge.

changes.case: United States v. Martin Linen Supply; Burks v. United States; United States v. Scott
changes.what: A judge's resolution of factual elements is an unappealable acquittal, an insufficiency reversal bars retrial, but a dismissal unrelated to guilt may be appealed.

changes.case: Smith v. Massachusetts; Evans v. Michigan

name: Patent claim construction (Phillips), indefiniteness and damages apportionment
description: Federal Circuit claim meaning, definiteness and damages, 2020-24 only, anchored by Phillips (2005): ordinary meaning in light of the specification, no importing of embodiments (Vitronics 1996; Innova 2004; Thorner 2012), prosecution history informs meaning (Personalized Media 2020). Nautilus (2014) set reasonable-certainty indefiniteness; Lucent (2009), VirnetX (2014) and Ericsson (2014) require damages apportionment; Halo (2016) frees enhanced damages.
history: Dominant rule: patent claims mean what they would to a skilled artisan reading them in light of the specification and prosecution history (Phillips, en banc 2005, anchor of the only slice, 2020-24). The lineage forms from the obviousness/PTAB unit and a related unit and splits off in 2025-29. How it developed: Markman (1996) assigned construction to judges, and Vitronics (1996) put intrinsic evidence first; Innova (2004) and Liebel-Flarsheim (2004) refused to confine claims to disclosed embodiments; Thorner (2012) limited departures from ordinary meaning to lexicography or disavowal; Columbia v. Symantec (2016) and Personalized Media (2020) read terms through the specification and prosecution history; World Class Technology (2014) on claim differentiation. Nautilus (2014) replaced the insolubly-ambiguous test with reasonable certainty, applied in Teva (2015) and Sonix (2017). Damages: Lucent (2009), i4i (2010), VirnetX (2014), Ericsson (2014) and CSIRO (2015) require apportionment and gatekeeping of expert theories; Halo (2016) returned enhanced damages to district-court discretion.
rule: Patent claims carry their ordinary meaning to a skilled artisan read in light of the specification and prosecution history, absent lexicography or disavowal (Phillips; Thorner); claims are indefinite unless they inform skilled artisans of their scope with reasonable certainty (Nautilus); damages must be apportioned to the patented features (VirnetX).

changes.case: Markman v. Westview Instruments; Vitronics v. Conceptronic
changes.what: Claim construction is for the court, reading claims in view of the specification; intrinsic evidence controls and a construction excluding the preferred embodiment is rarely correct.
Claims are read in light of the specification, but importing limitations from the written description is a cardinal sin; extrinsic evidence is secondary.

changes.case: Lucent v. Gateway; VirnetX v. Cisco; Ericsson v. D-Link
changes.what: Damages may not rest on the entire market value of multi-feature products; experts must apportion value to the patented features, including for standard-essential patents.
Only lexicography or clear disavowal departs from a term's plain and ordinary meaning.
A claim is indefinite unless, read with the specification and prosecution history, it informs skilled artisans of its scope with reasonable certainty.

name: Waiving counsel and self-representation: Zerbst, Faretta, McKaskle (1980-99)
description: Waiver of counsel and self-representation, 1980-99: counsel may be waived only knowingly and intelligently (Zerbst, 1938), and a competent defendant may conduct his own defence (Faretta, 1975, anchor 1980-84), limited by McKaskle (1984) on standby counsel. Gideon (1963) anchors 1985-99 as Argersinger and Scott tie the right to imprisonment; Custis (1994) confines collateral attacks on priors to Gideon claims. Competency and plea cases join later.

previous.name: Right to counsel: indigents, misdemeanors and waiver (1980-99)
previous.description: Gideon, Powell and Zerbst on appointed counsel and waiver, Argersinger and Scott on actual-imprisonment misdemeanors, Faretta self-representation and Custis on collateral attack of uncounseled priors.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session subagents, from cocite evidence; second pass differentiated near-duplicates)

history: Dominant rule: a defendant facing imprisonment has a right to counsel, applied to the states by Gideon (1963), that he may waive only by an intentional relinquishment of a known right (Zerbst, 1938), shown on the record (Gillies, 1948; Adams, 1943). A competent defendant may knowingly waive counsel and conduct his own defence (Faretta, 1975). How it changed: Faretta anchors 1980-84, with circuit cases on the waiver colloquy (Welty, 1982). Gideon anchors 1985-89 through 1995-99 as the founding cases join: Powell (1932), Tumey (1927) on a biased judge, Argersinger (1972) and Scott (1979) on misdemeanours, and Baldasar (1980). In 1990-94 competency to stand trial and waive (Dusky, 1960; Pate, 1966; Drope, 1975) and indigents' appellate rights (Griffin, 1956; Douglas, 1963) enter. McKaskle (1984) limited Faretta by allowing standby counsel, and Morris v. Slappy (1983) denied a right to a meaningful relationship with counsel. Custis (1994) allowed only Gideon-based collateral attacks on prior convictions at sentencing. In 1995-99 the guilty-plea unit merges in (Boykin, Alford, Brady), and in 2000-04 the unit splits.
rule: An accused facing imprisonment is entitled to counsel unless he knowingly and intelligently waives it (Gideon, Zerbst, Argersinger), and a competent defendant who validly waives counsel may represent himself, subject to standby counsel that does not destroy his control (Faretta, McKaskle).

changes.case: Powell v. Alabama; Johnson v. Zerbst; Griffin v. Illinois; Douglas v. California; Gideon v. Wainwright
changes.what: Due process and Sixth Amendment counsel rights, waiver as intentional relinquishment, and equal access for indigents on appeal. Gideon anchors 1985-99.

changes.what: Counsel required whenever imprisonment is imposed, but not when it is only authorised.

name: Federal habeas c. 1980: Sykes cause and prejudice, total exhaustion, conflicts
description: Federal habeas doctrine around 1980-84: Wainwright v. Sykes (1977) and Engle v. Isaac (1982) replaced Fay v. Noia's (1963) deliberate-bypass test with cause and prejudice for state defaults, and Frady (1982) applied it to § 2255; Rose v. Lundy (1982) required total exhaustion; Sumner v. Mata (1981) presumed state findings correct. Holloway (1978) and Cuyler v. Sullivan (1980), the anchor, set the conflict-of-interest rules.

previous.name: Federal habeas procedure and conflicts of counsel (c. 1980)
previous.description: Habeas doctrine around 1980: procedural default under Wainwright v. Sykes and Engle v. Isaac (replacing Fay v. Noia), deference to state findings (Sumner v. Mata), total exhaustion (Rose v. Lundy), and conflicts of interest (Holloway, Cuyler v. Sullivan).

history: Dominant rule: the gatekeeping rules for federal habeas review of state convictions, in a single 1980-84 slice anchored by Cuyler v. Sullivan (1980). How it changed: Fay v. Noia (1963) had allowed review of defaulted claims unless the prisoner deliberately bypassed state procedures, and Townsend v. Sain (1963) required evidentiary hearings in defined cases. Wainwright v. Sykes (1977), the heaviest case, limited Fay and required cause and prejudice for a default under a contemporaneous-objection rule; Engle v. Isaac (1982) held that a claim's novelty is not cause when other lawyers had perceived it, and Frady (1982) applied the same standard to § 2255. Sumner v. Mata (1981) extended the § 2254(d) presumption of correctness to state appellate findings, and Rose v. Lundy (1982) required dismissal of mixed petitions. On counsel, McMann (1970) and Herring (5th Cir. 1974) frame effective assistance; Holloway (1978) presumed prejudice from joint representation over objection, and Cuyler (1980) required an actual conflict adversely affecting performance. The Fifth Circuit's Washington v. Strickland (1982) appears just before the Supreme Court's 1984 decision.
rule: A state prisoner who defaulted a federal claim under a state procedural rule may obtain federal habeas review only by showing cause and actual prejudice (Wainwright v. Sykes, Engle), mixed petitions must be dismissed (Rose v. Lundy), state findings are presumed correct (Sumner v. Mata), and an actual conflict of interest that adversely affected counsel's performance violates the Sixth Amendment without further proof of prejudice (Cuyler v. Sullivan).

changes.case: Fay v. Noia; Townsend v. Sain
changes.what: Fay allowed habeas review of defaulted claims absent deliberate bypass, and Townsend set when an evidentiary hearing is required.

changes.case: Wainwright v. Sykes; Engle v. Isaac; United States v. Frady
changes.what: Cause and prejudice replaced Fay's deliberate-bypass test for defaults under contemporaneous-objection rules; a claim's novelty is not cause if others had raised it, and the standard also governs § 2255 motions.

description: ERISA benefit and fiduciary litigation, anchored by Firestone v. Bruch (1989) in every slice: de novo review unless the plan grants discretion. history: Dominant rule: under Firestone v. Bruch (1989), the anchor in every slice, benefit denials are reviewed de novo unless the plan confers discretion, and a conflict of interest is weighed in deferential review. How it changed: in 1990-94 the group carries plan-amendment and estoppel cases (Nachwalter 1986 barring estoppel to modify written terms, Hozier 1990, Musto 1988). In 1995-2004 the circuits split on conflicts: Brown (11th Cir. 1990), Doe (4th Cir. 1993), Atwood (9th Cir. 1995), Winters (1995), Woo (1998), Vega (en banc 1999) and Pinto; Wilkins (1998) confined review to the administrative record. Nord (2003) rejected a treating-physician rule. name: Eighth Circuit early post-Booker review: proportional justification for variances
description: Eighth Circuit sentencing review right after Booker, a single 2005-09 slice anchored by Haack (2005): within-range sentences presumed reasonable (Lincoln 2005), and large departures or variances needing proportionally compelling reasons, so extraordinary reductions were reversed (Dalton, Saenz 2005; Claiborne, McMannus, Gall 2006). The Supreme Court reversed the circuit's Gall in 2007, rejecting the proportionality approach.
history: Dominant rule: how the Eighth Circuit reviewed sentences for reasonableness in the two years after Booker made the Guidelines advisory. Haack (2005) anchors the lineage's only slice, 2005-09, which came from the Guidelines-departure lineage. How it changed: Haack adopted Crosby's account of post-Booker sentencing and treated a clear error of judgment as an abuse of discretion; Mashek (2005) kept the old standards for Guidelines application and required remand for misapplication; Lincoln (2005) presumed within-range sentences reasonable; and Long Soldier (2005) asked whether § 3553(a) supported the sentence. The circuit then policed downward departures and variances by their size: Dalton (2005) and Saenz (2005) held 68-75% reductions unreasonable, and McMannus, Claiborne, Bryant and Gall (2006) required more compelling justification the farther the sentence strayed, reversing probation for a drug offender. The Supreme Court reversed Gall in 2007 and vacated Claiborne, rejecting that proportionality rule. Also: Wade (1992) on substantial-assistance motions, Williams (2007) on mandatory minimums, Lazenby (2006) on co-defendant disparity, and Hadash (2005) on harmless sentencing error.
rule: In the Eighth Circuit's first post-Booker years, a within-range sentence was presumed reasonable (Lincoln), and the farther a sentence varied or departed from the range the more compelling the § 3553(a) justification had to be (McMannus), so extraordinary reductions such as probation for a drug offense were reversed (Dalton, Saenz, Claiborne, Gall) until Gall v. United States (2007) rejected that approach.

changes.what: A court may review the government's refusal to file a substantial-assistance motion only for an unconstitutional motive.

changes.what: Post-Booker review: Guidelines application keeps its standards, a sentence is an abuse of discretion if it reflects a clear error of judgment, and within-range sentences are presumptively reasonable. Haack anchors the slice.

history: Dominant rule: Arceo (1996), which enters and anchors 1995-99 and again 2005-09, holds that when the evidence shows separate acts each of which could support the charge, the jury must be told it must agree unanimously on the same act, unless the prosecution elects the act by the close of its case-in-chief; omitting the instruction was plain error. How it changed: the 1990-94 slice is a small civil remnant anchored by Amfac (1992). In 1995-99, Holbron (1995) read HRPP Rule 52(a) as requiring harmlessness beyond a reasonable doubt and overruled Tagaro, Gaylord (1995) set sentencing and restitution limits under HRS § 706-606, Toyomura (1995) addressed police lay opinion on intoxication, and Higa (1995) rejected a double-jeopardy bar after license revocation. Kelekolio (1993) anchors 2000-04 on police deception and confessions, with Klinge (2000) on alternative means. Also: from 2010-14 the line drifts away from criminal law into small slices of Hawaii public-trust water law, contested-case standing and agency review (In re Water Use Permit Applications 2000, Kaho'ohanohano 2007, Mauna Kea 2015, Flores 2018), which anchor through 2025-29.

history: Dominant rule: due process limits the use of prior official acts against a defendant. A deportation order used to prove a § 1326 offense is open to collateral attack where the hearing was fundamentally unfair and deprived the alien of judicial review, and the government may not convict for conduct an official affirmatively said was lawful. In 1995-99 illegal-reentry cases merge in and Mendoza-Lopez (1987) anchors: review of the deportation is required where waiver of appeal was not knowing. Proa-Tovar (en banc 1992), Encarnacion-Galvez (1992), Meraz-Valeta (1994) and Leon-Leon (1994) made prejudice an element the defendant must prove, and Trevino-Martinez (1996) held § 1326 a general-intent crime. Congress codified the collateral-attack limits in § 1326(d) in 1996. The unit splits toward immigration habeas review in 2000-04.

history: Dominant rule: since Department of Ecology v. Campbell & Gwinn (2002), Washington courts find plain meaning in the statute's words read with the whole act and related statutes. If that reading is unambiguous they stop; otherwise they may use legislative history, canons and the rule of lenity. Campbell & Gwinn anchors or co-leads every slice from 2000-04 to 2020-24. How it changed: the earlier text-in-isolation approach gives way to this contextual plain-meaning test in 2000-04, when Cockle (2001) on ambiguous terms in the workers' compensation wage statute and Davis (1999) on ejusdem generis lead alongside it. In 2005-09 J.P. (2003), Jacobs (2005, lenity), Roggenkamp (2005, noscitur a sociis) and Berrocal (2005) apply it. From 2010-14 Armendariz (2007), Engel (2009), Lake (2010) and Gonzalez (2010) lead, and from 2015-19 administrative-review cases join (Postema, 2000; Port of Seattle, 2004). Ervin (2010) on legislative acquiescence and Jametsky (2014) lead 2020-24. No change to the core rule appears.
rule: Washington courts derive a statute's plain meaning from its text read in the context of the whole statute and related statutes; if that meaning is unambiguous the inquiry ends, and only if ambiguity remains do courts turn to legislative history, canons and, in criminal cases, the rule of lenity.

history: Dominant rule: under Firestone v. Moon (2005), on jury selection and counsel: death-qualification by questionnaire (Avila 2006), Wheeler/Batson review (Guerra 2006), substitution of counsel (Barnett 1998) and self-representation (Lewis 2006); also consent searches after illegality (Boyer 2006) and premeditation (Stitely 2005). It splits from and rejoins the main capital lineage.
history: Dominant rule: the California Supreme Court's settled answers to recurring claims in capital appeals, with deference to the trial court. The lineage exists only in 2005-09, anchored by People v. Moon (2005), formed when two 2000-04 capital units merge; it rejoins the main California capital-appeals lineage in 2010-14. How it developed: no rule changes within the single slice. The leading cases concern jury selection (Avila 2006 allows excusal for cause on questionnaire answers; Guerra 2006 limits comparative juror analysis where no prima facie case was found), counsel (Barnett 1998 requires a good-faith effort before a conflict is irreconcilable; Lewis 2006 on self-representation asserted to plant error; Rogers 2006 on competency hearings under Penal Code § 1368), evidence (Boyer 2006 on consent searches after a Fourth Amendment violation; Roldan 2005 on motive; Panah 2005 on unobjected hearsay; Morrison 2004 on offers of proof), sufficiency of premeditation (Stitely 2005), lesser included offenses under the accusatory-pleading test (Moon), burglary (Hughes 2002), and the penalty factors upheld in Tuilaepa (1994).
rule: On automatic appeal the California Supreme Court defers to trial-court rulings on juror exclusion, Wheeler/Batson challenges, substitution of counsel and self-representation, and rejects standard Eighth Amendment attacks on the penalty statute (Tuilaepa).

changes.what: California's penalty factors, including the circumstances of the crime, are not unconstitutionally vague.
No irreconcilable conflict requiring new counsel exists where the defendant has not made a sustained, good-faith effort to work out disagreements.
Jurors may be excused for cause on written questionnaire answers alone when those answers show views that would substantially impair their duties.
Comparative juror analysis is problematic where the trial court found no prima facie case and the prosecutor gave no reasons.

name: Criminal contempt and the jury right: Mayberry, Bloom, Baldwin's six-month line
description: Criminal contempt and the jury right, 1970-89: a judge embroiled with the contemnor may not try the contempt (Mayberry, 1971, anchor 1970-74), post-trial contempt needs notice and a hearing (Taylor, 1974, anchor 1975-79), and serious contempt needs a jury (Bloom, 1968; Codispoti, 1974). From 1980-84 Baldwin's (1970) six-month line anchors, with jury size and unanimity (Williams, Apodaca, Ballew, Burch) and petty offenses.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, round 2 after the lineage re-link)

previous.name: Contempt: civil versus criminal
previous.description: Distinguishing civil and criminal contempt (Gompers, Shillitani, Bagwell), jury rights for serious criminal contempt (Cheff, Bloom, Duncan, Baldwin), summary contempt and the appearance of justice (Cooke, Mayberry, Taylor v. Hayes), and obeying orders until set aside (United Mine Workers).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: the procedural protections owed in criminal contempt and, increasingly, the scope of the jury right. How it changed: Mayberry (1971) anchors 1970-74, requiring another judge where the trial judge was embroiled, with Cooke (1925), Oliver (1948), Offutt (1954) and Sacher (1952) on summary contempt and bias. Taylor v. Hayes (1974) anchors 1975-79: contempt adjudicated after trial requires notice and a hearing; Bloom (1968) treats serious contempt as a crime for jury purposes and Codispoti (1974) aggregates contempt sentences; Tumey and Murchison govern biased adjudicators. In 1980-84 Baldwin (1970) anchors, and the cases turn to the jury right generally, with Williams (1970), Apodaca (1972), Ballew (1978) and Burch (1979) on jury size and unanimity. In 1985-89 Baldwin leads older petty-offense cases (Callan, 1888; Clawans, 1937; Colts, 1930; Schick, 1904) and state cases applying them. The rest of the lineage splits off in 1985-89, partly toward Batson.
rule: Serious criminal contempt, like any offense punishable by more than six months, carries the right to a jury (Bloom; Baldwin), and a judge personally embroiled with the contemnor must not adjudicate the contempt, which otherwise requires notice and a hearing (Mayberry; Taylor).

changes.case: Cooke v. United States; In re Oliver; Offutt v. United States; Sacher v. United States; In re Murchison
changes.what: Contempt outside the court's presence needs notice and a hearing; a judge may defer summary contempt to the end of trial, but one personally embroiled should yield to another judge.

changes.case: Duncan v. Louisiana; Bloom v. Illinois; Baldwin v. New York
changes.what: Jury trial binds the states; serious criminal contempt is a crime for jury purposes; any offense punishable by more than six months is serious.
Due process requires a different judge to try contempt arising from a defendant's insults that embroiled the trial judge.

changes.case: Taylor v. Hayes; Codispoti v. Pennsylvania
changes.what: Post-trial contempt adjudication needs notice and an opportunity to be heard; aggregated contempt sentences over six months require a jury.

changes.case: Williams v. Florida; Apodaca v. Oregon; Ballew v. Georgia; Burch v. Louisiana
changes.what: Six-person juries and nonunanimous twelve-person verdicts allowed; five-person juries and nonunanimous six-person verdicts not.

round1.name: Contempt: civil versus criminal (Gompers, Bagwell) and jury rights (Bloom)
round1.description: Contempt: civil contempt coerces or compensates and criminal contempt punishes (Gompers, 1911; Shillitani, 1966). Bloom (1968) required juries for serious criminal contempt, with Baldwin's (1970) six-month line, and Mayberry, Taylor and Codispoti (1971-74) limited summary contempt by embroiled judges. Hicks (1988) looked to the character of relief and Bagwell (1994) treated large noncompensatory fines as criminal; Bagwell anchors from 1995.
round1.history: Dominant rule: the civil-criminal line in contempt and the procedural protections that follow from it. How it changed: in 1970-74 Cheff (1966) anchors as Bloom (1968) holds serious criminal contempt is a crime for jury-trial purposes and Duncan and Baldwin (1968-70) set the six-month line. Taylor v. Hayes (1974) anchors 1975-79, with Mayberry (1971) on judges embroiled with the contemnor, Codispoti (1974) on aggregated sentences, and Tumey, Murchison and Ward on biased adjudicators; Muniz (1975) allowed a $10,000 union fine without a jury. Baldwin anchors 1980-84, as state courts follow Codispoti. In 1985-89 United Mine Workers (1947) anchors: orders must be obeyed until set aside, and Shillitani (1966) and Hicks (1988) look to whether the sanction is purgeable. Gompers (1911) anchors 1990-94, with Young (1987) on disinterested prosecutors and Hudson and Goodwin (1812) on inherent power. Bagwell (1994) anchors from 1995-99: noncompensatory fines for out-of-court violations of complex injunctions are criminal. In 2005-09 juvenile contempt cases (M.B.) and in 2010-14 FTC civil-contempt cases (McComb) enter.
round1.rule: Contempt is civil if it coerces compliance the contemnor can purge or compensates the complainant, and criminal if it punishes a completed act (Gompers, Hicks, Bagwell); criminal contempt carries criminal procedural protections, including a jury trial when the punishment imposed or authorized exceeds six months (Bloom, Baldwin), and an order must be obeyed until set aside (United Mine Workers).

changes.case: Gompers v. Buck's Stove; Cooke v. United States; United States v. United Mine Workers
changes.what: Civil contempt coerces, criminal contempt vindicates the court's authority; summary punishment is limited to contempt in the court's presence; and orders must be obeyed while challenged.

changes.case: Cheff v. Schnackenberg; Shillitani; Bloom v. Illinois; Duncan v. Louisiana; Baldwin v. New York
changes.what: Serious criminal contempt requires a jury trial, with seriousness measured by a six-month line, while coercive confinement with release on compliance is civil; Cheff anchors 1970-74.

changes.case: Mayberry v. Pennsylvania; Taylor v. Hayes; Codispoti v. Pennsylvania
changes.what: A judge personally embroiled with a contemnor must not try the post-trial contempt, notice and a hearing are required when punishment is deferred, and aggregated post-trial sentences over six months need a jury; Taylor anchors 1975-79.

changes.case: Young v. United States ex rel. Vuitton; Hicks v. Feiock
changes.what: Courts should appoint a disinterested prosecutor for criminal contempt, and the character of the relief, not the label, decides whether contempt is civil or criminal.

name: Ninth Circuit reasons to reject medical opinions and testimony (Magallanes to Woods)
description: Ninth Circuit rules on what reasons an ALJ must give, 1985-2029: specific-and-legitimate or clear-and-convincing reasons to reject treating and examining opinions (Magallanes 1989, Lester 1995), clear-and-convincing reasons to reject symptom testimony (Bunnell, Smolen), harmless error (Molina 2012) and credit-as-true remands (Garrison 2014). Woods v. Kijakazi (2022) held the 2017 regulations displace the treating-physician hierarchy.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Social Security disability review (Ninth Circuit)
previous.description: Ninth Circuit review of disability denials: substantial evidence and harmless error (Molina), weighing treating-physician opinions and the specific-and-legitimate standard (Lester, Bayliss), rejecting claimant testimony (Smolen, Tommasetti), and credit-as-true remands (Garrison).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: courts affirm a Social Security denial supported by substantial evidence, but the ALJ must give legally sufficient reasons for rejecting medical opinions and the claimant's testimony. How it changed: Baker (1984) anchors 1985-89 on the zone of choice under substantial-evidence review. Magallanes (1989) anchors 1990-99: treating opinions are not conclusive and may be rejected for specific, legitimate reasons; Bunnell (en banc 1991) barred discrediting pain testimony solely for lack of objective support. Lester (1995) anchors 2000-14, setting the opinion hierarchy and the credit-as-true rule, with Smolen (1996) on testimony and lay witnesses. Harmless error grew through Batson (2004) and Carmickle (2008), and Molina (2012) anchors from 2015-19. Garrison (2014) leads on credit-as-true remands. The 2017 regulations, applied in Woods v. Kijakazi (2022), replaced the treating-physician hierarchy for new claims; Woods anchors the partial 2025-29 slice.
rule: A Social Security denial is upheld if supported by substantial evidence and free of harmful legal error; in the Ninth Circuit an ALJ needed clear and convincing reasons to reject an uncontradicted treating or examining opinion (specific and legitimate if contradicted) and clear and convincing reasons to reject a claimant's symptom testimony, with errors excused if harmless.

changes.case: Magallanes v. Bowen; Bunnell v. Sullivan (en banc)
changes.what: A treating opinion is not conclusive but can be rejected only for specific, legitimate reasons; symptom testimony cannot be discredited solely for lack of objective medical support.

changes.case: Lester v. Chater; Smolen v. Chater
changes.what: Hierarchy of treating, examining and nonexamining opinions with clear-and-convincing and specific-and-legitimate standards; credit-as-true remand where crediting the evidence compels a disability finding.
Harmless-error review: an ALJ's error is harmless if other valid reasons support the decision or the error is inconsequential to the disability determination.
Credit-as-true remand for benefits is appropriate where its conditions are met, and symptoms that wax and wane do not justify rejecting testimony.
For claims filed on or after March 27, 2017, the revised regulations displace the treating-physician hierarchy and the specific-and-legitimate standard in favor of supportability and consistency.

before_differentiation.description: Ninth Circuit review of disability denials for substantial evidence and harmful error: specific-and-legitimate or clear-and-convincing reasons to reject treating and examining opinions (Magallanes 1989, Lester 1995), clear-and-convincing reasons to reject symptom testimony (Bunnell, Smolen), harmless error (Molina 2012) and credit-as-true remands (Garrison 2014). name: General procedural due process: Roth entitlements and Mathews balancing
description: Procedural due process outside the prison and creditor settings, 1970-2009: property requires a legitimate claim of entitlement (Roth, Perry 1972; Roth anchors 1975-99), not reputation alone (Paul 1976); fixed prior-hearing rules (Goldberg, Fuentes; Sniadach anchors 1970-74) gave way to Mathews (1976) balancing; Loudermill (1985) set pretermination process. Gagnon (1973) on revocations anchors 2000-04 and Mullane notice 2005-09.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Procedural due process: property, liberty and hearings
previous.description: What process is due before government deprives a protected interest: property interests in benefits and jobs (Goldberg, Roth, Perry, Loudermill, Bishop), the Mathews v. Eldridge balancing test, notice (Mullane), parole revocation (Morrissey), prejudgment remedies (Sniadach, Fuentes) and reputation (Paul v. Davis).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: whether a protected property or liberty interest exists, and what hearing is owed. Roth (1972) anchors 1975-99: property needs a legitimate claim of entitlement, and Perry (1972) found one in an implied tenure policy. How it changed: in 1970-74 the anchor is Sniadach (1969), with Goldberg (1970), Burson (1971) and Fuentes (1972) requiring prior notice and hearing. Mitchell v. W.T. Grant (1974) upheld judicially supervised ex parte sequestration, Di-Chem (1975) struck a garnishment law, and Mathews (1976) replaced fixed rules with balancing, allowing benefits to end before an evidentiary hearing. Paul (1976) required more than reputational harm, Bishop (1976) looked to state law for job interests, and Codd (1977) limited the stigma remedy to a chance to refute. Loudermill (1985) required pretermination process; Morrissey and Gagnon (1972-73) govern revocations and anchor 2000-04. Doehr (1991), Good (1993) and Homar (1997) apply Mathews. In 2005-09 the anchor is Mullane (1950), with Parratt, Hudson, Daniels and Zinermon on post-deprivation remedies.
rule: Due process protects property interests that rest on a legitimate claim of entitlement under state law or mutual understanding (Roth, Perry), not mere reputation (Paul), and the timing and form of the hearing owed are fixed by Mathews balancing rather than a uniform pre-deprivation evidentiary hearing.

changes.case: Sniadach; Goldberg v. Kelly; Fuentes v. Shevin
changes.what: Notice and a hearing are required before wages are garnished, welfare benefits terminated or goods replevied; Sniadach anchors 1970-74.

changes.case: Board of Regents v. Roth; Perry v. Sindermann
changes.what: Property interests require a legitimate claim of entitlement; a fixed-term teacher has none, but an implied tenure understanding can create one; Roth anchors 1975-99.

changes.case: Mitchell v. W.T. Grant; North Georgia Finishing v. Di-Chem
changes.what: Ex parte sequestration under judicial supervision with a prompt post-seizure hearing is valid, while a garnishment scheme without such safeguards is not.

changes.case: Mathews v. Eldridge; Paul v. Davis; Bishop v. Wood
changes.what: Disability benefits may end without a prior evidentiary hearing under three-factor balancing; reputation alone is not liberty; at-will status under state law defeats a property claim.

changes.case: Cleveland Board of Education v. Loudermill
changes.what: For-cause public employees are owed a pretermination opportunity to respond; the procedures are a matter of federal law, not the statute creating the interest.

changes.case: Connecticut v. Doehr; James Daniel Good Real Property; Gilbert v. Homar
changes.what: Mathews balancing extended to prejudgment attachment and civil forfeiture of real property (prior notice required) and allowed suspension without a prior hearing.

before_differentiation.description: Procedural due process: property interests need a legitimate entitlement (Roth, Perry, 1972), not reputation alone (Paul, 1976). Sniadach, Goldberg and Fuentes (1969-72) required prior hearings; Mitchell (1974) and Mathews (1976) moved to flexible balancing. Loudermill (1985) set pretermination process for for-cause employees; Morrissey and Gagnon govern revocations; from 2005-09 Mullane notice and Parratt post-deprivation remedies lead.

name: Indiana sentence review: Anglemyer abuse of discretion and Rule 7(B) (Cardwell)
description: Indiana appellate review of sentences under the advisory scheme: within-range sentences are reviewed for abuse of discretion in the sentencing statement, not the weighing of factors (Anglemyer 2007, anchor in most slices); Rule 7(B) revision for inappropriateness puts the burden on the defendant (Childress 2006) and looks at the aggregate sentence (Cardwell 2008, anchoring 2020-24). Stephenson (2015) requires compelling positive evidence.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, round 2 after the lineage re-link)

previous.name: Indiana criminal: sentence review and waiver
previous.description: Indiana appellate review of sentences: abuse of discretion within the statutory range (Anglemyer), Appellate Rule 7(b) revision for inappropriate sentences (Cardwell, Childress), and waiver of arguments lacking cogent reasoning or citation.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: Indiana appellate courts review sentences in two separate ways. Within the statutory range, the trial court's sentencing statement is reviewed for abuse of discretion, such as relying on improper aggravators or omitting clearly supported mitigators (Anglemyer, 2007, clarified on rehearing). Independently, Appellate Rule 7(B) lets the court revise a sentence the defendant shows is inappropriate given the offense and the offender. How it changed: Childress (2006) assigned the 7(B) burden to the defendant. Anglemyer anchors 2005-09 through 2015-19 and again in the partial 2025-29 slice, ending review of the relative weight of factors. Cardwell (2008) told courts to look at the forest, the aggregate sentence, and anchors 2020-24; King (2008) separated the two claims and Davidson (2010) allowed review of all penal consequences. Stephenson (2015) demanded compelling positive evidence and leads from 2015-19. Also: Cotto (2005) on arrest records as character evidence, waiver without cogent argument (Cooper 2006), and Conley (2012) on juvenile life without parole.
rule: Indiana appellate courts review a within-range sentence for abuse of discretion in the sentencing statement, and separately may revise it under Appellate Rule 7(B) if the defendant shows it is inappropriate in light of the offense and the offender.

changes.what: The defendant bears the burden of persuading the court that the sentence is inappropriate under Rule 7(B).
Within-range sentences are reviewed only for abuse of discretion in the sentencing statement, such as improper aggravators or omitted clearly supported mitigators, not the relative weight of factors.

changes.case: Cardwell v. State; King v. State
changes.what: Rule 7(B) review looks at the aggregate sentence (the forest, not the trees), and abuse-of-discretion and inappropriateness claims are analyzed separately.
Rule 7(B) review may consider all aspects of the penal consequences imposed, including suspension and placement.
Rule 7(B) relief is declined absent compelling evidence portraying the offense and the defendant's character in a positive light.

name: Louisiana manifest-error review of fault and causation: Rosell, Stobart, Housley
description: Louisiana appellate review of fault, its allocation and causation: set aside only for manifest error or when clearly wrong (Arceneaux, 1978; Watson, 1985; Rosell, 1989; Stobart, 1993), with de novo review after legal error and deference even on documentary records (Virgil, 1987). Causation is factual, with the Housley (1991) presumption. Stable throughout; the anchor alternates between Rosell and Stobart.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Louisiana manifest-error review of fault allocation and causation
previous.description: Louisiana appellate review of fact-finding under Rosell, Stobart, Arceneaux and Canter: fault allocation, causation (Housley) and damages are set aside only for manifest error or when clearly wrong.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session subagents, from cocite evidence; second pass differentiated near-duplicates)

history: Dominant rule: whether a defendant was at fault, how fault is allocated, and whether an accident caused the injuries are questions of fact. A Louisiana court of appeal may not set them aside absent manifest error, giving great deference even where the record is documentary (Virgil, 1987), but when a legal error interdicted the fact-finding it must decide the facts de novo (Rosell, 1989; Gonzales v. Xerox, 1975, on rendering judgment on appeal). How it changed: the rule is stable; the anchors restate it. Rosell anchors 1990-94 and 1995-99, Stobart (1993) from 2000-04 through 2010-14, and Rosell again from 2015-19. Watson (1985) supplies the factors for allocating fault. Housley (1991) treats causation as factual and presumes an accident caused a disability that appears afterward in a previously healthy plaintiff. Also: the rear-end presumption (Mart, 1987), the motorist's burden to show no dereliction (Ferrell, 1995), custodial liability (Sistler, 1990), plaintiff's burden on cause in fact (Lasha, 1993) and workers' compensation findings (Banks; Freeman).
rule: Findings on fault, its allocation and causation are facts that a Louisiana appellate court may set aside only if manifestly erroneous or clearly wrong, deferring even to findings on documentary evidence, unless legal error requires de novo review.

changes.what: Restated manifest-error review and de novo redetermination after legal error; Rosell anchors 1990-99 and from 2015-19.
Causation is a fact reviewed for manifest error, and an injury is presumed caused by an accident if the plaintiff was well before it and symptoms appeared after.
Two-part test and its application to fault allocation; Stobart anchors 2000-04 through 2010-14.

name: RICO: enterprise, pattern (H.J. Inc.), operation or management (Reves)
description: RICO in a single 1995-99 slice anchored by Sedima (1985): no prior conviction needed for civil RICO; a pattern requires related, continuous predicates (H.J. Inc. 1989); liability requires operation or management (Reves 1993); civil plaintiffs need proximate cause (Holmes 1992). Turkette (1981) separates enterprise and pattern. Also D.C. Circuit and Second Circuit gang prosecutions (Edmond 1995, Thai 1994, Wong 1994, Concepcion 1993 under § 1959).
history: Dominant rule: the elements of RICO, civil and criminal. Sedima (1985) anchors the lineage's only slice, 1995-99, which formed from RICO units and splits in 2000-04 into First Circuit criminal-appeals and antitrust lineages. How it changed: no change within the span; the leading Supreme Court cases set the elements. Turkette (1981) held enterprise and pattern are distinct elements whose proof may coalesce; Sedima (1985) rejected a prior-conviction or racketeering-injury requirement; H.J. Inc. (1989) defined a pattern by relationship plus continuity; Holmes (1992) required proximate cause for civil plaintiffs; and Reves (1993) required participation in operating or managing the enterprise. Haroco (7th Cir. 1985) applied Rule 9(b) to RICO fraud and Neapolitan (1986) read § 1962(d) conspiracy by traditional conspiracy law. Alongside: criminal RICO and § 1959 gang trials (Thai 1994, waiver of hearsay objections by procuring a witness's silence; Edmond 1995, anonymous juries; Wong 1994; Concepcion 1993 on the gang-membership motive), and prosecutorial argument (Childress 1995).
rule: RICO liability requires an enterprise distinct in proof from a pattern of racketeering (Turkette), a pattern of related predicates showing continuity (H.J. Inc.), participation in the operation or management of the enterprise (Reves), and, for civil plaintiffs, injury proximately caused by the predicate acts (Holmes), but no prior criminal conviction (Sedima).

changes.what: RICO reaches illegitimate enterprises; enterprise and pattern are separate elements whose proof may coalesce.
Civil RICO requires no prior criminal conviction on the predicates and no special racketeering injury; Sedima anchors the slice.

changes.case: H.J. Inc. v. Northwestern Bell Telephone Co.
changes.what: A pattern requires related predicates that amount to or threaten continued criminal activity.

changes.case: Holmes v. Securities Investor Protection Corp.
changes.what: A civil RICO plaintiff must show the predicate act proximately caused the injury; but-for causation is not enough.
Liability under § 1962(c) requires participation in the operation or management of the enterprise; an outside auditor was not liable.

history: Dominant rule: Article III requires a live controversy throughout; a claim is moot when the issues are no longer live or the parties lack a cognizable interest (Powell 1969, Murphy v. history: Dominant rule: Thornburg v. Gingles (1986) anchors 1990-99. A § 2 vote-dilution plaintiff must show a sufficiently large and compact minority, political cohesion and white bloc voting. name: Delaware controlling-stockholder transactions: entire fairness (Weinberger, Kahn)
description: Delaware review of conflicted and controller transactions: entire fairness under Weinberger (1983), which leads every slice, with controller status and special-committee burden shifting under Kahn v. Lynch (1994) and director-interest materiality under Cede and Cinerama (1994-95). Kahn v. M&F (2014) and Corwin (2015) restored business-judgment review for deals cleansed by committee and informed stockholder votes.
history: Dominant rule: when a controller or conflicted board stands on both sides, Delaware courts review for entire fairness, fair dealing and fair price (Weinberger, 1983, the 2010-14 anchor). How it changed: Kahn v. Lynch (1994) anchors 2015-19: a minority holder exercising actual control is a controller, and a coerced committee does not shift the burden; Kahn (1997) holds process and price intertwined. Cede (1994) and Cinerama (1995) require a director's interest to be material, judged by an actual-person test. Rosenblatt (1985), which adopted the TSC materiality standard for disclosure, anchors 2020-24, when Kahn v. M&F (2014) and Corwin (2015) lead: dual protections or a fully informed, uncoerced stockholder vote restore business-judgment review; Leal (2015) requires non-exculpated claims against each director, and Blasius and Schnell enter on vote manipulation. Trados (2013) shows a fair outcome despite an unfair process. Cede anchors the partial 2025-29 slice. Also: Revlon (1986) and QVC (1994) sale-of-control duties.
rule: A transaction with a controlling stockholder is reviewed for entire fairness (fair dealing and fair price), with the burden shifted by a well-functioning independent special committee or informed minority approval, and business-judgment review restored only if the deal is conditioned from the outset on both protections (Kahn v. M&F, 2014).

description: Wisconsin criminal appellate practice: undeveloped arguments are not addressed (Pettit, 1992, anchor in both slices). history: Dominant rule: across 2020-24 and the partial 2025-29 slice, Wisconsin appellate courts refuse to develop arguments for the parties (Pettit, 1992, the anchor in both slices; A.O. Smith, 1998, on abandoned issues). They decide ineffective-assistance claims through the Machner procedure. How it changed: the lineage forms in 2020-24 from Texas ineffective-assistance and Wisconsin statutory-interpretation groups and gathers earlier rules rather than new ones. Machner (1979) requires trial counsel's testimony. Bentley (1996) and Allen (2004) require objective factual allegations before a hearing, and Balliette (2011) applies them to postconviction motions. Thiel (2003) allows aggregation of counsel's errors, and Romero-Georgana (2014) sets the clearly-stronger test for postconviction counsel. Escalona-Naranjo (1994) bars successive § 974.06 claims without sufficient reason, overruling Bergenthal. Alongside: Poellinger (1990) on sufficiency, Sullivan (1998) on other-acts evidence and Bangert (1986) on plea colloquies. In 2025-29 civil and statutory cases join (Kalal, 2004; Data Key, 2014), which is drift.
rule: Wisconsin appellate courts decline to address undeveloped or inadequately briefed arguments (Pettit), and a defendant claiming ineffective assistance must preserve trial counsel's testimony at a Machner hearing, which is required only if the postconviction motion alleges sufficient material facts that would entitle him to relief (Bentley, Allen).

name: Enforcing plea agreements: Santobello breach and remedies
description: Plea-agreement enforcement, 1980-2004: Santobello (1971), anchor in every slice, binds the prosecution to promises that induced a plea, with specific performance or withdrawal as the remedy. Mabry (1984) gave unaccepted offers no constitutional weight; Wade (1992) limited review of refusals to file substantial-assistance motions. From 2000-04 Washington cases (Sledge, Talley, Van Buren) on prosecutors undercutting agreed recommendations lead.
history: Dominant rule: Santobello v. New York (1971), the anchor in all five slices, requires the government to keep a promise that induced a guilty plea. How it changed: in 1980-84 circuit cases order specific performance even of unauthorised or withdrawn promises (Palermo 1976, Cooper 1979, Correale 1973), and Blackledge (1977) stresses the weight of plea-colloquy statements. Mabry (1984) leads from 1985-89: an offer has no constitutional significance until accepted, and the plea must be induced by the promise; Harvey (4th Cir. 1986) applied contract principles, and Rowe v. Griffin (1982) enforced immunity promises. Wade (1992) enters in 1990-94 with circuit cases on cooperation agreements and § 5K1.1 or § 3553(e) motions, which are reviewable only for unconstitutional motive. In 2000-04 Washington cases lead: the defendant chooses the remedy (State v. Miller 1988), and a prosecutor breaches by eliciting contrary testimony or highlighting aggravating factors (Sledge 1997, Talley 1998, Jerde 1999, Van Buren 2000). Alongside: Alabama rules that agreements be disclosed before the plea (Yarber 1983).
rule: When a guilty plea rests on a prosecutor's promise, due process requires the promise to be kept; a breach entitles the defendant to specific performance or withdrawal of the plea, read under contract principles.

changes.what: A prosecutorial promise that induced a plea must be fulfilled; the remedy is specific performance or withdrawal.
An unaccepted plea offer has no constitutional significance; a Santobello claim requires the plea to have been induced by the promise.
Plea agreements are read like contracts, with ambiguities against the government, and a breach implicates due process.
A prosecutor's refusal to move for a substantial-assistance departure is reviewable only for unconstitutional motive.

history: Dominant rule: a federal court may entertain a constitutional challenge to state law unless it is so insubstantial as to be devoid of merit, and then may decide related statutory claims. How it changed: early slices are small and concern the three-judge court statute: Stratton (1930) anchors 1955-59 with Poresky (1933), letting a single judge dismiss insubstantial claims, and 1960-64 cases (Jacobs 1957 and others) mapped when a panel must be convened. Poresky anchors 1965-74, with Bailey v. Patterson and Epstein (1962) on foreclosed claims and abstention, Phillips (1941) on narrow reading, Swift v. Wickham (1965) removing Supremacy Clause claims from the statute, and Flowers (1967) excluding local ordinances. In 1975-79 King v. Smith (1968) anchors as welfare litigation arrives: it struck Alabama's substitute-father rule; Rosado (1970) confirmed pendent review, and Townsend (1971) and Carleson (1972) invalidated conflicting eligibility rules; Hagans (1974) and Goosby (1973) defined insubstantiality. Congress largely ended three-judge courts in 1976.

name: Tenth Circuit pro se appeals: inadequate briefing, waiver and plain error (Garrett)
description: Tenth Circuit appellate practice in pro se and habeas appeals, 2020-24: pro se filings are read liberally, but the court is no advocate (Hall v. history: Dominant rule: Tenth Circuit preservation and briefing rules applied to pro se litigants. Nixon (2015) requires the appellant to explain what was wrong with the district court's reasoning; Richison (2011) and Leffler (2019) treat an unpreserved issue as waived when the appellant does not argue plain error; Morales-Fernandez (2005) applies the firm-waiver rule to unobjected magistrate recommendations; Servants of the Paraclete (2000) limits reconsideration motions. Alongside: § 2241 and habeas matters (Garza 2010 on exhaustion futility; McIntosh 1997 on the habeas-civil-rights line), equitable tolling denied for limited English (Yang 2008), IFP showings (Debardeleben 1991), and stray ADA accommodation cases (Punt 2017; Lincoln 2018, which overruled the rule that ADA exhaustion is jurisdictional). history: Dominant rule: an at-will employee may be fired without cause, but the implied covenant of good faith bars a firing designed to deprive the employee of compensation already earned (Fortune, 1977), and public policy bars firings for reasons such as refusing to lie under oath. How it changed: Gram (1981) anchors 1990-94 and confined Fortune: lack of cause alone is not actionable, and recovery covers only identifiable earned compensation (Gram 1984 on renewal commissions). DeRose (1986) recognized a public-policy claim, but Mello (1988) and Smith-Pfeffer (1989) refused to extend it to internal complaints or all socially desirable conduct; Shea (1997) later allowed internal complaints about criminal conduct. Jackson (1988) held a personnel manual is not a contract absent mutual intent. Geltman (1990) adopted the Restatement's 'improper' interference element. Wright (1992) anchors 1995-99: a co-worker who interferes with employment is liable only for actual malice, and King (1994) held financial gain insufficient. Also: Chapter 151B exclusivity over MCRA claims (Mouradian, Sereni 1987). The line splits to Massachusetts summary judgment in 2000-04.
rule: A Massachusetts employer may end at-will employment without cause, but not in bad faith to deprive the employee of compensation already earned, nor in violation of a clearly established public policy; co-workers who interfere are liable only for actual malice.

Parker (1983) toll limits for class members; Cada (1991) separates the discovery rule, equitable tolling and estoppel. Baldwin County (1984) limits tolling.
history: Dominant rule: Zipes v. Trans World Airlines (1982), the anchor, holds that timely filing of an EEOC charge is not jurisdictional but works like a statute of limitations, subject to waiver, estoppel and equitable tolling. How it applied: Delaware State College v. Ricks (1980) runs the period from when the discriminatory decision is made and communicated, and United Air Lines v. Evans (1977) rejected continuing violations based on present effects of past acts. American Pipe (1974) and Crown, Cork & Seal v. Parker (1983) toll the period for putative class members. Baldwin County v. Brown (1984) refused tolling where entitlement was not shown. Cada v. Baxter Healthcare (7th Cir. 1991) distinguished the discovery rule from equitable tolling and estoppel; Early (1992) and Chakonas (1994) allowed tolling for misleading agency conduct. Background tolling doctrine comes from Bailey v. Glover (1875) and Holmberg (1946); Brown v. GSA (1976) makes Title VII exclusive for federal employees. Single slice.
rule: Title VII's charge-filing and suit deadlines are not jurisdictional but operate like statutes of limitations subject to waiver, estoppel and equitable tolling; they run from the discriminatory decision, not its later consequences, and a class action tolls them for putative members.

changes.case: United Air Lines v. Evans; Delaware State College v. Ricks
changes.what: The period runs from the discriminatory decision, and lingering effects of past acts are not continuing violations.

changes.case: American Pipe & Construction v. Utah; Crown, Cork & Seal v. Parker
changes.what: Filing a class action tolls limitations for all putative class members, including those who later sue separately.

name: Texas jury-charge error 2000-29: Almanza some harm v. egregious harm
description: Texas review of jury-charge error, 2000-29, under Almanza (1985), the anchor in every slice: once error is found, objected-to error needs some harm and unobjected error egregious harm. Lesser-included instructions follow Rousseau (1993) and Hall (2007, pleadings approach); Ngo (2005) found egregious harm from a non-unanimous charge, Cosio (2011) required actual harm, and Kirsch (2012) barred instructions commenting on the weight of evidence.

previous.name: Texas criminal: jury-charge error and egregious harm
previous.description: Texas review of jury-charge error under Almanza: some harm for preserved error and egregious harm for unpreserved error (Hutch, Ngo), lesser-included offenses and defensive instructions.

history: Dominant rule: Almanza (1985) anchors every slice from 2000-04 to 2025-29: an appellate court first asks whether the charge was erroneous (Hutch 1996, Abdnor 1994) and then whether the error caused some actual harm (if preserved; Arline 1986) or egregious harm (if not), weighing the entire charge, the evidence, argument and the record. How it changed: in 2000-04 lesser-included-offense cases lead (Rousseau 1993 and Bignall 1994 refining Royster; Moore 1998; Schweinle 1996), along with Huizar (2000) requiring a reasonable-doubt instruction on punishment-phase extraneous acts. In 2005-09 Ngo (2005) found egregious harm from a non-unanimous charge, Francis (2000) and Jefferson (2006) addressed unanimity and manner and means, and Stuhler (2007) adopted the Jefferson concurrence framework. Hall (2007) leads 2010-14 with the pleadings approach to lesser-included offenses. Cosio (2011) required actual harm, Kirsch (2012) barred instructions commenting on the evidence, and Reeves (2013) addressed provocation instructions; these lead 2015-24 with Villarreal (2015). Also: double-jeopardy unit-of-prosecution cases (Vick 1999, Cavazos 2006) that split off in 2010-14.
rule: Jury-charge error is reviewed in two steps: first whether error exists, then whether it caused 'some harm' if the defendant objected, or 'egregious harm' depriving him of a fair and impartial trial if he did not.

changes.what: Preserved charge error requires reversal unless harmless (some actual harm); unpreserved error requires egregious harm.

changes.case: Rousseau v. State; Bignall v. State
changes.what: Refined the Royster two-step test for a lesser-included-offense instruction: the lesser offense must be within the proof of the charged offense and some evidence from any source must permit a rational finding of guilt only of the lesser.
A non-unanimity charge error, compounded by the prosecutor telling jurors they need not agree, caused egregious harm.
The pleadings approach is the first step in deciding whether an offense is a lesser-included offense.
Egregious harm must be actual, not theoretical.
An instruction that focuses the jury on particular evidence supporting an element, such as defining 'operate' in a DWI case, is an impermissible comment on the weight of the evidence.

name: What is testimonial, 1995-99: physical evidence and act of production (Fisher)
description: Which compelled evidence the privilege covers, in a single 1995-99 slice anchored by Kastigar (1972): only testimonial communications. Schmerber (1966), Gilbert and Wade (1967) put blood, handwriting and voice samples outside it; Fisher (1976), Doe (1984) and Braswell (1988) limited document protection to the testimonial act of production; Doe (1988) and Muniz (1990) defined testimonial conduct. Kastigar immunity rides along.
history: Dominant rule: the Fifth Amendment protects only compelled testimonial communications that incriminate. Schmerber (1966), Gilbert (1967), Wade (1967) and Dionisio (1973) hold that blood, handwriting and voice samples are not testimonial. Kastigar (1972), the anchor, lets the government compel testimony under use and derivative-use immunity, with a heavy burden to show its evidence came from independent sources (North 1990, Harris 1992). How it changed: Fisher (1976), Doe (1984) and Braswell (1988) moved document protection to the act of production, leaving the contents of business records and collective-entity records unprotected; Doe (1988) defined testimonial conduct, and Muniz (1990) applied it to booking questions. Also: Neville (1983) allows use of a refusal to take a blood test. The lineage exists only in 1995-99 and then moves into special-needs searches.
rule: The Fifth Amendment privilege bars only compelled testimonial self-incrimination, not compelled physical evidence, and testimony may be compelled if the witness receives use and derivative-use immunity.

changes.what: Compelled blood samples are physical, not testimonial, evidence outside the privilege.
Use and derivative-use immunity is coextensive with the privilege and allows compelled testimony.
Only the testimonial act of producing documents is protected; the contents of business records are not, and collective-entity custodians cannot invoke the privilege.

changes.case: Pennsylvania v. Muniz; United States v. North
changes.what: A question calling for a testimonial answer is protected; North held the government must show immunized testimony did not shape later witness testimony.

name: Seventh Circuit injunctions and trademark confusion (2025)
description: A partial 2025-29 grouping of Seventh Circuit injunction and trademark cases. Injunctions must specify what they restrain and are clarified or modified by the issuing court (McComb 1949, Longshoremen 1967, Russian Media 2010, Eli Lilly 2018). Lanham Act merits turn on likelihood of confusion and distinctiveness (Sorensen v. WD-40 2015, Uncommon 2019, Booking.com 2020).

history: Dominant rule: this single partial 2025-29 slice, anchored by Sorensen v. WD-40 (7th Cir. 2015), combines the scope and enforcement of injunctions with Lanham Act merits. Injunctions: McComb (1949) allows a decree to obey a statute after persistent violations and tells a party in doubt to seek clarification; Longshoremen (1967) applies Rule 65(d) specificity to orders functioning as injunctions; Express Publishing (1941) cautions against broad obey-the-law decrees; Russian Media (2010) and Eli Lilly (2018) allow modification. Trademark: Sorensen treats actual confusion as especially important; Uncommon (2019) holds registration yields one distinctiveness presumption, not both; Booking.com (2020) rejected a per se rule that generic.com terms are generic; HANWJH (2022) found personal jurisdiction from a single online sale. Also: Califano v. Yamasaki (1979) on class relief. No rule change is visible within the slice.
rule: An injunction must state its terms specifically and is enforced and modified by the issuing court (McComb, Longshoremen, Rule 65(d)), and in Lanham Act cases relief turns on likelihood of confusion and the mark's distinctiveness (Sorensen v. WD-40, Uncommon v. Spigen).

changes.what: A record of persistent violations can justify a decree to obey the statute, and a party unsure of a decree's scope should seek clarification rather than risk contempt.

changes.case: International Longshoremen's Ass'n v. Philadelphia Marine Trade Ass'n
changes.what: Rule 65(d) applies to orders that function as injunctions, which must specify the acts restrained.

changes.case: Uncommon, LLC v. Spigen, Inc. (7th Cir.)
changes.what: Registration gives a mark one of two presumptions, inherent or acquired distinctiveness, not both; surveys help prove secondary meaning.

name: Mass. Appeals Court 2020-24: Chace unpublished decisions, Birchall contempt
description: A single 2020-24 slice of Massachusetts Appeals Court decisions, anchored by Chace (2008) on the persuasive weight of unpublished decisions, mixing criminal sufficiency under Latimore (1979; inferences need only be reasonable and possible) with civil appeals: contempt proved by clear and convincing evidence (Birchall 2009, Smith 2018), good faith (Carey 2006) and issues not raised below being waived.
history: Dominant rule: this one-slice lineage (2020-24) collects routine Massachusetts appellate review. On the criminal side Latimore (1979) governs sufficiency: a conviction stands if any rational trier of fact could find the elements beyond a reasonable doubt, inferences need only be reasonable and possible (2016), a victim's credited testimony alone can suffice (2021), but motive and consciousness of guilt alone cannot (2016); probable cause turns on the totality of the evidence (2013). Zanetti (2009) aiding-and-abetting language and the 2014 DiGiambattista instruction rule recur. On the civil side Birchall (2009) raised the standard for civil contempt to clear and convincing evidence (applied in Smith v. Smith, 2018), Carey (2006) defines good faith and bars arguments first raised on appeal. The 1954 case supplies the formula that unaddressed points were considered. The anchor, Chace (2008), is cited for the rule that unpublished Appeals Court decisions are persuasive but not binding.
rule: Massachusetts appellate courts sustain a conviction if any rational factfinder could find each element beyond a reasonable doubt (Latimore), and require civil contempt to be proved by clear and convincing evidence of disobedience of a clear and unequivocal command (Birchall).

changes.what: Rational-factfinder sufficiency standard remains a leading case.
Civil contempt now requires clear and convincing evidence of disobedience of a clear and unequivocal command.

history: Dominant rule: termination requires clear and convincing proof of a statutory ground and of best interests, with specific findings, because parental rights are fundamental (Stanley, 1972; Santosky, 1982). How it changed: Valentine (2002) anchors 2010-14 and 2015-19. One ground suffices, and substantial noncompliance with a permanency plan is reviewed de novo. Audrey S. In 2015-19 Kaliyah S. (2015) held reasonable efforts are not a precondition to termination, overruling Tiffany B. (2007), and Gabriella D. (2017) set the best-interest analysis. Carrington H. (2016) anchors 2020-24 and 2025-29, requiring appellate review of all grounds and rejecting post-conviction-type remedies. Braxton M. (2017) applies the statute in force at filing. Also: divorce and parenting cases join from 2020-24 (Kelly, 2014), which is drift.

history: Dominant rule: harassment because of sex that alters the conditions of employment violates Title VII. In 1980-84 the unit concerns constructive discharge, where intolerable conditions force a resignation (Young 1975, Muller 1975). Henson (11th Cir. 1982) anchors 1985-89 and set the elements of hostile-environment and quid pro quo claims, building on Bundy (1981). How it changed: Meritor (1986) anchors 1990-99, making hostile environments actionable without economic loss. The circuits divided on measuring hostility: Rabidue (1986) set a demanding standard, Ellison (1991) a reasonable-woman view, and Hicks (1987) and Hall (1988) counted nonsexual hostility. Harris (1993) required objective hostility but no psychological injury; Baskerville (1995) held mild incidents insufficient. In 1998 Oncale reached same-sex harassment, and Faragher and Ellerth made employers vicariously liable for supervisors subject to an affirmative defense; Faragher anchors 2000-04, when Morgan (2002) enters on timeliness.

history: Dominant rule: the anchor shifts from deference to plain-language interpretation. name: Fourth Circuit trial errors, 2005-14: Burgos sufficiency, Queen Rule 404(b)
description: Fourth Circuit criminal-trial appeals, 2005-14, anchored by Burgos (1996): a verdict stands on substantial evidence viewed for the government (Glasser 1942, Tresvant 1982), and knowledge may be proved circumstantially (Beidler 1997). history: Dominant rule: sufficiency review of federal convictions in the Fourth Circuit. Burgos (en banc 1996) anchors both slices, 2005-09 and 2010-14: a conviction is upheld if substantial evidence, taking the view most favourable to the government, supports it (Glasser 1942), the government gets all reasonable inferences (Tresvant 1982), and knowledge of illegality may be inferred from conduct (Beidler 1997). How it changed: within the span the leading cases stay fixed, while trial-error rules accompany them. Queen (1997) admits prior acts under Rule 404(b) when intent is at issue; Alerre (2005) set the standard for physicians dispensing controlled substances; Smith (2006) and Moye (2006) address the right to present a defence and instructions; Wilson (1997) the judge's questioning of witnesses. In 2010-14 Harvey (2008, clear error), Foster (2007, plain error from a sentence above the statutory maximum), and capital and Virginia cases enter: Lighty (2010) on requested instructions and argument, Basham (2009) on crime-spree evidence, Green (2010) and Kellam (2009) on searches and stops. rule: A Fourth Circuit conviction is sustained if substantial evidence, viewed most favourably to the government, supports it (Glasser, Burgos), with knowledge and intent provable circumstantially (Beidler); similar-act evidence is admissible under Rule 404(b) when relevant to an element such as intent, necessary and reliable (Queen); and inconsistent verdicts are not reviewed (Dunn, Powell).
