name: § 1981/§ 1983 limitations borrowing: Johnson v. REA, Tomanio, Wilson v. Garcia
description: Which state limitations period governs the Reconstruction-era civil-rights statutes, 1970-89: Jones (1968), Sullivan (1969) and Runyon (1976) applied §§ 1981-1982 to private discrimination. Johnson v. Railway Express (1975) held § 1981 independent of Title VII and not tolled by an EEOC charge; Tomanio (1980, anchor 1980-84) applied state tolling rules; Wilson v. Garcia (1985, anchor 1985-89) chose the personal-injury period, applied to § 1981 in Goodman (1987).
history: Dominant rule: borrowing state limitations periods for federal civil-rights claims. In 1970-74 the lineage begins with the scope of the Reconstruction statutes: Jones v. Alfred H. Mayer (1968) read § 1982 to bar private discrimination in property, Sullivan (1969) allowed retaliation claims, and Caldwell (1971) let § 1981 plaintiffs bypass Title VII procedures. How it changed: Johnson v. Railway Express Agency (1975) held § 1981 an independent remedy alongside Title VII but refused tolling during an EEOC charge, borrowing state limitations and tolling rules; Holmberg (1946), anchor in 1975-79, makes accrual and fraudulent concealment federal questions, and Hoosier Cardinal (1966) borrowed state periods for labor claims. Runyon (1976) applied § 1981 to private schools and McDonald (1976) protected white employees. Board of Regents v. Tomanio (1980), anchor 1980-84, applied state tolling rules to § 1983 claims. Wilson v. Garcia (1985), anchor 1985-89, characterized all § 1983 claims as personal-injury actions for limitations purposes, with Chevron Oil v. Huson (1971) governing retroactivity; Goodman v. Lukens Steel (1987) applied the same approach to § 1981 and Al-Khazraji (1987) extended § 1981 to ancestry discrimination. The unit splits in 1990-94.

history: Dominant rule: McDonnell Douglas (1973) anchors every slice except 1985-89, when Burdine (1981) does. The plaintiff makes a prima facie case, the employer articulates a legitimate reason, and the plaintiff must prove pretext. Furnco (1978) and Aikens (1983) keep the framework flexible and focused on intent, and Burdine makes the employer's burden one of production. 1980s age cases (Loeb, La Montagne, Kephart) adapted it to the ADEA, and Thurston (1985) held it inapplicable to direct evidence. How it changed: in 1990-94, as disparate-impact units merge in (Griggs, Watson), Price Waterhouse (1989) allows mixed-motive liability with a same-decision defense, and Hicks (1993) holds that disbelieving the employer permits but does not compel a finding of discrimination. Reeves (2000) enters in 2000-04 and rejects a pretext-plus requirement. Desert Palace v. Costa (2003) leads in 2005-09. From 2010-14, harassment and summary-judgment units merge in: Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Celotex and Matsushita lead, alongside Burlington Northern (2006) on retaliation, Harris (1993) and Faragher (1998) on hostile environments, and Gross (2009) on but-for causation. Babb (2020) and Comcast (2020) enter in 2020-24 on causation.
rule: A plaintiff relying on circumstantial evidence of disparate treatment makes out a prima facie case, the employer must then articulate (but need not prove) a legitimate nondiscriminatory reason, and the plaintiff bears the ultimate burden of persuading the factfinder that the reason is a pretext for discrimination; disbelief of the employer's reason, with the prima facie case, may but need not support liability.

changes.case: McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green; Furnco v. Waters; Sweeney

name: Federal conspiracy trials c. 1970: Glasser sufficiency, Kotteakos variance, Pinkerton
description: Federal conspiracy trials (one 1970-74 slice): a verdict stands on substantial evidence viewed for the government (Glasser, 1942), but a variance proving many conspiracies is reversible if it substantially swayed the jury (Kotteakos, 1946; Blumenthal, 1948 on chains), and a constructive amendment always is (Stirone, 1960). Also Pinkerton liability, aiding and abetting (Nye & Nissen, Pereira) and corroboration of admissions (Opper, 1954).
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Federal conspiracy and variance (c. 1970)
previous.description: Federal conspiracy prosecutions: variance between indictment and proof (Kotteakos, Stirone), Pinkerton liability, aiding and abetting (Nye & Nissen, Pereira), and corroboration of confessions (Opper).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: on appeal a federal jury verdict must be sustained if substantial evidence, taken in the view most favourable to the government, supports it (Glasser, 1942, the anchor), but a conviction cannot rest on a variance or amendment that departs from the grand jury's charge. How it changed: this lineage has a single slice (1970-74), so it shows the settled law of the period rather than change. Kotteakos (1946) held that proving at least eight separate conspiracies under one charge was not harmless and set the 'substantial and injurious effect' test, limiting Berger (1935); Blumenthal (1948) allowed a single chain conspiracy with a common objective. Stirone (1960) treated a broadening of the indictment as a constructive amendment. Pinkerton (1946) made conspirators liable for foreseeable acts in furtherance; Nye & Nissen (1949) adopted Judge Hand's view of aiding and abetting, and Pereira (1954) said it needs no agreement. Opper (1954) required independent corroboration of admissions, and Holland (1955) rejected the 'exclude every reasonable hypothesis' instruction. Also: Michelson (1949) on character evidence. The unit splits in 1975-79.
rule: A federal conviction stands if substantial evidence, viewed most favourably to the government, supports it (Glasser), but a variance proving several conspiracies under one charge, or a constructive amendment of the indictment, requires reversal when it substantially affects the verdict (Kotteakos, Stirone).

changes.case: Kotteakos v. United States; Blumenthal v. United States
changes.what: Proof of many separate conspiracies under a single-conspiracy charge is not harmless where it had substantial and injurious effect; Blumenthal limited Kotteakos for chain conspiracies with a common plan.
Conspirators are liable for co-conspirators' foreseeable acts in furtherance; aiding and abetting needs conscious participation, not agreement, and need not be charged.

changes.case: Opper v. United States; Holland v. United States
changes.what: Admissions need independent corroboration of trustworthiness; circumstantial cases need not exclude every reasonable hypothesis of innocence.
Broadening the bases of conviction beyond the indictment is a per se Fifth Amendment violation.

name: Booker's advisory Guidelines: remands, plain error and reasonableness (2005)
description: The 2005 wave applying Booker, anchor of this one-slice 2005-09 lineage: advisory Guidelines, still correctly calculated (Mashek), reasonableness review with a within-range presumption (Mykytiuk, Lincoln), and plain-error rules for unpreserved Booker claims (Pirani). Dean and Cunningham (7th Cir.) set the duty to explain; Moore and Melvin kept § 3582(c)(2) reductions within the amended range.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Booker remands (2005)
previous.description: The 2005 wave of federal appeals sorting out Booker error: whether a sentence imposed under mandatory Guidelines requires resentencing, plain-error treatment of unpreserved claims, and § 3582(c)(2) reductions.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: United States v. Booker (2005; listed as 2004 in the data) made the Guidelines advisory and anchors this single 2005-09 slice, drawn mostly from the Seventh and Eighth Circuits. How it changed: courts first had to decide what to do with sentences imposed under mandatory Guidelines. Pirani (8th Cir. en banc 2005) required a specific Sixth Amendment objection to preserve the claim and held that a bottom-of-range sentence alone does not show prejudice; George (2005) found failure to consider the Guidelines harmless. Mykytiuk (7th Cir.) and Lincoln (8th Cir.) adopted a presumption of reasonableness for within-range sentences, while Mashek and Haack held that misapplied Guidelines still require remand and defined abuse of discretion; Dalton reversed an extraordinary departure as unreasonable. Dean and Cunningham required adequate reasons and responses to principal mitigation arguments. Moore (2008) and Melvin (2009) held that Booker does not loosen § 3582(c)(2) limits. The lineage splits in 2010-14 into reasonableness review and plain-error lines.
rule: After Booker the Guidelines are advisory: courts must still calculate the range correctly and consider § 3553(a), sentences are reviewed for reasonableness (with a rebuttable presumption for within-range sentences in some circuits), unpreserved Booker error requires a showing of prejudice under plain-error review, and Booker does not expand § 3582(c)(2) reductions.

changes.what: Mandatory Guidelines violate the Sixth Amendment; the remedy makes them advisory with reasonableness review, applied to all cases on direct review.

changes.case: United States v. Pirani (8th Cir. en banc)
changes.what: Booker error is preserved only by an objection citing Apprendi, Blakely or the Sixth Amendment; a bottom-of-range sentence alone does not show prejudice on plain-error review.

changes.case: United States v. Mykytiuk (7th Cir.); United States v. Lincoln (8th Cir.)
changes.what: Rebuttable presumption of reasonableness for sentences within a properly calculated Guidelines range.

changes.case: United States v. Mashek; United States v. Haack (8th Cir.)
changes.what: Guidelines-application errors still require remand regardless of reasonableness, and abuse of discretion is defined by ignoring relevant factors, weighing improper ones, or a clear error of judgment.

changes.case: United States v. Dean; United States v. Cunningham (7th Cir.)
changes.what: A judge need not discuss every § 3553(a) factor but must give adequate reasons and address principal nonfrivolous mitigation arguments.

changes.case: United States v. Moore; United States v. Melvin (11th Cir.)
changes.what: Crack-amendment reductions under § 3582(c)(2) do not reach career offenders and cannot go below the amended range despite Booker.

name: Pennsylvania involuntary termination: abandonment and duties of incarcerated parents
description: Pennsylvania involuntary termination: a parent who fails to perform parental duties for the statutory period may lose parental rights, and an incarcerated parent must use available resources with reasonable firmness (McCray 1975, anchor 1975-79; Diane B. 1974; M.T.T. 1976). In re William L. (1978) anchors 1980-84, upholding termination to avoid the limbo of foster care, while D.J.Y. (1979) and B.D.S. (1981) refused termination where contact was obstructed.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Pennsylvania termination: abandonment and parental duty (1975-84)
previous.description: Pennsylvania Supreme Court involuntary-termination cases (McCray, William L., Burns, MTT, Orwick) on abandonment and parental duties, especially incarcerated parents who fail to use available resources.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session subagents, from cocite evidence; second pass differentiated near-duplicates)

history: Dominant rule: parental duty is an affirmative obligation, and failure to perform it for the statutory period supports involuntary termination, with needs and welfare examined only afterward (R.I. 1976). How it changed: McCray (1975) anchors 1975-79, applying abandonment analysis under the 1970 Adoption Act and requiring an incarcerated parent to resist obstacles with reasonable firmness; Diane B. (1974) held desire alone insufficient, and Orwick (1975) found a few letters inadequate. M.T.T. (1976) and Farabelli (1975) reversed or excused where an incarcerated father used available resources or contact would harm the child. In re William L. (1978) enters and anchors 1980-84: termination for incapacity was upheld for children long in foster care. Marshall (1978) required clear and convincing proof that removal was clearly necessary, Burns (1977) addressed whether adoption must be contemplated, and D.J.Y. (1979) and B.D.S. (1981) refused termination where the custodial side obstructed contact. The unit merges into family-privacy due process in 1985-89.
rule: Under Pennsylvania's Adoption Act, parental rights may be involuntarily terminated where a parent has failed for the statutory period to perform parental duties, which require affirmative effort and reasonable firmness against obstacles such as incarceration, unless the parent's efforts were obstructed or excused; the child's needs and welfare are considered only after a statutory ground is found.

changes.case: Appeal of Diane B.; In re Adoption of McCray; In re Adoption of Orwick
changes.what: A mere desire to parent is insufficient; an incarcerated parent who does not resist obstacles with reasonable firmness may forfeit rights; sporadic contact does not show performance of duty.

changes.case: In re Adoption of Farabelli; In re Adoption of M.T.T.
changes.what: Termination for abandonment is precluded where an incarcerated parent used available resources, or where contact would harm the child's situation.
An agency petition to terminate does not require a specific adoption to be pending, construing when adoption is contemplated.

changes.case: In re William L.; In re Marshall
changes.what: Upheld termination for incapacity where children had long been in foster care, declining to preserve a nonexistent family; removal requires clear and convincing proof that it is clearly necessary.

changes.case: In re D.J.Y.; In re Adoption of B.D.S.
changes.what: Termination denied where the custodial family impeded the other parent's contact; obstructive behavior will not be tolerated.

name: Ohio permanent-custody appeals: manifest weight (Eastley) and In re Z.C.
description: Ohio custody, dependency and permanent-custody appeals: parental custody is a fundamental right (In re Murray, 1990; In re Hayes, 1997) and the child's best interest governs disposition (In re Cunningham, 1979). Eastley (2012) applied criminal manifest-weight review in civil cases, displacing C.E. Morris; In re Z.C. (2023), which anchors 2025-29, set sufficiency and manifest-weight review for R.C. 2151.414 decisions.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Ohio custody and dependency appeals
previous.description: Ohio parental-rights and custody review: the parent's fundamental interest in custody (In re Murray, In re Hayes), manifest-weight review in civil cases (Eastley), and deference to the trial court's observation of witnesses (Seasons Coal).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: a parent's right to custody is fundamental, so termination and custody decisions need clear and convincing proof under the statutory best-interest factors (In re Murray, 1990; In re Hayes, 1997; In re Cunningham, 1979), and the appellate court defers to the trial court's observation of witnesses (Seasons Coal, 1984). How it changed: Seasons Coal anchors 2015-19, when the unit splits from the general Ohio abuse-of-discretion lineage. Eastley (2012), the heaviest case, held that Thompkins's manifest-weight standard governs civil cases and criticised C.E. Morris's 'some competent, credible evidence' test as merging weight with sufficiency. In re C.F. (2007) anchors 2020-24, as many permanent-custody decisions under R.C. 2151.414 enter. In re Z.C. (2023) anchors 2025-29: it distinguishes custody allocations under R.C. 3109.04, reviewed for abuse of discretion (Davis, 1997, a change of substance suffices to modify), from permanent-custody findings, reviewed for sufficiency and manifest weight. Also: adoption consent and parental contact (In re Adoption of Holcomb, 1985), continuances (Unger, 1981) and civil plain error (Goldfuss, 1997).
rule: Because parental custody is a fundamental right, a juvenile court's custody or termination decision must rest on the statutory best-interest factors and clear and convincing evidence, reviewed on appeal for sufficiency and manifest weight with deference to the trial court's view of witnesses.

changes.case: In re Murray; In re Hayes
changes.what: Parental custody is an important legal right, and parents facing termination must receive every procedural and substantive protection the law allows.
The criminal manifest-weight standard (Thompkins) applies in civil cases, rejecting C.E. Morris's 'some competent, credible evidence' test as merging weight and sufficiency.
Permanent-custody determinations under R.C. 2151.414 are reviewed for sufficiency and manifest weight, distinct from the abuse-of-discretion review used for R.C. 3109.04 allocations.

name: FOIA exemptions narrowly construed: Rose, Sears, Reporters Committee
description: FOIA litigation: disclosure is the rule and exemptions are narrowly construed (Rose 1976, Exemption 2 for housekeeping only). Mink (1973) and Sears (1975) set Exemption 5's deliberative-process scope; Vaughn (1973) requires a detailed index. Reporters Committee (1989), anchor 1990-2014, limits the privacy-balancing public interest to agency operations; Favish (2004) added family privacy. Safecard and Oglesby (1990-91) anchor 2015-19 on adequate searches.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Freedom of Information Act exemptions
previous.description: FOIA litigation over agency withholding: Exemption 2 (Rose), privacy under Exemptions 6 and 7(C) and the public-interest balance (Reporters Committee), deliberative-process privilege (Sears, Coastal States, Klamath), segregability (Mead Data), Vaughn indexes and adequate searches (Oglesby, Safecard, Morley); D.C. Circuit heavy.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: FOIA requires disclosure unless the agency carries its burden of proving that withheld material falls within a narrowly construed exemption, with segregable portions released. How it changed: Bristol-Myers (1970) anchors 1970-74, with Soucie (1971) on agency status and Getman (1971) on privacy. Mink (1973) anchors 1975-79, alongside Vaughn v. Rosen (1973) requiring itemized justification, Sears (1975) and Renegotiation Board (1975) defining predecisional material, and the 1974 amendments. Rose (1976) anchors 1980-84, confining Exemption 2 to housekeeping matters; National Parks (1976) set the commercial-information test for Exemption 4. Reporters Committee (1989) anchors 1990-2014: privacy is weighed only against information about what the government is up to, followed by Ray (1991), FLRA (1994), Landano (1993) on confidential sources, and Favish (2004). Coastal States (1980) and Klamath (2001) refined Exemption 5. From 2015-19 Safecard (1991) anchors procedural cases on search adequacy (Oglesby 1990, Morley 2007), official acknowledgment (Wolf 2007) and segregability (Mead Data 1977); Sears anchors 2020-24. Also: state public-records cases (Bradley 1997) in 2000-04.
rule: FOIA mandates disclosure of agency records unless the agency proves, with reasonably specific affidavits or a Vaughn index after an adequate search, that material falls within one of the narrowly construed exemptions, releasing reasonably segregable non-exempt portions; privacy exemptions balance personal privacy against the public interest in learning what the government is up to.

changes.case: EPA v. Mink; Vaughn v. Rosen (D.C. Cir.)
changes.what: Exemption 5 covers predecisional deliberation but not purely factual material, and agencies must justify withholdings with a detailed index rather than conclusory claims.
Congress authorized in camera review and narrowed Exemption 7, responding in part to Mink.
Exemption 5 incorporates executive and attorney privileges; predecisional documents are protected unless expressly adopted in a final decision, and FOIA does not require agencies to create records.

changes.case: Department of the Air Force v. Rose
changes.what: Exemption 2 is limited to internal housekeeping matters; disclosure, not secrecy, is the dominant objective.

changes.case: Mead Data Central v. Air Force; Coastal States Gas v. DOE
changes.what: Agencies must explain why factual portions cannot be segregated; the deliberative-process privilege does not cover working law the agency relies on.

changes.case: DOJ v. Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press
changes.what: Under Exemptions 6 and 7(C) the only relevant public interest is shedding light on an agency's performance of its duties; compiled rap sheets are exempt.

changes.case: Department of the Interior v. Klamath Water Users
changes.what: Exemption 5 requires an inter- or intra-agency source; communications from interested outside parties do not qualify.
Family members' privacy is protected, and a requester alleging misconduct must offer more than bare suspicion.

name: Patent obviousness, 1950s-80s: from the invention test to Graham v. John Deere
description: Pre-Federal Circuit validity: a patent fails if the claimed subject matter was obvious. The older 'invention' test (Cuno, 1942; A&P Tea, 1951, scrutinising combinations of old elements) gave way to § 103 (1952) and Graham v. John Deere (1966), the anchor from 1965-69. Anderson's-Black Rock (1969) and Sakraida (1976) then required a synergistic result for combination patents. Also Graver Tank on equivalents and Sears/Compco on preemption.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Patent validity: invention and obviousness (1945-80)
previous.description: Pre-Federal Circuit patent validity law: Hotchkiss, Cuno, A&P Tea, Graham v. John Deere and Adams, Anderson's-Black Rock and Sakraida on invention and obviousness, with Graver Tank on equivalents and Sears/Compco on preemption of state unfair-competition law.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session subagents, from cocite evidence; second pass differentiated near-duplicates)

history: Dominant rule: a patent is invalid if its subject matter would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill, decided on the scope of the prior art, the differences from the claims, the level of skill and secondary considerations (Graham, 1966). How it changed: the 1955-59 and 1960-64 slices apply the judge-made 'invention' requirement (Hotchkiss, 1851; Cuno, 1942) and A&P Tea (1951), the 1960-64 anchor, which told courts to scrutinise combinations of old elements. Section 103 (1952) replaced invention with nonobviousness, and Graham, the anchor from 1965-69 through 1980-84, read it as rejecting the 'flash of creative genius' test; Adams (1966) applied it and construed claims in light of the specification. Anderson's-Black Rock (1969) and Sakraida (1976) narrowed combination patents to those with a synergistic result, and Dann (1976) found a computerised banking system obvious. Lower courts add the presumption of validity and its weakening by uncited art (Saf-Gard, Republic Industries). Also: Graver Tank v. Linde (1950) on equivalents and Sears/Compco (1964) barring state protection for unpatented articles.
rule: A patent is invalid if the claimed subject matter would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill, judged under Graham's factual inquiries (prior art, differences, skill level, secondary considerations), with combinations of old elements closely scrutinised.

changes.case: Cuno Engineering; Great A&P Tea v. Supermarket Equipment
changes.what: Patentability required 'invention'; Cuno spoke of a 'flash of creative genius' and A&P Tea demanded close scrutiny of combinations of old elements.
Replaced the invention requirement with nonobviousness; Graham explains the second sentence disowned the 'flash of creative genius' test.

changes.case: Graham v. John Deere; United States v. Adams
changes.what: Graham set the factual framework for § 103, with secondary considerations; Graham anchors from 1965-69 to the end.

changes.case: Anderson's-Black Rock v. Pavement Salvage; Sakraida v. Ag Pro; Dann v. Johnston
changes.what: Combinations of old elements must produce a synergistic result; commercial success without invention does not make a patent valid.

name: New Jersey agency review: arbitrary, capricious or unreasonable (Stallworth)
description: New Jersey appellate review of final agency action: affirmance unless arbitrary, capricious or unreasonable or unsupported by substantial credible evidence (Henry 1980; Stallworth 2011, the anchor from 2015-19), with deference to expertise (Mayflower, 1973) but de novo review of law (Lavezzi, 2014). Herrmann and Carter (2007) govern public-employee discipline; Richardson (2007) and Russo (2011) accidental-disability pensions.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: New Jersey administrative-agency review
previous.description: New Jersey appellate review of agency decisions: affirmance unless arbitrary, capricious or unreasonable or unsupported by substantial credible evidence (In re Stallworth, Herrmann, Carter), with deference to agency expertise (Mayflower Securities).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: courts reverse an agency's final decision only if it violates express or implied legislative policy, lacks substantial evidence in the record, or reaches a conclusion that could not reasonably have been made on the facts (Mazza, 1995; In re Carter, 2007, the 2010-14 anchor; In re Stallworth, 2011, the anchor from 2015-19). Deference reaches agency expertise (Mayflower, 1973; Greenwood, 1992) and interpretations within the agency's sphere unless plainly unreasonable, but not purely legal questions (Lavezzi, 2014). How it changed: no change in the review standard. The slices add subject areas: public-employee discipline under Henry (1980), Herrmann (2007) and Carter (2007), which allow removal for serious infractions without progressive discipline; Richardson (2007) and Russo (2011) on accidental-disability retirement and the horror-inducing event standard for mental injury; parole future eligibility terms (McGowan, 2002); and in 2020-24 prison disciplinary hearings (Malacow, 2018) and licensing (Allstars Auto, 2018). The partial 2025-29 slice adds older public-utility and agency-powers cases.
rule: A New Jersey court will not reverse a final agency decision unless it is arbitrary, capricious or unreasonable, violates legislative policy, or lacks substantial credible evidence in the record, deferring to agency expertise but reviewing purely legal questions de novo.

changes.case: Mayflower Securities Co. v. Bureau of Securities; Henry v. Rahway State Prison
changes.what: Review of agency adjudications is limited, gives due regard to expertise, and asks whether the action was arbitrary, capricious or unreasonable.

changes.case: In re Herrmann; In re Carter
changes.what: Progressive discipline is not mandatory; some infractions justify removal despite an unblemished record, and courts reverse a sanction only if it shocks the sense of fairness.

changes.case: Richardson v. Board of Trustees, PFRS
changes.what: Accidental-disability benefits require an undesigned and unexpected traumatic event, replacing the earlier great-rush-of-force test.
Restated the three-part arbitrary-capricious inquiry and reviewed the Civil Service Commission's modification of a removal to a suspension.
Agency interpretations of statutes are reviewed de novo, and the challenger bears the burden.

name: Plausibility pleading (Twombly, Iqbal) for pro se and prisoner complaints
description: How a complaint must be pleaded, 2010-29, chiefly in pro se and prisoner suits: Twombly (2007) and Iqbal (2009) require facts stating a plausible claim, not conclusions, while Erickson (2007) and Haines require liberal construction of pro se filings and Neitzke governs frivolousness. Third Circuit cases (Grayson, Phillips) require leave to amend unless futile, and personal involvement is required (Rode, Dooley). The rule stays stable across the slices.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Pro se pleadings and Twombly/Iqbal in prisoner suits
previous.description: Dismissal of pro se and prisoner civil-rights complaints under the Twombly/Iqbal plausibility standard, with liberal construction (Erickson), frivolousness (Neitzke) and leave to amend unless futile. Third Circuit cases (Grayson, Allah v. Seiverling, Phillips) carry the leave-to-amend rule.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session subagents, from cocite evidence; second pass differentiated near-duplicates)

history: Dominant rule: plausibility pleading. Iqbal (2009) anchors three of four slices and Twombly (2007) anchors 2015-19: a complaint must contain factual matter that makes the claim plausible, and conclusions are disregarded. Twombly retired Conley's 'no set of facts' formulation, and Swierkiewicz (2002) survives for the point that a prima facie case need not be pleaded. How it changed: the core rule is stable across the slices; what varies is the setting. In 2010-14 Bivens claims and Third Circuit prisoner cases lead: Grayson (2002) and Phillips (2008) on leave to amend unless futile, Allah v. Seiverling (2000) on retaliation claims. In 2015-19 antitrust and securities units merge in, bringing Tellabs (2007) on documents incorporated by reference and the strong-inference scienter test. In 2020-24 Third Circuit personal-involvement rules (Rode; Dooley, 2020) and Murray (2011) on cell assignments lead. In 2025-29 Eleventh Circuit rules that issues not briefed on appeal are abandoned, even by pro se litigants (Timson, 2008; Sapuppo, 2014), and Heck (1994) enter.
rule: A complaint must plead factual content making the claim plausible, and legal conclusions get no presumption of truth (Twombly, Iqbal); pro se pleadings are construed liberally (Erickson), and in the Third Circuit a civil-rights plaintiff must be given leave to amend unless amendment would be inequitable or futile (Grayson, Phillips).

changes.what: Retired Conley's (1957) 'no set of facts' standard in favor of plausibility.
Pro se complaints must be liberally construed; a prisoner's allegations that officials stopped needed medication were not too conclusory.
Plausibility applies to all civil actions; bare allegations that supervisors adopted a discriminatory policy are conclusions not presumed true.

changes.case: Grayson v. Mayview State Hospital; Phillips v. County of Allegheny (3d Cir.)
changes.what: On dismissal of a civil-rights complaint, the court must allow a curative amendment unless it would be inequitable or futile; Phillips read Twombly as requiring facts suggestive of the proscribed conduct.
Reviewing and denying a grievance does not show a supervisor's personal involvement under Rode.

before_differentiation.name: Plausibility pleading (Twombly, Iqbal) for pro se and prisoner complaints
before_differentiation.description: Pleading in pro se and prisoner suits, 2010-29: Twombly (2007) and Iqbal (2009) require facts stating a plausible claim, not conclusions, while Erickson (2007) and Haines require liberal construction of pro se filings and Neitzke governs frivolousness. Third Circuit cases (Grayson, Phillips) require leave to amend unless futile, and personal involvement is required (Rode, Dooley). The rule stays stable across the slices.

distinct_from.how: Pleading sufficiency, 2010-29, not whether Bivens supplies a remedy.
Pleading sufficiency, not Heck's bar.
Pleading sufficiency, not Feres military immunity.

name: Texas mandamus: clear abuse of discretion and no adequate appeal (Walker)
description: Texas original mandamus: relief requires a clear abuse of discretion and no adequate remedy by appeal (Walker v. Packer, 1992, anchor from 1995-99 on), with the relator supplying the record. Johnson (1985) anchors 1990-94 on new-trial orders. Prudential (2004) made adequacy of appeal a practical balancing; ruling on a properly presented motion is ministerial (Garcia 1997, Chavez 2001); overbroad discovery (CSX 2003) and venue (Team Rocket 2008) support relief.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Texas mandamus
previous.description: Original mandamus proceedings in Texas: clear abuse of discretion and no adequate remedy by appeal (Walker v. Packer, In re Prudential), ministerial duties to rule on motions, new-trial orders (Johnson v. Fourth Court of Appeals, Columbia Medical), and discovery and forum orders.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: mandamus corrects a clear abuse of discretion, meaning a decision so arbitrary as to be clear error or a failure to analyze or apply the law correctly (Cerberus 2005), when the relator lacks an adequate remedy by appeal, and the relator must supply a record proving its right to relief. How it changed: Johnson v. Fourth Court of Appeals (1985) anchors 1990-94, with Downer (1985) on abuse of discretion and Powell and Braden (1991) on sanctions appeal cannot cure. Walker v. Packer (1992) anchors from 1995-99 to the partial 2025-29 slice, holding that expense and delay do not make appeal inadequate (Wittig 1994). In 2000-04 ministerial-duty cases lead: O'Donniley (1993), Garcia (1997), Barnes (1992), Chavez and Bates (2001) compel rulings on properly presented motions but not their outcome. Prudential (2004) recast adequacy of appeal as a balancing of benefits and detriments and enforced a contractual jury waiver; CSX (2003) allowed relief from overbroad discovery, Team Rocket (2008) from improper venue transfers, and Young (Tex. Crim. App. 2007) restated the criminal mandamus test. From 2015-24 insurance-appraisal and discovery mandamus (H.E.B. 2016, Garza 2018, National Lloyds 2014) join.
rule: Mandamus issues only to correct a clear abuse of discretion or violation of a legal duty, such as a failure to analyze or apply the law correctly or to rule on a properly presented motion, when the relator, on a record it must supply, has no adequate remedy by appeal.

changes.case: Johnson v. Fourth Court of Appeals
changes.what: On mandamus the relator must show the facts and law permit the trial court only one decision; granting a new trial in the interest of justice is within its discretion.

changes.case: Braden v. Downey; TransAmerican Natural Gas v. Powell
changes.what: Appeal is inadequate for sanctions that threaten a party's ability to continue the litigation or that preclude a decision on the merits.
Mandamus requires a clear abuse of discretion and no adequate remedy by appeal; the relator must supply a record, and more expense or delay does not make appeal inadequate.

changes.case: O'Donniley v. Golden (1993); In re Garcia (1997); In re Chavez (2001); Ex parte Bates (2001)
changes.what: Ruling on a properly filed motion brought to the court's attention is ministerial and can be compelled, though not its outcome; filing with the clerk is not notice to the court.
No adequate appellate remedy exists for an order compelling overbroad discovery unlimited in time.

changes.case: In re Prudential Insurance Co. of America
changes.what: Whether appeal is adequate depends on balancing the benefits and detriments of mandamus review; a knowing, voluntary contractual jury waiver is enforceable.

name: California capital appeals 1995-99 (Arias): penalty argument and voir dire
description: California capital appeals in 1995-99 only, anchored by Arias (1996), on the penalty phase and jury selection: Crittenden (1994) bars arguing that absent mitigation aggravates; Arias holds Simmons does not require concealing commutation; Ashmus (1991) allows limits on life-without-parole voir dire; Montiel (1993) refuses appellate comparative juror analysis; Davis (1995) on juror misconduct; Lucas (1995) on ineffective assistance.
history: Dominant rule: in death-penalty appeals the California Supreme Court rejects recurring penalty-phase and trial claims by reading instructions and argument as a whole and deferring to the trial court. The lineage exists only in 1995-99, anchored by People v. Arias (1996), continuing a 1980s California capital-appeals unit and splitting three ways in 2000-04. How it developed: Crittenden (1994) barred arguing that a missing mitigating factor is aggravating, while Arias (1996) held that Simmons does not require instructions concealing commutation and pardon; Ashmus (1991) allowed limits on voir dire about life imprisonment without parole. On jury selection, Montiel (1993) refused appellate comparative juror analysis of Wheeler challenges and Lucas (1995) treated accepting a jury as tactical. Davis (1995) required inquiry into alleged juror misconduct. Evidence rulings recur: mannequins as illustrative evidence (Cummings 1993), other-crimes evidence (Garceau 1993), brief non-responsive references (Price 1991), prior inconsistent statements (Zapien 1993) and mental-state instructions (Rodrigues 1994; Berryman 1993).
rule: On automatic appeal the California Supreme Court reviews penalty-phase arguments and instructions as a whole: a prosecutor may not treat the absence of mitigation as aggravation (Crittenden), and the jury need not be told commutation is impossible (Arias).

changes.what: An appellate court will not conduct its own comparative juror analysis to reassess a prosecutor's good faith in peremptory challenges.
The prosecutor may not argue that the absence of a mitigating factor is itself an aggravating factor.

name: Teague 2020-24: procedural versus substantive rules (Schriro, Welch), savings clause
description: Retroactivity on collateral review in the single 2020-24 slice, anchored by Sawyer (1990): new procedural rules do not reach final convictions (Saffle; Beard 2004; Whorton 2007 on Crawford; Chaidez 2013 on Padilla), while substantive rules do (Schriro 2004; Welch 2016 on Johnson) and statutory narrowing applies (Bousley 1998). history: Dominant rule: under Teague v. Lane (1989), a new rule of constitutional criminal procedure does not apply to convictions that were final when it was announced, while Griffith (1987) applies new rules to every case still on direct review. The lineage covers only 2020-24, with Sawyer v. Smith (1990) as anchor, after Padilla-retroactivity and § 2241 units merge. How it developed: Saffle (1990) and Sawyer held that a rule is new unless dictated by precedent; Lambrix and O'Dell (1997), Beard (2004), Whorton (2007, Crawford) and Chaidez (2013, Padilla) applied the bar, and Tyler (2001) required the Supreme Court itself to make a rule retroactive for successive petitions. Substantive rules escape the bar: Schriro (2004) drew the procedural-substantive line in refusing retroactivity to Ring, and Welch (2016) made Johnson retroactive. Bousley (1998) applied Bailey's statutory narrowing retroactively. Danforth (2008) let states give broader relief in their own courts. Also: the § 2255(e) savings clause for statutory claims (Webster 2015; Bruce 2017; McCarthan 2017; Cordaro 2019).

history: Dominant rule: Texas courts give effect to the parties' intent as expressed in the writing, read as a whole so that no provision is meaningless, and decide ambiguity as a question of law; only a contract still open to two reasonable meanings after construction admits extrinsic evidence. How it changed: 1975-89 slices are anchored by older Texas contract and oil-and-gas cases (Texas Co. v. State 1955, Phillips Petroleum v. Stahl 1978) and Cavnar (1985). Coker (1983) anchors 1990-2009, with Madeley (1981) and Reilly (1987). In 1995-2004 insurance cases join: Barnett (1987) and Hudson Energy (1991) construe exclusions for the insured, Forbau (1994) has specific terms control, CBI (1995) and Columbia Gas (1996) bar using extrinsic evidence to create ambiguity, and Merchants Fast Motor Lines (1997) applies the eight-corners rule. The lineage then shifts to arbitration agreements: Webster (2003) anchors 2010-14 with FirstMerit (2001) and Kellogg Brown & Root (2005), Labatt (2009) anchors 2015-19 on binding nonsignatory beneficiaries, with G.T. Leach (2015), Rachal (2013) and Royston Rayzor (2015), and Henry (2018) anchors 2020-29 with Jody James Farms and RSL Funding (2018).

Counsel of choice (Gonzalez-Lopez, 2006) and conflicts (Cuyler, 1980; Mickens, 2002) follow, along with Dusky (1960) competency and structural error under Fulminante (1991) and Neder (1999).
round1.history: Dominant rule: the right to counsel (Powell, 1932; Zerbst, 1938; Gideon, 1963) carries a right to self-representation on a knowing and intelligent waiver (Faretta, 1975), and Faretta anchors every slice. How it changed: McKaskle (1984) allowed standby counsel, Martinez (2000) denied a Faretta right on appeal, Tovar (2004) relaxed the warnings required for a waiver at a plea, and Indiana v. Edwards (2008) let States require counsel for defendants competent to stand trial but not to represent themselves. Competency follows Dusky (1960) and Drope (1975). On conflicts, Cuyler (1980) presumes prejudice from an actual conflict, which Mickens (2002) confined. Gonzalez-Lopez (2006) made denial of counsel of choice structural. In 2010-14 harmless-error and jury cases join (Neder, 1999; Recuenco, 2006; Gaudin, 1995; Winship, 1970), confirming that most errors are not structural. Tumey (1927) and Caperton (2009) on judicial bias run alongside. In 2015-19 public-trial (Waller, 1984) and identification cases (Wade, Neil, Manson, Perry) merge in before the lineage splits.
round1.rule: The Sixth Amendment guarantees appointed counsel (Gideon) and implies a right to waive counsel and represent oneself on a knowing, intelligent and voluntary waiver (Faretta), and denials of counsel, counsel of choice and certain other basic protections are structural errors that need no showing of prejudice.

name: Texas statutory construction: plain meaning, absurd results, agency deference
description: Texas statutory construction, 2000-14: legislative intent from the plain meaning of the enacted text, read as a whole, without adding words, unless absurd (Fitzgerald 1999, Shumake 2006, Hughes 2008, Summers 2009, anchor 2010-14). Agencies get serious consideration for reasonable readings (Moore 1993; Texas Citizens 2011) and their orders substantial-evidence and arbitrariness review (Charter Medical 1984, City of El Paso 1994, anchor 2005-09).

previous.name: Texas statutory construction and agency deference
previous.description: Texas courts reading statutes: legislative intent, presumed knowledge of existing law, avoiding absurd results, and deference to the agency charged with enforcement (Fitzgerald, Rylander, City of San Antonio v. Boerne), with DTPA coverage and immunity waivers.

history: Dominant rule: Texas courts construe statutes to effectuate legislative intent as expressed in the plain meaning of the enacted words, read in context and as a whole, presuming the Legislature chose its words and omissions purposely (Cameron 1981), without adding words or exceptions (Fitzgerald 1999), unless plain meaning yields absurd results. How it changed: Shelton (1994) anchors 2000-04, with Rylander (1999) refusing readings that make a statute meaningless, and Agan (1997) and Moore (1993) on agency and officer powers. City of El Paso v. PUC (1994) anchors 2005-09 on arbitrary-and-capricious review, alongside Charter Medical (1984) substantial-evidence review, City of San Antonio v. Boerne (2003) giving effect to every part, Wilkins (2001) on reading statutes as a whole, the APA's independent right of judicial review (2004), and City of Sunset Valley (2004) on immunity waivers. Summers (2009) anchors 2010-14, holding statutory definitions binding; Shumake (2006) and Hughes (2008) restate plain meaning; Texas Lottery (2010) and Texas Citizens (2011) addressed the role of extrinsic aids and agency deference, and Combs (2011) enters. Also: application to the DTPA, insurance code (Garrison 1998) and noncompete covenants (Sheshunoff 2006).
rule: Texas courts construe statutes to give effect to legislative intent as expressed in the plain meaning of the enacted words, read as a whole and without adding words, unless that meaning yields absurd results, giving serious consideration to reasonable agency readings and reviewing agency orders for substantial evidence and arbitrariness.

name: Washington res judicata and collateral estoppel: identities, full and fair hearing
description: Washington preclusion doctrine, 2015-29: res judicata requires identity of subject matter, cause of action, persons and parties, and quality of persons (Rains 1983; Pederson 2000; Berschauer Phillips 2013); collateral estoppel needs an identical issue decided after a full and fair hearing (Hadley 2001; Christensen 2004), with privity (Loveridge 1995). Hisle (2004), on Minimum Wage Act wages, anchors every slice. Stable; Weaver (2019) restates the elements.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, round 2 after the lineage re-link)

previous.name: Washington collateral estoppel and Minimum Wage Act claims
previous.description: Washington cases on res judicata and collateral estoppel from earlier proceedings, including agency hearings (Thompson, Christensen, Hadley, Rains), together with Hisle and Pederson on wage claims under the Minimum Wage Act and FLSA.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session subagents, from cocite evidence; second pass differentiated near-duplicates)

history: Dominant rule: claim and issue preclusion in Washington. Res judicata bars claims that were or could have been brought in a prior action resolved on the merits between the same parties, tested by identity of subject matter, cause of action, persons and parties, and quality of persons (Rains, 1983; Pederson, 2000, treating a confession of judgment as a consent judgment). Collateral estoppel bars an identical issue actually decided if the party had a full and fair hearing and preclusion works no injustice (Hadley, 2001; Christensen, 2004; Thompson, 1999, treating the State and its agencies as the same party); Loveridge (1995) addresses privity. How it changed: the doctrine is stable across the three slices. Hisle (2004) anchors throughout, a Minimum Wage Act decision holding arbitrated retroactive pay is wages, so the label pairs preclusion with wage claims. In 2020-24 Weaver (2019) restates the elements, Berschauer Phillips (2013) finds concurrence of causes of action, Williams v. Leone & Keeble (2011) enters, and Standlee (1974) keeps criminal acquittals from barring parole revocation. The partial 2025-29 slice has four cases.
rule: In Washington res judicata bars claims that were or could have been litigated to a final judgment between the same parties with identity of subject matter, cause of action, persons and parties, and quality of persons, and collateral estoppel bars an identical issue actually decided after a full and fair hearing where preclusion works no injustice.

changes.what: Four identities test for res judicata.
Privity, for example between the EEOC and employees, may support preclusion.

changes.case: Hadley v. Maxwell; Christensen v. Grant County Hospital District
changes.what: Collateral estoppel turns on whether the parties had a full and fair hearing on the issue; unemployment decisions under RCW 50.32.097 do not preclude later wrongful-termination claims.

round1.history: Dominant rule: claim and issue preclusion in Washington. Res judicata bars claims that were or could have been brought in a prior action resolved on the merits between the same parties, tested by identity of subject matter, cause of action, persons and parties, and quality of persons (Rains, 1983; Pederson, 2000, giving a confession of judgment that effect). Collateral estoppel bars an identical issue actually decided, if the party had a full and fair hearing and preclusion works no injustice (Hadley, 2001; Christensen, 2004; Thompson, 1999, treating the State and its agencies as one party). name: Presumption of mens rea in federal crimes: Morissette, Staples, X-Citement Video
description: A single 2015-19 slice on reading mens rea into federal crimes: knowledge is presumed and extends to the elements separating wrongful from innocent conduct (Morissette, 1952; Liparota, 1985; Staples and X-Citement Video, 1994, anchor; Flores-Figueroa, 2009; McFadden, 2015), but not to public-welfare offenses (Balint) or jurisdictional facts (Feola, 1975; Dancy on § 922(g)). Cheek (1991) defines willfulness.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Mens rea and federal criminal statutes
previous.description: Reading knowledge requirements into federal crimes: Morissette, Staples, X-Citement Video, Flores-Figueroa, Liparota, U.S. Gypsum and Cheek (willfulness), against regulatory public-welfare offenses (Freed). Distinct from the 2010 mandamus-and-mens-rea mix 26996.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, contrastive pass from family evidence)

history: Dominant rule: courts presume Congress intends a mens rea requirement in federal crimes and apply it to each element that makes otherwise innocent conduct criminal. How it changed: the lineage exists only in 2015-19, merged from a 2010-14 mens-rea and mandamus unit, and X-Citement Video (1994) anchors it. Balint (1922) allowed strict liability for regulatory offenses, but Morissette (1952) refused to extend it to conversion. Feola (1975) held knowledge of a victim's federal status unnecessary, U.S. Gypsum (1978) required intent for criminal antitrust, and Liparota (1985) applied knowledge to the unlawfulness of food-stamp use. Cheek (1991) let a sincere misreading of tax law negate willfulness. Staples (1994) and X-Citement Video extended knowledge to a weapon's features and performers' ages; Flores-Figueroa (2009) and McFadden (2015) carried it to identity theft and controlled substances, while Betancourt (2009) excluded drug quantity. Also: § 922(g) needs no knowledge of the interstate nexus (Dancy, 1988; Alcantar, 2013).
rule: Federal criminal statutes are presumed to require knowledge of the facts that make conduct criminal, and 'knowingly' is read to extend to each element that separates wrongful from innocent conduct, except in public-welfare offenses and jurisdictional or sentencing elements.

changes.case: United States v. Balint; Morissette v. United States

changes.case: United States v. Feola; United States Gypsum; Liparota v. United States
changes.what: Mens rea is the rule; knowledge need not extend to jurisdictional facts such as a victim's federal status, but does extend to the unlawfulness of food-stamp use.
Willfulness in tax crimes allows a good-faith misunderstanding of the law, however unreasonable, but not disagreement with its validity.

name: RICO: enterprise, pattern and civil standing (Turkette, Sedima, H.J. Inc.)
description: RICO doctrine: an enterprise may be wholly illegitimate (Turkette 1981, anchor 1980-84); civil suits need no prior conviction or racketeering injury (Sedima 1985, anchor 1985-99); a pattern needs relatedness and continuity (H.J. Inc. 1989, anchor 2000-04). Holmes (1992) required proximate cause, Reves (1993) operation or management, Agency Holding (1987) a four-year limit, and Salinas (1997) broadened conspiracy liability.

history: Dominant rule: RICO liability rests on an enterprise conducted through a pattern of racketeering, with civil standing for injured persons. Sedima (1985) enters and anchors 1985-99, rejecting conviction and racketeering-injury requirements; Seventh Circuit civil cases follow, including Haroco (1985) on Rule 9(b) and Morgan (1986) and Fulmer (1986) on pattern. H.J. Inc. (1989) and Holmes (1992) enter in 1990-94, setting the continuity test and proximate cause, while Arnett (1989) and U.S. Textiles (1990) applied pattern limits to single schemes. Reves (1993) and Agency Holding (1987) enter in 1995-99, along with distinctiveness cases (Riverwoods 1994). In 2000-04 H.J. Inc. anchors as Salinas (1997) and criminal RICO appeals return (Zwick 1999), before the unit splits.

description: The long-running speedy-trial line under Barker v. Wingo (1972), anchor in every slice but 2005-09, when Doggett (1992) anchors: Doggett allowed prejudice to be presumed from long negligent delay, and from 2000 Texas Court of Criminal Appeals cases (Munoz 1999, Zamorano 2002, Dragoo 2003, Cantu 2008) lead the applications. Marion (1971) and Lovasco (1977) confine the right to post-accusation delay; Klopfer (1967) applies it to the states.

history: Dominant rule: Barker v. Wingo (1972) anchors every slice from 1975-79 to 2025-29 except 2005-09, when Doggett (1992) anchors: speedy-trial claims are balanced on length of delay, reason, assertion and prejudice. How it changed: early slices pair Barker with Klopfer (1967, incorporation) and Hooey (1969) and Dickey (1970) on prisoners held elsewhere, and Strunk (1973) on dismissal as the remedy. In 1990-94 Marion (1971) and Lovasco (1977) enter, separating pre-accusation delay (due process) from the Sixth Amendment, with MacDonald (1982) and Loud Hawk (1986) excluding periods without pending charges. Doggett (1992) enters the same slice and becomes the second-heaviest case: negligent delay of extraordinary length can be presumptively prejudicial. From 2000-04 Texas Court of Criminal Appeals cases lead the applications: Munoz (1999) on plea negotiations and incarceration, Zamorano (2002) and Shaw (2003) on the one-year trigger, Dragoo (2003) on preservation, and Cantu (2008) on burdens. Balderas (2016) joins by 2020-24.
rule: Whether a defendant was denied a speedy trial is decided by balancing the length of the delay, the reason for it, the defendant's assertion of the right and prejudice to the defendant, with delay approaching one year triggering the full analysis and dismissal with prejudice the only remedy for a violation.

name: Second Amendment: Heller, the two-step framework, then Bruen's history test
description: The individual right to keep and bear arms (Heller 2008, McDonald 2010). Through 2020-24 Heller anchors as circuits apply a two-step test with intermediate scrutiny (Marzzarella, Chester, Heller II, Ezell). Bruen (2022) replaced that with a text-and-history test and anchors the 2025-29 slice, where Rahimi (2024) upheld disarming dangerous persons and Range and Duarte test § 922(g)(1) as applied.

previous.description: The individual right to keep and bear arms: Heller, its incorporation (McDonald), the circuits' two-step intermediate-scrutiny framework (Heller II, Marzzarella, Chester, Skoien, Ezell), and its replacement by Bruen's text-and-history test (and Rahimi).

history: Dominant rule: Heller (2008) anchors 2010-24, recognising an individual right of self-defense with presumptively lawful longstanding prohibitions, and McDonald (2010) incorporated it. How it changed: in 2010-14 circuit cases built a two-step framework, asking whether a law burdens protected conduct and then applying intermediate scrutiny unless the core right is hit (Marzzarella, Chester, Skoien, Reese, all 2010; Heller II and Ezell, 2011). In 2015-19 the framework was applied to assault-weapons and magazine bans (Cuomo 2015, Fyock 2015, Kolbe 2017), age limits (NRA 2012), and public carry, where the Ninth Circuit en banc (Peruta 2016) found no concealed-carry right; Binderup (2016) and Kanter (2019) addressed felon bans. Bruen (2022) enters in 2020-24 and anchors 2025-29: regulations must fit the Nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation. Rahimi (2024) upheld § 922(g)(8)-type disarmament, and Range (2023-24), Diaz (2024) and Duarte (2025) contest § 922(g)(1) as applied.
rule: The Second Amendment protects an individual right to keep and bear arms for self-defense, incorporated against the states (Heller, McDonald); from 2022 a firearm regulation is valid only if consistent with the Nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation (Bruen), replacing the circuits' two-step means-end scrutiny.

previous.name: Confrontation Clause under Ohio v. Roberts (pre-Crawford)
previous.description: Pre-Crawford Confrontation Clause law: hearsay admissible if firmly rooted or trustworthy under Ohio v. Roberts and Idaho v. Wright, Bruton limits on codefendant confessions (Lee, Lilly, Richardson v. Marsh), and Maryland v. Craig on child testimony. Fades after 2004.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session subagents, from cocite evidence; second pass differentiated near-duplicates)

history: Dominant rule: Ohio v. Roberts (1980), which anchors 1990-94 and 2000-04, admitted hearsay that was firmly rooted or bore particularized guarantees of trustworthiness; Idaho v. Wright (1990) anchors 1995-99. How it changed: Pointer (1965) applied confrontation to the states, Green (1970) admitted prior statements of testifying witnesses, and Dutton (1970) upheld reliable co-conspirator hearsay. Bruton (1968) barred a co-defendant's inculpating confession at a joint trial. Lee v. Illinois (1986) called accomplice confessions presumptively unreliable; Inadi (1986) and Bourjaily (1987) dropped unavailability and independent reliability for co-conspirator statements; Richardson v. Marsh (1987) allowed redacted confessions with instructions, and Cruz (1987) rejected the interlocking-confessions exception. Wright (1990) barred reliance on corroboration, Craig (1990) allowed closed-circuit child testimony, and White (1992) dispensed with unavailability for firmly rooted exceptions. Gray (1998) rejected obvious redactions, and Lilly (1999) held accomplice confessions not firmly rooted. Crawford (2004) enters the last slice and, for testimonial statements, displaced Roberts; Van Arsdall (1986) and Davis v. Alaska (1974) cover cross-examination limits.
rule: Before Crawford, hearsay against the accused satisfied the Confrontation Clause if it fell within a firmly rooted exception or bore particularized guarantees of trustworthiness (Roberts, Wright), and a nontestifying co-defendant's confession naming the defendant could not be admitted at a joint trial (Bruton) unless redacted with a limiting instruction (Marsh).

changes.case: Pointer v. Texas; California v. Green; Dutton v. Evans
changes.what: Confrontation binds the states; prior statements of a testifying witness are admissible; co-conspirator hearsay with indicia of reliability is permitted.
A nontestifying co-defendant's confession directly inculpating the defendant is inadmissible at a joint trial despite limiting instructions.
Unavailable declarants' statements are admissible if they bear adequate indicia of reliability, inferred from firmly rooted exceptions.

changes.case: Lee v. Illinois; United States v. Inadi; Bourjaily v. United States; Richardson v. Marsh; Cruz v. New York
changes.what: Accomplice confessions are presumptively unreliable; co-conspirator statements need no unavailability or separate reliability showing; redacted confessions with instructions satisfy Bruton.

changes.case: Idaho v. Wright; Maryland v. Craig; White v. Illinois
changes.what: Trustworthiness cannot rest on corroboration; child witnesses may testify by closed-circuit television on a case-specific necessity finding; firmly rooted exceptions need no unavailability.

changes.case: Gray v. Maryland; Lilly v. Virginia
changes.what: Redactions that obviously refer to the defendant violate Bruton, and accomplice confessions are not firmly rooted.
Replaced the Roberts reliability test for testimonial statements with a requirement of unavailability and prior cross-examination.

before_differentiation.name: Confrontation Clause under Ohio v. Roberts: reliability and Bruton limits
before_differentiation.description: Pre-Crawford Confrontation Clause law, 1990-2004: hearsay admissible if firmly rooted or particularly trustworthy (Roberts 1980, Wright 1990, White 1992), co-defendant confessions limited by Bruton (1968), Lee (1986), Marsh (1987), Gray (1998) and Lilly (1999), co-conspirator statements freed of extra requirements (Inadi, Bourjaily), and Craig (1990) on child testimony. Crawford (2004) replaced the Roberts test.

distinct_from.how: Hearsay reliability under Roberts, not cross-examination and presence after Crawford.
The mature Roberts regime of 1990-2004 (Wright, White, Lilly) through its replacement by Crawford, not its 1970-84 origins in Bruton and Green.
Admissibility of hearsay, not the right to cross-examine for bias and present a defense.

name: Illinois appellate practice: complete record (Foutch) and forfeiture by brief
description: Illinois appellate practice in 2020-24, anchored by Foutch (1984): the appellant must supply a complete record, and doubts from gaps are resolved against him (Corral 2005, Webster 2001). Briefs must comply with Rule 341; unargued points are forfeited (Hall 2012), and the court is not a repository for a party's research (Obert 1993; Talandis 1976). Also IHRA claims analyzed under federal frameworks (Zaderaka 1989, Owens 2010).
history: Dominant rule: Foutch v. O'Bryant (1984) anchors this single 2020-24 slice: an appellant must present a sufficiently complete record to support a claim of error, and absent one the reviewing court presumes the trial court's order conformed to law and had a sufficient factual basis (Corral, 2005; Webster, 2001, which also bars reversal on speculation). Brief rules reinforce it: points not argued are forfeited (Hall, 2012), the court is not a repository for an appellant's burden of argument and research (Obert, 1993), noncompliant briefs may be stricken or appeals dismissed (Epstein, 2005), though merits readily ascertained from the record may still be decided (Twardowski, 2001, which also treats unruled motions as abandoned), and the court need not act as the appellee's advocate (Talandis, 1976). Alongside: dismissal under section 2-619 for a missing certificate (Holzrichter, 2013), proof of judicial bias (Eychaner, 2002), and employment discrimination under the Illinois Human Rights Act analyzed like Title VII and ADEA claims (Zaderaka, 1989; Owens, 2010). No rule changes appear; the slice merges two 2015-19 units and splits in 2025-29.
rule: An Illinois appellant must present a sufficiently complete record, and any doubt from its absence is resolved against him with the trial court's order presumed correct; points not argued in a rule-compliant brief are forfeited, and the reviewing court will not search the record or research for a party.

changes.case: First Capitol Mortgage v. Talandis Construction
changes.what: A reviewing court need not act as appellee's advocate or search the record to sustain the judgment.
The appellant bears the burden of a complete record; without one the order is presumed lawful and factually supported. Anchors the slice.

changes.case: Zaderaka v. Illinois Human Rights Commission
changes.what: Illinois Human Rights Act discrimination claims follow the federal Title VII and ADEA frameworks.

history: Dominant rule: New Mexico appellate courts view the evidence most favourably to the verdict and ask whether any rational juror could find each element beyond a reasonable doubt; the factfinder may reject the defendant's version (Rojo, 1998; Sutphin, 1988; Cunningham, 2000). Rojo anchors 2005-09 through 2015-19, adding that the court will not search the record for preservation. How it changed: in 2005-09 Swafford (1991) leads beside Rojo: legislative intent is the only double-jeopardy limit on multiple punishments, analysed through unitary conduct; Alberico (1993) on scientific evidence also leads. Tollardo (2012) enters in 2010-14 and made non-constitutional harmless error turn on a reasonable probability of affecting the verdict; Swick (2012) applied the subsumed-elements bar, and Belanger (2009) addressed material defence testimony. Montoya (2015) enters in 2015-19 and anchors 2020-24 on preservation. Also: Franklin (1967) and Boyer (1985) on presenting a client's contentions; fundamental error for unpreserved instructions (Benally, 2001); ineffective assistance on direct appeal (Roybal, 2002; Aker, 2005). The partial 2025-29 slice merges with other units under Armendariz (2003).

name: Ohio Civ.R. 60(B) relief from judgment: the GTE Automatic Electric test
description: Ohio Civ.R. 60(B) relief from judgment, a single 2000-04 slice: GTE Automatic Electric (1976) requires a meritorious defense, a ground under (B)(1)-(5) and timeliness, and imputes counsel's neglect to the party. Adams (1988) denies relief if any element fails; Griffey (1987) and Strack (1994) set abuse-of-discretion review; Adomeit and Lohman confine (B)(5); Kay (1996) requires a hearing on operative facts.
history: Dominant rule: the GTE Automatic Electric (1976) test for Ohio Civ.R. 60(B) relief: a meritorious claim or defense, a ground under (B)(1)-(5), and a timely motion. GTE anchors the lineage's only slice, 2000-04, which split from the Ohio civil-appeals abuse-of-discretion lineage. How it changed: no change within the span; the leading cases restate the test. Adams (1988) holds that a motion fails if any one requirement is not met; Griffey (1987) and Strack (1994) commit the ruling to the trial court's discretion; Adomeit (1974) and Lohman (1983) keep (B)(5) for extraordinary cases and bar its use as a substitute for the specific grounds; Kay (1996) requires a hearing when the motion alleges operative facts that would warrant relief. Also: Moore (1985) and Doddridge (1978) on lack of notice as a ground, Colley (1980) and GTE on finality of 60(B) orders, and Knapp (1980) on the appellant's duty to supply a transcript.
rule: To obtain relief under Ohio Civ.R. 60(B) the movant must show a meritorious claim or defense, entitlement to relief under one of the grounds in (B)(1)-(5), and a timely motion; failing any one requires denial, and the ruling is reviewed for abuse of discretion.

changes.case: GTE Automatic Electric v. ARC Industries
changes.what: Set the three-part 60(B) test and imputed an attorney's neglect to the party under 60(B)(1).
60(B)(5) is reserved for extraordinary cases and is not a substitute for the more specific grounds; a motion without operative facts may be denied without a hearing.
Rulings are discretionary and reviewed for abuse of discretion; a motion fails if any requirement is unmet, and a hearing is required when operative facts warranting relief are alleged.

name: Procedural due process: Mathews balancing, property and liberty interests
description: Procedural due process, 2010-19: a protected interest (Roth, Loudermill; Sandin for prisoners), then Mathews (1976) balancing to set the process due, with Mullane notice. Morrissey and Gagnon revocation hearings anchor 2010-14 and Swarthout (2011) cut California parole review to notice and reasons; in 2015-19 Mathews anchors as civil commitment and forced medication cases (Addington, Foucha, Harper, Sell) enter.

previous.name: Procedural due process: Mathews, property interests, prison discipline
previous.description: Procedural due-process cluster (2010-19) built on Mathews balancing, Roth and Loudermill property interests, Morrissey parole revocation, and Wolff, Sandin, Hill and Wilkinson on prison discipline and atypical-hardship liberty interests.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session subagents, from cocite evidence; second pass differentiated near-duplicates)

history: Dominant rule: the two-step procedural due-process inquiry: is there a protected interest, and if so, what process does Mathews (1976) balancing require. Property comes from a legitimate entitlement under state law (Roth, 1972), so for-cause employees get a pretermination hearing (Loudermill, 1985); prisoners' liberty interests require atypical and significant hardship (Sandin, 1995; Wilkinson, 2005), with Wolff (1974) and Hill (1985) on disciplinary process; Parratt, Hudson and Daniels make post-deprivation remedies enough for random acts and exclude negligence. Notice must be reasonably calculated to reach the party (Mullane, 1950; Jones v. Flowers, 2006). How it changed: in 2010-14 Morrissey (1972) anchors, with Gagnon on revocation and the California parole 'some evidence' cases (Lawrence and Shaputis, 2008; Hayward, 2010) until Swarthout (2011) held federal due process requires only a hearing and reasons. In 2015-19 Mathews anchors and civil-commitment and medication cases merge in: Addington (1979, clear and convincing proof), Foucha (1992), Harper (1990), Sell (2003) and Washington sexually-violent-predator cases (Thorell, Post).
rule: Once a protected property or liberty interest is shown (Roth, Sandin), the process due is set by Mathews balancing of the private interest, the risk of error and value of added safeguards, and the government's interest, with notice reasonably calculated to reach the party (Mullane).

changes.case: Morrissey v. Brewer; Gagnon v. Scarpelli
changes.what: Parole and probation revocation require informal hearings with basic due-process protections; Morrissey anchors 2010-14.
Three-factor balancing to decide what process is due; Mathews anchors 2015-19.

changes.case: Cleveland Board of Education v. Loudermill
changes.what: A public employee removable only for cause is entitled to notice and an opportunity to respond before termination.
Indefinite supermax placement imposes an atypical and significant hardship, but informal nonadversary procedures suffice.

For California parole, federal due process requires only an opportunity to be heard and a statement of reasons; California's 'some evidence' rule (Lawrence, Shaputis, Hayward) is state law not enforceable on federal habeas.

name: Second Circuit criminal appeals: sufficiency (Autuori, Samaria), officer experts
description: Second Circuit criminal appeals in a single 2005-09 slice anchored by Autuori (2000): sufficiency review deferring to the jury, but requiring proof of knowledge and specific intent (Samaria 2001). Case-agent expert testimony is limited to criminal methods (Dukagjini 2002, Lombardozzi 2007); venue follows essential conduct (Anderson 1946, Cabrales 1998). Also RICO predicates (Bruno 2004, Reifler 2006), Rule 404(b) review (Downing 2002) and Salameh (1998).
history: Dominant rule: Second Circuit review of fraud, racketeering and conspiracy convictions for sufficiency and trial error. Autuori (2000) anchors the lineage's only slice, 2005-09, formed from First Circuit waiver and other criminal units and splitting in 2010-14. How it changed: no change within the span; the leading cases settle the circuit's rules. Autuori allowed mail-fraud liability for omissions where a duty to disclose exists and stressed deference to jury verdicts; Samaria (2001) reversed where the evidence showed only transport, not knowledge that goods were stolen; a 2004 decision required specific intent to violate the substantive statute for conspiracy. Dukagjini (2002) and Lombardozzi (2007) limited case agents testifying as experts, and Gaskin (2004) held a stipulated expert opinion cannot be challenged on appeal. Venue follows the essential conduct elements (Anderson 1946; Cabrales 1998 for money laundering). Alongside: RICO predicates need not further the enterprise (Bruno 2004) and Booker does not bar judge-found restitution (Reifler 2006); Downing (2002) on limiting instructions, Salameh (1998) on the World Trade Center bombing trial, Yousef (2003) and Jones (2004) on testimonial statements.
rule: The Second Circuit upholds a conviction if any rational juror could find the elements beyond a reasonable doubt, but conspiracy and knowledge require proof of specific intent and knowledge rather than mere association (Samaria); law-enforcement experts may explain criminal methods but may not relay hearsay or link the defendant to particular conduct (Dukagjini, Lombardozzi); venue lies where the essential conduct elements occurred (Anderson, Cabrales).

changes.case: United States v. Anderson; United States v. Cabrales
changes.what: Venue is determined by the essential conduct elements of the offense; money laundering is tried where the financial transactions occurred.
Mail fraud may rest on omitting information one has a duty to disclose, and a jury verdict supported by the evidence should not be set aside; Autuori anchors the slice.
Transporting stolen goods was insufficient to prove the defendant knew they were stolen or intended to join the conspiracy.

changes.case: United States v. Dukagjini; United States v. Lombardozzi (2d Cir.)
changes.what: A case agent testifying as an expert may not transmit hearsay or go beyond methods of criminal organizations, though the error may be harmless if the evidence was cumulative.

changes.case: United States v. Bruno; United States v. Reifler (2d Cir.)
changes.what: RICO predicates need not be in furtherance of the enterprise; Booker does not bar judge-found MVRA restitution.

history: Dominant rule: the North Carolina Supreme Court reviews each death sentence for proportionality against a pool of similar cases, and it applies ordinary preservation rules to capital defendants. Benson (1988) anchors 1995-99: constitutional issues not raised at trial are not reviewed. How it changed: Jackson (1983) placed proportionality review in the Supreme Court; Bondurant (1983), Young (1985) and Rogers (1986) found sentences disproportionate. McKoy v. North Carolina (1990) struck down the unanimity requirement for mitigating circumstances, and cases such as Neville were vacated for reconsideration. Green (1994) let jurors reject nonstatutory mitigators that they find have no mitigating value. Gaines (1997) anchors 2000-04, and Gaines and Vandiver overruled Rogers in part on other grounds; Rogers anchors the small 2005-09 slice. Also: prosecutorial argument reviewed for gross impropriety ex mero motu (Hill, Billings), Batson and juror-removal rulings (McCollum, Robinson), and aggravators such as 'great value' (Vandiver) and the officer and avoid-arrest circumstances (Nicholson).

name: Third Circuit pretext at summary judgment: Fuentes v. Perskie
description: Third Circuit employment-discrimination pretext at summary judgment, 1995-99 (one slice): Fuentes v. Perskie (1994, anchor) lets a plaintiff defeat summary judgment by showing weaknesses, implausibilities or inconsistencies that make the employer's reason unworthy of credence, or that discrimination was more likely a determinative cause. Armbruster, Waldron and Sheridan (en banc 1996) rejected pretext-plus; Miller (1995) required determinative effect in ADEA cases.
history: Dominant rule: Fuentes v. Perskie (3d Cir. 1994), the anchor, sets the plaintiff's burden at summary judgment once the employer articulates a legitimate reason: point to evidence from which a factfinder could reasonably disbelieve that reason or believe discrimination was more likely than not a determinative cause, showing weaknesses, implausibilities or contradictions; stray remarks and post hoc documentation alone do not suffice. How it applied: Chipollini (en banc 1987), Josey (1993) and Ezold (1993) supplied the framework, Ezold focusing on the employer's actual reasons. Armbruster (1994), Waldron (1995) and Sheridan v. DuPont (en banc 1996) held, after Hicks, that disbelief plus the prima facie case can support an inference of discrimination, rejecting pretext-plus. Miller v. CIGNA (en banc 1995) required age to have a determinative effect in ADEA cases, and Seman (1994) confined mixed-motive analysis to direct-evidence cases. The prima facie case is flexible (Torre 1994, Sempier 1995). Single slice.
rule: In the Third Circuit, a discrimination plaintiff survives summary judgment after the employer articulates a legitimate reason by pointing to evidence from which a factfinder could reasonably disbelieve that reason or believe discrimination was more likely than not a determinative cause; no pretext-plus showing is required.

changes.what: Plaintiff defeats summary judgment by evidence discrediting the employer's reason or showing discrimination was more likely a determinative cause.
McDonnell Douglas pretext analysis, not mixed-motive, applies absent direct evidence.

changes.case: Miller v. CIGNA Corp. (3d Cir. en banc)
changes.what: In ADEA pretext cases age must have had a determinative effect on the decision.

changes.case: Waldron v. SL Industries; Sheridan v. E.I. DuPont (3d Cir. en banc)

history: Dominant rule: Crawford (2004) anchors every slice from 2010-14 to 2025-29. Testimonial statements of an absent witness are admissible only if the witness is unavailable and was subject to prior cross-examination; Ohio v. Roberts's (1980) reliability test survives only as history. How it changed: the lineage forms in 2010-14 as the forensic line leads. Davis (2006) supplied the primary-purpose test and Giles (2008) limited forfeiture by wrongdoing; Melendez-Diaz (2009) and Bullcoming (2011) required the analyst; Bryant (2011) treated emergency statements as nontestimonial; and Williams v. Illinois (2012) split on expert reliance on DNA reports, which state courts read cautiously (Michaels, N.J. 2014). Bruton (1968) is confined to testimonial statements (Vasquez 2014). In 2015-19 Ohio v. Clark (2015) enters, with lower-court primary-purpose cases (Koslowski 2009). In 2020-24 California's Sanchez (2016) and gang-expert cases (Albillar 2010; Vang 2011) lead. In 2025-29 Smith v. Arizona (2024) enters. Van Arsdall (1986) and Davis v. Alaska (1974) govern limits on cross-examination, Craig (1990) allows child testimony by closed-circuit television, and Holmes (2006) protects third-party-guilt evidence.
rule: Testimonial statements of a witness absent from trial are admissible only if the witness is unavailable and the defendant had a prior opportunity to cross-examine (Crawford), with testimonial status turning on the statement's primary purpose (Davis; Bryant).

changes.what: Replaced Ohio v. Roberts's reliability test with a categorical bar on unconfronted testimonial statements.
Statements are testimonial when the primary purpose of police questioning is to establish past events for prosecution, not to meet an ongoing emergency.
Forfeiture by wrongdoing applies only where the defendant intended to prevent the witness from testifying.

changes.case: Melendez-Diaz v. Massachusetts; Bullcoming v. New Mexico
changes.what: Forensic lab reports and certificates are testimonial; the analyst who made the certification must testify.
Statements to police addressing an ongoing emergency, judged objectively, are not testimonial.
A fractured Court allowed an expert to rely on a non-testifying analyst's DNA profile, the plurality reasoning it was not offered for its truth.
Statements to persons other than law enforcement, such as teachers, are much less likely to be testimonial.
A gang expert may not relate case-specific testimonial hearsay as the basis of an opinion; disapproved Gardeley's not-for-truth reasoning.
Basis testimony that an expert relays to support an opinion is offered for its truth, rejecting the Williams plurality's approach.
