In 2015-19 Ohio v. Clark (2015) enters. In 2020-24 California's Sanchez (2016) and gang-expert cases (Gardeley, Vang, Prunty) lead. In 2025-29 Smith v. Arizona (2024) enters, along with right-to-present-a-defence cases (Chambers, Crane). Van Arsdall (1986) and Davis v. Alaska (1974) govern limits on cross-examination.
round1.rule: The Confrontation Clause bars testimonial out-of-court statements unless the declarant is unavailable and the defendant had a prior opportunity to cross-examine (Crawford); a statement is testimonial when its primary purpose is to establish past facts for prosecution rather than to meet an ongoing emergency (Davis, Bryant).

changes.what: Replaced Ohio v. Roberts's reliability test for testimonial hearsay with a categorical cross-examination requirement.

changes.case: Davis v. Washington; Hammon v. Indiana
changes.what: Primary-purpose test: statements to police to meet an ongoing emergency are nontestimonial; statements to prove past events are testimonial.
Crawford is not retroactive on collateral review, and nontestimonial hearsay falls outside the Clause.
Forfeiture by wrongdoing applies only where the defendant intended to prevent the witness from testifying.

changes.case: Melendez-Diaz v. Massachusetts; Bullcoming v. New Mexico
changes.what: Forensic certificates are testimonial, and a surrogate analyst who did not perform or observe the test cannot satisfy confrontation.
A mortally wounded victim's statements to police during an ongoing emergency were nontestimonial.
A fractured Court allowed an expert to rely on a DNA report not offered for its truth or not testimonial, leaving its precedential force unclear.
Statements to non-law-enforcement persons such as teachers are much less likely to be testimonial.

Arizona (2024) resolved against not-for-truth reasoning. Ohio v. Clark (2015) narrowed statements to non-police.

That sibling is the 2005-09 move from Roberts' reliability test to Crawford; this one applies Crawford in 2010-29 to forensic evidence, emergencies (Bryant) and statements to non-police (Clark).

name: ADA disability and accommodation: Sutton and Toyota's strict reading
description: Who is disabled under the ADA and what employers owe, 2000-09. Sutton (1999), anchor of both slices, with Murphy and Kirkingburg counted mitigating measures; Toyota (2002) required severe limits on activities central to daily life; Bragdon (1998) found asymptomatic HIV a disability. Circuit cases set interactive-process duties (Benson 1995, Midland Brake 1999). The ADA Amendments Act of 2008 superseded Sutton and Toyota.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, round 2 after the lineage re-link)

previous.name: Disability discrimination: ADA and Rehabilitation Act
previous.description: What counts as a disability and what employers owe: substantial limitation of a major life activity (Sutton, Murphy, Kirkingburg, Toyota v. Williams, Bragdon), reasonable accommodation, and Rehabilitation Act § 504 (Arline, Southeastern Community College v. Davis, Alexander v. Choate).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: a plaintiff must prove an impairment that substantially limits a major life activity and that he is qualified with or without reasonable accommodation. Sutton (1999) anchors both slices, 2000-04 and 2005-09: corrective measures count in deciding disability, as Murphy (1999) and Kirkingburg (1999) applied with individual assessment. Bragdon (1998) held asymptomatic HIV a disability. How it changed: Toyota (2002) enters in 2000-04 and demanded a severe restriction of activities central to daily life, rejecting a focus on job tasks. Circuit cases fill in the employer's duties: the plaintiff must show an accommodation is possible (Benson 1995), both parties must engage in good faith in the interactive process (Gile 1996, Fjellestad and Taylor 1999), the employer may choose among reasonable accommodations (Midland Brake 1999), and seniority limits reassignment (Dalton 1998). Courts also rejected claimed limits on sleeping, lifting and recreation (Colwell 1998, Thompson 1997, Weber 1999). In 2005-09 Head (9th Cir. 2005) eased proof of limitation and Kolstad (1999) governs punitive damages. The ADA Amendments Act of 2008 superseded Sutton and Toyota, and the unit splits in 2010-14.
rule: An ADA plaintiff must show an impairment that, considering mitigating measures, substantially limits a major life activity of central importance to daily life, and that he is qualified with a reasonable accommodation reached through a good-faith interactive process.

changes.what: Asymptomatic HIV substantially limits the major life activity of reproduction.

changes.case: Sutton v. United Air Lines; Murphy v. UPS; Albertson's v. Kirkingburg
changes.what: Disability is judged with mitigating measures taken into account and by individual assessment; a mere difference is not a substantial limitation.

changes.case: Benson v. Northwest Airlines (8th Cir.); Gile v. United Airlines (7th Cir.); Smith v. Midland Brake (10th Cir. en banc); Fjellestad v. Pizza Hut (8th Cir.); Taylor v. Phoenixville (3d Cir.)
changes.what: The plaintiff must show an accommodation is possible; both sides must engage in the interactive process in good faith; the employer need not give the preferred accommodation, and reassignment has limits.
Reassignment is not required where it would violate a seniority system or legitimate transfer policies.
A substantial limitation must prevent or severely restrict activities of central importance to most people's daily lives, not just job tasks.
Rejected Sutton's mitigating-measures rule and Toyota's demanding standard, requiring broad coverage.

round1.name: Disability under the ADA and § 504: Arline, then Sutton and Toyota's strict reading
round1.description: Who is disabled and what employers owe under the Rehabilitation Act and ADA (1990-2014): Arline (1987) anchors 1990-99 with individualized inquiry; circuits require proof that accommodation is possible and an interactive process (White 1995, Bultemeyer 1996). Sutton (1999) and Toyota (2002), anchors from 2000-04, narrowed disability by counting mitigating measures and requiring severe limits; the ADA Amendments Act of 2008 superseded both.
round1.history: Dominant rule: a plaintiff must prove an impairment that substantially limits a major life activity and that he is otherwise qualified. Arline (1987) anchors 1990-99: tuberculosis could be a handicap, others' reactions can limit working, and qualification is decided individually. Davis (1979) requires no fundamental alteration, and Alexander v. Choate (1985) sets meaningful access. Postal Service cases (Jasany 1985, Forrisi 1986) held that one job is not working in general. How it changed: under the ADA, the 1995-99 circuit cases lead. White (1995) and Benson (1995) put on the plaintiff the burden to show accommodation is possible, Bultemeyer (1996) found bad faith in the interactive process, and Wooten (1995) followed the narrow-job rule. Bragdon (1998) held asymptomatic HIV a disability. Sutton (1999), Murphy and Kirkingburg then counted mitigating measures and required individual assessment, and Sutton anchors 2000-09. Toyota (2002), the 2010-14 anchor, demanded a severe restriction of activities central to daily life, and Barnett (2002) favored seniority systems. The ADA Amendments Act of 2008 superseded Sutton and Toyota, which is why the unit fades after 2010-14, where claims arising before the Act still apply them.
round1.rule: A plaintiff under the Rehabilitation Act or ADA must show an impairment that substantially limits a major life activity (or a record of, or being regarded as having, one) and that he is otherwise qualified with or without reasonable accommodation; from 1999 to the 2008 amendments the Supreme Court read 'substantially limits' strictly, counting mitigating measures and requiring a severe restriction of activities central to daily life.

changes.case: Southeastern Community College v. Davis; Alexander v. Choate
changes.what: § 504 requires no fundamental alteration or affirmative action, only meaningful access for otherwise qualified persons.

changes.case: School Board of Nassau County v. Arline
changes.what: A contagious disease can be a handicap, and the negative reactions of others can substantially limit working; qualification needs an individualized inquiry.

changes.case: Jasany; Forrisi; Byrne; Wooten v. Farmland Foods
changes.what: Inability to perform one particular job is not a substantial limitation on working.

changes.case: White v. York International; Benson v. Northwest Airlines; Bultemeyer; Smith v. Midland Brake
changes.what: The plaintiff must show an accommodation is possible, and employers must engage in good faith in an interactive process, offering a reasonable (not the preferred) accommodation.
Asymptomatic HIV substantially limits the major life activity of reproduction.

changes.case: Sutton v. United Air Lines; Murphy; Albertson's v. Kirkingburg; Toyota v. Williams
changes.what: Disability is assessed with mitigating measures, individually, and requires a severe, long-term restriction on activities of central importance to daily life.
An accommodation that conflicts with a seniority system is ordinarily not reasonable.
Congress rejected Sutton and Toyota, excluding mitigating measures and directing a broad reading of disability.

name: Colorado criminal statutes: vagueness and equal protection for identical conduct
description: Colorado criminal law, 1975-84: equal protection bars punishing identical conduct more harshly under a separate statute without a real distinction (Calvaresi, 1975; Marcy, 1981), though harsher penalties for more specific conduct survive (Czajkowski, 1977). Statutes are saved from vagueness by constitutional construction (Blue; Garcia, 1975, anchor 1980-84). Bennett (1973, anchor 1975-79) dropped the circumstantial-evidence hypothesis rule.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Colorado criminal: equal protection and overlapping statutes
previous.description: Colorado Supreme Court decisions holding criminal statutes unconstitutional where they punish identical conduct differently (Calvaresi, Marcy on extreme-indifference murder) and deadly-weapon definitions.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, contrastive pass from family evidence)

history: Dominant rule: Colorado courts sustain criminal statutes against vagueness and overbreadth when a constitutional construction is available, but under the state's equal-protection guarantee a statute that punishes conduct indistinguishable from a lesser offense more severely is invalid. How it changed: Bennett (1973) anchors 1975-79; it replaced the rule that circumstantial evidence must exclude every reasonable hypothesis of innocence with a single sufficiency test. Calvaresi (1975) struck felony manslaughter as indistinguishable from criminally negligent homicide, while Czajkowski (1977) and Marques (1974) upheld distinct or presumptive-value provisions. In 1980-84 Garcia (1975) anchors and Blue (1975) leads, upholding the arson and weapon-possession statutes by reading in a voluntary act and a choice-of-evils defense; People in Interest of C.M. (1981) adopts the constitutional reading of an ambiguous statute. Marcy (1981) extended Calvaresi, holding the extreme-indifference murder definition indistinguishable from second-degree murder. Also: vagueness challenges to sexual-assault and child-abuse statutes (Smith, Taggart, Hoehl) and right-to-travel and licence cases (Heninger, Colorado Auto & Truck Wreckers).
rule: Under Colorado's equal-protection guarantee a statute may not punish the same conduct more severely under one offense than another without a reasonable distinction between them, and criminal statutes are upheld against vagueness and overbreadth where a constitutional construction is available.

changes.what: Discarded the rule that wholly circumstantial evidence must exclude every reasonable hypothesis of innocence; one sufficiency test applies to direct and circumstantial evidence. Anchors 1975-79.
The felony manslaughter statute violated equal protection because it could not be distinguished from criminally negligent homicide.

changes.case: People v. Blue; People v. Garcia
changes.what: Upheld the possession-of-weapon-by-previous-offender and arson statutes against vagueness and overbreadth, reading in a choice-of-evils defense and a voluntary-act requirement; Garcia anchors 1980-84.
A greater penalty for more specific conduct, such as stealing auto parts, does not violate equal protection.
The extreme-indifference murder definition violated equal protection because it was indistinguishable from second-degree murder.

name: Florida capital postconviction: strategic-choice IAC claims, then Hurst
description: Florida death-penalty postconviction law: Huff (1993) hearings and Strickland claims rejected for reasonable strategy or meritless issues (Occhicone, Freeman, 2000; Sochor, 2004, anchor 2010-14). Hurst v. Florida (2016) struck the advisory-jury scheme under Ring. Hurst v. State (2016) required unanimity, applied only to sentences final after Ring (Mosley, Asay, Hitchcock); Poole (2020) later receded from it.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Florida capital postconviction and Hurst
previous.description: Florida death-penalty litigation: Rule 3.851 postconviction claims and Huff hearings, strategic decisions of counsel (Occhicone, Sochor), and Hurst v. Florida's application of Ring to Florida's sentencing scheme.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: in Florida capital postconviction review, counsel's reasonable strategic choices and failures to raise meritless issues are not ineffective, and claims that could have been raised on direct appeal are barred. How it changed: Huff (1993) anchors 2005-09, guaranteeing a hearing on initial postconviction motions, with Occhicone, Freeman and Rutherford (2000). Johnson (2005) held Ring not retroactive in Florida. Sochor (2004) anchors 2010-14 with Maxwell (1986) and the older Michel and Affronti strategy cases, and lethal-injection challenges are rejected (Lightbourne, 2007; Baze, 2008). In 2015-19 the anchor shifts to Hurst v. State (2016), after Hurst v. Florida (2016) applied Ring to strike the advisory-jury scheme. Florida then required unanimous death recommendations and applied Hurst to sentences final after Ring (Mosley, 2016), but not earlier ones (Asay; Hitchcock, 2017). In 2020-24 Spencer (1993) anchors, with DiGuilio's (1986) harmless-error test, as Poole (2020) receded from the unanimity requirement.
rule: In Florida capital postconviction proceedings, ineffective-assistance claims fail where counsel made a reasonable strategic choice after considering alternatives or failed to raise a meritless issue, and claims that could have been raised on direct appeal are barred; from 2016 the lineage turns on Hurst's requirement that a jury find the facts needed for death.

changes.case: Huff v. State; Spencer v. State
changes.what: Capital postconviction movants get a hearing to determine whether an evidentiary hearing is needed, and trial courts must hold a post-penalty-phase hearing for additional evidence and argument.

changes.case: Occhicone v. State; Freeman v. State; Rutherford v. Moore
changes.what: Strategic decisions are not deficient if alternatives were considered and rejected reasonably; claims that could have been raised on direct appeal cannot be relitigated as IAC; appellate counsel is not ineffective for omitting meritless claims.
Both Strickland prongs are mixed questions reviewed with deference to findings of fact; anchors 2010-14.
Ring v. Arizona does not apply retroactively to Florida cases final when it was decided.
Florida's scheme, in which the jury's recommendation was advisory and the judge found aggravators, violated the Sixth Amendment under Ring.

changes.case: Hurst v. State (Fla.); Mosley v. State
changes.what: On remand Florida required a unanimous jury recommendation of death and applied Hurst retroactively to sentences that became final after Ring.

changes.case: Asay v. State; Hitchcock v. State
changes.what: Hurst relief is unavailable to defendants whose sentences were final before Ring (2002).
The Florida Supreme Court receded from Hurst v. State's requirement of a unanimous death recommendation, keeping only a unanimous finding of an aggravator.

name: Conflicted counsel and presumed prejudice: Cuyler, Holloway, Mickens, Cronic
description: When counsel's conflict or absence is presumed prejudicial, one 2000-04 slice anchored by Cuyler (1980): an actual conflict that adversely affects performance violates the Sixth Amendment without Strickland prejudice (Holloway 1978), courts must inquire into known conflicts (Wood 1981), and Cronic (1984) presumes prejudice when counsel fails entirely. Mickens (2002) required adverse effect; Wheat (1988) let courts refuse waivers.
history: Dominant rule: when the Sixth Amendment presumes prejudice from counsel's conflict or absence. In the single 2000-04 slice Cuyler v. Sullivan (1980) anchors: an actual conflict that adversely affected performance violates the right to counsel. How it changed: Holloway (1978) presumed prejudice when joint representation was forced over objection; Wood (1981) imposed a duty to inquire where a conflict is apparent; Wheat (1988) let trial courts refuse conflict waivers; Mickens (2002) held that a failure to inquire does not relieve the defendant of showing adverse effect, and suggested Cuyler's presumption may be limited to concurrent multiple representation. Cronic (1984) presumed prejudice where counsel is absent or fails entirely, building on Powell (1932), Hamilton (1961), White (1963), Herring (1975) and Geders (1976). Roe v. Flores-Ortega (2000) applied Strickland to failures to file an appeal. Circuit cases (Levy, 2d Cir. 1994; Schwarz, 2d Cir. 2002) found actual conflicts. The unit merged in from a Texas ineffective-assistance unit and passes on in 2005-09.
rule: A defendant whose lawyer labored under an actual conflict of interest that adversely affected performance, or who was denied counsel at a critical stage, need not show Strickland prejudice (Holloway; Cuyler; Cronic), but presumed prejudice requires an actual conflict affecting performance, not a mere theoretical division of loyalties (Mickens).

changes.case: Powell v. Alabama; Hamilton v. Alabama; White v. Maryland
changes.what: Counsel must be provided in a substantial sense, and denial of counsel at a critical stage such as arraignment or a preliminary hearing requires reversal without inquiry into prejudice.

changes.case: Herring v. New York; Geders v. United States
changes.what: Denying closing argument or barring consultation with counsel during an overnight recess violates the right to counsel without a showing of prejudice.
Requiring joint representation over a timely conflict objection is reversible without a showing of prejudice.

changes.case: Cuyler v. Sullivan; Wood v. Georgia
changes.what: An actual conflict that adversely affected counsel's performance violates the Sixth Amendment; a court must inquire into a conflict it knows or reasonably should know of.
Prejudice is presumed where counsel entirely fails to subject the prosecution's case to meaningful adversarial testing.
District courts have substantial latitude to refuse waivers of conflicts, limiting the right to counsel of choice.
A trial court's failure to inquire does not dispense with proof that the conflict adversely affected counsel's performance.

before_differentiation.name: Conflict-free counsel and presumed prejudice: Cuyler, Holloway, Cronic, Mickens
before_differentiation.description: Conflicts of interest and presumed prejudice in 2000-04: an actual conflict that adversely affects counsel's performance violates the Sixth Amendment without Strickland prejudice (Cuyler, 1980, anchor; Holloway, 1978), courts must inquire into known conflicts (Wood, 1981), and Cronic (1984) presumes prejudice for complete failures of counsel. Mickens (2002) required proof of adverse effect; Wheat (1988) let courts refuse conflict waivers.

distinct_from.how: Concerns presumed prejudice from counsel's conflict or failure, not automatic reversal for structural errors and Custis attacks.
Concerns defence counsel's conflicts, not a biased judge.
Concerns counsel's conflicts, not burden-shifting instructions.
Concerns presumed prejudice from conflicted counsel, not habeas harmless-error standards.
Is anchored by Cuyler on conflicts and Cronic, while that lineage is anchored by Faretta on self-representation.
Concerns conflicts of interest in 2000-04, not California self-representation and Marsden hearings in the 2020s.

name: Brady disclosure and knowing use of false testimony
description: The prosecution's due-process disclosure duties. Mooney (1935) and Napue (1959, anchor 1960-64) bar knowing use of false testimony; Brady (1963) anchors every slice from 1965-69, requiring disclosure of material favorable evidence. Giglio (1972) added impeachment evidence, Agurs (1976) duties without request, Bagley (1985) the reasonable-probability standard, Youngblood (1989) bad faith for lost evidence, and Kyles (1995) and Strickler (1999) police knowledge and prejudice.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Brady disclosure and false testimony
previous.description: The prosecution's due-process duties: suppression of exculpatory and impeachment evidence (Brady, Giglio, Agurs, Bagley, Kyles, Strickler), knowing use of false testimony (Mooney, Napue) and failure to preserve evidence (Trombetta, Youngblood).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: Brady (1963) anchors 1965-2004: suppressing material evidence favorable to the accused violates due process. How it changed: in 1960-64 Napue (1959) anchors the false-testimony line from Mooney (1935), Pyle (1942) and Alcorta (1957). Brady enters in 1965-69 with Giles (1967) and Barbee (4th Cir. 1964) imputing police knowledge to prosecutors. Giglio (1972) enters in 1970-74, extending the duty to witness-impeachment material. Agurs (1976) enters in 1975-79, recognizing a duty without a request but requiring materiality. In 1985-89 Bagley (1985) unified materiality as a reasonable probability of a different outcome, Trombetta (1984) and Youngblood (1989) required bad faith for unpreserved evidence, and Valenzuela-Bernal (1982) addressed deported witnesses. Ritchie (1987) enters in 1990-94 on in camera review of files. Kyles (1995) enters in 1995-99, charging prosecutors with police knowledge and requiring cumulative assessment, and Strickler (1999) leads 2000-04 before the unit splits into habeas and Florida capital postconviction units.
rule: Due process is violated when the prosecution suppresses evidence favorable to the accused, including impeachment evidence, that is material, meaning there is a reasonable probability of a different result (Brady, Giglio, Bagley, Kyles), or when it knowingly uses or fails to correct false testimony (Mooney, Napue).

changes.case: Mooney v. Holohan; Alcorta v. Texas; Napue v. Illinois
changes.what: A conviction obtained through testimony the prosecution knows to be false, or fails to correct, violates due process; Napue anchors 1960-64.
Suppression of evidence favorable to an accused and material to guilt or punishment violates due process regardless of good faith; anchors from 1965-69.
Brady covers evidence impeaching a key government witness, including promises of leniency.
The duty to disclose exists even without a request, but the mere possibility of help to the defense is not materiality.

changes.case: California v. Trombetta; Arizona v. Youngblood
changes.what: Failure to preserve potentially useful evidence violates due process only on a showing of bad faith.
A single materiality standard for exculpatory and impeachment evidence: a reasonable probability of a different result.

changes.case: Kyles v. Whitley; Strickler v. Greene
changes.what: Prosecutors are responsible for evidence known to police, materiality is assessed cumulatively, and a Brady claim requires favorable, suppressed and prejudicial evidence.

name: Tennessee suppression review and searches (Odom, Walton, Yeargan)
description: Tennessee review of suppression rulings, anchored by Odom (1996) in 2010-24 and Henning (1998) in 2025-29: findings stand unless the evidence preponderates otherwise, law is reviewed de novo (Walton 2001), the whole record may be used (Henning), video is reviewed independently (Binette 2000). Search rules: warrantless searches presumed unreasonable (Yeargan 1997), sworn affidavits (Keith 1998), informant reliability (Echols 2012).
history: Dominant rule: the standard for reviewing Tennessee suppression rulings and the search-and-seizure rules they apply. State v. Odom (1996) anchors 2010-14 through 2020-24, Henning (1998) the partial 2025-29 slice; the lineage forms from a Fourth Amendment unit in 2010-14. How it developed: Odom requires deference to the trial court's findings unless the evidence preponderates otherwise, Walton (2001) reviews the application of law de novo, Henning (1998) lets the court consider the entire record, and Binette (2000) reviews video evidence without deference. Substantive rules recur: warrantless searches are presumed unreasonable (Yeargan 1997; Garcia 2003); warrants need a sworn written affidavit (Keith 1998); consensual encounters versus seizures (Daniel 2000; Williams 2006); traffic stops on probable cause or reasonable suspicion (Cox 2005; Nicholson 2006; Berrios 2007), with article I, section 7 co-extensive with the Fourth Amendment (McCormick 2016); probable cause judged objectively (Bell 2014); and informant reliability (Echols 2012). Also: confessions after promises of leniency (Smith 1996) and invocation of counsel (Climer 2013).
rule: On review of a Tennessee suppression ruling the trial court's findings of fact are upheld unless the evidence preponderates otherwise (Odom), its application of law to facts is reviewed de novo (Walton), and a warrantless search or seizure is presumed unreasonable unless the State shows an exception (Yeargan).

changes.what: Credibility and factual findings at a suppression hearing are upheld unless the evidence preponderates against them, with the prevailing party given the strongest view of the evidence.
Warrantless searches and seizures are presumed unreasonable; a stop was valid where the officer knew the driver's license had been revoked.

changes.case: State v. Henning; State v. Keith
changes.what: The reviewing court may consider the entire record, including trial evidence; a written, sworn affidavit is required for a valid warrant.

changes.case: State v. Binette; State v. Daniel
changes.what: Video evidence is reviewed de novo; an encounter does not become a seizure from social pressure alone, but pursuing someone who departs is a seizure.
Application of law to the facts in a suppression ruling is reviewed de novo; the Fifth Amendment covers only testimonial evidence.
For traffic stops article I, section 7 and the Fourth Amendment are co-extensive.

name: Washington ineffective assistance (Strickland): Reichenbach, Kyllo, Grier
description: Washington ineffective-assistance claims on direct appeal and in personal restraint petitions, 2010-29, under Strickland as adopted in Thomas (1987) and McFarland (1995): failing to move to suppress can be deficient (Reichenbach 2004, anchor 2010-14); counsel must research the law (Kyllo 2009, anchor 2015-19), but an all-or-nothing strategy can be legitimate (Grier 2011, anchor 2020-24). Crace (2012) equated Strickland and collateral prejudice.

previous.name: Washington post-conviction ineffective assistance
previous.description: Washington personal restraint petitions on ineffective assistance: Strickland as applied in Grier (all-or-nothing strategy), McFarland, Kyllo, reference hearings for factual disputes, and failure to propose instructions.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: Washington's version of Strickland. The defendant must overcome a strong presumption of a legitimate tactic and show prejudice, and on direct appeal the court looks only at the trial record (McFarland, 1995). How it changed: Reichenbach (2004) anchors 2010-14, finding counsel ineffective for not moving to suppress evidence from an unlawful seizure, alongside Hendrickson (1996) on article I, § 7 searches and Davis (2004) on tactical choices in a personal restraint petition. Kyllo (2009) anchors 2015-19, holding counsel deficient for proposing a flawed pattern instruction. A.N.J. (2010) requires adequate investigation before a juvenile's plea, and Sutherby (2009) on units of prosecution joins. Grier (2011) anchors 2020-24 and allows all-or-nothing strategies, with Crow (2019) requiring that an omitted objection would likely have succeeded and Yarbrough (2009) on tactical omission of limiting instructions. Petition procedure follows Rice (1994), Yates (2013) and Crace (2012). Kyllo anchors the partial 2025-29 slice.
rule: Washington applies Strickland: the defendant must show deficient performance, overcoming the presumption of a conceivable legitimate tactic, and a reasonable probability of a different result, on the trial record for direct appeals or on competent evidence for a reference hearing in a personal restraint petition.

changes.case: State v. Thomas; State v. McFarland; State v. Hendrickson
changes.what: Washington adopted Strickland, failure on either prong defeats the claim, and direct review is limited to the record.

changes.case: In re Personal Restraint of Rice
changes.what: A petitioner must present competent, admissible evidence of facts entitling him to relief to obtain a reference hearing, and may not relitigate issues rejected on direct appeal absent the interests of justice.

changes.case: State v. Reichenbach; In re Personal Restraint of Davis
changes.what: Failing to move to suppress evidence from an unlawful seizure was deficient and prejudicial; forgoing objections to avoid highlighting evidence can be tactical. Reichenbach anchors 2010-14.
Reasonable conduct includes researching the law, and requesting a pattern instruction that case law showed was flawed is deficient; anchors 2015-19 and 2025-29.
Effective assistance may require consulting experts and adequately investigating before a juvenile's guilty plea.
An all-or-nothing strategy forgoing lesser-included instructions can be a legitimate tactic, and the defendant must show the absence of any conceivable legitimate tactic; anchors 2020-24.

changes.case: In re Personal Restraint of Crace
changes.what: A petitioner who meets Strickland prejudice necessarily shows the actual and substantial prejudice needed for collateral relief.

before_differentiation.name: Washington ineffective assistance on appeal and in PRPs: McFarland, Kyllo, Grier
before_differentiation.description: Washington ineffective-assistance claims on direct appeal and in personal restraint petitions under Strickland as adopted in Thomas (1987) and McFarland (1995). Counsel must research the law (Kyllo, 2009, anchor 2015-19), but an all-or-nothing strategy can be legitimate (Grier, 2011, anchor 2020-24). Reference hearings require competent evidence, and Crace (2012) equated Strickland prejudice with collateral prejudice.

This judges defense counsel's performance (Kyllo, Grier); that judges the prosecutor's argument (Emery, Thorgerson) after an earlier capital-review phase.

name: Takings doctrine over five decades: Mahon and Penn Central to Lucas and Sheetz
description: The long-running takings line, 1975-2029: regulation that goes 'too far' (Mahon 1922) is judged under Penn Central's (1978) balancing, with per se rules for permanent physical occupation (Loretto 1982) and total wipeouts (Lucas 1992), and nexus and proportionality for exactions (Nollan 1987, Dolan 1994). Lingle (2005) discarded Agins's test; Knick (2019) overruled state exhaustion; Cedar Point (2021) and Sheetz (2024) extend the rules.

previous.name: Takings Clause: regulatory and physical takings (1980 on)
previous.description: Modern takings law: Penn Central balancing, categorical takings (Loretto physical occupation, Lucas total wipeout), exactions (Nollan, Dolan), Agins and its rejection in Lingle, and ripeness (Williamson County). Its 1970s predecessor (18309) was built on Mahon's 'too far' test.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, contrastive pass from family evidence)

history: Dominant rule: a regulation is a taking when it goes too far. Before 1980 the anchors are Goldblatt (1962) and Mahon (1922), with police-power cases (Mugler, Hadacheck). How it changed: Penn Central (1978) anchors from 1980-84, setting the ad hoc balance of economic impact, investment-backed expectations and the character of the action. Agins (1980) added a 'substantially advances' test, Loretto (1982) a per se rule for physical occupation, and Williamson County (1985) ripeness rules. history: Dominant rule: whether a state prisoner's procedural default in state court bars federal habeas review. How it changed: in 1970-74 Fay v. name: Pre-Guidelines sentencing review: Tucker, Williams v. New York, Townsend
description: Appellate review of federal sentences before the Guidelines (single 1975-79 slice). Tucker (1972, anchor) set aside sentences based on misinformation of constitutional magnitude; Williams v. New York (1949) and Townsend (1948) allowed broad sentencing information but barred materially false assumptions; Dorszynski (1974) kept within-limits sentences unreviewable, while circuits policed rigid sentencing policies (Daniels, Hartford, Woosley).
history: Dominant rule: a federal sentence within statutory limits was not reviewable for severity (Dorszynski 1974), but courts would vacate a sentence that rested on false or constitutionally invalid information or on a refusal to exercise individual discretion. Tucker (1972) anchors the single 1975-79 slice: a sentence influenced by uncounseled prior convictions must be reconsidered. Williams v. New York (1949) and Williams v. Oklahoma (1959) let judges consider information beyond the trial record, while Townsend (1948) found a denial of due process where an uncounseled defendant was sentenced on false assumptions about his record. How it changed: in the late 1960s and early 1970s the circuits used these limits to vacate sentences that relied on thin presentence reports (Weston 1971), punished defendants for going to trial (Scott 1969), or reflected a fixed policy of maximum sentences for draft refusers or LSD dealers (Daniels 1971, Hartford 1974, Woosley 1973), and allowed consideration of acquitted charges (Sweig 1972). The unit splits in 1980-84, before the Sentencing Reform Act of 1984 changed review.

history: Dominant rule: Faretta (1975), the anchor in all four slices: a defendant who knowingly and intelligently waives counsel may conduct his own defence, though not as a licence to ignore procedural rules, and the competency needed to waive counsel is the same as to stand trial (Godinez, 1993), measured by Dusky (1960) and enforced by inquiry when doubt arises (Pate, 1966; Drope, 1975). How it changed: in 2000-04 conflicts of interest lead: Holloway (1978) and Cuyler (1980) presume prejudice from an actual conflict that affects performance, and Mickens (2002) limited that to multiple concurrent representation; Martinez (2000) denied a Faretta right on appeal and Tovar (2004) relaxed plea warnings. In 2005-09 structural-error cases join (Sullivan, 1993; Fulminante, 1991; Tumey, 1927), with Gonzalez-Lopez (2006) on chosen counsel. In 2010-14 Indiana v. Edwards (2008) lets states insist on counsel for gray-area defendants, and California practice appears (Marsden, 1970, on substitute counsel; Windham, 1977, on untimely Faretta requests). In 2015-19 public-trial cases merge in (Waller, 1984).
rule: A defendant competent to stand trial may knowingly and intelligently waive counsel and represent himself (Faretta, Godinez), but a state may insist on counsel for one competent to stand trial yet unable to conduct a defence (Indiana v. Edwards); denial of the right is structural error.

name: Facial vagueness and overbreadth of Texas criminal laws, 2005-09 (Ferber, Salerno)
description: Facial challenges to criminal statutes, a single 2005-09 slice mostly in Texas courts, joining vagueness with speech overbreadth: a law fails if ordinary people must guess at its meaning or police lack minimal guidelines (Connally 1926; Grayned 1972, anchor; Kolender 1983; Morales 1999); overbreadth must be substantial (Ferber 1982; Free Speech Coalition 2002 on virtual child pornography), and Texas applies Salerno's no-set-of-circumstances test (Santikos 1992).

history: Dominant rule: a penal law must give fair notice and set minimal guidelines for enforcement, and a law reaching speech is facially invalid only if its overbreadth is substantial. history: Dominant rule: the Illinois Post-Conviction Hearing Act proceeds in three stages. history: Dominant rule: equal protection forbids invidious classification and invidious enforcement. In 1970-74, anchored by Takahashi (1948), the lineage concerns state laws disadvantaging aliens and racial classifications: Graham v. Richardson (1971) made alienage a suspect class and struck welfare restrictions; Truax (1915), Oyama (1947) and Purdy & Fitzpatrick (1969) supply the background; McLaughlin (1964), Loving (1967) and Hunter (1969) condemn racial lines, with Korematsu (1945) cited for strict scrutiny. Sugarman and In re Griffiths (1973) extended Graham to civil-service and bar membership. How it changed: in 1975-79 Berrios (2d Cir. 1974) anchors and selective prosecution dominates. Oyler (1962) allows some selectivity, Yick Wo (1886) forbids enforcement with an unequal hand, and Snowden (1944) requires intent. Crowthers (4th Cir. 1972) and Falk (7th Cir. en banc 1973) gave the defense force for targeted war resisters; Berrios required a showing that similar offenders went unprosecuted and the selection rested on an impermissible ground, applied in Berrigan (1973) and Scott (1975). The lineage splits in 1980-84.
rule: State classifications based on alienage or race are suspect and need compelling justification, and a facially neutral law enforced with an evil eye and an unequal hand (Yick Wo) denies equal protection, though prosecutors may exercise some selectivity.

round1.history: Dominant rule: prosecutors may exercise some selectivity (Oyler 1962), but enforcing a facially neutral law with an evil eye and an unequal hand denies equal protection (Yick Wo 1886), and the discrimination must be intentional (Snowden 1944). Steele (9th Cir. 1972) reversed a census-refusal conviction aimed at vocal resisters, and Crowthers (4th Cir. 1972) found a prima facie showing that shifted the burden to the government. name: Ohio manifest-weight review 1980-2004: C.E. Morris to Martin, Jenks, Thompkins
description: How Ohio's evidence-review standards formed, 1980-2004: C.E. Morris v. Foley (1978, anchor 1980-89) held a judgment supported by some competent, credible evidence is not against the manifest weight; Martin (1983, anchor 1990-94) let the court reverse a conviction only where the jury clearly lost its way; Jenks (1991) adopted the rational-juror sufficiency test; Thompkins (1997, anchor 1995-2004) separated sufficiency from weight.

history: Dominant rule: Ohio's appellate review of the evidence, as it formed. In 1980-84 and 1985-89 the anchor is C.E. Morris Co. v. Foley Construction (1978): a judgment supported by some competent, credible evidence going to all essential elements will not be reversed as against the manifest weight. How it changed: Martin (1983) anchors 1990-94, letting the appellate court review the whole record as a thirteenth juror and reverse a conviction only where the jury clearly lost its way and created a manifest miscarriage of justice; DeHass (1967) leaves credibility to the factfinder. Jenks (1991) adopted the Jackson v. Virginia rational-juror test for sufficiency and abandoned the rule that circumstantial evidence must exclude every reasonable theory of innocence. Thompkins (1997) anchors 1995-99 and 2000-04: sufficiency is a question of law and manifest weight a separate question, and, following Tibbs (1982), a sufficiency reversal bars retrial but a weight reversal does not. Also: Bradley (1989) on ineffective assistance, plain error for unobjected-to instructions (Long 1978; Adams 1980), lesser-included instructions (Thomas 1988), and older Ohio criminal cases (Bridgeman 1978, Eley 1978).
rule: In Ohio, sufficiency of the evidence is a question of law asking whether any rational juror could find the elements proved, while manifest weight asks whether, on the whole record, the factfinder clearly lost its way so that a new trial is needed.

name: Massachusetts Latimore sufficiency 2010-19: constructive possession of drugs, guns

name: Asylum review (7th and 4th Cir.): persecution, credibility, social group
description: Circuit review of asylum denials, chiefly in the Seventh Circuit (Capric, Georgis, Dandan, 2003-04) and later the Fourth (Camara, 2004; Hernandez-Avalos, 2015). name: Texas sovereign and governmental immunity: clear waiver, pleas to the jurisdiction
description: Texas immunity from suit: the State and local governments are immune unless the Legislature waives immunity clearly (Federal Sign 1997, IT-Davy 2002, Tooke 2006). name: Gissel bargaining orders need stated reasons; Wright Line adopted (1980-84)
description: NLRB enforcement in 1980-84 (one slice), on limits to Gissel (1969) bargaining orders: circuits refused them without a reasoned explanation why a fair election was unlikely (Armcor 1976, Peerless 1973, Red Oaks 1980). history: Dominant rule: courts enforce Board findings supported by substantial evidence on the whole record (Universal Camera 1951, the anchor), giving weight to the administrative law judge who saw the witnesses (Penasquitos Village, 9th Cir. 1977). Wright Line (1st Cir. 1981) adopted the Board's mixed-motive test: once anti-union motive is shown, the employer must prove it would have taken the same action anyway (Delco-Remy 1979 on legitimate discharge). description: Early-1970s justiciability (one slice): voluntary cessation moots a case only if recurrence is not reasonably expected (W.T. Grant 1953, anchor; Concentrated Phosphate 1968); wrongs capable of repetition yet evading review stay live (Southern Pacific 1911); a backpay claim kept Powell (1969) alive. Declaratory suits need an actual controversy (Haworth 1937, Golden v. Zwickler 1969). Also Speech or Debate immunity (Johnson 1966, Gravel 1972).
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, round 2 after the lineage re-link)

previous.name: Mootness, Speech or Debate and justiciability (1970-74)
previous.description: Early-1970s justiciability cases: mootness and voluntary cessation (W.T. Grant, Southern Pacific Terminal, Munsingwear vacatur), Powell v. McCormack, Speech or Debate (Kilbourn, Johnson, Gravel), and challenges to the Vietnam War (Massachusetts v. Laird).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session subagents, from cocite evidence; second pass differentiated near-duplicates)

history: Dominant rule: W.T. Grant (1953) anchors this single 1970-74 slice. A defendant's voluntary cessation does not moot a case unless subsequent events make it absolutely clear the conduct will not recur, a heavy burden on the party urging mootness (Concentrated Phosphate 1968). Southern Pacific Terminal (1911) first applied the capable-of-repetition, yet-evading-review exception; Powell v. McCormack (1969) held that a live backpay claim keeps a case going though injunctive relief is obviated; Hall v. Beals (1969) found a case moot after a statutory amendment; Medical Committee (1972) found a shareholder-proposal dispute too speculative to stay live; Munsingwear (1950) directs vacatur when mootness arises on appeal; Alaska Steamship (1920) forbids deciding moot questions. Alongside: actual-controversy limits on declaratory judgments (Aetna v. Haworth 1937, Maryland Casualty 1941) and Golden v. Zwickler (1969), denying standing where future prosecution was wholly conjectural; and Speech or Debate immunity from Kilbourn (1881) through Johnson (1966) and Gravel (1972), protecting acts integral to the legislative process. The unit splits in 1975-79 into qualified immunity, mootness and standing units.
rule: A federal court decides only live, actual controversies: voluntary cessation moots a case only if recurrence cannot reasonably be expected, wrongs capable of repetition yet evading review remain reviewable, and declaratory relief requires a real, immediate dispute.

changes.what: Wrongs capable of repetition, yet evading review are not moot.

name: Guidelines departures under Koon v. United States (1995-2004)
description: Pre-Booker review of Guidelines departures: Koon (1996), anchoring 1995-2004, made departure decisions reviewable for abuse of discretion and allowed unmentioned factors outside the heartland, displacing stricter circuit bars (Brock 1997). Burns (1991) requires notice of upward departure, Williams (1992) treats policy statements as authoritative, and Wade (1992) limits review of refusals to move for substantial assistance. The PROTECT Act (2003) restored de novo review.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Guidelines departures (1990s)
previous.description: Pre-Booker review of Sentencing Guidelines departures under Koon's abuse-of-discretion standard, with Williams v. United States, Burns (notice of upward departure), Wade and § 5K1.1 substantial-assistance motions, and Buford.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session subagents, from cocite evidence; second pass differentiated near-duplicates)

history: Dominant rule: Koon (1996), the anchor of both 1995-99 and 2000-04, held that a sentencing court may depart when a case falls outside the Guidelines' heartland on a factor the Commission has not forbidden, and that appellate courts review the decision for abuse of discretion, which includes errors of law. How it changed: before Koon, Burns (1991) required notice of an upward departure, Williams (1992) held that a departure on a rejected ground misapplies the Guidelines, Wade (1992) let courts review the government's refusal to move for a substantial-assistance departure only for unconstitutional motive, and the First Circuit's Rivera (1993) set a deferential framework for 'unusual' cases while barring forbidden factors. After Koon the circuits relaxed: Brock (4th Cir. 1997) held Van Dyke overruled and allowed departures for extraordinary post-offense rehabilitation, Sally (1997) extended that to post-conviction rehabilitation, Collins (1997) adopted a unitary abuse-of-discretion test, and Farouil (1997) allowed departures for deportable aliens' conditions of confinement, while Rybicki (1996) rejected ordinary collateral consequences. Buford (2001) extended deference to fact-bound rulings. The PROTECT Act (2003) returned departure review to de novo, which Mallon (2003) applied. The line splits into post-Booker reasonableness review in 2005-09.
rule: Under the mandatory Guidelines, a sentencing court may depart for factors that take a case outside the heartland unless the Commission forbids them, and the decision to depart is reviewed for abuse of discretion, which includes any error of law (Koon).

changes.what: A court must give the parties notice before departing upward on a ground not identified in the PSR or the government's submissions.

changes.case: Williams v. United States; Wade v. United States
changes.what: A departure on a ground the policy statements reject is a misapplication of the Guidelines (Williams); the government's refusal to file a § 5K1.1 or § 3553(e) motion is reviewable only for unconstitutional motive (Wade).
Appellate courts review 'unusualness' with respect for the sentencing court's feel for the case, but forbidden factors may not support departure.
Departure decisions are reviewed for abuse of discretion, and the Guidelines generally do not limit the factors that may warrant departure; Koon anchors both slices.

changes.case: Brock (4th Cir.); Collins (11th Cir.); Sally (3d Cir.)
changes.what: Koon overruled bars on departing for extraordinary post-offense rehabilitation (Brock, overruling Van Dyke) and produced a unitary abuse-of-discretion standard (Collins).

changes.case: Buford v. United States; PROTECT Act; Mallon
changes.what: Buford deferred to fact-bound Guidelines rulings; the 2003 PROTECT Act made departure review de novo, which courts such as Mallon applied.

name: Plain error 2025-29 (partial): Puckett, Greer, preservation rules
description: A partial 2025-29 slice anchored by Puckett (2009): Olano's (1993) four prongs applied to pleas (Vonn 2002; Dominguez Benitez 2004) and plea breaches; Molina-Martinez (2016) and Rosales-Mireles (2018) made Guidelines errors ordinarily correctable; Greer (2021) required Rehaif defendants to show they lacked knowledge of status. Fifth Circuit preservation rules (Cano 2020) and Alabama capital plain-error cases (Ex parte Trawick 1997) also appear.
history: Dominant rule: an error not raised in the district court is reviewed only for plain error: there must be an error, it must be clear or obvious, it must affect substantial rights, and the court of appeals should correct it only if it seriously affects the fairness, integrity or public reputation of proceedings (Olano 1993; Puckett 2009, anchor of the only slice, 2025-29). The unit continues a Fifth Circuit plain-error lineage. How it developed: Frady (1982) bars using § 2255 as a substitute for appeal, and Young (1985) reviews unobjected prosecutorial remarks in context. Vonn (2002) and Dominguez Benitez (2004) applied the test to Rule 11 errors, requiring a reasonable probability the defendant would not have pleaded. Puckett (2009) extended it to plea-agreement breaches. Molina-Martinez (2016) held that an incorrect Guidelines range ordinarily shows prejudice, and Rosales-Mireles (2018) that such errors ordinarily satisfy the fourth prong. Greer (2021) required Rehaif claimants to show they lacked knowledge of felon status. Fifth Circuit cases hold that a general objection does not preserve a specific claim (Cano 2020; Zarco-Beiza 2022). Esteras (2025) bars retribution in revocation.
rule: A forfeited error is corrected on appeal only if it is plain, affected the defendant's substantial rights (a reasonable probability of a different outcome), and seriously affects the fairness, integrity or public reputation of judicial proceedings (Olano; Puckett).

changes.what: Four-part plain-error test; waiver, unlike forfeiture, is not reviewable.

changes.case: United States v. Vonn; United States v. Dominguez Benitez
changes.what: Plain error applies to unpreserved Rule 11 errors; the court may consult the whole record, and the defendant must show a reasonable probability he would not have pleaded guilty.
Plain error applies to an unpreserved breach of a plea agreement, and the showing of error cannot be recast as the effect on substantial rights.

changes.case: Molina-Martinez v. United States; Rosales-Mireles v. United States

A defendant raising a forfeited Rehaif claim must show he would have presented evidence that he did not know he was a felon.
A court revoking supervised release may not rely on retribution for the original offense.

name: Deference to agency interpretation: Udall v. Tallman to Chevron (1965-89)
description: Judicial deference to agency interpretation: Skidmore (1944) and Seminole Rock (1945) set the older framework; Udall v. Tallman (1965, anchor 1965-84) gave great weight to administrative constructions, limited by Volkswagenwerk (1968) and Zuber (1970). Chevron (1984, anchor 1985-89) replaced this with its two-step test, and Cardoza-Fonseca (1987) kept pure statutory questions for courts.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Agency deference: Udall to Chevron (1965-89)
previous.description: Judicial deference to agency interpretation from Skidmore, Seminole Rock (Bowles) and Udall v. Tallman through Chevron and Cardoza-Fonseca, including TVA v. Hill on the Endangered Species Act.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session subagents, from cocite evidence; second pass differentiated near-duplicates)

history: Dominant rule: courts defer to reasonable agency interpretations of statutes and regulations the agency administers, but decide clear statutory questions themselves. How it changed: Udall v. Tallman (1965) anchors 1965-84, drawing on Seminole Rock (1945) for an agency's reading of its own regulations, Skidmore (1944) for persuasive weight, American Trucking (1940) on purpose, and Power Reactor (1961) on contemporaneous construction. Mining and milk-marketing cases (Best, Coleman, Blair) applied that deference. Volkswagenwerk (1968) and Zuber (1970) required a reasonable basis in law and reserved the final word to courts. In 1975-84 Bell Aerospace (1974), Morton v. Ruiz (1974), Train (1975-76), TVA v. Hill (1978), GTE Sylvania (1980) and Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (1981) lead, alternating between deference and plain-text enforcement, and Red Lion (1969) joins. Chevron (1984) enters and anchors 1985-89 with its two-step framework, and Cardoza-Fonseca (1987) confined it where a pure question of statutory construction is presented. The unit then continues as the general agency-review lineage.
rule: Courts give great weight to an administering agency's interpretation of its statute and controlling weight to its reading of its own regulation unless plainly erroneous (Udall; Seminole Rock), and from 1984 accept an agency's reasonable construction of an ambiguous statute where Congress has not directly spoken (Chevron), while enforcing clear statutory text themselves.

changes.case: United States v. American Trucking Associations; Skidmore v. Swift; Bowles v. Seminole Rock
changes.what: Statutory purpose governs when plain meaning yields unreasonable results; informal interpretations carry weight according to their power to persuade; an agency's reading of its own regulation controls unless plainly erroneous.

changes.case: Power Reactor Development v. Electrical Workers; Udall v. Tallman; Zemel v. Rusk
changes.what: Great deference to contemporaneous administrative constructions of statutes and regulations; Udall anchors 1965-84.

changes.case: Volkswagenwerk v. FMC; Zuber v. Allen
changes.what: Deference only to constructions with a reasonable basis in law; courts keep the final responsibility to construe statutes.

changes.case: NLRB v. Bell Aerospace; Morton v. Ruiz; CPSC v. GTE Sylvania; FEC v. Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee
changes.what: Agencies may choose adjudication or rulemaking; agencies must follow their own procedures; clear statutory language is ordinarily conclusive; specialized agencies are presumptively owed deference.
The Endangered Species Act's plain terms required enjoining a nearly completed dam; Congress gave endangered species priority over agency missions.
Two-step test: apply Congress's clear intent; if the statute is silent or ambiguous, uphold a permissible agency construction; Chevron anchors 1985-89.
A pure question of statutory construction is for the courts; the 'well-founded fear' asylum standard is more generous than 'more likely than not'.

name: Washington government tort duty: take-charge supervision (Taggart, Hertog) and public duty
description: Washington government tort duty: a government that takes charge of a dangerous offender owes victims a § 319 duty (Petersen, 1983; Taggart, 1992; Hertog and Bishop, 1999, extending it to probation and pretrial release), while the public-duty doctrine bars claims for duties owed to the public (Taylor, 1988) absent a special relationship with express assurances (Beal, 1998; Babcock, 2001). Business duties against third-party crime (Nivens, 1997) and causation (Schooley, 1998) run alongside.

previous.name: Washington torts: public duty and negligent supervision
previous.description: Washington Supreme Court tort cases on government liability for supervised offenders and public duty: Taggart and Hertog (parole and probation officers who take charge), Bishop, Taylor's public-duty doctrine, Folsom and Schooley.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session subagents, from cocite evidence; second pass differentiated near-duplicates)

history: Dominant rule: when Washington governments and businesses owe a duty to protect against third parties. In 1995-99 the anchor is Hansen (1992, social hosts must not serve minors), with Christen (1989), Hutchins (1991, innkeepers) and Hartley (1985). How it changed: Hertog (1999) anchors 2000-04 and again 2015-19. Building on Petersen (1983) and Taggart (1992), it held city probation officers take charge of probationers and owe a duty to foreseeable victims; Bishop (1999) added pretrial-release monitoring and rejected the public-duty defence. Schooley (1998) addresses cause in fact and the liquor-to-minors protected class. Folsom (1998) anchors 2005-09 (no franchisor duty without control). Taylor (1988) anchors 2010-14: the public-duty doctrine shields duties owed to the public, with exceptions for special relationships, applied in Babcock (2001), Beal (1998), Osborn (2006, the duty runs to persons the entity can control) and Cummins (2006). Joyce (2005) leads 2015-19 on state liability for supervised offenders. In 2020-24 and 2025-29 Ranger Insurance (2008) and Young (1989) anchor on summary-judgment practice, which is drift.
rule: A Washington government entity that takes charge of a dangerous offender, as parole and probation officers do, owes a duty under Restatement § 319 to protect foreseeable victims (Taggart, Hertog); otherwise the public-duty doctrine bars liability for duties owed to the public at large unless an exception such as a special relationship with express assurances applies (Taylor, Babcock).

changes.case: Petersen v. State; Hartley v. State
changes.what: The state owes a duty to foreseeable victims when it controls and wrongly releases a dangerous person; proximate cause has cause-in-fact and legal-causation elements.
Building permit and inspection duties protect the general public, so the public-duty ('duty to all is duty to no one') doctrine bars individual claims.
Parole officers take charge of parolees, so physical custody is not required for § 319 liability.

changes.case: Nivens v. 7-11 Hoagy's Corner; Niece v. Elmview Group Home
changes.what: Businesses owe invitees a duty against foreseeable third-party crime, and group homes must protect vulnerable residents, though without nondelegable liability for employees' intentional acts.

changes.case: Beal v. City of Seattle; Folsom v. Burger King
changes.what: Justifiable reliance on a 911 operator's assurance creates a special relationship (Beal); a franchisor without control of daily operations owes employees no duty (Folsom).

changes.case: Hertog v. City of Seattle; Bishop v. Miche
changes.what: Extended the take-charge duty to municipal probation officers and pretrial-release counselors; the public-duty doctrine does not bar these claims.

changes.case: Babcock v. Mason County Fire District
changes.what: A special relationship requires the plaintiff to seek and the government to give an express, unequivocal assurance.

name: Nebraska juvenile proceedings: rehabilitation plans, final orders, termination
description: Nebraska juvenile court appeals: rehabilitation plans must rest on evidence and reasonably relate to the adjudication before noncompliance supports termination (In re J.S. 1987, anchor 1985-94); placement orders are final and appealable within 30 days (In re R.G. 1991, In re J.A. 1994); prior adjudications cannot be collaterally attacked (In re Joshua 1997, anchor 2000-04). Late cases apply the federal ASFA (Sarah K. 1999).

previous.description: Nebraska Supreme Court juvenile proceedings: final dispositional orders and appeal deadlines, rehabilitation plans and termination of parental rights.

history: Dominant rule: Nebraska juvenile proceedings move from adjudication to disposition to possible termination, and each step needs record support and timely appeal. How it changed: In re Interest of J.S. (1987) anchors 1985-94, reversing a termination where no evidence supported the rehabilitation plan; companion cases (A.H. 1991, M.P. 1991) set plan terms, D.S. (1990) protected the guardian ad litem's role, and A.G.G. (1988) barred a court-appointed attorney without client contact from waiving rights. In re R.G. (1991) enters and anchors 1995-99: placement orders are dispositional and appealable, with due process at removal; J.A. (1994) fixed the 30-day appeal period and O'Connor (1998) addressed finality. In re Joshua (1997) enters and anchors 2000-04, barring collateral attacks absent lack of jurisdiction. In that slice Tabatha R. (1998) allowed consideration of incarceration in plan decisions, Sarah K. (1999) applied federal ASFA guidelines, and Clifford M. (2001) the 15-month exception hearing.
rule: In Nebraska juvenile cases, a court-ordered rehabilitation plan must be supported by the evidence and reasonably related to the reasons for adjudication before failure to comply can support termination, dispositional placement orders are final and appealable within 30 days, and prior adjudications cannot be collaterally attacked except for lack of jurisdiction.

changes.what: Reversed a termination where the record lacked evidence supporting the rehabilitation plan entered at disposition, and required courts to inform parents of plan consequences.
An order determining a juvenile's placement is a dispositional, appealable order; analyzed due process at the removal stage. Anchors 1995-99.

changes.what: Failure to find facts supporting a plan is plain error, and a notice of appeal must be filed within 30 days of entry of the order.
Collateral attacks on earlier juvenile proceedings are impermissible unless based on lack of jurisdiction; anchors 2000-04.

changes.what: Courts may consider incarceration in deciding whether to adopt a rehabilitation plan, and applied the federal Adoption and Safe Families Act framework, including exception hearings at 15 months in foster care.

name: California self-representation and Marsden substitute-counsel motions
description: California practice on self-representation and replacing appointed counsel, anchored by Faretta (1975) in 2020-24 and 2025-29: a competent, knowing waiver permits self-representation (Godinez 1993; Tovar 2004), limited by Edwards (2008) for gray-area defendants; untimely requests are discretionary (Windham 1977); a Marsden (1970) hearing governs requests for new counsel (Sanchez 2011). In 2025-29 structural-error cases join.
history: Dominant rule: a defendant has a Sixth Amendment right to represent himself if he knowingly and intelligently waives counsel (Faretta 1975, anchor of both slices), and California defendants may seek substitute appointed counsel at a Marsden (1970) hearing. The lineage forms in 2020-24 from right-to-counsel units. How it developed: Adams (1943) and Zerbst (1938) frame waiver; Windham (1977) made untimely requests discretionary, and Marshall (1997) requires an unequivocal request. McKaskle (1984) allowed standby counsel but no hybrid representation. Godinez (1993) equated competency to waive counsel with competency to stand trial, and Tovar (2004) rejected a rigid admonition requirement (with Bush 2017 on advisements). Edwards (2008) let states insist on counsel for defendants competent to stand trial but not to conduct it. Sanchez (2011) requires a Marsden hearing only on a clear indication that the defendant wants new counsel, and Smith (1993) reviews such rulings for abuse of discretion. Also: Pitchess (1974) discovery of officer personnel records. In 2025-29 a structural-error unit merges in (Gideon, Waller, Tumey, Caperton).
rule: A competent defendant who knowingly and voluntarily waives counsel in a timely, unequivocal request may represent himself (Faretta), though a state may insist on counsel for one competent to stand trial but not to conduct it (Edwards); a request to replace appointed counsel requires a hearing on the reasons (Marsden).

changes.what: A defendant seeking substitute appointed counsel must be allowed to state the reasons and support the request.

changes.case: Faretta v. California; People v. Windham
changes.what: The Sixth Amendment implies a right to self-representation; untimely requests are left to the trial court's discretion after inquiry into the reasons.
Standby counsel's limited participation does not infringe the right, and there is no right to hybrid representation.
The competency standard for waiving counsel or pleading guilty is the same as for standing trial.
A valid waiver need not include a rigid, detailed warning about the usefulness of counsel when pleading guilty.

name: Fifth Circuit drug-conspiracy trials, 1990-94: Bourjaily statements, Zafiro severance
description: Fifth Circuit trials of co-conspirators in 1990-94, on coconspirator statements and severance: preliminary facts found by a preponderance (Bourjaily, 1987), severance only for specific, compelling prejudice (Arzola-Amaya, 1989; Zafiro, 1993), extrinsic offenses under Beechum (1978), and sufficiency under Glasser (1942) and Bell (Unit B en banc 1982, anchor). Drug cases infer intent to distribute from quantity (Hernandez-Palacios, 1988).

previous.name: Joint trials, conspiracy and severance
previous.description: Federal joint trials of co-conspirators: severance and antagonistic defenses (Zafiro), Bruton limits on co-defendant confessions, co-conspirator statements (Bourjaily), Pinkerton liability, and Fifth Circuit en banc law (Calverley, Beechum).

history: Dominant rule: in Fifth Circuit drug-conspiracy trials, a guilty verdict stands if a reasonable trier of fact could find guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. Bell (Unit B en banc 1982) anchors the single 1990-94 slice, with Glasser (1942) the heaviest case. How it changed: within the slice the rules are restatements: Bourjaily (1987) lets courts find coconspirator-statement prerequisites by a preponderance; Beechum (1978) governs extrinsic offenses; Arzola-Amaya (1989) requires compelling prejudice for severance, and Zafiro (1993) held that antagonistic defenses are not prejudicial per se. Sufficiency cases infer intent to distribute from large quantities (Hernandez-Palacios, 1988), find constructive possession (Molinar-Apodaca, 1989), give the Government only reasonable inferences (Tresvant, 1982) and reverse where a defendant was not shown to know of the conspiracy (Gardea Carrasco, 1987). Also: Bell v. United States (1983) on the Bank Robbery Act and prosecutorial remarks (Brockington, 1988). The lineage splits in 1995-99, partly into a plain-error unit.
rule: In Fifth Circuit multi-defendant drug-conspiracy trials, a verdict stands if a reasonable trier of fact could find guilt beyond a reasonable doubt (Glasser; Bell), coconspirator statements are admitted on preliminary facts found by a preponderance (Bourjaily), and severance requires specific, compelling prejudice that instructions cannot cure (Zafiro).

changes.what: A verdict must be sustained if substantial evidence, viewed for the Government, supports it.

changes.case: United States v. Beechum (5th Cir. en banc)
changes.what: Extrinsic-offense evidence is relevant only if the defendant committed the act, and its relevance turns on similarity to the offense charged.

changes.case: United States v. Bell (5th Cir. Unit B en banc)
changes.what: A verdict stands if a reasonable trier of fact could find that the evidence establishes guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.
Preliminary facts for coconspirator statements are found by a preponderance, may rest in part on the statements themselves, and need no separate reliability showing.
Mutually antagonistic defenses are not prejudicial per se; severance is required only on a serious risk of prejudice to a specific trial right.

round1.description: Fifth Circuit trials of co-conspirators: joinder is the norm and severance needs specific, compelling prejudice (Zafiro 1993: antagonistic defenses not prejudicial per se), within Bruton (1968) as narrowed by Marsh (1987). round1.history: Dominant rule: co-conspirators are tried together, and a defendant gets severance only by showing specific and compelling prejudice that a limiting instruction cannot cure (Faulkner 1994, Rocha 1990, Arzola-Amaya 1989); a guilty verdict stands if substantial evidence supports it (Glasser, 1942). name: Interim relief against federal policy: Winter injunction test, Nken stays

name: Louisiana 1980s: circumstantial-evidence rule fitted into Jackson (Captville)
description: Louisiana sufficiency review in 1980-89, right after Jackson v. Virginia (1979, anchor): the courts reconciled the statutory circumstantial-evidence rule with Jackson, treating it as a guide within the rational-juror test (Chism 1983; Wright 1984), and Captville (1984) held that once the jury rejects the defendant's hypothesis of innocence, guilt follows unless another reasonable hypothesis remains. history: Dominant rule: Jackson v. Virginia (1979) anchors both slices: a conviction stands if any rational trier of fact, viewing the evidence for the prosecution, could find guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. The cases are Louisiana appellate decisions. How it changed: in 1980-84 Jackson leads with Baldwin (1980), Fuller (1982), Crawford (1980) and Mathews (1979) applying it to intent and specific crimes, and Byrd (1980) allowing a court to enter a lesser included offense when the evidence does not support the greater. In 1985-89 the Louisiana Supreme Court's reconciliation of its statutory circumstantial-evidence rule with Jackson leads: Chism (1983) and Wright (1984) treat the rule as a guide within the Jackson standard, and Captville (1984) holds that once the jury reasonably rejects the defendant's hypothesis of innocence, guilt follows unless another hypothesis creates reasonable doubt. Korman (1983) applies the review to the courts of appeal after jurisdiction moved to them. Porretto (1985) and Rosiere (1986) apply these rules. The lineage splits in 1990-94.

Virginia), and the statutory rule that circumstantial evidence must exclude every reasonable hypothesis of innocence is a guide within that standard, not a separate test (Wright; Chism).

name: Connecticut Golding review and prosecutorial impropriety (Williams, Stevenson)
description: Connecticut criminal appeals, 1995-2014: Golding (1989) review of unpreserved constitutional claims anchors throughout, joined from 2000-04 by State v. Reasonable-doubt instruction cases (Hines, Whipper) lead early; DeJesus (2008), Salamon (2008) and Kitchens (2011, implied waiver of instructional claims) enter in 2010-14.

Stevenson (2004) held that the Williams analysis embodies Golding's fourth prong, so impropriety claims need no separate Golding review, and Warholic (2006) applied it. name: "Some evidence" review of prison discipline and California parole denials (Hill)

previous.description: Timeliness of employment-discrimination charges (1975-89): Zipes holding EEOC filing limits non-jurisdictional and subject to tolling, Ricks and Chardon accrual at notice of the decision, Love, Mohasco (Silver) and Evans.

history: Dominant rule: the EEOC charge-filing period is a statute-of-limitations-like requirement, not a jurisdictional bar. In 1975-79 the circuits lead, and Dartt v. Shell Oil (10th Cir. 1976) anchors. Love (1972) rejects procedural technicalities in a scheme run by laymen, and Sanchez (1970) lets the suit cover what the charge's investigation would reasonably reach. Reeb (1975) and Dartt tolled the period where the employer or agency misled the claimant, and Dartt (1978) carried tolling to the ADEA. How it changed: Robbins & Myers (1976) held that grievances do not toll the period, and Evans (1977) refused to treat the lingering effects of a time-barred act as a continuing violation. Oscar Mayer v. Evans (1979) required ADEA resort to state agencies, and Mohasco v. Silver (1980) applied the deferral rules strictly. Bonham (1978) anchors 1980-84 on tolling only for active deception. Ricks (1980) and Chardon (1981) fixed accrual at notice of the decision. Zipes (1982) anchors 1985-89 and confirmed tolling. Baldwin County (1984) limited equitable relief, and Martinez (1984) tolled where the EEOC misled the claimant. Also: Equal Pay Act and Bennett Amendment cases (Laffey, Brennan, Gunther) and Rehabilitation Act claims (Davis, Prewitt, Darrone), which split off to the disability unit.
rule: Timely filing of an EEOC charge is not a jurisdictional prerequisite but a requirement like a statute of limitations, subject to waiver, estoppel and equitable tolling (Zipes); the period runs from the date the employee is notified of the discriminatory decision, not when its effects are felt (Ricks, Chardon), and deferral-state filing rules are applied as Congress wrote them (Mohasco, Evans).

changes.case: Sanchez v. Standard Brands (5th Cir.); Love v. Pullman Co.
changes.what: Charges are read liberally, a suit may cover what the EEOC investigation reasonably grows out of the charge, and the EEOC may refer charges to state agencies for claimants.

changes.case: Electrical Workers v. Robbins & Myers; United Air Lines v. Evans
changes.what: A grievance procedure does not toll the period, and continuing effects of a time-barred act are not a continuing violation.

changes.case: Oscar Mayer v. Evans; Mohasco Corp. v. Silver

changes.case: Delaware State College v. Ricks; Chardon v. Fernandez

name: Texas ineffective assistance, 2010-19: Strickland anchor, Goodspeed hearing rule
description: Texas ineffective-assistance claims on direct appeal in 2010-19, anchored by Strickland (1984), adopted for the Texas Constitution in Hernandez (1986): a strong presumption of sound strategy when the record is silent (Jackson, 1994; Thompson, 1999; Mallett, 2001), claims firmly founded in the record (Bone, 2002), and denial where no hearing developed counsel's reasons (Goodspeed, 2005). In 2015-19 Delaware postconviction cases join (Outten, Bailey).
history: Dominant rule: Strickland's (1984) two-pronged test as the Texas Court of Criminal Appeals applies it on direct appeal. Strickland anchors 2010-14 and 2015-19, and Hernandez (1986) made it the standard under the Texas Constitution. How it changed: the rule is stable; the cases explain why such claims rarely succeed on direct appeal. Jackson (1994) and Thompson (1999) presume a valid strategy when the record is silent; Mallett (2001) notes the record is usually undeveloped; Bone (2002) demands that claims be firmly founded in the record; Rylander (2003) and Lopez (2011) require both prongs; Goodspeed (2005) refuses to find deficiency absent a hearing unless no competent attorney would have so acted; Andrews (2005) allows an exception for failing to correct a harmful misstatement of law. Texas habeas jurisdiction appears in Ex parte Young (1967) and Ex parte Rodriguez (1960). In 2015-19 Michel (1955) and Affronti (1956) on presumed strategy and Delaware postconviction cases (Outten, 1998; Bailey, 1991, Rule 61) join. The lineage splits in 2020-24.
rule: Under Strickland, adopted for the Texas Constitution in Hernandez, an appellant must prove both deficient performance and prejudice, and where the direct-appeal record is silent about counsel's reasons the court presumes a sound strategy, so the claim usually fails unless the conduct was so outrageous that no competent attorney would have engaged in it (Thompson; Goodspeed).

changes.what: Deficient performance plus a reasonable probability of a different result.
The Strickland standard governs ineffective-assistance claims under both the federal and Texas constitutions.

history: Dominant rule: the Ohio Civ.R. 56 burden. Dresher (1996) anchors every slice: the movant must inform the court of the basis for the motion and identify evidentiary material showing no genuine issue, and a conclusory assertion that the nonmovant has no evidence is not enough; the nonmovant then must set out specific facts. Harless (1978) and Temple (1977) supply the three-part standard, Mitseff (1988) bars unstated grounds, Murphy v. Reynoldsburg (1992) requires the trial court to examine all materials itself, and Grafton (1996) makes review de novo. How it changed: no rule change appears in the 2010-29 slices; the standard is applied to the merits issues on which Ohio appeals arise, such as open-and-obvious hazards (Armstrong, 2003), recklessness and wantonness for political-subdivision immunity (Anderson v. In 2025-29 Anderson v. Liberty Lobby (1986) joins as persuasive federal authority.

description: Fourth Circuit drug-conspiracy appeals in a single 1995-99 slice anchored by Glasser (1942): a verdict stands on substantial evidence viewed for the government, and a slight connection to a proven conspiracy suffices (Brooks 1992, Burgos 1996 en banc). history: Dominant rule: sufficiency review of federal drug-conspiracy convictions. Glasser (1942) anchors the lineage's only slice, 1995-99, which formed from a joint-trial and conspiracy unit and later joins the Olano plain-error lineage. history: Dominant rule: Firestone Tire & Rubber v. Herron (2005) anchors 2005-19: the court declined the State's request to adopt Olano and kept two disjunctive prongs, and Piatkowski (2007) placed the burden of showing prejudice on the defendant under the first prong while presuming it under the second. Glasper (2009) and Thompson (2010) held that Rule 431(b) violations in Zehr questioning are not structural, and Hillier (2010) required postsentencing motions. Sebby (2017) enters 2015-19 and treats the closely-balanced inquiry as qualitative. From 2020-24 Piatkowski anchors, with Krankel (1984) inquiries into pro se ineffectiveness claims and Stacey (2000) on excessive sentences.
rule: An Illinois criminal defendant preserves an issue only by a contemporaneous trial objection and a written posttrial (or postsentencing) motion (Enoch, Hillier); forfeited error is reviewable as plain error only if the evidence was so closely balanced that the error threatened to tip the scales, or the error was so serious it affected the fairness of the trial and the integrity of the process (Herron, Piatkowski).

changes.what: Albanese adopted Strickland for ineffectiveness claims, and Zehr required jurors be questioned on the presumption of innocence and related principles; Free (1983) anchors 1985-89.

name: Defendant's public-trial right and closures: Waller, Washington's Bone-Club
description: Closure of criminal proceedings, increasingly as the defendant's public-trial right: the federal access cases (Richmond Newspapers 1980; Press-Enterprise I and II, 1984-86) and Waller (1984) frame it, and from 2005-09 Washington cases lead: Bone-Club (1995) requires five-factor findings before closure, Orange (2004) and Brightman (2005) protect voir dire, and Wise and Sublett (2012) set structural error and the experience-and-logic test.
