previous.name: Public trial and press access to proceedings
previous.description: Openness of criminal proceedings: the First Amendment right of access (Richmond Newspapers, Globe Newspaper, Press-Enterprise I and II), the Sixth Amendment public-trial right and closure findings (Waller, Washington's Bone-Club factors), and the common-law right to judicial records (Nixon v. Warner Communications).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: courtrooms are presumptively open, and closure needs a compelling interest, narrow tailoring and findings. In 1980-84 DePasquale (1979) anchors, holding the Sixth Amendment right belongs to the defendant, with Nebraska Press v. Stuart (1976) on prior restraints and Nixon (1978) on records. How it changed: Richmond Newspapers (1980) anchors 1985-89 after recognising a First Amendment right to attend trials; Globe (1982) and Press-Enterprise I (1984) extended it to minor-victim testimony and voir dire, and Press-Enterprise II (1986), which anchors 1990-99, to preliminary hearings. Waller (1984) applied the same test to the defendant's right. Civil records and protective orders (Seattle Times v. Rhinehart, 1984; Public Citizen, 1988) and grand-jury secrecy (Douglas Oil, 1979) also appear. Nixon anchors 2000-04. From 2005-09 Washington's article I, §§ 10 and 22 cases dominate: Bone-Club (1995), Orange (2004), Brightman (2005), Momah and Strode (2009), with Presley (2010) and Washington's Wise, Paumier and Sublett (2012). Wise anchors 2015-19 and Bone-Club 2020-24.
rule: Criminal trials and related proceedings are presumptively open; a court may close them only on specific findings that closure is essential to an overriding interest and narrowly tailored after considering alternatives (Press-Enterprise, Waller), and in Washington only after the five-factor Bone-Club analysis on the record, failing which the error is structural.

changes.what: Gag orders on the press are presumptively invalid prior restraints, but the Sixth Amendment public-trial right belongs to the defendant, not the public.
The public has a common-law right of access to judicial records, subject to the trial court's discretion.

changes.what: The First Amendment gives public and press a right to attend criminal trials, voir dire and preliminary hearings; mandatory closure for minor victims' testimony fails strict scrutiny.

changes.what: Unjustified closure is structural error requiring a new trial (Wise, Paumier); whether a proceeding implicates the right turns on an experience-and-logic test (Sublett).

name: Jackson v. Virginia sufficiency review in Texas and Louisiana: Geesa, Clewis
description: Jackson v. Virginia (1979) sufficiency review: a conviction stands if any rational juror, viewing the evidence for the verdict, could find each element beyond a reasonable doubt. Louisiana read its circumstantial-evidence rule into Jackson (Wright, Captville 1984). Texas dropped the any-evidence test (Butler 1989) and the reasonable-hypothesis construct (Geesa 1991), then added factual-sufficiency review (Clewis 1996).
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Jackson sufficiency review in Texas and Louisiana (1980-2004)
previous.description: Jackson v. Virginia rational-juror sufficiency standard as applied by the Texas Court of Criminal Appeals (Geesa dropping the reasonable-hypothesis rule, Clewis factual sufficiency, Butler) and Louisiana courts (Captville, Mussall, Rosiere).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session subagents, from cocite evidence; second pass differentiated near-duplicates)

history: Dominant rule: Jackson v. Virginia (1979) anchors every slice: a conviction must be upheld if any rational trier of fact, viewing the evidence in the light most favorable to the prosecution, could find each element beyond a reasonable doubt, and credibility is for the fact finder (Moreno 1988, Matson 1991, Sharp 1986). How it changed: in 1985-89 Louisiana cases lead; Wright and Captville (1984) treated the state's circumstantial-evidence rule (exclude every reasonable hypothesis of innocence) as a guide to applying Jackson, not a separate standard, and Mussall (1988) restated the rational-juror test. In Texas, Butler (1989) rejected the any-evidence test, and Geesa (1991), leading 1990-94, abandoned the reasonable-hypothesis-of-innocence construct for cases tried after it. Clewis (1996), leading 1995-99, added factual-sufficiency review following Stone (1992). In 2000-04 Clewis and Geesa drop out and the lineage splits toward Texas sufficiency review after Brooks (2010), which later abolished separate factual-sufficiency review. Also: proof of intent to deprive from conduct (Griffin 1981).
rule: Evidence is legally sufficient if, viewed in the light most favorable to the verdict, any rational trier of fact could have found every element beyond a reasonable doubt, with conflicts and credibility resolved in favor of the verdict.

changes.what: Louisiana's circumstantial-evidence rule is not a separate standard but a guide to applying Jackson; once the jury reasonably rejects the defendant's hypothesis of innocence, the defendant is guilty unless another reasonable hypothesis remains.

Adopted factual-sufficiency review (Stone test) alongside Jackson legal-sufficiency review, with legal sufficiency addressed first.

name: Habeas review of state convictions: AEDPA deference (Williams, Harrington)
description: Federal habeas review of state (often capital) convictions, 1980-2029, with a shifting anchor: capital sentencing 1980-94 (Gregg, Lockett, Penry 1989); procedural default under Coleman (1991) in 1995-99; then AEDPA deference, with Williams v. Taylor (2000) anchoring 2000-14, Harrington (2011) 2015-19 and 2025-29, and Slack (2000) on certificates of appealability 2020-24. Harrington and Pinholster (2011) made deference near-absolute.

previous.name: Federal habeas: AEDPA deference and procedural default
previous.description: Federal collateral review under AEDPA: unreasonable application of clearly established law (Williams v. Taylor, Harrington, Pinholster), procedural default and cause (Coleman, Murray v. Carrier), certificates of appealability (Slack, Miller-El), Brecht harmlessness, and Strickland/Wiggins and Brady/Kyles claims.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: federal habeas courts defer to state adjudications and honor state procedural bars; under AEDPA (1996) relief requires a decision contrary to, or an unreasonable application of, clearly established Supreme Court law. How it changed: the early slices are capital-sentencing habeas: Gregg (1976) anchors 1980-84, Lockett (1978) 1985-89 and Penry (1989) 1990-94, with Eddings, Woodson and Zant on mitigation and narrowing. Coleman (1991) anchors 1995-99: cause and prejudice (Sykes 1977; Murray v. Carrier 1986; Keeney 1992) replaced Fay v. Noia's deliberate-bypass rule, Teague (1989) barred new rules on collateral review, McCleskey (1991) limited successive petitions, and Brecht (1993) and Schlup (1995) set the harmless-error and actual-innocence standards. AEDPA made § 2254(d) deference mandatory for new petitions (Lindh 1997). Williams v. Taylor (2000) anchors 2000-14, reading the contrary-to and unreasonable-application clauses; Wiggins (2003) and Rompilla (2005) bring Strickland investigation claims. Harrington (2011) anchors 2015-19 and the partial 2025-29 slice; with Pinholster (2011) it made deference near-absolute and confined review to the state record. Slack (2000), on certificates of appealability with Miller-El (2003), anchors 2020-24.
rule: A federal habeas court may not grant relief on a claim the state court adjudicated on the merits unless that decision was contrary to, or an objectively unreasonable application of, clearly established Supreme Court law, or rested on an unreasonable determination of the facts (28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)), and claims defaulted under an adequate and independent state rule are barred absent cause and prejudice or actual innocence.

changes.case: Wainwright v. Sykes; Murray v. Carrier; Coleman v. Thompson
changes.what: Cause and prejudice replaced Fay v. Noia's deliberate-bypass test; cause requires an objective external factor, and Coleman expressly rejected Fay. Murray and Coleman anchor 1990-99.
New constitutional rules of criminal procedure generally do not apply on collateral review to convictions already final.

Constitutional trial error warrants habeas relief only if it had a substantial and injurious effect on the verdict (Kotteakos standard).
A gateway actual-innocence claim requires new reliable evidence making it more likely than not that no reasonable juror would convict.

changes.case: Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act; Lindh v. Murphy
changes.what: AEDPA's deferential § 2254(d) standard governs petitions filed after April 24, 1996, but not cases already pending.

changes.case: Williams v. Taylor; Slack v. McDaniel
changes.what: The contrary-to and unreasonable-application clauses have independent meanings, and a certificate of appealability on a procedural ruling needs a debatable procedural ruling and a debatable constitutional claim.

changes.case: Lockyer v. Andrade; Miller-El v. Cockrell
changes.what: An application must be objectively unreasonable, not merely wrong; a COA needs only a showing that the claim is debatable.

changes.case: Harrington v. Richter; Cullen v. Pinholster
changes.what: Deference applies to unexplained summary denials, relief requires that no fairminded jurist could agree with the state court, and review is limited to the state-court record; Harrington anchors 2025-29.

name: Eyewitness identification, 1965-99: Wade lineup counsel to Manson reliability
description: Pretrial identification alone, 1965-99: Wade and Gilbert (1967) required counsel at post-indictment lineups, Kirby (1972) confined that to after formal charge, and Stovall (1967), Simmons (1968) and Foster (1969) opened due-process attacks on suggestive procedures. Neil v. Biggers (1972) and Manson v. Brathwaite (1977) then made reliability the linchpin, and they anchor from 1975-79. State-court applications follow.

previous.name: Eyewitness identification and lineups
previous.description: Pretrial identification: the right to counsel at post-indictment lineups (Wade, Gilbert, Kirby), suggestive procedures and due process (Stovall, Simmons, Foster), and reliability under Neil v. Biggers and Manson v. Brathwaite.

history: Dominant rule: identification testimony following an unnecessarily suggestive police procedure is admissible unless, under the totality of the circumstances, there is a very substantial likelihood of misidentification; the Biggers factors (opportunity to view, attention, prior description, certainty, time) decide reliability. How it changed: Wade (1967), the anchor through 1970-74, and Gilbert (1967) held a post-indictment lineup a critical stage requiring counsel, while Stovall (1967) applied that only prospectively and recognised a due-process challenge to suggestive show-ups. Simmons (1968) set the 'very substantial likelihood of irreparable misidentification' standard for photo arrays, and Foster (1969) applied it to exclude. Kirby (1972) limited the counsel right to identifications after formal charge, and Coleman (1970) made the preliminary hearing a critical stage. Neil v. Biggers (1972) anchors from 1975-79, and Manson v. Brathwaite (1977) adopted its factors and declined a per se exclusion rule; the two alternate as anchors through 1995-99. Later slices are state and federal applications (Massachusetts show-up and jury-instruction cases in 1975-84).
rule: An identification from an unnecessarily suggestive police procedure is excluded only if, under the totality of the circumstances, it is unreliable (Biggers, Manson); counsel is required at lineups held after formal charge (Wade, Kirby).

changes.what: Exclusion where a procedure gives rise to a very substantial likelihood of irreparable misidentification; Foster excluded an identification made all but inevitable by police.

name: Apprendi's statutory-maximum rule and plain-error review of Apprendi errors
description: The immediate Apprendi (2000) wave in this one-slice 2000-04 lineage: facts other than prior convictions that raise the statutory maximum must go to a jury, applied to drug quantity under § 841 (Aguayo-Delgado, Doggett), with Almendarez-Torres (1998) left standing (Dabeit). Unpreserved errors got plain-error review (Olano 1993, Johnson 1997, Cotton 2002) and harmless-error review (Neder 1999); Harris (2002) left mandatory minimums to judges.

previous.name: Apprendi: jury findings and the statutory maximum
previous.description: The immediate Apprendi wave: facts increasing a penalty beyond the statutory maximum must go to a jury, the prior-conviction exception (Almendarez-Torres), and plain-error and harmless-error treatment of Apprendi errors (Johnson, Neder, Cotton, Olano).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: Apprendi (2000), anchoring this single 2000-04 slice, requires jury findings beyond a reasonable doubt for any fact other than a prior conviction that increases the penalty beyond the statutory maximum, extending Jones (1999) to the states and confining McMillan (1986). How it changed: the circuits quickly overruled precedent treating drug quantity as a sentencing factor where it raised the § 841 maximum (Aguayo-Delgado, 8th Cir. 2000; Doggett, 5th Cir. 2000), while Dabeit (2000) held that Almendarez-Torres (1998) still treats prior aggravated felonies as sentencing factors. Because most Apprendi claims were unpreserved, the plain-error framework of Olano (1993) and Johnson (1997) dominated, and Cotton (2002) held that an indictment's failure to allege quantity is not jurisdictional and did not seriously affect fairness given overwhelming evidence. Neder (1999) allowed harmless-error review of an omitted element. Harris (2002) upheld judge-found mandatory minimums. Blakely (2004) closes the slice, and the lineage splits in 2005-09 into Booker remands and plain-error review.
rule: Any fact other than a prior conviction that increases a penalty beyond the statutory maximum must be charged and proved to a jury beyond a reasonable doubt, but unpreserved Apprendi errors are reviewed for plain error under Olano and Cotton, and omitting an element from the jury can be harmless under Neder.

changes.what: States may treat facts like visible firearm possession as sentencing factors raising a minimum; there is no Sixth Amendment right to jury sentencing.

changes.case: United States v. Olano; Johnson v. United States
changes.what: Four-part plain-error test for forfeited errors; an error need only be plain at the time of appellate review.

changes.case: Neder v. United States; Jones v. United States
changes.what: Failure to submit an uncontested element can be harmless; facts raising the maximum are elements that must be charged.

name: Rational-basis review of economic and social laws (Williamson, Dandridge, Cleburne)
description: The deferential tier of equal protection, 1945-99: economic and welfare classifications stand if any rational basis is conceivable (Williamson, 1955; Dandridge, 1970; Dukes, 1976, overruling Morey v. Doud), and Rodriguez (1973) refused heightened review for education and wealth. Cleburne (1985) and Romer (1996) struck classifications based on prejudice; Heller and Beach (1993) reaffirmed deference. Sex cases (Craig, 1976) merge in from 1980-84.

previous.description: The deferential tier of equal protection: economic and social-welfare classifications upheld if any rational basis exists (Williamson v. history: Dominant rule: classifications that neither burden fundamental rights nor target suspect classes are upheld if rationally related to a legitimate purpose on any conceivable facts (Lindsley, 1911; Williamson, 1955; McGowan, 1961). How it changed: in 1970-74 Reed (1971) anchors as Shapiro (1969), Loving (1967) and Graham (1971) show strict scrutiny for the right to travel, race and alienage. Dandridge (1970) anchors 1975-79, upholding AFDC caps, with Murgia (1976) declining to treat age as suspect and Dukes (1976) overruling Morey v. Doud. Rodriguez (1973) anchors 1980-84, holding education not fundamental, while sex and legitimacy units merge in with Craig (1976), Orr (1979) and Trimble (1977). Cleburne (1985) entered in 1985-89 and anchors 1990-94, striking a permit denial based on prejudice; state right-to-remedy cases (Carson, 1980) and Nordlinger (1992) on tax assessment join. In 1995-99 Heller (1993) and Beach (1993) confirmed that no evidence is needed, Romer (1996) struck an animus-based amendment, and a military unit merges in, so Feres (1950) anchors alongside challenges to military policies (Steffan, Watkins).

description: Alabama custody: a noncustodial parent seeking modification must show the change materially promotes the child's welfare (Ex parte McLendon 1984); a parent keeps a presumption against a nonparent unless unfit (Ex parte Terry 1986). Couch (1988) applied best interest to joint custody, Bryowsky (1996) applied McLendon to agreed joint legal custody, and from 2000-04 Ex parte Beasley's two-pronged termination test joins.

previous.description: Alabama custody-modification law under Ex parte McLendon, which requires a noncustodial parent to show a change would materially promote the child's welfare. history: Dominant rule: Ex parte McLendon (1984) anchors every slice from 1985-89 to 2000-04. history: Dominant rule: for most of the lineage, Massachusetts summary-judgment burdens under Rule 56, then the limits of at-will employment. How it changed: the tiny 1975-79 slice (Crane, Dawes, 1976) begins the summary-judgment line. Dawes (1976) anchors 1980-84 and 1985-89: the opponent must answer a supported motion with specific facts, not hypothetical allegations, and Massachusetts rules follow the federal construction (Rollins, 1975); interlocutory-appeal and affidavit cases join (Pollack, Madsen). Pederson (1989) anchors 1990-94 and required the movant to demonstrate affirmatively the absence of a triable issue, and Kourouvacilis (1991) adopted the Celotex approach that a movant may point to the opponent's lack of proof; Flesner (1991) warned against summary judgment on state-of-mind issues. In 1995-99 King (1994) anchors as the unit becomes employment law: Fortune (1977) and Gram (1981) limited the implied covenant to deprivation of earned compensation, Jackson (1988) the binding force of personnel manuals, and Smith-Pfeffer (1989), Mello (1988) and Wright (1992) confined the public-policy exception to clearly established policy. The unit then splits, with summary judgment and the implied covenant continuing separately.
rule: Under Mass. R. Civ. P. 56 the moving party must show there is no genuine issue of material fact, after which the opponent must set out specific facts showing a triable issue; and an at-will employee may sue on the implied covenant only for discharge that violates clearly established public policy or deprives him of earned compensation.

changes.what: Summary judgment is granted where the movant carries its burden and the opponent offers no specific facts, only hypothetical allegations; Dawes anchors 1980-89.

changes.case: Fortune v. National Cash Register; Gram v. Liberty Mutual
changes.what: An employer breaches the implied covenant by firing an at-will employee to deprive him of earned commissions or compensation, but discharge without cause alone is not actionable.
The moving party must affirmatively demonstrate the absence of a triable issue before the burden shifts; anchors 1990-94.
Adopted the Celotex approach: a movant without the burden at trial may prevail by showing the opponent has no reasonable expectation of proving an essential element.

changes.case: Jackson v. Action for Boston Community Development; Smith-Pfeffer; Mello; Wright v. Shriners Hospital
changes.what: Personnel manuals bind only in limited circumstances, and the public-policy exception is confined to clearly established public policy, not internal complaints or general social good.

name: Washington negligence: Young burden and take-charge duty (Taggart, Hertog)
description: Washington negligence decided on summary judgment: under Young (1989, anchor from 2010-14) a defendant may show the plaintiff lacks proof of an element. Public entities owe a take-charge duty for parolees and probationers (Taggart, 1992; Hertog, 1999, anchor 2000-04), but the public-duty doctrine bars other claims absent an express assurance (Taylor, 1988; Babcock, 2001). CPA claims under Hangman Ridge join in 2015-19.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Washington torts: government duty and the CPA
previous.description: Washington tort precedent on public entities' duties: take-charge duties of parole and probation officers (Taggart, Hertog), the public-duty doctrine (Taylor), and Consumer Protection Act claims (Hangman Ridge elements, Bain on deeds of trust).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: negligence requires duty, breach, injury and proximate cause (Folsom, Schooley, 1998). A Washington defendant can win summary judgment by showing the plaintiff lacks proof on one element, and the plaintiff must then come forward with specific facts (Young, 1989). How it changed: in 2000-04 Hertog (1999) anchors, extending Taggart's (1992) take-charge duty under Restatement § 319 from parole officers to probation and pretrial-release staff, with Hartley (1985) on legal causation and Schooley (1998) on factual causation. Folsom (1998) anchors 2005-09 with Taylor's (1988) public-duty doctrine, narrowed by Babcock (2001) and Cummins (2006) to cases of express, unequivocal assurances. Osborn (2006) restates the special-relationship duty. From 2010-14 Young anchors, with Ranger v. Pierce County (2008) on what defeats summary judgment and Seybold (2001) on expert proof in medical negligence. In 2015-19 Consumer Protection Act cases join (Hangman Ridge, 1986; Bain, 2012; Panag, 2009), and in 2020-24 Keck (2015) on late expert declarations and insurance bad-faith cases appear.
rule: In Washington a defendant may obtain summary judgment by showing the plaintiff lacks proof of an essential element of negligence (duty, breach, injury, proximate cause), after which the plaintiff must produce specific facts; a public entity owes a duty to control persons it has taken charge of, such as parolees and probationers, but otherwise owes duties to the public at large rather than to individuals.

changes.what: The public-duty doctrine: duties owed to the public generally, such as building inspection, support no individual tort claim absent an exception.
A moving defendant meets its initial burden by pointing to the plaintiff's lack of proof on an element, shifting the burden to the plaintiff; anchors from 2010-14.
Parole officers take charge of parolees under Restatement § 319 and owe a duty to protect others from their foreseeable dangers, without physical custody.
Extended the take-charge duty to city probation officers and county pretrial-release counselors.

changes.case: Babcock v. Mason County Fire Dist.; Cummins v. Lewis County
changes.what: The special-relationship exception to the public-duty doctrine requires an express assurance unequivocally given to the plaintiff.

changes.case: Hangman Ridge Training Stables v. Safeco; Bain v. Metropolitan Mortgage Group
changes.what: Consumer Protection Act claims require an unfair or deceptive act, in trade, affecting the public interest, injury and causation; Bain applied the Act to deed-of-trust beneficiary practices, leading 2015-19.

name: Idaho (later Kansas) termination of parental rights: Doe cases, Santosky, Troxel
description: Termination of parental rights in the Idaho Supreme Court's Doe decisions, later joined by Kansas: Troxel's (2000) parental liberty interest and Santosky's (1982) clear-and-convincing standard, rooted in Meyer and Pierce. Grounds under I.C. § 16-2005 are independent (Aragon, 1991), incarceration alone is not abandonment (Doe, 2002), and best interests come second. Georgia and Kansas cases join later (B.D.-Y., 2008; R.S., 2014).
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Idaho termination of parental rights
previous.description: Idaho Supreme Court termination and adoption cases (the Doe decisions) applying Santosky's clear-and-convincing standard and Troxel's parental liberty interest, rooted in Meyer and Pierce.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session subagents, from cocite evidence; second pass differentiated near-duplicates)

history: Dominant rule: termination requires clear and convincing proof of a statutory ground (Santosky, 1982) and then a best-interests finding, because parental rights are fundamental (Troxel, 2000; Meyer, 1923; Pierce, 1925). How it changed: in 2010-14 Troxel anchors a constitutional group (Santosky, Quilloin, Lassiter, Yoder, M.L.B.) drawn from substantive-due-process and Texas termination lines. From 2015-19 Idaho cases lead, with the 2014 termination decision as anchor. Grounds under I.C. § 16-2005 are independent (Aragon, 1991; Doe, 2007), incarceration alone is not willful abandonment (Doe, 2002), domestic violence can show neglect (Doe, 2006), and appellate review asks for substantial and competent evidence (Doe, 2009). Georgia cases on present unfitness and deprivation join (C.J.V., 2013; S.O.C., 2015), as do grandparent-visitation cases (Blixt, 2002). Doe (2006) anchors 2020-24, as Kansas decisions on the clear-and-convincing standard of review (B.D.-Y., 2008; R.S., 2014; M.S., 2019) enter. In the partial 2025-29 slice Kansas adoption cases lead (Baby Girl G., 2020), which is drift.
rule: Because parents have a fundamental liberty interest in the care, custody and control of their children (Troxel), the State must prove a statutory ground for termination by clear and convincing evidence (Santosky), each ground being independent, and must then show termination is in the child's best interests; Idaho appellate courts ask whether substantial and competent evidence supports the decision.

changes.case: Meyer v. Nebraska; Pierce v. Society of Sisters
changes.what: Parents' liberty to direct the upbringing of their children is protected by due process.
Due process requires clear and convincing evidence to terminate parental rights.
Parents have a fundamental right to make decisions about the care, custody and control of their children; Troxel anchors 2010-14.

changes.case: In re Aragon; Doe (2002); Doe (2006); Doe (2007)
changes.what: Statutory grounds under I.C. § 16-2005 are independent; incarceration alone is not willful abandonment where the parent tried to keep a relationship; persistent domestic violence can show neglect.

changes.case: In re Termination of Parental Rights (mother) (2014); Doe v. Doe (2015)
changes.what: Once a ground is proved the court must determine best interests, guided by nonexclusive considerations; an aggravated-circumstances finding is interlocutory.

changes.case: In re B.D.-Y.; In re R.S.; In re M.S. (Kan.)
changes.what: Kansas reviews termination findings under a standard incorporating clear and convincing proof, without reweighing credibility, and judges the foreseeable future from the child's perspective.

name: California resentencing: Estrada retroactivity and discretion to strike
description: California resentencing after the 2018-2022 reforms: ameliorative statutes reach nonfinal judgments (Estrada, 1965), and courts have discretion to strike priors and enhancements (Romero, 1996; Carmony, 2004). Dueñas (2019) anchors 2020-24 with an ability-to-pay requirement for fines; Stamps (2020) applied the new power to strike serious-felony enhancements to plea bargains. In 2025-29 the anchor shifts to Carmony and probation conditions (Lent, Ricardo P.).
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: California sentencing reform and resentencing (2020s)
previous.description: California's 2018-2022 sentencing changes: retroactive ameliorative statutes under In re Estrada, discretion to strike enhancements (Romero, Carmony), ability to pay fines (Dueñas), and youth-offender issues after Miller (Gutierrez).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: In re Estrada (1965) presumes that a statute reducing punishment applies to every judgment not final on its effective date, and trial courts may strike prior strikes and enhancements in furtherance of justice (Romero, 1996; Williams, 1998), with refusals reviewed for abuse of discretion (Carmony, 2004) and unobjected-to discretionary choices forfeited (Scott, 1994). How it changed: the lineage forms in 2020-24 from the merger of the Proposition 47, Proposition 36 and Apprendi sentencing units. Dueñas (2019) anchors that slice, requiring an ability-to-pay determination before fines (questioned in Kopp, 2019), and Buycks (2018) applied Proposition 47 to enhancements. Stamps (2020) applied the 2019 power to strike serious-felony enhancements while letting the prosecutor withdraw from a plea bargain. In 2025-29 Carmony anchors and the slice shifts toward probation conditions: Lent (1975), Sheena K. (2007) on vagueness, Olguin (2008) and Ricardo P. (2019) on conditions burdening privacy. Also: youth offenders after Miller (Gutierrez, 2014) and Cunningham resentencing (Sandoval, 2007).
rule: Ameliorative sentencing statutes apply to every judgment not yet final when they take effect (Estrada), and trial courts exercise reviewable discretion to strike prior strikes and enhancements (Romero, Carmony).

changes.what: A statute lessening punishment presumptively applies to defendants whose judgments are not final on its effective date.
Courts may strike prior strikes in furtherance of justice, judged by whether the defendant falls outside the Three Strikes scheme, and a refusal is reviewed for abuse of discretion.
Cunningham resentencings proceed under the amended § 1170(b), which gives the judge discretion among the three terms.
Due process requires an ability-to-pay determination before imposing certain fines and assessments.
The new discretion to strike a serious-felony enhancement applies retroactively, but a court that strikes it under a plea bargain lets the prosecutor withdraw from the bargain.

name: § 2255(e) savings clause, 2015-19: when federal prisoners may use § 2241
description: When the § 2255(e) savings clause lets a federal prisoner use § 2241, 2015-19 only: Dorsainvil (1997, anchor), Davenport and Reyes-Requena allowed it for a retroactive statutory decision showing innocence; a time bar or failed earlier motion does not suffice (Pack, Cradle). Prost (2011) and McCarthan (2017) narrowed the door; Brown v. Caraway (2013) opened it for career-offender errors. Jones v. Hendrix (2023) later closed the statutory-claim route.
history: Dominant rule: a federal prisoner normally attacks a conviction or sentence only under § 2255; § 2241 is for challenges to how the sentence is executed (Reyes-Requena, 2001), unless the savings clause applies because § 2255 is inadequate or ineffective. The lineage covers only 2015-19, with In re Dorsainvil (3d Cir. 1997) as anchor, after splitting from a habeas time-bar unit. How it developed: building on Davis (1974), Dorsainvil, Davenport (1998) and Reyes-Requena let prisoners convicted of conduct that a later statutory decision (Bailey) made non-criminal use § 2241, while insisting that AEDPA's gatekeeping limits alone do not make § 2255 inadequate. Pack (2000), Cradle (2002) and Okereke (2002) held that a time bar, successiveness or an Apprendi claim does not qualify; Kinder (2000) and Bradford (2011) excluded claims of innocence of a sentencing enhancement. The circuits then diverged: Prost (10th Cir. 2011) and McCarthan (11th Cir. en banc 2017) narrowed the clause, while Brown v. Caraway (7th Cir. 2013) and Webster v. Daniels (2015) allowed some sentencing and constitutional-ineligibility claims. Also: Simmons (4th Cir. en banc 2011) on prior-conviction exposure after Carachuri.
rule: A federal prisoner may bypass § 2255 and petition under § 2241 only when § 2255 is inadequate or ineffective, which a time bar, successiveness or a failed earlier motion does not show; most circuits allowed it for a retroactive statutory decision showing the prisoner was convicted of a non-crime.

changes.what: An intervening change in substantive law showing the act is not criminal can support collateral relief even on a nonconstitutional ground.

changes.case: In re Dorsainvil (3d Cir.); In re Davenport (7th Cir.); Reyes-Requena (5th Cir.)
changes.what: The savings clause opens § 2241 to a prisoner imprisoned for conduct an intervening, retroactive decision (such as Bailey) shows is not criminal, but not merely because the § 2255 gatekeeping limits bar relief.

changes.case: Pack (10th Cir.); Cradle (3d Cir.); Okereke (5th Cir.)
changes.what: A prior unsuccessful motion, the limitations period or successiveness does not make § 2255 inadequate, and Apprendi claims cannot be raised through § 2241.
§ 2255 is not inadequate when the prisoner could have raised the statutory argument in the first motion, even if circuit law then foreclosed it.
A pre-Booker career-offender misclassification is a miscarriage of justice that can be corrected under § 2241.

changes.case: McCarthan v. Director of Goodwill Industries (11th Cir. en banc)
changes.what: A change in statutory interpretation does not make § 2255 inadequate; § 2241 is for claims § 2255 cannot address at all, such as execution of the sentence.

before_differentiation.name: § 2255(e) savings clause: when a federal prisoner may use § 2241 (Dorsainvil, Prost)
before_differentiation.description: When the § 2255(e) savings clause lets a federal prisoner use § 2241. Dorsainvil (1997, anchor), Davenport and Reyes-Requena allowed it for a retroactive statutory decision showing innocence; a time bar or failed earlier motion does not suffice (Pack, Cradle). Prost (2011) and McCarthan (2017) narrowed the door; Brown v. Caraway (2013) opened it for career-offender errors. A single slice, 2015-19.

name: Comment on a defendant's silence and harmless error: Griffin, Doyle, Chapman
description: Use of a defendant's silence and harmless error. Griffin (1965, anchor 1975-79) bars comment on failure to testify; Doyle (1976, anchor 1980-84) bars impeachment with post-Miranda silence; Chapman (1967) and Harrington (1969) review such errors for harmlessness beyond a reasonable doubt. Jenkins (1980), Anderson v. Charles (1980) and Fletcher v. Weir (1982) allowed impeachment with pre-arrest or unwarned silence.
history: Dominant rule: the state may not use a defendant's exercise of silence against him, and violations are reviewed under Chapman's (1967) harmless-beyond-a-reasonable-doubt standard. Griffin (1965) anchors 1975-79: comment on a failure to testify violates the Fifth Amendment, as New York's Crimmins (1975) applied. Harrington (1969), Schneble (1972) and Milton (1972) found errors harmless on overwhelming evidence, and Fahy (1963) supplied the earlier reasonable-possibility test. How it changed: Hale (1975) and Doyle (1976) barred impeachment with silence after Miranda warnings, and Doyle anchors 1980-84. The Court then limited Doyle: Jenkins (1980) allowed impeachment with pre-arrest silence, Anderson v. Charles (1980) with prior inconsistent statements, and Fletcher v. Weir (1982) with post-arrest silence before warnings. Carter (1981) required a no-adverse-inference instruction on request (following Bruno 1939), and Hasting (1983) applied harmless-error review to comment on silence. Also: Raffel (1926) and Grunewald (1957) on testifying defendants. The unit then splits.
rule: The prosecution may not comment on a defendant's failure to testify or use post-Miranda-warning silence against him, but such errors are reviewed for harmlessness beyond a reasonable doubt, and pre-arrest or unwarned silence may be used to impeach.

changes.what: Prosecutorial or judicial comment on a defendant's failure to testify violates the Fifth Amendment.

changes.case: Chapman v. California; Harrington v. California; Schneble v. Florida; Milton v. Wainwright
changes.what: A constitutional error is harmless only if harmless beyond a reasonable doubt, which overwhelming evidence of guilt can show.

changes.case: United States v. Hale; Doyle v. Ohio
changes.what: Using silence after Miranda warnings to impeach violates due process (Doyle); Hale barred it under supervisory power as lacking probative value.

changes.case: Jenkins v. Anderson; Anderson v. Charles; Fletcher v. Weir
changes.what: Pre-arrest silence, post-arrest silence before warnings, and prior inconsistent statements may be used to impeach a testifying defendant.

changes.case: Carter v. Kentucky; United States v. Hasting
changes.what: A no-adverse-inference instruction must be given on request, and improper comment on silence is subject to harmless-error review.

name: New York Molineux rule on uncharged crimes, then harmless error (Crimmins)
description: New York's Molineux rule (1901): uncharged crimes are inadmissible to show propensity but admissible for motive, intent, absence of mistake, common scheme or identity, refined by Ventimiglia (1981, pretrial hearing) and Alvino (1987, anchor 1990-2004), with Sandoval (1974) impeachment. From 2005-09 the unit is anchored by Crimmins (1975) and Ashwal (1976) on harmless error and summation misconduct.

previous.name: New York criminal: Molineux uncharged-crimes evidence
previous.description: New York rules on evidence of uncharged crimes and prior bad acts admissible only for motive, intent, identity and similar purposes, not propensity (Molineux, Ventimiglia, Alvino, Allweiss), with Sandoval impeachment and Crimmins on harmless error.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session subagents, from cocite evidence; second pass differentiated near-duplicates)

history: Dominant rule: the Molineux rule, which bars uncharged-crime evidence offered to show propensity but admits it for motive, intent, absence of mistake, common scheme or identity. How it changed: Sandoval (1974) anchors 1975-79 with its procedure for impeaching a defendant with prior crimes. Allweiss (1979) anchors 1980-84 and Molineux itself 1985-89. Ventimiglia (1981) required a pretrial ruling and limited the 'inextricably interwoven' route; Crandall (1986) and Lewis (1987) elaborate. Alvino (1987) anchors 1990-94 through 2000-04 as the modern restatement of the balancing test, joined by Hudy (1988) on extrinsic proof of a motive to fabricate (abrogated in part by Carmell v. Texas, 2000). The dominant rule then shifts: from 2005-09 Crimmins (1975) leads and anchors 2010-14, with its significant-probability test for harmless error, and Ashwal (1976) anchors 2015-19 on summation misconduct, as the unit merges with the weight-and-preservation group. Dorm (2009) admitted background evidence of the parties' relationship.
rule: Evidence of a defendant's uncharged crimes or bad acts is inadmissible to show propensity but may be admitted for motive, intent, absence of mistake, common scheme or identity, or as inextricably interwoven background, when its probative value outweighs its prejudice.

changes.what: Other-crimes evidence is excluded as propensity proof but admissible for the five listed purposes.
Pretrial ruling on which prior convictions may be used to impeach a testifying defendant, weighing bearing on credibility against prejudice.

changes.case: People v. Crimmins; People v. Ashwal
changes.what: Non-constitutional error is harmless unless there is a significant probability the jury would have acquitted; prosecutorial summation misconduct can deny a fair trial.
Prosecutors should seek a pretrial ruling on uncharged-crime evidence, and 'inextricably interwoven' evidence is not admissible merely because it is part of an admissible conversation.
Restated the Molineux framework: the evidence must be relevant to a non-propensity issue and its probative value must exceed its prejudice.
Prior conflicts between defendant and victim may be admitted as background to the relationship and motive.

description: Private enforcement of federal statutes, 1970-99. Borak (1964) and Wyandotte (1967, anchor 1970-74) implied remedies freely; Cort v. Ash (1975) set four factors, but Redington and Lewis (1979, anchors 1980-89) made congressional intent controlling. For § 1983, Wright (1987) and Wilder (1990, anchor 1990-94) allowed suits; Suter (1992, anchor 1995-99) and Blessing (1997) narrowed them.

history: Dominant rule: whether a private party may sue to enforce a federal statute depends on congressional intent to create a private right and remedy. How it changed: Wyandotte (1967) anchors 1970-74 with Borak (1964) and Rigsby (1916), when remedies were implied to serve statutory purposes. Barbour (1975) anchors 1975-79 as Cort (1975) set four factors and Amtrak (1974) and Piper (1977) declined to imply remedies. Cannon (1979) found a Title IX remedy, but Lewis (anchor 1980-84) and Redington (anchor 1985-89) made intent decisive; Sierra Club, Sea Clammers, Northwest Airlines and Pennhurst (1981) restricted remedies and Spending Clause rights; Curran (1982) preserved implied Commodity Exchange Act actions; and Thompson (1988) treated Cort's factors as guides. In 1990-94 the focus moves to § 1983: Wilder (1990) anchors with Wright (1987), allowing suits to enforce Medicaid and housing provisions. Suter (1992) anchors 1995-99, requiring unambiguous conferral of rights, with Blessing (1997) and Dole (1987). The unit then joins the Eleventh Amendment lineage.
rule: Whether a private party may sue to enforce a federal statute, directly or through § 1983, depends on whether Congress intended to create a private right and remedy for that plaintiff.

changes.case: J.I. Case Co. v. Borak; Wyandotte Transportation v. United States
changes.what: Courts implied private remedies where needed to make a statute's purposes effective.

changes.case: National Railroad Passenger Corp. v. National Ass'n of Railroad Passengers; Cort v. Ash; SIPC v. Barbour; Piper v. Chris-Craft
changes.what: Cort set a four-factor test; express remedies weigh against implying others, and tender-offer competitors and SIPA customers had no implied action.

changes.case: Cannon v. University of Chicago; Touche Ross v. Redington; Transamerica Mortgage Advisors v. Lewis
changes.what: Cannon found a Title IX remedy, but Redington and Lewis made congressional intent the decisive question.

changes.case: California v. Sierra Club; Middlesex County Sewerage Authority v. Sea Clammers; Northwest Airlines v. Transport Workers; Pennhurst v. Halderman
changes.what: No implied rights under the Rivers and Harbors Act or for contribution; comprehensive remedial schemes preclude § 1983; Spending Clause conditions must be unambiguous.

changes.case: Merrill Lynch v. Curran; Thompson v. Thompson
changes.what: Congress's reenactment against a backdrop of implied remedies preserves them; Cort's factors are guides to intent.

changes.case: Wright v. Roanoke Redevelopment; Wilder v. Virginia Hospital Ass'n
changes.what: Section 1983 enforces statutory provisions that create enforceable rights, such as utility allowances and Boren Amendment rates.

changes.case: Suter v. Artist M.; Blessing v. Freestone
changes.what: A statute must unambiguously confer a right on the plaintiff; a 'reasonable efforts' requirement and Title IV-D's substantial-compliance standard do not.

description: A single 1970-74 slice on federal mootness: a case is moot when issues are no longer live (Powell, 1969; Rice, 1971), but survives for wrongs capable of repetition yet evading review (Southern Pacific, 1911, anchor; Moore v. history: Dominant rule: constitutional trial errors are reviewed for harmlessness, but structural errors require automatic reversal. Sullivan v. Louisiana (1993) anchors this single 1995-99 slice, with Chapman (1967) the heaviest case. Brecht (1993) adopted Kotteakos's substantial-and-injurious-effect test for federal habeas, and O'Neal (1995) held that grave doubt favors the petitioner. Sullivan (1993) made a defective reasonable-doubt instruction structural, building on Winship (1970), while Victor (1994) upheld instructions that, taken as a whole, conveyed the standard correctly. Alongside: Gideon, Zerbst and Faretta on counsel and waiver, and Estelle v. McGuire (1991) on the limits of habeas review. name: Press and public First Amendment access to proceedings, 1975-2009 (Richmond)

name: Builders' and architects' statutes of repose under state constitutions
description: State-court challenges to statutes of repose for architects and builders (1975-89): some courts uphold them because a repose statute keeps a claim from ever arising (Rosenberg 1972, anchor throughout; Freezer Storage 1978), while others strike them under special-legislation, open-courts or equal protection clauses (Skinner 1967, Saylor 1973, Sirmons 1979, Phillips 1980, Daugaard 1984).

history: Dominant rule: whether a statute of repose that cuts off claims against architects, engineers and builders a fixed number of years after completion is valid under state constitutions. history: Dominant rule: Anders v. name: Alleyne jury findings and punitive sex-offender registration, 2020-24
description: Jury findings and civil-versus-punitive sanctions, single 2020-24 slice: Apprendi (2000), Blakely (2004) and Alleyne (2013, anchor) require jury findings for facts that raise a sentence, with the Almendarez-Torres exception reaffirmed (Wallace 2014; Pervis 2019). history: Dominant rule: any fact other than a prior conviction that increases the penalty range, at the top (Apprendi 2000; Blakely 2004) or at the floor (Alleyne 2013, anchor of the only slice, 2020-24), is an element for the jury to find beyond a reasonable doubt. How it developed: the lineage forms in 2020-24 from three merging units. Almendarez-Torres (1998) treats recidivism as a sentencing factor, and circuit courts held it binding until the Supreme Court overrules it (Pineda-Arrellano 2007; Wallace 2014; Pervis 2019); Apprendi does not reach restitution (Sawyer 2016). A second strand asks when a nominally civil sanction is punishment: Mendoza-Martinez (1963) and Hudson (1997) supply the test, Smith v. Doe (2003) held Alaska's registration civil, and Does v. Snyder (6th Cir. 2016) and Commonwealth v. Muniz (Pa. 2017) found later registration schemes punitive. Building on Muniz, Commonwealth v. Butler (Pa. Super. 2017) held that sexually-violent-predator designations by judicial finding violate Apprendi and Alleyne. Haymond (2019) treated supervised-release terms as part of the sentence.

history: Dominant rule: AEDPA's one-year clock is tolled by properly filed state applications. Lee (4th Cir. 2001) anchors 2005-09 with Fourth Circuit gatekeeping cases. Winestock (2003) treats Rule 60(b) motions that attack the conviction as successive applications, and Reid (2004) requires a COA to appeal their denial. In 2010-14 Supreme Court law leads. Pace (2005) excludes untimely state petitions from statutory tolling, Gonzalez (2005) separates true Rule 60(b) motions from successive petitions, and Lawrence (2007) denies tolling during certiorari. Holland (2010) confirmed equitable tolling and allowed it for egregious attorney misconduct. Schlup (1995), Herrera (1993), Sawyer (1992) and House (2006) define the actual-innocence gateway, and Erickson (2007) requires liberal reading of pro se pleadings.

history: Dominant rule: Oregon courts seek the legislature's intent by examining text and context, then legislative history, then general maxims. How it changed: PGE (1993) anchors 1995-99 through 2005-09; context there includes related statutes and their history (Goodyear, 1995), prior judicial constructions (Davis, 1995) and preexisting common law, and the absurd-result maxim comes only after history (Young, 1999). Stull (1997) enters in 2000-04: the court must reach the correct interpretation whether or not the parties argue it. Gaines (2009) anchors from 2010-14, refining PGE after the 2001 amendment of ORS 174.020: text and context remain first, but history may be considered whenever useful. Later leading cases add rules of use: Cloutier (2011) on redundancy, Mowry (2011) on stare decisis for prior constructions, Comcast (2014) on legal dictionaries and Gonzalez-Valenzuela (2015) on their limits. Also: the 2005-09 slice carries speedy-trial (Johnson, Emery) and remedy-clause (Smothers, 2001, later overruled by Horton, 2016) cases, plus preservation rules (Wyatt, Stevens, Outdoor Media).

history: Dominant rule: the Second Circuit first checks a sentence for procedural error and then reviews its substance with deference, setting it aside only in exceptional cases outside the range of permissible decisions (Cavera, en banc 2008, anchor 2015-19 and 2020-24). How it changed: Fernandez (2006) presumed that judges consider the § 3553(a) factors (restated in Rosa 2020); Villafuerte (2007), Verkhoglyad (2008) and Marcus (2010) apply plain error to unpreserved procedural objections. Rigas (2009) reserved substantive relief for the rare case, and Broxmeyer (2012) left the weighing of factors to the judge; Muzio (2020) confined Dorvee (2010) to its narrow facts. Aldeen (2015) permits reliance on acquitted or uncharged conduct proved by a preponderance. Supervised-release conditions become a second focus: Matta (2015) barred delegating the choice of inpatient treatment, Betts (2018) requires conditions to be explained or self-evidently justified, and Eaglin (2019) treated total Internet bans as unusual and severe. In 2020-24 compassionate-release denials enter (Keitt 2021; Clenista 2022). Betts anchors the partial 2025-29 slice.

name: Conflict-free counsel in joint representation: Glasser and Holloway
description: The Sixth Amendment right to conflict-free counsel in joint representation of codefendants: Glasser (1942, anchor) held that forcing conflicting representation on a defendant is reversible without proof of prejudice. history: Dominant rule: Glasser (1942) anchors both slices. A defendant is entitled to counsel's undivided loyalty, and courts will not weigh the degree of prejudice once a conflict in joint representation is shown. How it changed: in 1970-74 circuit cases (Warner, 7th Cir. 1971; Lollar 1967; Sanders 1969) asked trial judges to inquire into joint representation, and Foster (1st Cir. 1972) prospectively shifted to the government the burden of showing prejudice was unlikely where no inquiry was made; Davenport (1973) treated even a remote possible conflict as enough. Illinois courts treated certain conflicts as per se: Stoval (1968) for counsel also representing the victim, and Kester and Coslet (1977) for counsel who had acted for the prosecution or a related party. Holloway v. Arkansas (1978) enters in 1975-79, holding that when counsel's timely objection is overruled without inquiry, prejudice is presumed. Also: the cluster carries unrelated criminal-evidence cases (Holland 1955 on net-worth proof, Falcone 1940 on conspiracy knowledge).
rule: The Sixth Amendment guarantees counsel's undivided loyalty, so when a court requires or permits joint representation over a timely objection or without adequate inquiry into a possible conflict, prejudice is presumed and reversal follows (Glasser, Holloway).

changes.what: Appointing one attorney to represent codefendants with conflicting interests over objection violates the Sixth Amendment without a showing of the degree of prejudice.

changes.case: People v. Kester; People v. Coslet (Ill.)
changes.what: A potential conflict, such as prior representation of the prosecution, required reversal without proof of actual prejudice.

history: Dominant rule: the process due before a prison deprives an inmate of a protected liberty interest. Wolff (1974) leads throughout: losing good time requires notice, a chance to call witnesses and a written statement. How it changed: Hewitt (1983) anchors 1985-94, finding interests where regulations used mandatory substantive predicates, with Olim (1983) and Thompson (1989) requiring explicit limits on discretion; Meachum (1976) denied any interest in a particular prison, Greenholtz (1979) treated parole statutes case by case, Dumschat (1981) found no interest in commutation, and Vitek (1980) found one in avoiding transfer to a mental hospital. Morrissey (1972) and civil-commitment cases (Addington 1979, Jones 1983) join in 1985-94. Hill and Ponte (1985) set evidence and witness rules. Sandin (1995) anchors 1995-2004, limiting interests to atypical and significant hardship, while Turner (1987), Bounds (1977) and Wolfish (1979) join the core; Heck (1994) and Edwards (1997), with Preiser (1973), bar damages claims implying invalid discipline. In 2000-04 Seventh Circuit cases (McPherson 1999, Webb 2000) apply these rules before the unit splits.
rule: A prisoner is owed procedural due process only when deprived of a protected liberty interest, which after Sandin (1995) means an atypical and significant hardship or a loss affecting the duration of custody; then Wolff's notice, witness and written-statement protections apply.

changes.what: Challenges to the fact or length of confinement, including good-time restoration, lie in habeas corpus, not § 1983.

history: Dominant rule: a guilty plea waives the privilege, jury trial and confrontation, so the record must affirmatively show that the defendant entered it knowingly, intelligently and voluntarily; waiver cannot be presumed from a silent record (Boykin, 1969, the anchor in every slice). How it changed: in 1970-74 McCarthy (1969) made Rule 11 noncompliance reversible, though Halliday (1969) denied it retroactive effect, and In re Tahl (1969) required California courts to enumerate the three rights; Wade v. From 1975-79 the Brady trilogy (Brady, McMann, Parker, 1970) holds that pleas induced by fear of a harsher penalty, or entered on reasonable but mistaken advice, are voluntary, and Alford (1970) allows pleas with protestations of innocence if the factual basis is strong. Santobello (1971) required the state to honour promises that induced a plea. Tollett (1973) held that a counselled plea bars independent pre-plea claims. Henderson v. Morgan (1976) required notice of the essential elements, and it leads in 1980-84 and 1985-89 with state cases on the factual basis and the colloquy (Marra 1978, Battle 1976).
