The 1970 trilogy (Brady, McMann, Parker) and Alford (1970) upheld bargained pleas; Santobello (1971) enforced plea promises; Tollett (1973) made counselled pleas waive pre-plea claims; Henderson v. Morgan (1976) required notice of elements.

distinct_from.how: This sub follows the colloquy and the notice of elements across 1970-89, largely in state courts; that cluster covers 1980-89 collateral relief (Timmreck) and counsel's plea advice (Hill v. Lockhart).
This sub runs 1970-89 and centres on the colloquy and Henderson v. Morgan; that cluster is the single 1970-74 slice centred on McCarthy's Rule 11 and the Brady trilogy.

name: California homicide instructions and harmless error: Barton, Breverman, Chun
description: California noncapital homicide instructions and the harmless-error tests applied to them: sua sponte imperfect self-defense (Barton 1995), voluntary manslaughter without intent to kill (Blakeley 2000), felony-murder merger (Chun 2009); omitted lesser-included instructions are tested under Watson (Breverman 1998). Watson (1956) anchors from 2010-14, with Chapman (1967) for federal error.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, round 2 after the lineage re-link)

previous.name: California harmless error: Watson, Chapman and structural error
previous.description: California appellate harmless-error analysis pairing Watson's state-law reasonable-probability test with Chapman, Neder, Fulminante and Sullivan on federal harmlessness and structural error, often for instructional error (Breverman, Moye).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session subagents, from cocite evidence; second pass differentiated near-duplicates)

history: Dominant rule: Watson (1956) governs state-law error, which is reversible only if it is reasonably probable the defendant would have obtained a better result; Chapman (1967) governs federal constitutional error. How it changed: the anchor moves from homicide-instruction cases to the harmless-error tests themselves. In 1995-99 (Pearson anchor) Flannel (1979) and Barton (1995) set the duty to instruct sua sponte on imperfect self-defense, superseding Wickersham (1982). Blakeley (2000) anchors 2000-04 and, with Lasko (2000), held that voluntary manslaughter needs no intent to kill; Breverman (1998) put noncapital lesser-offense omissions under Watson. Griffin (1965), on comment on a defendant's silence, anchors 2005-09 as Chapman enters. Watson anchors 2010-14 through 2020-24. Chun (2009) overruled Robertson on merger in felony murder; Moye (2009) and Beltran (2013) refined heat of passion, Beltran stating that Watson asks what a jury would likely have done. Also: battered-woman evidence (Humphrey 1996) and Kelly-Frye scientific evidence (Kelly 1976; Leahy 1994; Venegas 1998). The unit swaps cases with the California capital lineage in 2020-24 and splits in 2025-29.
rule: In California, state-law error, including a failure to instruct sua sponte on a lesser included offense in a noncapital case, reverses only if a better result was reasonably probable (Watson; Breverman), while federal constitutional error must be harmless beyond a reasonable doubt (Chapman).

changes.what: An honest but unreasonable belief in the need for self-defense negates malice, reducing murder to voluntary manslaughter.
Trial courts must instruct sua sponte on imperfect self-defense when substantial evidence supports it, rejecting Wickersham's treatment of it as a defense needing no sua sponte instruction.
Failing to instruct sua sponte on a lesser included offense in a noncapital case is state-law error reviewed under Watson.

changes.case: People v. Blakeley; People v. Lasko
changes.what: Voluntary manslaughter does not require intent to kill; an unintentional killing in heat of passion or imperfect self-defense qualifies.
Overruled People v. Robertson and applied the merger doctrine to assaultive felonies in second-degree felony murder.
Watson asks what a reasonable jury would likely have done absent the error, not what it could have done; heat of passion is measured by an ordinary person of average disposition.

round1.name: California harmless error: Watson, Chapman, and structural error (Fulminante, Neder)
round1.description: California harmless error: state-law error reverses only on a reasonable probability of a better result (Watson, 1956), which covers omitted lesser-included instructions in noncapital cases (Breverman, 1998); federal error must be harmless beyond a reasonable doubt (Chapman, 1967), save structural errors (Fulminante, 1991; Sullivan, 1993; Gonzalez-Lopez, 2006). Neder (1999) and Weaver (2017) narrowed automatic reversal. Watson anchors every slice; many cases concern homicide instructions.
round1.history: Dominant rule: Watson (1956) anchors all three slices. State-law error is reversible only if, on the whole record, it is reasonably probable the defendant would have obtained a better result; the inquiry is what a reasonable jury likely would have done, not what it could have done (People v. Beltran, 2013). Chapman (1967) governs federal constitutional error. How it changed: no shift in the core tests. Fulminante (1991) and Sullivan (1993) defined structural error, Neder (1999) held an omitted element can be harmless, Gonzalez-Lopez (2006) made counsel-of-choice violations structural, and Weaver (2017), entering in 2020-24, required prejudice when structural error is raised as ineffectiveness. Breverman (1998) and Barton (1995) set the duty to instruct sua sponte on lesser offenses and imperfect self-defense, with Breverman putting noncapital omissions under Watson. The cases applied are largely homicide instruction disputes: heat of passion (Moye, 2009; Beltran, 2013), imperfect self-defense (Christian S., 1994; Manriquez, 2005), diminished actuality (Steele, 2002; Saille, 1991) and merger in felony murder (Chun, 2009, overruling Robertson). The unit swaps cases with the California capital lineage in 2015-19 and 2020-24.
round1.rule: California courts reverse state-law error, including most instructional error such as an omitted lesser-included instruction, only on a reasonable probability of a more favourable result (Watson, Breverman); federal constitutional error must be harmless beyond a reasonable doubt (Chapman), except structural errors that require automatic reversal (Fulminante, Sullivan).

changes.case: Arizona v. Fulminante; Sullivan v. Louisiana
changes.what: Separated trial errors, subject to Chapman, from structural defects such as a defective reasonable-doubt instruction, which are never harmless.

changes.case: People v. Barton; People v. Breverman
changes.what: Courts must instruct sua sponte on lesser included offenses and theories such as unreasonable self-defense when substantial evidence supports them, but in noncapital cases the omission is state-law error reviewed under Watson.
Omitting an uncontested element from the jury charge is not structural and can be harmless.
Denial of counsel of choice is structural error needing no showing of prejudice.
Overruled People v. Robertson and applied the merger doctrine to bar second-degree felony murder based on assaultive felonies.
Watson asks what a reasonable jury is likely to have done absent the error; provocation for heat of passion must make an ordinary person react without reflection.
A preserved structural error gets automatic reversal on direct appeal, but raised through ineffective assistance it requires prejudice.

before_differentiation.name: California harmless error (Watson, Chapman) and homicide-instruction duties
before_differentiation.description: California harmless error: state-law error reverses only on a reasonable probability of a better result (Watson 1956, anchor from 2010-14), including omitted lesser-included instructions in noncapital cases (Breverman 1998); federal error must be harmless beyond a reasonable doubt (Chapman 1967). Most errors tested are homicide instructions: imperfect self-defense (Barton 1995), manslaughter (Blakeley 2000), merger (Chun 2009).

distinct_from.how: The 1995-2024 successor on homicide instructions and Watson; the 1970-84 cluster centres on Daniels kidnapping and Sedeno.
The harmless-error and homicide-instruction strand of the modern family, without its capital review, Batson, Crawford or SB 1437 strands.
Noncapital homicide instructions and harmless error, not 1995-99 capital special circumstances.
Noncapital homicide instructions, not 1985-94 death-penalty review.
Tests instruction error under Watson/Chapman in noncapital cases; the other unit sets forfeiture and misconduct standards in capital appeals.
Homicide instructions and harmless error, not 2005-09 capital jury selection.
Noncapital homicide instructions, not 1995-99 capital penalty argument and voir dire.

name: New York premises liability: notice of the condition (Gordon) on summary judgment
description: New York premises liability: an owner is liable only if it created the condition or had actual or constructive notice, and constructive notice needs a visible defect present long enough to be found (Gordon, 1986; Piacquadio, 1994). Gordon anchors 1990-99; from 2000-04 the Zuckerman/Alvarez/Winegrad summary-judgment burdens anchor. Also Basso's (1976) single duty, Derdiarian (1980) on intervening causes, Turcotte (1986) assumption of risk and Espinal (2002) on contractors.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: New York premises liability
previous.description: New York negligence on summary judgment: actual and constructive notice of a dangerous condition (Gordon v. American Museum, Piacquadio), contractors' duties to third parties (Espinal), intervening causes (Derdiarian), and the Alvarez/Winegrad/Zuckerman burdens.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: Gordon (1986) anchors 1990-94 and 1995-99: a slip-and-fall plaintiff must show the owner created the hazard or had actual or constructive notice, and constructive notice requires a visible and apparent defect that existed long enough to be discovered and fixed; speculation about how long a substance lay on the floor fails (Anderson, 1988; Torri, 1989; Bykofsky, 1994), and general awareness is not notice (Piacquadio, 1994). How it changed: from 2000-04 the unit merges with summary-judgment cases and the anchor becomes Zuckerman (1980), then Alvarez (1986) from 2005-09 and Winegrad (1985) in 2020-24, so the governing frame becomes the movant's prima facie burden. Basso (1976) supplies a single reasonable-care duty for landowners. Turcotte (1986) and Morgan (1997) treat primary assumption of risk as no duty in sports. Espinal (2002) enters in 2005-09 and limits contractors' duties to third parties to three exceptions. Mirand (1994) covers school supervision, Derdiarian (1980) intervening causes, and Trincere (1997) and Hutchinson (2015) trivial sidewalk defects.
rule: A New York property owner is liable for a dangerous condition only if it created the condition or had actual or constructive notice of it, constructive notice requiring a visible and apparent defect present long enough to be discovered and remedied (Gordon); a general awareness of a hazard is not enough.

changes.what: Replaced the invitee/licensee/trespasser categories with a single duty to maintain property in a reasonably safe condition.
An intervening act does not break causation if it is a normal or foreseeable consequence of the situation the defendant created; foreseeability is usually for the jury.

changes.case: Gordon v. American Museum of Natural History
changes.what: Constructive notice requires a visible, apparent defect existing long enough to be discovered; general awareness of litter is insufficient.
After comparative negligence, primary assumption of risk operates as a no-duty rule for participants in sports.
A general awareness that a dangerous condition may be present is legally insufficient notice of the particular condition.
A contractor owes no tort duty to third parties unless it launched a force or instrument of harm, induced detrimental reliance, or displaced the owner's duty entirely.

name: Texas parental-rights termination: endangerment grounds, Holley, C.H. review
description: Texas termination of parental rights: clear and convincing proof of a statutory ground, often endangerment under § 161.001(b)(1)(D) or (E), plus best interest under Holley (1976, anchor 1990-94) and G.M. (1980, anchor 1995-99). C.H. and J.F.C. (2002) set heightened sufficiency review and anchor from 2000-04. Boyd (1987) and J.O.A. (2009) allow endangerment to be inferred from conduct, and N.G. (2019) requires review of challenged (D) and (E) findings.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Texas parental-rights termination
previous.description: Termination of parental rights in Texas: statutory endangerment grounds under § 161.001(1), the Holley best-interest factors, clear-and-convincing evidence and heightened sufficiency review (In re C.H., In re J.F.C.), and incarceration as endangerment (Boyd).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: termination requires clear and convincing evidence of a § 161.001(b)(1) ground and of best interest. How it changed: Holley (1976) anchors 1990-94 with Boyd (1987), Holick (1985) and Sims (1990). G.M. (1980), which required clear and convincing proof, anchors 1995-99. Courts of appeals then applied ordinary sufficiency tests (Meadows, 1975; Neiswander, 1982), and Harris (1992) and D.T. (2000) held imprisonment alone is neither endangerment nor abandonment. In 2000-04 C.H. (2002) and J.F.C. (2002) enter and anchor every later slice (J.F.C. in 2015-19), adopting the firm-belief-or-conviction standard for factual and legal sufficiency. A.V. (2003) holds one ground suffices, J.T.G. (2003) and J.O.A. (2009) reach drug use and conduct not aimed at the child, and H.R.M. (2006) requires deference to the factfinder. M.S. (2003) recognized a right to effective counsel. E.N.C. (2012) limits endangerment from incarceration or deportation, and N.G. (2019) leads 2020-24, requiring review of challenged (D) and (E) findings.
rule: Texas termination requires clear and convincing evidence of a § 161.001(b)(1) ground, such as endangering conditions or conduct (subsections (D) and (E)), and that termination is in the child's best interest under the Holley factors, reviewed under the heightened legal and factual sufficiency standards of C.H. and J.F.C.

changes.what: Both a predicate ground and best interest must be proved, with best interest weighed by non-exclusive factors; anchors 1990-94.
Termination findings must rest on clear and convincing evidence; anchors 1995-99.

changes.case: Texas Department of Human Services v. Boyd; Harris (1992)
changes.what: Endangerment may be inferred from parental misconduct and imprisonment is a relevant factor, but imprisonment alone does not establish endangering conduct.

changes.case: In re C.H.; In re J.F.C.
changes.what: Adopted heightened factual- and legal-sufficiency review asking whether a factfinder could form a firm belief or conviction, replacing the courts of appeals' ordinary sufficiency formulations; C.H. anchors from 2000-04.

changes.case: In re A.V.; In re J.T.G.; In re J.O.A.
changes.what: One predicate suffices with a best-interest finding; drug use and violence can establish endangerment; endangering conduct need not be aimed at the child.
Not every offense that could lead to confinement or deportation establishes endangerment.
Because (D) and (E) findings carry collateral consequences, due process requires appellate review of a challenge to them even when another ground supports termination.

name: Texas default judgments: the Craddock test, defective service, bills of review
description: Setting aside Texas default judgments under Craddock (1939), the anchor in every slice but 2015-19 (Silver): no intentional failure or conscious indifference, a meritorious defense, and no delay or injury. Peralta (1988) and Wilson (1991) void judgments without notice or strict service; Evans (1994) accepts uncontroverted affidavits; Caldwell (2004) relieves non-served bill-of-review plaintiffs; Lerma (2009) leads from 2010-14.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, round 2 after the lineage re-link)

previous.name: Texas default judgments and restricted appeals
previous.description: Setting aside default judgments in Texas under Craddock v. Sunshine Bus Lines (no conscious indifference, meritorious defense, no undue delay), lack of notice (Peralta), defective service, bills of review and restricted appeals.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: Craddock (1939) anchors 2005-09, 2010-14, 2020-24 and the partial 2025-29 slice: a defaulting defendant gets a new trial by showing its failure was due to accident or mistake rather than intent or conscious indifference, a meritorious defense, and that a new trial will not cause delay or injury. Ivy (1966) extended the test to post-answer defaults. In 2005-09 Cliff (1987) and Peralta (1988) lead, treating lack of notice as decisive under due process, with Alexander (2004) holding a silent record shows no error and Villarreal (1999) on dismissal for want of prosecution. How it changed: Lerma (2009) enters and leads from 2010-14, requiring remand when a post-answer default rests on insufficient evidence, with Lejeune (2009) voiding judgments on defective returns. Silver (1994), requiring amendment of a defective return before judgment, anchors 2015-19 with Wilson (1991) and Uvalde (1985) on strict service and Norman Communications (1997) on sufficiency review in restricted appeals. Evans (1994) made uncontroverted affidavits binding, and Caldwell (2004), Gold (2004) and Drewery (2006) shaped bills of review. Also: lost-profits proof (Heine 1992) in 2020-24 and diligence in service (Proulx 2007).
rule: A Texas default judgment is set aside if the defendant shows its failure was not intentional or the result of conscious indifference, a meritorious defense, and that a new trial will cause no delay or injury; a judgment without proper service or notice is void.

changes.what: Three-part equitable test for setting aside a default judgment.
Craddock applies to post-answer defaults where the defendant fails to appear for trial.

changes.case: Cliff v. Huggins; Peralta v. Heights Medical Center
changes.what: A defendant without notice of the suit or trial setting is entitled to relief as a matter of due process, without a meritorious-defense showing.

changes.case: Wilson v. Dunn; Primate Construction v. Silver; Director, State Employees Workers' Comp. Div. v. Evans
changes.what: Strict compliance with service rules is required and a defective return must be amended before judgment; uncontroverted Craddock affidavits must be accepted.

changes.case: Caldwell v. Barnes; Gold v. Gold; Fidelity & Guaranty v. Drewery Construction
changes.what: A bill-of-review plaintiff who was not served need not show fraud or diligence, need not first pursue a restricted appeal, and may prove non-service by evidence outside the return.
A post-answer default supported by legally insufficient evidence is reversed and remanded, not rendered; Craddock relief should not be denied over a reasonable excuse.

round1.name: Texas default judgments: the Craddock test, defective service, bills of review
round1.description: Setting aside Texas default judgments under Craddock (1939), anchor in every slice: no intentional failure or conscious indifference, a meritorious defense, and no delay or injury. Peralta (1988) and Wilson (1991) void judgments without notice or strict service; Evans (1994) accepts uncontroverted affidavits; Caldwell (2004) relieves non-served bill-of-review plaintiffs; Lerma (2009) remands for insufficient evidence.
round1.history: Dominant rule: Craddock (1939) anchors every slice: a defaulting defendant gets a new trial by showing its failure was due to accident or mistake rather than intent or conscious indifference, a meritorious defense, and that a new trial will not cause delay or injury. How it changed: Ivy (1966) extended the test to post-answer defaults, and Strackbein (1984), Bank One (1992) and Smith (1996) held that an uncontroverted explanation negates conscious indifference. Peralta (1988) and Cliff (1987) treated lack of notice as decisive under due process. Wilson (1991), Uvalde Country Club (1985) and Silver (1994) required strict service and correct returns, and Evans (1994), leading 1995-2004, made uncontroverted affidavits binding. Norman Communications (1997) allowed sufficiency review in restricted appeals, and Alexander (2004) held a silent record shows no error on its face. Caldwell (2004), Gold (2004) and Drewery (2006) shaped bills of review and service challenges; Lerma (2009) leads from 2010-14, requiring remand for insufficient evidence. Also: lost-profits proof (Heine 1992, Texas Instruments 1994), dismissal for want of prosecution (Villarreal 1999), and diligence in service (Proulx 2007).
round1.rule: A default judgment must be set aside and a new trial granted if the defendant shows that the failure to answer or appear was not intentional or the result of conscious indifference but an accident or mistake, sets up a meritorious defense, and moves when a new trial will cause no delay or injury to the plaintiff; a judgment without proper service or notice is void regardless of the Craddock elements.

changes.what: The three-part equitable test for setting aside a default judgment.
Craddock applies to post-answer defaults where the defendant fails to appear for trial.
A bill of review plaintiff must present prima facie proof of a meritorious defense as a pretrial matter.

changes.case: Cliff v. Huggins; Peralta v. Heights Medical Center
changes.what: A defendant without notice of the setting satisfies Craddock, and due process voids a judgment entered without notice even absent a meritorious defense.

changes.case: Wilson v. Dunn; Primate Construction v. Silver; Director, State Employees Workers' Comp. Div. v. Evans
changes.what: Strict compliance with service rules is required and actual notice does not cure defective service; returns must be amended before judgment; uncontroverted Craddock affidavits must be accepted.
A bill-of-review plaintiff who proves non-service need not show a meritorious defense or extrinsic fraud.
A post-answer default resting on legally insufficient evidence is reversed and remanded, not rendered; Craddock's first prong requires accident or mistake.

name: Florida dissolution review: Canakaris discretion and Rowe fee lodestar
description: Florida domestic-relations review: Canakaris (1980), anchor 1980-99, treats spouses as partners, allows lump-sum alimony for equitable distribution, and reverses only if no reasonable person would agree; Shaw (1976), anchor 1975-79, requires competent substantial evidence. Rowe (1985), anchor 2000-04, adopted the lodestar for fee awards and Quanstrom (1990) restated the contingency multiplier.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Florida divorce: equitable distribution and alimony
previous.description: Florida domestic-relations law: equitable distribution and lump-sum alimony (Canakaris, including its abuse-of-discretion test), competent substantial evidence (Shaw v. Shaw), and attorney's fee lodestar findings (Florida Patient's Compensation Fund v. Rowe).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: Florida appellate courts defer to the trial court's discretion in dividing property, awarding alimony and setting fees, reversing only when no reasonable person would take its view (Canakaris 1980), and accept findings supported by competent substantial evidence (Shaw 1976). How it changed: Shaw anchors 1975-79, with Lash (1975) on rehabilitative alimony, Herzog (1977) against reweighing, and Ball (1976) on special equity. Canakaris anchors 1980-99, holding spouses are partners and lump-sum alimony may achieve equitable distribution; Kuvin and Conner (1983) and Marcoux (1985) reinforced deference, Duncan (1980) treated exclusive home possession as child support in kind, Tronconi (1985) allowed reciprocal lump-sum awards, Diffenderfer (1986) treated pensions as marital assets, and Hamlet (1991) required viewing remedies together. New-trial cases (Cloud 1959, Canty 1978, Baptist Memorial 1980) apply the same discretion standard. Rowe (1985) adopted the lodestar for fees, applied in dissolution cases under § 61.16 (Boyle 1986, Kuse 1988), and Quanstrom (1990) restated the multiplier; Rowe anchors 2000-04. Bowen (1985) required a present-ability finding for civil-contempt incarceration.
rule: Florida trial courts have broad discretion to fashion alimony and equitable distribution, treating spouses as partners, and are reversed only if no reasonable person would adopt their view, with findings upheld if supported by competent substantial evidence; attorney's fee awards must rest on lodestar findings of a reasonable hourly rate and hours reasonably expended.

changes.case: Lash v. Lash; Shaw v. Shaw; Ball v. Ball
changes.what: Rehabilitative alimony presupposes capacity for self-support; nonjury findings stand if supported by competent substantial evidence; special equity arises when one spouse supplies all consideration for entireties property.

Spouses are partners in distributing marital assets; lump-sum alimony may be used to achieve equitable distribution; discretion is abused only if no reasonable person would take the trial court's view.

changes.case: Kuvin v. Kuvin; Conner v. Conner; Marcoux v. Marcoux
changes.what: Whether a spouse was shortchanged is a factual question; appellate courts exceed their role by reweighing the trial court's discretionary judgment.

changes.case: Florida Patient's Compensation Fund v. Rowe
changes.what: Florida adopted the federal lodestar method; fee awards require findings on reasonable hourly rate and hours, with a possible contingency multiplier.
Pensions can be marital assets despite contingencies, and the same asset may not be counted twice for distribution and support.

changes.case: Standard Guaranty Ins. Co. v. Quanstrom
changes.what: Restated when a contingency multiplier applies, with factors including whether the relevant market requires one.

name: Double jeopardy same offense: Blockburger elements test, Grady overruled by Dixon
description: The Double Jeopardy Clause's same-offense rules (1975-2009): Blockburger (1931) anchors 1975-99. Brown v. Ohio (1977) bars successive prosecution for lesser included offenses; Whalen, Albernaz and Missouri v. Hunter (1980-83) make multiple punishment a question of legislative intent. Grady (1990) added a same-conduct test that Dixon (1993) overruled. From 2000 the anchor moves to vindictiveness (Pearce) and mistrials (Green 1957).
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Double jeopardy: same offense and multiple punishment
previous.description: The Double Jeopardy Clause: Blockburger's same-elements test, multiple punishments and legislative intent (Whalen, Albernaz, Missouri v. Hunter), successive prosecutions (Brown v. Ohio, Grady, Dixon), collateral estoppel (Ashe), incorporation (Benton) and vindictive resentencing (Pearce).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: Blockburger (1931) anchors every slice from 1975-79 to 1995-99. Offenses are distinct if each requires proof of an element the other does not. How it changed: Brown v. Ohio (1977) and Harris v. Oklahoma (1977) bar successive prosecution for greater and lesser included offenses, and Ashe (1970) adds collateral estoppel. In 1980-84 multiple-punishment cases enter. Whalen (1980) applied Blockburger to rape and felony murder, Albernaz (1981) allowed separate conspiracy punishments, and Missouri v. Hunter (1983) and Garrett (1985) held that clear legislative intent controls. In 1985-89 the vindictiveness unit merges in: Pearce (1969) and Blackledge (1974) presume vindictiveness after a successful appeal, but Bordenkircher (1978) and Goodwin (1982) reject it for plea bargaining and pretrial charging. Grady v. Corbin (1990) enters in 1990-94 with a same-conduct test, and Dixon (1993) overruled Grady. Pearce anchors 2000-04, and Green (1957) anchors 2005-09 as a mistrial unit merges in (Arizona v. Washington, Oregon v. Kennedy, Jorn), drift toward retrial rules.
rule: Two offenses are the same for double jeopardy purposes unless each requires proof of an element the other does not (Blockburger); in a single trial the test is a rule of construction yielding to clear legislative intent to impose cumulative punishment (Hunter), while successive prosecution for a greater and lesser included offense is barred (Brown v. Ohio) and an acquittal's necessary findings bind under collateral estoppel (Ashe).

changes.what: Same-elements test for whether two statutory offenses are the same.

changes.case: Benton v. Maryland; North Carolina v. Pearce; Blackledge v. Perry
changes.what: The Clause applies to the states; a harsher sentence after retrial carries a presumption of vindictiveness, extended to prosecutors' added charges.
Collateral estoppel is part of the double jeopardy guarantee.

changes.case: Brown v. Ohio; Harris v. Oklahoma
changes.what: Successive prosecution and cumulative punishment for greater and lesser included offenses are barred.

changes.case: Whalen v. United States; Albernaz v. United States; Missouri v. Hunter; Garrett v. United States
changes.what: Multiple punishment turns on legislative intent; Blockburger is a rule of construction that clear intent overrides.

changes.case: Bordenkircher v. Hayes; United States v. Goodwin
changes.what: No presumption of vindictiveness in plea bargaining or for pretrial charging decisions.
Added a same-conduct test barring a later prosecution that proves conduct already prosecuted.
Overruled Grady and restored the same-elements test as the sole test.

name: Guilty-plea voluntariness (Boykin) turning to Tennessee IAC, 1995-2004
description: Plea voluntariness, then counsel: in 1995-99 Boykin (1969, anchor) requires the record to show a knowing, voluntary plea, with Alford and Brady (1970), applied in Ohio and other state cases on Crim.R. 11 colloquies and plea misadvice. In 2000-04 Tennessee post-conviction law leads: Baxter v. Rose (1975, anchor) on competence, Hill (1985) for pleas, Goad (1996) and Henley (1997) on the two prongs, and Burns (1999) on lesser-included offenses.
history: Dominant rule: post-conviction review of guilty pleas and counsel's performance. How it changed: in 1995-99 Boykin (1969) anchors: a plea must affirmatively appear knowing and voluntary on the record. Alford (1970) allows a plea despite claimed innocence and Brady (1970) holds that a desire to avoid a harsher sentence is not coercion; Ohio and other state cases address plea colloquies under Crim.R. 11 (Nero, 1990) and counsel's misadvice about sentences (Alexander, 1992; Blankenship, 1993). In 2000-04 the unit merges with a Texas ineffective-assistance unit and Tennessee post-conviction law leads: Baxter v. Rose (1975) anchors on counsel's required competence, with Hill (1985) applying Strickland to pleas, Goad (1996) and Henley (1997) allowing denial on either prong and deferring to strategy, Hellard (1982) rejecting hindsight, and Fields (2001) leaving credibility to the post-conviction court. Burns (1999) on lesser-included offenses also leads. The lineage splits in 2005-09, partly into Ohio post-conviction and res judicata.
rule: A guilty plea is valid only if the record affirmatively shows it was knowing and voluntary (Boykin), even if the defendant maintains innocence (Alford), and a post-conviction claim that counsel was ineffective requires deficient performance and prejudice, which for a plea means a reasonable probability the defendant would have gone to trial (Hill), either prong's failure being enough to deny relief.

changes.case: Boykin v. Alabama; North Carolina v. Alford; Brady v. United States
changes.what: A plea waiving trial rights must affirmatively appear knowing and voluntary on the record; a plea may be accepted despite protestations of innocence where a strong factual basis exists; fear of a harsher sentence does not make a plea involuntary.
Tennessee requires counsel's representation to be within the range of competence demanded of criminal attorneys, including investigation of substantial defenses.
The Strickland test applies to guilty pleas.

changes.case: Goad v. State; Henley v. State (Tenn.)
changes.what: Failure to prove either deficiency or prejudice defeats the claim, and courts defer to counsel's informed strategic choices.
Tennessee adopted a Model Penal Code-based test for lesser-included offenses and requires instructions on those supported by the evidence.

phases.rule: voluntariness of guilty pleas (Boykin, Alford, Brady)
Tennessee post-conviction ineffective assistance (Baxter, Henley, Goad)

before_differentiation.name: Guilty pleas and ineffective assistance in state post-conviction review
before_differentiation.description: Guilty pleas and ineffective assistance on post-conviction review: in 1995-99 Boykin (1969, anchor), Alford and Brady (1970) govern plea voluntariness, applied in Ohio and other state cases on plea advice. In 2000-04 Tennessee post-conviction law leads: Baxter v. name: Officials' immunity, 1955-2029: Pierson to Pearson, Harlow test, Graham force
description: The long qualified-immunity lineage, 1955-2029: officials are liable only for violating clearly established law (Harlow 1982, anchor 1985-89 and 1995-2004; Anderson 1987, anchor 1990-94), denials are immediately appealable (Forsyth 1985), and force is judged by Graham (1989; anchor 2005-09, 2020-29). Pearson (2009, anchor 2010-19) made Saucier's order optional; Mullenix, White, Kisela and Wesby (2015-18) demand particularized precedent.

previous.name: Qualified immunity and § 1983 officer liability
previous.description: Suits against officials under § 1983 from Monroe v. Pape onward: qualified immunity and clearly established law (Harlow, Anderson v. Creighton, Pearson, Hope), interlocutory appeal of its denial (Forsyth, Johnson v. Jones), excessive and deadly force (Graham, Scott v. Harris) and municipal liability (Monell).

history: Dominant rule: qualified immunity for officials sued for damages. The lineage starts in 1955-64 with color-of-law cases (Classic, 1941; Screws, 1945; the white-primary cases) and Monroe (1961); 1965-69 is reapportionment drift (Reynolds, 1964). How it changed: Pierson (1967) anchors 1970-79, with Scheuer (1974) and Wood (1975) on good-faith immunity and Imbler (1976) on absolute prosecutorial immunity; Butz (1978) anchors 1980-84. Harlow (1982) made immunity objective and anchors 1985-89 and 1995-2004 (Anderson, 1987, anchors 1990-94); Forsyth (1985) allowed interlocutory appeal, limited by Johnson v. Jones (1995) and extended to the dismissal stage by Behrens (1996). Anderson (1987) required the right's contours to be clear, Malley (1986) protected all but the plainly incompetent, and Garner (1985) and Graham (1989) set force standards. Hope (2002) allowed obvious cases, Brosseau (2004) and Scott (2007) narrowed. Graham anchors 2005-09. Pearson (2009) anchors 2010-19 after ending Saucier's mandatory sequence, and al-Kidd (2011), Mullenix (2015), White (2017), Kisela and Wesby (2018) demand particularized law. Graham anchors again from 2020-24 through the partial 2025-29 slice, with Rivas-Villegas (2021) and Barnes v. Felix (2025).
rule: Officials performing discretionary functions are immune from § 1983 and Bivens damages unless they violated a constitutional right clearly established, in a particularized sense, at the time (Harlow, Anderson); excessive-force claims are judged by Fourth Amendment objective reasonableness (Graham).

name: Right to counsel after Gideon: actual imprisonment, waiver and Faretta
description: Right to counsel after Gideon (1963): no imprisonment for any offense without counsel or a valid waiver (Argersinger, 1972), with actual imprisonment the trigger (Scott, 1979). Waiver must be knowing and cannot be presumed from silence (Zerbst; Carnley); Faretta (1975, anchor 1980-84) adds self-representation. Uncounseled convictions cannot enhance or impeach (Burgett, Tucker, Loper); Geders (1976) bars blocking consultation overnight.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Right to appointed counsel (1970s)
previous.description: The right to counsel after Gideon: misdemeanors with imprisonment (Argersinger, Scott v. Illinois), waiver (Zerbst, Carnley), self-representation (Faretta), uncounseled prior convictions (Burgett, Loper), and denial of consultation during an overnight recess (Geders).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: the Sixth Amendment, applied to the states by Gideon (1963, the 1975-79 anchor), forbids imprisoning a defendant for any offense unless he was represented or validly waived counsel. How it changed: Argersinger (1972) extended Gideon to misdemeanors resulting in imprisonment, and Scott (1979) limited it to cases where imprisonment is actually imposed. Waiver must be the intentional relinquishment of a known right (Zerbst, 1938), shown on the record (Carnley, 1962; Gillies). Faretta (1975), the 1980-84 anchor, held that a defendant who knowingly waives counsel may represent himself. Burgett (1967), Tucker (1972) and Loper (1972) bar using uncounseled convictions to convict, enhance or impeach; Baldasar (1980) barred using an uncounseled misdemeanor to raise a later sentence to imprisonment (later overruled by Nichols, 1994), while Lewis (1980) allowed such a felony as a firearms predicate. Also: restrictions that interfere with counsel's role, such as barring consultation over an overnight recess (Geders, 1976), denying summation (Herring, 1975) or ordering the defendant to testify first (Brooks, 1972). Powell (1932) supplies the due-process roots.
rule: No defendant may be imprisoned for any offense unless he had or knowingly and intelligently waived counsel (Gideon, Argersinger, Scott), and a competent defendant may waive counsel and represent himself (Faretta).

changes.case: Johnson v. Zerbst; Carnley v. Cochran; Gideon v. Wainwright
changes.what: Waiver must be an intentional relinquishment of a known right and cannot be presumed from a silent record; Gideon extended the right to state felony trials.

changes.case: Burgett v. Texas; United States v. Tucker; Loper v. Beto
changes.what: Convictions invalid under Gideon may not be used to prove guilt, enhance a sentence or impeach.

changes.case: Argersinger v. Hamlin; Scott v. Illinois
changes.what: Counsel is required for any offense resulting in imprisonment, but actual imprisonment, not authorised imprisonment, triggers the right.
The Sixth Amendment implies a right to self-representation after a knowing waiver; Faretta anchors 1980-84.

changes.case: Baldasar v. Illinois; Lewis v. United States
changes.what: An uncounseled misdemeanor could not enhance a later sentence to imprisonment (Baldasar, later overruled by Nichols v. United States, 1994), while an uncounseled felony may serve as a firearms-disability predicate (Lewis).

name: Vienna Convention consular notice: no suppression remedy (Breard, Sanchez-Llamas)
description: Consular-notification claims by foreign defendants, 2000-09: the Vienna Convention is applied in conformity with domestic procedural rules (Breard 1998, anchor); circuits held Article 36 creates no suppression or dismissal remedy and perhaps no enforceable individual right (Lombera-Camorlinga 2000, Jimenez-Nava 2001, Emuegbunam 2001), and that prejudice must be shown. Sanchez-Llamas (2006) confirmed no suppression remedy and that state procedural bars apply.

history: Dominant rule: Breard v. Greene (1998), the anchor in both slices, held that the Vienna Convention must be applied in conformity with U.S. procedural rules, so an unraised consular-notice claim is defaulted on habeas (Murphy v. Netherland 1997). How it changed: in 2000-04 the circuits rejected remedies for Article 36 violations: the Ninth Circuit en banc (Lombera-Camorlinga 2000) and others (Chaparro-Alcantara 2000) refused suppression, noting only the legislature can create an exclusionary rule; Jimenez-Nava and Emuegbunam (2001) held Article 36 creates no judicially enforceable individual right; De La Pava (2001) and Duarte-Acero (2002) refused dismissal of indictments; Cordoba-Mosquera (2000) and Minjares-Alvarez (2001) required prejudice. In 2005-09 Sanchez-Llamas (2006) held that suppression is not an appropriate remedy and state procedural default rules apply, leaving open whether the treaty confers individual rights. Alongside: older treaty doctrine on self-execution and the last-in-time rule (Foster 1829, Edye 1884, Whitney 1888). The unit merges into immigration habeas in 2010-14.
rule: A violation of Article 36 of the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations does not warrant suppression of evidence or dismissal of an indictment, and consular-notice claims remain subject to domestic procedural-default rules.

changes.what: The Vienna Convention is applied in conformity with U.S. procedural rules, including federal habeas default.

changes.case: Lombera-Camorlinga (9th Cir. en banc); Jimenez-Nava (5th Cir.); Emuegbunam (6th Cir.)
changes.what: No suppression remedy for Article 36 violations, and no judicially enforceable individual right.

round1.name: International law in U.S. courts: Sosa's narrow ATS norms, Vienna Convention, FSIA
round1.description: International law in U.S. courts, 2005-14: ATS claims lie only for specific, universal and obligatory norms (Sosa, 2004, after Filartiga); Vienna Convention consular-notice claims yield to procedural default and carry no suppression remedy (Breard, Sanchez-Llamas); the FSIA is the sole basis for jurisdiction over foreign states (Amerada Hess, Altmann). Morrison (2010) and Kiobel (2013) applied the presumption against extraterritoriality.
round1.history: Dominant rule: the limits on enforcing international law in U.S. courts. Alongside, Amerada Hess (1989) and Weltover (1992) make the FSIA the sole basis for jurisdiction over foreign states and treat bond refinancing as commercial activity, and Altmann (2004) applied the FSIA retroactively. How it changed: Sosa (2004), building on Filartiga (1980), anchors 2010-14 and confines ATS claims to narrow, well-defined norms. Morrison (2010) revived the presumption against extraterritoriality (after Aramco, 1991), and Kiobel (2013) applied it to the ATS. Also: in 2010-14 Erie, Hanna, Gasperini and Shady Grove merge in on the federal-state choice of law, a separate topic.
round1.rule: The Alien Tort Statute supports federal common-law claims only for a narrow class of specific, universal and obligatory international norms (Sosa), and treaty provisions such as Vienna Convention Article 36 are applied subject to domestic procedural rules and do not generally create suppressible individual rights.

name: Vindictiveness after exercising rights: Pearce, Blackledge, Goodwin, Alabama v. Smith
description: Due-process limits on retaliation for exercising rights. Pearce (1969, anchor 1970-74) presumed vindictiveness in harsher resentencing; Blackledge (1974, anchor 1975-84) applied it to increased charges after appeal. Bordenkircher (1978), Goodwin (1982, anchor 1985-2004), McCullough (1986) and Alabama v. Smith (1989, anchor 2005-09) confined the presumption to a reasonable likelihood of actual vindictiveness; Wayte and Armstrong add selective prosecution.

previous.name: Vindictive prosecution and resentencing (Pearce, Blackledge)
previous.description: Due-process limits on harsher treatment after a defendant exercises rights: Pearce and Chaffin on resentencing, Blackledge and Goodwin on prosecutorial vindictiveness, Bordenkircher plea bargaining and Alabama v. Smith, with Wayte and Oyler on selective prosecution.

history: Dominant rule: penalizing the exercise of a procedural right offends due process, with a presumption of vindictiveness in defined settings. How it changed: Pearce (1969) anchors 1970-74, permitting harsher resentencing only on objective reasons in the record, with Ex parte Lange (1874) on double punishment. Blackledge (1974) anchors 1975-84, extending the presumption to prosecutors who increase charges after an appeal; Chaffin (1973) and Colten (1972) excluded jury sentencing and two-tier trial de novo, Bozza (1947) allowed correcting an illegal sentence, and Menna (1975) let a guilty plea leave double-jeopardy claims open. Bordenkircher (1978) enters in 1980-84, allowing plea-bargaining threats, and Goodwin (1982) enters and anchors 1985-2004, refusing a presumption for pretrial charging. Wasman (1984) and McCullough (1986) narrowed resentencing presumptions, and Wayte (1985), Oyler (1962) and Armstrong (1996) set selective-prosecution standards. Alabama v. Smith (1989) enters in 1990-94 and anchors 2005-09, denying the presumption after a withdrawn plea; Broce (1989) addresses guilty-plea waiver. The unit then joins the double-jeopardy lineage.
rule: Due process forbids penalizing a defendant for exercising a procedural right; a presumption of vindictiveness arises only where there is a reasonable likelihood that a harsher sentence or charge after the exercise of the right was retaliatory.

changes.what: A harsher sentence after retrial must rest on objective, on-the-record reasons, or vindictiveness is presumed.

changes.case: Colten v. Kentucky; Chaffin v. Stynchcombe
changes.what: No presumption for a two-tier trial de novo or for jury sentencing.
A prosecutor may not increase charges in response to a defendant's appeal for a trial de novo.
Threatening more serious charges in plea bargaining is not vindictive while the defendant is free to accept or reject the offer.
No presumption of vindictiveness for pretrial charging decisions after a demand for jury trial.

changes.case: Wasman v. United States; Texas v. McCullough
changes.what: The presumption is rebuttable and applies only where a reasonable likelihood of actual vindictiveness exists.

changes.case: Wayte v. United States; United States v. Armstrong
changes.what: Selective-prosecution claims require discriminatory effect and purpose, with a showing that similarly situated persons were not prosecuted.
No presumption when a sentence after trial exceeds one imposed on a later-withdrawn guilty plea, overruling Simpson v. Rice in part.

name: Texas Anders briefs: High, Stafford and Bledsoe on frivolous appeals
description: Anders (1967) and Penson (1988) as applied by Texas courts, Anders anchoring every slice 1990-2009: the brief must professionally evaluate the record (Currie 1974, High 1978), the court must independently review it and appoint new counsel if arguable grounds appear (Stafford 1991), and it may not decide the merits (Bledsoe 2005). Cooper (2001) limited what plea-bargaining defendants may appeal.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Texas Anders briefs (1990s-2000s)
previous.description: Anders and Penson as applied in Texas: what an Anders brief must contain (High, Currie, Stafford), the appellate court's independent review (Bledsoe), and notice-of-appeal limits on what can be raised.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: Anders v. California (1967) anchors every slice from 1990-94 to 2005-09: appointed counsel may withdraw from a frivolous appeal only with a brief referring the court to anything arguably supporting it. How it changed: Texas adopted the procedure in Currie (1974) and High (1978), which require a professional evaluation of the record and discussion of each objection and ruling. Penson (1988) held that a defective withdrawal leaving the defendant without counsel is presumptively prejudicial. Stafford (1991) entered in 2000-04: after its own review, a court that finds arguable grounds must appoint new counsel. In 1995-2004 notice-of-appeal rules for plea bargains changed: Lyon (1994) applied the general-notice rule, and Cooper (2001) held the Flowers doctrine did not survive amended Rule 25.2(b), so plea voluntariness cannot be raised without the trial court's permission. Bledsoe (2005) held that the court must not address the merits of an Anders appeal. Alongside: Ex parte Wilson (1997) on counsel's duty to tell the client about discretionary review, and probation-revocation review (Cardona 1984, Cobb 1993).
rule: Appointed counsel who finds an appeal frivolous may move to withdraw with an Anders brief that professionally evaluates the record and explains why no arguable issue exists; the Texas appellate court must then independently review the record and, if it finds an arguable ground, appoint new counsel rather than decide the issue.

changes.what: Counsel seeking to withdraw from a frivolous appeal must file a brief referring to anything in the record that might arguably support the appeal.

changes.case: Currie v. State; High v. State
changes.what: Texas adopted the Anders procedure; the brief must discuss trial objections and rulings and explain why there is no reversible error.
Denying counsel on appeal after an inadequate withdrawal is presumptively prejudicial; Strickland prejudice does not apply.
If the court of appeals finds arguable grounds after its own review, it must abate and appoint new counsel to brief them.

changes.case: Lyon v. State; Flowers v. State; Cooper v. State
changes.what: Under amended Rule 25.2(b), a plea-bargaining defendant may not challenge the plea's voluntariness on appeal without the trial court's permission, ending the Flowers doctrine.
It is error for the court of appeals to reach the merits of issues in an Anders case; it decides only whether the appeal is wholly frivolous or arguable grounds exist.

name: Erie, Hanna and Shady Grove: which law applies in federal court; party presentation
description: Which law federal courts apply: state substantive law in diversity (Erie, 1938; Klaxon, 1941), but a valid Federal Rule controls unless it alters substantive rights (Hanna, 1965, anchor 2020-24; Shady Grove, 2010), so state anti-SLAPP procedures do not apply (Abbas, Carbone). Alongside: party presentation (Greenlaw, 2008; Sineneng-Smith, 2020) and the presumption against extraterritoriality (Morrison, 2010). The partial 2025-29 slice adds federal common law.

previous.name: Party presentation, Erie and the Rules Enabling Act (2020s)
previous.description: Recent cases on what courts may decide and which law applies: the party-presentation principle (Greenlaw, Sineneng-Smith), Erie, Hanna and Shady Grove, extraterritoriality (Morrison, Aramco), and recharacterizing filings (Castro).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, contrastive pass from family evidence)

history: Dominant rule: federal courts sitting in diversity apply state substantive law and the forum's choice-of-law rules, while a Federal Rule that covers the point governs if it is within the Rules Enabling Act. How it changed: the lineage begins in 2020-24, merged from units on foreign sovereign immunity and international law and on the collateral-order doctrine, and Hanna (1965) anchors that slice. Erie (1938) and Klaxon (1941) set the base rule; Hanna and Burlington Northern v. Woods (1987) gave valid Federal Rules priority; Gasperini (1996) accommodated state verdict-review standards; Shady Grove (2010) applied Rule 23 over a state class-action bar, and the D.C. and Eleventh Circuits relied on it to keep state anti-SLAPP procedures out of federal court (Abbas, 2015; Carbone, 2018). Alongside: the party-presentation principle (Greenlaw, 2008; Sineneng-Smith, 2020), tempered by Kamen (1991) and Independent Insurance Agents (1993), and extraterritoriality (Morrison, 2010; Kiobel, 2013; RJR Nabisco, 2016; WesternGeco, 2018). In the partial 2025-29 slice Erie anchors and federal common law joins (Clearfield Trust, 1943; Kimbell Foods, 1979; Boyle, 1988).
rule: A federal court applies state substantive law in diversity cases (Erie) but a valid Federal Rule that answers the question in dispute governs unless it abridges, enlarges or modifies a substantive right (Hanna, Shady Grove), and courts decide the issues the parties present (Greenlaw, Sineneng-Smith).

changes.case: Erie R. Co. v. Tompkins; Klaxon v. Stentor
changes.what: There is no general federal common law; diversity courts apply state substantive law, including the forum state's choice-of-law rules.

changes.case: Hanna v. Plumer; Burlington Northern v. Woods
changes.what: A Federal Rule within the Rules Enabling Act's authority governs over conflicting state law; Hanna anchors 2020-24.
A state standard for excessive verdicts applies in diversity cases, administered by the trial court and reviewed for abuse of discretion.

changes.case: Shady Grove Orthopedic Associates v. Allstate
changes.what: Rule 23 displaced New York's bar on class actions for statutory penalties; circuits then held state anti-SLAPP motion procedures inapplicable in federal court (Abbas, 2015; Carbone, 2018).

changes.case: Greenlaw v. United States; United States v. Sineneng-Smith
changes.what: Under the party-presentation principle courts decide the questions the parties frame, though the principle is supple and courts may identify governing law (Kamen, 1991).

name: Indian country jurisdiction: state limits (Williams, McClanahan), then Montana
description: The long Indian-law line on who governs in Indian country, 1955-2019: tribes are sovereigns beyond state control (Worcester, 1832), so state courts and taxes may not infringe tribal self-government (Williams v. Lee, 1959; McClanahan, 1973, the usual 1975-94 anchor). Santa Clara Pueblo (1978) confirmed tribal immunity; Montana (1981), Strate (1997) and Hicks (2001) narrowed tribal power over nonmembers; Kiowa (1998) and Bay Mills (2014) reaffirmed immunity.

previous.description: Tribal sovereignty and state authority in Indian country: Worcester v. Georgia, infringement of tribal self-government (Williams v. Lee), state taxation (McClanahan, Moe, Colville, Bracker), tribal jurisdiction over nonmembers (Montana, Oliphant), sovereign immunity and ICRA (Santa Clara Pueblo, Wheeler).

history: Dominant rule: tribes retain inherent sovereignty and immunity subject only to Congress, and states may not apply their law in Indian country where it would infringe tribal self-government or is preempted by federal interests. How it changed: early slices rest on Worcester (1832), Cherokee Nation (1831), Kagama (1886) and McBratney (1882). Williams v. Lee (1959) anchors 1965-74, barring state jurisdiction over on-reservation claims against Indians, with Kennerly (1971) requiring tribal consent under Public Law 280. McClanahan (1973) anchors 1975-84, barring state income tax on reservation Indians, followed by Moe (1976), Bryan (1976) and Colville (1980), while Mescalero (Jones, 1973) allowed off-reservation state law and Bracker (1980) set interest-balancing preemption. In 1985-89 treaty fishing rights lead (Washington v. Fishing Vessel Ass'n, 1979). Santa Clara Pueblo (1978) anchors 1995-99 and 2005-14 on immunity, with Wheeler (1978) and Oliphant (1978). Montana (1981) anchors 2000-04, and Strate (1997) and Hicks (2001), the 2015-19 anchor, limited tribal court power over nonmembers; Lara (2004) upheld congressional restoration of tribal criminal jurisdiction over nonmember Indians. Also: Contracts Clause cases drift in during 2010-14.
rule: Tribes are separate sovereigns retaining inherent powers of self-government and immunity from suit unless Congress acts, so state law may not infringe tribal self-government or tax Indians in Indian country absent congressional authorization, but tribal authority over nonmembers is limited to the Montana exceptions.

changes.case: Worcester v. Georgia; United States v. McBratney; United States v. Kagama
changes.what: Tribes are distinct political communities beyond state law, though states may prosecute crimes between non-Indians and Congress holds plenary power.
State courts lack jurisdiction over a non-Indian's suit against an Indian for an on-reservation transaction because it would infringe tribal self-government; anchors 1965-74.

changes.what: States may not tax reservation Indians' income or property, Public Law 280 did not grant civil regulatory power, but states may tax sales to nonmembers, with interest-balancing preemption for non-Indians (Bracker). McClanahan anchors 1975-84 and 1990-94.

name: Ohio res judicata in postconviction relief (State v. Perry) and void sentences
description: Ohio postconviction law: res judicata bars claims that were or could have been raised at trial or on direct appeal (Perry, 1967, anchor most slices), with Cole (1982) and Jackson (1980) on hearings and counsel claims and Calhoun (1999) on discretion. Murnahan (1992) moved appellate-counsel claims to App.R. 26(B). Bezak (2007) and Fischer (2010) treated post-release control errors as void until Harper and Henderson (2020) made them voidable.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Ohio postconviction relief and res judicata
previous.description: Ohio's bar on relitigating in postconviction proceedings claims that could have been raised on direct appeal (State v. Perry, Cole), postconviction petitions (Calhoun), and resentencing for post-release control (Bezak, Fischer).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: State v. Perry (1967), which anchors 1990-94, 1995-99 and 2015-19 through 2025-29, bars relitigation in postconviction proceedings of claims that were or could have been raised earlier. How it changed: Jackson (1980) required operative facts before a hearing, and Cole (1982) let trial-counsel claims proceed where the same counsel handled the appeal or the claim rests on evidence outside the record. Murnahan (1992) sent appellate-counsel claims to the court of appeals (App.R. 26(B)). Szefcyk (1996) applied res judicata despite a change in law, and Calhoun (1999) called postconviction relief a collateral civil attack. In 2000-09 the unit absorbs plea-withdrawal law: Smith (1977) on manifest injustice under Crim.R. 32.1, Nero (1990, anchor 2005-09) and Xie (1992). Bezak (2007) held sentences without post-release control void, and Fischer (2010), anchor 2010-14, limited resentencing to that part. Harper and Henderson (2020) then held such errors voidable, restoring res judicata (knowledge). Civil res judicata (Grava, 1995) joins in 2015-19.
rule: Res judicata bars an Ohio defendant from raising in postconviction proceedings any claim that was or could have been raised at trial or on direct appeal (Perry), a postconviction petition being a collateral civil attack that warrants a hearing only on sufficient operative facts outside the record.

changes.what: Res judicata bars postconviction litigation of claims that were or could have been raised at trial or on direct appeal.

changes.case: State v. Jackson; State v. Cole
changes.what: A petition needs evidentiary documents with operative facts to get a hearing, and res judicata bars a trial-counsel claim only if new counsel handled the direct appeal and the claim did not depend on evidence outside the record.
Ineffective-appellate-counsel claims cannot be raised in postconviction proceedings and must go to the appellate court, leading to App.R. 26(B).

changes.case: State v. Szefcyk; State v. Calhoun
changes.what: Res judicata applies even after a change in law; postconviction relief is a collateral civil attack and the court has discretion to deny a hearing.

changes.case: State v. Bezak; State v. Fischer
changes.what: A sentence lacking required post-release control was void; Fischer confined resentencing to the post-release control portion and applied res judicata to the rest.

changes.case: State v. Harper; State v. Henderson
changes.what: Errors in imposing post-release control and other sentencing errors by a court with jurisdiction make a sentence voidable, not void, so res judicata applies; earlier void-sentence cases were overruled.

before_differentiation.description: Ohio postconviction law: res judicata bars claims that were or could have been raised at trial or on direct appeal (Perry, 1967, anchor most slices), with Cole (1982) and Jackson (1980) on hearings and counsel claims and Calhoun (1999) on discretion. Murnahan (1992) moved appellate-counsel claims to App.R. 26(B). Bezak (2007) and Fischer (2010) treated post-release control errors as void until Harper and Henderson (2020) made them voidable.

name: Eleventh Circuit sentencing reasonableness: Talley, Pugh and Irey (en banc)
description: Eleventh Circuit review of federal sentences after Booker: Talley (2005, anchor 2005-14) placed the burden on the challenger and expected within-range sentences to be reasonable; Rodriguez (2005) governed plain-error Booker claims; Pugh (2008) and Irey (en banc 2010, anchor from 2015 through 2025-29) vacated lenient sentences as substantively unreasonable; Rosales-Bruno (2015) upheld an upward variance. Bonner (1981) adopted pre-split Fifth Circuit law.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Eleventh Circuit sentencing reasonableness
previous.description: Eleventh Circuit review of federal sentences after Booker: substantive reasonableness (Talley, Pugh, Irey en banc), within-range sentences as indicators of reasonableness, and the Bonner v. City of Prichard rule adopting pre-October 1981 Fifth Circuit decisions as binding.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: the Eleventh Circuit reviews sentences deferentially for reasonableness. How it changed: Talley (2005) anchors 2005-09 and 2010-14, holding that the party challenging a sentence bears the burden and that a within-range sentence is ordinarily expected to be reasonable, though not presumed so (Hunt 2008). Rodriguez (2005) required defendants raising Booker error for the first time to show a reasonable probability of a different result, and Shelton (2005) found that showing made; Scott (2005) held a judge's acknowledgment of the § 3553(a) factors enough. Pugh (2008) vacated a probation-only sentence for failing to give the range real weight, and Gonzalez (2008) treated a sentence well below the statutory maximum as a sign of reasonableness. Irey (en banc 2010) entered in 2010-14 and anchors from 2015-19 through the partial 2025-29 slice, vacating a 42% downward variance and defining substantive abuse of discretion. Tome (2010) allowed consideration of uncharged conduct, and Rosales-Bruno (2015) upheld an upward variance. Bonner v. City of Prichard (1981) and Jernigan (2003, abandonment of issues) appear as circuit practice rules.
rule: The Eleventh Circuit reviews sentences for reasonableness under a deferential abuse-of-discretion standard, with the challenger bearing the burden; a within-range sentence is ordinarily expected to be reasonable but not presumed so, and a sentence is substantively unreasonable when the court gives significant weight to an improper factor, fails to weigh a relevant one, or commits a clear error of judgment in weighing them (Irey).

changes.case: Bonner v. City of Prichard (en banc)
changes.what: Fifth Circuit decisions issued on or before September 30, 1981 bind the Eleventh Circuit, and prior-panel decisions bind later panels.

changes.case: United States v. Rodriguez; United States v. Shelton
changes.what: On plain-error review of Booker error, the defendant must show a reasonable probability of a different sentence; Shelton found it shown.

changes.case: United States v. Talley; United States v. Scott
changes.what: The challenger bears the burden of showing unreasonableness; a within-range sentence is ordinarily expected to be reasonable; acknowledging the § 3553(a) factors suffices. Talley anchors 2005-14.

changes.case: United States v. Pugh; United States v. Gonzalez
changes.what: A probation-only sentence for child-pornography possession was unreasonable for giving the range no real weight; a sentence well below the statutory maximum indicates reasonableness.
Vacated a major downward variance as substantively unreasonable, defining abuse of discretion by improper factors, ignored factors and clear errors of judgment. Irey anchors from 2015-19.
Upheld an upward variance based on prior crimes, stressing the weight of factors is for the district court.

name: California capital appeals: prosecutorial misconduct, Ring and the death statute
description: California Supreme Court review of death judgments: prejudice review of prosecutorial misconduct (Hill, 1998), juror death-qualification (Witt), and settled rejection of challenges to the death statute under Ring (2002) and international law (Hillhouse, Brown). Johnson v. California (2005) loosened the Batson prima facie standard; Doolin (2009) anchors from 2010-14. The 2025-29 slice drifts into Watson and Chapman harmless error.

previous.name: California capital appeals
previous.description: California Supreme Court review of death judgments: Ring's jury-finding requirement for aggravating circumstances and the state court's repeated rejection of challenges to California's death-penalty statute, with Watson harmlessness.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: on automatic appeal the California Supreme Court reviews capital trial errors for prejudice and rejects, as a settled list, the standard constitutional challenges to California's death-penalty statute. Crittenden (1994) anchors 2000-04 and Hillhouse (2002) 2005-09; Doolin (2009) anchors 2010-14 through 2020-24, with Hill (1998) on prosecutorial misconduct and cumulative prejudice as a constant lead case. How it changed: Ring (2002) enters in 2005-09 and leads into 2010-14; the court held its penalty-phase weighing was not the kind of fact-finding Ring requires. Johnson v. California (2005) replaced California's more-likely-than-not Batson standard with an inference standard, and Cunningham (2007) struck down the judge-found upper term in noncapital sentencing; both leave by 2015-19. Alongside: Witt (1985) and Avila (2006) on death-qualifying jurors, Coffman (2004) on aider-and-abettor liability for foreseeable crimes, Hines (1997) on Proposition 8 and exclusion of evidence. In 2025-29 the anchor becomes Watson (1956), with Chapman (1967), as the unit merges with the harmless-error lineage.
rule: On automatic appeal from a death judgment, the California Supreme Court reviews claims of prosecutorial misconduct, jury selection and instructional error for prejudice, and repeatedly upholds the state's death-penalty statute against Ring, Apprendi and international-law challenges.

changes.what: Prosecutorial misconduct, alone or with other errors, can have a cumulative prejudicial effect that requires reversal.
A jury must find any aggravating circumstance that makes a defendant death-eligible; California's court treated its own penalty-phase weighing as outside Ring.
Batson's first step needs only evidence permitting an inference of discrimination, rejecting California's more-likely-than-not standard.

name: Strickland reaches Texas, 1980-2009: federal origins to Thompson's silent record
description: Strickland (1984) from federal origins to its Texas form, 1980-2009: a general right-to-counsel group (Cuyler 1980, then Strickland 1985-99 as anchor) becomes Texas law after Hernandez (1986) adopted it and Hernandez (1999, overruling Duffy) extended it to punishment. On direct appeal, claims must be firmly founded in the record (McFarland, 1996), and a silent record means presumed strategy (Jackson, 1994; Thompson, 1999, anchor 2000-09; Bone; Goodspeed).
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Texas criminal: ineffective assistance on direct appeal
previous.description: Strickland as applied by the Texas Court of Criminal Appeals: a silent record on direct appeal rarely shows deficient performance (Thompson, Bone, Goodspeed, Mallett), so counsel's conduct is presumed strategic unless it was so outrageous no competent attorney would engage in it.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: Strickland's deficient-performance and prejudice test, read in Texas to bar most direct-appeal claims on a silent record. How it changed: Cuyler v. Sullivan (1980) anchors 1980-84, on conflicts of interest in joint representation (with Holloway, 1978). Strickland anchors 1985-89 a general right-to-counsel group (Faretta, Gideon, Zerbst; Cronic, 1984). In 1990-94 and 1995-99 it is applied to pleas and federal collateral review (Hill, 1985; Frady, 1982; Lockhart, 1993; Boykin, 1969). Texas cases take over in 2000-04: Hernandez (1986) adopted Strickland under the state constitution, Jackson (1994) and McFarland (1996) require a record showing ineffectiveness, and Hernandez (1999) overruled Ex parte Duffy (1980) for the punishment phase. Thompson (1999) anchors 2000-04 and 2005-09, with Mallett and Garcia (2001), Bone (2002), Rylander (2003) and Goodspeed (2005) presuming strategy unless the conduct was outrageous and pointing to habeas as the better vehicle. The lineage ends in 2005-09; later Texas slices continue in other lineages.
rule: An ineffective-assistance claim requires deficient performance and a reasonable probability of a different result (Strickland), and in Texas a claim raised on direct appeal must be firmly founded in the record; where the record is silent about counsel's reasons, the court presumes sound strategy unless the conduct was so outrageous that no competent attorney would have engaged in it.

changes.case: Strickland v. Washington; United States v. Cronic; Hill v. Lockhart
changes.what: Two-part test, presumed prejudice only for complete failure of counsel, and application to guilty pleas; Strickland anchors 1985-99.
Texas adopted Strickland for claims under article I, section 10 of the Texas Constitution.

changes.case: Jackson v. State; McFarland v. State
changes.what: When the record is silent on counsel's reasons, courts presume a valid strategy, and ineffectiveness must be firmly founded in the record.
Strickland applies to the punishment phase, overruling Ex parte Duffy (1980) and its separate standard.

changes.case: Thompson v. State; Mallett v. State; Garcia v. State; Bone v. State; Rylander v. State; Goodspeed v. State
changes.what: The direct-appeal record is usually inadequate, counsel should normally get a chance to explain, habeas is the better vehicle, and only outrageous conduct is deficient on a silent record; Thompson anchors 2000-09.

before_differentiation.name: Strickland on direct appeal in Texas: silent record presumes sound strategy
before_differentiation.description: Strickland (1984) as applied by the Texas Court of Criminal Appeals, which adopted it in Hernandez (1986) and extended it to punishment in Hernandez (1999, overruling Duffy). On direct appeal, claims must be firmly founded in the record (McFarland, 1996), and a silent record means presumed strategy (Jackson, 1994; Thompson, 1999, anchor 2005-14; Bone, 2002; Goodspeed, 2005). Early and late slices are general federal Strickland law.

name: Frivolous in forma pauperis complaints and pro se pleading: Neitzke, Denton
description: Screening of in forma pauperis and pro se complaints (single 1990-94 slice). Neitzke (1989, anchor) limits frivolousness dismissals under § 1915(d) to claims lacking an arguable basis in law or fact, and Denton (1992) adds fanciful or delusional facts reviewed for abuse of discretion; Conley (1957) and Haines (1972) set liberal pleading for pro se plaintiffs, applied in Hall (1991) and Noll (1987).
history: Dominant rule: an in forma pauperis complaint may be dismissed before service as frivolous only if it lacks an arguable basis in law or fact. Neitzke (1989) anchors the single 1990-94 slice, holding that failure to state a claim is not the same as frivolousness, and Denton (1992) let courts dismiss factually fanciful or delusional claims, with abuse-of-discretion review. Conley (1957) supplies the notice-pleading standard and Haines (1972) the rule that pro se pleadings are construed liberally. How it changed: the circuits applied these rules to prisoner suits, giving pro se litigants notice and leave to amend unless futile (Noll 1987, McKeever 1991) while rejecting conclusory claims (Hall v. Bellmon 1991; Jackson 1989, a slippery floor stating no Eighth Amendment claim). Martinez (1978) supplied the special-report procedure, and Meade v. Grubbs (1988) addressed supervisory liability and limitations. The slice also gathers unrelated pleading cases on Title VII (Hishon 1984) and Massachusetts Chapter 93A (Nader 1977, Kotseas 1979). The unit then rejoins the prisoner-rights lineage, before the PLRA (1996) rewrote screening.
rule: A court may dismiss an in forma pauperis complaint as frivolous under § 1915(d) only if it lacks an arguable basis in law or fact, a standard distinct from failure to state a claim; pro se pleadings are construed liberally and leave to amend is given unless futile.

changes.what: A complaint suffices if it gives fair notice of the claim and its grounds, and is not dismissed unless no set of facts would support relief.
Pro se prisoner complaints are held to less stringent standards than lawyers' pleadings.
Courts may order prison officials to prepare a special report to resolve preliminary issues in prisoner suits.
A complaint is frivolous only if it lacks an arguable basis in law or fact; failure to state a claim does not make it frivolous.
Factual frivolousness covers fanciful, fantastic or delusional allegations, and § 1915(d) dismissals are reviewed for abuse of discretion.

changes.case: Noll v. Carlson (9th Cir.); Hall v. Bellmon (10th Cir.); McKeever v. Block (9th Cir.)
changes.what: Pro se litigants get notice of defects and leave to amend unless amendment would be futile, but conclusory allegations still fail.

name: Florida divorce: Canakaris equitable distribution and abuse-of-discretion review
description: Florida dissolution appeals: Shaw (1976) requires competent substantial evidence in nonjury cases and anchors 1975-79; Canakaris (1980), anchor 1980-94, sets equitable distribution with spouses as partners, lump-sum and permanent alimony, and a reasonableness test for abuse of discretion. Conner and Kuvin (1983) curbed appellate reweighing; later cases treat distribution, alimony and support as interrelated (Hamlet, 1991). The rule stays stable.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Florida divorce: equitable distribution and alimony
previous.description: Canakaris on equitable distribution, lump-sum alimony and abuse-of-discretion review, with Shaw on competent substantial evidence in nonjury cases.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session subagents, from cocite evidence; second pass differentiated near-duplicates)

history: Dominant rule: Canakaris (1980), which anchors 1980-94. Trial courts have broad discretion to divide marital assets equitably, treating spouses as partners, and may award lump-sum alimony to achieve that distribution or permanent alimony to maintain the marital standard of living; an abuse of discretion exists only when no reasonable person would adopt the court's view. How it changed: in 1975-79 the anchor is Shaw (1976): judgments in nonjury cases must rest on competent, substantial evidence, and appellate courts may not reweigh it (Herzog, 1977); Lash (1975) ties rehabilitative alimony to a capacity for self-support, and Ball (1976) recognizes special equities. After Canakaris, Conner and Kuvin (1983) held that district courts exceeded their role by reversing awards they found unfair, and Duncan (1980) treats exclusive use of the home as support. In 1985-89 district courts applied the framework to unequal divisions (Grimmett, Farkas, Berger) and reciprocal lump-sum awards (Tronconi), with Walter (1985) and Noah (1986) on permanent alimony. In 1990-94 Hamlet (1991) treats alimony, support and distribution as one scheme, and custody-relocation cases (D'Onofrio, Giachetti) drift in.
rule: A Florida trial court dividing marital assets and awarding alimony treats the spouses as partners and may use lump-sum alimony to achieve equitable distribution, and its ruling stands unless no reasonable person would take the view it adopted (Canakaris); findings in nonjury cases stand if supported by competent, substantial evidence (Shaw).

changes.case: Shaw v. Shaw; Herzog v. Herzog; Lash v. Lash
changes.what: Appellate courts do not reweigh evidence in nonjury divorce cases, and rehabilitative alimony presupposes a capacity for self-support; Shaw anchors 1975-79.
Equitable distribution of marital assets with spouses as partners, lump-sum and permanent alimony as tools, and the reasonableness test for abuse of discretion; Canakaris anchors 1980-94.

changes.case: Conner v. Conner; Kuvin v. Kuvin
changes.what: Whether a spouse was 'shortchanged' is a question of fact, and district courts exceeded their review by substituting their judgment, reinstating trial-court awards.

description: Commerce power and federal crimes, 1995-2009: Lopez (1995, anchor throughout) and Morrison (2000) bar regulating noneconomic intrastate conduct by aggregation, against the Wickard, Perez and Heart of Atlanta line. Circuits upheld § 922(g), carjacking and Hobbs Act prosecutions through jurisdictional elements; Jones (2000) read the arson statute narrowly; Raich (2005) upheld the CSA as applied to home-grown marijuana.
