history: Dominant rule: Congress may regulate the channels and instrumentalities of interstate commerce and activities that substantially affect it, but it may not reach noneconomic, intrastate conduct whose link to commerce depends on piling inference on inference. Lopez (1995) anchors every slice. How it changed: in 1995-99 the lineage measures Lopez against the expansive line of Jones & Laughlin (1937), Darby (1941), Wickard (1942), Heart of Atlanta and McClung (1964) and Perez (1971), with Scarborough (1977) and Bass (1971) on jurisdictional nexus and clear statement; circuits then upheld § 922(g)(1) (Bell), carjacking (Bishop) and the Hobbs Act (Bolton) after Lopez. In 2000-04 Morrison (2000) struck VAWA's civil remedy because noneconomic violence cannot be aggregated, Jones (2000) excluded owner-occupied homes from § 844(i), and Rodia (1999) and Wang (2000) tested jurisdictional elements; Gibbs (2000) upheld the Endangered Species Act on private land. Raich (2005) entered in 2005-09 and upheld the Controlled Substances Act as applied to home-grown marijuana, while statutory-construction cases (McNally, Staples) join. The unit then splits toward SORNA commerce-power challenges in 2010-14.
rule: Congress may regulate the channels and instrumentalities of interstate commerce and activities that substantially affect it, but not noneconomic intrastate conduct whose effect on commerce rests only on attenuated aggregation (Lopez, Morrison); a jurisdictional element ties a federal crime to commerce.

changes.what: Struck the Gun-Free School Zones Act as beyond the commerce power, the first such holding since 1937; anchors every slice.

changes.case: United States v. Bell; Bishop; Bolton; Rodia
changes.what: Circuits upheld § 922(g), carjacking and Hobbs Act prosecutions after Lopez, relying on jurisdictional elements and aggregation, though a jurisdictional element does not automatically save a statute.

changes.case: United States v. Morrison; Jones v. United States
changes.what: Congress may not regulate noneconomic violent crime by aggregation (VAWA civil remedy struck), and the federal arson statute does not reach an owner-occupied home.
Upheld application of the Controlled Substances Act to home-grown marijuana as part of a comprehensive regulation of an economic market.

name: Chapter 15 recognition and comity to foreign insolvency proceedings
description: Cross-border insolvency in 2010-14 only: comity under Hilton v. Guyot (1895), the anchor, extended to foreign insolvency proceedings (Overseas Inns 1990, Finanz AG 1999, Ephedra 2006), and Chapter 15 recognition and relief (Telecom Argentina 2008, Basis Yield 2008 on independent COMI findings, Metcalfe & Mansfield 2010, Qimonda 2010-11 on public policy).

previous.name: Chapter 15 bankruptcy and international comity
previous.description: Cross-border insolvency: recognition of foreign proceedings under Chapter 15 and center of main interests (SPhinX, Tri-Continental, Atlas Shipping), comity to foreign judgments (Hilton v. Guyot) and non-debtor injunctions.

history: Dominant rule: U.S. courts defer to foreign insolvency proceedings through comity and Chapter 15. Hilton v. Guyot (1895) anchors this single 2010-14 slice: a foreign judgment after a full and fair trial is not retried absent prejudice or fraud, with reciprocity a factor. Courts recognise foreign interests in winding up domestic entities (Overseas Inns, 1990), review comity decisions for abuse of discretion (Finanz AG, 1999) and honour foreign orders that meet due process even if they override a civil jury right (Ephedra, 2006). How it changed: Chapter 15 cases restate the rule: recognition no longer requires the five § 304(c) factors (Telecom Argentina, 2008); the court must find the center of main interests itself (Basis Yield, 2008); additional assistance under § 1507 may be unnecessary (Atlas Shipping, 2009); relief enforced from a foreign plan need not be available here (Metcalfe & Mansfield, 2010); and Qimonda (2010-11) addresses the public-policy exception. The round-1 equitable-mootness lineage is no longer part of this span.
rule: U.S. courts extend comity to foreign insolvency proceedings and judgments, and under Chapter 15 recognize foreign proceedings and grant relief, when the foreign court offers a full and fair process consistent with due process and U.S. public policy, without requiring identical relief to be available here.

changes.what: Foreign judgments rendered after a full and fair trial are generally not retried absent prejudice or fraud; anchors the slice.

changes.case: In re Telecom Argentina; In re Basis Yield Alpha Fund
changes.what: Chapter 15 dispensed with an explicit need to weigh the old § 304(c) factors for recognition; the court must determine the center of main interests independently even without objection.
Enforcing relief granted in a foreign plan does not require that identical relief be available in the United States.

round1.name: Bankruptcy appeals: statutory and equitable mootness; Chapter 15 recognition
round1.description: Mootness of bankruptcy appeals: sales to good-faith purchasers without a stay (Mills v. Green 1895; Rock Industries 1978; § 363(m)) and plans substantially consummated (Roberts Farms 1981; Chateaugay 1993; UNR 1994; Continental Airlines 1996, anchor 2000-04). In 2010-14 the anchor drifts to Chapter 15 recognition and center of main interests (SPhinX 2006, Bear Stearns 2008).
round1.history: Dominant rule: appellate courts will not disturb completed bankruptcy sales or substantially consummated plans when no stay was obtained and relief would harm reliance interests. How it changed: in 1975-84 sale-mootness cases lead, from Mills v. Green (1895) through Abingdon Realty (1976), Rock Industries (1978, anchor 1980-84) and Dutch Inn (1980), with § 363(m) codifying protection for good-faith purchasers. Roberts Farms (1981) extended mootness to implemented plans, and Algeran (1985) anchors 1985-89, applying judicial mootness beyond § 363(m). AOV Industries (1986) anchors 1990-94 with Miami Center and Texaco (1988). Roberts Farms anchors 1995-99 as Chateaugay (1993) and UNR (1994) recast the doctrine as equitable mootness, and Continental Airlines (1996, en banc) anchors 2000-04 with its multi-factor test; UNR anchors 2005-09 and 2015-19, when One2One (2015) entered. In 2010-14 a merger brings Chapter 15 cases: SPhinX and Tri-Continental (2006), Bear Stearns (2008, anchor), Ran and Condor (2010), alongside Pacific Lumber (2009) on releases and Hilton v. Guyot (1895) on comity.
round1.rule: An appeal from a bankruptcy sale to a good-faith purchaser or from a substantially consummated reorganization plan is moot, by statute (§ 363(m)) or as equitable mootness, where no stay was obtained and effective relief would unravel the transaction; in 2010-14 the lineage turns to Chapter 15 recognition, which depends on the debtor's center of main interests or an establishment in the foreign country.

changes.case: Mills v. Green; In re Abingdon Realty (4th Cir.); In re Rock Industries Machinery (7th Cir.); In re Dutch Inn of Orlando

Virginia (1979) sufficiency review as applied across several states: any rational trier of fact, viewing the evidence for the prosecution, could find the elements proved, with credibility for the jury. history: Dominant rule: Jackson v. Virginia (1979) anchors all three slices. A reviewing court asks only whether any rational trier of fact, viewing the evidence most favourably to the prosecution, could find each element beyond a reasonable doubt; the jury resolves conflicts, judges credibility and draws inferences from basic to ultimate facts. How it changed: the standard is stable, but the courts applying it shift. In 2010-14 the unit is Louisiana-led (Mussall, 1988; Captville, 1984, circumstantial evidence and rejected hypotheses of innocence; Hearold, 1992; King, 1983; Neal, 2001). In 2015-19 Louisiana cases split off and Georgia and Virginia lead: Malcolm (1993) on merger, Kelly (2011) adopting Rule 52(b)-style plain error for jury charges, Olds (2016) on Rule 403 and other-acts evidence, and Virginia's Kelly (2003, en banc). In 2020-24 Illinois cases (Siguenza-Brito, Cunningham, Gray) and Georgia's Lane (2020, cumulative error) lead, and Davenport (2020) ended routine sua sponte sufficiency review in Georgia non-capital cases. The lineage splits again in 2025-29.

name: Article III standing: injury in fact, traceability, redressability (Lujan)
description: Article III standing: the legal-right test (Ickes 1938, anchor 1965-69) gave way to injury in fact and zone of interests (Data Processing v. Camp 1970, anchor 1970-79). Warth (1975), Simon (1976), Valley Forge (1982), Lyons (1983) and Allen (1984) narrowed standing, settled in Lujan's (1992, anchor from 1995-99) three-part test. history: Dominant rule: a plaintiff must show a concrete, particularized and imminent injury, fairly traceable to the challenged conduct and redressable by the court. How it changed: in 1965-69 the anchor is Alabama Power v. Ickes (1938), whose legal-right test barred most competitor suits. Data Processing v. Camp and Barlow (1970) enter and Camp anchors 1970-79, replacing that test with injury in fact and zone of interests; Flast (1968) allowed Establishment Clause taxpayer suits, and Sierra Club (1972) and SCRAP (1973) set the outer edges. Schlesinger and Richardson (1974), Warth (1975) and Simon (1976) narrowed standing, and Warth anchors 1980-94 as Valley Forge (1982), Lyons (1983) and Allen (1984) join. Lujan (1992) enters in 1990-94 and anchors every slice from 1995-99, with Steel Co. (1998), Friends of the Earth (2000), Hein and Massachusetts v. EPA (2007) and Summers (2009). Clapper (2013) and Spokeo (2016) lead 2010-19, and TransUnion (2021), Uzuegbunam (2021) and Murthy (2024) enter in 2020-29.
rule: To sue in federal court a plaintiff must show a concrete and particularized injury in fact, actual or imminent, fairly traceable to the defendant's conduct and likely to be redressed by a favorable decision (Lujan), and a generalized grievance or speculative future injury does not suffice.

Dorthey (1993) allowed reduction of a mandatory habitual-offender sentence found excessive; Bradford (1997) anchors 2000-04 and Dorthey anchors 2005-19. history: Dominant rule: New York separates legal sufficiency from weight of the evidence. Contes (1983) anchors 1990-94 through 2000-04: sufficiency asks whether any rational factfinder could find the elements, viewing the evidence most favourably to the People. Baldi (1981) and Benevento (1998) set the meaningful-representation standard for counsel, Crimmins (1975) the harmless-error test, and Suitte (1982) the power to reduce sentences in the interest of justice. history: Dominant rule: courts enforce agreements to arbitrate labor grievances, presume arbitrability, decide only whether a dispute is arbitrable, and defer to awards that draw their essence from the agreement. How it changed: in 1955-59 Westinghouse (1955) anchors, and Lincoln Mills (1957) read § 301 to authorize enforcement under federal common law. The Steelworkers Trilogy (1960) enters in 1960-64 and anchors to 1990-94. Lucas Flour, Dowd Box, Evening News and Atkinson (1962) settled jurisdiction and federal law, and Wiley (1964) sent procedural arbitrability to arbitrators. In 1970-74 Vaca (1967) on fair representation leads before splitting off. Boys Markets (1970) overruled Sinclair (1962) to permit no-strike injunctions, Gateway Coal (1974) implied a no-strike promise, and Buffalo Forge (1976) excluded sympathy strikes. W.R. Grace (1983), AT&T Technologies (1986) and Misco (1987) enter in 1985-89; Misco anchors 1995-2009 as public-sector and public-policy vacatur cases (Stratford, New Haven, Eastern Associated 2000) lead.
rule: Under § 301, a collective-bargaining agreement's arbitration clause is presumed to cover a grievance unless it is clearly excluded, courts decide arbitrability but not the merits, and an award that draws its essence from the agreement must be enforced unless it violates an explicit, well-defined public policy.

history: Dominant rule: under Olano (1993), codifying Atkinson (1936), an appellate court may correct a forfeited but not waived error only if it is error, is plain, and affects substantial rights, and then only in its discretion where the error seriously affects the fairness, integrity or public reputation of judicial proceedings. How it changed: the lineage exists in one slice, 1995-99, anchored by Olano. Gaudin (1995) held that materiality of a false statement is a jury question, so convictions tried under the older rule raised unpreserved instructional errors. Griffith (1987) required the new rule to apply to cases on direct review. Circuits held an error plain when a supervening decision made it clear by the time of appeal (Retos 1994, David 1996) and found some Gaudin errors harmless to substantial rights (Kramer 1996). Johnson (1997) held that plainness is judged at the time of appellate consideration. Also: prosecutorial argument in context and vouching (Young 1985, Necoechea) and inconsistent verdicts (Powell 1984). The lineage splits into Apprendi in 2000-04.
rule: A forfeited (not waived) error may be corrected under Rule 52(b) only if it is an error, plain, and affects substantial rights, and the court then has discretion to correct it if it seriously affects the fairness, integrity or public reputation of judicial proceedings; plainness is judged at the time of appeal.

changes.what: Four-part plain-error test; forfeited but not intentionally waived errors are reviewable, and correction is discretionary.
Materiality of a false statement is an element that must be submitted to the jury, unsettling earlier law that treated it as a question for the judge.

It is enough that an error be plain at the time of appellate consideration, even if the rule was not established until after trial.

description: A single 1975-79 group on selective prosecution: Oyler (1962) allows conscious selectivity unless based on race, religion or another arbitrary classification. history: Dominant rule: selective-prosecution claims under equal protection, in a single 1975-79 slice anchored by Berrios (2d Cir. 1974). Oyler (1962) held that some selectivity in enforcement does not violate equal protection unless deliberately based on an unjustifiable standard. How it changed: in the early 1970s the circuits gave the defense teeth. Steele (9th Cir. 1972) reversed a census-resister conviction where the authorities targeted vocal protesters, Crowthers (4th Cir. 1972) recognized selective enforcement against war protesters, and Falk (7th Cir. 1973, en banc) criticized reflexive dismissals citing Oyler and found a prima facie case for a draft-card prosecution. Berrios framed the two-part test: the defendant was singled out while others similarly situated were not prosecuted, and the selection was invidious or in bad faith; it also addressed in camera review of the prosecutor's memorandum. Scott (1975) and Swanson (1975) applied the test to reject claims. Also: Oyler, Spencer (1966), Graham (1912), Moore (1895) and McDonald (1901) uphold recidivist statutes against due-process, double-jeopardy and ex post facto challenges.
rule: Some conscious selectivity in enforcement is constitutional (Oyler), but a prosecution is invalid if the defendant shows he was singled out while others similarly situated were not, and that the selection rested on an impermissible ground such as race, religion or the exercise of First Amendment rights (Berrios).

changes.what: Selective enforcement violates equal protection only if deliberately based on an unjustifiable standard such as race, religion or another arbitrary classification; recidivist statutes do not offend due process.

changes.case: United States v. Steele (9th Cir.); United States v. Crowthers (4th Cir.); United States v. Falk (7th Cir. en banc); United States v. Berrios (2d Cir.)

changes.case: United States v. Scott; United States v. Swanson
changes.what: A claim fails without proof that similarly situated persons were not prosecuted, and enforcement priorities such as targeting tax crimes by professionals are not unlawful discrimination.

history: Dominant rule: a witness may refuse to answer when he has reasonable cause to apprehend a real danger of incrimination (Hoffman, 1951; Marchetti, 1968), and the government can override the privilege only with immunity coextensive with it. Turley (1973) extended the employment line to contractors, and Mandujano (1976) held grand-jury targets have no right to warnings or counsel inside the room. name: Eleventh Amendment state immunity: Edelman, Ex parte Young, Seminole Tribe
description: State sovereign immunity: no private suit against a State without consent or valid abrogation, but Ex parte Young allows prospective relief against officers and Edelman (1974) bars retroactive treasury awards. Seminole Tribe (1996) ended Article I abrogation, overruling Union Gas, and Boerne, Alden, Kimel and Garrett (1997-2001) narrowed § 5 abrogation. From 2015-19 the unit drifts into collateral-order appeals.

history: Dominant rule: the Eleventh Amendment and Hans (1890) bar private suits against unconsenting States, subject to Ex parte Young's (1908) prospective relief against officers; Edelman (1974), which anchors 1980-94 and 2010-14, bars retroactive relief from the treasury. How it changed: Fitzpatrick (1976) allowed abrogation under § 5, while Quern (1979) held § 1983 does not abrogate. Pennhurst (1984) barred state-law claims against the State in federal court, and Atascadero (1985) demanded an unmistakably clear statement for waiver or abrogation. Will (1989) held States are not § 1983 persons; Hafer (1991) allowed individual-capacity suits. Seminole Tribe (1996) overruled Union Gas and anchors 1995-2009, followed by Boerne (1997), Alden and College Savings Bank (1999), Kimel (2000) and Garrett (2001); United States v. Georgia (2006) enters later. Puerto Rico Aqueduct (1993) allowed collateral-order appeal of immunity denials, and from 2015-19 the unit merges with the collateral-order lineage and is anchored by Cohen (1949) and Mohawk (2009): the dominant topic shifts to interlocutory appeals.
rule: A State and its agencies are immune from private suit without consent or valid abrogation, but a federal court may enjoin a state officer's ongoing violation of federal law prospectively (Ex parte Young) and may not award retroactive relief payable from the state treasury (Edelman).

changes.what: Relief against state officials is limited to prospective injunctions; retroactive monetary relief from the treasury is barred.

changes.case: Fitzpatrick v. Bitzer; Quern v. Jordan
changes.what: Congress may abrogate state immunity under § 5 of the Fourteenth Amendment, but § 1983 does not do so.
The Amendment bars state-law claims against the State whatever relief is sought, and waiver or abrogation must be unmistakably clear.

changes.case: Will v. Michigan Dept. of State Police
changes.what: States and officials sued in their official capacity for damages are not 'persons' under § 1983.
Congress cannot abrogate state immunity under its Article I powers, overruling Union Gas (1989); Seminole Tribe anchors 1995-2009.

changes.case: City of Boerne; Alden v. Maine; Kimel; Garrett
changes.what: Section 5 abrogation must be congruent and proportional, and immunity also bars suits on federal claims in state court.

name: Louisiana summary judgment (Penalber) then insurance-policy reading (LIGA, Reynolds)
description: Louisiana civil appeals in two phases. Penalber (1989) and Schroeder (1991) anchor 1990-2004 on the older summary-judgment burden and de novo review, with Hayes (1996) applying the amended art. 966. From 2005 LIGA v. Interstate Fire (1994) and Cadwallader (2003) anchor insurance-contract interpretation: policy words take their ordinary meaning and ambiguous exclusions are construed against the insurer (Reynolds 1994).
history: Dominant rule: across the span the anchor moves between two related lines of Louisiana civil appeals. In 1990-94 Penalber (1989) anchors on summary judgment: it is rarely appropriate on subjective facts, and once a motion is supported the burden shifts (Sanders 1980, Vaughn 1981). Schroeder (1991) anchors 1995-2004, with de novo review, and Hayes (1996) applies the amended art. 966, under which a complete failure of proof on an essential element ends the case; Sunbeam (2000) addresses expert evidence on summary judgment. How it changed: Reynolds (1994) and Smith v. Our Lady of the Lake (1994) join the core in 1995-99, bringing insurance interpretation. LIGA v. Interstate Fire (1994) anchors 2005-09 and 2015-19, and Cadwallader (2003) 2010-14: policy words get their plain, popular meaning, clear terms are enforced as written, and exclusions are strictly construed against the insurer. Peterson and Yarbrough (1999), Carrier (2000) and Bonin (2006) fill out the rules on public policy, the duty to defend and ambiguity. The small 2020-24 slice is anchored by Doerr (2000) on avoiding absurd literal readings.
rule: Louisiana courts interpret insurance policies by the common intent of the parties, giving words their general and popular meaning, enforcing clear terms as written and strictly construing ambiguous exclusions against the insurer; summary judgment, reviewed de novo, is granted when no genuine issue of material fact remains.

changes.what: Once a summary-judgment motion is properly supported, the opponent must show material facts in dispute; summary judgment is rarely proper on subjective facts such as intent or good faith; appellate review is de novo.

changes.case: La. Code Civ. Proc. art. 966 amendments; Hayes (1996)
changes.what: Summary judgment became favored, and a complete failure of proof on an essential element of the nonmovant's case renders other facts immaterial.

changes.case: Louisiana Ins. Guar. Ass'n v. Interstate Fire & Casualty; Reynolds v. Select Properties
changes.what: Policy words take their general, ordinary meaning, and exclusions that narrow coverage are strictly construed against the insurer when reasonably open to two readings.

changes.case: Peterson (1999); Yarbrough (1999); Carrier (2000); Cadwallader v. Allstate (2003); Bonin (2006)
changes.what: Policies are not to be read in a strained way, the duty to defend turns on the petition's factual allegations, undefined terms are read with dictionaries and jurisprudence, and ambiguity requires two reasonable readings.

changes.case: Independent Fire Ins. Co. v. Sunbeam Corp.

name: Alabama plain-error review of death records, 1995-2014 (Kuenzel, Hodges, Hyde)
description: The long Alabama plain-error line, 1995-2014: death records are searched for plain error, reversing only for egregious error affecting fairness (Price 1998, Williams 1996), and aggravators are upheld on the manner of the killing (Bankhead 1991, Haney 1991). Kuenzel (1990-91) anchors 1995-2004, Ex parte Hodges (2003) 2005-09 with Waldrop (2002), and Hyde (1998) 2010-14. Harris (1995) upheld the capital statute.
history: Dominant rule: Alabama's appellate courts search a death record for plain error, reversing only when the error seriously affects the fairness or integrity of the proceedings, and review aggravators and argument in context (Young 1985). How it changed: Ex parte Kuenzel (1991) anchors 1995-99 and Kuenzel (1990) 2000-04, with Taylor (1994-95) and Ex parte Bankhead (1991). In 2000-04 Haney (1991), Harris v. Alabama (1995), Wilson (1999, torture supporting the heinous aggravator) and Ingram (1999, 'recommendation' language consistent with Caldwell) enter, with Williams (1996) and Ex parte Williams (1997). In 2005-09 newer cases lead: Ex parte Hodges (2003) anchors with Ex parte Waldrop (2002), Stallworth and Turner (2003), and Gavin (2003) on dog-tracking evidence. In 2010-14 Hyde (1998) anchors with Price (1998) on the plain-error standard and Ex parte Belisle (2008), before the unit splits into a Batson lineage. Also: Ex parte Bankhead (1993) on a single unexplained strike of a black veniremember, and Lockhart (1986) on death qualification.
rule: In a death case Alabama appellate courts search the whole record for plain error but reverse only for errors so egregious that they seriously affect the fairness, integrity or public reputation of the proceedings (Price), while upholding aggravators such as heinous, atrocious or cruel on the manner of the killing.

changes.case: Ex parte Bankhead; Haney v. State

description: Arizona Supreme Court criminal appeals: capital review of aggravators under Knapp (1977) and Gretzler (1983); Anders (1967), Leon (1969) and Shattuck (1984) on whole-record review; Bible (1993) on Frye and fundamental error; Ring (2002) requiring jury-found aggravators; and Henderson (2005), anchor 2005-19, limiting unobjected-to error to fundamental, prejudicial error. history: Dominant rule: Arizona's standards of appellate review in criminal and capital cases, with the anchor moving among them. In 1980-84 the anchor is State v. Clark (1980), with Richmond (1976), Watson (1978), Knapp (1977) and Gretzler (1983) defining the pecuniary-gain, grave-risk and heinous, cruel or depraved aggravators and Valencia (1982) treating age 16 as mitigating. How it changed: in 1985-89 Anders (1967) anchors as no-merit appeals and capital cases (Tison) merge. Gretzler anchors 1990-94, with Walton (1989), Fierro and Amaya-Ruiz (1990); Atwood (1992) anchors 1995-99 and Bible (1993), on Frye admissibility of DNA evidence and fundamental-error review, anchors 2000-04. Ring (2002), overruling Walton, required juries to find aggravators, and State v. Ring (2003) reviewed the resulting sentences. Henderson (2005) anchors 2005-19: forfeited error is reviewed only for fundamental, prejudicial error. In 2015-19 Leon (1969) and Shattuck (1984) return as Anders review grows; Payne (2013) anchors 2020-24 in capital appeals, and Shattuck the partial 2025-29 slice.
rule: In Arizona, an unobjected-to trial error is reviewed only for fundamental error, which the defendant must show went to the foundation of the case and caused prejudice (Henderson); when counsel finds no arguable issue the court searches the whole record (Anders, Leon); and in capital cases the court strictly construes aggravators such as 'especially heinous, cruel or depraved' (Knapp, Gretzler).

changes.what: Independent capital review with narrowing definitions of the (F)(6) heinous, cruel or depraved aggravator, including Gretzler's five factors for heinousness or depravity; Clark anchors 1980-84 and Gretzler 1990-94.

history: Dominant rule: plain-error review in Alabama death-penalty appeals. The Court of Criminal Appeals and the Alabama Supreme Court notice errors not raised at trial (Brooks 1996), but only those that seriously affect substantial rights; Frady (1982) supplies the federal plain-error and default framing. Ex parte Gaddy (1997) anchors the lineage's only slice, 2005-09, which merged in from the 2000-04 Alabama plain-error unit and splits in 2010-14. How it changed: no change within the span. Ex parte Taylor (1995) and Ex parte Bankhead (1991) are the heaviest cases, on aggravators and the record. Batson strikes are a main companion issue: Ex parte Bankhead (1993) held an unexplained strike of a single black veniremember may require a new trial, Ex parte Brooks (1997) rejected bare age, employment or marital status as reasons, and Johnson (2001) found six strikes of nine black veniremembers insufficient for a prima facie case. Also: expert funds (Bush 1996), speedy trial (Coral 1992), accomplice corroboration (Burton 1993), Miranda predicate (Smith 2000).
rule: In Alabama death-penalty appeals the courts notice errors not raised at trial, but reverse only for plain error that seriously affects substantial rights, and review aggravators, photographs and Batson strikes on the record.

changes.what: Failing to give a sufficient race-neutral reason for striking even one black veniremember may require a new trial.
Age, employment and marital status are not sufficiently race-neutral when given as the sole reason for a strike without more.

description: Supplemental jurisdiction and remand (1990-99): Gibbs (1966) pendent claims, Cohill (1988, anchor 1990-94) remand once federal claims drop out, and Thermtron (1976, anchor 1995-99) on reviewing remands outside § 1447(c). In 2000-04 Zahn (1973) anchors: each plaintiff must meet the amount in controversy, and circuits split on whether § 1367 overruled it (Stromberg 1996).

history: Dominant rule: how far a federal court's jurisdiction reaches beyond the claims that independently support it. In 1990-94 Cohill (1988) anchors with Gibbs (1966): state claims sharing a common nucleus may be heard, and remanded once federal claims are gone; Finley (1989) and Kroger (1978) limited pendent-party and ancillary jurisdiction before § 1367 (1990). How it changed: in 1995-99 Thermtron (1976) anchors on review of remand orders outside § 1447(c), with Petrarca (1995) confirming the bar for removal defects and jurisdictional remands, and St. Paul Mercury (1938) holding post-removal reductions do not defeat jurisdiction. In 2000-04 the anchor moves to the amount in controversy: Zahn (1973) and Snyder (1969) bar aggregating separate claims, Allen (5th Cir. 1995) sets a 'more likely than not' standard for removal, and the circuits split on whether § 1367 overruled Zahn (Stromberg 1996; Cohen 2000; Leonhardt 1998). Also: complete diversity (Strawbridge 1806) and partnership citizenship (Carden 1990).
rule: A federal court may hear state claims forming one case with federal claims and may remand them once federal claims are gone, while in diversity cases each plaintiff traditionally had to meet the jurisdictional amount, a rule courts divided on after § 1367.

changes.what: Pendent jurisdiction reaches state claims from a common nucleus of operative fact, and is discretionary.
Remand orders on grounds not authorized by § 1447(c) can be reviewed despite § 1447(d).
A court may remand pendent state claims once the federal claims are gone, which some circuits read as overruling Thermtron's statutory-grounds limit.
Finley rejected pendent-party jurisdiction; Congress then enacted § 1367 on supplemental jurisdiction.
Section 1447(d) bars review of remands for removal defects or lack of subject-matter jurisdiction.

round1.name: Mandamus over district courts (Roche, Will), then diversity amount (Zahn, Allapattah)
round1.description: Mandamus to district courts: Roche (1943) anchors 1950-79 and Will (1967) from 1970: the writ corrects usurpation of power, not ordinary error (Holland 1953, Kerr 1976, Allied Chemical 1980), with La Buy (1957) and Schlagenhauf (1965) allowing supervisory use. From 1990 the anchor becomes Thermtron (1976) on reviewing remands, then Cohill (1988), Zahn (1973) and St. Paul Mercury (1938) on amount in controversy, ending with Allapattah (2005) and CAFA.
round1.history: Dominant rule: through 1985-89, the limits of mandamus. Roche (1943) anchors 1950-69 and again 1975-79: the writ confines an inferior court to its lawful jurisdiction and cannot substitute for appeal. Ex parte Fahey (1947) and Holland (1953) add that hardship and the cost of trial are not enough. La Buy (1957) allowed supervisory mandamus against routine references to masters, and Schlagenhauf (1965) reviewed a novel Rule 35 issue. How it changed: Will (1967) anchors 1970-74 and 1985-89, demanding exceptional circumstances amounting to usurpation, and Kerr (1976) and Allied Chemical (1980) require a clear and indisputable right, as Holland anchors 1980-84. In 1990-99 the anchor moves to Thermtron (1976), which allows mandamus review of remands on grounds outside § 1447(c), and Cohill (1988), which lets courts remand once federal claims are gone, alongside Gibbs (1966). In 2000-04 Zahn (1973) anchors: each plaintiff's separate claim must meet the jurisdictional amount, as Snyder (1969) held. St. Paul Mercury (1938) anchors 2005-09, as Exxon v. Allapattah (2005) holds that § 1367 overrides Zahn for co-plaintiffs and the Seventh Circuit's CAFA cases (Brill 2005, Hart v. FedEx 2006) set removal burdens.
round1.rule: Through 1985-89: mandamus is an extraordinary remedy, available only to confine a lower court to its lawful jurisdiction or correct a usurpation of power where the right is clear and indisputable and appeal is inadequate, not as a substitute for appeal (Roche, Will, Kerr); later slices turn to review of remand orders (Thermtron), supplemental jurisdiction (Cohill) and the diversity amount in controversy (St. Paul Mercury, Zahn, Allapattah).

changes.case: Roche v. Evaporated Milk Ass'n; Ex parte Fahey; Bankers Life v. Holland
changes.what: Mandamus confines courts to their jurisdiction and is not available merely to avoid the cost and delay of trial.

changes.case: La Buy v. Howes Leather; Schlagenhauf v. Holder
changes.what: Supervisory mandamus may correct a practice such as references to masters for congestion, and may address novel, important questions such as Rule 35 examinations.

history: Dominant rule: a court may certify a class challenging government action only after rigorous analysis shows that every Rule 23 requirement is satisfied, including a common contention whose resolution will decide all members' claims in one stroke, and the plaintiffs must have standing and actual injury for the relief they seek. How it changed: the lineage exists only in the partial 2025-29 slice, merged from a 2020-24 unit on class certification under Rule 23, and Wal-Mart (2011) anchors it. Califano v. Yamasaki (1979) supports classwide relief against federal benefit programs and frees (b)(2) classes from (b)(3) limits; Falcon (1982) requires rigorous analysis; Wal-Mart tightened commonality and barred using Rule 23 to change substantive rights. Lewis v. Casey (1996) requires actual injury for systemwide relief, and Kowalski (2004) limits third-party standing. Also: Ex parte Young (1908) suits against officers, executive power (Youngstown, 1952; Myers, 1926), equal protection for undocumented children (Plyler, 1982), and limits on equitable remedies (Grupo Mexicano, 1999). The slice is too short to show a rule change.
rule: A class challenging government action may be certified only after rigorous analysis shows each Rule 23 requirement is met, including a common question whose answer resolves all members' claims at once (Wal-Mart, Falcon), and plaintiffs must show their own standing and actual injury for the relief sought.

changes.what: Class relief is available in suits against federal programs where common questions of law apply in the same way to each member, and Rule 23(b)(2) classes are not limited as (b)(3) classes are.
Certification requires rigorous analysis that each Rule 23 requirement is met, and the order may be modified as the case develops.
Systemwide relief requires a showing of actual injury, not theoretical deficiency.
Commonality requires a common contention capable of classwide resolution, and Rule 23 cannot be read to alter substantive rights; anchor of the slice.

previous.name: Public trial and press access to proceedings
previous.description: The First and Sixth Amendment right to open criminal proceedings (Richmond Newspapers, Globe, Press-Enterprise I and II, Waller) growing out of pretrial-publicity cases (Sheppard, Irvin, Estes), with Washington's Bone-Club closure test in later slices.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session subagents, from cocite evidence; second pass differentiated near-duplicates)

history: Dominant rule: the anchor changes doctrine. Through 1975-79 the lineage protects fair trial against prejudicial publicity. Irvin (1961) anchors 1960-64 and Sheppard (1966) anchors 1965-79, with Rideau (1963) and Estes (1965), and Nebraska Press (1976) forbade most gag orders on the press. How it changed: DePasquale (1979) treated the public-trial right as the defendant's alone, but Richmond Newspapers (1980), the anchor in 1980-94, found a First Amendment right to attend trials. Globe (1982) and Press-Enterprise I and II (1984, 1986) extended access to voir dire and preliminary hearings, and Press-Enterprise II anchors 1995-2004, with Nixon (1978) on access to records. Waller (1984) leads 2005-09 and applies the closure test to the defendant's own right. From 2010-14 Washington's Bone-Club (1995) anchors, with Momah and Strode (2009), Presley (2010), and Wise and Sublett (2012) on waiver, structural error and the experience-and-logic test. Irby (2011), on the right to be present, anchors the partial 2025-29 slice.
rule: Criminal proceedings are presumptively open under the First Amendment and the Sixth Amendment public-trial right, and closure requires findings that it serves an overriding interest, is narrowly tailored and that alternatives were considered (Press-Enterprise, Waller; in Washington, Bone-Club); earlier slices protect fair trial against prejudicial publicity.

changes.case: Irvin v. Dowd; Rideau v. Louisiana; Estes v. Texas; Sheppard v. Maxwell
changes.what: Due process requires an impartial jury, and pervasive or televised publicity can deny a fair trial, so courts must control the trial atmosphere; Sheppard anchors 1965-79.
Gag orders forbidding the press to publish information about a criminal case are presumptively unconstitutional prior restraints.
The Sixth Amendment public-trial right belongs to the defendant and gives the public no independent right to attend a pretrial hearing.
The First Amendment gives the public and press a right to attend criminal trials, overcome only by powerful countervailing interests; anchors 1980-94.

changes.case: Globe Newspaper; Press-Enterprise I and II
changes.what: Mandatory closure for minor victims fails strict scrutiny, and the right of access reaches voir dire and preliminary hearings, though not grand juries.
The defendant's Sixth Amendment right covers suppression hearings and is at least as broad as the press's right; closure must meet a four-part test.
Washington requires a five-factor analysis on the record before closing any part of a trial, and a post hoc justification does not cure an unjustified closure; anchors 2010-24.
The Sixth Amendment public-trial right extends to jury voir dire, and courts must consider alternatives to closure on their own.

changes.case: State v. Momah; State v. Strode; State v. Wise; State v. Sublett (Wash.)
changes.what: Failure to object does not waive the right; an unjustified closure is structural error; an experience-and-logic test decides whether a proceeding implicates the right.

name: Washington collateral estoppel from agency findings: Williams, Reninger, Thompson
description: Washington collateral estoppel around 2000: identical issue, final judgment, same party or privity, and no injustice. Administrative findings can preclude later civil claims (Reninger, 1998), and the State and its agencies count as one party (Thompson, 1999; Cleveland, 1990), but public policy can bar estoppel against criminal prosecutions (Williams, 1997; Dupard, 1980). Only ultimate facts are precluded (McDaniels, 1987).
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Washington collateral estoppel
previous.description: Washington collateral-estoppel cases around 2000: State v. Williams, Reninger, Nielson, Thompson and Dupard on giving preclusive effect to agency and prior-proceeding findings (welfare fraud, paternity, licensing), including whether the State and its agencies are the same party.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session subagents, from cocite evidence; second pass differentiated near-duplicates)

history: Dominant rule: the four-part Washington test for issue preclusion (identical issues, a final judgment on the merits, the same party or one in privity, and no injustice), applied to findings from earlier administrative or other proceedings. This is a single slice (2000-04) anchored by State v. Williams (1997). How it changed: within the slice the cases mark the doctrine's limits. Williams held DSHS in privity with the prosecutor but refused, on public-policy grounds, to let a DSHS hearing finding bar a welfare-fraud prosecution, following Dupard (1980), which kept a parole board's acquittal from barring prosecution. In civil settings estoppel applied: Reninger (1998) gave Personnel Appeals Board findings preclusive effect over tortious-interference claims because the hearing resembled a trial, and Nielson (1998) treated a judgment as final despite appeal and settlement. Thompson (1999) and Cleveland (1990) treat different arms of the State as the same party; Bryant (2002) found issues in two hearings not identical; McDaniels (1987) limits preclusion to ultimate facts and arises from a paternity dispute.
rule: Collateral estoppel applies in Washington when the issue is identical, the prior proceeding ended in a final judgment on the merits, the party estopped was a party or in privity, and preclusion works no injustice; it may be withheld on public-policy grounds, especially to protect criminal prosecutions from prior administrative findings.

changes.what: A parole board's not-guilty finding does not estop a later prosecution for the new crime; estoppel may yield to public policy.
Collateral estoppel reaches only ultimate facts directly at issue, not merely evidentiary facts.
Although DSHS was in privity with the prosecutor, its administrative finding of no intentional overpayment did not bar a welfare-fraud prosecution, for public-policy reasons.

changes.case: Reninger v. Department of Corrections; Nielson v. Spanaway
changes.what: Personnel Appeals Board findings precluded later tort claims where the hearing was trial-like and no injustice resulted; a judgment remains final for estoppel during appeal and despite later settlement.
The State and its Department of Licensing are the same party even when represented by different counsel.

name: Asylum review: well-founded fear and nexus (Cardoza-Fonseca, Elias-Zacarias)
description: Circuit review of asylum denials, mainly in the Ninth Circuit. Stevic (1984, anchor 1985-89) set the clear-probability withholding test; Cardoza-Fonseca (1987) set a lower well-founded-fear standard for asylum. Elias-Zacarias (1992) requires proof of the persecutor's motive, and its compel standard anchors 1995-2004. Later: Ventura (2002) remand, REAL ID Act credibility (2005), and social-group and nexus limits (M-E-V-G-, 2014; Zetino, 2010).
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Asylum: persecution and nexus (Ninth Circuit)
previous.description: Circuit review of asylum denials, mainly in the Ninth Circuit: persecution on account of a protected ground and nexus (Elias-Zacarias), well-founded fear (Cardoza-Fonseca, Stevic), corroboration after the REAL ID Act, and remand to the agency (INS v. Ventura).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: an asylum applicant must show persecution, or a well-founded fear of it, on account of a protected ground, and the court reverses only if the record compels it. How it changed: Stevic (1984) anchors 1985-89 with its clear-probability withholding standard, and Cardoza-Fonseca (1987) anchors 1990-94, setting a more generous well-founded-fear test for asylum. Elias-Zacarias (1992) enters then and anchors 1995-99 and 2000-04: motive must be shown, and agency findings stand unless compelled otherwise. Ventura (2002) requires remand of undecided issues. In 2005-09 Farah (2003) anchors on credibility, with Barron (2004) on jurisdictional exhaustion, as the REAL ID Act (2005) changes credibility rules (Shrestha, 2010). Wakkary (2009) anchors 2010-14 on what compels a finding of past persecution, with Zehatye (2006) on economic harm and conscription. M-E-V-G- (2014) anchors 2015-19 on social distinction of a particular social group, and Zetino (2010) anchors 2020-24 on nexus. Duran-Rodriguez (2019) leads the partial 2025-29 slice.
rule: An asylum applicant must show past persecution or a well-founded fear of persecution on account of a protected ground, proved by evidence of the persecutor's motive, and a court may reverse the agency's factual findings only if the record compels a contrary conclusion.

changes.what: Withholding of deportation requires a clear probability of persecution, a more demanding standard than asylum.
The asylum well-founded-fear standard is more generous than the more-likely-than-not withholding standard.
The applicant must show the persecutor's motive is tied to a protected ground, and the agency's finding stands unless the evidence compels the contrary.
A court of appeals should remand to the agency an issue it has not decided rather than resolve it in the first instance.

changes.case: Farah v. Ashcroft; Barron v. Ashcroft (9th Cir.)
changes.what: An adverse credibility finding on key elements forecloses asylum and withholding, and § 1252(d)(1) exhaustion is jurisdictional.

changes.case: REAL ID Act of 2005; Shrestha v. Holder (9th Cir. 2010)
changes.what: For applications filed after May 11, 2005, credibility may rest on the totality of circumstances, including inconsistencies not going to the heart of the claim.
Harm from random theft or violence bears no nexus to a protected ground; anchors 2020-24.
A particular social group must be shown to exist and be perceived as distinct in the society, and general harm from gang violence is not enough; anchors 2015-19.

before_differentiation.name: Asylum review: well-founded fear and nexus (Cardoza-Fonseca, Elias-Zacarias)
before_differentiation.description: Circuit review of asylum denials, mainly in the Ninth Circuit. Cardoza-Fonseca (1987) set the well-founded-fear standard, lower than Stevic's (1984) withholding test. Elias-Zacarias (1992) requires proof of the persecutor's motive, and its compel standard anchors 1995-2004. Later changes: Ventura (2002) remand, REAL ID Act credibility (2005), and nexus and social-group limits (Zetino, 2010; M-E-V-G-, 2014).

name: Third Circuit sentencing reasonableness review after Booker (Tomko, Gunter, Cooper)
description: Third Circuit appellate review of federal sentences after Booker, as it stood in 2010-14: Gunter's (2006) three-step procedure, no presumption of reasonableness (Cooper 2006), preponderance fact-finding within the statutory maximum (Grier, en banc 2007), and Tomko (en banc 2009, anchor) holding a sentence substantively unreasonable only if no reasonable court would impose it. Levinson (2008) and Merced (2010) police the explanation.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, round 2 after the lineage re-link)

previous.name: Post-Booker judicial fact-finding: acquitted conduct, ex post facto
previous.description: Circuit decisions after Booker (Cooper, Grier, Tomko, Gunter, Vaughn, Dupas) on reasonableness review and judicial fact-finding by a preponderance, including acquitted conduct, and ex post facto/fair-warning challenges.
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session subagents, from cocite evidence; second pass differentiated near-duplicates)

history: Dominant rule: the Third Circuit reviews a federal sentence for procedural error and then substantive reasonableness, with great deference to the district court. This lineage covers only 2010-14, when Tomko (en banc 2009) anchors it. How it took shape: Gunter (2006) set the three-step sentencing process (range, departures, § 3553(a)); Cooper (2006) rejected a presumption of reasonableness and kept refusals to depart unreviewable; Grier (en banc 2007) held that judges may find sentencing facts by a preponderance so long as the sentence stays within the statutory maximum; Bungar (2007) refused to reweigh mitigating factors. Tomko then held a sentence substantively unreasonable only if no reasonable court would have imposed it, upholding probation. Levinson (2008) found an explanation inadequate for a large unexplained variance, and Merced (2010) required the court to show it considered the factors, without a mandatory script. Also: Anders briefs (Youla 2001, Marvin 2000) and plain-error review (Wise 2008).
rule: In the Third Circuit a sentence is reviewed for procedural soundness under Gunter's three steps and is substantively unreasonable only if no reasonable sentencing court would have imposed it on the reasons given (Tomko); facts may be found by a preponderance within the statutory maximum (Grier).

changes.what: Three-step process: calculate the Guidelines range, rule on departure motions, then consider the § 3553(a) factors.
No presumption of reasonableness for within-Guidelines sentences, and a refusal to depart remains unreviewable after Booker.

changes.case: United States v. Grier (3d Cir. en banc)
changes.what: Sentencing facts may be found by a preponderance without violating the jury right so long as they do not raise the sentence above the statutory maximum.

changes.case: United States v. Tomko (3d Cir. en banc)
changes.what: A procedurally sound sentence is affirmed unless no reasonable sentencing court would have imposed it for the reasons given; a probationary sentence was upheld.

round1.name: Post-Booker judicial fact-finding by a preponderance and Third Circuit reasonableness review
round1.description: Circuit decisions after Booker on judicial fact-finding: preponderance findings, including acquitted conduct under Watts (1997), remain valid within the statutory maximum (Vaughn, 2005; Grier, en banc 2007), and applying Booker to earlier offenses raises no ex post facto or fair-warning problem (Dupas, Jamison, 2005; Rogers v. Tennessee). Third Circuit reasonableness review follows (Cooper, Gunter, 2006; Tomko, en banc 2009).
round1.history: Dominant rule: after Booker made the Guidelines advisory, the jury right limits only sentences above the statutory maximum, so sentencing judges may still find facts, including conduct underlying an acquittal, by a preponderance of the evidence (Watts, 1997; Vaughn, 2d Cir. 2005, anchor in 2005-09; Grier, 3d Cir. en banc 2007). How it changed: defendants resentenced after Booker argued that its remedial holding operated as an ex post facto law; the circuits rejected this (Dupas, Jamison, Scroggins, Lata, 2005), relying on Rogers v. Tennessee (2001), which grounds limits on retroactive judicial change in due process and bars only unexpected and indefensible changes. The Third Circuit then built its reasonableness review: Cooper (2006) declined a presumption of reasonableness and kept refusals to depart unreviewable, Gunter (2006) set a three-step sentencing process, and Tomko (en banc 2009), anchor in 2010-14, held a sentence substantively unreasonable only if no reasonable court would impose it, upholding a probationary sentence; Levinson (2008) and Merced (2010) applied it. Also: Rines (2005) on harmless non-constitutional Booker error. The unit splits in 2015-19.
round1.rule: After Booker, judges may find sentencing facts, including acquitted conduct, by a preponderance of the evidence so long as the sentence stays within the statutory maximum, and applying Booker's remedy to pending cases does not violate ex post facto or fair-warning principles.

changes.what: Sentencing courts may consider acquitted conduct proved by a preponderance.
Limits on retroactive judicial decisions come from due process fair warning, not the Ex Post Facto Clause, and bar only unexpected and indefensible changes.

changes.case: United States v. Vaughn (2d Cir.); United States v. Dupas (9th Cir.); United States v. Jamison; United States v. Scroggins
changes.what: Watts survives Booker; applying the remedial holding to offenses committed before Booker gives fair warning because the statutory maximum was unchanged. Vaughn anchors 2005-09.

changes.case: United States v. Cooper; United States v. Gunter (3d Cir.)
changes.what: No presumption of reasonableness for within-range sentences; refusals to depart stay unreviewable; a three-step process (calculate, rule on departures, apply § 3553(a)).

changes.case: United States v. Grier (3d Cir. en banc)
changes.what: The relevant maximum is now the statutory maximum, so preponderance fact-finding does not violate the jury right or due process.

changes.case: United States v. Tomko (3d Cir. en banc)
changes.what: A sentence is substantively unreasonable only if no reasonable court would impose it for the reasons given; upheld a probationary sentence. Tomko anchors 2010-14.

before_differentiation.name: Third Circuit sentencing reasonableness review after Booker (Tomko, Gunter, Cooper)
before_differentiation.description: Third Circuit appellate review of federal sentences after Booker, as it stood in 2010-14: Gunter's (2006) three-step procedure, no presumption of reasonableness (Cooper 2006), preponderance fact-finding within the statutory maximum (Grier, en banc 2007), and Tomko (en banc 2009, anchor) holding a sentence substantively unreasonable only if no reasonable court would impose it. Levinson (2008) and Merced (2010) police the explanation.

distinct_from.how: That one is the nationwide Gall-Rita framework and the circuit split on explanation and preservation, 2005-29; this one is the Third Circuit's version in 2010-14, which declines Rita's within-range presumption (Cooper) and defines substantive unreasonableness through Tomko.

name: New Jersey sentencing review: Roth deference, Fuentes and Case factors
description: New Jersey criminal appeals: sentences reviewed deferentially under Roth (1984), anchor of every slice, with Yarbough (1985) for consecutive terms, Fuentes (2014) and Lawless (2013) against double-counting, and Case (2014) requiring a stated weighing of factors. Alongside: Macon plain error, Frost on summation, Cofield on other-crimes evidence, and Henderson (2011) on eyewitness identification.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: New Jersey criminal sentencing and trial error
previous.description: New Jersey criminal precedent: sentencing review of aggravating and mitigating factors (State v. Roth, Fuentes, Case), consecutive sentences (Yarbough), prosecutorial summation (Frost), and cumulative error (Weaver).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: appellate review of a New Jersey sentence is deferential; the court checks that the guidelines were followed, that competent evidence supports the aggravating and mitigating factors, and that the sentence does not shock the judicial conscience (Roth, 1984, anchor in all three slices). How it changed: the lineage forms in 2015-19 from merged suppression-appeal units, so its rules come from earlier decisions. Yarbough (1985) set the criteria for consecutive sentences. Lawless (2013) and Fuentes (2014) barred double-counting offense elements as aggravating factors, and Case (2014), which leads from 2020-24, required judges to explain how the factors were found and balanced. Alongside: Macon's (1971) plain-error standard (error clearly capable of producing an unjust result), Frost (1999) and Reddish (2004) on prosecutorial summation and cumulative error, Cofield (1992) and Rose (2011) on other-crimes and intrinsic evidence, jury-charge cases (Jordan, R.B., Funderburg), and Henderson's (2011) prospective overhaul of eyewitness-identification evidence, entering in 2020-24.
rule: A New Jersey appellate court affirms a sentence unless the guidelines were not followed, the aggravating and mitigating factors lack competent, credible support, or applying the guidelines makes the sentence clearly unreasonable so as to shock the judicial conscience (Roth).

changes.what: Three-part, deferential appellate review of sentences under the Code of Criminal Justice.
Criteria for choosing concurrent or consecutive sentences.

changes.case: State v. Lawless; State v. Fuentes
changes.what: Sentencing courts must not double-count elements of the offense, including those that set its grade, as aggravating factors.
The judge must explain why each factor was found or rejected and how the factors were balanced, to allow meaningful review.
Overhauled the framework for admitting eyewitness identifications, prospectively, with enhanced jury instructions.

name: Copyright: Feist originality, idea-expression line and fair use (Campbell)
description: Copyright protects only original expression, not facts or ideas (Feist, 1991, anchor 1995-2004 and 2015-19), and fair use weighs the four factors with transformative use (Sony, 1984; Harper & Row, 1985; Campbell, 1994). Software cases filtered out unprotectable elements (Altai, 1992; Lotus, 1995); Napster (2001) and Grokster (2005) extended secondary liability. The 2020-24 slice drifts to party presentation on appeal (Greenlaw, Sineneng-Smith).
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, round 2 after the lineage re-link)

previous.name: Copyright: originality, infringement and fair use
previous.description: Copyright law: originality (Feist), idea versus expression (Baker v. Selden, Computer Associates v. Altai), fair use (Sony, Harper & Row, Campbell v. Acuff-Rose), derivative works (Stewart v. Abend), fee awards (Fogerty), and online secondary liability (Perfect 10).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: copyright covers original expression only, and copying of protected elements is excused where the fair-use factors favour the use. How it changed: Feist (1991) anchors 1995-99 and 2000-04, rejecting sweat-of-the-brow protection; Altai (1992) set abstraction-filtration-comparison for software, and Lotus (1st Cir. 1995) held menu hierarchies uncopyrightable. Harper & Row (1985), Sony (1984) and Campbell (1994) lead fair use throughout, Campbell stressing transformative use. In 2000-04 music-infringement cases enter (Smith v. Jackson, 1996; Ellis v. Diffie, 1999; Three Boys Music v. Bolton, 2000). Sony anchors 2005-09 as Napster (2001) and Grokster (2005) extended secondary liability. Harper & Row anchors 2010-14, with Bill Graham Archives (2006), Blanch (2006) and Perfect 10 (2007) on transformative uses, Castle Rock (1998) on derivative works and Stewart v. Abend (1990). Feist anchors again in 2015-19 as online-platform cases enter (Viacom, 2012; Columbia Pictures v. Fung, 2013; UMG, 2013; Global-Tech, 2011). Also: in 2020-24 Harper & Row anchors a merged slice dominated by appellate party presentation (Greenlaw, 2008; Sineneng-Smith, 2020) and Erie (1938), which is drift.
rule: Copyright covers only original expression, never facts, ideas, systems or methods of operation, and copying of protected expression is excused where the four fair-use factors, weighed together with transformative use, favour the use.

changes.case: Sony Corp. v. Universal City Studios
changes.what: Home time-shifting is fair use, and selling a device capable of substantial noninfringing uses is not contributory infringement.
Taking the heart of an unpublished work is not fair use even if the quantity is small.

changes.case: Feist Publications v. Rural Telephone Service
changes.what: Originality is a constitutional requirement; facts and unoriginal compilations are unprotected, rejecting sweat of the brow.

changes.case: Computer Associates v. Altai; Lotus v. Borland
changes.what: Unprotectable elements of software are filtered out, and a menu command hierarchy is an uncopyrightable method of operation.
Fair use is weighed case by case with transformative use central; commercial parody can be fair use.

changes.case: A&M Records v. Napster; MGM v. Grokster; Perfect 10 v. Amazon
changes.what: Secondary liability reaches services that induce or materially contribute to infringement, while search thumbnails may be transformative fair use.

round1.history: Dominant rule: copyright covers original expression only, never facts, ideas, systems or methods of operation, and copying of protected elements is excused where the four fair-use factors favour the use. How it changed: Feist (1991) anchors 1990-94 through 2000-04, rejecting sweat-of-the-brow protection, with Baker v. Selden (1880), Nichols (1930) and Mazer (1954). Software cases follow: Altai (1992) set abstraction-filtration-comparison, Apple (1994) applied virtual-identity review to thin protection, and Lotus (1st Cir. 1995) held menu hierarchies uncopyrightable. Harper & Row (1985), Sony (1984) and Campbell (1994) lead fair use from 1995-99, Campbell stressing transformative use; Fogerty (1994) set even-handed fee awards and Reid (1989) the agency test for works for hire. round1.rule: Copyright protects only original expression, not facts, ideas or methods of operation (Feist, Baker v. Selden), and infringement requires copying of protected elements, subject to fair use judged case by case on the four statutory factors (Sony, Harper & Row, Campbell).

changes.case: Feist Publications v. Rural Telephone Service
changes.what: Originality is a constitutional requirement; facts and sweat of the brow are unprotected, and a compilation is protected only for original selection or arrangement. Anchors 1990-2004 and 2015-19.

changes.case: Computer Associates v. Altai; Gates Rubber v. Bando; Lotus v. Borland
changes.what: Abstraction-filtration-comparison removes unprotectable elements from software comparisons, and a menu command hierarchy is an uncopyrightable method of operation.
The fair-use factors are weighed together, commerciality creates no presumption against fair use, and transformative use weighs heavily.

changes.what: Secondary liability reaches file-sharing services and those who induce infringement, despite Sony's safe harbour for devices capable of substantial noninfringing use; Sony anchors 2005-09.

changes.what: Abandoned the inverse-ratio rule and limited 1909 Act music claims to the deposit copy; anchors the partial 2025-29 slice.

name: Connecticut termination of parental rights: statutory ground, then best interest
description: Connecticut's two-phase termination scheme, 1985-2004: the state must prove a statutory ground by clear and convincing evidence and then that termination serves the child's best interest. Juvenile Appeal (1979) anchors to 1994; In re Luis C. (1989) set the failure-to-rehabilitate test, Sean H. (1991) reached emotional injury, Valerie D. (1992) excluded prenatal conduct alone, and In re Eden F. (1999) anchors 2000-04.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Connecticut termination of parental rights
previous.description: Connecticut child-protection appeals: termination grounds and reunification efforts (In re Eden F., In re Luis C., In re Juvenile Appeal decisions), family integrity, and prenatal conduct (In re Valerie D.).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, contrastive pass from family evidence)

history: Dominant rule: termination is the ultimate interference with family integrity (In re Migdalia M. 1986), so the state must prove a statutory ground in an adjudicatory phase and then best interest in a dispositional phase. How it changed: Juvenile Appeal v. Commissioner (1979) anchors 1985-94, treating no ongoing parent-child relationship as a no-fault ground; the 1983-84 Juvenile Appeal decisions required preponderance proof to continue temporary custody, allowed termination without fault, and let courts consider incarceration. In 1990-94 In re Luis C. (1989) and Nicolina T. (1987) enter: rehabilitation must be foreseeable within a reasonable time, and termination can rest on inability to parent rather than mental condition. Migdalia M. anchors 1995-99 as Sean H. (1991, emotional injury counts), Valerie D. (1992, prenatal drug use alone insufficient), Kezia M. and Christina V. (rehabilitation as a parent) join. In re Eden F. (1999) enters and anchors 2000-04 with Savanna M. and John G. on the two phases.
rule: Connecticut may terminate parental rights only on clear and convincing proof of a statutory ground (such as failure to rehabilitate within a reasonable time, acts of commission or omission, or no ongoing parent-child relationship) and a separate finding that termination is in the child's best interest.

changes.case: Juvenile Appeal v. Commissioner of Children & Youth Services
changes.what: Construed the no-ongoing-relationship ground as a no-fault statutory ground for termination.

changes.case: In re Juvenile Appeal (83-CD); In re Juvenile Appeal (83-BC)
changes.what: Due process requires the state to prove by a preponderance that temporary custody should continue, and the legislature may permit termination without parental fault.
Failure to rehabilitate turns on whether the parent's rehabilitation is foreseeable within a reasonable time given the child's needs.

changes.case: In re Sean H.; In re Valerie D.
changes.what: Acts of commission or omission include serious emotional injury (Sean H.), but prenatal drug use alone cannot ground termination (Valerie D.).
Read § 17a-112 in light of legislative policy, separating the adjudicatory phase from the dispositional best-interest phase; anchors 2000-04.

(1992) excluded prenatal conduct alone, and In re Eden F. (1999) anchors 2000-04.

distinct_from.how: Connecticut's statutory grounds (no ongoing relationship, failure to rehabilitate) and two-phase structure over 1985-2004, not South Dakota's 1985-89 best-interests and reunification-effort cases.

name: Sixth Circuit Booker remands (Barnett, Oliver) with § 924(c) 'in furtherance' rules
description: Sixth Circuit drug and firearm appeals in a single 2005-09 slice anchored by Barnett (2005): mandatory-Guidelines sentencing affects substantial rights because a lower sentence was possible, so Booker cases are remanded (Oliver 2005). Companion rules: § 924(c) 'in furtherance' possession needs more than presence (Mackey 2001, Ceballos-Torres 2000, after Bailey 1995) and conspiracy membership inferred from repeat dealings (Martinez 2005).
history: Dominant rule: how the Sixth Circuit disposed of drug and firearm appeals pending when Booker (2005) made the Guidelines advisory. Barnett (2005) anchors the lineage's only slice, 2005-09, which formed from Guidelines-departure and circuit units and continues into reasonableness review in 2010-14. How it changed: Oliver and Barnett (2005) held that mandatory-Guidelines sentencing is plain error that affects substantial rights, because the defendant might receive a lower sentence, and that it impairs the integrity of proceedings, so the cases were remanded; Barnett also kept prior convictions outside Apprendi. McDaniel (2005) treated objections to enhancements as preserving the Sixth Amendment issue. Alongside, the trial issues in the same appeals: Bailey (1995) required active employment for 'use', Congress added possession 'in furtherance of', and Ceballos-Torres (2000) and Mackey (2001) require a nexus beyond presence, with Kincaide (1998) and Layne (1999) on constructive possession through dominion over premises; Gibbs (1999) and Martinez (2005) on proving conspiracy by circumstantial evidence; Combs (2004) on constructive amendment; and Schreane (2003) and Salgado (2001) on speedy trial.
rule: In the Sixth Circuit, a sentence imposed under mandatory Guidelines affects substantial rights and is remanded under plain-error review because a lower advisory sentence is possible (Barnett, Oliver); possession 'in furtherance of' a drug crime under amended § 924(c) requires a specific nexus beyond mere presence (Mackey, Ceballos-Torres), and conspiracy membership may be inferred from repeated dealings (Martinez, Gibbs).

history: Dominant rule: the standards for taking a case from the jury or ordering a new trial. Pedrick (1967) anchors 1995-99 and stays second throughout: a directed verdict or judgment n.o.v. is proper only if the evidence, viewed most favourably to the opponent, so overwhelmingly favours the movant that no contrary verdict could stand. From 2000-04 Maple (1992) anchors every slice: new trials only for verdicts against the manifest weight of the evidence. How it changed: the standards themselves are stable; the cases applying them are mostly medical malpractice. Holton (1997) rejects a better-result requirement; Leonardi (1995) allows a sole-proximate-cause defense; Simmons (2002) requires expert causation testimony; Purtill (1986) and Sullivan (2004) govern the standard of care and expert qualification. Copeland (2000) and Radfar (2000) enforce Rule 213 disclosure; Gilbert (1993) and York (2006) set apparent agency for hospitals; Snelson (2003) defers to juries in battles of experts and requires specific objections. Also: jury-instruction discretion (Schultz, 2002) and offers of proof (Dillon, 2002).

Smith (1968), with Rosado (1970), Townsend (1971) and Carleson (1972) striking state AFDC rules under the Supremacy Clause, decided through pendent jurisdiction over substantial constitutional claims (Hagans, 1974; Goosby). How it changed: from 1980-89 Gibbs (1966) anchors: a common nucleus of operative fact, with discretion to dismiss state claims once federal claims fall. Aldinger (1976) and Kroger (1978) limited pendent-party and ancillary jurisdiction, Cohill (1988) allowed remand of pendent claims, and Finley (1989) rejected pendent-party jurisdiction, leading Congress to enact § 1367 in 1990. From 1990-2004 Thermtron (1976) anchors: § 1447(d) bars review only of remands on § 1447(c) grounds, so other remands are reviewable by mandamus, and Quackenbush (1996) allowed appeal of abstention-based remands, with circuit mandamus cases (Shell Oil, Continental Casualty, FMC) alongside.
rule: A federal court may hear state claims sharing a common nucleus of operative fact with a substantial federal claim (Gibbs) but has discretion to decline or remand them (Cohill); remand orders on § 1447(c) grounds are unreviewable, while remands on other grounds may be reviewed (Thermtron, Quackenbush).

name: Due-process vagueness, 1990-99: Grayned fair notice and Bouie fair warning
description: The due-process vagueness test in 1990-99, mostly in state courts: Grayned (1972, anchor) requires fair notice and guards against arbitrary enforcement (Connally 1926, Papachristou 1972); Hoffman Estates (1982) relaxes review for economic regulation and requires considering limiting constructions; Kolender (1983) stresses enforcement guidelines. Bouie (1964) and Marks (1977) add fair warning against retroactive judicial enlargement.

previous.name: Void for vagueness and overbreadth (to 1984)
previous.description: Connally and Lanzetta fair-notice vagueness through Grayned, Papachristou, Coates and Goguen, with Gooding and Broadrick on overbreadth of speech and breach-of-peace laws.

history: Dominant rule: due process voids a law so vague that people of common intelligence must guess at its meaning (Connally 1926, Lanzetta 1939) or that leaves enforcement to officials' discretion; Grayned (1972), the anchor in both slices, restated the test and its special force where speech is affected (Coates 1971, Papachristou 1972, Goguen 1974). How it was applied: Hoffman Estates (1982) allowed facial challenges only where a law reaches substantial protected conduct or is vague in all applications, gave economic regulations more leeway, and directed courts to consider limiting constructions; Kolender (1983) struck a stop-and-identify law for lacking enforcement guidelines; Parker v. Levy (1974) denied standing to one whose conduct was clearly covered. In 1995-99 Bouie (1964) and Marks (1977) enter on due-process limits to retroactive judicial expansion of criminal statutes. State courts applied the test to loitering, dangerous-dog and drug-paraphernalia laws, often saving statutes by intent requirements or narrowing constructions (Cameron 1985, Newstrom 1985). The unit splits in 2000-04 into speech and criminal-vagueness units.
rule: A penal law is void for vagueness if it fails to give a person of ordinary intelligence fair notice of what is forbidden or invites arbitrary enforcement, with stricter scrutiny where it reaches protected expression and allowance for limiting constructions.

round1.name: Void for vagueness and overbreadth: Connally fair-notice rule to Grayned
round1.description: Void for vagueness: from early price and antitrust statutes (Nash 1913, Cohen Grocery 1921) to Connally's (1926) common-intelligence test and Lanzetta (1939), with greater rigor for speech (Winters 1948). Coates (1971), Papachristou (1972) and Goguen (1974) added arbitrary enforcement; Grayned (1972, anchor 1980-84) restated the test, and Broadrick (1973) required substantial overbreadth.
round1.history: Dominant rule: due process voids a penal law so vague that people of common intelligence must guess at its meaning, a standard applied with special strictness to laws affecting speech. How it changed: in 1920-34 the anchors are International Harvester (1914), Nash (1913) and Omaechevarria (1918), on whether economic statutes gave fair warning; antitrust cases (Standard Oil, American Tobacco) lead 1935-39. Cohen Grocery (1921), Connally (1926) and Cline (1927) struck price and wage standards, and Connally anchors most slices from 1945-49 to 1970-74, with Lanzetta (1939) anchoring 1965-69. Winters (1948) and Screws (1945) brought the speech and narrowing-construction strands in 1950-54; Harriss (1954) and National Dairy (1963) narrowed facial review. In 1970-74 First Amendment cases enter: Coates (1971), Papachristou, Gooding and Grayned (1972). Papachristou anchors 1975-79 with Goguen and Parker (1974). Grayned anchors 1980-84 with Broadrick (1973) and Hoffman Estates (1982) before the unit merges into general speech doctrine.
round1.rule: A penal law is void for vagueness if people of common intelligence must necessarily guess at its meaning or it invites arbitrary enforcement (Connally; Papachristou), with stricter scrutiny where it touches First Amendment freedoms, and a law reaching protected expression may be struck as overbroad only if the overbreadth is substantial (Broadrick).

name: Punitive damages 2000-04: Gore guideposts, Cooper de novo review, Kolstad
description: How the constitutional limits on punitive damages took shape, 2000-04 only: BMW v. Gore (1996, anchor) set three guideposts on Haslip (1991) and TXO (1993); Cooper Industries (2001) required de novo appellate review, and State Farm v. Campbell (2003) struck a 145-to-1 award. Alongside: Kolstad (1999) on Title VII punitive damages, and Erie, Hanna and Gasperini (1996) on which law governs excessiveness review in diversity.

previous.name: Punitive damages and due process
previous.description: Constitutional limits on punitive damages (Haslip, TXO, BMW v. Gore, State Farm v. Campbell, Cooper Industries de novo review) and Kolstad under Title VII, cited with Erie, Hanna and Gasperini on the law a federal court applies in diversity (2000-04).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session subagents, from cocite evidence; second pass differentiated near-duplicates)

history: Dominant rule: BMW v. Gore (1996) anchors the single 2000-04 slice. Due process bars grossly excessive punitive awards, judged by reprehensibility, the ratio to actual or potential harm and comparable civil penalties; a $2 million award on $4,000 of harm failed, and a state may not punish lawful out-of-state conduct. How it developed: Browning-Ferris (1989) held the Excessive Fines Clause inapplicable to private awards. Haslip (1991) upheld an Alabama award, finding instructions and post-trial review under Hammond (1986) and Green Oil v. Hornsby (1989) adequate, and TXO (1993) upheld a large award by counting potential harm. Cooper Industries (2001) then required de novo appellate review, and State Farm v. Campbell (2003) held a 145-to-1 award excessive, said few awards beyond a single-digit ratio will satisfy due process, and barred punishing dissimilar conduct. Alongside: Kolstad (1999) makes Title VII punitive damages turn on malice or reckless indifference with a good-faith-compliance defense (Lowery 2000 on managerial agents). Erie (1938), Guaranty Trust (1945), Hanna (1965) and Gasperini (1996) govern review of state-law damages in federal court. The unit splits in 2005-09.
rule: The Due Process Clause forbids grossly excessive punitive awards, measured by the reprehensibility of the conduct, the ratio of punitive to actual or potential harm and comparable civil penalties (BMW v. Gore), with single-digit ratios ordinarily the limit (State Farm v. Campbell), and appellate courts review the constitutional question de novo (Cooper Industries).

changes.what: The Excessive Fines Clause does not apply to punitive damages between private parties.

changes.what: Alabama trial courts must state the factors considered in reviewing a verdict for excessiveness, using post-trial factors such as culpability and deterrence.

changes.what: Due process limits punitive damages, but instructions confined to deterrence and retribution with post-trial review sufficed, and potential harm counts.

name: Constitutional challenges to 1970s medical-malpractice reform statutes
description: State constitutional challenges to 1970s medical-malpractice reforms. Courts upheld mandatory screening and mediation panels and admission of their findings (Comiskey 1976, Eastin 1977, Paro 1977, Attorney General v. Johnson 1978, Johnson v. St. Vincent 1980), but split on damages caps: Prendergast (Neb. 1977) and Johnson upheld them, while Wright (Ill. 1976) and Arneson (N.D. 1978) struck them.

previous.name: Medical-malpractice tort reform challenges (1975-80)
previous.description: Constitutional challenges to 1970s medical-malpractice reforms: pre-trial screening panels and the jury right (Eastin, Prendergast, Paro, Attorney General v. Johnson) and damages caps (Wright v. Central Du Page).

history: Dominant rule: legislatures responding to the malpractice insurance crisis could channel claims through pretrial panels and alter common-law recovery rules, subject to review under equal protection, due process and the jury right. How it changed: in 1975-79 Comiskey (N.Y. 1976) anchors, upholding admission of a unanimous panel recommendation, with Carter (Fla. 1976) relying on the imminent danger to health care and Eastin (Ariz. 1977) upholding abolition of the collateral-source rule. Jones (Idaho 1976) applied a fair-and-substantial-relation test to caps and remanded for facts, and Wright (Ill. 1976) struck a $500,000 cap. Prendergast (Neb. 1977) enters as anchor in 1980-84, upholding Nebraska's act and its elective $500,000 limit. In that slice Paro (Mass. 1977), Attorney General v. Johnson (Md. 1978), Wilkie (Wis. 1978), Woods (Fla. 1979) and Johnson v. St. Vincent (Ind. 1980) upheld panels, while Arneson (N.D. 1978) struck a $300,000 cap. The unit then merges into general rational-basis review in 1985-89.

changes.what: Mandatory malpractice panels, admission of their findings and abolition of the collateral-source rule did not violate equal protection, due process or the jury right.

changes.what: Damages caps were struck as arbitrary special legislation or a denial of equal protection (Wright, Arneson), or remanded for factual findings (Jones).
