name: New York legal sufficiency and its preservation 1990-2004: Contes, Gray
description: New York legal-sufficiency review, 1990-2004, before weight review dominates: Contes (1983), anchor of 1990-99, asks whether any valid line of reasoning and permissible inferences could lead a rational jury to find guilt, viewing the evidence for the People. Gray (1995), anchor of 2000-04, requires a specifically directed trial motion to preserve the claim; Hines (2001) applied that to post-verdict motions. Ryan (1993) and Hill (1995) on drug-weight knowledge.
history: Dominant rule: People v. Contes (1983) anchors 1990-94 and 1995-99: a verdict is legally sufficient if, viewing the evidence most favourably to the People, there is a valid line of reasoning and permissible inferences from which a rational jury could find each element beyond a reasonable doubt; older cases on circumstantial proof (Gaimari 1903) and Garafolo (1974) remain leading. Suitte (1982) explains when the Appellate Division may substitute its own discretion, and Udzinski (1989) leads with them. How it changed: Gray (1995) enters in 1995-99 and anchors 2000-04, requiring that a motion to dismiss be specifically directed at the alleged error to preserve a sufficiency claim, and Hines (2001) barred unpreserved insufficiency arguments on a post-verdict motion. Ryan (1993) and Hill (1995) address the knowledge-of-weight element in drug cases, and Okehoffurum (1994) enters with them. Alongside: accessorial liability and mere presence (Allah 1988, Cabey 1995) and recklessness inferred from post-shooting conduct (Roe 1989). The lineage merges into the broader New York weight-of-evidence and preservation lineage in 2005-09.
rule: A New York conviction is legally sufficient if, viewing the evidence in the light most favourable to the People, any valid line of reasoning and permissible inferences could lead a rational jury to find each element proved beyond a reasonable doubt, and a sufficiency claim is preserved only by a trial motion specifically directed at the alleged defect.

name: Civil forfeiture as punishment: Halper, Austin, Kurth Ranch, then Ursery
description: Whether civil sanctions are punishment, 1985-99: Halper (1989) let disproportionate civil penalties trigger double jeopardy, Austin (1993) put forfeitures under the Excessive Fines Clause and Kurth Ranch (1994) treated a drug tax as punishment, leading circuits to bar prosecutions after forfeiture ($405,089.23, 1994). Ursery (1996) held in rem forfeiture is not punishment, and Hudson (1997) overruled Halper in part. Calero-Toledo (1974) anchors earlier.
written_by: claude (Claude Code subagents, rule-centred pass from rule-history evidence)

previous.name: Civil forfeiture, double jeopardy and excessive fines
previous.description: Whether civil sanctions are punishment: civil penalties and forfeitures under the Double Jeopardy Clause (Halper, Kurth Ranch, Ursery, Hudson), forfeiture under the Excessive Fines Clause (Austin), and innocent-owner forfeiture (Calero-Toledo).
previous.written_by: claude (Cowork session, from cocite evidence)

history: Dominant rule: the lineage turns on whether civil forfeitures and penalties are punishment. Calero-Toledo (1974) anchors 1985-89 and 1990-94, allowing seizure without prior hearing, with currency and vessel forfeiture cases ($8,850, 1983, applying Barker to delay; the Tahuna, 1983) and innocent-owner defences (Four Million, 1985). Emerald Cut Stones (1972) and 89 Firearms (1984) held forfeiture civil and not barred by acquittal. How it changed: Halper (1989), anchor 1995-99, held that a civil penalty disproportionate to the government's loss could be punishment for double jeopardy. Austin (1993) applied the Excessive Fines Clause to civil forfeiture, and Kurth Ranch (1994) held Montana's drug tax punitive. The Ninth Circuit in $405,089.23 (1994) and the Sixth in Ursery (1995) then held civil forfeitures punishment, while others (Tilley, 1994) disagreed and Torres (1994) and Baird (1995) found no jeopardy in uncontested forfeitures. The Supreme Court in Ursery (1996) held in rem forfeiture not punishment, and Hudson (1997) overruled Halper in part. Helvering v. Mitchell (1938) supplies the civil-penalty baseline; the unit splits toward ex post facto law in 2000-04.
rule: Whether a civil sanction counts as punishment for double jeopardy turned under Halper on whether it served retributive or deterrent rather than purely remedial goals, until Ursery (1996) held in rem civil forfeitures are not punishment; separately, forfeitures that are partly punitive are subject to the Excessive Fines Clause (Austin).

history: Dominant rule: Blockburger's same-elements test, anchoring every slice except 1965-74 and 1990-94. How it changed: Gore (1958) and Prince (1957) anchor 1965-74 on federal statutory multiplicity, with Bell (1955) applying lenity to the unit of prosecution. Brown v. Ohio (1977) enters in 1975-79 with Iannelli (1975) and Jeffers (1977). Whalen (1980), Albernaz (1981), Vitale (1980) and Missouri v. Hunter (1983) enter in 1980-84, treating Blockburger as a presumption of legislative intent; Garrett (1985) and Ball (1985) follow. Grady v. Corbin (1990) enters and anchors 1990-94, adding a same-conduct test; Dixon (1993) enters and overruled it, and Felix (1992) addressed conspiracy and substantive offenses. Rutledge (1996) enters in 1995-99. Texas Court of Criminal Appeals cases (Ervin 1999, Cavazos 2006, Bigon 2008) lead 2010-14. In 2015-19 mistrial cases merge in, and the partial 2025-29 slice drifts toward vindictive resentencing (Pearce, Alabama v. Smith, Goodwin).

Ohio), but within a single trial cumulative punishment is permitted where the legislature clearly intends it (Hunter).

name: Texas deed and mineral-conveyance construction, 2020-24: URI, Hysaw, Wenske
description: Texas construction of mineral conveyances and other unambiguous instruments, 2020-24: construed de novo as a matter of law to effectuate intent expressed in the whole text (Coker 1983; URI 2018, anchor). Luckel (1992), Hysaw (2016) and Wenske (2017) favour holistic harmonisation over mechanical rules; Pathfinder (2019) gives every provision effect. Also merger clauses (Italian Cowboy 2011) and royalty calculation (NationsBank 1997).
history: Dominant rule: whether a contract is ambiguous, and the meaning of an unambiguous one, are questions of law reviewed de novo; courts ascertain the parties' intent from the instrument as a whole, giving effect to every provision and letting specific terms control general ones (Coker 1983; Frost National Bank 2005; Pathfinder 2019). URI v. Kleberg County (2018) anchors the single slice (2020-24): surrounding circumstances may inform, but a court may not interlineate terms not expressed in an unambiguous agreement. How it changed: in mineral conveyances the Texas Supreme Court moved from arbitrary rules to a holistic, harmonising approach (Luckel 1992; Hysaw 2016; Wenske 2017, holding that a mineral owner's reservation of an NPRI burdens only the grantor's interest), and NationsBank (1997) tied royalty to the lease's terms. Only an ambiguous contract admits extrinsic evidence (National Union 1995). Alongside: merger clauses do not bar fraudulent-inducement claims absent a clear disclaimer of reliance (Italian Cowboy 2011), the contractual-liability exclusion (Gilbert, 2010), definiteness and part performance (Fischer 2016), and third-party beneficiaries (Brumitt 2017).
rule: Texas courts construe an unambiguous contract or conveyance as a matter of law, de novo, to give effect to the parties' intent as expressed in the whole instrument, harmonising all provisions and rejecting mechanical rules, and look to extrinsic evidence only if the text is ambiguous.

changes.what: A contract that can be given a definite legal meaning is unambiguous and construed as a matter of law, considering the whole writing.
